caption: Midday sun hammers the cobblestone roadway of an old stone arch bridge spanning a Mumbai creek, its rusted lampposts leaning and wooden skiffs moored in the channel below. Three adults stand alone on the empty span: a wiry man in his twenties in a mustard vest, a broad-shouldered woman around forty in teal track pants, a lean man near fifty in a faded grey kurta. All three begin fully in frame, feet planted on the rounded stones, then fold one leg up and hop into bumping duels, shoulders colliding, arms crossed, staggering a couple of meters before recovering. Beyond the parapet, distant traffic drags light trails across the haze. One continuous shot, camera tracking sideways at a steady walking pace, gritty documentary grain.

Inside a cramped loft yoga studio above a Mumbai printing lane, rolled mats lean in a corner and cheap trussing carries colored stage lamps over pale bamboo flooring. Only two adults occupy the room: a stocky Black woman in her thirties wearing a maroon crop top and grey shorts, and a slight South Asian man near forty-five in a blue singlet. Both stand fully visible, bare feet flat on the boards for the opening beats, then tuck one leg behind and hop forward into a bumping duel, chests and shoulders knocking, each staggering a meter and hopping back in. Haze drifts as spotlights sweep magenta and green across their sweat. One continuous shot from a static tripod at eye level, raw documentary texture.

A single man commands an old akhara-style wrestling hall in Mumbai, where chalk-dusted pillars flank a red foam mat and clerestory windows drop hard shafts of daylight through the dust. He is tall and heavily muscled, mid-thirties, East Asian, in black compression shorts and a torn white tank, hair tied back. He starts fully in frame, both feet on the mat, arms swinging, then fires a standing broad jump, lands deep, rebounds instantly into a second and a third, bounding a few meters and turning to bound back. Torn paper scraps and confetti tumble through the light beams, kicked up by each landing. One continuous shot, handheld camera slowly circling at chest height, epic cinematic scale.

Two adults open the shot fully visible, feet planted on tapered concrete planks of a disused rail viaduct converted into a garden promenade above Mumbai, rusted signal masts and a bougainvillea tunnel flanking them. A tall Marathi man in his thirties, shaved head, saffron singlet, accelerates first; a lean Filipina woman in her twenties, braided hair, teal shorts, chases him down and slaps a blue baton into his outstretched palm mid-stride. They sprint the full width of the deck in one continuous shot, both bodies staying entirely inside the frame. Steam curls from vent grilles beside them, bruised purple storm clouds hang low, and onlookers watch from a raised terrace behind railings. The camera dollies slowly out, revealing more surroundings.

Inside a pedestrian subway under a Mumbai flyover, cracked white tile underfoot and a faded mural along one wall, two adults train alone. Both stand fully framed at first, feet on the tiled concrete, and neither leaves the frame. A stocky Punjabi woman in her forties, grey crop top, thick braid, drives a snap-down into an ankle pick; her partner, a wiry Somali man in his twenties in red compression shorts, sprawls, then reverses with a low single-leg lift and sets her down. They repeat, trading positions within two meters. Flickering neon from a shuttered kiosk and a searchlight sweeping past the vents cross daylight shafts falling from high slot windows. One continuous shot; the camera cranes from ceiling height down to eye level.

Under the ridge of a vast commercial glasshouse outside Mumbai, gutter pipes overhead and tables of seedling trays receding into green haze, two adults hold one spot on the wide concrete walkway. A broad-shouldered Nigerian man in his fifties, silver stubble, black tank top, and a compact Korean woman in her thirties, undercut hair, orange leggings, drop chest-to-floor, snap their feet in, and explode into tuck jumps that slap knees to palms. They repeat the cycle hard, footprints never leaving a meter of floor, both fully in frame from the first second and staying there. Bright even ceiling lamps flatten every shadow; the air is completely still. One continuous shot, the camera tracking sideways at a walking pace.

Blue hour on the open top deck of a Mumbai mall parking structure, faded yellow bay lines across the painted concrete, a bent ticket barrier and a stack of orange cones near the ramp. Four adults in white training jackets stand fully in frame, feet planted: a tall Bengali woman with a grey-streaked bob, a freckled Irish man, a broad Ethiopian man with a shaved head, a short Vietnamese woman. In pairs they drill alternating uchi-mata entries, sweeping a partner's thigh, lifting, then rolling out and rising to swap roles, drifting only a few meters. All four stay wholly in frame. Distant fireworks bloom over the skyline. One continuous shot, the camera craning from high above down to eye level.

Misty sunrise over a stone-paved square in an old Portuguese quarter of Mumbai, a chipped fountain basin and shuttered arcades ringing the rounded cobblestones. Five adults stand fully in frame at the far side, feet on the stones: a tall Egyptian woman in maroon, a slight Japanese man in white, a muscular Brazilian woman with a bleached crop, a lanky Sudanese man in grey, a stocky Chilean woman with a red headband. One after another they run a long diagonal, snapping round-off into two back handsprings finishing with a whip-back and a punch front. The air is dead calm. The last tumbler keeps coming toward the lens and finishes cropped at the waist, one continuous shot from a static tripod at eye level.

A truck loading dock bay inside a Mumbai warehouse: sealed concrete underfoot, corrugated roller doors half raised, stacked pallets and a dead forklift shoved against the wall, everything flattened by bright even overhead lighting. One man occupies the bay, a lean Afro-Caribbean sprinter in his early thirties, shaved head, wearing a charcoal singlet and yellow spikes. He stands fully in frame with both shoes flat on the concrete, then settles over the starting blocks, hips rising, and explodes out, driving four punishing strides down the bay before pulling up and jogging back to reset. Loose invoice paper and torn confetti tumble across the concrete in the wake of each start. One continuous shot from a static tripod at eye level, moody neo-noir contrast.

A mown launch meadow outside Mumbai where two deflated envelopes lie folded like collapsed sails beside a wicker basket and a propane trailer; slate-black thunderheads press down, the air heavy and unmoving. Six adults begin fully in frame, boots on the short grass: three broad men and three strong women, buzzed and braided heads, mixed Marathi, Kenyan, Turkish and Danish, in muted olive and charcoal work clothes. Working in twos, they wedge fingers under a battered tractor tire, drive hips through, flip it end over end twice, then hurdle through the opening and reset a couple of meters on. Grease darkens their forearms. One continuous shot, handheld, circling slowly at chest height; the nearest flipper drifts toward the lens and ends cropped.

Dawn mist on a chalk plateau above the Mumbai coast road, a weathered trig pillar and a broken flint wall marking the rim; fog banks roll through in slow grey ribbons. Two adults dance on the springy turf, both fully in frame, feet grounded from the opening beat and never leaving the frame. A silver-haired Cuban woman in a fuchsia wrap dress leads, spinning under her own arm into a hammerlock turn; her partner, a young Assamese man in a loose sky-blue shirt and black trousers, answers with a duck-under, a quick copa, and a spiralling dip that skims the grass. They travel three meters and back. One continuous shot, the camera tracking sideways at a steady walking pace.

Soft overcast light flattens a bare grey granite plateau inland from Mumbai, its surface scored by ancient glacial grooves, a stunted wind-bent tree and a small stone cairn marking the far edge. Everything is motionless. A single dancer holds the rock: a Spanish-featured woman in her late thirties, strong-shouldered, hair pinned tight, wearing a scarlet skirt with a black fringed shawl and hard-heeled shoes. She stands fully in frame, both feet on the stone, then unleashes zapateado — machine-gun heel and toe bursts cracking off the granite — while her arms wheel through slow braceo curls above her head, her footprint never leaving one small square of rock. One continuous shot, camera craning down from high above to eye level, playful upbeat commercial energy.

Sunrise mist floats over a drained rice paddy outside Mumbai, harvest stubble in ragged rows, cracked dry mud underfoot and a tilted wooden irrigation gate rotting at the bund. Rain streaks slant down and puddles jump around them. Five dancers, nobody else: two men and three women in their twenties to forties — Indian, white, Black, Vietnamese — in braces, rolled trousers, polka-dot skirts and scuffed brogues. All stand fully in frame with feet on the mud, then explode into lindy hop, a woman whipped over her partner's hip and flipped clean overhead, another pair firing a back-flip aerial, the group churning on one spot without travelling. One continuous shot, camera in a slow orbit around them, dreamy music-video haze and soft bloom.

Inside a timber-banked velodrome on Mumbai's outskirts, the steep track curving away and a scoreboard gantry hanging dark above the flat grey infield concrete. Three adults stand fully in frame, spikes on the slab: a rangy Jamaican man in a purple singlet, a strong Uzbek woman with a blonde ponytail and white tights, an older Tamil man with a grey moustache in blue. Each strides out and links five alternating bounds down a long runway line, knees driving high, arms cycling, finishing with a double-leg landing that skids on chalk dust. All three stay fully framed. Spectators watch from the seating tiers beyond the track, never on the infield. The air is still under even white lamps. One continuous shot, slowly dollying in.

The last light after sunset drains blue across a stepped marble quarry near Mumbai, benches of white sawn stone glowing faintly, a rusted wire saw spool and stacked blocks behind. Four adults grin and swing across a few meters of flat sawn marble, all fully in frame with feet down from the first moment and never leaving it. A curvy Ghanaian woman in a polka-dot skirt and a wiry Greek man in braces launch a candlestick lift, her legs scissoring overhead before she lands running; beside them a tall Nepali woman in yellow and a bearded Australian man in rolled sleeves answer with a hip-flip and a quick swing-out. Nothing else stirs in the quarry. One continuous shot, the camera orbiting slowly around them.

Harsh noon light hammers a small brick-paved square in a Mumbai fishing village, a dry stone trough and peeling blue doorframes closing three sides, shadows cut hard and black. One adult holds a single square meter of red pavers: a lean, sharp-jawed Mexican woman in her forties, hair oiled flat, wearing a charcoal waistcoat, cropped trousers and steel-shod shoes. She hammers a cramp roll, snaps a pullback, slides into a paddle-and-roll that rattles across the brick, then closes with an over-the-top and a scuffing riff, arms loose, chin low. Pale fireworks pop soundlessly far beyond the rooftops. She stays fully in frame throughout, one continuous shot, the camera orbiting slowly around her.

Floodlights blaze over the rolled dry clay of a cricket pitch's centre strip at a Mumbai ground, rolled tarpaulin covers parked at the boundary and rope flags snapping hard in a strong wind. Five capoeiristas hold the strip, no one else in the stadium: a sinewy Brazilian man near thirty in white trousers, a powerful Black woman about thirty-five in yellow, an older Indian man with grey dreadlocks, a stocky white woman in green, and a young Thai man barefoot in blue. All begin fully in frame with feet on the clay, then flow into ginga sway, snapping into au cartwheels, ducking esquiva dodges and sweeping kicks within a few meters. One continuous shot, slow dolly-in, epic cinematic contrast under the towers.

Night on a solar farm outside Mumbai: compacted red dirt runs like a road between tilted panel rows, humming inverter cabinets throwing pink neon glow across the dust, and torn windbreak fabric flapping wildly on the perimeter fence. Five adults share the strip, nobody else: two women and three men, twenties to fifties, Indian, Somali, white and Pacific Islander, in olive shirts, taped gloves and heavy boots. All start fully in frame, boots on the dirt, then shoulder a huge timber log and jog it far down the lane, shouting counts, before dropping it in unison in a burst of dust. One jogs back toward the lens and ends partly out of frame at the chest. One continuous shot, slow orbit, epic cinematic grandeur.

A cavernous foundry casting hall outside Mumbai, packed black sand underfoot, cold ladles hanging from an overhead rail, sand molds ranked along one wall. Two adults work the length of the floor. A broad Russian woman in her thirties, red hair knotted, navy coveralls, grabs the brass coupling of a canvas hose and sprints twenty meters, the flat line paying off its reel behind her; a slim Kenyan man in his fifties, grey beard, tan overalls, runs the far end out, spins the coupling home, then drops it and sprints back. Torn paper scraps tumble through the hard floodlight raking in from one side. Both stay fully in frame. One continuous shot, craning down from high above to eye level.

Rain hisses over a black lava shelf on the Mumbai coast, tide pools glinting between ropey basalt folds, a leaning navigation marker rusted orange, breakers exploding white on the reef behind. Three adults line up across the wet stone, fully framed, soles flat. A shaven-headed Croatian man in a black singlet tears off first, hands a scuffed aluminium baton back-to-front without looking; a tall Ivorian woman in silver receives, accelerates, and pushes it into the palm of a compact Peruvian man in olive, who drives away through the spray. Water sheets under their spikes, reflections smearing. All three remain fully in frame, one continuous shot from a static tripod at eye level.

Mist hangs in a canyon between stacked shipping containers at a Mumbai port yard, concrete paver blocks underfoot, a gantry crane looming pale at the far end and lashing rods heaped against a rust-streaked box. The air is utterly still and no one else is present. Six adults line up: three women, three men, twenties through fifties, South Asian, Black, white and Central Asian, in dark grey and navy training kit. All stand fully in frame, feet on the pavers, then tear off in shuttle sprints between cones set far apart, dropping a hand to touch the ground, cutting hard and driving back, crossing the whole length of the canyon. One continuous shot, handheld camera slowly circling at chest height, moody noir grade.

A black volcanic sand beach south of Mumbai lies under a swollen, purple pre-rain sky, bleached driftwood spars half-buried and a jagged basalt sea stack standing offshore. Nothing stirs — no wind, no movement but his own. A single man works the sand: broad-chested, Māori, mid-forties, in cut-off denim shorts and a soaked white tee, hair plastered flat. Beginning fully in frame with both feet on the dark grit, he takes three thundering strides and launches headfirst into a belly-flop dive, skidding through a spray of black grains, then rolls up and repeats the run and dive a few meters along the beach. One continuous shot, slow dolly-out revealing the vast empty shoreline, gritty documentary texture and raw grain.

Thick fog rolls across a cargo apron beside a corrugated hangar at a Mumbai airfield, yellow guidance stripes and a chained tow bar fading into white; far off, headlight trails streak along the perimeter road. One adult crouches into starting blocks set on the painted concrete: a heavyset Maori man in his thirties, tattooed shoulders, cropped black hair, grey vest and red spikes. He rocks into set, holds, then explodes out, driving four powerful low strides with his shins almost flat, chest rising on the fifth. He begins fully in frame, feet down, and finishes so close that the lens crops him at the ribs. One continuous shot, the camera tracking sideways at a steady walking pace.

Neon from shuttered juice kiosks bleeds pink and green across a weathered wooden promenade on the Mumbai seafront, the iron railing beaded with spray while heavy surf pounds the seawall below. Two adults own the decking: a fast, small Vietnamese woman in her twenties in a cropped black hoodie and cyan shorts, and a tall Greek man near forty-five in a white shirt and grey joggers. Both start fully in frame with feet on the boards, then break into a tag chase, cutting hard off the planks, faking, reversing, one lunging with an outstretched hand as the other swerves and sprints away down the promenade. Onlookers watch from behind the railing on a raised terrace. One continuous shot, slow orbit, moody neo-noir sheen.

Blue-hour calm in a grain silo loading yard on the Mumbai docks, three fat concrete towers, a hopper chute swung out overhead, dusty slab underfoot streaked with spilled husks. Two adults take turns on one spot. A grinning Sri Lankan woman with a thick plait and taped forearms squats over a round concrete ball, laps it to her belt, drives her hips and rolls it onto a chest-high barrel platform; her friend, a burly Polish man in a yellow tee and cut-off shorts, dumps it back down and repeats faster, chalk clouding around them. Warm steam drifts from vent grilles beside the chute. Both stay entirely in frame. One continuous shot, the camera craning down to eye level.

Snow falls thickly into a small tiled courtyard in a Mumbai heritage hotel, blue-and-white ceramic patterns vanishing under white, a dry fountain at the back. Four adults drill in a taped goalmouth, all four fully framed on the ceramic from the first second and never leaving the shot. A rangy Nigerian-Danish woman in green gloves throws herself low to smother a rolling ball, pops back up, and tips the next one over an imagined bar; three others—a stocky Iranian man, a Colombian woman with braids, a grey-haired Italian man—feed shots and dive in turn, sliding on wet tile. Dry petals swirl low between snow gusts. Hotel guests watch from the balcony above, off the tiles. One continuous shot, slowly orbiting.

Storm light turns a painted intersection plaza in central Mumbai violet-grey: giant orange and turquoise shapes brushed across the asphalt, concrete planters and a striped bollard ring at the edges. One adult works a single spot, ball hammering the paint. A springy Filipino-American man in his twenties, hair bleached at the tips, wearing a loose lilac jersey and mismatched socks, snaps a double crossover, wraps the ball behind his back, yanks it into a hard snatch-back, then pounds a low pocket dribble before spinning it on a fingertip. He stays fully in frame, feet never leaving the painted circle. Onlookers lean on the planter railings, off the plaza floor. The air is dead still. One continuous handheld shot, circling at chest height.

Thick fog drifts through an olive grove terrace outside Mumbai, gnarled silver trees fading into white, a low dry-stone retaining wall and a wooden harvest ladder propped against a trunk on the dusty pale earth. Nothing else moves. One athlete trains alone: a sinewy Turkish man in his early thirties, close-cropped beard, in a sky-blue tee, black shorts and worn trainers. He stands fully in frame with both feet on the dirt beside a flat agility ladder, then attacks it — in-in-out-out, lateral shuffles, quick icky-shuffle cuts — feet blurring, dust puffing, working a few meters up the ladder and jogging back to run it again. One continuous shot, handheld camera slowly circling at chest height, bright playful commercial mood softened by the mist.

Golden light slants between mahogany trunks into a clearing in the forest above Mumbai's ghats, a fallen log furred with moss and a ring of packed earth swept clear of leaf litter. Two adults hold that ring, both fully framed, feet down from the opening frame and staying in shot. A tall Zulu man in high-waisted brown trousers and braces crouches; his partner, a compact Swedish woman with copper curls in a green polka-dot dress, springs off his thigh, tucks over his shoulder, and lands beating out the rhythm; they swap, and he vaults her back in a low scissor vault, both landing on the same worn patch. Nothing else moves. One continuous shot craning from the canopy down to eye level.

Portable floodlights on scaffold masts blaze over a firm red interdune flat inland from Mumbai, tall ridged dunes rising behind and a rattling generator cabled across the sand. The night air is completely still. Three adults are out there alone: a grinning Indian man in his twenties in a lime tee, a freckled white woman about thirty-five in a blue swimsuit and shorts, and a lean Korean man near forty-five in white. All three stand fully in frame, bare feet on the packed sand, then run a few paces and launch headfirst into belly-flop dives, skidding through the grit in sprays of red, rolling over laughing and jogging back to dive again. One continuous shot, camera in a slow orbit, playful upbeat commercial brightness.

A dim training hall in an old Mumbai mill building: a worn blue spring floor, chalk handprints on a wall pad, ropes coiled on a hook, dust hanging in the shafts of daylight that fall from high clerestory windows. One adult occupies a single square of carpet — a compact Argentinian man in his thirties, dark curls tied back, black long-sleeve leotard and white socks. He sets his arms, snaps a tight straight somersault backward, absorbs the landing without a step, then immediately punches into a half-twisting layback, spotting the floor. Sweat glints. Nothing in the room moves but him, and he remains fully in frame the whole time. One continuous shot, the camera orbiting him slowly.

Scarlet chilies lie raked into drying beds on a whitewashed rooftop in a Mumbai spice quarter, a stilted water tank and laundry lines above the parapets, mist thinning as the sun comes up. Five adults hold a loose row on the whitewashed cement, all fully in frame with bare feet planted and none leaving the shot: a silver-haired Ugandan woman, a squat Malay man with wrapped hands, a freckled Canadian woman in a grey vest, a tall Tamil man in blue shorts, a broad Chilean woman in orange. They snap one-twos, slip under imagined counters, roll off the back foot, and pivot laterally a meter or two before firing again. Low dust drifts across the terrace. One continuous shot, tracking sideways at walking pace.

Fine rain glazes a red sandstone bench above the Mumbai backwaters, the rock cross-bedded in swirls, an old survey cairn and prayer pennants snapping hard in the wind at the rim. One adult plays there: a lithe Tunisian woman in her forties, dark curls soaked flat, wearing a rust-colored bodysuit and bare feet. She sends a wooden ring skimming across the wet stone with heavy backspin, chases it three strides, and folds her body through the gap as it rolls back, then hooks it up with a toe and repeats. Reflections streak beneath her. She begins fully in frame, then steps toward the lens and ends cropped mid-thigh. One continuous shot, slowly dollying out.

Hazy afternoon wind carries dust through a timber yard south of Mumbai, teak logs stacked in a wall, a silent bandsaw shed, sawdust drifted ankle-deep over the dirt. Two adults, fully framed with boots planted, race side by side with wide steel shovels. A wiry Rajasthani man in his fifties, white stubble, faded green shirt, and a strong Haitian woman in her twenties, headwrap and denim cut-offs, bite into their piles, twist, and fling long golden arcs onto a screening frame, shovels ringing. They shuffle a few meters along their heaps, never leaving the frame, sweat cutting tracks through the dust on their necks. Fireworks flicker over the distant skyline. One continuous shot, the camera tracking sideways at a steady walking pace.

An emptied exhibition hall in a Mumbai convention centre: grey commercial carpet seamed with tape, bare truss towers, half-struck booth skeletons along one side, everything lit flat and even from the ceiling. Two adults have their inner ankles lashed with a red bandage. A tall Lebanese woman with a dark ponytail in a mustard tracksuit and a shorter Korean-American man in a white tee count a rhythm, then run a long aisle together, hips clashing, lurching, catching each other, breaking into a real sprint before wheeling around a taped cross and hammering back. Nothing else stirs in the hall. Both stay fully in frame from the first second. One continuous shot, craning from the roof trusses down to eye level.

A curling rink converted for a late-night event outside Mumbai: pebbled ice glowing magenta and cyan under stage bars, haze rolling low, spotlights swinging across the house rings. One adult guards a portable net on the ice — a broad-shouldered Icelandic woman in her thirties, blonde braid, teal leg pads, blocker and catching glove. She stands square on her blades, fully framed, then drops into a butterfly, seals the ice, slides post to post on her knees, kicks a puck away with her right pad, then pops upright and repeats a meter to the left, skate edges spraying frost. She stays fully in frame the whole time. One continuous shot, the camera tracking sideways at a steady walking pace.

Noon glare bleaches a lone hard court wedged between Mumbai tenements, faded blue acrylic inside white lines, a sagging net and a chain-link fence threaded with faded cloth strips. One adult trains alone on the surface: a tall Hungarian man in his forties, close-cropped grey hair, black compression sleeve, red shorts. Standing fully in frame, feet on the paint, he steps left, plants a four-step approach, broad-jumps off both heels, and rips a cross-court arm swing at an imaginary ball, then repeats with a soft wrist-away roll shot. Paper scraps tumble across the baseline. Neighbours watch through the fence, never on the court. His final approach carries him past the lens, cropping him at the chest. One continuous shot, panning slowly left to right.

Low golden sun rakes a tidal flat below a Mumbai causeway, rippled wet sand holding the last light, a stranded mooring buoy and the black ribs of a wrecked hull far out. Three adults, feet planted on the sand, drive a plate-loaded sled across the flat: a huge Samoan man with a shaved head in a grey vest, a sinewy Ethiopian woman in navy, and a stocky German man in orange. They shove it twenty meters in a hard sprint, hands locked on the uprights, then turn, hook a strap over their shoulders and drag it back, heels tearing troughs in the sand. Fireworks bloom silently over the far shore. All three remain fully in frame. One continuous shot, slowly dollying out.

Harsh midday sun beats on an open-pit quarry bench inland from Mumbai, compacted rock aggregate underfoot, a stepped grey wall behind pocked with drill holes and a dead excavator parked far along the ledge, while fog banks roll slowly through the pit below. One athlete works the bench alone: a stocky Egyptian woman in her late thirties, thick thighs, hair under a black bandana, in a maroon tank and grey shorts. She stands fully in frame with both shoes on the gravel, then hammers repeated box jumps onto a steel plyo box, arms whipping, landing soft, stepping down and firing again without her feet leaving one small patch of stone. One continuous shot, slow pan from left to right, gritty documentary texture and hard shadow.

Shafts of daylight fall from high dusty windows onto an indoor sprint track in Mumbai, blue polyurethane laid in crisp lanes, a shallow banked turn at the far end and a hurdle rack shoved against the wall. The air is completely still. A single athlete stands on the blue: a lean Jamaican man in his mid-twenties, wiry and cut, in a black singlet, red shorts and bare feet, hair in short twists. Fully in frame with both feet on the track, he swings his arms and throws a standing back tuck, sticks the landing, immediately fires a second, then a standing layout, never leaving one lane square. Spectators watch from a raised gallery behind the rail. One continuous shot, slow dolly-in, moody neo-noir grade.

Inside a disused crop-duster hangar tucked against Guilin's karst peaks, six adults form a loose roda on painted grey concrete streaked with old tow lines. A tall Black man in a mustard tank, a wiry Vietnamese woman in cropped white, a broad Brazilian man in red shorts, a silver-haired Korean woman in navy, a freckled Irish man in olive, and a compact Nigerian woman in teal all begin fully framed, feet planted. They swing into ginga, drop into cartwheel au, and sweep low meia-lua kicks that miss by inches, staying within a few metres. Haze rolls between moving spotlights; deep shadows swallow the far wall. One continuous shot, a slow dolly-in toward the people.

Midday sun bakes a disused runway threading the karst valleys near Guilin, grooved asphalt streaked with lichen, limestone spires rising sheer on both sides, a toppled windsock mast in the grass. One adult works alone: a powerfully built Han Chinese woman in her thirties, hair in a tight bun, chalk on her palms, black vest and yellow shorts. She squats to a truck tire, drives her hips forward and lands it flat three times, then leaps onto the rubber, springs off, and turns to flip it back the other way. She stays fully in frame, feet on the asphalt from the first second. Pale daytime fireworks burst over the ridgeline. One continuous shot, slowly dollying out.

Pale limestone paving spreads before a riverside Guilin museum, its dry scallop fountain and bronze karst relief half-swallowed by thick drifting fog. Four adults grip wrists in a chain: a lanky Ethiopian man in orange, a stocky Japanese woman in lime, a middle-aged Danish man in white, and a rangy Mexican woman in cobalt at the tail. All four start fully in frame, shoes flat on stone. They wind into a crack-the-whip spin, the chain accelerating until the tail runner is slung wide, sprinting and skidding to a laughing stop. Ticket-line onlookers watch from behind a rope barrier on the upper steps. One continuous shot, a slow orbit; the tail runner swings close and ends partly out of frame.

Rain beads on painted black asphalt behind a village school in the karst valley, a bent hoop with a chain net, a bamboo fence, wet green peaks blurred beyond. One adult woman plays: a tall Filipina guard, hair in a soaked braid, lavender jersey and grey shorts clinging, feet fully on the glossy court as the shot begins. She attacks from the wing, crosses over, splits an imaginary help defender with a long euro-step, and lays the ball high off the glass, then gathers the rebound and repeats. Villagers watch from a covered walkway behind the fence. One continuous shot, a slow dolly-in; her final drive brings her partly out of frame.

Raked red dirt rings a half-forgotten diamond by a river bend, its sagging chain backstop tangled with vine, three limestone peaks stacked behind the outfield. Four adults train under a punishing noon sun with no shade to steal: a leggy Kenyan woman in faded red, a broad Ukrainian man in a grey compression top, a middle-aged Thai woman in yellow, a bearded Turkish man in black. Each begins fully framed, spikes in the dirt. In turn they carry a training javelin back, accelerate along the baseline with crossover steps, plant hard and launch the shaft arcing toward centre field, then jog wide to reset. One continuous shot, a handheld camera slowly circling at chest height.

A red painted tarmac cycle expressway runs on slim stilts above flooded paddies, its steel railing beaded with humidity, karst towers black against a bruised pre-storm sky. Four adults line up on the lane, all fully visible with shoes on the tarmac: a sinewy Colombian man in white, a tall Somali woman in electric blue, a stocky German man in orange, a lean Chinese woman in pink. Water bottles mark the turns. They explode into shuttle sprints, slapping each cone, hips dropping low on every touch-and-turn, covering fifteen metres out and back with breath tearing. Air is dead still; only they move. One continuous shot, a slow dolly-out revealing more of the surroundings.

Crusted white salt flats stretch between low mud dikes and a rusted sluice gate, a distant chalk-blue karst ridge floating in soft overcast light. Two adults occupy the pan: a broad-shouldered Ghanaian man in a charcoal long-sleeve and black shorts, and a lean Argentinian woman with a bleached crop and a slate grey kit. Both stand fully in frame, boots crunching salt. They lash power shots at a bent metal frame, then feed each other lifted balls and hammer full volleys out of the air, chasing rebounds far across the flat and drilling long-range strikes back. Salt dust puffs from their studs. One continuous shot, a slow orbit around the people; both stay framed.

Mist hangs low between gnarled apple trees on a terraced hillside above a sleeping village, clover and grass soft underfoot, a leaning wooden ladder and a crate of windfalls at the row's end. Three adults stand fully in frame as sunrise light filters gold through the fog: a willowy Swedish woman in oat linen, a compact Peruvian man in rust, an athletic Ivorian woman in cream. On a clap they drop flat, then explode up into two hard strides; next round they start seated, then falling forward, each time recovering into a three-metre burst before resetting. The orchard air is utterly calm. One continuous shot, a handheld camera slowly circling at chest height.

Blue hour drapes a green synthetic pitch laid across a headland where karst hills meet the coast; two floodlight masts stand dark, and swells break white against the cliff below, spray catching the last light. Three adults dig into the turf, all fully framed: a huge Māori man in deep red, a tall Egyptian woman in graphite, a stocky Scottish man in navy. They haul a thick hemp rope anchored to a sled, heaving in unison, heels skidding backwards two metres, then a lurch drops them onto their backs before they scramble up and haul again. Waves boom steadily behind. One continuous shot, a camera tracking sideways at a steady walking pace.

Snow falls thick over a hillside lavender plot in the karst country, greyed rows bowed under white, a chalky gravel path cutting straight between them toward a stone drying shed. One adult marches it: a broad Puerto Rican woman in a bright red bandsman's jacket, black trousers, a snare slung at her hips, sticks flashing. She begins fully in frame, boots crunching gravel, then rolls into a crisp cadence, high-stepping down the path for several metres, snapping a sharp pivot turn, a backward eight-count, another turn, grinning through the flakes settling on her shoulders. One continuous shot, a handheld camera slowly circling at chest height as she covers ground and stays framed.

Golden hour floods a strip of dry cracked soil edging a sunflower field that runs to a low bluff; beyond it, surf folds and crashes in slow white lines, karst stacks glowing offshore. Three adults hold speed ropes, each rooted to a single patch: a bouncy Korean man in canary yellow, a curvy Nigerian-British woman in mint, a silver-bearded Portuguese man in sky blue. Ropes blur into arcs as they rip crossovers, snap into double-unders, then a burst of high-knee singles, all inside a metre of ground, dust ticking up at their toes. Sunflower heads glow behind them. One continuous shot, a slow dolly-in toward the people, everyone fully framed.

Fired clay tiles pave a small brickworks yard in the karst countryside, kiln-fresh bricks stacked in herringbone towers, a tin-roof drying shed and a green ridge behind. Soft overcast light flattens every colour. Four adults ring a fat truck tire, feet planted and fully in frame: a burly Fijian man in a lilac tee, a compact Vietnamese woman in coral, a lanky Dutch man in stripes, a grinning Ethiopian woman in bright green. They take turns whipping sledgehammers overhead and cracking them down onto the rubber, which bucks and thumps, then swap sides without stepping away, cheering each hit. The air is completely still. One continuous shot, a static tripod camera at eye level.

A road tunnel bored through a karst hill sits closed to traffic, sodium lamps buzzing over asphalt, ventilation shafts dropping pale blades of daylight through the gloom onto tiled walls and a stalled barrier arm. Two adults work the bore, both fully framed at the start with cleats on the asphalt: a thick-necked Samoan-American man in a black practice jersey, and a rangy Sudanese woman in grey with taped fingers. He takes a five-step drop, sets, and fires a tight spiral thirty metres down the tunnel; she runs deep routes into the light shafts and rifles the ball back. One continuous shot, a camera tracking sideways at a steady walking pace; late, she sprints toward the lens and ends partly out of frame.

Misty sunrise softens a rail freight depot wedged among karst peaks, weathered concrete platform edged with rusted loading cleats, faded containers stacked two high, dew on the rails. Fireworks from a distant village festival bloom faintly above the fog. Four adults hold their own square metre, all fully in frame: a muscular Brazilian woman in hot pink, a wiry Indian man in white, a stocky Polish woman in tangerine, a tall Kenyan man in cobalt. They drop chest to concrete, snap the feet in, and launch into clapping vertical jumps, landing to drop again, a hammering rhythm, breath steaming. One continuous shot, a camera tracking sideways at a steady walking pace.

Low golden light rakes an open rural railway platform where dust skims the tactile-edged concrete in restless ribbons; a shuttered ticket kiosk at one end, karst spires beyond the empty track. Six adults are here and no one else. A bulky Tongan man in white and a lean Japanese woman in red take the near sleds; behind them a bearded Iranian man in grey, a tall Haitian woman in violet, a stocky Finn in green and a sinewy Chilean man in black set their grips. All six begin fully in frame with feet on the concrete, then drive the loaded sleds thirty metres down the platform in staggered sprints, heads low, chains rasping. One continuous shot, a slow pan from left to right.

Snow falls hard over a wind-packed field on a high karst plateau, black limestone teeth breaking the white and a bent survey pole leaning near a buried fence line. One adult trains alone: a barrel-chested Croatian man in a soaked navy thermal, taped wrists, snow crusted in his beard. He starts fully in frame, boots stamped into the crust, the iron ball tucked against his neck. He coils low, glides back across a metre, whips his hips open with a guttural shout and launches the shot into the storm, then resets on the same spot and repeats, exhaling steam. One continuous shot, a slow pan from left to right.

Golden hour pours through the arcade arches of a small hillside monastery, laying long warm bars across worn flagstone; a pomegranate tree drops fruit near a stone basin, incense smoke gone still in the calm air. One adult performs: a lithe Uyghur woman with a long dark braid, in a saffron wrap top and loose grey trousers, barefoot and fully in frame. She spins a bamboo hoop out across the stones, lets it roll back to her, catches it upright, then dives cleanly headfirst through the spinning ring, tucks into a shoulder roll and rises to flick it out again, working a small patch of the yard. One continuous shot, a slow orbit around her.

Fog drifts thick across a coffee drying patio below the karst hills near Guilin, beans raked into long dark stripes on the smooth concrete, bamboo rakes leaning on a low wall, a green ridge dissolving behind. One adult moves through it: a slender Hui man in his twenties, buzzed hair, loose white shirt knotted at the waist, grey trousers, barefoot. He whips a side aerial with both hands raised, lands, immediately spins a low crescent kick over the beans, then chains an aerial round-off into a soft landing two meters on. Paper scraps tumble past his ankles. He remains fully in frame with feet returning to the slab each time. One continuous shot, tracking sideways at walking pace.

A county theater in the karst hills keeps its house lamps low; only moody practice lights wash the black painted plywood stage, throwing deep shadows past a half-flown backdrop of painted limestone peaks and a dusty velour leg. Four adults work centre stage, fully in frame: a springy Cambodian man in white, a tall Jamaican woman in purple, a stocky Russian man in grey, a grinning Mexican woman in gold. Two hold hand paddles high while the others charge two steps and snap flying front and side kicks, cracking the pads, then swap roles with a whoop. Staff and students watch from the front row of seats below the stage lip. One continuous shot, a slow dolly-in.

A raised park terrace of crushed decomposed granite overlooks a slow green river; a chipped stone balustrade, two dead lampposts and a lone banyan frame the view, while far below a highway drags long red and white light trails across the dusk. Golden hour lights only the rim of things. Two adults circle, both fully framed with shoes in the gravel: a lean Vietnamese-French man in a black rash guard, and a broad-shouldered Kazakh woman in dark green with a taped forearm. They trade padded-stick strikes, high slashes turned by quick parries, shoulder slips, a duck-under and a sharp counter to the ribs, working a few metres. One continuous shot, a camera craning down from high above to eye level.

Night neon from the plant gate stains the black coal-dust ground magenta and green; a conveyor gantry crosses overhead and safety banners snap violently in the wind, karst silhouettes standing behind the stacks. One adult trains: a stocky Filipino sprinter in a lemon crop hoodie and black tights, grinning, resistance band cinched at his waist and anchored to a loaded sled. He starts fully in frame, spikes biting the dust, then leans forty-five degrees and claws forward, chopping short furious strides, dragging the sled fifteen metres across the yard. One continuous shot, a slow orbit around him; on the last run he charges the lens and finishes partly out of frame.

Daylight falls in bright shafts through the high clerestory of a riverside cultural centre's colonnaded arcade, terrazzo gleaming between square pillars while haze drifts and rigged spotlights sweep slowly across the columns. Five adults start fully in frame, boots planted on the terrazzo: a tall Senegalese keeper in lime gloves, a compact Italian woman in charcoal, a broad Korean man in maroon, a freckled Australian woman in slate, a wiry Bolivian man in cobalt. They take turns blasting balls at each other, low and high; the receiving keeper springs sideways, smothers, hits terrazzo hip-first, rolls up instantly and resets a metre away. Visitors watch from a balcony behind the railing above. One continuous shot, a slow dolly-out revealing more of the surroundings.

Harsh floodlights blaze in from one side of a turbine hall serving a river hydro station, raking across checker plate steel and lighting the flanks of green machine casings while the far end drops into blackness. One adult owns the floor: a towering Dominican pitcher in a sleeveless grey shirt and pinstriped pants, forearms corded, fully in frame with cleats on the plate. He rocks back, lifts a high knee, strides long and unloads a fastball down the hall into a padded backstop, then walks the ball back and repeats, drifting many metres along the walkway. One continuous shot, a slow orbit around him; the final delivery brings him partly out of frame.

Light rain glazes the painted asphalt of a film backlot street built in the karst valley, blank false shopfronts and a plywood teahouse facade reflecting in the sheen, real limestone peaks rising past the flats. Snowflakes from an overhead effects rig drift through the lamp beams. Six adults each stand over their own stone, all fully framed: a giant Icelandic man in black, a thick-armed Brazilian woman in white, a bearded Punjabi man in grey, a stocky Greek woman in wine, a broad Ugandan man in blue, a compact Norwegian woman in rust. They lap the stones and heave them onto a low platform, over and over. One continuous shot, a slow dolly-in.

Dawn mist lies over the flat grey asphalt of an old garrison parade ground, a flagless mast, a whitewashed inspection stand, and a wall of karst dissolving into pale vapour behind it. One adult crouches into starting blocks: a lean Ethiopian-American woman in an iridescent teal skinsuit, braids tied back, spikes set, entirely in frame. She rocks up, holds, then detonates forward, driving low through six powerful strides and sweeping thirty metres across the ground into the haze before easing off. A handful of caretakers watch from the inspection stand's raised balcony. Air is windless; only she moves. One continuous shot, a slow dolly-out revealing more of the surroundings, keeping her fully framed.

A storm stacks purple-black above a cracked white salt crust that runs from the feet of karst spires toward a distant shoreline where waves keep folding over and booming. Three adults play, all fully framed with shoes on the crust: a tall Danish woman in tangerine, a compact Filipino man in mint, a broad Nigerian woman in lemon. A disc floats out; one sprints two steps and launches horizontal, snagging it inches above the salt and skidding in a spray of white grit, then flicks it up for the next diving layout, laughing and dusting off. Nobody strays more than a few metres. One continuous shot, a slow dolly-out revealing more of the surroundings.

Under a riverside resort, a parking garage glows with strips of magenta and cyan stage light bouncing off epoxy-coated concrete, numbered bays and a ventilation duct running the ceiling's length. Four adults grapple, feet flat and all fully framed: a thick-set Turkish man in a blue singlet, a compact Chinese woman in red, a rangy Cuban man in white, a muscular Belarusian woman in black. In pairs they change levels, shoot low double-legs, drive through and finish, then reset a metre back, alternating shots and hard sprawls, shoes squeaking, chalk clapping off their palms. The air is dead quiet between impacts. One continuous shot, a slow pan from left to right.

Late gold light slices between six-storey walls into an apartment courtyard paved with interlocking concrete pavers; laundry hangs on lines, a steam vent by the boiler room breathes drifting white across the shadows, karst rock looming beyond the roofline. One adult trains: a wiry Uruguayan man with a shaved head, in a black long-sleeve and grey shorts, chalk on his hands, fully in frame with both feet down. He sprints four steps and kongs over a low concrete utility box, hands slapping, legs threading through, lands rolling and circles back to repeat higher and faster. Residents watch from balconies above. One continuous shot, a camera tracking sideways at a steady walking pace.

Floodlights blaze on light travertine tile beside a still rooftop pool at a riverside hotel, folded loungers stacked at the parapet, and beyond the glass rail, fireworks crack open in gold and green above the black karst skyline. One adult plays: a tall Dutch-Indonesian woman with a high ponytail, in a fuchsia tank and white shorts, knee pads on, standing fully in frame on the tile. She tosses, steps left-right-left into a booming spike approach, swings her arm through and hammers the ball down at the deck, chasing it two metres and resetting for the next, again and again. One continuous shot, a camera craning down from high above to eye level.

Storm light presses down over granite setts in a Guilin old-town pedestrian street, shuttered tea shops, faded red lanterns hanging dead still, and a wet karst ridge rearing at the end of the lane. Three adults perform on one patch of stone, all fully framed: a tall Congolese man in a fringed black coat, a stocky Vietnamese woman in silver, a sinewy Spanish woman in oxblood. Arms cut hard angles, wrists snap, and each whips into a spin that collapses into a death-drop dip, back leg folded, then rises to strike again without shifting position. Shoppers cluster beyond a low planter barrier at the lane's mouth. One continuous shot, a slow dolly-out revealing more of the surroundings.

Blue hour settles over a packed dirt farmyard ringed by bamboo drying racks, a hand tractor parked under a tin lean-to, and karst peaks going indigo above. Loose dust skims low across the ground in soft gusts. Three adults stand around a worn tractor tire, feet planted and fully in frame: a heavyset Malay man in a bright orange tee, a wiry Ecuadorian woman in yellow, and a grey-haired Australian man in teal. They alternate sledgehammer swings, hips whipping, heads snapping down as rubber booms and dust jumps, teasing each other between reps without leaving their spots. One continuous shot, a slow dolly-out revealing more of the surroundings around them.

Soft overcast light lies flat on the red rubber tartan of a school track set in the karst valley, white lane lines curving past an empty steel bleacher and a bank of green peaks. One adult trains: a compact Trinidadian woman in a white crop top, black tights and neon shoes, hair wrapped, fully in frame with both feet on the track. She rockets through an agility ladder, two-in-two-out, then icky shuffles, then lateral in-in-out-outs, feet blurring, before jogging back and running it again, never straying beyond a few metres. Everything else is windless and quiet. One continuous shot, a slow dolly-in; on the last pass she surges toward the lens and ends partly out of frame.

Frost furs the concrete of a cold storage warehouse in the karst foothills, breath hanging in slabs of warm tungsten work-lamp light while a flickering neon sign near the dock and a sweeping security searchlight strobe across towering pallet racks. One adult labours there: a heavily built Congolese-Belgian athlete in a black thermal, taped hands, frost in his beard, starting fully in frame with cleats on the frosted slab. Harnessed to a banded sled, he leans in hard and drives it twenty-five metres down the aisle, ice crackling under the runners, then resets and repeats. One continuous shot, a handheld camera slowly circling at chest height; his final drive carries him partly out of frame.

Noon sun hammers a flat of powdery white gypsum sand that laps against the feet of grey limestone towers; torn festival confetti tumbles across the dunes on hot air. Two adults face off, each rooted to a single patch and fully in frame: a broad Kazakh man in a white gi top with the sleeves cut off, and a tall Somali-Swedish woman in a black rash guard, both barefoot. They whip spinning hook kicks and jumping tornado kicks that flare huge arcs of sand into the light, landing, resetting on the same spot and firing again, sweat cutting tracks through the dust on their faces. One continuous shot, a slow pan from left to right.

A small-town badminton hall keeps one floodlight bank blazing from a single side, hard light stretching net-post shadows across the green vinyl and a spread of damp sand raked over the centre court. Big pedestal fans push loose scoresheets and dust in slow spirals. Two adults work that patch, fully in frame with bare feet dug in: a stocky Mongolian woman in a maroon singlet, and a lean Brazilian-Japanese man in white shorts. They tie up, snap a hip throw down into the sand, scramble instantly for position, wrestle up and reset in the same square metre, sand clinging to their shoulders. One continuous shot, a slow dolly-in toward the two of them.

A hydroelectric dam crest carries a concrete roadway with faded white lane lines high over a karst gorge, spillway gates yawning below and a settled dust haze bronzing the motionless afternoon air. Two adults face each other, both fully in frame with bare feet on the concrete: a tall Japanese-Peruvian man in indigo hakama, and a compact Norwegian woman in navy with her hair knotted tight. Shinai crack together as they exchange men strikes, sliding forward with sharp fumikomi stamps, retreating, then lunging again with shouted kiai, ranging a few metres along the crest. Nothing else on the crest stirs. One continuous shot, a camera tracking sideways at a steady walking pace beside them.

A pre-storm sky bruises purple over a cobbled quay in a karst water town; bamboo punts knock against mooring rings, a noodle kitchen's vent breathes steam across the grey setts, and a stone arch bridge closes the far end. One adult trains: a rangy Ghanaian-British long jumper in a faded red singlet and black shorts, calves scarred, fully in frame with spikes on the cobbles. She measures a run-up, sprints twenty metres down the quay, hits a chalk mark and launches, hanging with arms high before landing hard into a sand pile, then walks back to repeat. One continuous shot, a camera tracking sideways at a steady walking pace.

An abandoned subway platform beneath the karst city sits half-lit, daylight dropping in dusty shafts from a broken street grate onto tiled concrete, blank enamel signage boards and a rusted bench along the wall. Two adults work a short bucket line, both fully framed with feet on the platform: a stocky Puerto Rican woman in a lime work shirt, and a lanky Korean man in denim overalls. They swing sloshing pails hand to hand, jog three metres, pass again, water arcing and slapping the tiles, both laughing as they speed up. One continuous shot, a camera tracking sideways at a steady walking pace; the last pass carries her toward the lens, ending partly out of frame.

Heavy snow buries a closed county-town street, the crosswalk stripes ghosting through white asphalt, shuttered shopfronts and a stalled bus at the corner, torn red paper scraps tumbling on the wind with the flakes. Five adults labour there, all fully in frame at the start: a broad Chilean man in a soot-stained coat, a tall Kenyan woman in yellow, a stocky Bulgarian man in grey, a wiry Vietnamese woman in orange, a bearded Canadian man in navy. Gripping the coupling, they sprint the hose off its reel forty metres down the street, snow spraying, then drop the charged line and haul the next length. Bystanders watch from behind barricades on the sidewalk. One continuous shot, a static tripod camera at eye level.

In a faded river hotel's grand ballroom, dust hangs in shafts of daylight falling through tall clerestory windows onto scuffed parquet; the chandeliers are unlit, gilt mirrors face away under sheets, and stacked banquet chairs line one wall. Three adults each stand over a stone, all fully in frame: a huge Estonian man in a sweat-dark singlet, a thick-armed Nigerian woman in black, a squat Uzbek man with a taped back. They tack the stones to their laps, take a breath, then heave them onto a wooden platform, drop them and reload without moving their feet, skin scraped raw. Hotel staff watch from a mezzanine balcony above. One continuous shot, a slow dolly-out revealing more of the surroundings.

Neon tubing above a shuttered Miami commuter terminal washes the forecourt pink and cyan; palm shadows lie still across dark basalt setts. Five adults stand feet-planted on one spot, fully in frame throughout: a tall Black man in a mustard tank top, a stocky Latina woman with a shaved head, a lean white man in ripped denim, a broad Filipino woman in teal, and a wiry older Indian man in grey. Each spins a wooden staff into figure-eights, rolls it across shoulders and forearms, then flips it up and catches it blind. Commuters watch from behind a chest-high railing on the raised platform. One continuous shot, the camera craning down from high above to eye level, gritty and unpolished.

Cropped dry grass stretches flat under punishing midday sun on an inland Florida prairie strip, marked only by a rusted windmill and a sagging barbed fence hung with torn plastic sheeting that whips and cracks in the strong wind. Two adults stand alone here: a broad-shouldered Samoan man in a sweat-darkened black singlet, and a tall red-haired woman in a faded maroon tee and canvas trousers. Both stay fully in frame, boots rooted to the turf, footprints barely shifting. They squat over a battered steel keg, drive their hips, and launch it backward over one shoulder, then reset and repeat. One continuous shot, a slow dolly-out revealing more of the surroundings. Hard shadows, bleached highlights, moody neo-noir contrast.

Before the rain lands, a bayfront festival main stage sits under bruised cloud, its aluminium deck dulled to pewter, scaffold towers rising on both sides, torn banners and loose fabric snapping violently in the wind. Six adults work the deck in three pairs: a lanky Korean man in a blue singlet, a muscular Black woman with braided hair, a bearded white man in grey, a compact Mexican woman in yellow, a broad Somali man in maroon, a silver-templed woman in teal. All six start fully in frame, feet on the deck, and stay framed while shooting level-change double-leg takedowns, driving a few metres and resetting. One continuous shot, a slow dolly-out revealing more. Festivalgoers press behind the barricade below. Dreamy, desaturated, wind-blown.

A freak snow squall whitens a refinery service road outside Miami, flare stacks pluming behind chain fencing, a gravel verge crunching underfoot, floodlight beams full of drifting flakes. One adult owns a small patch of gravel: a striking Afro-Brazilian man in his thirties, tall and lean, hair shaved to a fade, silver mesh top, wide black trousers, boots. He snaps precise hand performance around his face, drops into a low duckwalk on the spot, rises with a catwalk pivot, then folds backward to the ground in one sharp descent and rolls straight up again, arms slicing. Snow settles on his shoulders. He stays fully in frame throughout. One continuous shot, the camera panning slowly left to right.

Snow drifts improbably over a beach volleyball court behind a shuttered boardwalk, settling on the sagging net, the leaning poles and the raked fine sand, while a broken neon sign flickers and a searchlight sweeps in from the marina. One adult is here, nobody else: a stocky white man in his late forties, grey stubble, black thermal shirt, ochre shorts, bare calves reddened by cold. He works a two-metre patch, spinning a wooden staff in tight helicopters, rolling it across his back, tossing it high and catching it blind, sand kicking up under his heels. One continuous shot, a slow orbit around him, keeping him fully framed. Handheld grain, cold documentary honesty.

Golden hour turns a white coral sand beach amber; a mangrove spit and a half-buried wooden skiff anchor the far edge, and beyond the dune line distant traffic streaks its light trails along an unseen causeway. Three adults share the sand alone: a slender Vietnamese woman in a lilac swimsuit, a broad Nigerian man in cut-off denim, a freckled thirty-something redhead in a faded green tee. All three begin fully in frame, heels sunk into the sand, and stay framed as they take three-step run-ups and hurl themselves headfirst into shallow belly-flop dives, skidding, rolling up, sand spraying gold. One continuous shot, camera tracking sideways at a steady walking pace. Soft haze, dreamy music-video warmth.

Dust hazes the afternoon in a scrap metal yard south of the port: towers of crushed cars, an idle magnet crane, and torn tarpaulins lashed to the fence whipping hard in the gusting wind. An oil-stained concrete pad lies clear beneath three adults, the only people for miles. A heavyset Haitian man in black shorts locks a plum clinch with a tall Ukrainian woman in a grey sports top; a lean Japanese man in his fifties, hand wraps loose, feeds and resets beside them. Feet planted, they drive alternating knees into pads and body, tight and repeated, never leaving their metre of concrete. One continuous shot, camera tracking sideways at a steady walking pace, all three fully framed. Epic, burnished, cinematic.

Inside a hurricane-shuttered cathedral nave, harsh floodlights rake in from one side, throwing column shadows far across worn stone flagstones; stacked chairs line the aisle and scaffolding wraps a restoration bay near the transept. The air is utterly still. Two adults occupy the open floor: a compact Puerto Rican woman in her thirties, hair tied back, navy rash guard and knee pads, and a tall grey-bearded Black man in a faded olive shirt. Both begin fully in frame, feet on stone, and remain framed while sparring with padded practice sticks: quick angled strikes, ducks, shoulder rolls, footwork carrying them only a couple of metres. One continuous shot with a slow dolly-in toward them. Raw handheld texture, gritty documentary flatness.

Floodlights on iron posts wash the sandstone forecourt of a twin-belltowered coral-stone cathedral, a dry fountain ringed with sandbags, a shuttered flower kiosk at the edge. Nothing stirs but four adults alone in the night. A rangy Colombian man in a white kit, a muscular Ghanaian woman in red, a stocky white man in his forties wearing black, and a tall Indian woman in blue all stand fully in frame at the start, boots on the stone. They stay framed while driving a ball hard between them, running the full width of the square, sprinting onto crosses and smashing full volleys that crack against the fountain wall. One continuous shot from a static tripod at eye level. Moody neo-noir shadows.

A frozen lake surface stretches out below a row of neon-lit warehouses, their pink and green signage smeared across snow-dusted ice; steam drifts from shoreline vents and pools in low clouds over the pressure cracks. A single adult skates here, no one else: a broad-chested Egyptian man in his forties, close-cropped beard, black thermal top, orange gloves, blades scoring long white arcs. At first he is fully in frame, feet on the ice, then he pushes into long backward crossovers, snaps forward-to-backward pivot transitions, and carves toward the lens until he ends partly out of frame, shoulders cropped. One continuous shot, a slow dolly-out revealing more of the surroundings. Gritty documentary, cold neon grain.

A wave-polished limestone shelf at the edge of a hazy Miami shoreline, ankle-deep pools trapped in hollows, a corroded iron ring, spray hanging in the wind. Two adults face off in the shallow water. A broad Puerto Rican woman in her forties, wet hair slicked back, black swim shorts and grey tee, scoops a sheet of water with the flat of her foot and hurls it; a lanky Norwegian man in his twenties, freckled, blue shorts, answers by dropping a hip and slamming both cupped hands into the pool. Rain streaks past, puddles bursting. Both start fully in frame on the rock; she charges the lens and ends cropped at the shoulders. One continuous shot craning from high above down to eye level.

Golden hour lacquers a beachfront promenade paved in black-and-white mosaic waves, leaning palms throwing long stripes across it while fireworks burst silently far out over the bay. Four adults own the empty walkway: a broad Tongan man in a sleeveless grey top, a wiry Iranian woman with a long braid, a sandy-haired man in his fifties wearing navy, and a tall Ethiopian woman in white shorts. All four stand fully in frame, feet on the tile, before breaking into a running line, flipping a rugby ball backward hand to hand, covering thirty metres of promenade; the lead runner drifts toward the lens and finishes half out of frame. One continuous shot, a slow pan from left to right. Moody neo-noir amber.

Thick fog swallows a rooftop helipad above downtown, leaving only the painted concrete circle, a folded windsock and two antenna masts fading into white; the air hangs perfectly still, no wind, no sound. Two adults share the pad and nobody else appears. A slim Chinese-American man in his twenties wears a white tee and silver track pants; beside him a muscular Black woman in her thirties wears a cobalt bodysuit, hair pinned tight. Rooted inside the circle, footprints barely a metre wide, they snap robotic chest and shoulder hits, freeze, then pass a liquid arm wave back and forth, dime-stopping on each beat. One continuous shot with a slow pan from left to right. Crisp, bright, energetic sports-ad polish.

A shuttered car plant outside Miami, warm tungsten work lamps hanging over a glossy epoxy floor, an idle overhead conveyor and skeletal body jigs receding into darkness. Four adults march it with snare drums strapped to their hips: a tall Colombian woman with a shaved head, a heavyset Irish-American man in a black tee, a slim Ethiopian-American woman in maroon, a grey-bearded Portuguese man in denim. They roll a thundering cadence down a long lane, snap a sharp about-face in unison, cross the floor the other way, and break into rim-shot accents. Big fans stir loose paper and dust around their boots. All four begin fully framed with boots on the epoxy and never leave the shot. One continuous shot, slowly orbiting them.

Bright, even light floods a glass-canopied transit plaza laid in grey porcelain tile, ticket gates along one wall, hanging planters dead still in the windless air, a mezzanine balcony ringing the space overhead. Four adults stand fully framed on the tile: a broad Dominican man in a mustard tee, a tall Swedish woman with cropped blonde hair, a stocky Black man in his fifties, and a compact Thai woman in a purple track top. Each holds their own square metre, loading and uncorking hard baseball swings at a rubber tee, ball after ball cracking away, then resetting on the same spot. Travellers watch from the mezzanine above, never on the tile. One continuous shot craning down from high above to eye level. Gritty documentary realism.

A bruised storm sky hangs low over the weather deck of a container ship riding calm water, lashed boxes stacked two high, a rust-streaked crane arm folded aft, painted steel deck plating clear and flat underfoot. The air is dead still. Six adults work the deck alone, all fully framed: a huge Serbian man in a grey singlet, a broad Jamaican woman in black, a bearded Turkish man in blue, a tall Maori woman in maroon, a silver-haired white man in olive, a stocky Korean woman in red. Each holds a spot barely a metre wide, coiling low, gliding back, and punching a shot put out over the rail. One continuous shot craning down from high above to eye level. Epic cinematic weight.

Warm tungsten work lamps light a small octagon cage inside a converted warehouse gym, chain-link fencing throwing diamond shadows over a scuffed vinyl-covered mat while torn paper scraps tumble down through the beams from an overhead vent. Three adults train inside, nobody else in the building: a heavily built Samoan woman in a black crop top, a lean white man in his forties with taped ribs, and a tall Sudanese man in yellow shorts. Each stays on one spot, feet planted, hoisting a heavy medicine ball overhead and smashing it into the mat, catching the bounce, immediately loading again, breath fogging under the lamps. One continuous shot from a static tripod at eye level, all three fully framed. Gritty documentary grain.

Warm tungsten lamps and a drifting haze fill an old indoor rink, moving spotlights sliding across white ice striped with faded painted lines, boards scuffed, glass fogged. Two adults skate the surface: a tall Argentinian man in a soft grey jersey, dark curls loose, and a strong-shouldered Black woman in her thirties wearing a cream turtleneck, hair braided back. Both start fully in frame with blades on the ice and remain framed throughout, gripping wrists and whipping each other around in crack-the-whip pulls, one anchoring while the other slingshots wide, carving from one end of the rink to the other. Spectators fill the seats beyond the boards. One continuous shot with a slow dolly-in. Dreamy, glowing, music-video softness.

Snow falls thickly on a university library plaza laid in herringbone brick, drifting past bike racks and a bronze abstract sculpture while fog banks roll through the colonnade and blur the tall reading-room windows. Two adults hold the plaza alone: a broad-shouldered Nigerian man in his thirties, black hoodie sleeves shoved up, and a wiry Italian woman with a dark ponytail in a rust-coloured windbreaker. Both start fully in frame, boots on brick, and stay framed as they fire rubber dodgeballs at each other from a few metres apart, twisting away, ducking low, diving flat onto the snow-dusted brick and scrambling upright. One continuous shot, camera tracking sideways at a steady walking pace. Vast, epic, silver-toned grandeur.

Bright overhead panels flood a roller skating rink's glossy maple floor while broken neon wall stripes flicker and a searchlight sweeps across the dead disco ball above. Five adults stand on the wood, alone in the building: a towering Black man in a grey vest, a compact Filipino man in blue, a strong Slavic woman with a blonde bob, a lean Moroccan woman in olive, and a barrel-chested white man in his fifties. Each anchors a spot under a metre wide, hammering thick battle ropes into alternating waves, then slamming both ends down hard so the coils crack against the maple. One continuous shot, a slow orbit around them, all five fully framed, feet planted throughout. Epic, weighty, cinematic contrast.

Shafts of daylight fall through high clerestory windows onto the non-slip ceramic tile of an indoor pool deck, lane ropes coiled at the wall, big wall fans stirring loose paper and dust through the beams. Four adults claim the dry tile, no one else present: a tall Spanish-descended woman in a black skirt, a slim Black man in a white shirt and high-waisted trousers, a broad Mexican man in charcoal, and a silver-haired white woman in deep red. Each holds a single square metre, hammering flamenco zapateado bursts, heel drills and sharp toe accents, with braceo arms curling overhead, chins high. One continuous shot with a slow pan from left to right, all four fully framed. Moody neo-noir chiaroscuro.

Snow sweeps across the striped tarmac of a coastal race circuit's pit lane, piling on empty pit-box thresholds and a row of stacked tyres, while surf crashes loudly beyond the far barrier. A single adult runs the lane: a powerfully built Mexican woman in her thirties, hair in a tight bun, wearing a sleeveless white top and blue leggings, breath steaming. She starts fully in frame, shoes flat on the tarmac, then shoves a steel barrel into a rolling sprint, chasing it hard down eighty metres of pit lane, cutting around a cone and driving it back. Spectators cheer from the grandstand behind the wall. One continuous shot, handheld camera slowly circling at chest height, keeping her fully framed. Bright, punchy sports-ad energy.

Harsh floodlights blast in from one side of a film sound stage, splashing a matte black floor with hard white edges while flickering neon strips and a sweeping searchlight rig cross the cyclorama; coiled cable and sandbags ring the mark. Four adults occupy it, nobody else: a lively Cuban woman in a hot-pink crop top, a lanky Vietnamese man in mint shorts, a stocky Black man with a fade in yellow, and a freckled woman in her forties wearing turquoise. In two facing pairs they stay rooted on their marks, ripping fast jab-cross-hook combinations into focus mitts, mitts popping loud, shoulders rolling, feet barely shifting. One continuous shot, a slow orbit around them, all fully framed. Playful, upbeat, saturated commercial gloss.

Bright, even ceiling light fills a courthouse great hall floored in checkerboard marble, brass rails and towering panelled doors at the far end, while a flickering neon repair lamp and a sweeping searchlight from outside skate colour across the stone. Two adults have the hall to themselves: a beaming Puerto Rican man in his twenties, mustard tee and white sneakers, and a tall Kenyan woman in a violet tracksuit, hair cropped short. Both begin fully in frame, feet on the marble, and stay framed as they drop prone, sit cross-legged, or topple sideways, then explode upright on a clap and burst three metres before resetting, laughing. One continuous shot with a slow dolly-in toward them. Playful, bright, upbeat commercial polish.

Pearl light seeps over a gravel outwash flat beside a drainage canal at sunrise; a concrete culvert mouth gapes, leaning marker posts trail off toward mangroves, and the mist sits motionless with not a breath of wind. Three adults own the calm: a cheerful Indian man in his thirties in a lime tee, a sturdy woman with a copper braid in navy, a lanky Black man in orange shorts. They begin fully in frame, shoes grinding fine grey gravel, and never leave the wide shot. Rubber balls fly hard between them across three or four metres — a shoulder-first dive, a spin, a scoop off the stones, and a delighted counter-throw from one knee. One continuous shot, a slow orbit around them, bright and buoyant.

Light rain slicks the smooth cast concrete flat bottom of a coastal skatepark, the bowl walls behind layered with old paint, a bent flood lamp reflecting in the standing water. The air is still, drizzle falling straight down. Two adults work the flat: a squat Guatemalan man in his forties, soaked grey tank top, and a tall Black woman with a shaved head in a black long-sleeve. Both begin fully in frame, feet on wet concrete, and stay framed while heaving a heavy sandbag chest-to-chest between them, hurling it a couple of metres, absorbing the catch, immediately launching it back. Onlookers watch from behind the perimeter fence above. One continuous shot from a static tripod at eye level. Gritty documentary texture.

Low practice lights leave deep shadows over a small boxing ring in an old gym, steam drifting from a wall vent and curling through the ropes, the canvas mat pale and scuffed beneath. Three adults are inside the ropes: a lean Colombian man with taped hands, a broad Black woman in a red crop top and headgear, and a grey-haired white coach in a faded blue shirt directing them. All three start fully in frame, feet on canvas, and stay framed as the two spar, sharp jabs answered by slips, rolls under hooks, quick pivots that carry them only a couple of metres before they reset. Spectators lean on the ring apron rail below. One continuous shot, a slow dolly-in. Moody neo-noir shadow.

Rows of looms fill a converted textile mill in Miami, cotton lint hanging in the air, a hard floodlight raking in from one side so the wooden plank floor glows in stripes. Two adults use the long aisle. A rangy Nigerian-American woman in a cropped grey jersey and a stocky Chilean-American man in white gloves start fully in frame, cleats on the boards. She fires off the line, plants hard, runs a deep post, and hauls in a ball over her inside shoulder; he mirrors her with a sharp comeback route and a low scoop. Paper scraps tumble in the light. On her last route she runs almost into the lens, ending cropped at the waist. One continuous shot, panning slowly left to right.

Golden hour filters through a dense bamboo grove, striping a clearing of packed earth and dry leaves; stacked cut canes lean against a trunk and, oddly, a broken neon sign and a distant searchlight from a roadside festival flicker colour across the stalks. One adult trains alone: a compact Brazilian woman in her twenties, gloves taped, black keeper jersey and grass-stained shorts. She begins fully in frame, boots on the earth, then flings herself sideways into low diving saves, palms scooping the ball from the leaves, popping instantly back to her feet, working a few metres of the clearing; on the last save she lunges toward the lens and ends cropped at the knees. One continuous shot, slow pan left to right. Dreamy, warm.

Harsh floodlights blaze in from one sideline of an indoor basketball court, glaring off polished maple and leaving the retracted bleachers in blackness while steam drifts lazily from a floor vent near the baseline. Four adults own the hardwood, nobody else: a springy Puerto Rican woman in a neon-green top, a tall Ghanaian man in white shorts, a stocky Korean-American man in navy, and a lean woman in her forties with a grey-streaked ponytail in orange. All four stay fully in frame, sneakers squeaking on the wood, snapping a flying disc between them and launching into full layout dives across a few metres of court, skidding on their hips before bouncing up. One continuous shot, a slow orbit around them. Bright, punchy sports-ad energy.

Misty sunrise softens a broad civic plaza of polished granite pavers, a dry stepped fountain basin at one end and steam curling up from grates near the flagpoles. A single adult crosses it: a tall Nigerian-American man in his thirties, close-shaved head, a plain white singlet and blue shorts, spikes clicking on stone. He starts fully in frame, feet on the granite, then builds a long approach across twenty-five metres of plaza, hips turning into crossover steps, blocking hard on the left leg and firing a javelin low over the basin, following through into a stumble-step recovery, still fully framed. Onlookers watch from a raised terrace behind the balustrade. One continuous shot, camera tracking sideways at a steady walking pace. Bright, crisp, sports-ad clarity.

Stage lights rigged along the gantries of a decommissioned steel mill throw magenta and cyan across a vast rolling floor of dull steel plate, cold rollers and coiled strip stacked in the shadows; the air hangs perfectly still. One adult occupies the floor: a lean Cape Verdean woman in her twenties, hair braided into a crown, wearing a charcoal crop top and teal shorts. She begins fully in frame, spikes flat on the plate, then leans forty-five degrees into a long resistance band anchored behind her, hammering short driving strides that haul her fifteen metres down the floor before she resets and repeats, never leaving the frame. One continuous shot, a slow orbit around her. Dreamy, saturated, music-video atmosphere, nobody else present.

Coloured stage lights installed for an unopened show wash a long gallery hall in violet and amber, blank white walls and a single empty plinth flanking pale oak plank flooring; nothing moves in the still air. Two adults face each other on the boards: a broad Lebanese man in his forties, hand wraps and a grey vest, and a tall Black woman with locs pinned up, wearing a rust-coloured sports top and holding focus mitts. Both stay fully in frame, feet rooted within a metre, as she calls angles and he rips jab-cross-hook-uppercut sequences into the pads, leather cracking, sweat catching the coloured light. One continuous shot, camera tracking sideways at a steady walking pace. Epic, burnished, cinematic gravity.

A bruised storm sky presses over a stadium concourse plaza of stamped concrete, its shuttered ticket gates and bare banner masts standing dead still in the heavy pre-rain calm. Five adults line up alone out there: a rangy Jamaican man in a white singlet, a powerful Polish woman in navy, a compact Filipino man in red, a tall Somali woman in yellow, and a silver-bearded white man in grey.
