They launch into grand allegro down the diagonal — grand jeté, chassé, another soaring split leap, a tour jeté landing deep — travelling forty meters past the shopfronts. Passersby line the street behind metal barriers, never on the run. One continuous shot, camera craning down from high above to eye level. Handheld grain, honest and unglamorous.

Blue hour settles over a packed-dirt farmyard outside Paris, a stone byre and a rusted plough at the edges, dry leaves and husks swirling low across the ground, one bulb burning over the barn door. Five adults are fully in frame, feet in the dirt: a broad Japanese man in a black keikogi, a tall Senegalese woman in indigo, a grey-haired French farmer type in a hakama, a compact Argentinian man, a lean Dutch woman with a plait. With wooden practice shinai they drill strikes — lunging step, sharp overhead cut with a shout, retreat, a wrist cut, then a fast advancing sequence a few meters forward and back. Nobody else appears. One continuous shot, handheld camera circling slowly at chest height. Raw, plain, unstyled.

Dawn mist hangs over the red rubber tartan of an athletics oval near Paris, dew beading on the inside rail, stacked hurdles and a portable volleyball net set up on the back straight. Three adults stand fully in frame, shoes on the track: a towering Serbian woman in a white jersey, a muscular Haitian man in yellow, a lean Japanese woman with taped fingers. They run spike approaches — three-step gather, arms swinging back, a hard vertical jump and a full arm swing cracking the ball over the net — landing, jogging two meters back, and going again, alternating hitters. The air is still. A handful of joggers watch from the outer fence, off the surface. One continuous shot, slow dolly-in. Bright and vivid.

Inside a frozen storage hall on the Paris ring, pallet racks vanish into blue haze, frost furs the door seals, and someone has rigged pink and green stage lamps that stain the misted air. Three adults work a lane of frosted concrete, all fully in frame, shoes gripping the rime. A springy Malaysian woman in a yellow crop hoodie skips forward and snaps a flying front kick between two hand paddles; a tall Sudanese man in white holds them and resets a step back; a stocky Croatian woman in purple follows with a spinning back kick, cracking the pad. They cover barely three metres. One continuous shot, the camera dollying slowly in toward them.

Golden hour turns a powdery white gypsum flat outside Paris to warm cream, low dunes ridged by wind, an abandoned wooden fence line half-buried in the distance. One man stands fully in frame, cleats sunk in the sand: late thirties, Puerto Rican, thick through the shoulders, a faded grey jersey, dark trousers, cap pulled low. He sets, lifts the front knee high, coils, and drives through into a hard throw, the ball flying far down the flat; then he walks off ten paces, sets again, and hurls further, working steadily across the open ground. Snowflakes drift improbably through the low sunbeams. Nobody else is out here. One continuous shot, handheld camera circling slowly at chest height. Grainy, honest, unpolished.

Bright even ceiling lights fill a municipal badminton hall in Paris: green vinyl mat, white court lines, a sagging net, steam drifting from ventilation grilles. A worn truck tire lies flat near the service line. Two adults work it, both fully in frame at the start, shoes on the mat: a broad Ukrainian man in his fifties with a shaved head and faded blue tee, and a compact Filipina woman with taped wrists and a buzzed undercut. They trade sledgehammer blows in metronomic rhythm, hauling the head past the ear, driving it into rubber that bucks and thuds, neither leaving their patch. Spectators fill the raised gallery behind a railing, off the court. One continuous shot, static tripod at eye level, documentary-plain.

Blue hour on the crest road of a dam in the hills east of Paris, white lane lines running to a gatehouse, fog banks pouring over the spillway lip and swallowing the valley. Five adults in dark hakama hold the concrete, all fully in frame, bare feet down. A tall Senegalese woman drives a stamping overhead strike at her partner's raised bamboo shinai, a grey-bearded Japanese man; two paces on, a stocky Mexican woman and a lanky Czech man trade wrist-then-head combinations, shinai cracking. A fifth, a broad Iranian woman, calls the rhythm and lunges in turn. Nobody travels more than three metres. One continuous shot, dollying slowly toward them.

Snow falls thick on a canal quay in northeast Paris, barge cleats iced over, a bar's broken neon stuttering red across the water while a searchlight swings from a distant crane. One dancer holds the grey cobble setts, fully in frame: a stocky Turkish-German man in his thirties, shaved head, black puffer, taped grey trainers. He shuffles an Indian-step toprock, drops a hand to the wet stone, spins a three-step, then whips a low leg sweep around himself. Spectators cluster behind the railing on the bank above. He rises, prowls two metres toward the lens and his torso crops out of frame. One continuous shot tracking sideways at a walking pace.

A decommissioned subway platform under Paris runs long and empty, tiled concrete underfoot, a bricked-up arch, blank advert frames, and big industrial fans stirring loose paper and dust down the length of it under bright even ceiling lights. Five adults begin fully in frame, feet on the tiles: a wiry Moroccan man in red shorts, a powerful Black woman in a grey crop top, a lean Swedish man in white, a compact Vietnamese woman in orange, a bald older man in blue. They kick into handstands and race the platform on their hands, hopping, wobbling, correcting, covering twenty-five meters. One continuous shot, camera orbiting slowly; late on, the leader hand-walks toward the camera and ends cropped at the frame edge. Vast and heroic.

Low golden light rakes along a barricaded Kreuzberg side street, its crosswalk stripes freshly painted across warm asphalt between shuttered shopfronts and a leaning traffic mast. Six adults in white fencing jackets and mesh masks begin planted on the tarmac, all fully in frame: a tall Black man with a shaved head, a stocky pale-skinned woman in silver-grey trousers, a lean Korean woman, a broad Turkish man, a wiry blond man, a copper-haired woman in her forties. In one continuous shot they split into three pairs, sport foils flashing as they advance, lunge deep and snap back with parry-ripostes, travelling many metres down the empty street. The camera orbits slowly around them; nobody else appears anywhere.

Inside a faded Berlin ballroom with cracked parquet, tarnished gilt mirrors and a stucco ceiling flaking above, magenta and cyan stage lamps wash the room while two industrial fans in the wings hurl loose paper and dust across the floor in long streaks. One adult woman, athletic and freckled with red hair knotted up, wears a teal jersey and stands fully in frame, both feet on the wood, legs already inside a burlap sack. In one continuous shot she explodes into hopping bounds the length of the hall, crashes into a tumbling roll, scrambles upright and hops on toward a chalk finish line. The camera dollies in slowly. She stays wholly visible; the ballroom is otherwise empty.

Blue hour settles over the dark basalt setts of a Berlin station forecourt, where tram rails curve past a spindly clock pylon and three shuttered kiosks. Fine grit skims low across the stones in thin ribbons. Three adults hold one spot: a broad-shouldered Punjabi man in an orange kurta, a silver-haired white woman in a black tracksuit, a young mixed-race man in a yellow vest. All three start fully in frame, feet firm on the stone. One continuous shot follows their pounding bhangra: high hops with arms punched overhead, dropping into squat kicks, shoulders bouncing, spinning wrists — the footprint never wider than a metre. The camera dollies slowly out, revealing the deserted square around them.

Mist lies knee-deep over a cropped dry grassland on a former Brandenburg training range; a ruined concrete watchtower leans on the horizon, and far behind it the raised autobahn drags long red and white light trails across the pale sunrise. Two adults face off, both fully in frame with boots pressed into the flattened grass: a heavyset Samoan man in a navy singlet and a tall Ethiopian woman with braided hair in maroon shorts. In one continuous shot they collar-tie, snap down, shoot a double-leg, drive three metres through the wet stalks, sprawl, scramble to a reversal and reset, breath steaming. The camera dollies slowly inward. No one else stands anywhere on the plain.

Mist burns off a festival ground east of Berlin at sunrise: a black scaffold main stage, cable ramps taped down, banners hanging limp in windless air. Four adults spread along the aluminium deck, all fully in frame, boots on the metal. A heavy-set Ghanaian woman in a wet grey vest hauls a brimming pail from a tub, sprints six paces, and swings it to a rangy Estonian man in denim; he pivots and slings it on to a short Peruvian woman in orange, who pounds down the deck to a tattooed Australian man tipping pail after pail into a steel drum. Water sheets across the metal. Onlookers crowd the pit below. One continuous tracking shot moving sideways at a walking pace.

Grey sunrise fog clings to a gravel service road threading a Brandenburg refinery: a flare stack breathing pale flame, pipe racks dripping condensate, a torn banner and loose plastic sheeting snapping violently on the chain-link in hard wind. Three adults stand fully in frame on the crunching stone — a weathered white man in oil-stained coveralls, a muscular Turkish woman in a red windbreaker, a young Filipino man in a hooded sweatshirt. In one continuous shot they grip hands and run a crack-the-whip chain, wheeling faster until the anchor plants and the tail runner is slung wide across the road, boots skidding gravel. He is flung toward the lens and ends partly out of frame. The camera dollies slowly back. No one else is present.

Raked fine sand fills a small beach volleyball court on a Spree sandbank, net posts strung with a sagging net, a willow screen behind, mist sitting flat and motionless over the water. Three adults begin fully in frame, barefoot in the sand: a stocky Japanese man in a white gi jacket, a tall Somali woman in a black rash top, a ginger-bearded man in grey shorts. One continuous shot captures their grappling round — collar grips, an inside trip, a hip throw dumping a body into a spray of sand, then a scramble that rolls them two metres sideways. Afterwards one lunges toward the lens and finishes partly out of frame. The camera tracks sideways at a steady walking pace; nobody else is around.

Hazy afternoon wind drags dust across a riverside beach bar where trucked-in white coral sand covers the bank; a rusted barge sits moored, deck chairs are stacked, and a row of grates behind the sand exhales drifting steam that curls low. Five adults crouch shoulder to shoulder, all fully in frame with hands and feet in the sand: a shaved-headed Ghanaian man, a tanned white woman with a blonde plait, a slim Indian man in green, a broad Polish woman in navy, a grey-templed man in a black tee. In one continuous shot they explode into a bear-crawl race, scrambling flat-backed twenty metres along the strand. The camera orbits slowly. The beach holds no one else.

Blue hour at a metals recycler in Berlin's south, where colour-sorted bales of copper and crushed aluminium form low walls, a weighbridge booth glows with a single blue lamp, and an elevated motorway carries streaking headlight trails behind the fence. One athlete owns the oil-stained concrete: a tall Somali-German woman in her twenties, cornrows tied back, teal singlet, black tights, spiked shoes. Fully in frame, she settles at a scratched start line and drives out over a row of five hurdles set down the yard lane, three strides between each, lead leg snapping flat, trail knee whipping through. She covers the whole run. One continuous shot, panning slowly from left to right.

A deconsecrated brick cathedral nave, columns half wrapped in scaffolding and a dry font pushed aside, has been rigged with cheap colour cans; haze machine fog rolls between the piers while spotlights sweep hard green and red across worn stone flagstones. Three adults stand fully in frame, chalked hands, feet on the stone: a sinewy Moroccan man in black shorts, a broad Dutch woman with cropped platinum hair, a compact Chinese man in a grey tank. In one continuous shot they run chained tumbling the length of the nave — cartwheel into cartwheel, round-off, stepped hurdle, another round-off — covering fifteen metres of flagstone. A handheld camera circles them slowly at chest height. Nobody else occupies the church.

Floodlights on temporary masts blast a sandstone cathedral forecourt, throwing a long shadow past a dry fountain basin and a scaffolded spire; steam curls up from grates at the square's edge and drifts through the beams like slow silk. One adult woman — tall, Afro-German, close-cropped hair, in a plum jacket with white piping — stands fully in frame, boots on the pale paving, snare drum strapped at her hip. In one continuous shot she marches out across the stone, sticks rolling into buzzed rudiments, throwing crisp pivot turns every eight steps and carving a wide dreamlike path over thirty metres. The camera orbits slowly around her. The square holds no other soul.

A bruised storm sky presses down on a frozen Berlin lake, snow-dusted ice stretching to a fringe of dead reeds and a jetty stranded above the freeze. The air is utterly still, the light silver and heavy before rain. One adult man skates alone — slender, Latin American, dark curls, in a wine-red long-sleeve and black trousers — starting fully in frame with both blades on the ice. In one continuous shot he swings into back crossovers within a few metres, springs a single axel, lands cleanly on a curving edge, then chains a toe-loop and a dreamy trailing spiral, snow crystals spraying. The camera orbits slowly around him. Nothing else moves out on the lake.

Night floodlights on a lake shore south of Berlin throw hard white across a wave-worn rock shelf, ankle-deep water skinning its surface, a rusted diving ladder and a black reed line at the edge. Three adults stand out there, all fully in frame, feet in the shallows: a lean Ethiopian man in a soaked white shirt, a broad Finnish woman with cropped blonde hair, a compact Filipina woman in black. They stomp great sheets of water at one another, scooping with flat hands, dodging and slipping across two metres of stone. The lake beyond lies dead calm. One of them charges the lens and crops at the waist. One continuous shot craning down from high above to eye level.

Light rain lacquers a black-and-white mosaic promenade beside a lake lido, wave-patterned tiles mirroring shuttered ice kiosks and a row of dripping palms in concrete planters. Five adults stand fully in frame, shoes planted on the wet mosaic: a heavily built Croatian man in a soaked grey tee, a lean Japanese woman in blue, a bald Caribbean man, a tall auburn-haired woman, a bearded man in his fifties. In one continuous shot they run fireman's-carry relays, hoisting a partner across the shoulders and sprinting twenty metres through spray, setting them down, swapping and going again. Onlookers watch only from the raised terrace behind the railing, never on the promenade. The camera dollies slowly in.

Harsh midday sun bleaches a helipad on a Berlin office roof, its painted concrete circle chalky white, an antenna mast humming at the parapet and dead planters lining the edge; dry leaves skitter and swirl low across the deck. One adult woman — powerfully built, Korean, hair in a tight bun, wearing a lime crop top and black tights — lies prone at the circle's rim, fully in frame, hands and toes on the concrete. In one continuous shot she snaps up into a five-metre sprint, drops flat, fires again from a seated start, then from a falling stumble, closing on the lens until her legs leave the frame. The camera tracks sideways at a walking pace. The roof is otherwise empty.

An idle car plant assembly floor stretches under an overhead body conveyor, epoxy-coated concrete gleaming green-grey between folded robot arms and yellow safety cages. Floodlights blaze in from one side while flickering neon strips and a sweeping searchlight rake the aisle with punchy colour. Two adults start fully in frame, trainers squeaking on the coating: a broad-chested Mexican man in a white tank top, a tall Nigerian-German woman in a citrus-yellow tee. In one continuous shot they shoulder a heavy timber beam and jog it thirty metres down the aisle, matching stride, then hit a synchronized count and drop it with a boom before hammering out a fist bump. The camera orbits them slowly. The hall holds nobody else.

Under a vast glass canopy, a transit plaza of grey porcelain tile glows in flat even light; ticket columns stand in a row, escalators climb to a mezzanine, and confetti scraps from some earlier event still tumble and lift in the draught. One adult man — compact, Turkish-German, buzzed hair, in a slate compression shirt and orange shorts — begins fully in frame, both feet on the tile. In one continuous shot he loads deep and fires a standing broad jump, sticks the landing, immediately rebounds into two more bounding jumps, arms slashing, covering only a few metres before resetting. Commuters watch from behind the mezzanine railing above, never on the plaza floor. The camera pans slowly left to right.

Hazy afternoon wind pushes a brown dust across the painted steel deck of a rusting feeder ship, its hatch covers streaked with salt, a lashing bridge throwing lattice shadows, the bleached sky empty overhead. Two adults begin fully in frame, boots wide on the plating: a squat Chilean man in a faded orange boiler suit, a strong-shouldered white woman with a grey braid in a canvas jacket. One continuous shot follows them heaving a mooring timber onto their shoulders and jogging it the full length of the deck, adjusting grip, hips rolling, then counting down and dropping it together with a ringing clang. The camera dollies steadily out to reveal the ship's beam. No one else is aboard.

A cramped basement octagon, chain-link stretched between padded posts, sits under a ceiling grid of cheap colour cans that soak the vinyl mat in deep violet and cold cyan; the air is dead still, dust hanging. Three adults hold a single patch of mat, all fully in frame with bare feet down: a scarred Ukrainian man in black shorts, a broad Cuban woman in a purple rash guard, a lean Bangladeshi man in grey. One continuous shot follows their tight drill — collar tie, snapdown, a hip throw planting one body, an instant scramble to back control, then a reset — bodies rotating within a metre, shadows sliding over the mat. A handheld camera circles slowly at chest height. Nobody else is in the room.

An empty Berlin ice arena under flat white lights, dasher boards scuffed with old paint, a zamboni door ajar, torn paper scraps from an earlier event still tumbling down through the cold air. Four adults hold four spots of white ice, all fully in frame, blades down. A slim Korean woman in black winds into a camel, free leg locked high, then folds into a sit spin; opposite her a tall Nigerian man in charcoal pulls a fast upright spin, arms drawing in. A grey-haired Swedish woman arches into a layback, and a stocky Chilean man wraps a scratch spin, each turning on one spot. One continuous shot, craning down from high above to eye level.

An overcast afternoon on a herringbone brick plaza outside a concrete university library, a dry fountain basin, chained bicycles, glass doors reflecting flat grey sky. Five adults have strung a rope between two lamp posts, all fully in frame, shoes on the brick. A tall Kenyan woman sets high; a broad Turkish man in yellow takes three quick steps, loads both arms, and hammers the ball down. Across the rope a lean Canadian woman in white and a stocky Italian man in blue leap into a double block, palms pressed over the line, while a silver-haired Indian woman digs the rebound. They range only a few metres. One continuous shot, static tripod at eye level.

A shuttered roller rink in Berlin, its maple floor glossed to honey under a few dim practice lamps, disco ball hanging dead, painted arrows curving off into shadow. Three adults work a taped grid on the boards, all fully in frame, feet down. A wiry Colombian man in grey shorts runs an in-out shuffle, toes tapping each box, knees high; a tall Ghanaian woman in a black bodysuit follows with lateral two-in, two-out hops; a stocky Belarusian woman in red drives a hopscotch pattern, arms pumping. The air is still. The man then strides at the camera until his chest fills and crops the frame. One continuous shot orbiting slowly around them.

Warm tungsten work lamps on stands light a small municipal pool hall, their glow bouncing off non-slip ceramic tile and lane water that lies perfectly flat and unmoving; a rolled lane rope and a stack of kickboards sit against the wall. One adult woman — athletic, Afro-Brazilian, hair in twists, in a bright coral top and black shorts — stands fully in frame, bare feet on the tile deck. In one continuous shot she sets, whips a 540 kick with a snapping foot high above her head, lands running, then launches a butterfly twist and touches down clean, shifting only a few metres along the deck. The camera dollies slowly out. She is the only person there.

Harsh midday sun burns down on the striped tarmac of a Brandenburg circuit pit lane while a sudden shower needles across it, rain streaks flashing silver and puddles bursting under foot. Open garage bays yawn behind, fuel rigs and tyre stacks inside. Two adults stand fully in frame, boots on the wet stripes: a broad Armenian man in black holding focus mitts, and a tall Danish woman with a bleached crop, gloved, in charcoal. One continuous shot follows their combinations — jab, cross, hook, slip, rolling counter — pivoting across two or three metres of streaming tarmac, water bursting off the mitts. Spectators watch only from the grandstand beyond the pit wall. The camera tracks sideways at a walking pace.

A cavernous Berlin sound stage: matte black floor, a half-struck plywood set at the back, sandbags and a stack of empty apple boxes, daylight falling in hard shafts from high clerestory windows. Two adults own one square of that black, both fully in frame, feet down. A springy Vietnamese-German woman in an orange crop top loads low, whips a butterfly kick flat and horizontal, lands clean, then rips a spinning hook kick through the air. Facing her, a lean Brazilian man in white swings up a twisting kick, corking off one foot and sticking the landing on the same spot. Paper scraps tumble through the beams. One continuous shot craning down from high above to eye level.

A disused courthouse great hall keeps its checkerboard marble and brass balustrades, but gelled par lamps on tripods now flood the space with hot pink and electric blue, and confetti scraps drift down through the beams from the coffered ceiling. One adult man stands fully in frame, barefoot on the polished squares: mid-thirties, Punjabi, densely muscled, in a white singlet and red shorts. In one continuous shot he snaps his arms down, swings up and throws a standing back tuck, sticking the landing on the same tile, then immediately loads and throws two more, chest high, chalk puffing, hair flying. His footprint never shifts. The camera holds locked on a tripod at eye level. The hall is completely empty of anyone else.

Neon signage on an old gasworks throws red and green across a wide grey gravel flat at night, a lone floodmast humming while fine dust streams low over the stones. Five adults are spread across it, all fully in frame with boots on the gravel: a rangy Senegalese man in a green shirt, a stocky Bosnian woman in black, a bald Portuguese man, a young woman with braids in orange, a greying man in a hoodie. One continuous shot, shot rough and observational, follows a running dribble game — step-overs, drag-backs, sharp cuts — carrying the ball forty metres across the flat, gravel spraying. A handheld camera circles slowly at chest height. Nobody else is out there.

Flat grey light over a Berlin skatepark bowl, its concrete flat bottom scarred with wax marks, a graffitied quarterpipe and a bent handrail at the rim. Six adults gather on the smooth cast concrete, all fully in frame, feet planted. Three bases — a broad Tongan man, a tall Somali woman, a heavyset Polish man — lace hands into a cradle while a grey-haired Argentine woman braces as backspot. A small Thai woman steps in, dips, and is punched skyward, arms locked, toes pointed, before dropping back into their arms; a sixth, a compact Egyptian man, spots from a step away. They stay on one square metre. One continuous handheld shot circling slowly at chest height.

Warm tungsten work lamps hang over a basement gym's boxing ring, the canvas mat scuffed grey, ropes sagging, taped heavy bags motionless in the still air beyond. Three adults stand fully in frame, bare feet on the canvas: a squat Georgian man with cauliflower ears in blue shorts, a tall Jamaican woman in a black rash top, a wiry Czech man in a faded singlet. Filmed plainly and roughly in one continuous shot, they run a throw drill — grip fight, hip throw, the thrown partner slapping out, an instant scramble across two metres of canvas, then a reset and a swap of roles. Sweat drips, breathing is loud. The camera dollies slowly out through the ropes. The gym holds nobody else.

An abandoned weaving hall runs long and low, rusted looms lined up under a sawtooth roof, its wooden plank floor grey with lint; gelled lamp bars wash amber and deep blue down the central aisle, and the air is perfectly still. Five adults begin fully in frame, spikes on the boards: a tall Kenyan man in yellow, a muscular German woman with a blonde crop, a lean Malaysian man, a Black woman in scarlet, a greying man in white. In one continuous shot they run a relay the length of the hall, sprinting flat out and slapping the baton into outstretched hands at full speed, three exchanges blurring past the looms. The camera dollies steadily out. The mill holds no one else.

A bamboo stand behind a Berlin garden centre, green canes clacking overhead, a coiled hose and stacked clay pots at the edge; storm cloud presses low while a club's neon stutters through the stems and a searchlight rakes past. Five adults stand on the packed earth and dry leaves, all fully in frame, feet down, before two pairs drop into position. A wiry Indonesian man walks on his palms while a tall Danish woman lifts his ankles, racing a grinning Nigerian woman held by a stocky Portuguese man. A bald Chilean man whoops and waves them on. They cover three metres, swap roles, and charge back. One continuous shot dollying slowly out.

Sunlight falls in solid shafts from the high windows of an old school gymnasium, crossing haze that a fog machine has laid over the polished maple court while two spotlights swing lazily through the drift. Folded bleachers line one wall. A single adult woman stands fully in frame, shoes squeaking on the boards: mid-forties, Filipina, compactly muscled, in a lavender crop top and grey shorts, hair braided tight. In one continuous shot she loads and drives onto a plyo box, lands soft, steps down, and repeats — six explosive box jumps, arms whipping, dust glittering in the beams — never leaving her single square of floor. The camera dollies slowly out through the haze. She is entirely alone in the gym.

Fine rain glazes a granite civic plaza where polished pavers hold a low sheen of the ministry colonnade and a dark, drained fountain; grit skates low across the stone in the wind. Everything reads cold and noirish. Five adults stand fully in frame, spikes down on the wet granite: a tall Sudanese man in black, a lean Slovak woman in silver, a heavyset Italian man, a woman with a shaved head in dark green, a greying man in navy. In one continuous shot they attack a row of hurdles strung across the plaza, snapping lead legs over five barriers, spray flying, and running sixty metres past the fountain. The camera dollies slowly toward them. The square holds no other person.

A disused rolling mill in Berlin's north: a long steel plate floor between idle roller tables, overhead cranes parked, someone's magenta and blue concert lamps left burning in the girders. Three adults line up abreast, all fully in frame, boots on the plate. A powerful Fijian-German woman in a black jersey carries the ball, sprints, and flips a flat pass left to a lanky Irish man in white; he draws and shifts it on to a stocky Colombian man in red, who cuts back inside and returns it. They run the full length of the hall in one line. The last carrier bursts at the lens, cropping past the frame. One continuous shot panning slowly from left to right.

A white gallery hall lies under bright, even ceiling light: pale oak planks, tall unframed canvases in muted colour, two empty plinths and a bench pushed to the wall. Nothing in the room stirs. Four adults are fully in frame, trainers on the oak: a sharply built Kenyan-German man in orange, a blonde Finnish woman in white, a broad Peruvian man in blue, a woman with a black bob in yellow. One continuous shot follows their punchy jump chain — deep load, standing broad jump, immediate rebound, two bounding strides, stick — travelling only a few metres between plinths, arms slashing, shoes thudding the boards. The camera dollies smoothly toward them. The gallery contains no one but the four.

Twilight has gone blue over a stadium concourse plaza of stamped concrete, a ramp helix curling up behind it, ticket booths shuttered, floodlight pylons dead against the deepening sky. The air hangs still. Four adults stand fully in frame, boots on the concrete: a stocky Fijian man in a mud-flecked jersey, a tall Latvian woman with a plait, a shaven-headed Black man in grey, a bearded man in a torn training top. Filmed plain and unglamorous in one continuous shot, they sprint abreast across the plaza, spinning rugby laterals down the line, one dropping back to recover a bobbled pass before they surge on forty metres toward the ramp. The camera dollies slowly inward. The concourse is completely deserted.

A black storm sky presses over a suburban club's red clay court, crushed brick swept into soft lines, a sagging net and a heavy roller parked by the ivy-covered fence. The air is heavy and still, colours popping under the bruised light. One adult man stands fully in frame, sneakers printing the clay: early thirties, Afro-Caribbean, wiry, in a mustard tracksuit and a backwards cap. In one continuous shot he bounces into cheerful toprock, kicks and crosses, then drops his hands into the clay for a six-step, legs sweeping a tight circle, red dust puffing, before popping back up grinning — all on one spot. Club members watch from the small stand behind the fence. The camera dollies slowly in.

Golden light slants under a passing shower onto a striped grass tennis lawn, warm rain streaking through the beams, puddles splashing at the baseline, a wooden umpire chair and clipped hedges framing the court. Six adults stand fully in frame, shoes on the wet turf: two turners — a bald Ghanaian man and a laughing red-haired woman — plus a slim Korean woman, a stocky Greek man, a tall woman with locs, and a bearded man in a bucket hat. In one continuous shot two ropes whip into double dutch and the jumpers cycle in, bouncing knees high, spinning, swapping mid-rhythm, all inside one small patch of grass. Friends cheer from the benches behind the fence. The camera dollies slowly out.

Six adults work a bucket line on the broad concrete slabs of a Spree-side esplanade — mooring bollards, a barge café alongside, a rust-red bridge crossing upstream under flat grey light. Every one stands whole in frame, shoes on the concrete. The pail comes up from a water tank in the hands of a grinning Ivorian woman in yellow, then goes hand over hand: a bearded Greek man, a tall Icelandic woman, a compact Vietnamese man, a broad Mexican woman, water slopping across the slabs. A lanky Kenyan man takes the last leg, sprinting thirty paces to dump it into a paddling tub before racing back. Onlookers cheer down from the bridge. One continuous shot, static tripod at eye level.

Hard wind rips across a corporate campus lawn, snapping banner flags on their poles and rippling a loose tarp by the hedged path while a glass office block reflects the flat overcast sky. Four adults square off on the mown grass, all fully in frame, boots planted: a heavyset Ukrainian man in a grey vest, a compact Ethiopian woman in black, a tall Norwegian man with taped hands, a broad Colombian woman in maroon. Shot rough and observational in one continuous take, the two pairs spar with gloves and headgear — jabs, slips, ducking under hooks, rolling shoulders, circling a couple of metres of turf. Staff watch from the terrace behind the low railing. A handheld camera circles slowly at chest height.

Inside a narrow glass-backed squash court in a Vancouver athletic club, floodlights rake the pale hardwood from one side, throwing two long shadows across the service lines. Two adults train: a tall Black woman in her thirties with cornrows and a teal crop top, and a stocky Filipino man in his forties in faded red shorts. They start fully in frame, bare feet planted, then lock a plum grip and drive alternating knees into each other's guarded ribs, pivoting a couple of metres along the tin. Big floor fans stir loose scorecards and dust into slow glitter. Spectators watch from the raised gallery behind the glass. One continuous shot, a slow dolly-in toward the people, dreamy and soft-edged.

Five adults train alone on a wide flat of short golden grass north of Vancouver, snow falling thick and windless past a leaning cedar fencepost and a coil of rusted wire. A broad Samoan man in orange, a lean white woman with a blonde braid, a wiry Korean man in grey, a tall Somali woman in purple and a freckled redhead in white all begin fully in frame, boots pressed into the crisp grass. They take three-step volleyball approaches, arms swinging back and up, hammering imaginary sets down over a taped-rope net and landing in soft crouches within a few metres. Bright, punchy, clean colour. One continuous shot with a slow dolly-out revealing more of the snowy plain.

Where two farm roads meet on packed gravel outside Vancouver, a tilted signpost and a row of half-buried mailboxes frame the view. Heavy snow pours down, and far beyond the treeline fireworks bloom and fade in silent gold. Three adults stand fully in view, boots crunching grit: a heavyset Punjabi man in a canvas coat, a silver-haired white woman in a red parka, and a young Métis man in a black hoodie. Each drives a wide shovel into the drifted gravel and hurls arcing sprays of snow sideways, racing, stamping, reloading, never straying beyond a few paces. Epic, cold and enormous. One continuous shot, a slow orbit around them.

Polished concrete runs matte grey down an emptied Vancouver distribution aisle, bare blue racking towering on both sides, a goal mouth chalked between two pallet jacks. Harsh floodlights blast in from one flank, cutting the far end into black. One adult stands fully in frame from the first second, feet set on the concrete: a lean Vietnamese-Canadian man in his late twenties, shaved head, black keeper jersey and padded green gloves. He shuffles, then throws himself low left, smothers, springs up, dives high right and rolls back to his line, working a few metres of floor. Industrial fans push loose packing slips and dust through the light beams. One continuous shot, the camera craning down from high above to eye level, noir and severe.

A rehearsal studio above a Vancouver dance school: mirrors covered with brown paper, a barre along one wall, a work floodlight throwing everything hard from the left, paper scraps from a party still spiralling down through the beam. Three adults claim one bright patch of black marley, all fully in frame, feet down. A cheerful Métis woman in a pink sweatshirt rips a chain of flap-heels, then springs into a maxi-ford leap and lands ticking. A tall Iranian man in yellow balances up onto his toe tips and riffs there; a round-cheeked Chinese woman in blue answers with a rattling paddle. Nobody moves off their square. One continuous handheld shot circling slowly at chest height.

Bare damp concrete stretches the length of a disused civil-defence bunker under Vancouver, fat pipe runs overhead, an old blast door cracked open at the far end. Magenta and cyan stage lights wash the walls; the air is perfectly still. From the first second one adult is fully in frame, sneakers squeaking on the wet floor: a muscular Cree woman in her thirties, high ponytail, lime tank top and grey joggers. Grinning, she crouches behind a steel barrel, shoves off and sprints it clean across the hall, hands slapping the ribs to keep it spinning, then whips it around a traffic cone and drives it back. The playful, brightly lit run plays out in one continuous shot, the camera dollying slowly toward her.

A cramped club dojo on a Vancouver side street, green tatami wall to wall, a frayed rope banner and a stack of crash pads in the corner under flat even ceiling lights. Three adults in worn white jackets stand on the mats, all fully in frame, feet down. Two — a stocky Cree man and a tall Vietnamese woman — grab an ankle behind them, fold their arms, and hop in, ramming shoulder to shoulder until one staggers off balance. The third, a wiry Portuguese woman, hops in to take the loser's place. They stay within two mats. One duellist hops right up to the lens and crops out of frame. One continuous shot panning slowly from left to right.

An arena with the ice stripped out for summer: painted concrete slab where the rink was, faded blue lines still ghosting through, boards pulled aside, one bank of work floodlights blazing from a single side. Four adults occupy the lit slab, all fully in frame, shoes down. A stocky Haitian man crouches, hands on knees; a lean Korean woman plants both palms on his back and vaults clean over, landing to crouch herself. A tall Ukrainian man and a broad Ojibwe woman leap the growing line in turn, the chain rolling a few metres across the concrete. A handful of watchers sit up in the seating bowl. One continuous shot, static tripod at eye level.

Numbered bays are striped in white across the asphalt of a cavernous Vancouver bus depot parking hall, charging posts standing in rows, one bus door left open at the back. Neon tubes flicker pink and green while searchlight beams sweep the columns. One adult occupies the frame from the first second, feet flat on the asphalt: a long-limbed Ethiopian-Canadian man in his late twenties, close-cropped hair, canary yellow tee and soft grey trousers. Laughing, he launches into grand allegro, chaîné turns into a huge grand jeté, then another, covering the diagonal in long airborne bounds. One continuous shot, a slow dolly-out revealing the whole hall; on his final leap he charges toward the lens and ends partly out of frame.

Mist glows over a deserted waterfront parking lot in Vancouver at sunrise, faded asphalt cracked into a jigsaw, a snapped light pole leaning over the bumper blocks, grey surf breaking against the seawall behind. Four adults begin fully in frame with shoes on the asphalt: a thickset Māori-descended man in a mud-streaked jersey, a tall Ukrainian woman with a blonde bun, a bald Black man in navy, and a short Mexican woman in yellow. One continuous shot, raw and grainy, follows them as they break into a spread line and sprint the length of the lot, flicking a rugby ball backward hand to hand, calling and accelerating, while the camera pans slowly from left to right. The lot holds nobody else.

Portable floodlights on a grey ash flat below a Vancouver-Island volcano throw three long shadows; fog banks roll in low and swallow the pumice ridges behind. Three adults stand in the fine ash, all fully in frame, boots sunk slightly. A broad Haida woman in a soaked black hoodie hinges low, grips the tyre lip, drives with her legs and slams it over; ash puffs up. A bearded Norwegian man takes the next flip; then both grab a bigger truck tyre and heave it end over end together while a lean Pakistani woman resets and steadies it. They work a four-metre lane. One continuous shot panning slowly from left to right.

Blue hour settles over a natural-grass stadium pitch in Vancouver, the mow stripes running dark and light toward empty benches and a bank of unlit towers, headlights streaking in long ribbons along the elevated road beyond the stands. One adult holds the centre of frame throughout, cleats pressed into the turf: a powerfully built Japanese-Canadian woman in her early thirties, taped fingers, black compression top and white shorts. She drops flat to the grass, snaps her feet in, explodes upward with both arms punching the sky, lands and repeats, never leaving her single patch of turf. Scattered spectators watch from the lower seating tier behind the barrier. One continuous shot, a slow orbit around her, vast and cinematic.

Loaded barbells and coiled ropes line a Vancouver crossfit box, black rubber tiles running wall to wall; neon strips and colored stage lights throw red and blue through air that never stirs. Four adults stand fully in frame with shoes on the rubber: a heavily tattooed white woman with a shaved side cut, a stocky Ghanaian man in a green vest, a slim Vietnamese woman in black, and a bearded Portuguese man in grey. Three sink into low crouches while the fourth leapfrogs the whole line, palms slapping shoulders, then drops in as the next launches, the chain rolling a few metres across the tiles. The camera tracks sideways at a steady walking pace through one continuous shot. Nobody else trains here.

A drained dry dock in a Vancouver shipyard: wet concrete scored with drainage channels, rows of timber keel blocks, sheer steel walls climbing into thick drifting fog while paper scraps tumble through the damp air. Five adults begin fully in frame, trainers splashing on the slab: a tall Sudanese woman in orange, a compact Japanese man in blue, a broad Croatian man in white, a freckled Irish woman in green, and a lithe Brazilian man in yellow. Hurling wooden hoops ahead of them, they chase, snap the rings back with a wrist flick and dive headlong through as they roll, covering the whole dock floor in bright bursts. The camera orbits slowly around the group in one continuous shot. Not another soul is down here.

Golden hour turns a broad stretch of packed damp sand near Vancouver into hammered bronze, a grey driftwood pile at one edge, three bleached marker flags standing upright, the inlet glassy and motionless behind. Three adults lie face down in the first second, toes and palms flat on the sand, all fully in frame: a muscular Fijian man in navy briefs, a lean Danish woman with a wet blonde plait, and a wiry Filipino man in red. On a whistle they scramble up and sprint the long stretch to the flags, arms driving, then launch into full-length dives, hands stretched, sand exploding around them. Grand, warm, cinematic. One continuous shot, a slow dolly-in toward them.

Harsh midday sun bleaches a Fraser Valley vineyard, the tractor row a strip of compacted soil between wire trellises heavy with leaf, weathered end posts leaning at both ends, the air completely still. Two adults stand fully in frame, feet planted on the dirt: a sinewy Korean-Canadian woman in her twenties in a lilac leotard, and a broad-shouldered Black man in white shorts, bare-chested. They hurdle forward into round-offs, snap through back handsprings and finish with tight back tucks, dust puffing, working down the row and covering its length. Soft haze blooms, dreamy and sun-drunk. One continuous shot, a slow pan from left to right; on the last pass she tumbles toward the lens and ends partly out of frame.

Snow falls hard into a sunken plaza in Vancouver's bank district, black granite paving swept nearly clear, steam curling from grates beside a dry fountain basin, mirrored towers rising into white sky. One adult is fully in frame from the first second, spikes set on the granite: a tall Jamaican-Canadian woman in her late twenties, braids tied back, purple singlet and black tights over a thermal. She drives out low, attacks a row of four closely spaced hurdles, covering only a few metres, snapping her lead leg down, trail knee whipping through, and pulls up past the last one. Office workers watch from the railed terrace above. One continuous shot from a static tripod at eye level, grainy and unstaged.

An unfinished rail tunnel under Vancouver: raw grey shotcrete underfoot, ribbed steel arches vanishing into blackness, cable spools and a dead survey tripod parked against the wall. A few low practice lamps carve pools of light and leave deep shadow, and nothing else stirs. Two adults are fully in frame throughout, boots planted on the shotcrete: a thickset Portuguese man in his forties with grey stubble and a sweat-soaked navy shirt, and a strong Anishinaabe woman with a long braid in a black tank top. Each hauls a heavy medicine ball overhead and drives it down at their feet, catching the bounce and slamming again, never shifting off their spot. Unpolished, sweaty, real. One continuous shot, a slow pan from left to right.

Shafts of hard daylight fall through high grimy windows into a shipyard fabrication shed on Vancouver's north shore, landing on a floor of rust-stained steel plate, a silent gantry crane parked overhead and a half-cut hull section chocked in the corner. The air is dead calm. Two adults stand fully in frame, shoes squeaking on the plate: a broad Māori-descended woman in a bright orange singlet and a lanky Polish man in a blue tee with taped knees. They whip rubber dodgeballs at each other, twist away, shuffle sideways and throw themselves into rolling dives, springing straight back up within a few metres. Vivid, crisp, athletic energy. One continuous shot, a slow orbit around them.

A fencing salle in an old Vancouver drill hall, three metallic strips laid over red rubber, foils racked on the wall, someone's leftover magenta and green stage lamps painting the ceiling trusses. Three adults hold one strip, all fully in frame, feet down. A silver-haired Japanese-Canadian man in black rattles brush-slap pickups, chin low. Beside him a tall Nigerian woman in a plum jumpsuit springs a buffalo hop and lands ticking; a compact Bolivian woman in grey machine-guns toe-tip clicks. None of them leaves a square metre of metal. Spectators watch from bleachers along the far wall. One continuous shot, the camera tracking sideways at a steady walking pace.

Inside a timber barn on Vancouver's delta farmland, wide plank boards worn silver, tungsten work lamps clipped to the posts throwing amber cones, hay dust hanging motionless in the beams. Three adults face the lens on the planks, all fully in frame, bare feet down. A heavyset Samoan man in a black singlet drops chest-to-board, snaps his knees back under him, and explodes into a tuck jump, knees to chest. A lean Egyptian woman in grey and a grizzled Irish man in olive match him rep for rep, hands slapping the wood, boards booming. Nobody shifts a step. One continuous shot, the camera dollying slowly out to reveal the barn.

Warm tungsten work lamps hang from a cable strung the length of an abandoned brick factory hall near the Vancouver rail yards, lighting a floor of broken brick tile, three cold kiln mouths and a rusted rail trolley pushed aside. The air is still, motes hanging gold. Three adults start fully in frame, shoes on the brick: a tall Somali woman with a shaved head in a red jersey, a bearded white man in mustard, and a compact Chilean man in white. They spread into a line and run the whole hall, spinning laterals backward hand to hand, calling and shifting angles, crossing from one end of the frame to the other. Soft, glowing, unhurried. One continuous shot, a slow pan from left to right.

An old circular threshing floor of worn flagstone sits on a rise above Vancouver farmland, ringed by a low stone rim, a leaning stone roller parked at its edge, the hazy afternoon dusty and bright. Four adults stay fully in frame on the flagstones: a wiry Trinidadian man in a lemon tee turning one end, a tall Dutch woman with a blonde crop turning the other, and in the middle a compact Korean woman in orange and a stocky Egyptian man in blue. Two ropes slap the stone in fast alternation while the pair inside skip, criss-cross their ankles and pump their knees high, never leaving the same metre of floor. Crisp, joyful, punchy. One continuous shot from a static tripod at eye level.

Golden hour lights a flat mesa top of hardpan and sparse silver scrub, a stacked stone cairn at the rim and the valley falling away in warm haze behind. Nothing moves but the athletes. Three adults are fully in frame, boots on the hardpan: a huge Tongan man in a bright teal singlet, a broad-shouldered Ukrainian woman with a red headband, and a stocky Mexican man in orange shorts. Each tucks a steel shot under the jaw inside a chalked ring, sinks into a low glide across the ring, whips the hips open and punches the throw skyward with a grin, then resets on the spot. Sunny, playful, high-spirited. One continuous shot, a slow dolly-out revealing more of the plateau.

Concrete pavers cover a rooftop terrace above a Vancouver warehouse block, chest-high planters of grass along one edge, an aluminium vent housing behind, the skyline flattened by dusty haze, the air itself dead still. Five adults start fully in frame, shoes on the pavers: a tall Nigerian woman in white, a stocky Serbian man in blue, a slim Vietnamese-Canadian man in grey, a red-haired woman in green, and a broad Samoan man in black. They rotate through spike approaches at a rope net, three quick steps, arms swinging back and slashing over, landing hard within a few metres. Rough, natural, documentary. One continuous shot, a slow orbit around them; at the end one hitter strides at the lens and ends partly out of frame.

Tight-packed dark pebbles armour a wide desert flat in the dry interior beyond Vancouver, a single dead juniper twisting up at one side, blue ridges stacked in the far distance under golden hour light. The air is glassy and still. Four adults begin fully in frame, shoes crunching stone: a lean Kenyan-Canadian man in pale blue, a curvy Italian woman with dark curls in cream, a bald Korean man in rust, and a freckled woman with silver hair in olive. They break into a tag game, cutting hard, faking, sprinting far across the flat and lunging with outstretched fingertips, laughter thin in the open air. Hazy, golden, hypnotic. One continuous shot with a handheld camera slowly circling at chest height.

Cracked pale clay tiles the floor of a dry lakebed under a dust-hazed afternoon sky, a leaning survey stake with a faded ribbon and old tire ruts curving off toward nothing. Four adults hold the middle of the frame, fully visible, shoes on the clay: a long-limbed Ethiopian woman in charcoal and a bearded Russian man in black work the rope ends, whipping them into a blur; between them a compact Filipina woman in slate and a broad Jamaican man in deep grey trade the beat, hopping heel to heel, snapping tuck jumps, feet flicking out and back, both pinned to one small patch of hardpan. Desaturated, hard-shadowed, tense. One continuous shot, the camera tracking sideways at a steady walking pace.

A closed highway overpass outside Vancouver holds nothing but lane-marked asphalt, cracked white dashes, concrete barriers pushed end to end and construction cranes standing gold in the low sun. The air is completely still. One adult stands fully in frame, boots planted on the asphalt: a huge Icelandic-Canadian man in his thirties, red beard, chalked hands, a sweat-dark grey singlet and a wide leather belt. He squats over a steel keg, rips it up between his knees and slings it backward over his shoulder, watching it clang down behind him, then resets on the same square of road and does it again. Rough grain, honest sweat, no polish. One continuous shot with a handheld camera slowly circling at chest height.

Tar-and-gravel roof membrane crunches underfoot on an industrial loft rooftop in Vancouver, a low brick parapet, a boxy elevator housing and a snarl of conduit behind, the skyline dimmed by dusty afternoon wind while headlight trails streak along the viaduct below. Four adults stay fully in frame, shoes on the gravel: a stocky Iraqi man in a black tee, a tall Ojibwe woman with a long braid in maroon, a wiry Scottish man with a shaved head in grey, and a heavyset Chinese woman in navy. Each drives up onto a wooden plyo crate, snaps the hips through, steps down and rebounds, all four rooted to their own spot. Grainy, unstaged, sunburnt. One continuous shot, a slow orbit around them.

Blue hour washes an abandoned drive-in theatre lot outside Vancouver, rows of rusted speaker posts standing in cracked asphalt and gravel, the blank white screen looming pale at one end. The evening is windless. Six adults stand fully in frame, shoes gritting on the asphalt: a broad Puerto Rican man in red gloves, a lean Vietnamese woman in blue, a bald Nigerian man in white, a freckled Irish woman in black, a stocky Greek man in green, and a tall Norwegian woman in yellow. In three pairs they spar light, slipping punches, rolling under hooks, firing quick counters and pivoting a couple of metres between the posts. Bold, clean, energetic. One continuous shot, a slow dolly-in toward the fighters.

Painted steel plate decks a waterfront festival pier in Vancouver, bolt heads raised in rows, faded bunting sagging between two light posts, moored barges dulled by dusty afternoon wind. Four adults stand fully in frame the whole time, boots on the plate: a massive Fijian man in a black singlet, a heavyset Ukrainian woman with taped forearms, a bearded Métis man in a grey tee, and a broad Ghanaian woman in navy. In turn each wraps a concrete atlas stone, laps it onto a thigh, drives up and rolls it onto a timber platform, then lowers it back down and resets on the spot, chalk clouding. Unvarnished, hard-edged, tired-eyed. One continuous shot, a slow dolly-out revealing more of the pier.

Fine rain glazes a red-earth walkway between clipped tea rows on a Vancouver Island hillside estate, a bamboo drying rack and a rusted pruning cart at the row's end, mist smoothing the ridge behind. Two adults face each other on the trodden earth, both fully in frame, bare feet planted. A broad Japanese-Canadian woman in a faded blue jacket grips sleeve and lapel, pivots her hips under her partner, and loads a lean Ethiopian man across her back before setting him down; three entries in, she completes the throw and he slaps out, rises, and offers the grip again. They never leave their spot. One continuous handheld shot circling slowly at chest height.

An emptied hotel lobby in downtown Vancouver has been cleared out: polished cream marble underfoot, a long brass reception desk, a chandelier still wrapped in dust cloth. Floodlights blaze in from one side of the room and the air is perfectly calm. Two adults stay fully in frame throughout, shoes squeaking on the marble: a broad Colombian man in his thirties with taped wrists and red gloves, and a lean Chinese-Canadian woman with a high ponytail in blue gloves and a white tee. They circle a few metres of floor, snapping jabs, slipping straight shots and weaving beneath wide swings, firing bright combinations and resetting. Vivid colour, crisp shadows, high energy. One continuous shot, a slow dolly-out revealing more of the lobby.

Blue hour settles over the floor of a sand and gravel pit outside Vancouver, packed sand ribbed by loader tracks, a dead conveyor angling up a spoil heap, four yellow flags planted in a line at the far end. The air is dead calm. Four adults lie prone in the opening second, hands and toes on the sand, all fully in frame: a tall Kenyan-Canadian woman in pink, a stocky Croatian man in lime, a slim Thai woman in white, and a grinning bald Dutch man in orange. A shout lifts them; they claw upright, devour the long run-in and go in headfirst, fingers raking the flags, grit fanning. Bright and cheerful. One continuous shot, the camera craning down from high above to eye level.

Storm cloud swallows the Fraser Valley horizon over a cut wheat field, round bales dotting the stubble, a leaning power pole and torn paper scraps blowing loose across the rows. Two adults stand at the far end of a mown lane, both fully in frame, boots in the straw. A rangy Sikh-Canadian man in a soaked grey tee runs the lane with a training javelin drawn back, crosses his legs over the last five strides, blocks, and rips it out flat. A powerful Ukrainian woman in maroon retrieves the shaft and runs her own approach back toward the camera, finishing so close her legs pass out of frame. One continuous handheld shot circling slowly at chest height.

Night sits over a dry riverbed sandbar outside Vancouver, pale sand ridged by old current, a bleached driftwood snag lodged at one end and neon signage across the far bank bleeding pink and green into the channel. Flags on a survey line and a loose tarp whip hard in the wind. Three adults stand fully in frame, bare feet dug into the sand: a muscular Korean woman in a blue rash guard, a lean Somali man in black shorts, and a broad Portuguese man in white. Each pivots and rips spinning hook and tornado kicks, heels flinging bright arcs of sand into the neon glow, all three anchored to their own spot. One continuous shot with a handheld camera slowly circling at chest height.

A Vancouver indoor skate park at night: a smooth plywood flat between painted quarterpipes, a scuffed funbox pushed aside, neon and colored stage lights throwing magenta and cyan while steam drifts from a floor vent. One adult is fully in frame from the first second, hands and feet on the plywood: a compact Brazilian-Canadian woman in her mid twenties, dark curls tied up, a lime crop top and black leggings. She whips into a cartwheel, links a second, then snaps a round-off with a hard rebound, chaining the sequence back and forth across a few metres of deck. Onlookers lean over the railed viewing platform above. One continuous shot, a slow orbit around her, bright and punchy.

Sunrise mist softens a working quay on the Burrard inlet, blue gantry cranes stepping away into the haze, mooring lines coiled on bollards, headlight trails streaking along the causeway beyond the fence. Three adults hold a patch of reinforced concrete, all fully in frame, bare feet on the cold slab. A tall Thai-Canadian woman in a green crop top locks a plum grip behind her partner's neck, breaks his posture, and drives alternating knees into his belly pad; a heavyset Māori man absorbs them, then swims an arm inside and turns her two steps sideways. A wiry Chilean man circles, calling corrections. One continuous shot craning down from high above to eye level.

A tree-lined boulevard median walk in Vancouver runs on compacted fine gravel between rows of plane trees, cast-iron benches and a dry drinking fountain, dust skimming low across the path in the hazy afternoon wind. Four adults stay fully in frame, shoes gripping the gravel: a lanky Cambodian man in a white dobok top, a strong Black woman with locs in blue, a red-bearded man in grey, and a small Peruvian woman in yellow. In pairs they hold hand paddles high while their partner runs two steps and snaps a jumping flying kick, cracking the target and landing lightly, then swapping roles. Passersby watch from the sidewalk behind the low railing. One continuous shot from a static tripod at eye level.

Night on a small grass airstrip outside Vancouver: mown turf running flat between reflector cones, a windsock snapping stiff on its pole, loose tarp corners flogging against a hangar whose old neon throws red and blue across the field. One adult stays fully in frame throughout, cleats set in the turf: a broad-shouldered Dominican man in his early thirties, close beard, a bright orange jersey and white pants. He toes an improvised rubber, rocks back, lifts the knee high and unloads a hard throw into a padded net a few metres away, follows through hard and struts back to reset, grinning. Snappy, colourful, upbeat. One continuous shot, the camera tracking sideways at a steady walking pace.

Two adults face each other across the faded lane arrows of a disused Highland toll plaza: three shuttered booths, a bent barrier arm, heather-covered slopes beyond. A tall Black woman in her thirties with cropped hair and a plum tracksuit, and a stocky white man in his forties, ginger beard, mustard shirt. Both stand fully in frame, feet planted on the painted concrete, then trade a pepper drill — forearm bump, overhead set, controlled spike — shuffling only a couple of metres. Bruised storm clouds hang low, and stray snowflakes drift through slanted light. One continuous shot, the camera orbiting slowly around them, dreamy and weightless.

On the raw poured concrete slab of an unfinished tower deck above a Highland glen, five adults stand shoulder to shoulder, feet flat on the wet surface: a broad Nigerian man with a shaved head in an orange vest, a slim Korean woman with a black braid, a freckled red-haired Scotsman in grey, a silver-bearded Greek man, and a tall Brazilian woman in cobalt. One continuous shot; the camera cranes down from high above to eye level. Their footprints stay inside a metre as they hammer shuffle-ball-changes into pullbacks, then flam-and-wing beats, heels ringing on concrete. Light rain lacquers the slab; brown leaves swirl low. Storm-grey grandeur, all five fully framed from the first beat.

Wind scours a stone amphitheater cut into a Highland hillside — cracked seat tiers, a rusted lighting mast, torn banner fabric whipping from its poles. One adult holds the flat concrete stage alone: a lean Filipino man in his late twenties, taped shins, orange jersey, hair blown flat. He begins fully in frame, feet firm, then works a stickhandling slalom through six cones, toe-drags, quick pulls, a heel-clip finish, covering only a few metres before circling back. Dust hazes the low afternoon light. Documentary grain, unpolished and honest, filmed as one continuous shot with the camera craning down from high above to eye level.

On a flat alpine meadow bench high in a Highland pass, a portable neon rig and two battery floodlights bathe the flowering turf in magenta and cyan; puddles between clumps of bog cotton splash with each footfall. Two adults square off: a muscular Māori woman in her thirties, black rash top, and a compact white man near fifty, shaved head, grey singlet. Both start fully in frame, bare feet gripping wet grass, then chain snap-downs into a body-lock trip, a hip throw, and a scrambling reversal, staying within a few metres. Rain streaks the neon. Bright, punchy sports-ad energy, one continuous shot, handheld camera circling slowly at chest height.

Blue-hour light drains from a single-arch packhorse bridge over a black Highland river, its mossy parapets slick, cobbles polished by centuries of cartwheels. One adult stands squarely mid-span, wholly in frame, boots on the rounded stone: a broad-shouldered Somali man in his thirties in a worn navy sweatshirt with the sleeves cut off. He drops into a discus wind-up: two preparatory swings, a coiling heel-to-toe spin across barely a metre, then an explosive release with a shout, resetting to repeat. Snowflakes drift through a lamp's cone of light. Raw documentary texture, cold and unglamorous, captured in one continuous shot as the camera orbits slowly around him.

Inside a converted stone byre turned yoga studio, whitewashed walls swallow the light except for two hard shafts falling through high slit windows onto pale bamboo boards; folded bolsters sit stacked in shadow. The air is perfectly still. Two adults train: a tall Brazilian woman in her late twenties, braided hair, charcoal shorts, locks a plum clinch on a thickset Japanese man in his forties wearing faded red trunks. Both remain fully in frame, bare feet on the boards, alternating knee strikes to a padded belly shield, breaking, resetting, drifting only a metre or two. Neo-noir mood, deep blacks and hard edges, filmed as one continuous shot with a handheld camera circling slowly at chest height.

A village hall wrestling room in the Highlands: red foam mats wall to wall, sagging rafters, a battered rope hoist in the corner. Dim practice lamps carve deep shadows, while a fairground's flickering neon and a sweeping searchlight rake through the rain-blurred casement windows. Four adults work in two pairs — a rangy Ethiopian man in white, a freckled Scottish woman with a red ponytail, a heavyset Turkish man in navy, a compact Vietnamese woman in grey. All start fully in frame, feet on the mat, then launch jumping flying kicks onto held hand paddles, landing, resetting, ranging a few metres. Epic and thunderous, one continuous shot, camera craning from high above down to eye level.

An elevated park walkway built on a disused Highland viaduct: tapered concrete planks, rusted wildflower troughs, cable stays humming. The air is dead still under a bruised sky heavy with unfallen rain. Five adults — a burly Māori man in black, a lean Kenyan woman in yellow, a pale redheaded man in grey, a stocky Mexican woman in maroon, a silver-bearded man in olive — start fully in frame, boots on the planks, then drill penetration steps into double-leg takedowns, driving and resetting over a few metres. Onlookers watch from a railed stairwell platform and the street far below, never on the walkway. Midway one wrestler drives toward the lens and ends partly out of frame. Gritty, one continuous shot, camera orbiting slowly.

Four adults pair off under a tiled pedestrian underpass beneath a Highland trunk road, its walls washed magenta and lime by rigged stage lights, a dead payphone alcove behind them. Two hold belly pads; the others lock plum grips and drive alternating knees, switching to a swim-through arm and a long guard knee, then trading roles on the same tile. Cast: a stocky Māori man in gold shorts, a lean Somali woman in teal, a tanned Italian woman in her forties, a pale ginger man in white. Big fans hurl loose paper and grit past their ankles. One continuous shot, handheld, circling slowly at chest height; all four stay grounded and fully framed.

A vast commercial greenhouse in the Highlands, glass misted, vine rows hanging in green corridors, irrigation pipes ticking. Floodlights blast in from one side of the wide concrete walkway; industrial fans push dust and torn leaf scraps tumbling past ankles. Four adults plant themselves on the concrete, all fully in frame throughout: a huge Samoan man in a blue singlet, a broad-backed Danish woman in black, a bearded Sikh man in yellow, a stout Colombian woman in white. Each in turn wraps a smooth stone sphere, rocks it onto a braced knee, explodes upright and dumps it onto a chest-high timber platform, resetting without moving a foot. High-energy sports-ad polish, one continuous shot, the camera craning down from above to eye level.

The top deck of a Highland ski-centre car park is empty save for wind-bent banners and a lopsided ticket kiosk; hazy afternoon dust drifts across the painted concrete and loose tarpaulin cracks like a whip. Two adults grin at opposite ends: a lanky Jamaican man in his twenties, yellow shorts, and a freckled Irish woman in her thirties, blue windbreaker. Both begin fully in frame, trainers on the paint, then play red-light-green-light — explosive sprint bursts across the deck, comic mid-stride freezes, wobbling arms, another burst that carries them clean across the frame. Playful, sunny, commercial-bright. One continuous shot, the camera craning down from high above to eye level.

Grey overcast light flattens a Highland market town square — rounded cobbles, a weathered mercat cross, shuttered stone arcades, grit blowing low across the stones. Not a soul but two adults: a tall Sudanese woman in her twenties, teal singlet, calves like cable, and a heavyset white man in his forties, greying crew cut, faded green vest. Both stand fully in frame, spikes on cobble, before exploding into a relay exchange — the incoming runner closing hard, the outgoing accelerating on the call, baton slapped into an upturned palm at full stride as they cover the whole square. Epic scale, cool and monumental, staged as one continuous shot with the camera tracking sideways at a steady walking pace.

Inside a Highland distillery's loading dock bay — half-raised roller shutter, stacked oak pallets, a strip of hard floodlight raking one wall of the sealed concrete floor. Everything is motionless but the dancers. Two adults start fully in frame, feet on the concrete: a radiant Punjabi woman in her thirties in a gold-trimmed kurta, and a lean Afro-Caribbean man in his twenties in a violet shirt. They drive into bhangra: high hops with arms punched overhead, squat kicks, shoulder bounces, spinning a few metres apart. Near the end the man bounds toward the lens and finishes partly out of frame. Dreamy, saturated, music-video soft. One continuous shot, camera tracking sideways at a steady walking pace.

A mown launch meadow in the Highlands holds a slack balloon envelope, a wicker basket on its side, and a row of gas cylinders; fog banks roll through while a bruised pre-rain sky presses down. Two adults work the short grass, both fully in frame from the start: a broad Pacific Islander woman in her forties, orange tee, and a slim Iranian man in his twenties, grey hoodie. They run a two-person bucket brigade — hauling sloshing pails from a trough, swinging them hand to hand, sprinting three steps back, water arcing and slapping the turf. Bright, kinetic, sports-ad clean. One continuous shot with the camera tracking sideways at a steady walking pace.

Hazy afternoon light hangs dust over a chalk-veined plateau of close-cropped turf, a leaning standing stone at its edge and ridgelines fading into ochre distance. The air itself is still. Six adults space themselves across the springy grass, every one fully in frame, boots planted: a rangy Senegalese man in black, a shaven-headed Bulgarian woman in oxblood, a wiry Thai man in slate, a tall Argentine woman in grey, a stocky Scot in charcoal, a silver-haired Italian in dark green. Each juggles a ball in place — laces, thigh, shoulder, header — never straying past a stride. Neo-noir palette, moody and desaturated, captured in one continuous shot with a slow pan from left to right.

Bare grey granite spreads flat above a Highland corrie — a house-sized glacial erratic, wind-scoured runnels, a cairn on the lip. The air is dust-hazed and quiet. Two adults hold the slab, fully in frame with boots on stone: a tall Vietnamese woman in her twenties, white bodysuit with a scarlet sash, and a broad Nigerian man in his thirties, cobalt tunic. They snap into color-guard work — flat spins, drop-spins, an angled toss that turns twice overhead and lands clean in the palm, exchanges made with two quick steps sideways. Bright, crisp, sports-ad energy. All in one continuous shot as the camera dollies slowly out to reveal the plateau and the drop beyond.

A drained coastal field in the Highlands has baked to cracked mud, its low turf dykes crumbling; beyond the dunes, heavy breakers thump and spray. Under soft overcast light six adults spread out on the hard ground, all fully in frame, boots pressed into the fissured mud: a huge Tongan man in a green vest, a broad Estonian woman in grey, a bearded Iraqi man in ochre, a muscular Haitian woman in white, a lean Norwegian man in blue, a stocky Peruvian woman in rust. In sequence each swings a small keg between the knees and hurls it backward over one shoulder, stepping clear. Dreamy and slow-burning. One continuous shot, slow pan left to right.

Inside a timber velodrome in the Highlands, the pine track banks steeply around a flat grey concrete infield chalked with old lane marks; shafts of daylight drop from high roof lanterns through motionless air. Four adults work in two pairs, all fully in frame with feet on the concrete: a lean Cuban man in red, a tall Somali woman in navy, a freckled Scottish man in white, a compact Korean woman in gold. They spar light and fast — flicking jabs, shoulder rolls, ducks beneath wide swings, pivots — drifting only a few metres. Spectators fill the banked seating above the track, none on the infield. Bright, punchy sports-ad clarity, one continuous shot, camera tracking sideways at a steady walking pace.

Mist pools in a Highland marble quarry at sunrise, gold seeping over sawn white benches, a rusting wire-saw rig, and sheer cut walls streaked with slurry. Torn paper scraps from a wind-scattered logbook tumble through the light. Two adults stand fully in frame on the smooth sawn floor: a springy Ethiopian woman in her twenties, coral leggings, and a broad Croatian man in his thirties, grey shorts, taped ankles. They break into a tag chase across the quarry floor — hard cuts, jackknife changes of direction, a lunging tag, an instant reversal of roles — covering the whole width of the frame. Dreamy and luminous. Filmed as one continuous shot, the camera dollying slowly in.

Soft overcast light sits on a brick-paved Highland village square: a granite war memorial, painted shopfronts, chestnut trees shedding leaves that swirl low across the red pavers. One adult occupies the open bricks — a compact Japanese woman in her thirties, black leggings, teal crop jacket, hair tied tight. She begins fully in frame, shoes flat on the brick, then fires a chain of standing broad jumps, arms swinging, landing deep, bounding again across three or four metres before turning back, staying fully framed throughout. Villagers watch from a low wall and the café terrace behind railings, none on the open square. Bright, energetic sports-ad tone, one continuous shot, camera craning down from high above to eye level.

Mist lies waist-deep over a Highland estate cricket ground at sunrise, the pavilion's white boards ghostly, a wind-bent sightscreen at one end. Two adults stand on the rolled clay strip, fully in frame, boots on the packed surface: a strapping Barbadian woman in her thirties, lemon vest, and a wiry Nepali man in his twenties, sky-blue shirt. On a shout they set two wooden barrels rolling and chase them at a sprint, hands slapping the staves, driving them the full length of the strip and across the frame. Spectators watch from the pavilion balcony and behind the boundary rope. Nothing else stirs. Bright sports-ad energy, one continuous shot, camera tracking sideways at walking pace.

A service strip of compacted red dirt runs between tilted panel rows on a Highland solar farm; an inverter hut throws blue and pink neon across the ground while fog banks roll through the array at night. Four adults line up abreast, all fully in frame, boots on the dirt: a barrel-chested Fijian man in maroon, a lean Norwegian woman in white, a tattooed Chilean man in black, a tall Ghanaian woman in emerald. They sprint down the strip firing flat lateral passes back along the line, hands soft, feet churning, covering the full length. Near the end the outside runner angles at the lens and finishes partly out of frame. Bright and kinetic, one continuous shot, camera craning down to eye level.

A working foundry casting hall in the Highlands: packed black sand underfoot, a ladle crane parked overhead, steam creeping from floor vents into low, moody work lights that leave half the hall in shadow. Three adults use the long floor, all fully in frame throughout, boots sunk slightly in the sand: a rangy Ghanaian man in a torn grey tee, a broad Serbian woman in navy, a wiry Mexican man in orange. One throws while the other two run crisp routes — hard stem, out-break, deep post — sprinting thirty feet and hauling in over-the-shoulder catches. Handheld documentary grit, unvarnished. One continuous shot, the camera circling slowly at chest height.

Sunrise mist hangs motionless over a flat expanse of dark basalt pavement in a Highland glen, split into hexagonal columnar cracks, moss-furred boulders at the margins, still water pooled in seams. Four adults spread along the slab, every one fully in frame with bare feet on stone: a springy Vietnamese woman in pink, a lean Nigerian man in white, a freckled Welsh woman in yellow, a compact Turkish man in blue. Each takes a run-up and fires a round-off into a back handspring and a snapped back tuck, travelling several metres across the pavement before the next goes. Playful, sunlit, commercial-bright. One continuous shot, the camera craning from high above down to eye level.

Between two towering stacks in a Highland port container yard, a lane of concrete paver blocks runs long and grey under flat overcast light, steam curling from drain vents along the wall. One adult trains here, nobody else: a powerful Kenyan man in his thirties, shaved head, black compression top, chalk on his palms. He begins upright, fully in frame, feet flat on the pavers, then drops into a fast bear crawl down the lane, hips low, shoulders churning, covering ten metres, resets and repeats harder. On the last effort he crawls straight at the lens and ends partly out of frame. Neo-noir, cold and shadowed. One continuous shot, camera tracking sideways at walking pace.

Blue hour bleeds indigo over a black volcanic sand beach at the head of a Highland sea loch — bleached driftwood spars, a wrecked dinghy rib, water flat as slate with no wind at all. One adult occupies the sand: a lithe Colombian woman in her late twenties, navy leotard, sand crusting her forearms. She stands fully in frame, bare feet sinking slightly, then throws a chain of cartwheels into round-offs, hands slapping the sand, travelling right across the beach in a straight line. On the final pass she rebounds toward the camera and finishes partly out of frame. Gritty documentary texture, grainy and cold. All in one continuous shot, camera tracking sideways at a steady walking pace.

Dust hazes the afternoon over a Highland airstrip apron: a corrugated hangar with its door half-open, a straining windsock, a parked fuel bowser, painted taxi lines running away across the concrete. Torn paper scraps tumble through the air. Five adults, all fully in frame with feet on the paint: a tall Kenyan woman in red, a stocky Greek man in white, a freckled Scottish woman in green, a lean Indonesian man in grey, and a broad Brazilian man in black. Two pairs, ankles bound with cloth straps, stagger-sprint the length of the apron while the fifth runs beside them roaring the count. Epic, sweeping, monumental. One continuous shot, handheld camera circling slowly at chest height.

Blue hour settles over a weathered wooden promenade on a Highland coast — iron lamp standards, a shuttered ice-cream kiosk, the sea beyond flat and windless. Five adults own the decking, all fully in frame, feet on the boards: a tall Māori woman in indigo, a slim Iranian man in cream, a silver-haired Dutch woman in grey, a broad Jamaican man in rust, a compact Filipina in violet.
