Gripping a rope along the strip, they haul each other back and forth a few meters, skidding, dropping to knees, scrambling back up. On the final heave the woman staggers backward into the lens and her shoulders leave frame. One continuous shot, camera tracking sideways. Cold, moody, noir.

An old dairy barn stands cleared to its wide plank wood floor, hay dust settled in the seams, tungsten work lamps clamped to the posts, a cracked door showing blue dusk outside. The air is utterly still. Two adults work the boards, nobody watching, both fully framed with feet down: a stocky Mexican-American man in his thirties in a padded green keeper shirt and shorts, and a tall white woman near forty, hair in a low braid, wearing black training gear. Over a few meters she fires low drives and lofted balls; he throws himself sideways, palms them off the planks, rolls onto his shoulder, springs back to his stance and resets. One continuous shot, the camera orbiting them slowly. Plain, gritty, observational.

Salvaged neon tubes strung along an abandoned brick factory hall flicker pink and green over a broken brick tile floor, roof holes dropping pale shafts, a security beam sweeping through the far arches. One adult trains here alone, fully in frame throughout with shoes on the brick: a powerfully built Black woman in her early thirties, hair in tight cornrows, wearing a lemon-yellow crop top and black tights, chalk on her palms. Hands locked on the uprights of a plate-loaded sled, she drives it in explosive sprints the full length of the hall, bricks grinding under the runners, turns it hard and pushes back, quads burning. One continuous shot, the camera dollying steadily in toward her. Bold, saturated, high-energy commercial polish.

Thick fog swallows the spruce around an old flagstone threshing floor beside an abandoned homestead, a mossed stone rim and a leaning grain cradle just visible, rain streaking down and splashing bright in shallow puddles between the stones. Six adults use the floor, no onlookers, all fully framed with feet on wet stone: a broad Fijian man in orange, a slim Danish woman in white, a bearded Iranian man in blue, a Black woman with silver braids in green, a red-cheeked white man in yellow, a compact Vietnamese woman in red. Half crouch as backs; the others vault them in a rolling leapfrog chain, swapping roles, splashing across a few meters. One continuous shot from a static tripod at eye level. Punchy and bright.

A storm wall stacks black over a flat bluff plateau above the Yukon, hardpan crusted with sparse scrub, thin steam venting from ground fissures near the rim and shearing off in the wind. Four adults hold the plateau, no one else in sight, all fully framed with boots on the hardpan: a heavy-shouldered Alaska Native man in canvas, a tall Black woman in a charcoal turnout coat, a wiry Portuguese man in olive, a blonde white woman in slate. Gripping a rolled fire hose, they sprint it out across thirty meters of hardpan, the flat line snaking behind them, then plant, brace and drop the coupling in unison. One continuous shot, the camera orbiting slowly around them. Bleak, silvered, noirish.

Misty sunrise floods a concrete-paver rooftop terrace above a harbor town, steel planters of dead grasses along the parapet, a radio mast overhead and the skyline dissolving into pale haze; the air is completely calm. Six adults have the roof to themselves, all fully framed, feet on the pavers: a lanky Sudanese man in mint, a curvy white woman in lavender, a broad Japanese man in grey, a freckled Irish woman in blush, a compact Colombian man in cream, a tall Black woman in pale blue. Within a few meters they hurl foam dodgeballs hard, twist away, drop to slide across the pavers, dive, and pop up throwing again. One continuous shot from a static tripod at eye level. Soft, glowing, dreamlike.

Harsh midday sun bleaches a wind-scoured barren near Delta Junction, tight-packed dark pebbles forming an endless desert pavement, a bleached driftwood snag and a hazy mountain range the only landmarks; the air hangs dead calm. Six adults train on the flat, nobody else for miles, all six fully framed with feet down: a rangy Jamaican man in white, a muscular Ukrainian woman in blue, a short Filipino man in orange, a tall Black woman in fuchsia, a lean white man in green, a stocky Peruvian woman in yellow. One after another they sprint in, hit the hop, snap the step and blast the final jump, then jog back. One continuous shot, camera craning from high above down to eye level. Vivid, energetic.

Heavy snowfall settles over a dry lakebed playa of cracked pale clay, fog banks rolling low across the polygons, a half-buried survey stake tilting and a dark ridge appearing and vanishing behind the mist. One adult plays here alone: a curly-haired mixed-race woman in her mid-twenties in a bright coral jacket and white leggings, cheeks pink with cold. Whipping a long turquoise ribbon wand, she carves big spirals and snaking figure-eights overhead, chases the ribbon into skipping leaps, spins twice under it and catches it, drifting only a few meters across the visible clay. One continuous shot, handheld camera circling slowly at chest height. Bright, buoyant, cheerfully absurd.

Soft overcast light flattens a closed highway overpass, jersey barriers pushed across both ends, orange cones scattered on lane-marked asphalt, a spruce valley far below, and shredded paper scraps from a torn sign bag tumbling along the deck in the draft. Three adults use the roadway, no one else: a wiry Ghanaian man in a faded red shirt, a stocky white woman with a buzzcut in grey, a tall Chilean man in a black tracksuit. They spread across the lanes, driving power shots into a barrier, chasing rebounds, jogging fifteen meters to strike full volleys out of the air, boots scuffing paint. One continuous shot, camera craning down from above to eye level. Plain, unpolished.

Misty sunrise turns the air pearl-grey over an industrial loft rooftop in a mill district, a rusted water tank on stilts behind a low brick parapet, gravel crunching across the tar membrane, no wind at all. Four adults work up here, unobserved: a heavyset Black man in a sweat-soaked grey tee, a sinewy Vietnamese woman in navy, a bearded white man in a cut-off hoodie, a broad Mexican-American woman in maroon. Each anchored on one spot, they whip battle ropes into alternating waves, then drop into squats and slam both ends into the gravel, grit jumping with every strike, breath ragged. One continuous shot, the camera craning down from high above to eye level. Unvarnished, documentary-real.

Blue hour settles over an old drive-in theater lot on a bluff above a bay, rusted speaker posts standing in rows on cracked asphalt and gravel, the blank screen pale against the water while surf breaks steadily below. A handful of onlookers sit on a grass berm behind a rope at the lot's edge, off the asphalt entirely. Two adults duel across the lot: a slim Indian woman in white kit and a tall Black man in charcoal, both with sport foils. They advance and retreat down twenty meters of lane, lunging deep, parrying, ripping quick ripostes. One continuous shot, camera craning down from high above to eye level. Cool, gauzy, dreamlike.

Light rain lacquers the painted steel plate deck of a waterfront festival pier, shuttered food stalls edging it with stuttering neon while a searchlight barge sweeps beams across the harbor and the reflections smear underfoot. One adult owns the deck: a compact Filipino man in his late twenties, hair bleached blond, wearing a bright green windbreaker, white tee and black joggers. Locked to a single spot, he drops into windmills, hands slapping the wet plate, swings into airflares, kicks up a short headspin and pops back to a freeze, water spraying off his sleeves. One continuous shot, the camera tracking sideways at a steady walking pace. Loud color, crisp, high-energy.

A bruise-colored storm sky hangs over a terraced herb-tea plantation cut into a coastal hillside, clipped rows dropping away and a wooden drying rack at the walkway's head; the trodden red earth path lies still, not a leaf moving. Four adults work the walkway alone: a barrel-chested Nepali man in a faded blue shirt, a tall Black woman in olive, a sunburned white man in grey, a strong Chinese woman in rust. In two facing pairs a few meters apart they heave weighted grain sacks chest-high across the gap, absorb the catch, pivot and throw back. Finally one steps toward the lens, cropping to the waist. One continuous shot, camera tracking sideways.

One bank of harsh floodlights on a stand rakes the emptied lobby of a mid-century hotel, brass columns throwing hard bars across polished marble, the reception desk stripped bare and big floor fans skidding loose paper and dust past the plinths. Three adults are here and nobody else: a lean Black man in his twenties in a bright orange tank, a compact Turkish woman near thirty in electric blue, a broad white man in his forties in white. Each pinned to one spot, they shadow box — snapping jab-cross combinations, slipping, rolling under, pivoting, digging body hooks — sneakers squeaking on the marble. One continuous shot, the camera dollying out to open up the lobby. Punchy and bright.

Harsh midday sun bakes the packed sand floor of a working gravel pit, terraced walls stepping up on all sides, an idle conveyor throwing one hard shadow, the air perfectly still and glassy with heat. Six adults sprawl across the bowl and nobody else: a tall Black man in white shorts, a muscular Polish woman in yellow, a wiry Indonesian man in red, a broad Nigerian woman in cobalt, a tanned white man in green, a lean Mexican woman in violet. They fling big hoops far out, chase them down the pit, dive through the rolling rings and shoulder-roll up in sand. At the end one charges past the lens, half out of frame. One continuous shot, handheld, circling.

Neon from a roadhouse across the section road bleeds red and blue over a cut wheat stubble field, straw rows crunching underfoot, a leaning irrigation wheel silhouetted, the night air hanging dead still and cold. Two adults train on the stubble, unwatched: a broad-shouldered Korean man in his thirties in a black hoodie with the sleeves shoved up, and a rangy white woman near forty with a blonde crop, in a dark grey tank. Sharing one small footprint, they alternate explosive box jumps onto a battered wooden plyo box — deep swing, snap up, quiet landing, step down — breath pluming through the colored glow. One continuous shot, the camera tracking sideways at walking pace. Saturated, shadowy, noirish.

Portable floodlights on a truck bed blast a dry riverbed sand bar into hard white and long shadow, a bleached log jam piled at one end and old bridge piers beyond, dead leaves skittering low across the pale river sand. Four adults are out on the bar, alone: a heavyset Alaska Native woman in a canvas jacket, a wiry white man with a moustache in flannel, a tall Black man in a grey sweatshirt, a compact Mexican woman in denim. Hands linked, they run the chain into a widening crack-the-whip spin until the tail runner is slung stumbling many meters across the sand. One continuous shot, dollying in. Grainy, unposed, documentary.

Low practice lights leave most of an indoor skate park in deep shadow, plywood quarter pipes rising around a smooth plywood flat, steam curling from a heating vent under the mezzanine where a few onlookers watch from behind the rail, never stepping down. Two adults dance on the flat: a tall Ethiopian woman near thirty in a smoke-grey wrap skirt, and a slender white man in his forties in black trousers and a loose ivory shirt. Rooted on one spot each, they spot and spin — clean double pirouettes, then long strings of fouettés, whipping leg cracking the dim air. One continuous shot, handheld camera circling slowly at chest height. Hazy and hypnotic.

Soft overcast daylight sits over a container port quay, stacked boxes walling one side, gantry legs straddling the reinforced concrete apron, mooring bollards along the edge and grey water beyond, while headlights on the elevated haul road streak past in long trails behind the stacks. One adult uses the apron: a lean Black man in his early thirties, close-cropped hair, wearing a faded maroon long-sleeve and black shorts. He drops flat on the concrete, snaps up on a whistle and sprints four meters, walks back, repeats from seated, then from a forward fall, hands slapping the deck. One continuous shot, static tripod at eye level. Plain, cold, unstyled.

Three adults hold the gravel median of a floodlit causeway at a polar research base, where transplanted wind-stunted pines line both sides and a snow-crusted signpost leans nearby. A tall Kenyan woman with cropped hair in a teal thermal top, a stocky white man with a red beard in orange coveralls, and a slim Korean man in grey fleece all begin fully in frame, boots on the compacted fine gravel. One continuous shot from a static tripod camera at eye level: two drop into wheelbarrow position, palms slapping gravel while the third grips ankles, driving a few meters and swapping roles. Fog banks roll through the floodlight beams. Bundled staff watch from a raised catwalk railing well behind, dreamy and glowing.

Soft overcast daylight flattens a mown turf skiway apron at a polar station, an orange wind sock hanging limp above buried fuel bladders and a red-nosed ski plane parked far off. Five adults stand spaced across the grass, feet planted: a broad Samoan man in yellow shorts, a lean Ethiopian woman in purple, a silver-haired white man in navy, a freckled Irish woman in mint, and a compact Filipino man in orange. The camera cranes down from high above to eye level in one continuous shot as each winds up, coils through a full discus spin on one spot, and releases with a shout, footwork chalking the turf. Nobody else is present. Bright, playful, upbeat.

Fog swallows a disused toll plaza that guards the tractor route into an Antarctic station: four striped booths, a frozen boom gate, faded lane arrows on concrete. Four adults claim one lane apiece and stay fully in frame, feet on the paint. A muscular Brazilian man in a lime windbreaker drops into windmills; a tattooed white woman with a blonde bob spins flares over the lane line; a wiry Nigerian man in a red beanie holds a headspin; a broad Kazakh woman in blue tracks him with freezes. The camera pans slowly left to right in one continuous shot. Air is calm, the fog simply hangs. No spectators anywhere, only bouncing color and grins.

On the raw poured slab of a half-built dormitory tower at a polar research station, rebar bristles at the edge and an idle yellow crane leans against flat overcast sky. Six adults form a loose ring, boots planted on the concrete: a tall Sudanese woman in coral, a barrel-chested Chilean man in white, a ginger-haired Scottish woman in green, a slight Vietnamese man in yellow, a grey-bearded Greek man in blue, a young Māori woman in lilac. In one continuous shot the camera cranes down from high above to eye level as they keep a football alive — instep flicks, thigh bounces, headers snapped across the circle. Still air, nobody else on the deck. Sunny, cheerful energy.

Golden hour rakes across a small concrete amphitheater stage cut into a snowbank behind the mess hall of an Antarctic station; empty stone tiers curve upward and a strung line of pennants sags overhead. Three adults grip one thick rope: a heavyset Tongan woman in a red vest, a lanky Danish man in a yellow sweater, and a compact Peruvian woman in blue. They stay on their spot, boots skidding on flat concrete, heaving and rocking until one loses footing and the trio collapses laughing, then resets. Snowflakes drift through the low light beams. One continuous shot, camera tracking sideways at a steady walking pace. The tiers are entirely empty.

Floodlights on tall poles wash a rectangle of short flowering turf beside a weathered bench outside the greenhouse dome of a polar research base; cables snake toward a humming generator shed. One adult woman — muscular, Mexican, black ponytail, magenta long-sleeve and grey shorts — starts fully in frame, both trainers on the grass beside a taped agility ladder. In one continuous shot a handheld camera circles slowly at chest height as she rips through in-and-out steps, lateral shuffles and icky-shuffle patterns, shifting a couple of meters down the rungs. Near the end she drives forward at the lens and finishes cropped at the waist, still pumping. The night air is dead calm, nobody else around.

A cobbled stone arch bridge spans a frozen meltwater channel between modules of an Antarctic station, iron lamp posts furred with rime and orange marker flags at both ends. Six adults work the roadway end to end: a rangy Jamaican man in grey, a broad Turkish woman in orange, a stubbled Polish man in black, a tall Somali woman in white, a stocky Argentine man in maroon, a wiry Japanese woman in teal. In one continuous shot the camera cranes down from high above to eye level while they sprint slant and post routes across the cobbles, snapping over-the-shoulder catches, cutting hard and jogging back. Golden light cuts through drifting snowflakes. Cold reportage texture; the bridge holds nobody else.

Inside the small bamboo-floored yoga room of an Antarctic station's recreation module, magenta and cyan lamps clipped to the ceiling bathe rolled mats and a frosted porthole window. Two adult women stand fully in frame, bare feet on the pale planks: one tall and Ghanaian in a gold crop top and black leggings, the other soft-built and Norwegian with a platinum braid in a violet unitard. In one continuous shot from a static tripod camera at eye level, each folds a leg up and hops in, shoulders and hips colliding, hopping a meter or two sideways to reclaim balance, laughing as one nearly topples. Big floor fans stir loose paper and dust through the colored haze. Slow, dreamy, saturated.

The wrestling room of a polar station gym: red foam mat wall to wall, taped-over insulation panels, a bank of harsh floodlights blazing from one side so bodies throw long shadows. Four adults pair off within a few meters, socked feet on the mat: a heavyset Iranian man in black, a lean Colombian woman with braids in yellow, a bald white man in a blue rashguard, a stocky Thai woman in grey. In one continuous shot the camera dollies slowly in as padded sticks crack overhead, sidesteps and ducks answer, and both pairs rotate and reset, breathing hard. Outside a porthole, neon flicker and a sweeping searchlight pulse across the frost. No onlookers; raw, grainy documentary texture.

An elevated walkway of tapered concrete planks rides above the pipe runs of an Antarctic station, orange handrails on one side and a lattice of vent stacks breathing steam below. Three adults hold the deck: a broad Inuit man in a rust parka shell, a tall Egyptian woman with a headscarf in olive, a wiry white man with dreadlocks in grey. They link hands and wind up a crack-the-whip chain, pivoting in place before the anchor snaps them around and the tail runner is slung several meters down the planks, catching herself grinning. Hazy afternoon wind carries dust across the light. One continuous shot, slow pan left to right. Off the walkway entirely, crew look on from a service gantry railing further back.

A tiled service tunnel links two modules of a polar research base, snow crusted at the far hatch, colored practice lights someone rigged along the pipework washing the walls violet and green. One adult — a broad-shouldered Norwegian woman in her thirties, freckled, blonde hair taped back, thermal leggings and a cut-off orange base layer — attacks a rubber agility ladder taped to the concrete: in-in-out-out, then a lateral icky shuffle down its length and a hopping return. She starts fully framed, boots planted. Air in the tunnel is dead still. One continuous shot, the camera panning slowly left to right as she drives toward the lens, shoulders finally cropping out of frame.

Warm tungsten work lamps hang over a wide concrete aisle in the glass greenhouse of an Antarctic station; racks of pale lettuce line both sides and condensation beads on frost-edged panes. Four adults stand fully in frame on the walkway, feet planted: a tall Senegalese man in a white dobok, a compact Chinese woman in black, a freckled Australian man in blue, a sturdy Bulgarian woman in red. In one continuous shot the handheld camera circles slowly at chest height while they fire spinning hook kicks and back kicks at hand pads, shifting a couple of meters up and down the aisle. The air is dead still. At the end one drives forward and leaves frame at the shoulders. No spectators, bright and punchy.

Heavy snowfall stacks on the open top deck of a vehicle garage at a polar research base, faded yellow bay lines still visible under the drift and a rime-caked railing ringing the edge. One adult man — long-limbed, Haitian, shaved head, charcoal thermal top and navy joggers — stands fully in frame, cleats on the painted concrete. In one continuous shot the camera orbits slowly around him as he takes a five-step drop-back, resets, and rips a spiral the length of the deck, then jogs down after it and repeats from the far end. Fog banks roll between the parked machines and pour over the railing. Nobody else appears. Low contrast, blue shadow, moody noir stillness.

Between the oldest timber huts of an Antarctic station lies a square of rounded cobblestones, a rusted bell frame at one edge and grates exhaling steam near a stacked woodpile. Under a bruised storm sky moments before rain, three adults crouch fully in frame on the stones: a powerful Nigerian woman in gold, a lanky Czech man in white, a sinewy Bolivian woman in pink. In one continuous shot the camera dollies out to reveal more of the square as they burst into a head-to-head sprint, spikes clattering across the cobbles, and lunge chests-first over a chalk finish line at the far side. Station staff cheer from a hut porch behind a railing. Buoyant and cheeky.

Inside a truck loading dock bay in an Antarctic station warehouse, roller doors sit half open, low practice lamps carve deep shadows across stacked crates, and floor vents leak drifting steam. Six adults hold their own square of sealed concrete, all fully in frame: a stocky Ghanaian woman in silver, a rangy Dutch man in orange, a Chinese man with bleached hair in white, a curvy Puerto Rican woman in teal, a bearded Lebanese man in black, a tall Finnish woman in yellow. One continuous shot orbits slowly around the group as they snap robotic chest hits, ripple arm waves down the line and freeze in unison. No audience, just grinning, glossy, upbeat mischief.

Behind an Antarctic station, a mown launch flat holds a deflated weather-balloon envelope, a wicker basket on its side, and a tethered orange marker pole. The storm sky above is bruised and motionless, not a breath of wind. Two adults begin the take fully in frame, trainers planted on the short grass: a broad Russian woman with a copper crop in a black long-sleeve, and a slender Sri Lankan man in a mustard tee. Side by side down a laid agility ladder they blitz quick lateral hops, in-in-out-out, crossovers, drifting two meters before spinning back for another pass. Nobody else stands on the field. One continuous shot, the camera orbiting slowly around them. Silvered green, soft and dreamlike.

Light rain glazes a plateau of short springy turf over chalk above an Antarctic station, where a whitewashed survey cairn and a guyed instrument mast stand dripping and the ground shines wet. One adult man — heavy-shouldered, Mexican-American, black hair plastered flat, grey hoodie and dark trousers — begins fully in frame, cleats on the turf. In one continuous shot the camera dollies out to reveal the sweep of the plateau while he lifts into a full pitching windup, strides and hurls hard downfield, then walks off ten paces and repeats, covering ground across the frame. The air is otherwise still. No other soul appears. Desaturated, shadowed, quietly ominous.

Blue hour settles violet over a bare grey granite plateau above an Antarctic station; wind-scoured boulders squat at the rim and a distant antenna array pricks the horizon. Six adults stay fully in frame on the rock: a tall Kenyan man in white, a strong German woman in navy, a lean Bangladeshi man in orange, a broad Cuban woman in yellow, a grey-haired Italian man in green, a young Sámi woman in blue. In one continuous shot the camera orbits slowly as they cycle three-step spike approaches, jumping and swinging at a tossed volleyball, landing and rotating a few meters each time. The air is utterly still. No onlookers. Hazy, romantic, slow-motion sheen.

Cracked dry mud spreads across a drained tank flat beside the hydroponics hall of a polar research station, where a neon sign over the door throws pink and green across the plates and coiled hoses lie abandoned. Three adults start fully in frame, bare feet on the mud: a lithe Angolan man in white trousers, a muscular Filipina woman in a red tank, a wiry Portuguese man in yellow. One continuous shot tracks sideways at a steady walking pace while they swing a capoeira ginga, threading cartwheels, ducking sweeps and dodging within a few meters. The night is windless. Late in the take one rolls toward the lens and finishes cropped at the hip. Slick, shadowed, neon-noir.

Inside a vast supply hangar at a polar station, the crew's home-built timber cycling ring encircles a flat grey concrete infield; ski crates and a parked snow tractor sit along the wall. Cold shafts of daylight drop from high clerestory windows. Three adults take turns across four metres: a willowy Chilean woman with a long braid hurdles two steps into a front aerial; a compact Japanese man in a navy thermal answers with a chain of one-handed cartwheels; a tall grey-eyed Estonian woman in her forties floats a slow no-hands walkover. The air is perfectly still, dust suspended. Off-duty crew watch from the banked ring above. One continuous shot, camera dollying slowly out, all three fully framed.

Rain slicks the sawn white marble cutting floor of a quarry serving an Antarctic station, where a wire saw hangs slack over a half-cut block and stacked slabs glisten under grey light. Five adults begin fully in frame, boots on the wet stone: a towering Zulu man in red, a compact Japanese woman in gold, a thickset Croatian man in black, a tall Brazilian woman in white, a sinewy Indonesian man in orange. In one continuous shot the camera orbits slowly while they sink into deep crouches and explode into lion-dance style pounces, bounding the length of the floor in a chained line. Late on, the lead man leaps at the lens and ends cropped mid-torso. Air still, grand and thunderous.

Snow falls thickly on a small square of red brick pavers outside the chapel hut of an Antarctic station; benches wear white caps and a line of pennants snaps hard in strong wind alongside a flapping canvas awning. Four adults grip a thick rope and hold one spot, boots scraping brick: a burly Maori man in a yellow singlet, a tall Ethiopian woman in blue, a wiry Scottish man in green, a strong Uzbek woman in orange. In one continuous shot the camera dollies out to widen the square while they heave in rhythm, slide, and pile into a laughing collapse before hauling back upright. Wrapped-up crew lean over a snowed-in balcony railing above, well clear of the bricks. Crisp, high-energy, vivid.

A rolled dry clay strip runs down the middle of a fenced recreation field at an Antarctic station, tall floodlight masts unlit under soft overcast and a painted crease still faintly visible. Four adults shoulder one heavy timber log, boots on the clay and all fully in frame: a broad Nigerian woman in white, a rangy Serbian man in red, a compact Nepali woman in yellow, a bearded Canadian man in navy. In one continuous shot the camera dollies out as they jog the log the whole length of the strip, chanting a count, then drop it in unison with a thud and dust. Fireworks bloom silently in the far sky. Staff watch from bleachers beyond the fence. Ethereal, drifting mood.

Between two long banks of solar arrays serving a polar research station runs an access strip of compacted red dirt, a cabling trench half-backfilled along one edge and a leaning inverter cabinet at the far end. Hazy afternoon wind hangs dust in the light. Two adults start fully in frame, palms and boots down on the dirt: a heavyset Māori woman in a grey vest, and a lean Egyptian man in a faded orange shirt. In one continuous shot the camera cranes down from high above to eye level as they bear crawl flat-out along the strip, hips low, crossing the frame neck and neck to the cabinet. Flickering neon from a work rig and a sweeping searchlight strobe the haze. Nobody else present.

The casting hall of an Antarctic station foundry: packed black sand underfoot, rows of sand moulds, a ladle crane parked overhead and harsh floodlights blasting from one wall so shadows stretch far. Five adults line up fully in frame, feet on the sand: a powerful Trinidadian woman in white, a slim Vietnamese man in red, a broad Polish woman in yellow, a tall Somali man in blue, a compact Chilean woman in green. In one continuous shot the camera orbits slowly as each sprints a long run-up, snaps a round-off into back handspring and finishes a tucked flip, chalk puffing on landing. Flickering neon and a searchlight sweep the girders. No spectators. Punchy, saturated, athletic.

Golden hour lies long over a pavement of flat dark basalt below the ridge of an Antarctic station, cracked jointing underfoot, orange marker poles staggered across it and a rust-streaked emergency cache box at the edge. Three adults begin fully in frame, boots on the stone: a broad Māori man in charcoal, a tall Somali-Swedish woman in white, a wiry Argentine man in ochre. In one continuous shot the camera pans slowly left to right as a tag chase erupts, the runners covering the whole pavement with hard cuts around the poles, skidding turns and lunging fingertip tags. The air is completely still. No one else in sight. Vast, burnished, epic scale.

Blue hour paints a lane of concrete paver blocks between two stacks of weathered shipping containers in an Antarctic station's supply yard, a bent forklift fork leaning against steel and frost feathering the door seals. One adult man — thickset, Pakistani, grey-streaked beard, brown canvas jacket and heavy gloves — stands fully in frame, boots on the pavers. In one continuous shot the camera tracks sideways at a steady walking pace as he swings baled sacks up onto a rising stack, hips snapping, moving a step or two between grabs, breath clouding. The air is dead still. Nobody else in the yard. Grainy, unpolished, honest documentary light.

Floodlights on a cliff mast pour white over a cove of black volcanic sand below an Antarctic station, ice-glazed boulders ringing the beach and a beached wooden dinghy half buried. Three adults hold one patch of sand, all fully in frame: a tall Colombian man in a silver mesh top, a curvy Nigerian woman in fuchsia, a slight Korean-American person with a bleached crop in white. In one continuous shot the camera cranes down from high above to eye level as they snap vogue hand performance, spin on the spot and slam into death-drop dips, popping back up grinning. Confetti scraps tumble through the beams. Nobody else on the sand. Glossy, playful, high-contrast.

Blue hour cools the painted concrete apron outside an aircraft hangar at a polar research station, a ski-equipped plane silhouetted in the doorway and taxiway lights beading off toward the drifts. Three adults stand fully in frame, boots on the paint: a tall Ivorian woman in red, a stocky Norwegian man in yellow, a lean Filipino man in black. In one continuous shot the camera dollies slowly in as they link hands, wind a crack-the-whip chain across the apron and sling the tail runner far across the markings; he skids, recovers and sprints back into the chain, all three staying fully in frame. Distant vehicle light trails streak past behind the fence. No one else present. Crisp, punchy sports energy.

Rain lashes a weathered wooden promenade running along the shoreline of an Antarctic station, rope handrails sagging between posts, puddles splashing on the boards and a lamp swinging above a shuttered kiosk. Blue hour dims everything to indigo. Four adults begin fully in frame, feet on the decking: a tall Brazilian woman in a soaked white shirt, a stocky Korean man in orange, a lanky Nigerian man in green, a strong Danish woman in navy. In one continuous shot from a static tripod camera at eye level, a tag chase runs the promenade end to end with sharp changes of direction, spray kicked from puddles and lunging outstretched tags. Onlookers cluster under a raised shelter behind railings. Slow, gauzy, dreamlike.

Night at the ration-silo apron of a polar base: squat steel silos, a frosted auger chute, pink service neon buzzing over the dusty concrete slab. Six adults line up behind a chalk mark — a broad Brazilian woman, a wiry Korean man, a tall Nigerian man, a stocky Scottish woman, a slim Indian man, a silver-haired Norwegian woman, all in cut-off thermals and mismatched beanies. Each starts planted and fully framed, then bounds a long approach and hangs in a one-legged jump into a raked gravel patch. Steam gusts from a floor vent across the run-up. One continuous shot, camera dollying slowly out; the last jumper charges the lens and lands half out of frame.

Rain hisses over the patterned blue-and-white ceramic tiles of a courtyard behind an old coastal whaling station, its colonnade half-glazed with ice. Fog rolls thick between the pillars. Six adults in bright waterproof shells hold one square of tile: a burly Samoan man and a lanky Czech woman turn a pair of long ropes in an eggbeater rhythm; a shaven-headed Egyptian man and a curvy Jamaican woman skip inside, trading high-knee sprint steps for turn-jumps; a wiry Finnish man and a grey-braided Peruvian woman time their entries and swap in without the ropes stopping. Puddles burst under their shoes and rain streaks the fog. One continuous shot from a static tripod at eye level; all six stay on the tile, fully in frame.

Dense fog sits motionless over a painted crossroads outside a polar station's vehicle bay: yellow chevrons and a faded compass rose on the asphalt, fuel drums stacked under a guy-wired mast. Three adults hold a tight circle barely a metre across and trade solo rounds — a heavy-shouldered Trinidadian man in a black thermal snaps jabs and a stomp-driven kill-off; a small, sinewy Filipina woman answers with a stuttering chest-pop lock; a bearded Russian man in his forties buck-ups, arms whipping, then freezes. Nothing else in the scene moves; the air is dead. One continuous shot from a static tripod at eye level, all three grounded and fully in frame.

Stunted olive trees stand in ranks on a terraced flat of dusty pale earth behind an Antarctic station's greenhouse row, a dry stone retaining wall and a coiled irrigation hose at its edge. A stormy sky bruises purple just before rain while fog banks roll through the trunks. Two adults square up, fully in frame with feet on the earth: a tall Japanese woman in indigo hakama, hair braided tight, and a broad Nigerian-French man in white. The camera pans slowly left to right in one continuous shot as their shinai crack together — men strikes, kote counters, lunging footwork that drives each of them two metres before a sharp reset. Dust puffs at every stamp. Nobody else is out here. Bright, punchy, high-energy.

A sheltered clearing opens among transplanted conifers in the arboretum trial plot of a polar research station, packed earth and leaf litter underfoot, a split log bench at one edge and numbered stakes among the trunks. Hazy afternoon wind hangs dust in the light and swirls leaves low across the ground. Two adults stand fully in frame, boots on the litter: a stocky Turkish woman in a red training top, and a lanky Norwegian man with a blond topknot in grey. In one continuous shot the handheld camera circles slowly at chest height while they spar with padded sticks — overhead cracks, slipping sidesteps, quick counters — ranging a few meters through the clearing. No one else appears. Vivid, energetic, sunlit.

Neon tubes rigged on a survey trailer throw pink and blue over a firm red sand flat between dunes at an Antarctic station's ground-test range, ribbed marker poles leaning and a half-buried anemometer whirring. Sand blows low across the ground. Four adults hold their footing fully in frame: a heavyset Iraqi man in black, a strong Kenyan woman in white, a tattooed Australian woman in grey, a compact Peruvian man in maroon. In one continuous shot the camera cranes down from high above to eye level while they hurl weighted sacks between partners in pairs, absorbing the catch, pivoting and slinging back across a couple of meters. No one else is there. Cold shadows, hard neon edges, noir chill.

Warm tungsten work lamps hang over a sprung carpet floor in the gymnastics room of an Antarctic station recreation block; foam blocks are stacked against padded walls and a ceiling vent leaks slow steam through the amber light. Six adults hold their own spot, feet on the carpet and all fully in frame: a broad Nigerian woman in black, a lean Chilean man in grey, a tall Latvian woman in maroon, a stocky Korean man in olive, a bearded Israeli man in navy, a wiry Jamaican woman in rust. In one continuous shot the handheld camera circles slowly at chest height as they drive medicine balls overhead and slam them down again and again. Staff watch from a mezzanine railing above. Dark, sweat-lit, noir.

Harsh midday sun bleaches a whitewashed cement drying terrace on the kitchen block of an Antarctic station, shallow trays of chilies laid in rows and blue tarps whipping hard on a line beside a rusted water tank. One adult woman — tall, powerfully built, Dominican, box braids, a yellow tank and black shorts — starts fully in frame, feet on the cement. In one continuous shot the camera tracks sideways at a steady walking pace while she runs three-step spike approaches, jumping and cracking her arm through a tossed ball, landing and resetting a couple of meters over. Strong wind snaps the fabric around her. At the finish she drives at the lens and ends cropped at the waist. Nobody else up here.

Golden hour sets a smooth red sandstone bench alight above the shoreline of an Antarctic station, a stack of bleached driftwood at one end and a weathered survey bolt drilled into the rock; below, heavy waves crash against the cliffs and throw spray into the light. Three adults crouch fully in frame, spikes set on the stone: a powerful Bahamian man in white, a lean Korean woman in red, a rangy Ukrainian man in black. In one continuous shot the camera pans slowly left to right as they detonate out of block starts, driving through hard first strides and covering the whole bench before easing up and walking back. Nobody else appears. Vast, burnished, sweeping.

Harsh midday sun beats on the sawdust-covered dirt yard of a timber mill serving an Antarctic station, stacked logs banded in steel, an idle bandsaw shed with its door hooked open and a slab offcut pile throwing hard shadow. The air is completely still. One adult woman — sinewy, Kazakh, short black hair, faded green work shirt with sleeves rolled and dark trousers — stays fully in frame, boots on the sawdust. In one continuous shot the handheld camera circles slowly at chest height while she blitzes an agility ladder laid on the dirt: two-in-two-out, lateral shuffles, quick crossovers, dust kicking up with every contact as she works a few meters back and forth. Nobody else. Bleached highlights, deep shadow, quiet menace.

Three adults drill judo on grey commercial carpet inside a shuttered Manhattan expo hall, bare booth skeletons and a boarded concession counter looming behind them. One continuous shot, the camera orbiting them slowly. A tall Black woman in a violet gi loads a stocky Filipino man across her hip for o-goshi, lowers him, and a lean fifty-year-old redhead in navy steps in so the trio alternate uchi-mata entries, gripping sleeves, spinning, lifting, landing back on the same square metre of carpet. Magenta and cyan stage lamps hang in perfectly still air. All three stay fully in frame, feet down, the hall otherwise empty.

Pebbled ice glitters across a small Brooklyn curling club where painted house rings glow under a gantry of colored lamps. Two adults in goalie gear begin standing, fully framed, skate-boots planted: a broad Korean man in teal pads and a freckled Irish-American woman with a blonde braid under her mask. Filmed as one continuous shot with the camera dollying slowly inward, they hammer a stationary drill — dropping into butterfly, sealing the ice, flashing blockers at rubber balls, popping up and dropping again, spraying frost. Shredded confetti and paper scraps tumble lazily through the neon beams. Nobody else occupies the sheet, and both stay wholly in view.

Fine drizzle beads on the faded blue acrylic of a Queens tennis court, its sagging net and rusted chain-link fence darkening with wet. Two adults stand fully in frame at the baseline, sneakers gripping the slick paint: a wiry Mexican-American man in orange shorts and a broad-shouldered Nigerian woman in a white crop top, both soaked. One continuous shot, the camera dollying slowly backward to reveal the empty court and dripping fence line. They alternate sledgehammer strikes onto a battered truck tire — overhead, hips snapping, water exploding off rubber — then trade sides without leaving their spot. The air is otherwise motionless, and no one else appears.

Ribbed wet sand stretches across a tidal flat off Jamaica Bay, the hazy skyline reduced to grey teeth on the horizon. Four adults crouch in a staggered row, hands and feet pressed into the sand, all fully in frame: a shaved-headed Samoan man, a tall Danish woman in black, a compact Vietnamese woman in crimson, and a bearded thirties runner in grey. One continuous shot, the camera orbiting slowly. On a shout they explode forward, driving low, arms tearing, water flicking from their heels as they cover twenty metres across the flat and pull up together, still entirely within frame. Dust-thick afternoon light hangs motionless; nobody else is out here.

On a quarry bench of compacted rock aggregate, terraced walls rise behind an idle crusher silhouette. Four adults hold a tight square of ground, fully framed from the first moment: a broad Ukrainian woman in olive, a slim Ethiopian man in yellow, a tattooed forty-something in a cut sleeveless tee, and a stocky Puerto Rican man in grey. Captured as one continuous shot, the handheld camera drifting slowly around them at chest height. They drop, chest to gravel, snap their feet in, and launch upward with both arms overhead, landing to repeat — grit puffing under each rep. Far off, fireworks bloom silently in the dusty haze. No spectators anywhere.

Blue polyurethane runs the length of an old Bronx armory converted to an indoor sprint track, girders lost above the colored gels. Two adults stand shoulder to shoulder in lane four, both fully in frame with shoes flat on the surface: a muscular Jamaican-American woman in lime, an athletic white man in his thirties wearing black. One continuous shot, the camera dollying steadily back to open up the empty straightaway. They swing their arms, load their knees, and rip standing back tucks — tucking tight, spotting the floor, sticking the landing — then a whip-back and a stepless twist, never leaving their marks. Steam curls out of floor vents around their ankles.

Inside a half-empty hangar, painted grey concrete stretches beneath hanging work lamps, one aircraft wing shrouded in canvas tarps at the far wall. Three adults stand fully in frame, feet flat: an ash-blonde Polish woman in slate silk, a lithe Ghanaian man in bare feet and grey trousers, and a Japanese-American woman in her forties wearing dusty rose. Rendered as one continuous shot, the camera drifting slowly toward them. They chain pirouettes — doubles into triples — then whip fouetté after fouetté on the same worn spot, skirts flaring, heels stabbing the concrete. Big floor fans stir loose paper and dust past their ankles. The hangar holds no one else.

Fog swallows a decommissioned runway; grooved asphalt and a ghosted centerline emerge only a few metres ahead, with hangar shapes hinted beyond. One adult stands alone at the mark, fully in frame, barefoot on the cold surface — a sinewy Brazilian man in his late twenties, cropped dark hair, black shorts, chalk on his palms. One continuous shot, the camera panning slowly left to right to follow him. He kicks up into a handstand, walks steadily along the centerline for several metres, then breaks into sharp hand-hops, shoulders punching, legs stacked and shivering, before stepping down and repeating. Steam drifts from a vent grate through the fog. He remains entirely within frame.

Heavy snow settles on the pale limestone forecourt of a columned museum, the fountain basin frozen and rimmed with white. The air is dead calm; flakes fall straight down. Two adults stand fully in frame with boots planted on swept stone: a lean Haitian-American man in a charcoal overcoat and a silver-haired woman in her fifties wearing a long black coat, both breathing steam. Shot as one continuous take from a static tripod at eye level. They alternate swings at a rubber tee — hips rotating, wooden bat cracking a ball into the falling snow, then resetting and swinging again — shoulders dusted white. Deep shadows pool between columns. The forecourt is otherwise deserted.

Fog drowns a painted black asphalt court under bent rims and faded key lines, its chain-link perimeter dissolving into grey. Three adults anchor a small patch of blacktop, fully in frame with sneakers set wide: a heavyset Dominican man in a maroon hoodie, a braided Kenyan-American woman in teal, and a wiry man in his forties, shirtless under a windbreaker. One continuous shot, the camera orbiting them slowly. They drive alternating battle rope waves, then rise together for double-arm overhead slams that whip the ropes flat against the asphalt. Beyond the fence, a handful of onlookers watch from the sidewalk, none stepping onto the court. Dreamy, desaturated, hushed.

Harsh midday sun bakes the raked red dirt of a derelict city ballpark, chalk lines crisp, sun-bleached dugouts empty behind. Six adults line up along the baseline, all fully in frame with bare feet on the dirt: a tall Sudanese woman, a stocky Greek man, a red-haired woman in her thirties, a wiry Filipino man and a broad Ghanaian woman in twin-toned singlets, and a silver-bearded athlete in grey. One continuous shot, the camera tracking sideways at a steady walking pace. They kick into handstands and race, hand-walking across the infield, some breaking into hopping bunny-jumps, dirt smudging their palms — covering the stretch from third toward second, everyone staying in frame. Air perfectly still. No spectators exist here.

A red painted tarmac bike highway runs between concrete barriers, arrows baking under vertical noon sun, towers hazed behind. Two adults occupy one stretch of lane, fully in frame, boots gripping the paint: a barrel-chested Armenian man in a sweat-dark tank, and a powerful Black woman in her late thirties with taped wrists. Documentary in feel, one continuous shot, the handheld camera circling slowly at chest height. Each hikes a steel keg between their knees, then hurls it backward over one shoulder, tracking its flight, before resetting on the same spot to throw again, grunting, hands chalked. Shredded paper scraps tumble past on the lane. Nobody else is present.

Coastal evaporation pans spread out in cracked white salt, ankle-deep brine glowing under the pink and green neon of a small pump shed. Four adults stand in one shallow square, fully in frame with feet flat in the water: a grinning Chinese-American man in a yellow shirt, a curly-haired Colombian woman in denim shorts, a lanky Somali man, and a laughing woman in her forties with cropped platinum hair. One continuous shot as the camera dollies backward, uncovering more pans. They stomp huge splashes at each other, scooping and flinging brine, hopping and ducking, never leaving that patch. The night air is otherwise perfectly still and empty.

Floodlights on aluminium poles blast a mown clearing in an apple orchard, clover and grass silver-green, gnarled trunks and stacked crates ringing the edge. Six adults spread across the turf, every one fully in frame with shoes on the grass: a compact Thai woman in orange, a tall Sikh man in a black patka, a freckled runner in her twenties, a broad Samoan man, a grey-templed coach in blue, and a lean Egyptian woman. One continuous shot, the camera orbiting the group slowly. Their ropes blur into speed skipping, then crossovers snapping past their hips, then double-unders, each holding a single square of clover. The night air hangs still, orchard otherwise deserted.

Mist hangs over a green synthetic pitch at sunrise, a rusted goal frame and low warehouse rooftops silhouetted beyond the touchline. Two adults face each other on the centre circle, fully in frame with boots on the turf: a heavily built Turkish man in a grey compression top, and a tall Trinidadian woman with locs tied back, in cobalt. One continuous shot, the camera dollying out to reveal the wide empty pitch. They lift medicine balls overhead, rise onto their toes, and hammer them down into the rubber-crumb turf, catching the bounce and repeating, faster, until crumb sprays around their ankles. The air is glassy still. Nobody else is on the field.

Blue hour settles over a lavender field where a chalky gravel path splits rows of purple spikes beside a wooden drying rack. Two adults stand on the path, fully in frame, boots crunching gravel: a broad Korean-American woman in a cream hoodie, and a wiry man in his fifties, grey stubble, sleeves shoved up. One continuous shot, the camera tracking sideways at an even walking pace. She tees a ball, coils, and lashes the barrel through it so the ball disappears over the purple rows; he steps in, re-chalks his grip and rips his own swing, gravel grinding under tight footwork. Fine snowflakes drift through the last shafts of light. The field holds nobody else.

At the seaward edge of a community sunflower plot on the Rockaway peninsula, heads droop over a strip of dry cracked soil, a leaning deer fence and rusted irrigation drum behind. Two adults claim one patch: a sinewy Dominican man in his thirties, cornrows, oversized grey tee; and a stocky Korean-American woman in a red bandana and baggy carpenter pants. He rocks an Indian step, drops to a three-step, then rides a coffee-grinder sweep into a shoulder freeze; she answers with a CC-step and a hollowback hold. Hot hazy wind lifts grit; surf pounds beyond the dune. One continuous shot, handheld, circling slowly at chest height; both stay grounded, fully framed.

Blue hour over a brickyard behind a Brooklyn kiln shed: fired clay tiles laid flat and stacked in pallets, a chalked hopscotch grid faded on the surface. Two adults work practice poi on tethers, sock heads whistling: a broad Puerto Rican man in his twenties, tank top and taped wrists, and a lean Nigerian-American woman with short bleached twists and lime shorts. He runs a three-beat weave, dips into a butterfly, and turns under his own leads; she chases with fast wall-plane stalls, stepping three metres across the tiles and back. Everything else is dead calm, sky deepening indigo. One continuous shot tracking sideways at a walking pace; both stay fully framed.

A river tunnel closed to traffic runs long and low, its asphalt orange under sodium lamps, tiled walls slick, a dark barrier plugging the far mouth. Four adults stand in the roadway, all fully in frame, cleats on the asphalt: a rangy Black quarterback in a grey cutoff, a thick-necked Serbian man, a tall Chilean woman in navy, and a receiver in her thirties with taped fingers. One continuous shot, the camera craning down from high above to eye level. Two drop back five steps, plant, and fire spirals seventy feet down the lane while the others break long and haul them in, sprinting the tunnel's length. Paper scraps tumble through the beams; nobody else appears.

Floodlights on a freight depot rake the weathered concrete platform, container stacks and idle boxcars sitting dark behind. One adult occupies the platform, fully in frame with cleats squared on the slab: a powerfully built Filipina woman in her thirties, hair in a low bun, wearing a white jersey and grey pants, batting gloves cinched. One continuous shot, the camera dollying slowly backward to open the depot's scale. Balancing a ball on the tee, she coils, then whips the barrel through with a crack that ricochets off steel containers, reloads and fires the next swing harder, her stride tightening each rep. The night air is dead calm and nobody else is here.

An outer railway platform edges the harbor, tactile strips ribbing its concrete, neon signage staining the puddles, heavy surf breaking beyond the seawall. Six adults stand in a line at one end, fully in frame with feet on the platform: a muscular Cuban man, a tall Norwegian woman in white, a compact Indian woman, a bearded tumbler in his forties, a lean Korean man, and a broad-shouldered athlete in red. One continuous shot, the camera panning slowly left to right. One after another they hurdle into round-offs, snap back handsprings, and rip back tucks, travelling the platform's length in a chain of passes. Epic, cold, and utterly unpeopled otherwise.

Crusted wind-packed snow covers a marsh flat where buried fence posts poke up in a crooked line under flat overcast light. Three adults crouch in a row, hands sunk into the crust, everyone fully in frame: a grinning Puerto Rican woman in a pink beanie, a lanky Nordic man in yellow, and a stout Cambodian-American man in black thermals. One continuous shot, the camera dollying backward to widen the white expanse. They punch out of their starts, driving hard for fifteen metres, snow crunching and spraying off their shoes, then wheel around laughing to reset. The air is windless and clean, and there is no one else on the field.

A cloister courtyard of worn flagstone sits inside arcaded columns, a dry stone basin at its center, sky drained to blue-hour indigo. Three adults claim the open flags, fully in frame with feet planted: a lean Algerian man in a black tank, a tall Swedish woman with a French braid, and a compact Peruvian woman in her forties, hands wrapped. One continuous shot, the handheld camera circling slowly at chest height. One holds focus mitts while another slips and fires jab-cross-hook-uppercut, drifting a couple of metres along the flags before they rotate and the third steps in to throw. Air perfectly still, cold, dreamy. No one watches from the arcades.

Fog rolls off the harbour onto the concrete drying patio behind a Red Hook roastery, burlap sacks slumped by the rake rack, green beans swept into a low ridge. Three adults start planted on the slab and dance hard over four metres: a rangy Jamaican-American man in braces, a petite Ukrainian woman in a swing skirt, and a broad-shouldered Mexican-American woman in her forties who counts them in and swaps places each chorus. The pair swing out, kick through a Charleston, then hit a hip-to-hip snatch lift that flips her clean over his back to a landing on the slab. Wind snaps the drying tarps and flags overhead. One continuous handheld shot circling at chest height; all three stay fully framed.

Two adults square off midstage in a faded Queens vaudeville house, black plywood decking scuffed pale, a half-lowered fire curtain and dusty gilt boxes framing them. Low practice lamps leave deep pockets of shadow. A trim Japanese-American man in his fifties, hair tied back, and a tall Nigerian-American woman with taped forearms run kirikaeshi with bamboo shinai: she stamps a fumikomi lunge and cracks a straight head cut; he receives, then feeds alternating left-right diagonals as they drive three metres downstage and back, shouting on every strike. Stage fans send loose paper skittering past their heels. A scatter of onlookers watches from the seats. One continuous shot tracking sideways at a walking pace, both fully framed.

Rain streaks through floodlights on a raised park terrace of crushed decomposed granite, puddles splashing along a low stone wall with lit trees glowing behind. Two adults square off on the grit, both fully in frame with shoes dug in: a huge Tongan man in a soaked grey tee, and a tall Russian woman in her thirties, hair plastered flat, forearms taped. One continuous shot, the handheld camera circling slowly at chest height. They haul a thick rope in savage heaves, boots skidding a metre or two through gravel and water, one dropping to a knee, both scrambling back up to heave again. Cinematic and drenched; the terrace holds no one else.

A coal stockyard lies under a conveyor gantry, ground powdered black, hazy stacks fading into dusty afternoon light while fireworks bloom silently far beyond them. Six adults hold a loose ring, all fully in frame with bare feet in the dust: a shaved-headed Brazilian man, a tall Kazakh woman in white, a wiry Vietnamese man, a heavyset Ghanaian woman, a grey-bearded fighter, and a compact athlete in her twenties wearing a red belt. One continuous shot, the camera craning down from high overhead to eye level. Each spins through hook kicks and jumping crescents that blast up black clouds around their spots. Epic and grimy, with no spectators.

Matte terrazzo runs down a colonnaded arcade lined with repeating columns and glass doors at the far end, lit flat and even from above. Four adults are fully in frame at the start, feet flat on the dull stone floor: a thick-necked Bulgarian man, a lean Black woman in a singlet, a stocky Mexican-American wrestler, and a woman in her forties with a taped ear. The air hangs perfectly still. One continuous shot, the camera dollying slowly toward them. In pairs they drill double legs — level change, penetration step, drive two metres and finish — then reset. As the camera closes, one wrestler shoots forward past it and ends partly out of frame, torso cropped. Nobody else occupies the arcade.

A decommissioned turbine hall on the East River, checker plate steel underfoot, a gutted casing the size of a bus and coiled tarps behind. Harsh floodlights blast from one side; haze drifts and a rigged spotlight swings across the girders. Two adults grin, chalk up and go to work on one spot: a huge Serbian man in a stretched blue singlet, and a thick-set Haitian-American woman in her thirties with tape on her forearms and a shaved fade. Each laps a tacky concrete atlas stone onto the thighs, hugs it to the chest and loads it onto a chest-high steel drum, then rolls it down and swaps. One continuous shot, the camera dollying slowly in; both stay fully framed.

Noon glare bounces off a studio backlot street where painted asphalt runs between false brownstone facades, scaffolding and dead light towers stacked behind them. Six adults spread down the roadway, every one fully in frame with cleats on the paint: a broad Samoan lineman, a tall Argentinian woman in gold, a bleached-blond receiver, a bearded Ukrainian passer in grey, a compact Korean-American athlete, and a long-limbed Ethiopian-American woman throwing left-handed. Everything unfolds as one continuous shot with the camera easing slowly toward them. Passers drop back, pump once, and rip spirals thirty yards down the street; receivers tear routes past the stoops and haul the ball in, sprinting the whole block. Air dead still; nobody watches, and all six stay in frame.

A disused parade ground of flat grey asphalt stretches out, faded formation marks ghosting under noon sun, flagless poles standing along one side. One adult begins fully in frame, feet on the asphalt inside a burlap sack pulled to the waist — a stocky Greek-American man in his thirties, curly hair, striped shirt, grinning hugely. One continuous shot, the camera panning slowly left to right to follow him. He hops hard across the tarmac, gaining speed, wobbles, crashes onto his shoulder in a laughing tumble, scrambles upright and hops on toward a chalk finish line. Dry leaves swirl low across the ground around him. Not another soul in sight.

Snow falls thick over a cracked white salt crust near the shore, a driftwood line marking where heavy surf breaks and booms beyond. Three adults hold one patch, all fully in frame with shoes on the crust: a tall Somali woman in a mustard coat, a compact Portuguese man in black, and a woman in her forties with silver-streaked hair and red mittens. One continuous shot, the camera tracking sideways at an even walking pace. Two turn long ropes in steady opposition while the third jumps between them, switching to high knees, spinning a full turn mid-jump, snow melting on her shoulders. Dreamy and soft-focused. No one else is anywhere near.

An underground parking level runs off in epoxy-coated concrete, painted bay numbers and a low ceiling of pipes swallowed by shadow between weak practice lamps. One adult stands fully in frame, sneakers on the smooth floor — a bouncy Vietnamese-American man in his twenties, backwards cap, oversized green jersey, wooden stick in gloved hands. One continuous shot, the camera tracking sideways at a walking pace. He rips a ball through a tight cone lane, toe-drags, pulls it between his feet, fakes forehand and snaps backhand, feet shuffling but never leaving his little box. Big service fans lift loose paper and dust past him. Playful, bright-hearted, and completely alone down here.

Snow tumbles into an apartment courtyard paved with interlocking concrete, brick balconies stacked overhead, bike racks and frozen planters at the margins. One adult crouches at a taped line, fully in frame with hands and shoes on the pavers — an energetic Nigerian-American woman in her twenties, braids tied back, orange windbreaker, breath steaming. One continuous shot, the handheld camera circling slowly at chest height. She fires out of a three-point start, drives four or five metres, decelerates, jogs back and does it again, harder. Grit and dry snow skitter low across the pavers. Neighbours lean over the balcony railings above, watching and clapping, none of them down on the courtyard.

Blue hour on the travertine pool deck of a small Manhattan boutique hotel, drained plunge pool, folded loungers, a steel handrail edging the parapet. Five adults begin planted on the dry tile in a stunt group: three broad bases — a Puerto Rican man, an Egyptian woman, a rangy Irish-American man in his thirties — a compact Chinese-American backspot, and a small, wiry Black flyer in navy. They dip, drive, and press a walk-in half-up to extension, then load and pop her straight up for a snapping toe-touch before she drops into a clean cradle. The evening air is glassy and still. Hotel guests watch from behind the glass balustrade above. One continuous shot, static tripod at eye level, all five fully framed.

Granite setts pave a pedestrianized shopping street, striped awnings and stone planters lining both sides under blistering noon sun, with a strip of raked sand laid across the setts as a landing pit. Three adults stand at the top of the runway, fully in frame with spikes on stone: a springy Brazilian woman in yellow, a tall Sikh man in blue, and a grinning Italian-American man in his forties. One continuous shot, the camera orbiting slowly around them. Each pounds down the setts, hits the board, hangs with arms cycling, and slams into the sand — then jogs back past the planters. The air is dead still; the street is otherwise empty.

Mist sits low over a packed dirt farmyard, a leaning barn and rusted plough emerging in grey, fence rails beaded with damp. One adult holds the middle of the yard, fully in frame with bare feet pressed into the dirt — a tall Vietnamese woman in her thirties, dark hair coiled tight, wearing a slate leotard and long charcoal skirt. One continuous shot, the camera orbiting her slowly. She whips a ribbon wand into tall spirals and snaking figure-eights, leaps through the loops, and drills fast turns that wrap the silk around her, all on one small circle of ground. The air is utterly still. Moody, dim, and no one else appears.

Golden hour pours across an athletics oval, red rubber tartan glowing, lane lines stretching toward a distant curve. Two adults stand chest to chest in lane one, fully in frame with bare feet on the track: a wiry Thai man with taped shins, and a tall Black woman in her thirties, hair braided flat, gloves cinched. One continuous shot, the camera orbiting them slowly. They lock a plum clinch, pummel for inside control, and drive alternating knees into a body pad, snapping each other's posture down, feet pivoting on the same spot. Snowflakes drift through the low beams like sparks. Spectators sit scattered in the stands above, none on the track.

A cold storage warehouse opens into frosted concrete aisles between ice-glazed racking, colored beams slicing haze that pours off the chillers. Four adults stand fully in frame, boots gripping the rime: a huge Nigerian man in a black thermal, a compact Norwegian woman with a blonde crop, a broad Mexican-American athlete in red, and a lean Chinese man in grey. One continuous shot, the camera craning down from high above to eye level. Two shoulder their partners in fireman's carries and sprint four metres through the fog, set them down, then the carried pair pick up their carriers and charge back. Breath billows white. Nobody else is inside.

Powdery white gypsum stretches into low dunes at sunrise, bleached yucca stalks poking through, mist glowing pink along the horizon. Six adults form a wide ring, all fully in frame with bare feet in the sand: a compact Japanese woman in white, a tall Ghanaian man in a black rashguard, a tattooed Latina fighter, a broad Turkish man, a sinewy runner in her forties, and a young athlete in a blue belt. One continuous shot, the camera dollying backward to reveal the flats. Each rips spinning hook and jump-spin crescent kicks that blast sand up into the light, staying on their marks. Air perfectly calm; no onlookers.

Inside an empty badminton hall in a lakeside Patagonian town, faded shuttle-line decals glow on a green vinyl mat while ceiling vents breathe slow ribbons of steam. Four adults hold the court: a tall Black woman in teal rashguard, a wiry Mapuche man in grey shorts, a broad blond Scandinavian man in navy, a compact Filipina woman in orange. One continuous shot from a static tripod at eye level. All four begin fully in frame, feet planted, then break into paired double-leg entries, sprawls and hip-throw scrambles inside a few meters. Near the end the blond man drives forward until his shoulder and hip pass out of frame. Dreamy, soft-bloom color.

Dawn mist pools over a reservoir as six adults warm up along the lane-striped concrete crest of a Patagonian hydroelectric dam, spillway gates yawning below and a rusted gantry crane parked at the far abutment. Loose paper scraps and pale confetti tumble past on the valley draft. A silver-haired Korean woman, a freckled ginger man, a stocky Guaraní man, a lean Somali woman, a tattooed Latina, a bearded south-Asian man each stay rooted to their own square meter, snapping jabs, slipping under imagined hooks, rolling shoulders, pivoting on the ball of the foot. One continuous shot, the camera dollying slowly out to reveal the whole rose-lit crest. All six stay fully framed throughout, shoes flat on the concrete from the first beat.

Bruised violet clouds stack over a canal quay in southern Patagonia, grey cobble setts running past moored steel fishing hulls and a leaning tower of stacked crab traps. Improbable snowflakes drift through low shafts of light. Five adults shoulder a peeled beech log: a towering Māori man, a rangy Ethiopian woman, a silver-bearded Basque man, a muscular Vietnamese woman, a young Argentine man with cropped curls. They start fully in frame, feet on stone, then jog the log twenty meters along the quay, calling cadence, and slam it down in unison. The camera dollies out steadily across one continuous shot as the lead runner surges close, his torso cropping out of frame. Epic, storm-grey grandeur.

A decommissioned subway platform under a Patagonian port city: tiled concrete, warm tungsten work lamps clamped to pillars, and a dark trackbed where a stalled service car rests. Through the sealed mezzanine glass, neon flickers and a searchlight sweeps, throwing colored bands across the tiles. Five adults train here — a broad Samoan man, a lithe Danish woman, a bald Nigerian man, a compact Peruvian woman, a lanky Turkish man in a yellow tee. One continuous shot, static tripod at eye level. Feet on the tiles and all five fully framed from the first beat, they sprint five-step drop-backs down the long platform, plant, and rifle tight spirals to one another as they cut past the pillars. Bright, punchy sports-ad energy; nobody else is underground.

Blue hour settles over a closed street in a windswept Patagonian city, asphalt still holding a painted crosswalk, wool-shop awnings furled, steel barricades at both corners where spectators press and film from behind the railings. The air is dead calm. Three adults drive weighted sleds: a burly Māori-Chilean man in a red singlet, a broad-shouldered Ukrainian woman with a blonde braid, a lean Jamaican man in white. From a first beat with all three fully framed and feet down, they launch and grind the sleds thirty meters up the block, plates chattering, breath ragged. One continuous shot, the camera orbiting slowly around them. Deep cinematic indigo, headlights unlit, everyone stays in frame.

A faded estancia ballroom in Patagonia: warped parquet, dark chandeliers wrapped in dust sheets, tungsten work lamps on stands, and boarded French doors leaking flickering neon and the slow sweep of a searchlight from the yard outside. Three adults run shuttles between chalk-marked cones set fifteen meters apart — a tall Ghanaian woman in a purple crop top, a stocky Japanese man in black, a rangy Chilean man with a bleached fade. All three begin fully in frame with feet on the wood, then explode into touch-and-turn sprints, hands slapping the boards, shoes shrieking on parquet. One continuous shot, camera panning slowly left to right. Epic, high-contrast amber and cold blue.

Rain glazes the dark basalt setts of a Patagonian train station forecourt, an iron-and-glass canopy dripping overhead, a dead clock tower behind and a rank of empty taxis along the far kerb. Onlookers cluster under the arcade behind steel railings, none on the open stone. Two adults work the wet square: a sinewy Egyptian woman in a black unitard, a broad Norwegian man in a charcoal tracksuit. Both stand fully framed, feet down, then launch chained cartwheels and round-offs, hands slapping puddles, crossing eight meters of glossy stone. One continuous shot, camera tracking sideways at a steady walking pace. Neo-noir: sodium reflections, wet blacks, no other movement in the air.

On a wide Patagonian steppe of cropped dry grass, a sagging wire fence runs to a lone stone corral, and beyond it an ice-capped ridge sits under flat overcast light. Low dust snakes across the ground on a steady wind. Three adults spar with foam-padded practice sticks: a weathered Aymara woman in a grey vest, a tall Dutch man with a red beard, a broad Korean-Chilean woman in olive. Feet on the turf and all three fully in frame from the first beat, they trade overhead cuts, slip aside, counter to the ribs, circling within a few meters. One continuous shot, the camera panning slowly left to right. Muted, moody, desaturated greens and gunmetal.

Heavy snow falls on the aluminium deck of an open-air festival stage pitched in a Patagonian valley, scaffold towers dressed with limp bunting, a stack of silent speaker cabinets, and far below a highway where distant traffic drags long light trails through the flurries. One adult occupies the deck: a tall Brazilian woman with box braids, in a bright yellow windbreaker and black leggings. She stands fully framed, boots on the deck, then bursts into a deep three-step drop, plants hard, and rips a spiral the length of the stage, sprinting after her own throw to do it again. One continuous shot, camera orbiting slowly around her. Playful, upbeat, snow-bright color; she stays fully in frame.

Night at an oil refinery on the Patagonian coast: a gravel service road, a flare stack burning orange above cracking towers, a gatehouse washed in green and magenta neon, and fireworks blooming silently over the far bay. Four adults work in two pairs — a stocky Sudanese man in a red tank top, a tall Czech woman with a bleached crop, a wiry Bolivian man, a strong Tongan woman in blue. All four start fully in frame, boots crunching gravel, then heave weighted sandbags chest-high across two meters, absorb the catch in a deep squat, and fire them straight back. One continuous shot, camera dollying slowly out. Saturated, energetic, sweat catching the neon.

Fog crawls across a raked sand volleyball court by a Patagonian lake town, spectators bundled on driftwood benches beyond the sideline, a sagging net at one end. Six adults spin practice poi in a loose ring — a broad Mapuche man, a tall Danish woman with a wind-blown bob, a bearded Argentine man in his forties, a slim Ghanaian woman in coral, a stocky Japanese woman, a wiry Welsh man. All start planted on the sand, fully framed, then break into hyperloops, antispin flowers and passing spins, drifting a few metres through each other's arcs. Fireworks bloom silently over the water. One continuous shot tracking sideways at a walking pace; one spinner sidesteps toward the lens and ends half out of frame.

A pale cove of fine white coral sand on the Patagonian shore, a bleached whale rib half-buried near the tideline and shell drifts curving toward a low grey surf under soft overcast light. Dry petals and torn kelp leaves swirl low across the ground. One adult is here: a lean middle-aged Japanese-Argentine man in cyan board shorts, hair salt-stiff. He begins fully in frame, barefoot and standing, then runs three strides and launches into a headfirst belly-flop dive, skidding through the sand, springing up and repeating it a few meters along the beach. One continuous shot, camera tracking sideways at a steady walking pace. Dreamy pastel greys, sand hanging in the air.

A scrap metal yard on the edge of a Patagonian port at night: oil-stained concrete apron, stacked cubes of crushed cars, a magnet crane hanging idle, and a buzzing pink-and-blue neon sign over the office shed. The air is perfectly still. Five adults line up — a tall Kenyan man in white, a muscular Mexican woman in green, a bald Russian man, a slight Thai woman in orange, a lanky Afro-Argentine man. Fully framed with feet on the concrete, they drop prone, sit, then explode upright on their own barked count and burst three meters forward, resetting again and again. One continuous shot, the camera craning down from high above to eye level; the Kenyan man finishes half out of frame. Vivid, high-energy.

Inside a granite cathedral in a Patagonian city, stone flagstones stretch between columns; a touring rig has left colored stage lights on the triforium, washing the vaults magenta and green while smoke drifts up from floor vents. Four adults hold one spot beneath the lantern: two bases, a broad Fijian man and a strong Polish woman; a Chilean man spotting; a compact Vietnamese-Canadian woman as flyer. All four are fully in frame, feet on stone, from the first beat. The bases crouch, snap their arms and rocket her skyward into a straight pike, pluck her out of the air into a cradle, then set her down and fire the launch again. One continuous shot, handheld camera slowly circling at chest height. Bright, playful, candy-colored.

Mist hangs over a cathedral forecourt in a Patagonian town at sunrise, sandstone paving still cold, a dry bronze fountain to one side and a scaffolded bell tower catching the first pink light. Early onlookers sit on the steps behind a stone balustrade, well off the open paving. The air is still. One adult trains alone: a tall mixed-race woman in her thirties, black tank top, red shorts, hair in a tight bun. Fully in frame with shoes on the stone, she paces her four-step spike approach, swings her arms back, jumps, and cracks an imaginary ball down, landing and repeating a couple of meters over. One continuous shot, camera craning from high above down to eye level. Plain documentary realism.

A frozen lake below black glacial peaks in Patagonia, its snow-dusted ice scored by old skate lines, an abandoned plywood ice-fishing hut leaning near a pressure ridge. Storm clouds pile low and heavy; the air itself is dead still. Four adults are out on the surface: a stocky Inuk woman in a mustard parka, a tall Colombian man in black, a freckled Irish woman in red, a wiry Chinese-Argentine man in blue. From a first beat with everyone fully framed and boots down, they scoop and hurl snowballs, dodging, sliding, diving flat and scrambling up as the fight ranges twenty meters across the ice. One continuous shot, camera tracking sideways at walking pace. Raw, handheld documentary grade.

Night on a flat wave-worn rock shelf below a Patagonian fishing village, tide pools glassy in the still air, mussel beds glinting, and a fish plant's green-and-red neon sign spilling color across the smooth stone. One adult occupies the shelf: a strong Argentine woman in her late twenties, magenta cropped hoodie, black tights, hair whipped into a knot. She stands fully in frame, bare feet on rock, then flops onto her back, springs up on a beat, sprints two meters, drops seated, twists and bursts again — grinning between reps. One continuous shot, camera craning down from high above to eye level; her final burst carries her close until her legs leave the frame. Bright, playful, poppy.

Midday sun hammers a beachfront promenade in a Patagonian resort town, its black-and-white mosaic laid in rolling wave patterns between wind-bent palms and a low seawall where a scattered crowd leans and watches, none stepping onto the tiles. Torn confetti and paper scraps from a morning parade tumble along on the sea breeze. Four adults square off in pairs on one small patch, all fully framed with shoes on the mosaic: a broad Lebanese man in white linen, a tall Haitian woman in lime, a compact Korean woman in denim, a sunburnt Australian man. Arms folded, each hops on one leg, barging shoulder to shoulder, hopping, twisting, staggering, never leaving their meter. One continuous shot, camera orbiting slowly. Sun-bleached, dreamy highlights.

An overcast morning on the rooftop helipad of a Patagonian regional hospital: a chipped painted circle on concrete, guy-wired antenna masts at the parapet, and a grey fjord stretching past the town's tin roofs. Nothing stirs but the man himself. He is one adult, mid-forties, Chilean, wiry, in a faded maroon tee and black shorts, calves corded.
