Fully in frame with trainers on the concrete from the first beat, he hammers through a rubber agility ladder — high knees, in-in-out-out, lateral shuffles — turning at the end and driving straight back over three meters of deck. One continuous shot, camera tracking sideways at a steady walking pace. Flat documentary light, sweat and breath, nothing staged.

An idle car assembly hall in Patagonia: epoxy-coated concrete lanes, unpainted body shells hanging still on an overhead conveyor, robot arms folded, and long shafts of daylight dropping through high clerestory windows into the dust. No air moves. Five adults chalk their palms — a compact Ecuadorian woman, a tall Ivorian man, a stocky German woman with cropped grey hair, a slim Malaysian man, a bearded Uruguayan man. All five stand fully framed, feet on the floor, then kick to handstands and race a marked ten-meter lane, walking and hopping on their hands, legs scissoring for balance, collapsing and resetting. One continuous shot from a static tripod at eye level. Gritty, unglamorous, honest documentary tone.

Under the glass canopy of a Patagonian transit interchange, grey porcelain tile runs between shuttered ticket kiosks and a dry planter of black stones; only a few dim practice lamps burn, leaving deep shadow between pools of light. Commuters watch from the mezzanine walkway above, none on the floor. Nothing else stirs. Five adults set up on a taped line: a heavyset Tongan man, a lean Iranian woman, a tall Swedish man, a muscular Brazilian woman, a slight Japanese man. Fully framed, hands and feet planted, they surge into bear crawls, hips low, racing four meters, turning and crawling back. One continuous shot, camera tracking sideways at a steady walking pace. Grainy, low-key, unpolished realism.

On the weather deck of a bulk carrier anchored off the Patagonian coast, painted steel plating runs between lashed containers and a rust-streaked crane pedestal; a dusty, hazy afternoon wind blurs the horizon to brass. The deck itself is quiet, no gear swinging. Two adults train on a ladder taped out in yellow: a broad Filipino man in a grey boiler suit with sleeves knotted at the waist, and a tall Nigerian-British woman in black thermals. Both fully in frame, boots on steel, they rip through quick in-and-out patterns, lateral hops and crossover steps, shuffling a couple of meters along the plating before turning back. One continuous shot, camera tracking sideways at walking pace. Neo-noir amber haze, hard shadows.

A cramped fight gym in a Patagonian industrial shed: an octagon of chain-link over a vinyl-covered mat, blank canvas banners, tungsten work lamps clamped to the cage posts, and two floor fans stirring loose paper and dust in the corners. A handful of members watch from benches outside the fence, never on the mat. One adult is inside: a lean Kazakh woman in her early thirties, black rashguard, red shin pads, hair braided tight. Fully in frame with bare feet on the mat, she chambers and fires spinning hook kicks, then back kicks, checking her balance, resetting a step or two each time. One continuous shot, handheld camera circling slowly at chest height. Rough, sweat-lit documentary texture.

A small-town Patagonian ice rink after a ceremony: bright even overhead lighting on white ice with faded painted lines, dasher boards patched with tape, and confetti and paper scraps still tumbling down from the roof trusses. A thin scatter of fans sits high in the stands behind the glass. Three adults skate — a tall Icelandic woman in a lavender jacket, a broad Argentine man in black, a compact Korean man in white. All three begin fully in frame, blades on the ice, then link hands, build speed the length of the rink, and whip the tail skater in a wide slinging arc. One continuous shot, camera dollying slowly out; the whipped skater sweeps close and exits frame at the hip. Dreamy pastel glow.

Mist softens a university library plaza in a Patagonian city at sunrise, herringbone brick damp underfoot, a green bronze sundial at the centre and a brutalist facade behind where a failing neon sign flickers and a maintenance searchlight sweeps slowly across the glass. Two adults hold a single square meter each: a Roma-Spanish woman in her forties, dark hair pinned, in a red ruffled skirt; a slim Senegalese man in a black shirt and high-waisted trousers. Fully in frame with heels on the brick, they drill zapateado — heel-toe machine-gun bursts, sharp stops, floreo wrists spiralling overhead, chins raised. One continuous shot from a static tripod at eye level. Grainy, unvarnished, cold morning color.

A shuttered roller rink in a Patagonian town, glossy maple boards scuffed by decades of wheels, an unlit mirror ball hooked over the centre, a closed skate-hire counter, and only low practice lamps leaving long shadows. A few club members lean on the perimeter rail, off the floor. The air is still. Three adults spar with padded practice sticks: a heavyset Māori woman in grey, a tall Iranian-Argentine man in a black tee, a wiry older Korean man in white. Fully framed with shoes on maple, they cut, parry, duck and counter, shuffling within three meters. One continuous shot, camera craning down from high above to eye level. Flat, honest, slightly grainy documentary color.

A municipal indoor pool in Patagonia, lane ropes coiled at the wall, non-slip ceramic tile ringing the basin, and a hired lighting rig throwing magenta and cyan across the still water and the tile. Spectators fill the tiered seating behind the glass barrier, none on the deck. Nothing moves in the air. Four adults stand on one small patch of tile: a bald Trinidadian man, a tall Slovak woman with a blue undercut, a compact Peruvian man, a broad Chinese-Chilean woman. Facing off in two pairs, feet fixed, they pass juggling clubs in fast four-count and then six-club showers, hands snapping, clubs spinning through the colored beams. One continuous shot, camera dollying slowly out. Fully framed throughout, gritty realism.

Storm light bruises the sky over a race circuit pit lane in Patagonia, striped tarmac running past open, empty garages, tyre stacks and a dead timing gantry; wind is absent, the air heavy and waiting. Fans line the grandstand across the main straight, safely behind the wall. Two adults work the lane: a broad Māori-Argentine man in an orange crew shirt and a tall Ukrainian woman with a grey buzz cut. Fully in frame with boots on tarmac, they run a two-person bucket brigade — filling, swinging, sprinting twenty meters, slinging sloshing pails hand to hand and dumping them into a drum, then hammering back. One continuous shot from a static tripod at eye level. Vast, epic, storm-grey contrast.

A converted wool shed on the Patagonian steppe now works as a sound stage: matte black floor, blacked-out windows, a shearing rail still bolted overhead. Practice lamps sit low, carving long shadows. Four adults form a roda on the boards — a lean Bolivian man with a shaved head, a muscular Angolan woman in white trousers, a freckled Argentine woman in her thirties, and a heavy-set Korean man. Two play in the centre: a sweeping meia-lua de compasso answered by a ducking esquiva and a queda de rins, feet whispering over two metres; the others clap the rhythm and rotate in. The air is dead still. One continuous shot tracking sideways at a walking pace, all four fully framed.

The great hall of a Patagonian provincial courthouse after hours: checkerboard marble, brass rails, tungsten work lamps left by restorers, and through the tall windows a flickering neon hotel sign and a slow sweeping searchlight. Five adults stand rooted on the marble, all fully in frame with shoes down from the first beat, each within a stride: a silver-haired Argentine woman in a green blouse, a tall Somali man, a stocky Portuguese man, a slender Korean woman, a broad Māori woman with a shaved side. In shifting pairs and a triangle they trade clubs — singles first, then doubles and triples arcing overhead, every catch cracking clean. One continuous shot, camera craning from high above down to eye level. Dreamy amber and cold blue.

A grey glacial outwash plain in Patagonia, fine gravel braided by shallow meltwater channels, a shattered moraine ridge on one side and fog banks rolling steadily across the flats in the dusty, hazy afternoon wind. Four adults hold their own patches of gravel: a tall Sudanese woman in a bright coral top, a compact Nepali man, a broad Danish woman with a red braid, a lean Chilean man in electric blue. Fully in frame with boots planted, they spin long wooden staffs — figure eights, hand rolls across the shoulders, high vertical tosses caught blind — never shifting their feet more than a step. One continuous shot, camera craning down from high above to eye level. Punchy, saturated, high-energy grade.

Floodlights blaze over a skatepark's smooth cast-concrete flat bottom in a Patagonian suburb, graffiti-scrawled quarterpipe walls rising on both sides, boards and bags dumped by the fence. Poplar leaves swirl low across the concrete in the night breeze. Four adults hold one spot: two bases, a broad Argentine man in a grey hoodie and a strong Nigerian woman in black; a Vietnamese-Chilean man spotting behind; a small freckled Canadian woman as flyer. All four fully in frame, shoes on concrete, they load, dip and basket-toss her high, her whole body staying inside the frame, catching her in a cradle, then setting and tossing again. One continuous shot, camera tracking sideways at walking pace. Grainy, cold-white documentary look.

A tiny boxing gym in a Patagonian mill town: a low ring with a stained canvas mat, sagging ropes, unmarked banners, tungsten work lamps overhead and steam curling from wall vents behind the corner post. Three adults occupy the canvas, each on their own square: a heavyset Cuban man in a grey sweatshirt, a lean Ethiopian woman in maroon, a middle-aged Croatian woman with a grey ponytail. Fully in frame, feet planted from the first beat, they hoist heavy medicine balls overhead and hammer them down into the canvas, catching the low bounce, exhaling hard, again and again in ragged unison. One continuous shot from a static tripod at eye level. Dreamy, hazy, warm amber glow.

A wool mill's weaving hall in Patagonia, rows of silent cast-iron looms threaded with dusty warp, a worn wooden plank floor, tungsten work lamps strung between posts and steam drifting up from floor vents near the boiler wall. Six adults each claim a tight ring of small cones: a broad Finnish man, a quick Colombian woman, a tall Punjabi man, a stocky Argentine woman with a blonde bob, a lean Haitian man, a compact Korean woman in red. Fully in frame, shoes on the planks, they stickhandle pucks through the cones — toe drags, quick dekes, rapid side-to-side — feet barely shifting. One continuous shot, camera craning from high above down to eye level. Bright, snappy, energetic color.

A bamboo grove in a Patagonian valley garden, lit at night by tripod floodlights: packed earth strewn with dry leaves, tall motionless culms overhead, a mossy stone lantern at the edge. The air is calm and the leaves lie undisturbed until he moves. One adult performs: a compact Malaysian-Chilean man in his thirties, gold sash over a black tee, hair cropped. Fully in frame with feet on the earth, he sinks into a deep crouch, freezes, then explodes into a lion-dance style pounce, landing wide, stalking sideways, and springing again across three meters of clearing. One continuous shot, camera tracking sideways at a steady walking pace. Bright, punchy contrast, leaf dust flaring in the beams.

A school gymnasium in a Patagonian mountain town, polished maple with faded key lines, blank felt banners in the rafters, and industrial fans at the doorways stirring loose paper and dust through the bright even overhead light. Students crowd the pull-out bleachers, none on the court. Two adults face each other over a thick hemp rope: a towering Samoan-Argentine man in a black singlet and a broad-shouldered Mongolian woman in red, both chalked and braced. Fully in frame, feet locked in place, they heave in surges, heels skidding a hand's width, dropping to a knee, hauling back up, the rope shivering. One continuous shot, camera dollying slowly in. Epic scale, deep contrast, dust in the beams.

Blue hour over a granite civic plaza in a Patagonian capital, polished pavers holding the last violet sky, a welded wind-turbine-blade monument at the centre and a dark glass tower reflecting the fading horizon. Nothing else stirs; no wind, no passersby. One adult crosses the stone: a tall Ojibwe-Argentine woman in her late twenties, silver puffer jacket, black leggings, long hair loose. Fully in frame, boots on granite, she runs deep drop-backs the length of the plaza, sets her feet, and launches long spirals into the dusk, chasing each throw fifteen meters before resetting. One continuous shot, camera tracking sideways at a steady walking pace. Dreamy, cool indigo grade, breath fogging.

The rolling floor of a mothballed steel mill in Patagonia: heavy steel plate underfoot, cold roller stands and a rusted ladle crane above, with a leftover event rig throwing red and violet beams through dust that big fans keep churning. Four adults gather: a tall Angolan man in a white vest, a stocky Georgian woman with a black braid, a lean Filipino man, a broad Argentine woman in yellow. All fully in frame, boots on plate, they link hands and wind a crack-the-whip chain across fifteen meters, accelerating until the tail runner is flung wide, sprinting toward the lens and cropping out at the waist. One continuous shot, camera tracking sideways at walking pace. Dreamy, smeared color.

Hard bars of daylight tilt down from high windows into a converted wool-warehouse gallery in a Patagonian port town, unhung canvases leaning against lime-washed walls, a floor vent breathing steam across the pale oak planks. Three adults trade fours on one square of floor: a rangy Chilean man in braces and hard-soled shoes; a compact Nigerian-British woman with a silver crop; a stout Argentine man in his fifties, sleeves rolled. Paddle-and-roll riffs answer cramp rolls; a maxie ford snaps out and back, heels drilling the oak, nobody moving off their spot. Steam curls through the light. One continuous shot, the camera panning slowly left to right; all three stay fully framed.

Stamped concrete patterned like slate spreads across a stadium concourse plaza in Patagonia, night floodlights beating down on shuttered ticket gates and a ring of bare planters; dry leaves swirl low over the ground. Fans linger behind the perimeter railing above the ramp, off the plaza itself. Two adults hold one spot of concrete: a tall Afro-Cuban man in a sheer black mesh top and wide silver trousers, and a slim Thai woman in a magenta bodysuit, hair slicked. Fully in frame, heels planted, they slice through sharp hand performance, duckwalk a half-step, then spiral into death-drop dips and snap back up, again and again. One continuous shot from a static tripod camera at eye level. Dreamy, glossy, saturated color.

Golden hour floods a crushed red brick clay court behind a Lagos tennis club, torn bunting and a windsock snapping hard in the gusts, palm crowns thrashing past the chain fence. Two adults dance on one small patch: a tall Nigerian man in his thirties, lean, close-cropped hair, in a loose saffron shirt, and a curvy Filipina woman in her forties with a long black braid and a teal skirt that flies open in the wind. He leads her through three fast salsa spins, catches her hand, and sweeps a cross-body lead, feet grinding clay dust, all in one continuous shot. Spectators watch from a shaded bleacher outside the fence. A static tripod camera at eye level holds them fully in frame, dreamy and warm.

Thin rain glazes a close-mown turf lawn behind a shuttered Lagos racquet club, the white service lines shining like wet chalk, a rolled net cart parked at the edge. Nobody else is anywhere near; the surrounding hedges stand empty. Four adults train shoulder to shoulder on one patch of grass: a broad Ghanaian man in his twenties in a red singlet, a wiry Korean woman in her thirties in navy shorts, a stocky Brazilian man in his forties, and a tall Somali woman with cropped hair in yellow. In pairs they snap off body-lock throws and scramble back to their feet, spraying water. One continuous shot, a slow dolly-out revealing more of the surroundings, bright and energetic, everyone fully framed.

Along the lagoon, broad concrete slabs of a Lagos riverside esplanade glow orange in windless golden hour, moored ferries motionless below the seawall and a shuttered kite stall at the far end. Four adults take turns bounding: a lanky Nigerian man in his twenties in lime shorts, a muscular Mexican woman in her thirties in white, a bald Indian man in his forties, and a freckled Irish woman with red curls in purple. Each explodes into a hop, a long step and a final jump, landing hard within a few meters, then jogs back. Onlookers cheer from behind the railing above. The camera makes a slow pan from left to right in one continuous shot, playful and upbeat, all four fully in frame.

Floodlights on tall poles bleach the mown lawn of a corporate campus in Lagos; a mirrored office tower looms behind with one lit stairwell, an idle shuttle bus parked at the kerb. Two adults work the grass from end to end: a heavyset Nigerian woman in her forties with locs tied back, wearing a grey warm-up jacket, and a slim Vietnamese man in his twenties in a white tee. She strides through a full pitching windup and fires a hard throw the length of the lawn; he catches, jogs wide, and rifles it back, both crossing the frame. Staff watch from a raised terrace behind a railing. Filmed as one continuous shot, camera tracking sideways at a steady walking pace, gritty and documentary.

Inside a small squash court in a Lagos hotel basement, pale hardwood is scuffed with black ball marks, the tin telltale dented, warm tungsten work lamps clamped to the balcony rail. Haze drifts and two little spotlights sweep across the front wall. One adult occupies the space: a stocky Afro-Caribbean man in his thirties, shaved head, orange jersey and black shorts. He weaves a ball through six plastic cones with a stick, dropping his shoulder for quick dekes, cutting back and forth over a few meters of floor with sneakers squeaking. Nobody else is inside. One continuous shot, the camera tracking sideways at a steady walking pace, playful and bright; he stays fully in frame, feet on the wood.

Thick fog drowns a stretch of short golden grass on the savanna edge beyond Lagos, a lone flat-crowned thorn tree and a line of leaning rusted fence posts fading into white. Pale flakes drift through the shafts of light cutting the mist. Two adults are alone out here: a tall Kenyan woman in her thirties with a shaved head in a slate tracksuit, and a broad Turkish man in his forties, dark beard, in a maroon top. Each carries a javelin, accelerates through crossover steps across many meters of ground, plants hard and launches; then they walk out to retrieve and repeat. Epic and cinematic, one continuous shot, the camera tracking sideways at a steady walking pace, both fully in frame.

A packed gravel crossroads outside Lagos sits under a bruised, swollen sky minutes before rain; a leaning wooden signpost with its plates stripped bare and a broad mango tree mark one corner, dust hanging dead still. Six adults spar in three pairs across a few meters: a rangy Nigerian man in his twenties in white, a compact Japanese woman in her thirties, a grey-bearded Lebanese man, a tall Dutch woman in green, a stocky Peruvian man, and a lean Ethiopian woman in blue. Padded sticks crack together as they lunge, slip, and counter, gravel skidding under their heels. No one else for miles. One continuous shot, camera tracking sideways at a steady walking pace, epic and cinematic.

Deep in an empty Lagos distribution warehouse, polished concrete runs like a black river between towering bare racks; magenta and cyan stage lights bleed across the columns while haze hangs thick and two spotlights swing. Four adults line up abreast on the floor, no one else in the building: a powerful Nigerian woman in her thirties in a red crop top, a wiry Chinese man in his twenties in white, a tall Polish man with blond stubble in blue, and a broad Jamaican woman in her forties in gold. On a shout they burst into a flat-out sprint, arms hammering, covering the long aisle to a taped finish line. Moody neo-noir, one continuous shot, a slow dolly-in toward the runners keeps all four framed.

A rehearsal studio above a Lagos music school: black marley vinyl, a long mirror with one cracked panel taped at the corner, wooden barres washed in violet and cold green neon from a rig in the corner. The air is perfectly still. Two adults share the floor with nobody else present: a slender Nigerian woman in her twenties, hair in a high bun, in a rust leotard, and a muscular Argentinian man in his thirties, dark ponytail, bare-chested in grey joggers. She launches a no-hand cartwheel; he answers with a front aerial, and they trade whipping passes back and forth across a few meters. Dreamy music-video mood, one continuous shot, a slow pan from left to right, both fully in frame throughout.

Under Lagos, a disused bunker hall arches overhead in bare damp concrete, water beading on fat pipes, two cable spools shoved against the wall. Low practice lamps carve deep shadows while haze glows and spotlights swing slowly. Four adults play alone down here: a broad Nigerian man in his forties in a grey vest, a small athletic Thai woman in her twenties, a tall Russian man with sandy hair, and a curvy Egyptian woman in a purple tee. Two crouch low, the others sprint in and leapfrog clean over their backs, then swap roles instantly, the chain drifting a few meters across the wet floor. One continuous shot, the camera cranes down from high above to eye level, playful and bright.

A small judo dojo in Lagos, green tatami mats seamed with tape, a row of white judogi hanging on pegs and a dented water urn by the door. Harsh floodlights rake in from one side only, cutting hard shadows across the mats; the air is dead calm. One adult trains here alone: a powerfully built Nigerian woman in her thirties, hair in tight cornrows, in a black sports top and red shorts, barefoot on the tatami. She whips two heavy ropes into fast alternating waves, drops into a squat, then slams both ends down again and again, never shifting off her single square of mat. One continuous shot, the camera in a slow orbit around her, upbeat and bright, feet always visible.

An off-season ice rink in Lagos with the ice long gone: a painted concrete slab inside scarred dasher boards, a taped-over scoreboard hanging dark, big industrial fans stirring loose paper and dust across the surface. Red and blue stage lights slice the gloom. Six adults train alone in three pairs, moving within a few meters: a lean Nigerian man in his twenties, a tall Ukrainian woman with a blonde ponytail, a stocky Filipino man, a muscular Ethiopian woman in orange, a bearded Moroccan man, and a compact Korean woman in black. Three hold hand paddles high; the others sprint two steps and launch flying kicks that crack the pads. One continuous shot, a slow pan from left to right, moody neo-noir.

Inside a cavernous Lagos bus depot, asphalt bays striped in faded yellow stretch away between concrete pillars; shafts of daylight pour through high clerestory windows and big fans push loose paper and glittering dust through the beams. Three adults occupy one bay, nobody else in the hall: a tall Nigerian woman in her thirties with braids coiled up, in a lilac top, a compact Bolivian man in his twenties, and a silver-haired Australian woman in her forties. Two hold focus mitts and circle; the third rips jab-cross-hook combinations, then they rotate, drifting a couple of meters over the bays. Dreamy, hazy music-video tone, one continuous shot, the camera cranes down from high above to eye level.

Snow falls thick over a faded asphalt parking apron on a Lagos film lot, drifts collecting along the painted bays while fireworks burst silently far beyond the plywood hoardings. Five adults are alone out here in sport fencing jackets: a tall Nigerian man in his twenties, a stocky Hungarian woman in her forties, a lean Indian man, a broad Nigerian-British woman with silver locs, and a young Portuguese man. With foils they trade explosive lunges and parry-ripostes, blades ringing, footwork sliding through the snow within a few meters. After the opening seconds one of them advances hard toward the lens and ends partly out of frame. One continuous shot, the camera cranes down from high above to eye level, playful and bright.

A wide plain of fine grey ash beside a cement quarry outside Lagos, spoil heaps dusted white and a rusted conveyor angling into the sky. Snow falls heavily while dry leaves skitter low across the ash in ribbons. One adult stands out here alone: a tall Nigerian-Brazilian man in his thirties, athletic, hair in short twists, wearing a scarlet marching jacket with gold cord and black trousers, a snare drum slung at his hip. He hammers out a rattling roll, marches a long line across many meters of ash, snaps a sharp pivot turn, and marches back drumming, boot prints trailing behind. One continuous shot with a slow pan from left to right, bright and playful, he stays fully in frame.

Blue hour settles over a Lagos football stadium: striped natural grass, a blank scoreboard glowing faintly, half the seats in shadow. Flurries drift through the floodlight beams. One adult works the pitch, a broad-shouldered Nigerian man in his forties with a greying beard, in a sleeveless white kit and long socks; his boots are already dark with wet grass. Crouched low, he drives a wooden barrel forward at a full sprint, chasing it the length of the field, slapping it straight when it wobbles. Fans watch from the stands high behind the advertising boards. One continuous shot, a slow dolly-in toward him; after the opening beat he barrels close to the lens and ends partly out of frame.

A converted Lagos crossfit box: black rubber tiles, chalk-dusted barbells racked along a corrugated wall, a rope hanging from an exposed beam, everything washed in hot pink and cold blue stage light. Paper scraps and confetti tumble down through the beams from a fan overhead. Four adults train alone in two pairs across a few meters: a rangy Nigerian woman in her twenties in a black gi top, a stocky Swedish man in his forties, a tall Sri Lankan man in indigo, and a compact Mexican woman with a tight bun. Wooden practice swords crack together as they drive forward in lunging strikes and snap back. One continuous shot from a static tripod camera at eye level, moody neo-noir.

Rain glosses the wet concrete floor of a Lagos dry dock, keel blocks lined up like teeth beneath a rust-streaked hull wall, a gantry crane dripping overhead and confetti scraps tumbling on the damp air. Two adults are the only people down here: a tall Nigerian woman in her twenties in a yellow raincoat over shorts, and a stocky Colombian man in his forties in a soaked blue tee, their inside ankles lashed together with a red strap. They stagger, sync up, and sprint the length of the dock in laughing lurches, water fanning from their shoes. One continuous shot, a slow pan from left to right; near the end they surge at the camera and one ends partly out of frame.

Harsh midday sun hammers a wide beach of packed damp sand east of Lagos, a black timber groyne running seaward and a weathered lifeguard tower with peeling paint; the air is calm, the breakers distant. Two adults are alone on the sand: a lean Nigerian man in his twenties in navy trunks, and a strong Samoan woman in her thirties with hair tied high, in a red one-piece. Both lie prone facing away, then spring up on a whistle, sprint many meters down the beach, and dive full-length for a rubber flag stuck in the sand, skidding through the spray. Bright and energetic, one continuous shot, a handheld camera slowly circling at chest height, both fully in frame.

Blue hour over a hillside vineyard outside Lagos: a tractor row of compacted soil runs between wire trellises heavy with leaves, a tin shed and a parked trailer at the far end. Flurries drift through the last work-lamp beams. Four adults race alone down the row: a broad Nigerian man in his thirties in a green vest, a small wiry Nepali woman in her twenties, a tall Danish woman with a blonde crop, and a bearded Iraqi man in a grey shirt. Each shoves an oak barrel, sprinting bent double, wheels of wood churning dust as they cover the whole length of the row. One continuous shot from a static tripod camera at eye level, playful and bright, all four fully framed.

In the bank district of Lagos, a sunken plaza of black granite lies still under golden hour, a dry fountain basin at its center and mirrored towers throwing long amber reflections across the stone behind. Onlookers lean on the upper railing, watching from above. Four adults hold the stone floor: a tall Nigerian woman in her forties in a navy gi top, a slim Japanese-Nigerian man in his twenties, a stocky Greek man with a shaved head, and a lean Malaysian woman in white. In two pairs they drive forward with lunging steps, bamboo practice swords snapping down on head and wrist cuts, shifting a few meters. One continuous shot, a slow pan from left to right, dreamy and golden.

An unfinished road tunnel under Lagos: raw shotcrete floor still gritty, ribbed steel arches overhead, a parked drilling jumbo and stacked precast segments against one wall, warm tungsten work lamps strung along the arch in a receding chain. The air hangs still. Five adults play alone in the bore, moving a few meters: a lean Nigerian man in his twenties in a yellow tee, a tall Canadian woman in her thirties, a stocky Nigerian-Indian man, a short muscular Chilean woman, and a grey-templed Kenyan man. A disc floats out and two of them launch into full layout dives, skimming the shotcrete, then bounce up laughing. One continuous shot, the camera cranes down from high above to eye level, bright and energetic.

Bright even overhead lighting fills a Lagos shipyard fabrication shed, the floor a patchwork of rust-stained steel plate; half-built hull sections stand on stands and a gantry crane hangs still above. Big fans stir loose paper and welding dust in slow spirals. Two adults have the shed to themselves: a tall Nigerian man in his thirties, heavy shoulders, in a white sleeveless top, and a fast Puerto Rican woman in her twenties with a curly ponytail, in teal. He backpedals through a deep drop-back, sets, and launches a long spiral down the shed; she sprints many meters across the plates and hauls it in, then jogs it back. One continuous shot, the camera cranes down from high above to eye level, bright and energetic.

A fencing hall in Lagos, its metallic piste laid over grey rubber flooring, coiled reel cables at each end and faded club banners lit hot magenta and green by a stage rig. The air is still. Two adults dart along the strip: a wiry Nigerian man in his twenties in a white tracksuit, and a tall Brazilian woman in her thirties with a dark bob, in a yellow tee. Forget blades: they play tag, cutting sharply left and right, feinting, then lunging with an outstretched hand to slap a shoulder before scrambling back, all inside a few meters. Club members watch from a raised gallery behind the railing. One continuous shot, a handheld camera slowly circling at chest height, playful and upbeat.

Inside a timber barn outside Lagos, wide plank floorboards creak underfoot; hay bales are stacked to one wall and old leather tack hangs from nails. Harsh floodlights blast in from one side through the open door, hard-edged and dusty, and nothing else stirs. One adult holds the floor, alone: a slim Nigerian woman in her twenties, hair wrapped in an ochre scarf, wearing a white marching tunic with black piping, a snare drum strapped at her waist. Fully in frame, she rips a tight roll, marches three steps, snaps a crisp pivot turn on the ball of her foot, and marches back, staying within a couple of meters. One continuous shot, camera tracking sideways at a steady walking pace, upbeat and warm.

An abandoned brick factory hall in Lagos: broken brick tile underfoot, two collapsed kiln mouths gaping in the far wall, iron girders overhead washed in orange and green stage light while haze rolls and spotlights swing. Six adults train alone in three pairs, working a few meters of floor: a lean Nigerian man in his twenties in red shorts, a tall Dutch-Surinamese woman in black, a stocky Uzbek man, a muscular Nigerian woman with a shaved head, a young Italian man in blue, and a compact Filipina woman. Each pair locks a plum clinch and fires alternating knees into belly pads, breaking and resetting fast. One continuous shot, a slow dolly-out revealing more of the hall, playful and punchy.

Light rain turns an old flagstone threshing floor near Lagos into a sheet of reflections, a low crumbling stone wall ringing it and a rusted winnowing fan tipped on its side; fireworks bloom small and bright over the ridge beyond. One adult is out here alone, no one else in sight: a compact Nigerian woman in her thirties, powerful legs, hair in short twists, wearing a cobalt long-sleeve top and black leggings. She swings her arms, drops, and snaps a standing back tuck on one spot, sticking the wet stone, then immediately throws another, and another, spray flicking off her shoes. Bright, energetic sports-ad tone, one continuous shot, a slow dolly-in toward her, feet always visible.

Snow drives sideways across a mesa-top plateau far beyond Lagos, hardpan crusted with sparse scrub and a wind-carved rock stack marking the drop; rain streaks slant through it and puddles splash underfoot. Two adults are alone up here: a rangy Nigerian man in his twenties in a soaked grey hoodie, and a strong Croatian woman in her forties with a wet blonde plait, in black. She fires a ball long; he runs a hard post route across many meters of ground, cuts, and hauls in an over-the-shoulder catch at full speed, then they swap and run it again. Gritty documentary feel, one continuous shot, the camera tracking sideways at a steady walking pace, both fully framed.

Harsh midday sun bleaches a rooftop terrace of concrete pavers high over Lagos, the skyline hazy behind a rusted water tank while steam curls lazily from a bank of vent stacks. Neighbours watch from a balcony on the next building, well behind the parapet. One adult works up here: a heavyset Nigerian man in his forties, thick arms, hair shaved to stubble, in a sweat-darkened olive tank top and grey shorts. Planted over a battered tractor tire, he raises a sledgehammer overhead and drives it down, again and again, alternating hands, never moving off his spot as rubber shudders. Dreamy, sun-drunk music-video mood, one continuous shot, a slow pan from left to right keeps him fully in frame.

Blue hour drains the color from a desert pavement flat outside Lagos, tight-packed dark pebbles stretching to a leaning survey marker and a pale seam of salt crust; dust blows low and fast across the ground. One adult moves alone through the emptiness: a lithe Nigerian-Lebanese woman in her twenties, close-cropped bleached hair, in a charcoal unitard and taped hands. She launches a cartwheel, links a round-off, then another and another, chaining passes many meters across the flat with her hands slapping stone and grit spitting up. Moody neo-noir, cold shadow with one last blue rim on the horizon. One continuous shot, a handheld camera slowly circling at chest height keeps her fully in frame, feet on the pebbles.

Golden hour lies flat across a dry lakebed of cracked pale clay outside Lagos, an abandoned water trailer half-sunk at the margin and a low escarpment burning orange far off. The air is completely still, not a soul around. Two adults run the playa: a tall Nigerian woman in her thirties, long braids bound back, in a white singlet, and a lean Bangladeshi man in his twenties in maroon. She winds up to full speed, calls, and slaps the baton into his back-turned palm as he accelerates away, both covering long ground across the frame before jogging back to reset. Gritty documentary texture, one continuous shot, the camera cranes down from high above to eye level, both fully in frame.

Golden hour turns a closed highway overpass outside Lagos amber; lane-marked asphalt runs empty between concrete barriers, a shredded advertising banner cracking violently in the wind and tower cranes standing far off. No one else is up here. One adult works a single spot: a huge Nigerian man in his forties, thick beard, in a chalk-smeared black singlet with a leather belt, wrists taped. He squats over a rough stone ball, laps it onto his thighs, roars, and heaves it onto a steel platform, drops it, resets, and hoists again, his footprint never shifting. Epic cinematic weight, dust and chalk flying in the gusts. One continuous shot from a static tripod camera at eye level, feet planted on the asphalt.

Blue hour deepens over an industrial loft rooftop in Lagos, tar-and-gravel membrane crunching underfoot inside a low brick parapet, a bolted steel water tower and a forest of aerials black against the fading skyline. The air is dead calm. Two adults are alone up here: a broad Nigerian man in his thirties, bare-chested with taped fists, and a tall Serbian woman in her forties, blonde hair braided tight, in a black rash guard. She holds a hand paddle high; he takes two hard steps and explodes into a flying kick that snaps the pad, then they switch roles, drifting a few meters over the roof. Epic cinematic scale, one continuous shot, a slow dolly-in toward them, both fully in frame.

A derelict drive-in theater lot outside Lagos bakes gold in late light: cracked asphalt seamed with gravel, rows of rusted speaker posts leaning, and a blank weather-eaten screen tower at the head of the field. Flurries drift through the projector-booth beam. Four adults train alone: a stocky Nigerian man in his thirties in a faded orange tee, a tall Sudanese woman with close-cropped hair, a lean Vietnamese-Nigerian man in grey, and a broad Chilean woman in her forties. A rope ladder is laid on the asphalt; each burns through it with hammering in-and-out footwork, then peels off a few meters and jogs back. Gritty documentary texture, one continuous shot, camera tracking sideways at a steady walking pace.

Midday sun hammers a festival pier on the Lagos lagoon: painted steel plate deck, limp bunting strung between light poles, moored wooden boats nudging the piles. Six adults take turns across three metres of hot plate — a tall Yoruba man in yellow shorts, a muscular Igbo woman with cornrows, a lean Ghanaian man in white, a curvy Nigerian-Lebanese woman, a wiry man in his forties with a grey beard, a broad woman in emerald. Each runs two steps and throws something different: a raiz kicking over, a cheat-setup hook kick spinning past head height, a low swing-through twist landing flat. Air hangs motionless. Spectators crowd the railed walkway behind. One continuous shot, static tripod at eye level, all six fully framed.

Harsh midday sun beats down on a trodden red-earth walkway cutting through a tea plantation in the hills near Lagos, clipped green bushes rolling away on both sides, a tin picking shed and a stack of woven baskets at the bend. Nothing moves but him. One adult stands alone on the path: a wiry Nigerian man in his twenties, athletic, hair in short twists, in a sky-blue vest and black shorts, dust on his bare calves. He sets his feet, swings his arms, and snaps a standing back tuck, landing on the same spot, then immediately throws another, and a third, red dust puffing at each landing. Bright energetic sports-ad tone, one continuous shot with a slow orbit around him.

The atrium lobby of a deserted Lagos business hotel, polished marble under even ceiling light, a dry terrazzo planter and a bank of shuttered reception desks behind. One adult owns the floor: a tall, slender Nigerian man in his late twenties, sculpted flat-top, wide black trousers, a sleeveless white top. Standing on one marble slab, he cuts precise hand performance, snaps a catwalk pivot into a fast spin, then folds backward into a controlled dip, one leg extended, and rises again without a wobble. Big fans push loose paper and dust skidding past him. One continuous shot, the camera craning down from high above to eye level; he stays fully framed throughout.

Mist hangs over the packed sand floor of a sand and gravel pit outside Lagos, a dead conveyor and steep spoil cones looming through the haze while flickering neon from a site sign and sweeping searchlights cut the sunrise gloom. Four adults are alone on the pit floor: a powerful Nigerian woman in her twenties in a pink crop top, a lanky Ethiopian man in white, a stocky German man in his forties, and a compact Nigerian-Chinese woman in yellow. They coil into starting blocks, fire out on a shout, and drive through long accelerating strides over many meters. One continuous shot, a slow dolly-in toward them; after the opening one runner surges close and ends partly out of frame. Bright and energetic.

Portable floodlights on a trailer blaze across a harvested field near Lagos, straw stubble bristling in neat rows with round bales scattered and a pale grain silo standing far off in the dark. The night air is completely still, nobody else around. Four adults play across the ground: a broad Nigerian man in his thirties in a green kit, a fast Nigerian-Portuguese woman in her twenties with a bleached buzzcut, a tall Ivorian man in white, and a stocky Turkish woman in her forties. They spread wide, ping crosses through the light, and hammer power shots and full volleys into a portable goal, sprinting many meters between strikes. One continuous shot from a static tripod camera at eye level, playful and upbeat.

Golden hour warms a dry riverbed outside Lagos, a broad sand bar of pale river sand curling between banks of bleached driftwood, a low stone bridge with two arches spanning the empty channel. The air is perfectly still and nobody else is around. One adult trains here: a strong Nigerian woman in her thirties, hair in tight cornrows, in a bright coral one-piece and taped fingers. She lies face down in the sand, springs up on a whistle, sprints many meters along the bar with sand flying from her heels, and launches into a full-length dive to snatch a rubber flag, sliding to a stop. Playful and upbeat, one continuous shot with a slow orbit around her, always fully in frame.

Inside a converted woolshed skate park in inner-west Sydney, plywood quarter-pipes curve away under rusted roof trusses and two industrial fans push loose paper scraps and glittering dust across the floor. Exactly two adults work a short water relay on the smooth plywood flat: a tall Filipino man in his thirties, wiry, in an orange singlet, swings a full pail sideways to a broad-shouldered white woman in her forties with cropped grey hair and teal shorts, who pivots, sloshes it three metres on, and sprints the empty pail back. Harsh floodlights rake in from one side, carving epic shadows. One continuous shot, a slow pan from left to right, both fully in frame, feet on the wood.

Big hoops go out with heavy backspin, skidding along the reinforced concrete of a container quay in Sydney's inner harbour. Six adults — a rangy Vietnamese-Australian man, a strong Tongan woman, a bald Croatian man in his fifties, a tall Ethiopian woman in orange, a freckled woman with a sandy plait, a compact Chilean man — begin in a line, feet on the slab, all fully framed, then chase the returning rims and dive clean through them mid-roll, covering twenty metres past stacked boxes and a dead straddle carrier. Noon sun bleaches the twistlock-scarred quay; fog banks push off the water and swallow the far cranes. One continuous shot from a static tripod at eye level, all six staying fully in frame.

Golden hour floods a long gravel median walk beneath Moreton Bay figs on a Sydney boulevard, cast-iron benches and low bollards flicking past as distant traffic streaks the flanking lanes with smeared red and white light trails. Two adults crouch on the compacted fine gravel, both fully in frame with spikes dug in: a lean Vietnamese-Australian woman around thirty in a green crop top and black shorts, and a broad Māori man in his late twenties, shaved head, grey singlet. On an unspoken cue they explode out of the crouch, shins low, gravel spraying, driving hard through the first eight strides and away down the strip. Gritty documentary grain, one continuous shot from a static tripod at eye level, no one else around.

Six adults lock wrists into a chain on the mown turf of a grass airstrip west of Sydney: three broad men in orange singlets, three lean women in navy tracksuits, hair braided, buzzed or greying, twenties through fifties, Korean, Anglo and Nigerian faces. Fat snowflakes fall past two tin hangars and an ice-stiffened windsock; steam creeps from a fuel-shed vent. They sprint in a widening arc, the leader skids and plants, the line snaps around, and the tail runner is slung free, bolting across the strip with arms wheeling. One continuous shot, camera tracking sideways at a steady walking pace, all six on the grass, fully framed.

A decommissioned toll plaza on a Sydney orbital sits abandoned under heavy snowfall, booths shuttered, boom gates frozen half-raised, fog banks rolling between the lanes and softening the yellow arrows painted on concrete. One adult plays the whole race alone: a cheerful Lebanese-Australian man in his thirties, stocky, wearing a bright pink beanie and a canary windbreaker, both legs inside a hessian sack. He bounds down the lane paint in big two-footed hops, wobbles, tips, tumbles shoulder-first into slush, laughs, wriggles upright and hops on toward an imaginary finish forty metres away. Playful, upbeat and colourful; one continuous shot with a slow pan from left to right. He stays fully in frame, feet on the concrete, entirely alone.

Blue hour settles over the raw poured slab of an unfinished Sydney tower, rebar bundles and flapping blue tarps at the edge, harbour lights blooming beyond, snowflakes drifting bright through a work-lamp beam. Four adults take turns at a cheerful strength game on the flat concrete, all four fully in frame with boots down at the start: a burly Tongan woman in a fluoro vest, a lanky Dutch-Australian man in red overalls, a silver-haired Chinese-Australian man in grey, and a freckled woman in a blue jumper. Each squats over an empty steel keg, swings it twice and flings it backward over one shoulder, whooping. The last thrower then strides toward the lens, ending cropped at the waist. One continuous shot, slow dolly-out revealing the deck.

On the flat concrete apron of a sandstone amphitheater carved into a Sydney headland, two adults train: a tall Māori woman in a maroon crop top and black shorts, and a wiry silver-haired man in his fifties, brown skin, grey sweatpants, holding curved pads. She drills a switch-step body kick, then a spinning back kick that thuds into the leather, resetting on the same square metre. Overcast light lies flat and silver; fireworks bloom silently over the harbour beyond, and spectators watch from the tiered stone seats above, none on the stage. One continuous shot, a slow dolly-in toward them, both fully in frame, feet on concrete.

Rain falls lightly on a flat alpine meadow bench high above the Blue Mountains west of Sydney, the short flowering turf slicked and reflective between two granite boulders and a stunted snow gum. Otherwise the air is dead still. Three adults train there, all fully in frame at first with bare feet in wet grass: a tall Ethiopian-Australian man in his thirties in a white dobok top, a muscular Croatian-Australian woman around forty in black, and a slim Japanese-Australian man in blue. They alternate spinning hook kicks and stepping back kicks, whipping heels through the drizzle, spray flicking from their heels. Midway one steps toward the camera and finishes cropped at the chest. Epic cinematic mood, one continuous shot orbiting slowly around them.

Light rain lacquers the cobblestone roadway of an old sandstone arch bridge spanning a creek in Sydney's south, iron lamp standards glowing faintly, ivy trailing from the parapet, the air otherwise perfectly still. One adult occupies the crossing: a willowy Māori woman in her late twenties, long dark hair loose and wet, wearing a lilac windbreaker, legs zipped into a burlap sack. She bunny-hops the shining stones with knees driving high, gathers pace across the span, catches a raised cobble and sprawls into a puddle, then worms the sack under her, rocks upright and pumps on toward the far parapet. Dreamy, saturated reflections; one continuous shot with a slow dolly-in toward her. She remains fully in frame the whole time, alone on the bridge.

A small Surry Hills yoga studio has been rigged strangely tonight: haze-machine fog drifts low over pale bamboo flooring while two spotlights sweep slowly across rolled mats and a wall of hanging straps, the rest sunk in deep shadow. Two adults have turned it into a water line. A stocky Polish-Australian woman in her twenties, bleached hair and a maroon crop top, dunks a pail in a drum and swings it dripping to a sinewy Sri Lankan-Australian man in his forties, bare-chested with a towel at his waist; he lunges two paces, empties it into a tub, and skims the empty pail back across the boards. Water slaps the bamboo. Gritty documentary texture, one continuous shot, a slow dolly-out revealing the studio.

Daylight drops in hard shafts through high windows of a wrestling room under a Sydney suburban grandstand, red foam mats seamed with tape, steam curling from a wall vent. Three adults work: a stocky Samoan man in a yellow rashguard, a freckled redhead woman in blue, and a lean Vietnamese-Australian in his thirties, grey singlet. Two tuck into tight crouches a stride apart; the third vaults the first with both hands planted, dives flat under the second, springs up and swaps in, the trio rotating over a few metres of mat. One continuous shot, a slow dolly-in toward them, all three fully framed with feet on the mat. Bright, punchy sports-ad energy.

Floodlights mounted on old signal posts wash an elevated park walkway built on a disused Sydney rail viaduct, its tapered concrete planks running between steel handrails and planted beds of ferns; the night air is completely still. One adult trains alone on the planks: a powerfully built Nigerian-Australian woman in her thirties, hair in tight cornrows, wearing a charcoal long-sleeve and neon-green shorts. She sinks, swings both arms and fires off a standing broad jump, sticks the landing, spins back to her mark, and chains three more bounds that keep her inside a few metres of decking, breath clouding in the light. Epic cinematic contrast against the black city. One continuous shot, camera tracking sideways at a steady walking pace; she stays fully framed.

Under a rail embankment in inner Sydney, a tiled pedestrian underpass glows amber from tungsten work lamps clamped to scaffold poles; steam seeps from a grated vent and pools along the floor. Three adults drill on a taped grid chalked across the tiles: a tall Sudanese-Australian woman in a green windbreaker, a compact man in his forties with a salt-and-pepper beard, and a broad blonde woman in maroon. They rip through in-in-out-out hops, then lateral scissor steps, then a sudden 180 and a two-step burst back, all inside three metres. One continuous shot, the camera panning slowly from left to right, everyone fully in frame, shoes hammering the concrete.

A vast commercial glasshouse on Sydney's outskirts stretches into haze: endless trellised tomato rows, overhead misting pipes, and long shafts of daylight dropping through the high glass onto a wide concrete walkway. The air hangs perfectly still. One adult runs the aisle, a lithe Argentinian-Australian woman in her twenties with a dark ponytail, in a cream leotard and soft shoes, two four-metre silk streamers, rose and pale gold, knotted to her wrists. She sprints, breaks into long galloping leaps, carves the ribbons into looping spirals above the plants, spins mid-stride and pours on speed down thirty metres of walkway. Dreamy, sun-bleached music-video palette. One continuous shot, handheld camera slowly circling at chest height; she stays fully in frame, alone.

A bruised purple storm sky presses down on the open top deck of a Parramatta parking garage, faded bay markings on painted concrete, a squat lift block and a rusted vent stack at the far corner, the air heavy and unnaturally still before the rain. Two adults work a hose drill: a rangy Egyptian-Australian man in his forties in a charcoal tee, and a stocky Vietnamese-Australian woman in her thirties with a bleached buzzcut and orange gloves. She yanks the nozzle and sprints across forty metres of deck, canvas hose unreeling and snapping flat behind her, while he feeds coils fast off the reel; she drops it, spins, and sprints back. Moody neo-noir, one continuous shot, slow dolly-in toward them. No one else present.

Midday sun hammers a cobbled colonial square in Sydney's Rocks district while low fog banks slide between sandstone arcades and pool around a dry stone fountain, giving the rounded cobblestones a soft, unreal glow. Six adults line up shoulder to shoulder, all fully in frame with feet on the stones: a tall Ghanaian-Australian woman in coral, a wiry Turkish-Australian man in white, a broad blonde woman in denim shorts, a bearded Punjabi-Australian man in mustard, a freckled redheaded man in green, and a compact Filipino woman in violet. They burst forward together and race the length of the square to a chalked line, arms pumping, hair streaming. Dreamy diffused music-video haze, one continuous shot tracking sideways at a steady walking pace.

Bright even fluorescents flatten every shadow inside a warehouse loading dock bay in Sydney's south, roller doors half-open onto blackness, pallet stacks and a dented dock leveller behind, big pedestal fans dragging loose paper and dust in slow spirals across the sealed concrete. One adult performs alone on a single spot: a slender Korean-Australian man in his twenties, hair bleached platinum, wearing a boxy grey suit jacket over a black tee and wide trousers. He fires sharp popping hits through chest and shoulders, rolls a clean arm wave from fingertip to fingertip, snaps into stiff robotic angles, glides a half-turn and locks. Moody neo-noir grading despite the flat light. One continuous shot, handheld camera slowly circling at chest height, feet always on the concrete.

Heavy snow settles on a hot-air balloon launch paddock west of Sydney; a half-deflated striped envelope lies slack across the mown grass beside a wicker basket and a propane trolley, and the still air lets each flake fall straight down. Two adults dance on one patch of white-dusted turf: a tall Brazilian-Australian man in his thirties in a fringed silver jacket, and a heavyset Indigenous woman in her forties with a shaved head and a scarlet bodysuit. They snap through arm-length vogue lines, catwalk quarter-turns and hand performance, then whip a spin and drop into a death-drop dip, backs to the grass, before ratcheting straight back up. Gritty documentary texture, one continuous shot orbiting slowly around them. The paddock is empty.

Golden hour turns a chalk downland plateau south of Sydney amber, its short springy turf broken by pale limestone outcrops; far below, headlights smear the coast road into ribbons of light. One adult crosses the plateau, a muscular Fijian-Australian man in his late twenties, hair cropped, in a sleeveless white top and cobalt shorts, gripping two long crimson streamers on short handles. He drives into a bounding gallop, arms scything so the ribbons crack open behind him, then flattens into an all-out sprint that carries him clear across the frame, the crimson braiding and unfurling in the low sun. Bright energetic sports-ad clarity. One continuous shot, camera tracking sideways at a steady walking pace; he stays fully in frame and alone.

A bare grey granite plateau above the Sydney basin lies flat as a table between weathered tors and a leaning stone cairn, while a black storm front stacks up on the horizon; the air is completely calm, pre-rain and electric. Six adults sprint a hurdle row of six portable barriers set across the rock: a tall Kenyan-Australian woman in yellow, a stocky Maltese-Australian man in blue, a lean woman with silver-dyed hair in pink, a bearded Iranian-Australian man in white, a broad Samoan woman in green, and a freckled man in orange. They attack in a stagger, lead legs snapping over each hurdle, arms driving, covering thirty metres of stone. Bright sports-ad energy, one continuous shot, slow dolly-out revealing the plateau.

A bank of night floodlights on the levee spills hard white light across a drained rice paddy on Sydney's western fringe, cracked mud plates glowing between low bunds while rain slants through the beams and bursts in puddles beside a rusted pump shed. Four adults run a long-jump session, all fully in frame with feet on the mud: a rangy Sudanese-Australian man in black, a compact Japanese-Australian woman in red, a broad Scottish-Australian man with a ginger beard in grey, and a tall woman with locs in white. Each pounds out a fifteen-metre run-up, hits a scraped takeoff mark, hangs with knees driving, and lands heels-first into wet mud, spraying water. Moody neo-noir contrast, one continuous shot orbiting slowly around them. No spectators.

Flat grey concrete fills the infield of an ageing Sydney velodrome, the steep timber track curving up on all sides under flat, even ceiling lamps. Four adults work two long ropes: a heavyset Fijian man and a grey-braided woman in her fifties turn the arcs steadily, while a slim Indian-Australian in a black tee and a freckled woman in orange take turns diving in, hammering high-knee speed jumps, spinning a full turn between beats, then ducking out and tagging the next. Spectators watch from the tiered seats behind the railing above the banking, none on the concrete. One continuous shot, a slow pan from left to right; all four stay fully in frame.

Rain hisses across the flat marble cutting floor of a quarry west of Sydney, sawn white slabs slick and running, puddles bursting underfoot, a rusted slab sled and a stack of pallets against the bruised storm sky. Three adults play a caller's game: a broad Tongan man in a soaked black tank shouts and turns away, and two sprinters — a wiry woman with buzzed hair, a bearded man in his forties in red — tear twenty metres across the marble, then lock into dead statue holds when he spins. All three start fully framed, feet on the wet stone. On the last burst the woman charges the lens and ends half out of frame. One continuous shot, panning slowly left to right.

Thick fog swallows a small brick-paved square in a village on Sydney's rural edge, leaving only a stone war memorial, a shuttered bakery awning and a cast-iron water pump half visible; nothing else stirs. One adult trains alone on the red pavers: a lean Chilean-Australian woman in her early thirties, dark hair knotted, wearing a faded burgundy hoodie with sleeves pushed up and grey wraps on her hands. She circles a few metres of brick, snapping doubled jabs into the mist, slipping an imagined counter, rolling under, pivoting off the lead foot, then firing a fast hook-cross before resetting her guard. Dreamy diffused music-video softness, breath and fog blending. One continuous shot, camera tracking sideways at a steady walking pace; she stays fully in frame.

Floodlights on four steel pylons pour white light onto the rolled dry clay strip at the centre of a suburban Sydney cricket ground, a weathered picket fence and a timber scoreboard hut ringing the calm, windless outfield. One adult claims the strip: a heavyset Croatian-Australian man in his forties, thick forearms, wearing a sun-bleached blue singlet, chalk dust on his fingers. He settles his feet, swings the discus back twice to load, drops into a coiled crouch, spins hard through one and a half turns on the clay and slings it flat and low into the dark, staggering to hold his spot. Spectators cheer only from the small grandstand beyond the fence. Playful upbeat tone, one continuous shot, handheld camera circling slowly at chest height.

Snow drifts over a solar farm on Sydney's western plains, dusting endless tilted panel rows and grey inverter cabinets, while paper scraps and confetti tumble along a compacted red dirt access strip between them. Four adults charge down the track, all fully in frame with boots on the dirt: a tall Ethiopian-Australian woman in a scarlet coat, a broad Ukrainian-Australian man in navy, a slim Malaysian-Australian man in gold, and a grey-haired white woman in emerald. Each grips a long ribbon streamer that uncoils into snapping spirals as they sprint, break into stretched galloping bounds and cross the frame end to end. Epic cinematic scale, snowlight and colour. One continuous shot, slow dolly-out revealing the panel rows. Nobody else is there.

A cavernous foundry casting hall in Sydney's industrial belt spreads packed black sand between mould flasks and an idle ladle crane; bright overhead lamps flatten everything while flickering neon tubes and a sweeping searchlight beam skate across the far wall. Three adults race head-to-head over thirty metres of sand, all fully in frame with feet planted at the start: a tall Nigerian-Australian woman in a silver tank top, a wiry Chinese-Australian man in a red singlet, and a heavyset Irish-Australian man with a ginger beard in white. They drive out low, sand kicking up in dark plumes, and the leader finishes by charging past the lens, cropped at the shoulders. Dreamy saturated music-video colour, one continuous shot with a slow dolly-out revealing the hall.

A flat plate of dark basalt stretches beside a neon-lit fisherman's shed on the coast north of Sydney, its pink and cyan tubes buzzing while fireworks crack silently above the water far offshore. Six adults form three facing pairs on the stone, all fully in frame with feet on the rock: a lanky Sri Lankan-Australian man in teal, a stocky white woman in orange, a tall Sudanese-Australian woman in white, a bearded Portuguese-Australian man in black, a silver-haired woman in blue, and a compact Māori man in yellow. Clubs arc between partners in fast crossing patterns, spinning through the neon, the pairs stepping a metre in and out as the rhythm speeds up. Gritty documentary grain, one continuous shot tracking sideways at walking pace.

Between two towering stacks in a Sydney container yard, a narrow canyon of concrete paver blocks catches dusty afternoon wind and sudden rain streaks that pit the puddles and darken the corrugated steel walls. One adult trains on a single spot: a compact Vietnamese-Australian woman in her twenties, hair in a tight bun, wearing a lime crop top, black shorts and worn trainers, a scuffed wooden plyo box in front of her. She loads, swings her arms and snaps both feet onto the box, stands tall, steps down, and immediately fires the next jump, rain flicking off her shins, chest heaving. Bright energetic sports-ad colour despite the haze. One continuous shot with a slow pan from left to right; she stays fully in frame, alone.

Blue hour drains colour from a black volcanic sand beach south of Sydney, driftwood and a low seawall behind, dry petals and leaf scraps swirling in curls across the dark grains. One adult works alone beside a half-built stack of small hay bales: a broad-shouldered Croatian-Australian man in his fifties, forearms roped with muscle, in a sweat-marked grey singlet and canvas trousers, straw dust on his skin. He hooks a bale with a short pitchfork, dips, drives from the hips and heaves it up onto the stack, catching the next off the ground and repeating without moving his boots more than a step. Gritty documentary texture and grain. One continuous shot, handheld camera circling slowly at chest height; he stays fully framed.

Snow blows across an airport apron beside a hangar on Sydney's outskirts, the painted guidance lines fading under white while safety flags and a loose tarp corner whip hard in the wind and a wind-cone snaps taut. Two adults train on the painted concrete, both fully in frame with feet down: a tall Egyptian-Australian man in his thirties in black trousers and a sleeveless top, and a stocky Danish-Australian woman in her forties with a blonde crop, gripping two round hand paddles. He steps twice, launches into a flying front kick that cracks a paddle, lands, retreats, then leaps a switch-side kick as she resets the targets high. Epic cinematic scale against the hangar. One continuous shot from a static tripod at eye level.

Light rain glazes a weathered timber promenade along a Sydney beachfront, the decking mirroring a flickering neon kiosk sign while a searchlight sweeps out over black surf. Four adults run the boards, all fully in frame with feet on the wood: a lean Brazilian-Australian man in a yellow jersey, a tall Nigerian-Australian woman in purple, a stocky Italian-Australian man in white, and a short-haired Korean-Australian woman in orange. They chain quick step-overs, drag the ball back, cut sharply and burst past each other, working a football thirty metres down the promenade in tight combinations, spray flying from their studs. Onlookers watch only from behind the railing on the seawall above. Moody neo-noir palette, one continuous shot from a static tripod at eye level.

Misty sunrise softens a grain silo loading yard on the Hawkesbury plain outside Sydney, three corrugated silos and a rusted auger looming over a dusty concrete slab while faint fireworks pop over a distant showground. One adult drills alone on the slab: a rangy Chilean-Australian man in his late twenties, curly hair, wearing a padded green goalkeeper jersey, grey shorts and scuffed gloves, a football rebounding off the silo wall. He shuffles, springs sideways into a full dive, smothers the ball on the concrete, rolls up fast, throws it back and dives the other way, dust puffing at each landing. Epic cinematic light through the mist. One continuous shot with a slow pan from left to right; he stays fully in frame, alone.

Midday sun hammers a small courtyard behind a Sydney terrace house, floor laid in blue-and-ochre patterned ceramic tile, a dry wall fountain and a lemon-yellow door framing the space. Torn paper scraps and confetti tumble through the glare. Two adults trade a low game: a compact Brazilian-Australian woman with box braids in a lime crop top drops into a crouching duck as a lanky East African man in white shorts sweeps a wide crescent kick over her head; she answers with a one-handed floor spin, he escapes into a handstand cartwheel. Neighbours cheer from a balcony behind iron railings. One continuous shot, handheld, circling slowly at chest height, both fully framed on the tile.

Fog rolls in slow banks across a suburban Sydney intersection painted with big overlapping circles of coral and teal, bollards and a bike rack at the edge, everything soft under flat overcast light. Three adults hold one spot on the asphalt: a tall Filipino-Australian woman in a grey crop top locks a double collar tie on a stocky bald man in blue shorts, turning him off balance and driving short knees to his covered belly; he pummels an arm inside and answers. A silver-haired coach in a black hoodie counts and taps corrections. One continuous shot, handheld, drifting in a slow circle at chest height, all three fully in frame, bare feet on painted asphalt.

A flat dirt terrace inside an olive grove on the Sydney basin's western fringe: gnarled silver trees in rows, a stone retaining wall, a chalk circle scuffed into the dusty pale earth. The air is dead still under low grey cloud. Five adults ring the circle — a heavy-shouldered Greek man in a black shirt, two women in charcoal singlets, a slim Chinese-Australian in his twenties, a grey-bearded veteran. They drive a sand-filled ball overhead and smash it down, catching the bounce and whipping it sideways to the next pair, hips snapping, dust jumping. One continuous shot, the camera craning down from high above to eye level, all five fully framed, boots planted.

Golden hour slants through tall gum trunks into a small forest clearing north of Sydney, packed earth and leaf litter underfoot, a rope-strung tarp and a hanging lantern snapping and cracking in a strong gusting wind. Two adults train there, both fully in frame with feet on the ground: a tall Māori woman in her thirties in a padded black keeper jersey and taped gloves, and a wiry Portuguese-Australian man in his forties in a faded orange tee, firing a ball low and hard between two branch goalposts. She shuffles, launches into a full-stretch dive, palms the ball into leaf litter, scrambles up and resets in a heartbeat. Moody neo-noir grade with warm rim light. One continuous shot, slow pan from left to right.

Behind coastal dunes south of Sydney a firm red sand flat runs between spinifex tussocks and a bleached fence line, black storm cloud stacked overhead and heavy surf booming and breaking beyond the dune crest. Three adults push weighted sleds across it, all fully in frame with feet in the sand: a broad Tongan woman in her thirties in a grey singlet, a lanky Indian-Australian man in a blue tee, and a silver-haired white man in his fifties in black. Shoulders low, arms locked, they drive the loaded sleds twenty-five metres in grinding surges, sand ploughing up in dark furrows, then reset and go again. Dreamy saturated music-video colour under the storm light. One continuous shot with a slow pan from left to right.

A Sydney gymnastics hall glows under flat overhead lighting, the blue spring carpet floor bordered by chalk bowls and stacked wedge mats, while a flickering neon strip on the mezzanine and two slow searchlight beams wash colour across the wall. Five adults juggle on the sprung surface, all fully in frame with feet down: a tall Ethiopian-Australian woman in silver, a wiry Polish-Australian man in green, a stocky Filipino-Australian woman in red, a bearded white man in mustard, and a slim Chinese-Australian man in violet. They pass clubs in facing pairs while the fifth cuts between them, feeding extra clubs, everyone bouncing a few metres in and out of range. Dreamy music-video colour, one continuous shot with a slow dolly-in toward them.

Thick fog sits on a whitewashed cement rooftop above a Sydney back lane, wide woven trays of split red chillies drying in rows, a water tank and a sagging clothesline at the parapet. One adult works the centre: a broad-shouldered woman in her forties, dark hair knotted tight, black long-sleeve top and loose olive trousers, swinging two weighted tethers. She builds a three-beat weave, folds it into a butterfly across her chest, then turns under her own arm into a flat buzzsaw that hums past her hip, feet fixed on one square of cement. One continuous shot, the camera tracking sideways at a steady walking pace, she stays fully in frame.

Smooth red sandstone, carved into a broad bench beside an abandoned Bangkok riverside sculpture park, holds a lone pitcher: one tall woman in her thirties, East Asian, wiry, black hair braided tight, charcoal jersey and rust shorts. Harsh midday sun burns white while stray snowflakes drift through the light beams like ash, a moody neo-noir contrast against cracked stone planters and a dead fountain. In one continuous shot she plants, coils into a high leg lift, and fires a fastball, then jogs many meters down the sandstone to repeat the windup, covering ground each throw. A handheld camera slowly circles at chest height. She stays fully in frame, feet on the stone, nobody else present.

Two adults work a pair of thick ropes anchored to a rusted band-saw frame in a teak sawmill yard on Bangkok's outskirts, walls of stacked lumber and a leaning corrugated shed behind them. Both stay fully in frame: a stocky Thai man near fifty in a sweat-soaked olive tank, and a lean Black woman in her twenties, cropped bleached hair, maroon crop top and grey shorts. Misty sunrise filters gold through the haze while petals and dry leaves swirl low over sawdust-covered dirt. In one continuous shot they hammer alternating waves, then double slams, boots rooted to a single patch of ground. A handheld camera slowly circles at chest height. Gritty, unglamorous, nobody else anywhere.

Inside a cavernous Bangkok exhibition hall stripped after a trade fair, taped booth grids scar the grey commercial carpet and skeletal truss hangs overhead. Two adults begin the run fully visible, feet planted: a broad-shouldered South Asian man in his forties, shaved head, navy compression top, and a tall white woman near thirty with red ponytail in a teal singlet. Bright even overhead lighting floods everything cinematically; big floor fans stir loose paper and dust into slow spirals. One continuous shot from a static tripod at eye level: they explode into shuttle sprints between cones twenty meters apart, slapping the floor at each turn. On the final rep the woman charges straight at the lens and passes partly out of frame.

On a curling sheet inside a Bangkok shopping-mall ice rink, painted house rings glow under pebbled ice and vents breathe curling steam across the surface. Two adults in goalie pads guard a taped crease, both fully in frame, skates on the ice: a compact Latina woman in her twenties, curly dark hair, lime chest protector; and a lanky Southeast Asian man in his thirties, orange helmet and white pads. Harsh floodlights rake in from one side. Behind the boards and up in the frosted glass gallery, spectators lean and cheer, never on the ice. One continuous shot with a slow dolly-in: they drop into butterfly slides, snap pad saves on sliding stones, and pop back up, staying on one spot. Bright, playful energy.

Golden hour glazes a rooftop tennis court above a Bangkok condo tower, its acrylic-coated concrete faded, net sagging, rooftop vent stacks breathing steam that drifts through the low sun. Four adults spar in two playful pairs: a freckled white man in his twenties with gloves over a yellow tee; a muscular Thai woman near forty in pink wraps; a slim Black man in his thirties, dreadlocks tied back; a stocky Filipina woman in her fifties, blue headband. They bob, slip crisp jabs, roll shoulders and counter, drifting only a couple of meters. Friends watch from a railed stairwell landing above, off the court. One continuous shot, slow dolly-in, everyone fully in frame throughout, grinning.

Low mist sits on a vast tidal sand flat south of Bangkok, rippled wet sand stretching to stranded bamboo fish traps and stilt shacks fading into grey. Sand blows in thin sheets across the ground. Five adults line up, all fully visible with bare feet on the flat: a tall Thai man in his forties in black; a sinewy white woman near thirty, silver buzzcut; a broad Pacific Islander man in maroon; a slender Indian woman in her twenties, teal leggings; a grey-bearded Middle Eastern man in charcoal. Moody neo-noir tones. One continuous shot, camera panning slowly left to right as they attack long run-ups, hop, step and jump far down the flat, spraying wet sand. No one else.

A quarry bench cut into limestone terraces northeast of Bangkok: compacted rock aggregate underfoot, an idle crusher and cone-shaped stockpiles behind. Misty sunrise hangs perfectly still, air soft and dreamlike, dust untroubled. Four adults stand fully in frame, boots on the aggregate: a heavyset Māori man in his fifties, red coveralls tied at the waist; a lean Thai woman near thirty, yellow helmet; a tall Nordic man in his twenties, blue tee; a compact Black woman in her forties, grey tank. One continuous shot as they haul a rolled fire hose off a rack and sprint it out across forty meters of bench, uncoiling flat line, then drop it and skid to a stop. A handheld camera slowly circles at chest height.

Blue polyurethane lanes of an indoor sprint track in Bangkok have been given over to a strongman exhibition; banked turns curve away and rigging hangs above. Neon and colored stage lights wash magenta and cyan across the surface, air perfectly still. One adult works alone on the track, fully in frame, boots on the lanes: a barrel-chested Pacific Islander man in his forties, forearms taped, sleeveless grey shirt, mud-brown trousers. Behind a low barrier and up in the raked seating, a scattered audience watches, none on the track. One continuous shot, camera panning slowly from left to right, as he grips a hay bale, swings it up and hurls it onto a growing stack, striding a few meters between lifts. Raw documentary honesty.

A disused cargo hangar at a Bangkok airfield: painted grey concrete striped with faded safety lines, empty maintenance stands, a vast door cracked open. Low practice lamps carve deep shadows while flickering neon from a distant apron sign and sweeping searchlights slide across the floor, epic and enormous. Two adults face each other four meters apart, fully in frame with feet planted: a tall Ethiopian woman in her thirties, shaved head, emerald bodysuit, and a wiry white man near fifty, silver stubble, black vest and orange trousers. One continuous shot, camera tracking sideways at a steady walking pace, as they pass six spinning clubs, adding doubles and quick side-steps that carry them a few meters across the concrete, both staying fully in frame.

Storm light bruises the sky above a decommissioned runway outside Bangkok, grass splitting the grooved asphalt, a derelict control tower far off. Confetti and torn paper scraps tumble past on the pre-rain gusts, dreamlike. Three adults hold the frame, feet on the asphalt: a compact Korean woman in her twenties with a plum rashguard, a tall Somali man in his thirties in white gi trousers, and a broad Brazilian woman near forty, blonde braid, grey tank. Two hold hand paddles while the third explodes into jumping switch kicks, then they rotate roles, shifting only a few meters. One continuous shot, the camera dollying slowly in. Nobody else on the field, all three fully visible.

Fog hangs over the pale limestone forecourt of a Bangkok museum, a low ring fountain breathing mist, gilded eaves and stone urns behind. Boulevard neon flickers pink through the haze as a searchlight sweeps the façade. Five adults tumble in turns: a compact Thai woman in a red crop top, a tall Black man in yellow shorts, a broad Indian man, a lean woman with a bleached crop, a wiry man in white. All five start fully framed on the stone. Each runs three steps into a round-off, punches a front somersault, then a hands-free side aerial. Onlookers press behind the fountain railing. One continuous shot, craning down from high above to eye level; the last tumbler finishes close, partly out of frame.

Under a Bangkok expressway, a painted black asphalt basketball court glows in drifting fog; one bent hoop, a chain-link wall, neon shopfront light flickering and a security searchlight raking through the haze. Dreamlike, saturated, slightly unreal.
