Colored stage lights left from a show sweep violet and amber across polished maple in an empty Buenos Aires school gym, bleachers retracted, big floor fans stirring loose paper and dust into slow spirals through the beams. One adult stands at center circle: a tall Argentine woman in her thirties, dark curls bound in a scarf, black cropped top and loose white training trousers, feet bare. She loads her hips and rips a spinning back kick that snaps just above the paint, lands, then chains a jump spinning hook, breath sharp, hair flying, staying inside the circle through every repetition. Dreamy, glowing, slow-burn color. One continuous shot, handheld camera slowly circling at chest height, she stays fully framed.

Wide polished granite pavers spread across a civic plaza in a steppe town, a blunt stone monument at one end, flagpoles standing bare, grassland running flat to the sky beyond. Cloud light is soft, the air motionless. Four adults have set a row of portable hurdles down the plaza: a broad Mongolian man in a red singlet, a tall woman with a thick black braid, a wiry man in his forties, a short-haired woman in grey. All four start fully framed, feet on the granite, then sprint the row together, lead legs snapping over, three strides between each. One continuous shot, the camera craning down from high above to eye level; the nearest sprinter finishes past the lens, partly out of frame.

Bright and grinning, four adults take turns bounding over a low steel toolbox on the rolling floor of an idle steppe steel mill, roller tables and cooled slab coils stacked behind, chain hoists hanging overhead. A wiry Korean woman with cropped bleached hair in mint, a heavyset Mongolian man in red, a freckled white man in denim, a tall Black woman in purple each begin standing fully visible on the steel plate, then dive forward, plant both palms, tuck knees through and land clean, rotating in a fast loop within a few meters. Paper scraps tumble through the harsh side floodlights. One continuous shot from a static tripod at eye level, all four staying fully framed, the hall otherwise empty.

Inside a converted grassland art gallery, felt banners and suspended horsehair sculptures hang above a pale oak plank floor washed by neon magenta and cold blue stage light. Four adults stand fully in frame, feet planted: a silver-haired white woman in charcoal, a young Mongolian man in a sleeveless indigo tunic, a South Asian woman in emerald, a broad Latino man in bone white. They drive wooden staffs into fast figure-eight spins, roll them across shoulders and backs, then toss them spinning overhead and snatch them mid-drop, footwork shifting only a couple of meters. Air is dead still. One continuous shot, a slow pan gliding from left to right, epic and monumental.

Under a ribbed canopy, five adults line up on the stamped concrete concourse plaza of a steppe arena, shuttered ticket kiosks behind and a ring road beyond the railing where distant traffic drags soft light trails. Two men hoist teammates across their shoulders and sprint the full width, a tall Mongolian man in white carrying a lean Black woman in lime, a bearded white man in grey hauling a compact Filipina in coral, while a fifth adult, a muscular Han woman in navy, paces them shouting counts. Harsh midday sun bleaches the slabs. Spectators watch only from the raised balcony behind railings. One continuous shot, camera craning down from high above to eye level, dreamy and floating; all five stay fully in frame.

Mist hangs over a crushed red brick clay court behind a steppe rail depot, its net sagging, a rusted windbreak fence catching the pale sunrise. Four adults hold a tight circle, each rooted to a single patch of clay: a rangy Black man in oxblood, a heavyset Mongolian woman with a shaved side and long tail in slate, a middle-aged white man in a black vest, a small Chinese woman in bruised violet. They hammer stomps that puff faint clay dust, snap chest pops, throw jab-fast arm swings and buck-drop into low freezes, never traveling more than a stride. The air is utterly still. One continuous shot, slow dolly-out widening the shadowed court, neo-noir and cold.

Storm light stacks purple over a mown turf court at a lakeside club on the steppe, reed beds bending and whitecaps crashing against the shore wall beyond the low hedge. Six adults pair off on the close-cropped grass, all fully visible: a lanky white man in mustard braces, a curvy Mongolian woman in a red swing dress, a Black woman in teal, a stocky Japanese man in cream, a tall Nigerian man in sky blue, a freckled redhead in green. They swing out, then launch aerials — partners flipped over hips and backs, landing in triple-step rhythm within a few meters. One continuous shot from a static tripod at eye level, bright and punchy.

Along a broad concrete esplanade beside a steppe river, willows line the balustrade, a low arched bridge spans the water and a rusted barge sits moored. Four adults in club kit stand fully in frame on the slabs, then hit full stride: a rangy Mongolian woman in scarlet, a compact Vietnamese man in white, a tall Black man in cobalt, a muscular white woman in gold. Each runner drives into the exchange zone, hand slapping back, palm up, and slams the baton home without breaking speed, then peels off as the next accelerates away. Paper scraps and confetti tumble across the pavement. Onlookers cluster behind the railing above, never on the walkway. One continuous shot, a slow dolly-in toward the runners.

Neon signage from the glass office wings throws pink and cyan bars across a mown lawn quad on the steppe edge of a research campus, gravel berms and dark hedges beyond. One woman stands alone on the grass, fully in frame from the first beat: broad-shouldered, Mongolian, hair pinned tight, in a black training shell and grey shorts. She settles the iron ball against her neck, coils low with her back to the throw line, glides a half-step across the same square meter, then uncorks a violent hip drive and release, arm snapping, weight rebounding onto the front foot. Night air hangs still. Distant staff watch from a lit balcony. One continuous shot, a slow pan from left to right.

A squash court in a sports centre on the steppe: pale hardwood underfoot, white plaster walls scuffed with ball marks, a glass back wall where a few club members stand watching from the corridor. Even ceiling light fills the box; the air is perfectly still. One adult trains inside — a broad-shouldered woman in her forties, weathered brown skin, black hair tied short, plum tee and grey shorts, wristband soaked. She explodes from the service line to a red cone, taps it low, pivots, drives back, touches the wall, and repeats in shrinking shuttles, shoes squealing on the boards. One continuous shot, a slow dolly-in toward her, she stays fully framed.

A swell of short golden grass runs to a lone stone cairn and a sagging fenceline on the open steppe, a bruised storm front massing overhead while fireworks pop silently far along the horizon. One woman is there alone — mid-thirties, Mongolian, athletic, in a canary leotard and loose white wrap, standing fully in frame with bare feet on the grass. She whips a long ribbon into climbing spirals, then breaks into a running sequence, chaîné turns and split leaps carrying her thirty meters across the slope. One continuous shot, a slow dolly-in as she charges the lens and ends cropped at the waist, ribbon still coiling, bright and buoyant.

Work floodlights on a tilted signpost blaze over a packed gravel crossroads on the steppe, a squat grain silo and dark shelterbelt behind, headlights on the far highway smearing into thin streaks. Three adults set up shoulder to shoulder, feet on the gravel, all fully in frame: a stocky Mongolian man in a yellow windbreaker, a tall Black woman in white, a wiry Korean man in orange. They swing arms, load deep and fire off standing broad jumps, landing and immediately rebounding into bounding chains that eat a few meters of stones with each cheerful, grinning effort. One continuous shot, camera tracking sideways at a walking pace as the woman bounds close and ends half out of frame.

Sunlight drops in hard shafts from high windows onto polished concrete between rows of stripped-bare pallet racking in a steppe distribution warehouse, faded lane tape running off into the gloom. Three adults square up inside a taped circle, feet on the slab and fully in frame: a barrel-chested white man in a dust-grey tee, a tall Mongolian woman in a black tank, a lean Indian man in a faded red hoodie. Each folds one leg up, grips the ankle and hops, then drives shoulder into shoulder, ramming, absorbing and pivoting to stay upright, sweat showing, footprints staying inside a meter. Nothing else stirs. One continuous shot, camera tracking sideways at a steady walking pace, raw and observational.

Two adults face off across black marley vinyl in a steppe town's old ballet rehearsal hall, where a splintered pine barre and a chalky rosin box line the wall. Floodlights rake in from one side. A broad-shouldered Mongolian man in his forties, shaved head, orange tank top, drives alternating single-arm rope whips at hip level. Beside him a lean Kenyan woman in her twenties, braids tied high, teal crop top, hammers rainbow slams side to side, then drops to one knee and pounds both ropes flat. Steam curls from floor vents. Neither leaves their spot; both stay fully in frame, feet on the vinyl. One continuous shot, a handheld camera slowly circling at chest height.

Deep in a decommissioned concrete bunker hall beneath the steppe, a riveted blast door stands ajar and moisture beads on the vaulted ceiling; low practice lamps carve hard shadows while haze drifts and two spotlights sweep the damp concrete. One man works the floor alone — mid-twenties, white, wiry, in a plain grey singlet and black shorts, standing fully in frame with both feet down. He measures a run of fifteen meters, hurdles into a round-off, snaps a whipping back handspring and rips a tight back tuck, sticking the landing with a slap of chalked hands, then jogs back to repeat. One continuous shot, static tripod at eye level, unvarnished and documentary.

A small dojo on the steppe smells of chalk and canvas: green tatami mats, sliding wood screens, rope banners hung across the beams, floodlights blazing in from one side through slow haze while a spotlight drifts. Three adults stand centered on the mats, fully in frame: a shaven-headed Mongolian man in black, a compact Brazilian woman with taped wrists in red, a tall greying white man in navy. Two spar in gloves, jabs drawing slips and shoulder rolls, a lead hook answered by a duck-under and body counter, feet shifting a few meters; the third circles as coach, calling angles. Their shadows stretch enormous. One continuous shot, camera craning down from high above to eye level, monumental.

The ice is long gone from a steppe town rink; only a painted concrete slab remains inside battered dasher boards, the scoreclock dead, low practice lamps pooling light while a neon exit sign flickers and a rented searchlight sweeps the roof trusses. Five adults train on the slab, all fully in frame: a rangy Mongolian man in a grey vest, a broad white woman with a blonde bun in black, a Black man in taped red gloves, a small Thai woman in blue, a greying Turkish man calling time. Two pairs spar, a double jab drawing a pull-counter, a hook slipped into a rolling uppercut, feet shifting a couple of meters. Onlookers lean over the boards. One continuous shot, slow dolly-in.

Inside a steppe bus depot parking hall, bright ceiling panels flood the striped asphalt bays; fuel columns and half-open roller doors line the far wall and painted bay numbers hang from the girders. One woman owns the empty bay — early thirties, Mongolian, strong-shouldered, in a lemon crop jacket, white joggers and clean high-tops, standing fully in frame with both feet on the asphalt. She detonates into krump: heel stomps that echo, whip-fast chest pops, arm swings slashing across her body, jab-steps that carry her a few meters up the lane. The hall air hangs still. One continuous shot, a slow pan left to right as she drives at the lens and ends cropped mid-torso.

Light rain glazes a faded asphalt surface lot outside a shuttered steppe wholesale market, painted stall numbers ghosting through the water, bare light masts leaning against grey cloud. Four adults spread across the slick lot, all fully in frame with feet planted: a compact Mongolian man in gold satin, a tall Black woman in crimson, a stocky white man in green, a lithe Chinese woman in orange. They sink into deep bent-knee crouches and explode into paired pouncing leaps, one springing onto the other's braced thigh and dropping into a low prowl, chaining bounds thirty meters across the reflections. One continuous shot, camera craning down from high above to eye level, gritty and unglamorous; nobody else is present.

Neon tubes strung on a cabled rig throw magenta and green across a fine grey ash plain near a steppe cinder cone, guy-wired banner poles snapping loose fabric in a stiff night wind. Six adults stand on the ash, fully in frame with feet down, then drop into prone, seated and kneeling starts: a tall Mongolian woman in silver, a broad Samoan man in black, a lean white man in violet, a Black woman in white, a stocky Korean woman in teal, a bearded Iranian man in rust. On a clap they burst up, palms punching the ash, hips snapping up, driving four or five explosive meters before decelerating and resetting. One continuous shot, a slow orbit around them, hazy and hypnotic.

Midday sun hammers the striped natural grass of a steppe football stadium, one cantilevered stand throwing a knife of shadow, sun-bleached boards ringing the pitch while dry leaves swirl low across the turf. Four adults chalk their palms and stand fully in frame on the grass: a whip-thin Mongolian man in black, a muscular white woman with a red braid, a tall Black man in bone, a compact Peruvian woman in olive. They kick up into handstands and race, walking on hands the length of the penalty area, breaking into hopping bounds, one flaring legs to hold balance. Spectators sit only in the distant stand. One continuous shot, handheld camera circling at chest height; the leader walks close and ends partly cropped.

Deep in a converted grain depot turned crossfit box on the Inner Mongolian steppe, two adults tap on black rubber tiles between chalk-dusted barbell racks and a hanging rope. A stocky Brazilian man near fifty, grey stubble, faded maroon vest, rattles cramp rolls into a pullback. Opposite him a tall Korean woman in her thirties, blunt bob, mustard shorts, answers with paddle-and-roll riffs and an over-the-top. Practice lights carve deep shadows; big floor fans stir loose paper scraps and dust past their ankles. Both stay on one spot, fully in frame, feet on the rubber. One continuous shot, the camera craning down from high above to eye level.

Storm cloud presses low over a drained dry dock at a steppe reservoir shipyard, rows of keel blocks and a rusted caisson gate framing wet concrete; stray confetti from some earlier launch ceremony tumbles across the puddles. One man works alone — late twenties, Filipino, compact and grinning, in a bright teal tee, white shorts and orange shoes, standing fully in frame with both feet down. He drops flat, rolls, then punches up into an explosive start; next round he flops sideways, scrambles and rockets out again, each burst covering three or four meters. One continuous shot, camera tracking sideways at walking pace; his last start carries him close, shoulder clipping out of frame.

A shuttered kiosk and a tilted lifebuoy post edge a wide beach of packed damp sand along a steppe reservoir, cheap neon tubing on the kiosk staining the ground pink and green while dry leaves skitter low across the flats. One woman stands alone, fully in frame — early forties, white, thick-thighed and strong-backed, in a black long-sleeve, grey shorts and bare feet pressed into the sand. From a dead stop she coils, hurls both arms through and blasts a flat broad jump, sticks the landing, then links three alternating-leg bounds that kick sand up behind her, before pacing back and firing again down a few meters of flats. One continuous shot, a slow orbit around her, unpolished and documentary.

Dusty afternoon wind combs a steppe vineyard, wire-trained rows shivering and a canvas windbreak snapping hard on its posts above a compacted soil tractor lane. Two adults face off there, masks on, both fully in frame with feet on the earth: a tall Mongolian woman in white with a long dark plait spilling from her mask, and a stocky Greek man in cream, sleeves rolled. Sport foils flicker — advance, feint, deep lunge, a beat parry and snapping riposte — the exchanges driving them thirty meters down the lane and back, blades ringing under haze-gold light. One continuous shot, a slow orbit around them, soft-focus and lyrical; both stay entirely within frame.

Blue hour flattens a sunken black granite forecourt beneath a steppe city's finance block; a curved bronze relief wall and eight bent flagpoles ring it, salt crust whitening the planter troughs. Two adults square off, arms folded, each balanced on one leg. A wiry Uzbek man in his thirties, wind-tangled black hair, grey thermal, hops in and bumps shoulders with a broad Danish woman in her forties, cropped blonde hair, red windbreaker; she absorbs it, hops sideways, and drives back. Both start fully in frame, feet on the granite; wind snaps loose banner fabric. Late in the duel she hops toward the lens and ends partly out of frame. One continuous shot, the camera craning down from high above to eye level.

An unfinished road tunnel bores under a steppe ridge: raw shotcrete floor and walls, cable trays bolted overhead, a parked lighting rig throwing hard glare from one side into a soft vanishing dark. Five adults are inside, all fully in frame with boots on the shotcrete: a tall Mongolian man in white, a broad Black woman in navy, a lean white man in grey, a compact Japanese woman in red, a bearded Latino man in olive. One drops back seven steps, sets his feet and rifles a tight spiral forty meters down the bore to a sprinting receiver; they rotate roles and run it again, cleats grating. One continuous shot, a slow dolly-in, drifting and dreamlike.

Shafts of daylight drop through clerestory windows of a steppe shipyard fabrication shed, striking rust-stained steel plate between stacks of cut sections and a silent gantry crane. Five adults stand ready on the plate, all fully in frame: a tall Mongolian woman in cobalt, a muscular Black man in white, a lithe Vietnamese woman in fuchsia, a broad white man in lemon, a greying Indian woman in jade. Long ribbons crack to life in overhead spirals and boustrophedon waves as they burst into running leaps, chassé turns and switch jumps that carry them the full sixty-meter length of the shed. Air is otherwise still. One continuous shot, a slow orbit, crisp and exuberant.

Colored gels wash a steppe fencing hall in magenta and cyan; haze curls above the metallic pistes bonded to rubber flooring, reel cables coiled at the ends, spotlights sweeping slowly. Six adults stand spaced along the strips, feet planted and fully in frame: a lean Mongolian man in black, a tall Nigerian woman in white, a stocky white man in navy, a compact Korean woman in coral, a greying Brazilian man in grey, a red-haired woman in olive. Each shadow boxes in place — jab-cross-hook combinations, slipping under imagined counters, pivoting on the ball of the foot, shoulders rolling, never leaving their meter of strip. One continuous shot, a slow pan from left to right, hypnotic and drifting.

Gelled lamps clamped to the rafters bleed red and green across a wide plank barn floor on the steppe, hay dust and torn paper scraps drifting through the beams above empty tack hooks. Three adults hold their positions on the wood, fully in frame from the first breath: a slim Mongolian woman in a black slip dress, a heavyset white man in braces and a stained shirt, a Black woman with silver-streaked hair in deep burgundy. Their tap shoes rattle out paddle-and-roll triplets, then stamp-heel riffs, pull-backs and a traded wing on the offbeat, arms low, heads down, feet never straying beyond a hand's width. One continuous shot, static tripod at eye level, shadowed and cool-toned.

Warm tungsten work lamps swing on cords inside an abandoned steppe brick factory hall, collapsed kiln arches and broken brick tile underfoot while big fans stir loose paper and red dust through the light. Four adults chase a scuffed ball across the tile, all fully in frame with feet down: a quick Mongolian man in a yellow tee, a tall Black woman in white, a stocky white man in blue, a lithe Chilean woman in pink. They rip double step-overs, drag the ball back, cut hard at ninety degrees, nutmeg a defender and burst thirty meters down the hall laughing. One continuous shot, static tripod at eye level, bright and playful.

Blue hour settles over a flagstone threshing floor above a steppe village, a low dry-stone wall ringing it and bundled winnowing forks stacked at one edge. Four adults face off across the stones, all fully in frame with feet planted: a broad Mongolian woman in a red tee, a lean Black man in white, a stocky white woman in blue, a tall Malay man in yellow. Soft balls whip flat across the gap; they twist, drop into limbo bends, snap catches out of the air and dive sideways onto the flagstones, rolling up firing immediately, all inside a few meters. Air is dead calm. One continuous shot, a slow dolly-out revealing the walled floor, crisp and energetic.

Portable floodlights bleach a mesa plateau above the steppe, hardpan and sparse scrub running to a tilted survey marker, a chest-high timber platform rigged near the edge. Three adults work it, all fully in frame with boots on the hardpan: a huge Mongolian man in a black singlet, tacky-slick forearms; a thick-set white woman with cropped grey hair in a brown tee; a broad Samoan man in dark green. In turn they lap a heavy round stone onto the thighs, wrap the arms, roar and extend it onto the platform, drop it thudding and reset, feet barely shifting. Night air is still. One continuous shot, a slow dolly-in, cold and shadowed.

Blue hour bruises the skyline seen from a concrete-paver rooftop terrace above a steppe city, satellite dishes clustered at the parapet and fine dust blowing low across the pavers. Three adults hold a loose triangle, all fully in frame with feet on the concrete: a tall Mongolian woman in a white tank, a lean Black man in charcoal, a broad Turkish woman in coral. A volleyball snaps between them — forearm bump, tight set, controlled downward hit, then a scrambling dig and shuffle to keep it alive within a few meters. One continuous shot, the camera craning down from high above to eye level as the man chases a ball toward the lens and ends cropped at the chest.

Portable floods on a rattling generator throw white light across a desert pavement flat at the steppe fringe, its tight dark pebble crust running to a wind-scoured ridge under a black sky. Four adults stand rooted in a diamond, all fully in frame with feet on the pebbles: a slim Mongolian man in a grey mesh top, a tall Black woman with braids in white, a stocky white woman in plum, a compact Indonesian man in silver. Weighted poi blur into three-beat weaves, butterflies and behind-the-back catches while their bodies turn on the spot, cords humming. The night is windless. One continuous shot, a slow orbit around the group, soft and trance-like.

A cracked pale clay playa stretches under a slate storm wall on the steppe, salt crusting its rim, a half-buried tire marking the far end. Three adults shoulder a heavy timber log, all fully in frame with boots on the clay: a broad Mongolian woman in a dark grey shell, a rangy white man in a black tee, a heavyset Black man in olive. They jog it forty meters in step, calling cadence, then on a shout drop it in unison with a dull crack, reset grips underneath, and drive it back overhead. One continuous shot, the camera craning down from high above to eye level; the lead woman jogs close and ends cropped at the hips. Air hangs dead still, colors bruised and cold.

A closed highway overpass arcs above a steppe reservoir spillway, faded lane markings running its length, taped barriers at both ends and outflow waves crashing white below. Two adults own the deck, both fully in frame with spikes on the asphalt: a tall Mongolian man in a bright orange singlet and a broad-shouldered white woman in lime with a blonde ponytail. Each carries a javelin back, breaks into an approach run, throws into fast crossover steps, plants hard and slings the shaft skimming forty meters down the lane, laughing at the result. Overcast light stays soft. One continuous shot, a slow dolly-in until the woman's follow-through carries her past the lens, shoulder cropped.

A brick-parapet rooftop above a steppe loft factory has a small net lashed between two vent stacks; tar-and-gravel membrane crunches underfoot and a water tank looms behind, everything flattened by soft overcast daylight. One man stands alone as keeper — late thirties, Mongolian, thickset, in a slate green jersey, black shorts and worn gloves, fully in frame with both boots on the gravel. He sets, shuffles, then hurls himself sideways to parry a ball ricocheting off the parapet, hits the membrane hip-first, scrambles up and springs the other way for a low smothering dive, working a few meters of goal line. Nobody else is on the roof. One continuous shot, camera craning down from high above to eye level, grand and weighty.

Neon from a repaired marquee stains the cracked asphalt and gravel of an abandoned steppe drive-in, its leaning screen tower pale against the night while fireworks bloom far beyond the shelterbelt. Four adults pair off on the lot, all fully in frame with feet on the ground: a stocky Mongolian man in a green jacket, a tall Black woman in white, a lean white man in maroon, a small Chinese woman in gold. Free knees tucked high, they hop in circles hunting an angle, then crash chest-to-shoulder; one is bumped hopping backward, catches balance and lunges straight back in, all inside a few meters of asphalt. Onlookers watch from parked cars along the back berm. One continuous shot, a slow pan left to right.

Floodlights on scaffold masts blaze over a painted steel plate pier deck on a steppe reservoir, mooring bollards and coiled hawsers at the edge, black water beyond. Five adults command the deck, all fully in frame with feet on the plate: a tall Mongolian woman in white, a muscular Black man in red, a lean Korean man in blue, a broad white woman in yellow, a wiry Mexican man in teal. Staffs whirl into overhead helicopter spins and reverse-grip switches, snake around waists and necks, then launch in high vertical tosses traded partner-to-partner, the group shifting only a few meters. Night air is still. Festival crowds watch from behind railings on the shore ramp. One continuous shot, a slow dolly-in.

Neon tubing on a greenhouse below throws green and pink over a trodden red earth walkway between terraced tea rows at a steppe foothill, dry leaves swirling low along the path and a stone drainage lip catching the light. One man works alone — early fifties, Mongolian, wiry and weathered, in a dark quilted vest, canvas trousers and mud-caked boots, fully in frame with feet planted. He drives a shovel into a mound of sand at his feet and flings arc after arc sideways at racing tempo, blade flashing, torso rotating, breath steaming, boots never leaving their patch of earth. One continuous shot, camera craning down from high above to eye level, shadowed and severe.

Four adults own the marble floor of a Chicago hotel lobby stripped for an after-party, brass luggage carts pushed aside, a bare check-in counter glowing under magenta and cyan stage lamps. A tall Nigerian-American man in his twenties, high fade, gold shorts, pounds two balls at once. A short Filipina woman in her thirties, ponytail, purple jersey, whips a behind-the-back wrap and a no-look pocket pass. A stocky white man near forty, buzzcut, grey tee, answers with figure-eight lows; a lanky Black woman in her twenties finishes with a spin and pull-back. Paper confetti tumbles overhead. All four stay fully in frame, drifting only a few meters across the marble, one continuous shot, the camera tracking sideways at a steady walking pace.

Heavy snow falls across the packed sand floor of a gravel pit south of Chicago, rusted conveyor towers and frozen aggregate heaps rising at the edges, tire ruts filled white. The air is otherwise dead calm. One woman occupies the frame from the first second, boots flat on the sand: mid-thirties, East Asian, athletic, black hair whipped into a braid, magenta windbreaker over grey leggings, legs zipped into a burlap sack. She launches into hard two-footed hops, driving the length of the pit, arms clamped on the sack rim, tumbling once into the sand and bouncing straight back up to hop the last stretch. One continuous shot, a slow pan from left to right.

Rain falls thin over a harvested Illinois wheat field, straw stubble slicked dark and glossy, a leaning grain elevator and a broken fence line dissolving into grey at the far edge. Nothing else stirs. Three adults are visible head to toe from the opening beat, boots in the wet straw: a broad white man in his fifties with a grey crew cut and a soaked charcoal coat, a tall Nigerian woman in a maroon tracksuit, and a wiry Filipino man in black. They explode into sprint bursts across the stubble, then lock rigid mid-stride, chests heaving, before bursting again. One continuous shot, a slow dolly-in toward them.

Snow pours over a wide sand bar in a dry bend of the Fox River, pale grains crusted white between snow-dusted driftwood snags and bare cottonwoods. Dead leaves swirl low, skating across the sand in ribbons. Two adults hold the frame entirely, feet sinking slightly: a lean Black woman in her twenties in a scarlet long-sleeve and grey shorts, and a compact Korean man in a blue thermal and black joggers. They chain cartwheels down the bar, one hand then the other punching the sand, finishing with round-offs that snap them upright, then reversing direction with matched timing. Energy stays high and bodies stay whole in frame. One continuous shot, a slow pan from left to right.

Under flat, even ceiling lights, a Chicago indoor skate park's flattest patch of smooth plywood becomes a tap floor: two adults stand on the deck beside a mellow quarterpipe and a bin of loose coping bolts. A round-faced Vietnamese-American woman in her forties, silver-streaked ponytail, lime hoodie, rips a maxie ford and lands a clean five-tap wing. Facing her, a slim Ethiopian man in his twenties, short locs, red-and-white striped shirt, answers with a buffalo step and a chattering pullback, grinning. Neither leaves their spot; both stay fully in frame with feet on the plywood. Vent steam drifts across the ramps. One continuous shot, a slow orbit around them.

Wind hauls dust low across the reinforced concrete quay of a Lake Michigan container port, gantry crane legs straddling the frame and a rust-streaked hull moored beyond, the afternoon gone hazy amber. Two men fill the frame completely, boots on the concrete, and stay whole in it: a heavyset Pacific Islander in black shorts, shaved head, hands wrapped; a lean Ukrainian in his thirties with a blond fade and grey shorts. They lock a muay thai clinch, wrenching each other's heads down and firing alternating knees into the belly and ribs, pivoting a couple of meters over the grit. Vast and cinematic. One continuous shot, the camera tracking sideways at a walking pace.

Fog swallows a Chicago boulevard median promenade, elms dripping over a compacted fine-gravel path, iron benches and a stone drinking fountain barely legible. Rain streaks down and puddles burst underfoot. Behind a low railing along the traffic side, bystanders in raincoats watch from the sidewalk, never on the gravel. Four adults hold the center of the frame the whole time, feet on the path: a Mexican man with a black ponytail in a lime jacket paired with a freckled redhead woman in purple, and a Japanese woman in a white anorak paired with a bearded Black man in navy. Ankles tied, both pairs stumble-sprint a few meters and back, laughing. One continuous shot, static tripod at eye level.

Neon tubing rimming a hangar door washes green and pink across a small grass airstrip outside Chicago, where a windsock hangs dead still beside a cracked fuel drum. One adult stands on the mown turf: a heavyset Puerto Rican man in his thirties, shaved sides, black tracksuit with white piping. He drops into a low buck, fires two hard jabs across his body, snaps a rapid arm-swing combo, then explodes upward into a buck jump and lands with a stomp-out that flattens the wet grass. He shifts a few meters, never leaving frame, feet always on the turf. The air is windless. One continuous shot, a slow dolly-out revealing more of the airstrip.

Floodlights blast an abandoned Illinois toll plaza, lane paint bright on the concrete, empty glass booths under a long canopy, steam curling from a grate near lane four. Two adults are fully visible from the opening second, shoes on the painted concrete, and remain so: a tall Ethiopian woman in a white crop top and red shorts, and a thick-set white man in his fifties with a grey beard, black compression shirt. They run a tag chase down the lanes, cutting hard around booth pillars, reversing direction, one lunging with an outstretched hand to slap a shoulder before the roles flip and they tear back. Monumental and cinematic. One continuous shot, static tripod at eye level.

Snow drifts across the raw poured slab of an unfinished Chicago high-rise, rebar stubs and taped plastic sheeting fluttering at the open edge, a tower crane fading into white above. Torn paper scraps tumble through the flakes like slow confetti. Five adults begin fully in frame, shoes flat on the concrete, and stay whole throughout: a tall Indian woman in violet, a pale Irish man in grey, a broad Samoan man in black, a Black woman with silver braids in coral, a slim Vietnamese man in teal. They sprint the slab's length and clear a row of low hurdles, lead legs snapping down. Dreamlike. One continuous shot, a slow dolly-out.

Golden hour floods a lakefront amphitheater outside downtown Chicago: a flat concrete stage deck ringed by weathered steel arches and faded banners, dust skimming low across the boards in the warm wind. Beyond the stage lip, spectators fill the sloped seating, all of them off the deck. One woman occupies the stage, fully framed, feet on the concrete throughout: early thirties, Puerto Rican, compact and muscular, dark hair in a high knot, white uniform with rolled sleeves and a cobalt sash. She pivots on one spot, whipping spinning hook kicks and snapping back kicks into empty air, hips torquing, foot slapping down exactly where it started. Bright and playful. One continuous shot, a slow pan left to right.

Blue hour settles over a wide flowering bench of turf above a lake bluff, wild bergamot and clover underfoot, a split-rail fence and an old vent pipe from a buried utility line puffing white plumes that drift sideways. Three adults hold the frame entirely, shoes in the turf, and never leave it: a tall Ghanaian man in a lemon singlet, a stocky white woman with cropped platinum hair in a red tee, and a lanky Chilean man in blue. Two run tied at the ankles, lurching in a rough three-legged sprint far across the bench while the third pounds alongside shouting cadence, then they swap ties and tear back. One continuous shot, camera craning down from high above to eye level.

Mist hangs over the cobblestone roadway of an old limestone arch bridge on Chicago's far south shore, iron lamp posts still lit, sunrise turning the fog rose. Beyond the parapet, lake waves smash the breakwater in slow white bursts. One man is fully in frame from the first beat, feet on the cobbles, and remains fully in frame: late twenties, Brazilian, wiry, dark curls, a faded lavender long-sleeve and grey shorts. He drops flat to the stones, then explodes upward into a three-meter burst; he repeats it seated, then falling sideways, each time scrambling up and driving forward before resetting. Soft, dreamlike, saturated. One continuous shot, camera tracking sideways at a steady walking pace.

A small second-floor yoga studio in a Chicago walk-up: light bamboo flooring, a wall of folded mats and cork blocks, warm tungsten work lamps clamped to a pipe, steam rolling from a humidifier vent near the window. One man fills the frame completely, bare feet on the bamboo, never stepping out of it: mid-fifties, Punjabi, sturdy build, salt-and-pepper beard, a loose saffron kurta over black track pants, wrists ringed with bells. He bounces into bhangra, springing high with both arms thrown overhead, dropping into squat kicks and popping back up, shoulders shrugging in time, all inside a single arm's-length patch. Upbeat and sunny. One continuous shot, a slow pan from left to right.

A basement wrestling room in a Chicago field house: wall-to-wall red foam mat, taped padding on the walls, two big floor fans stirring loose paper and dust in the beam of a harsh floodlight aimed in from one side, the far corner nearly black. One woman is fully framed from the first second, bare feet on the mat, and stays whole in frame: late twenties, mixed Black and white, powerful thighs, tight box braids, a lime sports top and black shorts. She sets, swings her arms, and whips a standing back tuck, landing on the same square of mat, then adds a tucked-to-layout variation, chalk dust puffing. Bright, cheerful energy. One continuous shot, handheld camera slowly circling at chest height.

Soft overcast light greys an elevated rail-line park on Chicago's near northwest side, tapered concrete planks underfoot between steel planters of dry grasses and a mural-scabbed retaining wall. Neon from a bar sign below flickers up and searchlights sweep the low cloud. Onlookers watch from a stair landing behind the railing, none on the walkway. Five adults hold the planks, fully in frame the whole time: a slim Black man in olive, a tall Danish woman in rust, a broad Puerto Rican woman in grey, a bearded Iranian man in navy, a wiry Thai man in white. Each spots and drives through pirouettes into fouetté chains, staying pinned to one spot. One continuous shot, a slow pan from left to right.

A tiled pedestrian underpass beneath a Chicago boulevard: tiled concrete floor scuffed grey, cracked wall tile, a rusted drain grate at center, one work floodlight blasting from the mouth so the shadows stripe hard down the tunnel. The air is completely still. Two adults are fully framed from the first beat and remain so, shoes braced on the tile: a barrel-chested Polish man in his forties, buzzed hair, orange tee; and a tall Kenyan woman in a royal blue singlet, hair shaved close. Gripping a thick rope, they heave against each other, heels skidding inches on the tile, dropping low, one collapsing to a knee then hauling back up, footing never leaving one small patch. One continuous shot, camera orbiting slowly.

A commercial glass greenhouse north of Chicago, its wide concrete walkway running between endless tomato rows on hanging wire, misting pipes overhead. Haze pools between the benches and a couple of stray spotlights swing through it while a hard floodlight rakes in from one flank. One man occupies the aisle, entirely in frame throughout, boots on the concrete: mid-thirties, white, heavily built, ginger beard, sweat-dark grey tee and canvas work trousers. He squats over a steel keg, rips it up between his legs and launches it backward over his shoulder, turns, chases it two paces, and repeats. Raw and unpolished, documentary-plain. One continuous shot, a slow dolly-out revealing more of the greenhouse.

Blue hour bleeds violet over the open top deck of a Chicago parking garage, painted arrows fading on the concrete, a crooked light mast and a chained equipment shed at the far end. Fog banks roll through the parapet gaps. One adult works the empty lane: a lean Korean-American woman in her twenties, taped fingers, black singlet over teal tights, hair in a tight knot. She sprints eight strides, punches into a single-leg bound, drives the same leg through a second bound, then swings into a long two-foot landing, skids, jogs back, and repeats down the deck. She covers the whole level and stays fully in frame, feet on the concrete. One continuous shot, a slow dolly-out revealing more of the rooftop.

Golden light cuts sideways through fog banks rolling across a cobbled old-town market square on Chicago's northwest side, shuttered timber stalls, a green clock tower and a dry stone fountain looming out of the murk. Spectators cluster on the raised church steps and behind a chain barrier, none on the cobbles. Two adults hold center frame the whole time, feet on the rounded stones: a broad Croatian man with a black beard in a burgundy shirt, and a tall Cameroonian woman in a gold jacket, hair wrapped high. Each grabs one ankle behind them and hops, slamming shoulders and hips together, wobbling, laughing, fighting to stay upright on a single square of stone. One continuous shot, a slow orbit.

Inside a truck loading dock bay on Chicago's industrial corridor: sealed concrete floor, a half-open roll-up door, stacked pallets and strapped crates, tungsten work lamps throwing long amber shadows. The air is dead calm. Three adults start fully in frame with feet on the concrete: a tall Haitian man in a mustard hoodie, a compact white woman with a bleached crop in a green tank, and a broad Mongolian man in grey. Two crouch and the third vaults them in sequence, palms slapping backs, then they rotate and repeat, covering a few meters of floor. Near the end one of them leapfrogs toward the lens and finishes partly cropped out of frame. Epic, monumental. One continuous shot, a slow pan left to right.

Snow sweeps a mown balloon launch field west of Chicago, folded nylon envelopes lashed under tarps and two wicker baskets tipped on their sides, a wind sock stiff at the fence. Gusts drag loose dirt low over the grass between the flakes. One woman is fully framed from the opening second, spikes in the turf, and never leaves the frame: late twenties, Egyptian, lean and long-legged, dark hair braided under a beanie, a plum long-sleeve and black tights. She drives out of a crouched start and attacks a row of hurdles set down the field, lead leg slicing over each, trail knee cutting through, running well past the last one. Hazy, dreamlike. One continuous shot, a slow pan from left to right.

Midday sun hammers a springy turf plateau on a chalky river bluff south of Chicago, white rock breaking through the grass, a wind-bent hawthorn at the rim, the valley haze below. Everything is motionless but the people. Four adults stand fully in frame, shoes in the turf, and stay whole in it: a tall Swedish woman with a blonde plait in a white training jacket, a stocky Black man in red shorts, a slim Bangladeshi man in blue, and a muscular Mexican woman in black. Two hold hand paddles chest-high while the others sprint two steps and launch flying kicks, feet cracking the pads, then land, backpedal and swap roles. Sunny and playful. One continuous shot, a slow dolly-in.

Portable floodlights on tripods ring a bare grey granite plateau north of Chicago, a rusted survey marker at its edge. Five adults stand upright in a tight circle, feet on the rock, before taking turns without leaving their patches. A wiry Peruvian man in his thirties drops into six-step footwork and locks a chair freeze. A tall Somali woman in her twenties, orange headwrap, spins swipes into a shoulder freeze. A stocky white man near fifty backspins to an airchair; a slim Japanese woman in her forties threads a baby freeze; a broad Haitian man in his twenties finishes with a hollowback. The night air stays still, all five fully in frame. One continuous shot, a slow pan from left to right.

A drained paddy flat outside Chicago after harvest, cracked dry mud curling into plates, a rusted irrigation gate and a ragged willow break at the margin, the sky bruised purple-green before rain. Dust skims low across the crust in the pre-storm gusts. Boots pressed into the mud, three adults own the flat and stay whole in frame from start to finish: a freckled white man in a canary shirt, a tall Sudanese woman in fuchsia, and a stocky Peruvian man in turquoise. They pass juggling clubs in a fast triangle, doubles flipping between them, sidestepping a couple of meters to chase a wobble, whooping when a club skitters into the dirt. Bright and playful. One continuous shot, a slow orbit around them.

Low practice lights leave the infield of an indoor Chicago velodrome half in shadow, the banked timber track curving up on all sides, faded bunting sagging from the rail, flat grey concrete underfoot. Spectators sit high in the far grandstand behind the balustrade, well off the infield. Two adults hold the frame fully throughout, boots on the concrete: a thick-necked Greek man with a shaved head in a black singlet, and a tall Black woman in a deep red top, hair cornrowed tight. Together they wrestle a tractor tire upright and drive it over, chasing it a few meters to flip it again, hips exploding, chalk-white hands slapping the rubber. Cold, moody, noir. One continuous shot, static tripod at eye level.

Sunrise mist hangs over the cutting floor of a marble quarry, sawn white stone underfoot scored with blade tracks, house-sized blocks stacked behind a gantry saw, a stray neon work sign stuttering while a searchlight sweeps the rock wall. Three adults are fully in frame from the opening second and remain so, shoes on the marble: a tall Argentine man in white fencing kit, a compact Korean woman in the same, and a grey-haired Black man in a padded jacket. With sport foils, two exchange lunges and parry-ripostes across a few meters, blades ringing, while the third calls the phrase and then takes a turn on the strip. Cold blue-white, noirish. One continuous shot, a slow dolly-in.

Sunrise mist softens a small brick-paved village square in a Chicago suburb, red pavers laid in herringbone around an iron bandstand, bare planters and a taped café awning snapping in a strong wind that whips loose banner fabric sideways. Neighbors watch from the bandstand steps and behind a low chain, off the bricks. Two women hold the paving fully in frame the whole time: a tall Ukrainian in her thirties, blonde bun, sky-blue leotard and grey wrap skirt; and a curvy Jamaican woman in coral with braids piled high. Each carves huge ribbon spirals overhead, running two steps into split leaps and spinning turns, the silk coiling around them. Bright, cheerful. One continuous shot, the camera cranes down from above to eye level.

Blue hour drains the color from a cricket ground on Chicago's far west edge, the rolled dry clay strip pale between shorn outfield grass, a sagging boundary rope and a line of pennants cracking hard in the wind, a marquee's loose canvas whipping. Two adults stand fully in frame from the first second and stay entirely in frame: a slender Vietnamese woman in white fencing kit, dark ponytail through the mask strap; and a broad Nigerian man in the same whites, sleeves pushed up. With sport foils they run long attacks the full length of the strip, advancing, lunging deep, parrying and riposting, retreating meters at a time. Soft, floating, dreamlike blues. One continuous shot, static tripod at eye level.

Thick fog swallows the turning loop at the dead end of a solar array outside Chicago; a leaning weather mast, a stack of split pallets, and one panel washing rig fade into white. One adult owns the compacted red dirt: a powerfully built Mexican-American woman in her thirties, forearms taped, cobalt tank, hair braided flat. She squats, hooks her fingers under a mud-caked tractor tire, drives her hips through, and stands it upright, then punches it over with a knee. Four more flips carry her a few meters along the lane, breath steaming. The air is dead calm, and she stays fully in frame with feet on the dirt. One continuous shot, the camera tracking sideways at a steady walking pace.

Shafts of daylight cut through the high clerestory windows of a foundry casting hall, striping a packed black sand floor lined with green sand molds and an overhead ladle crane. A stuttering neon shop sign and a swinging inspection lamp throw sweeping beams through the dust. Three adults work the sand floor, framed head to toe from the opening second and never cropped: a broad Italian-American man in a yellow tee, a tall Kenyan woman in white, and a compact Indonesian man in blue. Two go hands-down while the third hoists their ankles, and they charge across a few meters in a wheelbarrow crawl, arms hammering the sand, then swap. Bright and punchy. One continuous shot, camera tracking sideways at a walking pace.

Blue dusk over a shelf of flat dark basalt on a wild stretch of Lake Michigan shore, tide pools glinting between hexagonal cracks, driftwood wedged in a seam, surf detonating white against the rocks behind. Four adults are fully in frame from the first second and remain so, shoes on the stone: a tall Ecuadorian man in teal, a lean Black woman with a shaved head in silver, a stocky Turkish woman in plum, and a rangy Australian man in white. Two lean hard into resistance bands anchored by partners, then swap to hauling a weighted sled, grinding long strides right across the shelf. Soft, saturated, dreamlike. One continuous shot, handheld camera slowly circling at chest height.

A narrow corridor between container stacks in a Chicago rail yard, concrete paver blocks underfoot, corrugated walls of rust-orange and faded blue rising on both sides, hazy afternoon wind dragging dust while rain streaks down and pocks the puddles. Two adults are fully in frame from the opening beat and never leave it, boots on the pavers: a burly French-Canadian man in his forties, dark stubble, black jersey; and a lean Chinese woman in a white jersey, hair in a low knot. With sticks and a puck each, they rattle dekes through a tight cone line, shoulders faking, blades snapping the puck side to side, feet chopping within a single meter. Vast, cinematic scale. One continuous shot, a slow dolly-in.

Flat overcast light over a black volcanic sand beach, the dark grains packed hard near the waterline, bleached driftwood and two sea stacks standing off in the grey. The air is windless and the surf barely breathes. Four adults stand fully in frame at the start, feet planted in the black sand, and never leave the frame: a rangy Somali man in charcoal, a muscular white woman with a red buzz cut in black, a broad Filipino man in slate, and a tall Brazilian woman in deep green. On a call they drop prone, scramble up, sprint fifteen meters down the beach and dive full-length for planted flags, sand exploding. Cold, hard, noirish. One continuous shot, static tripod at eye level.

Light rain glosses the painted concrete apron beside a hangar at a small Chicago airfield, yellow taxi markings doubled in the wet, huge hangar doors cracked open on darkness, chocks and a tug parked at the edge. Nothing else moves. Three adults are fully framed from the first second and stay whole in frame, shoes on the wet concrete: a powerfully built Black woman in a lemon tee, a lean Norwegian man in cobalt, and a stocky Filipino man in white. One hoists another across the shoulders and sprints far across the apron, sets them down, and the fresh pair takes off the other way, spray kicking behind. Bright and punchy. One continuous shot, a slow dolly-in.

Mist softens a lakefront timber promenade in Chicago, its silvered decking edged by a paint-blistered bandstand and a rail of chipped blue balusters. Six adults work one spot. Two turners, a tall Ghanaian man in his forties and a compact Chilean woman in her twenties, spin twin ropes in steady eggbeater rhythm. Inside, four jumpers rotate through: a freckled Irish woman in her thirties hammering a fast speed round, a wiry Vietnamese man in his twenties dipping to touch the boards mid-turn, then two more swapping in on the beat without a stumble. Beyond the railing, early walkers watch; car light trails streak the far shoreline. All six stay fully in frame on the decking. One continuous shot, a slow orbit around them.

Rain slicks the dusty concrete slab of a grain silo loading yard on the Illinois river flats, three white silos and a swung-out auger chute above, the wet ground throwing back their reflections. Torn feed-bag paper tumbles through the drizzle like confetti. Four adults stay fully in frame from the first second, boots on the slab: a tall Puerto Rican woman in a pink shell jacket, a broad Ukrainian man in green, a wiry Indian man in yellow, and a silver-haired white woman in blue. In two pairs they spar with padded foam sticks, swinging overhead strikes and hooks, ducking and pivoting a couple of meters, laughing at every clean hit. One continuous shot, camera craning down from high above to eye level.

Dust skims low across the patterned ceramic tile of a walled courtyard behind a Chicago social club, terracotta pots and a leaning trellis along one wall. Three adults train in hazy afternoon light. A rangy Algerian man in his forties, taped shins, black shorts, holds a belly pad. A compact Swedish woman in her twenties, blonde undercut, grey vest, fires low kick, cross, then a switching head kick; a broad Indian man in his thirties, in green, feeds the same combination back. Onlookers watch from a balcony above, off the tiles. All start fully in frame, feet down; later the pad holder backpedals toward the lens and ends partly out of frame. One continuous shot, a slow dolly-out revealing more of the courtyard.

Sunrise mist hangs over a neighborhood intersection in Chicago painted with a huge sunburst mural, planters and a striped barrel closing the street. Three adults run a water relay across the painted asphalt. A burly Samoan man in his forties, red beanie, swings a full galvanized pail up from a trough; a freckled white woman in her twenties, dungarees, catches and pivots it along; a tall Kenyan man in his thirties sprints the last two meters and dumps it into a drum, water arcing. Snowflakes drift through low light beams. All three begin fully in frame, boots on the paint; then the last runner charges the camera and ends partly out of frame. One continuous shot, a handheld camera slowly circling at chest height.

Sunrise mist threads a small olive grove terrace above a rocky shore, gnarled trunks in rows on dusty pale earth, a dry stone wall at the drop, and heavy surf breaking white on the rocks below. Four adults hold the frame fully at the start, feet in the dust: a tall Croatian woman with a blonde ponytail in lilac, a broad Black man in white, a compact Filipino woman in gold, and a lean Iranian man in navy. Under a rope strung between two trees, they run three-step spike approaches, arms swinging through hard overhead hits while partners set. Near the end the tallest steps in toward the camera and finishes partly out of frame. One continuous shot, a slow dolly-out.

Packed earth and dark leaf litter carpet a beech clearing above Istanbul, a moss-furred fallen trunk and a ring of charred stones at its edge, the sky draining to deep blue just after sunset; fog banks slide between the trunks. One adult holds the space: a lean Turkish woman in her forties, close-cropped silver hair, deep-red leotard over black leggings. Her ribbon wand carves tall overhead spirals, drops into low snake ripples that skim the leaves, then whips a boomerang throw she catches under a lifted leg while pivoting on the spot. She never leaves her patch of earth and stays fully in frame, feet down. One continuous shot, a slow dolly-in toward her.

Fog rolls thick over a firm red-sand flat between dunes on Istanbul's Black Sea shore, marram tufts and a bleached driftwood post marking the hollow; surf booms unseen beyond the ridge. One adult dances alone: a barrel-chested Punjabi-Turkish man in his fifties, grey beard, saffron kurta knotted at the waist, blue sash. He drives a bouncing chaal step, shoulders snapping, then springs into jhummar turns, drops to a deep squat and kicks out hard with both fingers punched skyward, repeating faster. His footprints stay inside one small ring of sand, and he remains fully in frame throughout. One continuous shot, the camera craning down from high above to eye level.

Warm tungsten work lamps hang low over the spring carpet of an Istanbul gym hall, stacked foam bumpers and a coiled climbing rope against a chalk-smudged wall. Three adults grip one thick rope, feet braced on the carpet in dead-still air. A heavyset Turkish woman in her thirties, black leggings and gold tee, anchors at the back, leaning until her heels squeal. Ahead of her a wiry Nigerian man in his twenties in blue, then a broad Georgian man in his forties, grey singlet, heave in sharp bursts, slide a hand's width, and dig back in. On the last pull they collapse laughing onto the mat, still fully in frame. One continuous shot, a handheld camera slowly circling at chest height.

Fog sits thick over a whitewashed cement rooftop terrace in Balat, trays of split red chilies drying along the parapet, a rusted forest of TV aerials and a slack laundry line fading into grey. Two adults work the small open patch: a lanky East Asian man in his late twenties, mint-green tee and cuffed jeans, and a curvy Middle Eastern woman, early thirties, curls tied up, wearing a coral jumpsuit. Facing off a few paces apart, they pass juggling clubs in fast crossing arcs, stepping sideways, adding double spins, one club clattering and getting scooped up mid-stride. Playful and bright. One continuous shot, camera craning from high above down to eye level; both stay fully in frame.

Soft overcast daylight, no wind, nothing moving but one man. He stands on a wide bench of smooth red sandstone above a dry streambed inland from Istanbul, three stacked cairns behind him and a rain-hollowed pothole holding still water. Sixties, Latino, silver hair cropped short, sinewy build, a faded navy windbreaker over a white vest and grey sweatpants. Feet planted, he throws crisp toprock — Indian steps, a hook-and-cross — then drops his hands to the stone and grinds through six-step footwork, knees swinging, before popping back upright and repeating. The rock stays clearly visible beneath him and he never leaves the frame. Filmed as one continuous shot from a static tripod at eye level. Plain, gritty, documentary flat.

Hazy afternoon light hangs dusty over a timber yard on Istanbul's outskirts: stacks of raw-cut planks curing under tarps, a silent bandsaw shed, sawdust drifted like snow over the packed dirt. The air is completely still. One adult practices there, a tall Turkish woman in her twenties, wide shoulders, black tank and cargo pants, a silk flag on a wooden pole. She rips through fast drop spins, snaps it into a low peggy roll, then launches a four-rotation toss, tracks it up past the plank stacks, and catches it blind behind her back. Two steps of travel, no more; she stays fully in frame with boots on the sawdust. One continuous shot, a slow pan from left to right.

Bare aluminium booth frames and coiled cable runs fill a vast, emptied exhibition hall by the airport, floodlights raking in hard from one side so long shadows stretch over acres of grey commercial carpet. Two adults carry harness snares: a tall Middle Eastern woman, thirties, shaved sides and a dark braid, in a red athletic top and black shorts, and a heavyset white man in his fifties, ginger beard, blue polo and khakis. They roll into a fast marching cadence, covering ground the length of the hall, snapping crisp pivot turns and back-marching, sticks flashing. Air completely still. One continuous shot, camera orbiting slowly around them; both remain fully framed. Upbeat, glossy, playful.

Bright even overhead lighting floods a small curling rink tucked under a shopping complex; painted house rings glow through the pebbled ice and a glassed viewing balcony runs along one wall, where a handful of spectators lean on the railing well above the sheet. Two adults in sneakers play broomball across a few metres of ice: a compact Black man, late twenties, in a yellow hoodie and grey shorts, and a tall white woman, forties, auburn ponytail, navy fleece and leggings. They scramble, slip, shuffle-chop at a small ball, one skidding onto a knee and bouncing up. Everything else is motionless. One continuous shot, the camera dollying slowly out to reveal the rink.

Harsh midday sun bleaches an acrylic-coated concrete tennis court wedged behind pastel apartment blocks, its net sagging, bougainvillea flaring purple through the chain-link, faded service lines ghosting under the paint. Three adults stand near the baseline: a slim South Asian woman, twenties, high ponytail, lilac crop top and white shorts; a broad Black man, thirties, teal tank and grey joggers; a lean older white woman, fifties, silver bob, in a pale blue tracksuit. Rooted to their spots, they swing and punch into standing back tucks, then a standing half-twist, landing tight and resetting. No breeze at all. Dreamy, sun-hazed color. One continuous shot, camera orbiting slowly; all three stay fully in frame.

Night, and portable floodlights on tripods throw hard white light across a rippled wet sand flat left by the outgoing tide, a beached orange buoy and a line of rusted groyne posts behind. Loose confetti and torn paper scraps tumble low over the sand from some party further up the beach. One man works the lit patch alone: mid-thirties, heavyset, Middle Eastern, thick dark hair plastered flat, in a soaked grey rash vest and black shorts. He runs three steps and launches headfirst into a belly-flop skid, sliding on the slick sand, scrambles up, jogs back and does it again, harder. Unpolished documentary feel, one continuous shot, handheld camera circling slowly at chest height.

A storm sky presses low and bruised over an open-pit quarry bench, terraced grey walls stepping away behind an abandoned conveyor and cone-shaped aggregate piles; fog banks roll through the cut, softening everything to slate. One woman stands on compacted rock aggregate, forties, powerfully built, white, with a blonde undercut, wearing a charcoal thermal top, black shorts and dusty boots. She squats over a steel keg, drives up through her hips and hurls it backward over her shoulder, turns, walks two paces to it, resets and throws again, breath steaming. Moody neo-noir, low contrast, cold silver highlights. One continuous shot, handheld camera circling slowly at chest height, ground always visible.

Shafts of daylight fall through high clerestory windows onto a blue polyurethane sprint track, hurdles stacked along the wall and lane numbers stenciled crisp underfoot. Three adults share a few metres of it: a tall Black woman, thirties, box braids, in an orange jersey; a stocky Turkish man, fifties, greying moustache, navy tee and shorts; and a slight East Asian man, twenties, in a white singlet. They run a volleyball pepper drill, bumping, setting and cutting sharp downward hits, shuffling and diving to dig. All three start fully framed with feet on the track; midway the woman chases a ball straight toward the lens and ends half out of frame. Air is dead still. One continuous shot, static tripod at eye level.

Neon tubes and colored stage lamps rigged to the roof trusses wash magenta and cyan across the painted grey concrete of an enormous aircraft hangar, folded scaffolding towers and taped-out aircraft outlines receding into the dark. Five adults begin fully in frame, feet on the floor: two pairs and one runner, mixed — a Black woman with a shaved head in red, a burly white man in a grey vest, a slim Middle Eastern woman in green, a South Asian man in blue, an older Latina in black. Two hoist partners into fireman's carries and sprint the hangar's length while the fifth pounds ahead, ending close to the lens and partly out of frame. Air still. One continuous shot, camera dollying out. Epic scale.

Light rain silvers a decommissioned runway on the coast, faded threshold bars and a canted windsock the only markings, distant motorway traffic streaking its light trails along the horizon. Two adults face off on the grooved asphalt, armored in plain indigo kendo gear: a rangy Latina woman in her thirties and a compact Turkish man, twenties, both gripping wooden shinai. They advance and retreat within a few metres, hammering men and kote strikes, stamping the wet surface, whipping into a lunging attack and a sharp step-back parry, spray flicking from their heels. Nobody else on the strip. Bright, punchy sports-ad energy. One continuous shot, camera orbiting slowly; both stay fully in frame throughout.

Rain has just glazed the pale limestone forecourt of a small archaeology museum, where a low octagonal fountain sits quiet beside a row of clipped cypresses and carved capitals rest on plinths. Six adults form three wheelbarrow pairs — a Black man in mustard, a white woman with red curls, a Turkish man in stripes, a South Asian woman in violet, an older Black woman in teal, a lanky white man in grey. Each front partner crawls fast on hands while their teammate holds their ankles, scuttling a few metres, wobbling, one pair spilling gently onto the wet stone. Onlookers watch from the museum steps behind a rope, off the paving. The air is dead calm. Playful, one continuous shot, camera orbiting slowly.

Fog banks spill over the chain-link fence of a hilltop asphalt court in Istanbul despite the harsh midday sun, bleaching the painted black surface, bent rims and a faded mural of geometric tiles on the end wall. Six adults play within a few metres of the key: a heavy Turkish man in a white vest, a tall Black woman with braids in maroon, a wiry Latino in a green tee, a white woman with a bleached crop in orange, an older South Asian man in grey, a stocky Black man in navy. They attack the rim with driving layups, euro-step finishes and hard closeouts. Neighbours watch from a wall above, off the court. One continuous shot, camera panning slowly right. Documentary grain.

Fog sits low on a raked red-dirt infield outside Istanbul, bases pulled, a leaning backstop and a dead scoreboard fading into white. Six adults shoulder one long peeled log and jog it across the diamond in step: a broad Turkish man in his fifties calling cadence at the front, a lanky Sudanese woman in her twenties behind him, a stocky Dutch man in his thirties, a wiry Japanese woman in her forties, and two more in bright club shirts bringing up the rear. On a shout they drop the log to the dirt together, dust puffing. Paper scraps tumble past. Spectators cheer from bleachers beyond the fence. All six stay fully in frame. One continuous shot, the camera tracking sideways at a steady walking pace.

A red-painted tarmac cycle highway runs beside a canal on the city's western edge, steel railings vanishing into thick fog, snowflakes drifting through the beams of low lamp posts. Two adults own the empty lane: a tall white man in his forties, shaved head, black thermal and grey shorts, and a broad Middle Eastern woman, thirties, dark ponytail, wearing a deep-purple long-sleeve. Both start fully in frame with feet on the tarmac, then take turns squatting over a small keg and flinging it backward over one shoulder, stepping a few metres after each throw. Near the end the man drifts toward the lens and finishes cropped at the waist. Dreamy, cool blues. One continuous shot, camera orbiting slowly.

Floodlights on a pump shed throw long white blades across coastal salt evaporation pans, low crusted dykes dividing the flats and a skin of ankle-deep brine mirroring nothing but glare. Two adults stand on the crusted salt: a lean East Asian man, twenties, in a soaked grey tee and rolled trousers, and a strong Black woman, forties, hair wrapped in a bronze scarf, in a sleeveless olive top. They stomp-splash at each other, kicking sheets of brine, sidestepping a few metres along the dyke, scooping water two-handed and ducking away laughing. The air itself is dead calm. Epic, high-contrast cinematic. One continuous shot, camera orbiting slowly, both fully in frame.

Blue hour settles over an old apple orchard outside the city, clover and grass thick underfoot, branches propped with forked poles, crates stacked at the row's end; leftover confetti from a harvest party tumbles through the cooling air. Two adults hold one spot between the trees: a slim Turkish woman, late twenties, blunt black bangs, in a silver satin shirt and black shorts, and a compact Latino man, thirties, bleached fade, wearing a lavender jacket. They snap through sharp unison choreography — pointed arm hits, quick body rolls, a synchronized drop to one knee and a spinning recovery — knees popping in time. Soft, dreamlike violet tones. One continuous shot, handheld camera circling slowly at chest height.

Dusty afternoon haze hangs over a full-size synthetic turf pitch beside the ring road, four floodlight pylons standing over sagging goal nets. Four adults strung across the green turf run a bucket brigade: a tall Black man in a white vest, a wiry white woman with a red braid, a heavyset Turkish man in a blue shirt, a young South Asian woman in yellow. They sling sloshing water pails hand to hand, running the chain from the corner flag toward the centre circle, water arcing and darkening the turf. Neighbours watch from a raised terrace behind the barrier, never on the pitch. Nothing else moves in the still air. Soft, dreamy grade. One continuous shot, static tripod at eye level.

A storm builds black and swollen over lavender rows on the Thracian side, dust blowing low across a chalky gravel service path, a squat stone hut and a rusted irrigation reel breaking the purple lines. One man works alone: early fifties, thickset, South Asian, greying beard, in a sleeveless charcoal top, taped wrists and dirt-caked boots. He drops into a wide stance, drives a heavy tractor tire up onto its edge and slams it over, chases it two steps, and flips it again down the lane, three, four times, gravel scattering. Epic and cinematic, air electric before rain. One continuous shot, the camera dollying slowly in toward him; he remains fully framed, feet on the gravel.

Blue hour drains the color from a sunflower field east of the city, heads bowed along a strip of dry cracked soil where irrigation pipes lie coupled and a broken standpipe leaks steam that drifts low across the ground. One woman holds the strip: mid-twenties, athletic, Black, hair in a high puff, wearing a white dobok top loose over black leggings, barefoot. She begins fully in frame, feet planted, then fires a spinning hook kick, a back kick into the fading light, hopping a metre or two between combinations. On her last spin she strides toward the camera and finishes cropped from the knees up. Bright sports-ad snap. One continuous shot, camera craning down from high above to eye level.

A brickmaker's drying yard outside Istanbul goes cobalt in the last light after sunset: fired clay tiles stacked in herringbone rows, a squat kiln chimney, neon tubing on a roadside hoarding flickering along the wall while a searchlight sweeps overhead. One adult chalks a line on the tiles, a lean Somali-Turkish man in his twenties, shaved head, white singlet, jade shorts. He rocks back, takes four quick strides, hops off his right foot, floats a long step phase with arms cycling, and finishes in a tucked jump, landing soft and skidding half a meter. He resets and repeats within a few meters, fully in frame, feet on the clay. One continuous shot, a slow pan from left to right.

A road tunnel closed to traffic, tiled walls streaked with grime, ventilation grilles humming, sodium lamps overhead while daylight pours in shafts through high vent openings near the mouth; a stray neon work lamp flickers and a maintenance searchlight sweeps the asphalt. One woman trains alone: forties, muscular, Turkish, dark hair in a tight bun, in a cobalt training top, black shorts and orange trainers. She explodes between four cones a few metres apart, touching the asphalt at each turn, chopping her feet and driving back. On the final rep she sprints straight at the camera and passes half out of frame. Bright, punchy sports-ad look. One continuous shot, camera craning down to eye level.

Mist hangs over a freight depot platform at sunrise, weathered concrete stretching between parked boxcars, a flickering neon depot sign and a yard searchlight swinging across the rails. One man does the work: sixties, lean and weathered, Latino, silver stubble, in a faded olive shirt with sleeves rolled and heavy canvas trousers. He grips a hay bale by its twine, swings it low and hurls it up onto a growing stack, steps two paces to the next, twists and throws again, chaff clouding in the cold light. Nothing else stirs on the platform. Moody neo-noir palette, deep shadow and amber. One continuous shot, camera panning slowly left to right; he stays fully framed.

Fog erases the tracks beyond a long suburban railway platform, tactile-edged concrete running under an iron canopy, empty sign frames and one wooden bench half-visible in the grey. Six adults stand spaced along it: a burly Black man in a black thermal, a broad Turkish woman with a copper braid, a tall white man in charcoal, a stocky East Asian woman in navy, a lean Middle Eastern man in olive, an older white woman in slate. Each keeps one small footprint, sinking into a shot put glide, driving the hip through and releasing an iron ball with a grunt, then resetting. Nothing else moves. Moody neo-noir, near-monochrome. One continuous shot, handheld camera circling slowly at chest height.

Drizzle beads on a crusted, wind-packed snowfield along a ridge above the city, a half-buried wire fence curving toward dark firs while distant fireworks bloom silently over the valley. Four adults spread across the open snow: a tall Black woman in a red parka, a compact Turkish man in a mustard jacket, a broad white man in his fifties in blue, a slim South Asian woman in a white anorak. They wage a running snowball fight, sprinting between drifts, packing fast, dodging, one diving flat and rolling up to throw again. Reflections shimmer in the wet crust. Dreamy, soft-focus music-video mood. One continuous shot, camera orbiting slowly; all four stay fully in frame.

Harsh midday sun cuts the cloister courtyard of an old monastery into hard geometry: worn flagstones, a shaded arcade of squat columns, a capped dry well and one fig tree in a corner. Five adults line up on the stone — a lean Black man in orange shorts, a strong white woman with a grey crop, a young Turkish man in a green tee, a curvy Latina in yellow, an older East Asian man in white. They chain standing broad jumps down the sunlit strip, arms swinging, sticking each landing before rebounding into the next, covering a few metres before turning back. Visitors watch from the shaded arcade behind a rope. Air perfectly still. One continuous shot, camera craning down to eye level.

Dust skims low across a smooth concrete drying patio behind a small roastery, wooden rakes leaning on a wall, burlap sacks slumped in a doorway, a bruise-dark storm sky about to break. Three adults occupy the slab: a broad Black woman in a lime tank, a wiry Turkish man in a grey tee, and a tall white man in his forties with a red beard, in blue. Two take turns hoisting the third across their shoulders in a fireman's carry and powering a few metres across the concrete before setting them down and swapping, all three grinning and gasping. Bright, playful commercial energy against the gloom. One continuous shot, camera panning slowly left to right, everyone fully framed.

Big stage fans stir loose paper and dust across the black painted plywood of an old proscenium stage, hemp ropes hanging in the fly space, faded velvet drapes bunched at the wings, floodlights blasting in hard from stage left. Three adults hold the boards: a slight East Asian woman, twenties, silver bob, in a black harness top; a tall Middle Eastern man, thirties, in a white shirt and wide trousers; a muscular Black woman, forties, in a red jumpsuit. They lock into unison: knife-edge hand flicks, a hip-snap freeze, a two-count body wave rolling down the line, then a hard three-step travel sideways and a stamp back to centre. Raw documentary texture, sweat and dust. One continuous shot, camera dollying slowly out.

Midday sun hammers a raised park terrace overlooking the Bosphorus, crushed decomposed granite crunching underfoot, a bare pergola casting striped shadow and a stone balustrade edging the drop. Two adults work the open patch: a tall Latina woman, thirties, dark ponytail, in a white sports top and navy shorts, and a stocky white man, fifties, grey buzz cut, in a faded blue tee. They keep a volleyball pepper rally alive — forearm pass, high set, controlled roll-shot spike — swapping hitter and digger, sprawling a couple of metres to dig low balls off the gravel. Onlookers rest on benches up behind the balustrade, off the terrace floor. Air completely still. Epic, high-contrast cinematic. One continuous shot, camera panning slowly left to right.

Thick fog hangs between ridges of coal in a power station stockyard, a conveyor gantry striding overhead, bucket-wheel machinery ghosted at the far edge, the ground a flat black dust that shows every footprint. Six adults line up on one side: a Black man in a scarlet tee, a white woman with a blonde bun in cobalt, a Turkish man in white, a South Asian woman in gold, an older Latina in green, a lean East Asian man in orange. One after another they bound the full diagonal in grand allegro leaps — split jumps, cabrioles, long travelling assemblés — kicking up soot. The air itself is motionless. Bright, energetic sports-ad drive. One continuous shot, camera dollying slowly in, all fully framed.

Tungsten work lamps clamped to scaffolding throw amber pools down a colonnaded arcade in old Istanbul, its terrazzo floor scuffed pale between marble piers, plaster dust ghosting the vaults. Paper scraps tumble through the arches on a draft. One adult stands under the third arch: a broad-shouldered Turkish-German man in his fifties, salt-and-pepper beard, waistcoat over a rolled-sleeve shirt, hard-soled shoes. He hammers a shim sham break, adds stinging heel drops, then rattles a double pullback and holds, chest lifted, before starting again faster. He never leaves that one square of terrazzo and remains fully in frame, feet on the floor. One continuous shot, the camera craning down from high above to eye level.

Inside a power plant turbine hall, buzzing neon tubes and swivelled stage lamps paint the green machine casings amber and deep teal, checker plate steel decking ringing underfoot beneath a dormant crane. Two adults start fully in frame with feet on the plate: a powerfully built Turkish woman, forties, dark braid, in a black training top, and a lean white man, twenties, buzzed hair, in a grey vest.
