She hoists him into a fireman's carry and pounds the length of the hall past the casings, sets him down, and he immediately shoulders her and hauls back the other way. The air hangs still. Bright, kinetic sports-ad energy. One continuous shot, camera tracking sideways at a steady walking pace.

Golden hour rakes down a film studio backlot street, false shopfronts with blank sign boards, a fake tram rail set into painted asphalt, rain streaking through the light and splashing in standing puddles. Two adults hold one spot on the wet pavement: a compact Black woman, twenties, cornrows, in a soaked grey crop top and joggers, and a broad Middle Eastern man, thirties, in a black tee clinging wet. Swinging their arms in sync, they whip backward into full standing tucks, water bursting around their shoes on landing, then answer with a back handspring stepped straight into a second tuck. Handheld, unpolished, documentary grain. One continuous shot, camera circling slowly at chest height, both fully in frame.

Heavy snowfall sweeps a vast flat grey asphalt parade ground, painted formation lines showing through the slush, a row of flagless poles clanging and low brick barracks fading at the edges while loose snow-dust blows low across the surface. Four adults cross the emptiness: a tall Black man in a red thermal, a slender white woman with a dark bob in ivory, a strong Turkish woman in emerald, a lean South Asian man in navy. They chase each other corner to corner, attacking the long diagonal with a huge sissonne, a tour jeté landing deep in the slush, then chassé steps into another soaring leap. Dreamy, desaturated music-video wash. One continuous shot, camera dollying slowly in; all four stay fully framed.

A thin reflective film of drizzle lies over the cracked white salt crust, low dust still skating across the drier patches, crooked marker stakes and a line of pylons shrinking toward the horizon. Six adults spar in three pairs on the flat: a broad Black woman in orange, a wiry white man with a topknot in grey, a Turkish man in a blue rash vest, a tall Latina in white, an older East Asian woman in green, a stocky white woman in black. Padded sticks crack together as they strike, slip, duck and counter within a few metres. All begin fully framed; one duellist backs toward the lens and ends partly out of frame. One continuous shot, handheld camera circling at chest height.

Daylight falls in sharp shafts through high slot windows and the ramp mouth of an underground parking garage, epoxy-coated concrete stretching between painted bays and yellow columns, confetti scraps skittering across the floor on the draught. Two adults crouch at a painted line: a heavyset Middle Eastern man, forties, thick beard, in a maroon tee and black shorts, and a sinewy white woman, thirties, blonde braid, in a lime tank. They launch into bear crawl races, hands and feet slapping the floor, driving the full length of the empty bays and slamming a far column before scrambling back. Epic, high-contrast cinematic. One continuous shot, handheld camera circling slowly; both stay fully in frame.

Midday sun drops hard shadows across an apartment complex inner courtyard paved in interlocking concrete, one plane tree in a square planter, balconies bristling with satellite dishes, a geometric mural on the end wall. Three adults train on the pavers: a compact Turkish man, twenties, in a grey singlet; a tall Black woman, thirties, cornrows, in a red rash guard; a broad white man, fifties, shaved head, in navy. They drill double-leg takedowns, level-changing, penetrating on one knee, driving a partner two or three metres and lowering them under control before resetting. Nothing else stirs in the still air. Bright, snappy sports-ad energy. One continuous shot, handheld camera circling slowly at chest height.

Storm light presses down on the travertine pool deck of a cliffside alpine spa hotel, where an empty infinity pool mirrors black cloud and fog banks pour over the ridge behind the loungers. Three adults hold the deck: a broad Black man in yellow shorts, a wiry Southeast Asian woman in a white tank, a lean grey-bearded white man barefoot. All three start fully in frame, feet planted on the pale tile, swaying through low ginga, then trading slow cartwheels, ducking au and rasteira sweeps past each other's heads. One continuous shot, the camera craning down from high above to eye level. Gritty documentary texture, damp stone, no rain yet.

Hard noon light bounces off the granite setts of a car-free alpine shopping lane, flower boxes blazing on carved wooden balconies, a bronze fountain standing dry at the corner. Four adults stand on the stone: a tall Kenyan woman in orange, a stocky Turkish man in denim, a freckled redheaded woman in mint, a silver-haired Japanese man in a track jacket. All four are fully framed, shoes on the setts, before a whistle drops them into prone and seated starts and fires them back up into scrambling bursts, cutting sideways and slapping the pavement. Shoppers watch from behind café railings only. One continuous shot craning down from high above to eye level; the redhead surges toward the lens and leaves frame at the edge.

Cobalt dusk pools in a high alpine farmyard, packed dirt swept smooth between a stone barn, a tipped hay wagon and rusted milk cans. Two adults face off: a compact Filipina woman in a white plastron and blue socks, and a rangy older Swiss man with a grey ponytail in faded grey. Both stand fully in frame, boots on the dirt, saluting with sport foils, then explode into repeated lunges, beat-attacks and quick parry-riposte exchanges, retreating and advancing along a few metres of packed earth. Their soles squeak and puff dust; the still evening air carries every clang. One continuous shot with a handheld camera slowly circling at chest height. Bright, playful energy under the fading light.

Black thunderheads stack over an alpine stadium, and the red tartan of the throwing area glows sick orange under the pre-rain light; empty banners hang dead on the fence. Three heavy-shouldered adults occupy one small circle of track: a Samoan woman in navy, a pale Slavic man with a shaved head, an older Brazilian man in a grey singlet. All three stay fully in frame, feet on the rubber, cycling through crouched glide-and-release shot put attempts, each rocking back, driving low across a metre, twisting and punching the ball skyward with a grunt. Spectators watch only from the distant concrete grandstand. One continuous shot, the camera craning down from above to eye level. Moody, near-monochrome noir.

Inside a mountain cold-storage warehouse, frosted concrete stretches between towering racks of pallets, and coloured stage lights someone rigged for a shoot wash the frost magenta and cyan while vapour drifts from ceiling vents. One athlete works the aisle alone: a muscular mixed-race woman in a lime crop top and black shorts, hair in tight braids. She begins fully in frame, bare feet on the icy slab, then kicks to a handstand and travels the long aisle on her hands, hopping, pivoting, chasing her own shadow. One continuous shot dollying slowly in until she walks her hands close and her legs cross out of frame. Bright, punchy sports-ad energy.

Neon spills from a shuttered ski-resort bar's window tubes across a white gypsum flat high in the Swiss Alps, sand ghosting low over the ground, a cable-car pylon dark against the peaks. One adult performs alone: a tall Brazilian-Swiss woman in her thirties, box braids under a wool cap, oversized black jacket, magenta laces. She swings both arms in wide power arcs, snaps a chest pop that ripples through her jacket, throws down hard as if flinging the air away, then locks into a trembling freeze before releasing into another round. Her boots never leave one small patch of gypsum; she stays fully in frame. One continuous shot, a slow dolly-out revealing the empty basin.

A village sports hall high in the mountains: green vinyl badminton court, sagging nets pushed aside, haze curling through moving spotlights while the practice lamps leave the corners black. Five adults share the court — a broad Māori man in red, a blonde white woman in teal, a white woman with a dark bob in grey, a slight Korean man in yellow, a grey-templed Iranian man in black. Every one of them is fully framed with shoes on the vinyl, then they burst into a tag game: sharp cuts, skidding lunges, hands slapping shoulders, bodies reversing direction in a single stride. Friends spectate from the wooden bleachers along the wall. One continuous shot from a static tripod at eye level. Playful, bouncing, commercial-bright.

Fog swallows the crest roadway of an alpine hydroelectric dam; white lane lines run off into grey nothing past a lichened parapet and a dead floodlight mast. Three runners crouch on the concrete, all fully in frame with spikes down: a slender Ethiopian woman in violet, a thickset Māori-featured man in charcoal, a blonde woman in a faded blue singlet. They rock back and detonate into a head-to-head sprint, arms scything, crossing dozens of metres of dam crest toward a chalked finish line, all three staying fully framed as they lean together at the tape. The fog hangs dead still around them. One continuous shot, a handheld camera circling slowly at chest height. Dreamy, diffuse, music-video softness with silver light.

Hazy afternoon wind scours an alpine canal quay, dust skimming the grey cobble setts past moored wooden boats and a row of chestnut trees gone pale with grit. Two adults face each other over three metres of stone: a tanned Greek woman with a long plait in a red vest, and a lanky Nigerian man in yellow suspenders. Both are fully in frame, boots planted on the setts, and they stay on their spots, whipping juggling clubs back and forth in fast crossing showers, doubles and triples spinning through the dusty light, arms snapping, knees bouncing. Passers-by watch from the far bank railing. One continuous shot, the camera tracking sideways at a steady walking pace. Cheerful, sunlit, commercial.

A decommissioned station under an alpine town: long tiled concrete platform, dead tracks, cracked enamel signage stripped blank, moody practice lamps throwing deep shadow along the tiles, big salvage fans stirring loose paper and dust down the tunnel mouth. Four adults line up, all fully framed on the tiles — a burly Indian man in a soaked grey tee, a short muscular white woman in navy, a tattooed Latina in cutoffs, a wiry older Vietnamese man barefoot. On a shout they drop and bear-crawl hard along the platform, hips low, palms slapping tile, covering its full length, paper skittering past their hands. Nobody else is down here. One continuous shot, camera dollying slowly out to reveal the empty vault. Raw, grainy, documentary.

Harsh midday sun bleaches a closed street in an Alpine town, barrier poles at both ends, geranium balconies above, a crosswalk baked into the asphalt; grit skims low across the paint. Four adults dance in two pairs on the stripes. A silver-haired Cuban man in his sixties leads a compact Thai woman in her twenties through an enchufla doble into a sombrero, hands sweeping over her head. Beside them a tall Nigerian woman in her forties, yellow wrap dress, spins a stocky Austrian man in his thirties into a hammerlock and unwinds him with a dile que no. Nobody drifts off their square meter; all four stay fully in frame, shoes on the asphalt. One continuous shot from a static tripod at eye level.

An old grand hotel ballroom in the Alps has been cleared for training: waxed parquet, dust-furred chandeliers, radiator steam curling through shafts of daylight that fall from tall arched windows. Four adults work one square of floor, all fully in frame with feet down throughout: a scarred Thai man holding pads, a tall Danish woman kicking, a heavyset Puerto Rican man in a sweat-black tee, a compact Somali woman with taped shins. They stay on their spots, hammering roundhouse kicks into the pads, switching stance, checking and returning, the cracks echoing off gilt plaster. One continuous shot in a slow orbit around them. Gritty handheld-documentary grain, sweat, warm dust.

Golden hour rakes the dark basalt setts of an alpine railway station forecourt; banners and a tarp over a bike rack whip in hard wind, and funicular sheds glow amber above the platforms. Two adults train there alone: a shaven-headed Egyptian man in wrapped hands and grey sweats, and a broad-shouldered Norwegian woman in a faded black hoodie. Both stand fully in frame, boots on the stone, then move a few metres through shadow boxing — slipping, rolling under imagined hooks, doubling jabs, pivoting off the back foot. One continuous shot, the camera tracking sideways at walking pace, and near the end the woman drifts toward the lens until her shoulder crops out of frame. Documentary rough, wind-loud.

Heavy snow falls on a high grass shelf beneath alpine ridges, cropped brown stalks poking through white, a leaning fence line and torn festival paper tumbling on the wind. Five adults hold a tight patch of ground, every one fully framed with boots on the grass: a towering Sudanese man in black, a compact Peruvian woman in orange, a blond Czech man shirtless and steaming, a tattooed Filipino man in grey, a lean Greek woman in navy. Each takes turns from a single spot, launching 540 kicks, corks and butterfly twists, snow bursting off their landings. One continuous shot with the camera tracking sideways at a steady pace. Epic, wide, cinematic cold.

Sunrise mist hangs around an open-air festival stage built on an alpine meadow: bare aluminium deck, scaffold towers strung with dead cable, a banner of blank canvas sagging behind. Three adults work the deck, all fully in frame with boots on the metal at the start: a sunburnt Australian woman in a knotted shirt, a stout Mexican man in a straw hat, a lanky Sri Lankan man in a grey vest. They swing small hay bales up hand to hand, hurling them onto a stack that grows past head height, straw spinning through the pale light. One continuous shot, slow dolly-in, until the woman steps close and her torso fills and exits the frame edge. Sunny, upbeat, commercial.

Snow pours over a gravel service road threading an alpine refinery, pipe racks furred white, a cold flare stack above, dry leaves swirling low with the flakes. Two adults face each other across the gravel, both fully in frame with boots down: a broad Inuit woman in a scuffed orange parka, and a wiry bearded Portuguese man in a blue boiler suit. They dig a shovelling race, ranging a few metres up and down the road, blades biting, flinging bright arcs of snow sideways, stamping, resetting, breath ripping in the cold as their heaps grow. One continuous shot, handheld camera circling slowly at chest height; the man finally lunges toward the lens and his shoulder leaves frame. Grainy documentary realism.

Mist burns off an alpine lake at sunrise and waves keep slapping the shingle beyond a raked sand volleyball court, its net posts leaning, a wooden boathouse black against the water. Two adults work the sand, both fully in frame, barefoot: a rangy Colombian man in navy shorts, and a strong-shouldered Polish woman in a grey two-piece kit. They take turns launching a few metres sideways into headfirst belly-flop dives, arms outstretched, skidding through the sand, bouncing up and resetting, sand sheeting off their ribs. Nobody else is around. One continuous shot with a handheld camera circling slowly at chest height. Cold silver light, deep shadow, noir mood.

Storm cloud stacks black over pale cliffs, and a long strip of fine white sand along an alpine lake glows unnaturally bright before the rain; driftwood and an overturned rowboat mark the far end. Three adults spread across the sand, all fully framed with bare feet down: a broad Tongan man in a cut-off jersey, a tall ash-blonde woman in grey compression gear, an older Black man with silver stubble in maroon. They run route after route across the beach, one dropping back with quick shuffling steps and firing long spirals downfield while the others sprint, catch and jog back. One continuous shot, the camera craning down from high above to eye level. Harsh, grainy, documentary.

Night in a scrap yard wedged in an alpine valley: oil-stained concrete apron, towers of crushed cars, a magnet crane hanging dead, and a buzzing violet-and-orange neon tube on the office shack throwing colour over everything. One dancer works a single square metre, fully in frame from first frame to last, sneakers on the stained slab: a lean Puerto Rican man in a grey mechanic's jumpsuit unzipped to the waist, a white singlet beneath. He fires robotic pops, dime stops and slow arm waves that ripple shoulder to fingertip, hitting hard on unheard beats. One continuous shot from a static tripod at eye level. Rough documentary grain, oil-slick reflections, cold neon.

An alpine cathedral nave stands empty: worn stone flagstones between massive columns, daylight falling in hard shafts from clerestory windows while flickering neon and sweeping searchlights from a street festival stutter through the coloured glass. One athlete occupies the aisle, fully in frame with trainers on the flagstones: a heavily built Māori woman in a black long-sleeve top and red shorts, hair scraped back. She drives a weighted sled the length of the nave, body angled low, legs pistoning, steel grinding on stone, resetting and going again. One continuous shot dollying slowly in, until she pushes so close her arms and head crop out of frame. Neo-noir, cold and cavernous.

Mist smokes off a sandstone forecourt square below an alpine cathedral, tall pennants and a loose tarp cracking in the wind, a worn stone cross at the square's centre. Three adults hold one small patch of paving, all fully in frame with feet down: two bases — a burly Argentinian man in black and a tall Nigerian-British woman in grey — and a small, wiry Vietnamese-American flyer in white. They lock wrists and punch a basket toss skyward, the flyer snapping straight, kicking a twist and dropping back into their arms, then reloading and going again. Onlookers watch from the cathedral steps far behind a rope. One continuous shot with a slow pan left to right. Cold, silvery noir.

A frozen alpine lake stretches black-green under night, its dry snow dust lying dead still, the neon of a lakeside village bar smearing red and blue over the ice. One skater is out there alone: a powerfully built Korean-Canadian man in a battered navy jersey and black pants, breath tearing white. He starts fully in frame, skates flat on the snow-dusted ice, then explodes into sprint starts, crossing dozens of metres before slamming into hockey stops that fire long plumes of ice into the neon. One continuous shot, handheld camera circling slowly at chest height; on the last stop he skids nearly into the lens and his skates leave the frame. Epic, cinematic, huge.

A flat wave-worn rock shelf runs out into an alpine lake, slick and dark, lit by the neon of a floating pontoon bar while confetti from some earlier party tumbles across the stone. One tricker owns the shelf: a compact Brazilian-Japanese woman in yellow shorts and a black long-sleeve top, hair in a high bun. Fully in frame with bare feet on the rock, she strings together 540 kicks, butterfly twists and a low sweeping cork, travelling a couple of metres between landings, confetti kicking up around her. One continuous shot, handheld camera circling slowly at chest height; she finishes by bounding toward the lens until her legs crop out. Playful, glossy, colour-popping.

Golden hour floods a lakeside promenade laid in black-and-white mosaic waves, palms replaced by clipped limes, an old bandstand and a stone jetty catching the last amber. One runner works the whole length: a thickset Basque man in his forties, sleeves rolled, canvas shoes, sweat darkening a blue shirt. Fully in frame with feet on the mosaic, he crouches and drives a wooden barrel rolling ahead of him at a run, chasing it fifty metres down the promenade, slapping it straight, wheeling it around a marker and racing back. Tourists watch from behind the seawall railing above. One continuous shot with a slow dolly-in. Warm, hazy, dreamy music-video glow.

A painted concrete landing circle tops an alpine clinic, its faded ring flaking, a windsock and lashed tarps snapping hard, snow peaks stacked behind under soft overcast. Four adults share the circle, all fully in frame with sneakers on the concrete: a lean Dominican man in a red tracksuit, a muscular Ukrainian woman with a bleached crop, a heavyset Filipino man in olive, a tall Ethiopian woman in white. They bounce through toprock, then drop one after another into fast six-step footwork, spinning on palms, kicking up, popping back to their feet within a couple of metres. One continuous shot with a slow dolly-in. Bright, bouncy, upbeat commercial energy.

Deep inside a decommissioned car plant in an Alpine valley, only a few practice lamps burn, leaving the epoxy-coated concrete in long shadow; an empty paint-booth tunnel gapes at one end and stripped parts racks line the aisle. Paper scraps tumble in a draft from a loading door. Two adults race loaded sleds down the yellow lane markings: a thickset Turkish-Swiss man in his forties, shaved head, black thermal, driving low with straight arms, and a rangy Jamaican woman in her thirties, locs bound back, orange tee, matching him stride for stride. They push forty meters, turn, and grind back, sweat dripping onto the concrete, both fully in frame. One continuous shot, a slow orbit around them.

Under the glass canopy of an alpine transit hall, grey porcelain tile stretches between ticket columns and frosted escalators, warm tungsten work lamps hanging on cables while steam drifts up from floor vents. Two adults dance there alone: a slim Korean man in a cropped black jacket and wide trousers, and a strong-lined Kazakh woman in silver with a long ponytail. Both stay fully in frame, shoes on the tile, moving only a few metres as they hit hard synchronized choreography — sharp pointing lines, snapped head turns, unison drops to a knee, whip-fast arm isolations. One continuous shot, the camera dollying slowly out to reveal the vast empty hall. Epic, burnished, cinematic.

A lake freighter lies moored beneath alpine cliffs, its painted steel weather deck streaked with rust between low hatch covers and a hunched deck crane, thunderheads piling black above the peaks. One performer commands the deck: a compact Chinese man in his thirties, red sash at the waist over black trousers, bare-chested and taut, no costume. He begins fully in frame with feet on the steel, then works the deck end to end in lion-dance style bounds — deep crouches, explosive pounces along the flat plating, sharp head-snapping stances, landing and springing again. One continuous shot, the camera craning down from high above to eye level. Epic, monumental, storm-lit cinema.

A small octagon sits in a converted alpine barn gym, chain-link stretched around a scuffed vinyl mat, low practice lamps leaving the corners in deep shadow while confetti from a fight-night promo still drifts through the air. One fighter works inside: a wiry Moroccan woman in a burgundy rash guard and black shorts, hair braided tight, hands taped. Fully in frame with feet on the mat at the start, she drops flat, then explodes up from prone, seated and rolling-fall positions, scrambling to her stance, shooting a step forward, resetting and falling again within a couple of metres. One continuous shot with a slow pan left to right. Soft, floating, dreamy tones.

An alpine arena sits half-lit, white ice ruled with faded painted lines, vapour drifting from the compressor vents, low practice lamps pooling on the boards. Six adults skid across one corner in sneakers, all fully in frame with feet on the ice: a barrel-chested Finnish man, a quick Vietnamese woman in red, a tall Nigerian man in yellow, a freckled Scottish woman, a grey-haired Italian man, a stocky Mexican woman in blue. They scramble at broomball, hacking at a battered ball, sliding, colliding gently, spinning to recover in a few metres of ice. One continuous shot with a slow dolly-in. Hazy, luminous, dreamlike music-video softness.

Soft overcast light lies flat on a herringbone brick plaza outside an alpine university library, a glass reading room glowing dully behind slender birches and a low granite bench. One dancer occupies a single spot: a striking Spanish woman in her thirties, black hair pinned severe, a deep green ruffled skirt and dark heeled shoes. Fully in frame throughout, heels on the brick, she drills bursts of zapateado — heel-toe volleys hammering the pavers, escobilla flurries, arms curling overhead in slow braceo between the storms of sound. The plaza is empty around her. One continuous shot with a slow dolly-in. Crisp, bright, high-energy sports-ad clarity and contrast.

Daylight falls in dusty shafts from high clerestory windows onto the glossy maple of a mountain-town roller rink, its rental counter shuttered and a broken disco rig throwing flickering neon while a searchlight beam swings across the boards. Three adults tap in a loose triangle. A slight Japanese-Swiss woman in her fifties, pearl-grey slip dress, rides a soft waltz clog. A muscular Colombian man in his twenties, mesh vest, answers with brush-heel riffs and a stomp-brush-hop-step turn. A freckled Scottish woman in her thirties, denim overalls, threads syncopated toe stands between them. Each stays on one board-width of floor, fully in frame, feet down. One continuous shot, a slow dolly-out revealing more of the rink.

Floodlights rake one side of an indoor alpine pool hall, throwing long hard shadows across the non-slip ceramic deck; lane ropes coil by the blocks and confetti from a meet still drifts on the humid air. One athlete trains beside a plyo box: a powerfully built Brazilian woman in a black one-piece and cropped hoodie, calves flexing. She stays fully in frame with feet on the tile, dipping and firing into repeated box jumps, landing soft, stepping down, resetting on the same square metre, breath sharp. A handful of coaches watch from the raised gallery behind glass. One continuous shot, the camera craning down from high above to eye level. Hard-edged neo-noir contrast.

A bruise-colored storm front stacks over an alpine race circuit; the pit lane's striped tarmac lies dead calm, garage shutters down, a bare marshal's flag stand and stacked tire barriers along the wall. Five adults drill volleyball on the stripes. A broad Croatian man in his forties digs low, a compact Brazilian woman in her twenties sets tight, and a lean Filipino man in his thirties rolls a controlled attack back; a tall Ethiopian woman in her forties and a stocky Finnish man in his fifties mirror the triangle beside them, chasing shanked balls a few paces. Fans watch from the grandstand above the wall. All five stay fully in frame, shoes on tarmac. One continuous shot, a slow orbit around them.

A converted alpine sound stage swallows light: matte black floor, black drapes on rails, cable coils along the walls, big fans stirring dust and loose paper while daylight cuts down in hard shafts from high clerestory panels. One gymnast owns the space: a wiry Mongolian man in white shorts and a black singlet, chalk on his hands, feet bare. He stands fully in frame on the black floor, then runs a long tumbling line across the stage — hurdle, round-off, back handspring, snapping into a back tuck, sticking it and jogging back to start again. One continuous shot from a static tripod at eye level. Vast, epic, high-contrast cinema.

Warm tungsten work lamps on stands light the great hall of an alpine courthouse: checkerboard marble underfoot, scaffolding against a frescoed vault, big fans stirring dust and loose paper through the beams. Six adults ring one patch of marble, every one fully in frame with feet down: a broad Nigerian woman in gold, a wiry Lebanese man in white, a blonde Russian woman in black, a heavyset Hawaiian man in red, a slim Ecuadorian man in grey, a silver-haired French woman in blue. Each in turn swings and rips a standing back tuck or standing full, landing on the same square. One continuous shot, camera dollying slowly out. Grand, golden, epic cinema.

Golden hour burns along a grey gravel outwash plain below a hanging alpine glacier, braided meltwater channels catching fire, fireworks bursting soundlessly over a distant ridge town. Two adults square up on the stones, both fully framed with boots dug in: a tall silver-braided Sámi woman in a worn canvas jacket, and a stocky Nepali man in a red flannel shirt. Neither leaves their spot; gripping long-handled shovels they compete blow for blow, blades crunching into the gravel, grit spraying up in glittering fans, hips torquing, shoulders burning, their piles climbing fast. One continuous shot, the camera in a slow orbit around them. Cool shadows against amber, hard-edged neo-noir mood.

Light rain glazes the cast concrete flat bottom of an alpine skatepark cut into a hillside, coping beading with water, tagged transitions and a road above where headlights streak past in long trails. A single athlete has the slab to himself: a lean Vietnamese-French man in a black hoodie and grey joggers, soaked hair pushed back. Fully in frame with shoes on the concrete, he chains a hook-kick feint into a 540, lands, whips a butterfly twist, then a cheat-360 tornado kick, shifting a few metres across the slab while water sprays off his heels. A few onlookers watch from the railing above the bowl. One continuous shot in a slow orbit. Epic, glossy, cinematic reflections.

Daylight falls in hard shafts through the high windows of an alpine gym onto a small boxing ring, its canvas grey with rosin, ropes sagging, corner buckets stacked. Three adults share the mat, all fully in frame with sneakers down: a shaven-headed Cuban man in a white tee, a broad Nigerian-German woman in denim shorts, a lean older Japanese man in black. Anchored to one small square of canvas, they trade rounds — indian steps and shuffles up top, then each sinking to hands for a six-step, legs carving circles, before rising back into the bounce. Gym members watch from behind the ropes and the raised gallery. One continuous shot, the camera craning down from high above to eye level. Stark, moody noir.

In a shuttered alpine weaving hall, rows of silent looms stand under a few low practice lamps, their frames throwing long shadows across a wide plank floor; paper scraps from old pattern cards tumble in the draft. One adult trains the empty aisle: a compact Swiss-Tamil man in his thirties, wiry, headband, grey compression top, red shorts. He explodes off a chalk mark, sprints five meters to a marker cone, slaps the plank, cuts hard on one foot, drives back ten meters to the far cone, touches again, and finishes flat out through the start, chest heaving. He covers the whole aisle yet stays fully in frame, feet on the boards. One continuous shot, a handheld camera slowly circling at chest height.

Inside a bamboo grove behind a derelict Victorian glasshouse in east London, rusted iron arches lean under the canes and packed earth is littered with dry brown leaves. Three adults train in one continuous shot: a tall Black man in a charcoal jersey, a wiry Filipina woman in slate grey, a broad white man in oxblood. All three start fully in frame, feet on the leaf-strewn soil, as the camera cranes down from high above to eye level. The thrower takes a five-step drop-back, plants, and fires a tight spiral a few metres; the receiver cuts and catches, then jogs toward the lens until she is cropped at the waist. The still air holds. Muted, moody neo-noir grey.

Floodlights rake in from one sideline of a converted drill-hall basketball court in east London, half the polished maple left in shadow; a broken neon strip flickers over the tunnel mouth and a security beam sweeps the far wall. One adult works the wing: a tall Anglo-Caribbean man in his thirties, sleeve tattoo, black hoodie, grey shorts. He pounds a hesitation in-and-out, snaps a hard between-the-legs into a retreat step-back, freezes, then attacks again with a wrap and a spin, ball ringing off the boards. A handful of onlookers sit in the raised bleachers behind the barrier. He stays fully in frame within a few meters, shoes squeaking on the maple. One continuous shot, the camera tracking sideways at a steady walking pace.

Five adults own an empty granite forecourt beside a City office block, its polished pavers streaked pale by a dusty hazy afternoon wind, three low stone planters and a dry runnel edging the space. Nobody else is in sight. A stocky Māori man in mustard, a slim Korean woman in mint, a freckled English woman in coral, a grey-bearded Black man in white, and a tall Latina in cobalt all begin fully in frame with feet on the stone and remain so. Held on a static tripod at eye level, one continuous shot: each takes a short run of two metres, dives hands-first into a kong vault over a low box, lands popping upright, and claps the next one in. Bright, sunny, cheerful.

Shafts of daylight drop through high clerestory windows of a disused Thameside rolling mill, striking a vast steel plate floor beside two idle rollers and a hanging chain hoist. Paper scraps and torn shipping tags tumble slowly through the beams. One woman — early forties, Ethiopian, close-cropped hair, in a lavender kit and worn boots — begins fully in frame with both feet on the metal and stays wholly visible. A static tripod at eye level holds one continuous shot as she carries a ball the width of the hall: double step-over, sharp cut left across the plate, scissor again, drag-back, then a long acceleration past the rollers and a stop-turn at the far edge. Soft, floating, dreamlike colour.

A stripped gallery hall in Southwark: blank white walls, four empty plinths, pale oak planks buffed by decades of visitors. Steam drifts from a floor vent and harsh floodlights blast in from one side, throwing long hard shadows. Six adults hold their own small patches of floor and stay fully framed, feet down at the start — a burly Samoan man in white, a lithe Vietnamese woman in orange, a silver-haired white woman in navy, a lanky Black man in lime, a compact Turkish man in red, a tattooed Irish woman in teal. One continuous shot dollies slowly in as they drop into windmills, kick into flares, and spike headspins, each rooted on one spot. Bright, punchy, athletic.

Storm light presses down on an empty concourse plaza outside a Stratford arena — shutters pulled over ticket windows, steel ramps curving away, stamped concrete pale and dry before the rain. Torn programme pages tumble past in the gusts. Three adults, alone here, remain fully in frame with feet on the slabs: a heavyset Jamaican man in a grey hoodie, a small Japanese woman in plum, a tall pale Ukrainian man in navy. One continuous shot, camera tracking sideways at a walking pace, follows a line of orange cones as each player stickhandles a ball-puck through it — toe drags, quick dekes, a backhand slip between cones, then a snap pass down the line. Dreamy, desaturated, cinematic blue.

Pale sunrise light filters through mist onto a red clay tennis court behind a London leisure club, the net taken down, a rusted umpire chair and a stack of ball hoppers at the fence; a faulty floodlamp flickers neon-blue while a maintenance searchlight swings past. Two adults train on one spot of crushed brick. A stocky Somali-British woman in her forties, cornrows, teal rashguard, holds thick Thai pads chest-high, feet planted. A lanky Polish man in his twenties, bleached crop, red shorts, snaps two quick teeps, then drives a switch kick and finishes with a leaping knee into the pads, dust puffing off the clay. Both remain fully in frame. One continuous shot; the camera dollies slowly back to take in the whole court.

Heavy snowfall settles on the close-mown turf of a suburban London tennis lawn, a wooden pavilion behind, benches stacked under a bare hedge; a handful of onlookers watch from the pavilion veranda, off the grass entirely. Three adults grip a thick rope and stay fully in frame, boots planted: a burly Scottish man in a soaked green fleece, a strong-shouldered Ghanaian woman in maroon, a lean older Chinese man in grey. Filmed as one continuous shot, the camera dollying slowly out to show the whitening court, they heave in unison, skid a metre through slush, dig in, then lose it and collapse backwards laughing into the snow before scrambling up. Cold, grainy, documentary honesty.

Soft overcast daylight flattens a broad concrete esplanade under old Thames wharf cranes, mooring bollards spaced along the low tide wall, no one else about. Far downriver, fireworks bloom silently over the rooftops. Three adults begin fully in frame, feet on the slabs, and remain visible: a rangy Somali man in an amber kit, a muscular white woman with a dark ponytail in slate, a stocky Brazilian man in cream. In one continuous shot the camera cranes down from high above to eye level as they work the length of the walkway — a driven power shot rifled twenty metres into a stack of crates, a sprint after the rebound, a first-time volley struck flat, then a lofted half-volley returned. Lush, dreamy, glowing.

Dusty haze rolls across a clipped corporate lawn in Chiswick, a glass atrium reflecting the wind-blown afternoon, hedges trimmed into low blocks. Colleagues watch from the raised terrace behind the railing, never on the grass. Far off, fireworks crack faintly above the rooftops. Two adults lock up and hold one patch of turf, fully in frame with feet down the entire time: a shaven-headed Turkish man in navy shorts, and a tall Black woman in a red rash top with taped hands. One continuous shot orbits slowly around them as they fight for the clinch — collar ties swapped, hips broken, alternating knees driven up to the body, a hard sweep of the head, then reset without travelling. Raw, handheld, documentary texture.

A small basement squash court beneath a Bloomsbury club: chipped plaster walls, a faded red service line, a scarred glass back panel. Low moody practice lights leave the corners in deep shadow and the air is perfectly still. One man — late twenties, mixed Caribbean heritage, wiry with a fade and a thin gold chain, in a white tee and black shorts — begins fully in frame, both feet on the pale hardwood, and stays fully visible. In one continuous shot the camera tracks sideways at a steady walking pace as he stickhandles a ball through five short cones set along the wall: quick toe drags, a wide deke around one, a between-the-feet pull, then a snap flick into the tin. Hazy, slow, dreamlike.

Harsh midday sun bleaches a wide paddock of short golden grass on London's outer green belt, a split-rail fence running away toward distant pylons and a lone hay bale. Nobody else shares the field, and the air is dead still. Two adults stay fully in frame with feet on the grass throughout: a compact Mongolian woman in a blue rash guard, and a broad ginger-bearded man in grey. A static tripod at eye level records one continuous shot as they drill inside a few metres — a snapping double-leg shot finished into a lift, a hip throw reversed mid-air, then a scramble on the ground into a back-take before both bounce up grinning and reset. Bright, sunny, cheerfully commercial.

Where two lanes meet at the London fringe, packed gravel spreads under a leaning wooden signpost, dry hedgerow either side, empty fields beyond. Dusty haze blows through the late afternoon while stray snowflakes drift down through the low beams of light, improbable and lovely. Two adults, alone, keep both feet on the gravel and stay fully in frame: a young Punjabi man in a saffron shirt, and a freckled woman in her fifties with silver-streaked hair and a violet jacket. One continuous shot circles them handheld at chest height as their poi build from a two-beat weave into a fast three-beat, they turn under their arms, step a metre sideways, and finish with crossed extensions. Playful, bright, buoyant.

Bare steel racking lines an emptied Barking distribution warehouse, taped lanes marking the polished concrete, a roller door shut at the far end under bright even overhead lighting. The air is completely still and no one else is present. Four adults stand fully in frame, boots on the floor: a broad Polish man in orange, a tall Kenyan woman in navy, a stocky Vietnamese man in grey, a strong white woman in olive. One continuous shot tracks sideways at a steady walking pace as they haul a flat hose from a reel and sprint it the length of the aisle, feeding coils hand over hand, hitting the far marker, dropping the line flat with a slap, then racing back along the lane. Bright, high-energy, athletic.

Black marley stretches across a rehearsal studio near Islington, a bare brick wall and two wooden barres along one side, rosin dust in the corners. Torn paper programme scraps tumble through the air from an open skylight while the overheads burn evenly. Four adults hold the floor alone, fully in frame with feet down from the start: a tall Japanese woman in indigo, a heavyset white man in charcoal, a lean Ethiopian man in navy, a short Spanish woman in slate. Handheld, the camera circles slowly at chest height in one continuous shot as they drill with wooden practice swords — sliding forward a metre into a men strike, retreating, then paired kote and do cuts snapping in unison. Cold, low-key, noir contrast.

Warm tungsten work lamps hang from riveted girders in a wartime concrete bunker hall under Clapham, cable spools stacked against the sweating walls, steam curling from a ventilation grille. Only six adults are down here, each pair holding a single patch of damp concrete, fully in frame with feet on the floor and never travelling: a broad Cuban man in a red shirt, a slender Indian woman in gold, a bald Greek man in white, a tall Black woman in emerald, a stocky Dutch man in blue, a curly-haired Colombian woman in fuchsia. One continuous shot, static tripod at eye level, catches triple spins, cross-body leads and hammerlock turns. Bright, kinetic, ad-slick.

Green tatami covers a small dojo above a Bethnal Green shop, a wooden weapon rack on one wall, a shuttered window leaking flickering neon from the street while a searchlight beam sweeps the ceiling. Only two adults train here: a powerfully built Nigerian woman in a white gi jacket and black shorts, and a lean grey-templed Italian man in navy. Both start fully in frame, bare feet on the mats, and stay visible. Handheld, the camera circles slowly at chest height in one continuous shot as they take turns with a padded box set low on the tatami — three running steps, a kong vault with hands slapping the top, tuck through, land soft, roll clear, then the other follows. Grand, dark, cinematic.

Off-season, the ice is gone from a rink built inside a Victorian market hall in London: painted concrete slab, cast-iron roof trusses overhead, coiled refrigeration pipe and a folded penalty bench pushed to one side. Practice lamps leave the corners black. Three adults stand in a tight feed pattern, feet fixed on the slab: a broad Ukrainian man in his fifties, braces over a striped shirt, showers clubs to a compact Brazilian woman in her twenties, who fires doubles straight back while a rangy Indian-British man in his thirties, orange vest, cuts triples across the middle. The air is still. Staff watch from the seating tiers behind the boards. All three stay fully in frame. One continuous shot, a slow dolly-in toward them.

Empty bays stripe the asphalt of a Battersea bus depot hall, a fuel gantry at the far end, faded stencil marks worn between the lines under bright even overheads. Haze-machine fog drifts thick while moving spotlights swing across the floor, and nobody else is inside. Three adults start fully in frame, boots on the asphalt: a huge Fijian man in a grey vest, a sinewy Iranian woman in black, a stocky Portuguese man in navy. One continuous shot dollies slowly toward them as each drives a weighted sled the length of two bays in a flat-backed sprint, chops the feet at the line, then turns and hauls it back by straps. Rough, honest, documentary grain.

Heavy snow falls on an empty surface car park behind a London retail shed, faded bay lines barely showing, a bent lamp column and a chained trolley bay at the edge; grit skitters low across the asphalt between drifts. One adult throws long: a broad-backed Japanese-British woman in her forties, hair tied under a beanie, navy warm-up jacket, mitt tucked under her arm. She sets on an imaginary rubber, rocks into a high leg lift, drives forward, and fires a ball the length of the lot into a chain-link backstop, then jogs down to collect and repeats from the far end. She stays fully in frame, boots on the asphalt. One continuous shot, a handheld camera slowly circling at chest height.

Fine grey ash covers a levelled flat beside a demolished London gasworks, low slag heaps and twisted pipe stubs breaking the horizon, hazy wind lifting dust while fog banks roll slowly through. Two adults are alone out here, both fully in frame with feet in the ash as the shot opens: a tall Sudanese man holding two hand paddles, in black; a compact Vietnamese woman in a red vest and grey wraps. One continuous shot cranes down from high above to eye level as she runs three steps and snaps a flying front kick into the paddles, lands, spins, launches a jumping side kick — then stalks straight toward the lens and ends cropped at the chest, breathing hard. Gritty, cold, documentary.

Floodlights blaze over a rain-lashed pitch in north London, striped grass churning to puddle at the touchline, corner flags bending, the stands utterly empty. Rain streaks slash the beams and splash off the turf. Four adults work alone on the grass, all fully in frame with boots planted and staying visible: a broad Maltese man in soaked grey, a tall Nigerian woman in yellow, a wiry Scottish woman in green, a heavyset Bangladeshi man in maroon. One continuous shot pans slowly from left to right down their line as they swing brimming pails hand to hand across ten metres, water arcing and slopping over their arms, the last emptying it into a drum and sprinting the empty back. Rain-black neo-noir.

Under a Vauxhall railway arch, black rubber tiles run between chalk bins and rigs bolted into brick, warm tungsten work lamps swinging on cables while steam drifts from a vent in the wall. Six adults hold the floor with nobody else inside, all fully in frame, feet down, moving only a couple of metres: a bald Bulgarian man in olive, a tall Somali woman in teal, a heavyset Māori woman in rust, a lean Korean man in black, a freckled redhead in cream, a silver-haired Indian man in indigo. One continuous shot dollies slowly out to reveal the arches as wooden staffs blur through figure-eights, roll across shoulders and backs, and fly up in low tosses caught clean. Smoky, amber, noir.

Soft overcast daylight fills a drained shipyard dry dock on the lower Thames — wet concrete underfoot, rows of keel blocks, iron ladders climbing the streaked walls, a puddle mirroring nothing but sky. Snowflakes drift through the pale beams that fall between the dock walls. Two adults have the floor to themselves and stay fully in frame, boots on the wet slab: a lanky Filipino man in a cobalt tunic, and a strong-shouldered Nigerian-British woman in white with braids tied back. One continuous shot circles them handheld at chest height as their flags snap through spins and drops, they step two metres apart, launch simultaneous high tosses that turn four times, and catch on the run. Grainy, sober, documentary.

Neon spills from an estuary promenade onto a wide beach of packed damp sand, black breakwater posts marching to the water, distant pier lights doubled in the flat wet shine. The night is still, and no one else is out. Six adults start fully in frame with bare feet on the sand and remain visible: a tall Sri Lankan man in magenta, a stocky Croatian woman in cyan, a lean Black man in white, a curvy Mexican woman in lime, a wiry Japanese man in orange, a silver-cropped Dutch woman in violet. One continuous shot cranes down from above to eye level as they hurl hoops thirty metres, roll them back with reverse spin, then sprint and dive cleanly through. Bright, saturated, athletic.

A tractor row runs between wire trellises on a chalky Kentish slope outside London, vines heavy, an oast house cowl turning at the top of the field. Hazy wind lifts dust while distant traffic streaks light trails along the ridge road. Six adults have the row entirely to themselves, all fully in frame with feet on the compacted soil at the start and visible throughout: a tall Senegalese woman in gold, a slim Russian man in white, a muscular Brazilian woman in coral, a lanky Chinese man in sky blue, a broad Greek woman in peach, a grey-haired Australian man in sage. One continuous shot dollies out as they bound the length in grand jetés and sissonnes. Sunny, playful, buoyant.

Thick fog pools in a sunken plaza among City bank towers, black granite slick with it, a dry fountain trough and sheer glass walls vanishing upward into grey. The air itself is calm and nobody else is down here. Two adults each claim a single square of stone, fully in frame with feet on the granite and never leaving their spot: a broad-shouldered Trinidadian man in a canary tracksuit, and a small tattooed Czech woman in white with a pink beanie. One continuous shot pans slowly left to right across the plaza as he spins into windmills, kicks up into a flare and holds it, then she drops in, hits a headspin, and pops out into a freeze, both grinning. Playful, poppy, upbeat colour.

A half-bored tunnel runs away into the dark beneath London, raw grey shotcrete underfoot, ring lights bright and even along the arch, stacked concrete segments waiting at the side. The air is dead calm and no one else is down the bore. Two adults lock up on one patch of floor, fully in frame with feet planted and never travelling: a tall Albanian man in black shorts and taped hands, and a broad Jamaican-British woman in a burgundy crop top and wraps. One continuous shot dollies slowly out, revealing the tunnel's throat, as they wrestle for double collar ties, snap the posture down, spear short knees into the ribs, pummel inside, and finish with a hard turn and a leaping knee. Soft-focus, dreamlike, glowing.

Floodlights blaze in from one open side of a Thames shipyard fabrication shed, throwing five long shadows down the rust-stained steel plate floor; gantry rails and a half-cut hull section loom in the gloom. The air is dead still. Five adults stand at a chalked start line, drop, and launch into a bear crawl race, hips low, palms slapping steel: a huge Nigerian-British man in his thirties, a wiry Vietnamese woman in her twenties skittering ahead, a freckled Irish man in his forties, a strong Turkish woman in her fifties, and a compact Chilean man in his twenties. They tear twenty meters to a painted line and back, all five fully in frame. One continuous shot from a static tripod at eye level.

A London community centre's fencing hall glows under warm tungsten work lamps, its metallic piste running down rubber matting between scoring reels and a rack of masks. The air is still. Two adults hit a hard unison routine on the strip: a sharp-featured Korean-British woman in her twenties, blunt fringe, white cropped blazer over black trousers, and a broad Ghanaian man in his thirties, twists tied back, silver-grey suit. They snap through a chest-hit-and-point sequence, drop into synchronized floor slides, spring up and stab arms out in the same beat. Both begin fully in frame, feet on the strip; then he advances at the lens and finishes half out of frame. One continuous shot, a handheld camera slowly circling at chest height.

Wide plank boards creak in a timber barn on the London green belt, hay bales stacked to one side, tack hanging from a beam, the overhead strip lights bright and even. Torn paper feed-sack scraps tumble in the draught from the open doors. Two adults have the barn to themselves and stay fully in frame, feet on the planks: a tall Nigerian man in a green tee and canvas trousers, and a compact Portuguese woman in a rust jumper with a dark bob. One continuous shot dollies slowly toward them as they play a hard chase inside a few metres — sudden jab-step cuts, a fake right and a burst left, a lunging tag on the shoulder, an immediate switch of roles. Grand, warm, cinematic.

Cast-iron columns march down an abandoned brick factory hall in Bow, the floor a patchwork of broken brick tile, a tarnished skylight and bright temporary work lights washing everything evenly. Paper scraps and old ledger pages tumble across the floor in the draught. Four adults have the hall alone and stay fully in frame with trainers on the tile: a broad Turkish man in grey, a lean Jamaican woman in yellow, a tall Finnish man in navy, a stocky Indian woman in maroon. The camera circles them handheld at chest height in one continuous shot as they hammer an agility ladder laid over the brick — icky-shuffles, in-in-out-out, lateral hops, then a fast two-metre burst out the end. Raw, unpolished, documentary.

Fog drifts thick over a round flagstone threshing floor on a hillside above London's greenbelt, a toppled millstone at its rim and a lichened stone wall curving away. Nothing stirs but five adults. Two pairs work the clinch: a tall Thai-British woman in her thirties locks a plum grip on a stocky Greek man in his forties and drives alternating knees to his belt pad; nearby a lean Somali man in his twenties turns a broad Danish woman in her fifties off balance and knees her shield. A silver-haired Nepali coach in his sixties circles, correcting elbows. They drift a few paces at most, all five fully in frame, bare feet on the stone. One continuous shot, a slow pan from left to right.

Light rain lacquers a hardpan plateau above a Thames chalk quarry, sparse scrub tufts and a wind-bent survey pole marking the rim, dust skittering low across the ground between showers. Three adults are alone up here, all fully in frame with feet on the wet hardpan as the shot opens: a burly Serbian man in a black shell jacket, a tall Ghanaian woman in mustard, a stringy Chilean man in grey. One continuous shot cranes down from high above to eye level as they fold one leg up, arms crossed, and hop in to barge shoulders — one staggers, one crashes down laughing — then the winner hops straight at the lens and ends cropped mid-torso. Slick, silvered, noir.

Rain glazes the concrete pavers of a Shoreditch rooftop terrace, planter boxes along the parapet, the skyline stacked and glittering beyond, steam curling from a vent cowl. Onlookers watch from a raised bar deck behind glass, off the terrace floor. Five adults hold one small patch, fully in frame with feet down and never leaving it: a tall Eritrean woman in olive, a stocky Welsh man in navy, a lean Filipino man in white, a curvy Polish woman in wine, a grey-locked Black woman in teal. Two turn long ropes while three take turns inside, in one continuous shot as the camera dollies slowly out — high knees, a full turn between beats, criss-cross entries. Wet, dark, neon-flecked noir.

Midday sun beats down on a wind-scoured gravel flat east of London, tight-packed dark pebbles running to a lone concrete pillbox and leaning fence posts far off. The air hangs dead. Four adults stand facing off in pairs, feet on the gravel and fully in frame, before two hoist their partners across their shoulders and sprint: a burly Fijian-British man in his forties carrying a slim Egyptian woman in her twenties, and a tall Ukrainian woman in her thirties hauling a compact Korean man in his fifties, both pounding thirty meters over the stones, laughing. The leading pair then charges past the lens and ends partly out of frame. One continuous shot, a handheld camera slowly circling at chest height.

Storm cloud stacks black over a drained London reservoir, its bed cracked into pale clay plates, a brick sluice tower standing out in the middle and a tide-marked bank ringing the basin. Torn paper scraps tumble through the heavy air ahead of the rain. One woman is out there alone — late thirties, Argentinian, powerfully built with a dark braid, in a slate vest and black leggings — fully in frame with both feet on the clay and never leaving her spot. One continuous shot tracks sideways at a steady walking pace as she hoists a medicine ball overhead and hammers it down again and again, dust bursting from the cracks, catching each rebound and reloading. Vast, grand, cinematic.

Floodlights on tall masts blaze down a closed overpass above London, lane markings glossy, crash barriers beaded with water, rain streaking through the beams and bursting in the puddles. No one else is on the deck. Two adults stay fully in frame with boots on the asphalt: a broad Nepali man in a soaked grey hoodie, and a tall white woman with a shaved head in black waterproofs. Held on a static tripod at eye level, one continuous shot watches them work wooden staffs within a couple of metres — fast figure-eights flinging water, a roll across the shoulders, a behind-the-back switch, a low toss spinning up through the floodlight and slapped back into the palm. Rough, wet, documentary honesty.

Light rain lacquers the tar-and-gravel roof of a former piano workshop in east London; a glass-block skylight dome glows from below, chalk-white pipe runs snake past a slumped satellite dish, and wet petals from a street tree swirl low across the membrane. Two adults play capoeira in the puddled shine. A slender Brazilian woman in her fifties, grey braid, white trousers rolled to the calf, rocks a low ginga; a stocky Turkish-British man in his twenties, bare-chested under an open shirt, sweeps past her hip, and she answers with a cartwheel-dodge and a slow rising kick. They circle within a few meters, fully in frame, bare feet on the wet roof. One continuous shot from a static tripod at eye level.

Floodlights on scaffold poles glare across a retro drive-in lot outside London, speaker posts leaning in rows, a blank screen tower at the far end, torn bunting and a big flag snapping hard in the wind. Five adults skip in a line on the cracked gravel-strewn asphalt. A muscular Jamaican-British man in his thirties rattles side-swing crossovers; a lithe Iranian woman in her twenties fires triple-unders; a freckled Welsh man in his forties adds high-knee sprint steps; a stocky Chinese woman in her fifties and a lean Sudanese man in his twenties trade criss-crosses on the beat. Onlookers cheer from the snack-bar terrace. All five stay planted and fully in frame. One continuous shot, the camera craning down from high above to eye level.

Mist burns off the Kamo delta as one continuous shot orbits slowly around four adults locked in pairs on the painted steel plate of a festival pier: a tall Japanese man in faded red shorts, a stocky Black woman with cornrows in grey tape and a tank top, a lean white man with a shaved head, a broad Korean woman in blue. They fist-tie behind each other's necks and fire alternating knees into braced forearms, pivoting on one spot, breath steaming. Festival banners and loose fabric whip violently on the pole line. Spectators press behind rope railings on the seawall, never on the deck. Gritty documentary grain, cold sunrise colors, feet planted on visible steel plate throughout.

Wind hauls dust across a service walkway of trodden red earth cutting between clipped tea rows on an Uji hillside, where torn survey pennants and a loose tarp snap against bamboo stakes. One woman, mid-thirties, South Asian, wiry, in a mustard crop top and black leggings, stands fully in frame with both feet on the earth, then drops to a chest-to-ground burpee, snaps her hips back under her, and detonates upward into a tuck jump, landing on the same footprint. She repeats it hard, five, six times, never drifting. One continuous shot tracks sideways at a steady walking pace. Hazy amber afternoon light, epic cinematic scale, ridges fading behind her.

Inside a hushed Kyoto business hotel lobby, marble underfoot, black lacquer screens and paper globe lamps overhead, five adults hold a loose arc, all fully visible with feet on the polished stone. A tall Nigerian man in a silver bomber, a petite Japanese woman in a white suit, a heavyset Latino man in olive, a freckled Irish woman with a red braid, an older Chinese man in a charcoal vest. They snap into isolated chest hits, elbows locking, then pass a liquid arm wave down the line and freeze in staggered angles, feet rooted. Haze drifts as narrow practice lights swing across them, carving deep shadows. One continuous shot dollies slowly in. Epic cinematic contrast, no one else present.

Fog sits thick in a disused gravel pit south of Kyoto, rusted hoppers and a raw cut-earth wall dissolving into grey. Two adults face off on the packed sand basin, fully in frame, barefoot: a lean Vietnamese man in black cropped trousers, and a tall blonde woman in a slate wrap top, forearms taped. They alternate spinning heel kicks and low sweeping hook kicks, each pivot tearing a pale arc of sand into the fog, resetting on the same square of ground without travelling. Far beyond the pit rim, traffic light trails streak in long horizontal ribbons. One continuous shot pushes slowly toward them. Moody neo-noir palette, desaturated blues, only the two of them here.

Six adults work a harvested field of straw stubble ringed by a fogbound cedar windbreak and one leaning bale stack. Three pairs: a heavy Samoan man and a rangy Japanese man, a muscular Black woman and a compact white woman with a bleached crop, a bearded Turkish man and a wiry Filipino man in singlets and mismatched shorts. All start upright, feet in the stubble, fully framed. On a shout they penetrate low, drive double-leg entries a couple of metres across the field, finish, slap the ground and reset. Air is dead still; only bodies move, stalks crackling. One continuous shot, handheld, circling slowly at chest height. Epic cinematic haze, cold silver light, nobody else for kilometres.

Harsh noon light hammers a broad sand bar in a dry Kizu riverbed, bleached driftwood snagged against a low concrete weir, hills hazing beyond. Three adults stand together on the pale sand, all fully in frame, feet down: a tall Kenyan woman in a lime crop top, a sandy-haired Australian man in navy, a stocky Japanese woman in orange. Grinning, they charge one after another down the bar, hitting hop, step and jump phases, blasting sand from each contact, and land laughing metres apart. The last runner keeps coming toward the lens and finishes cropped at the waist, half out of frame. Far overhead, daytime fireworks pop in pale grey bursts. One continuous shot dollies slowly in. Playful, bright, upbeat.

A converted warehouse skate park in southern Kyoto: smooth plywood flat between two quarter pipes, cable spools hanging from the trusses, bright even lights overhead. One man in his late twenties, Afro-Brazilian, compact and heavily muscled, wears a lilac tracksuit and a knit cap. He begins upright, feet on the plywood, fully in frame, then drops into continuous windmills, shoulders skimming wood, flips into an airflare, and screws up into a slow headspin before freezing on one hand. His footprint never leaves a small circle. Flickering neon from a side wall and a sweeping searchlight beam wash him in shifting magenta. One continuous shot from a static tripod at eye level, dreamy music-video haze, no one else inside.

Blue hour settles over a container quay, gantry crane legs and stacked boxes cut flat against a still harbour. Six adults ring a patch of reinforced concrete, all in frame with feet down: a tall Ethiopian woman in a yellow windbreaker, a chubby Japanese man in denim, a pale Polish woman with a shaved side, a Mexican man in mint, a lanky Indian man in white, a Black woman in patterned tights. One at a time they drop into the middle of the tight circle for windmills, a flare, a snapped headspin freeze, then bounce back into the ring, clapping. Air is dead calm. One continuous shot dollies gently in. Bright, playful, commercial energy, nobody else on the quay.

Dust hangs gold along a long median walk of compacted fine gravel running under two ginkgo rows, hazy afternoon wind combing the leaves. One woman, early forties, Japanese-Brazilian, broad-shouldered, in a cropped grey hoodie and black shorts, hands wrapped in blue tape, stands fully in frame with both feet on the gravel. She snaps out a jab-cross, slips left, rolls under an imagined hook, steps two metres up the path and back with sharp pivots, exhaling in bursts, gravel scuffing. Neon signage flickers through the trunks and a searchlight sweeps the haze above her. One continuous shot pans slowly left to right. Epic cinematic warmth, deep amber and dust, nobody else on the median.

A limp windsock hangs over a small grass airstrip outside Kyoto, one glider parked beside a low tin hangar, harsh midday sun burning the mown turf shadowless. Four adults stand on the grass, fully framed with feet down: a tall Danish woman with a blonde ponytail, a stocky Japanese man in red, a bearded Black man in cobalt, a compact Peruvian woman in yellow. Splitting into two pairs, they snap grips, hit an inside trip and a shoulder throw, land hard, scramble for top position across a couple of metres, then pop back up and reset. The air is completely still, only bodies and turf in motion. One continuous shot tracks sideways at a steady walking pace. Bright, saturated sports-ad energy, no spectators anywhere.

An abandoned expressway toll plaza west of Kyoto stands in dusty afternoon haze: faded lane paint on concrete, glass booths with dead signal heads, grit lying undisturbed across the surface. One man, late thirties, Māori, heavyset and powerful, in a soot-stained tan work shirt and canvas trousers, stands fully in frame with boots on the concrete. He shoulders a coiled fire hose, then sprints hard down three lanes, the flat hose snapping and unreeling behind him in a long yellow line, before he plants, slams the coupling down and doubles over. Nothing else in the plaza moves, the hazy air completely still. One continuous shot cranes down from high above to eye level. Gritty documentary look, bleached highlights, nobody else present.

Rain streaks across the raw poured concrete slab of an unfinished Kyoto tower, rebar clusters bristling at the edges, plastic sheeting drumming on scaffold pipe, harsh midday sun burning through the shower. Two adults crouch at a chalked start line, fully in frame, feet down: a tall Somali man in a red singlet and a broad-thighed Japanese woman in white with a soaked bun. They explode into a flat-out sprint the length of the slab, feet blasting spray from shallow puddles, arms driving, and lunge together at a taped finish twenty metres on. One continuous shot pans slowly left to right to hold them. Bright energetic sports-ad color, wet concrete glare, no one else on the deck.

A hillside amphitheatre above Kyoto: a flat concrete stage, curved stone tiers, cedars behind, soft overcast light with no wind at all. Three adults stand in burlap sacks at stage left, fully in frame with feet on concrete: a lanky Ghanaian man in a green tee, a round-cheeked Japanese woman in pink, a grey-bearded Italian man in stripes. They hop furiously across a few metres of stage, one crashing onto his hip and scrambling upright still gripping the sack. Spectators cheer from the stone tiers, none on the stage. One continuous shot dollies out to reveal the bowl; the leading hopper closes on the lens and ends cropped at the chest. Bright, energetic, cheerful color.

A flat alpine meadow bench high north of Kyoto, short flowering turf, one lichened boulder and a weathered shrine post, under a bruised sky loaded for rain. Three adults stand shoulder to shoulder, fully in frame, feet on the turf: a tall Japanese woman with a black bob in a coral tee, a red-bearded Scottish man in grey, a slim Colombian man in blue. Two have ankles bound with cloth; all three link arms and stampede across the meadow, stumbling, catching each other, then rebalancing into a ragged sprint that crosses the whole frame. The air stays perfectly still under the storm. One continuous shot cranes from high above down to eye level. Bright, punchy, sports-ad energy, nobody else here.

Light rain glazes the cobblestones of an old stone arch bridge over a Kyoto canal, iron lamp posts dripping, willows sagging on the far bank, reflections pooling between the stones. One woman in her fifties, Japanese, thick-armed and sun-worn, wears a navy work jacket, canvas gloves and rolled trousers. She stands fully in frame, boots on the cobbles beside a low stack of straw bales, then hooks each bale, swings it up from her hips and hurls it onto the growing pile, stepping a metre or two between throws, water flicking off the twine. The air is otherwise still. One continuous shot, handheld, circles slowly at chest height. Epic cinematic mood, silver rain light, no one else on the bridge.

Shafts of daylight cut through high windows into a small Kyoto yoga studio, bamboo floor glowing, folded mats stacked against a lime-plaster wall, two big floor fans stirring loose paper and dust through the beams. Two adults stand a couple of steps apart, fully in frame, barefoot on the boards: a tall Senegalese woman in a teal crop top and shorts, and a compact Japanese man in a white tee with taped ankles. They keep a football alive between them, flicking from laces to thigh to shoulder to head, spinning under it, never leaving their small patch of floor. One continuous shot, handheld, circles slowly at chest height. Bright energetic sports-ad color, warm and clean, nobody else inside.

A basement wrestling room in Kyoto, wall-to-wall red foam mats, a scuffed mirror strip and colored stage lamps throwing magenta and green across the surface. Six adults work in three pairs, all in frame with feet on the mat: a heavy Russian man holding mitts for a small Thai woman, a Black woman with locs feeding a lanky Japanese man, an older Mexican man catching for a red-haired Canadian woman. Combinations crack out — jab, cross, hook, body rip — the mitt holders backing up a metre and circling as their partners follow with tight steps. Still air, sharp leather claps. One continuous shot pans slowly left to right along the line. Gritty documentary texture, sweat sheen, no spectators.

An elevated linear park built over a Kyoto rail cut: tapered concrete planks running between beds of wild grass, a rusted signal gantry arching overhead, city roofs low in the sunrise mist. One man, early thirties, Korean, lean and long-limbed, in a washed-out grey vest and black shorts, starts standing fully in frame, feet on the planks. He drops to hands and toes and bear-crawls hard down the walkway, hips low, hands slapping concrete, covering ten metres and driving past the far planter. Dry leaves and petals swirl low across the deck around him. One continuous shot, handheld, circles slowly at chest height as he goes. Gritty documentary grain, pale gold mist, nobody else on the walkway.

Warm tungsten work lamps on tripods light a tiled concrete pedestrian underpass beneath a Kyoto ring road, peeling paper curling off the walls, big ventilation fans pushing dust and loose sheets along the floor. Six adults line up down the tunnel, all in frame, feet on the tiles: a tall Sudanese man, a stocky Japanese woman in a maroon hoodie, a silver-haired white man, a broad Tongan woman, a slim French man, a Chinese woman in olive. Three crouch, three vault, hands slapping backs, then swap roles and leapfrog steadily a few metres deeper. One continuous shot orbits slowly around the group. Moody neo-noir amber and black, long shadows raking the tile, no bystanders.

Floodlights rake in from one side of a commercial glasshouse near Kyoto, a wide concrete walkway running between endless staked tomato rows, steam creeping from floor vents and fogging the panes. Three adults stand together on the walkway, fully in frame, feet down: a tall Brazilian woman in a scarlet unitard, a bald Japanese man in black, a muscular Nigerian man in gold. They fling wooden hoops down the aisle with backspin, sprint after them, and dive headlong through the rolling rings, tucking into shoulder rolls and popping up further along, covering fifteen metres. One continuous shot cranes down from high overhead to eye level; the last performer runs at the lens and finishes cropped at the thighs. Epic cinematic contrast.

Neon from the streets below stains the top deck of a Kyoto station parking garage, faded stall paint on concrete, vent stacks breathing lazy steam across the surface, radio masts blinking beyond. Three adults set up along a painted line, all fully in frame with hands and feet on the deck: a wiry Japanese man in a citrus tracksuit, a strong Black woman in purple with a headwrap, a stocky Turkish man in white. On a shouted count they bear-crawl flat out across the whole deck, palms slapping, knees skimming, laughing and jostling as one surges ahead near the far kerb. One continuous shot cranes down from above to eye level. Playful upbeat commercial color, hot magenta and cyan, empty rooftop otherwise.

Snowflakes drift through the neon spilling across an old-town square in Kyoto, rounded cobblestones slick under machiya eaves and iron bollards, shutters half down on the arcade. One man, mid-forties, Japanese, barrel-chested, in a padded orange vest, work gloves and heavy boots, stands fully in frame with feet on the cobbles behind a wooden barrel. He tips it, then drives it at a run right across the square, hands hammering the staves, the barrel bouncing and rumbling over the stones, and pivots it hard around a bollard before pushing on. One continuous shot dollies steadily toward him. Playful upbeat commercial color, candy neon reflections in wet stone, nobody else out.

Inside a Kyoto distribution centre, a truck dock bay stands empty: sealed concrete floor, a half-raised roller door, shrink-wrapped pallet stacks and dock levellers along one wall. Harsh floodlights blast in from one side and haze drifts through moving spotlight beams. One woman, late twenties, Japanese-Peruvian, athletic with a tight bun, wears a copper leotard and soft shoes. She stands fully in frame, feet on the concrete, then whips into a triple pirouette, holds, and rolls straight into a run of fouetté turns, whipping leg snapping, staying on one small square of floor with the spot chasing her. One continuous shot cranes from high above down to eye level. Bright, energetic, sports-ad crispness, no one else present.

Heavy snow drops onto a hot air balloon launch field north of Kyoto: mown short grass showing dark through the white, a deflated envelope crumpled beside a wicker basket, a sagging wire fence along the tree line. A single adult works there — one man in his forties, Turkish, barrel-shouldered, in a quilted maroon jacket, gloves and a wool cap — standing fully framed with boots on the grass. He lifts each straw bale two-handed, swings it past his knees and pitches it up overhead onto a chest-high stack a few paces off, snow bursting from the twine. Nothing else stirs. Then he hauls the last bale straight at the lens, ending cropped at the chest. One continuous shot pushes slowly in. Moody neo-noir monochrome.

Night neon from the valley town glows up onto a chalk downland plateau, short springy turf over pale rock, a concrete trig marker and a leaning fence line, fireworks blooming silently far off across the sky. Three adults spread out along the ridge, fully in frame, feet on the turf: a tall Jamaican woman in electric blue, a slight Japanese man in silver, a broad Ukrainian woman in white. The first sprints flat out down the plateau, slaps a baton into the second's outstretched hand, who accelerates and feeds the third, all three crossing the frame at full pace. One continuous shot cranes down from high above to eye level. Dreamy music-video color, soft neon bloom, nobody else on the ridge.

Golden hour pours across a bare grey granite plateau above the Kyoto valley, wind-bent pines clinging at the rim, a low stone cairn casting a long shadow, air perfectly still. Two adults face each other on the slab, fully in frame, feet planted: a tall Māori woman in a black rash guard with taped forearms, and a lean grey-templed Spanish man in a rust tee. Gripping padded practice sticks, they trade fast overhead and angled strikes, parry with a snap, and shuffle a few metres in and out, one ducking under a sweep and countering to the ribs. One continuous shot tracks sideways at a steady walking pace, holding both. Bright energetic sports-ad warmth, honeyed rim light, no one else on the rock.

Soft overcast light flattens a drained rice paddy outside Kyoto, cracked dry mud curling in plates, low earth bunds squaring the field, an expressway smearing white and red light trails along the far horizon. Two adults toe a scratched start line, fully in frame, feet on the mud: a long-legged Ethiopian man in a yellow singlet and a powerful Japanese woman in black with taped fingers. They accelerate down a row of five improvised hurdles set across the paddy, snapping lead legs over each, trail knees whipping through, dust bursting on landing, and run the full length of the field side by side. One continuous shot, handheld, circles slowly at chest height. Epic cinematic grey-green, wide horizon, empty fields.

Inside a Kyoto velodrome, the banked track vanishes into darkness while practice lamps pool weakly on the flat grey concrete infield; steam creeps from floor vents past stacked foam crash pads. Five adults join hands in a chain out on the slab, all fully in frame, feet planted. The anchor, a heavyset Japanese man in his fifties, plants and pivots; a lanky Russian woman in her thirties, a wiry Mexican man in his twenties and a strong Nigerian woman in her forties run the arc faster until the tail, a rangy Australian man in his twenties, is slung loose and sprints wide, ending partly out of frame near the lens. One continuous shot, the camera craning down from high above to eye level.

Cold pink and blue neon tubing strung along scaffolding turns a coastal marble quarry unearthly, the sawn white cutting floor glowing under it, stacked blocks squared like a drowned city, surf detonating on the cliff below. One woman works the stone alone: broad-shouldered, Ghanaian, in her forties, braids tied back, in a sleeveless indigo top, canvas trousers and steel-capped boots. She begins fully framed, feet flat on the marble, hands on a steel-banded barrel, then flips it end over end at a jog before dropping it flat and driving it in a long roll the length of the floor, chasing it thirty metres past the block stacks. One continuous shot tracks sideways at a steady walking pace. Dreamy saturated glow, deserted quarry.

Snowflakes drift through beams from strung lanterns over a small brick-paved village square outside Kyoto, red pavers swept clear, an old stone well head and bare plane trees at the edges, soft overcast light above.
