Four adults stand spaced across the bricks, fully in frame, feet down: a tall Kenyan man in a white tee, a Japanese woman in a sky-blue tracksuit, a stocky Greek man with a beard, a young German woman with a blonde crop. Ropes blur into arcs as they rip out fast crossovers, then double-unders, shoes ticking the same square of brick, breath clouding. One continuous shot orbits slowly around them. Bright energetic sports-ad color, clean whites and reds, square otherwise empty.

A sun shower lashes a cricket ground outside Kyoto: rolled dry clay at the centre strip, a sagging boundary rope, a tin sightscreen, rain streaks flashing white under harsh midday sun with puddles bubbling at the crease. One man, mid-twenties, Indonesian, compact and springy, in a lemon vest and grey shorts, stands fully in frame, feet on the clay. He whips a cork kick, lands clean, chains into a 540 kick with water bursting from his heel, then a butterfly twist across a few metres of pitch. On the last landing he strides at the lens and ends cropped at the waist. One continuous shot pans slowly left to right. Playful upbeat commercial brightness, nobody else on the ground.

A compacted red dirt service strip runs between tilted rows of a Kyoto solar farm, panels throwing hard noon glare, inverter cabinets venting drifting steam across the lane. Five adults hold a staggered wedge on the dirt, all fully in frame, feet planted: a tall Sri Lankan man in a white boiler suit, a Japanese woman with a pink bob in silver, a burly Black man in charcoal, a slim Chilean woman in orange, a wiry older Korean man in denim. They hit sharp robotic chest pops, freeze at angles, then pass a wave from fingertip to fingertip along the wedge, feet locked in place. One continuous shot cranes down from high overhead to eye level. Bright energetic sports-ad color, hard shadows, no one else.

Warm tungsten work lamps hang low over a foundry casting hall, packed black sand underfoot, overhead ladle rails and rows of cooling moulds fading into the dark, the air completely still and dusty. Two adults stand in heavy hessian sacks pulled to their waists, fully in frame, boots sunk in the sand: a broad Japanese man in a soot-marked yellow tee, and a tall Nigerian woman with box braids in a green tank. Grinning, they launch into big two-footed bounds a few metres toward a chalked line; one over-jumps, pitches face-first into the sand, somersaults through it and bounces up still inside the hessian. One continuous shot tracks sideways at a steady walking pace beside them. Playful commercial warmth, orange lamp glow, empty hall.

Storm light presses down on a flat pavement of dark basalt on a lava field near the Kyoto coast, hexagonal seams cracked with pale lichen, one bleached driftwood post leaning at the edge, distant highway lights streaking in long ribbons behind. One woman, forties, Māori, powerfully built, in a faded olive jacket and gloves, stands fully in frame with boots on the basalt beside scattered straw bales. She drags a bale onto her thigh, rocks it once, then punches it up overhead onto a shoulder-high stack at her side, snatching the next without shifting her boots from one small patch of rock, chaff spraying with every heave. One continuous shot dollies out to reveal the black plain. Moody neo-noir slate and bruise-purple, completely alone.

Rain falls steadily in a narrow lane between two container stacks in a Kyoto freight yard, concrete paver blocks slick and reflective, puddles jumping under the drops, gantry lights smearing above the corrugated walls. One man, late thirties, Samoan, enormous through the chest, in a black singlet, chalked hands and taped forearms, stands fully in frame with feet on the pavers. He squats over a rounded stone ball, laps it onto his thighs, then explodes upward and rolls it onto a steel platform, drops it back and repeats, never shifting his stance. One continuous shot cranes down from high above to eye level. Gritty documentary texture, wet grey light, nobody else in the yard.

Heavy snow falls on a black volcanic sand beach, flakes drifting through the beam of a lone pole lamp, driftwood half-buried and concrete tetrapods stacked along the water. One woman, early thirties, Japanese, sturdy and short-haired, wears a rust parka, gloves and heavy boots, standing fully in frame with feet on the dark sand. She drives a wide shovel down and slings arc after arc of snow-crusted sand sideways, hips snapping, building a ridge beside her, never moving off her small patch. Her breath tears out in clouds. One continuous shot orbits slowly around her. Epic cinematic monochrome, black sand against white flurries, no one else on the beach.

Floodlights blaze across an apron beside a hangar at a small airfield near Kyoto, painted guide lines on concrete, rubber chocks and a tug parked in the doorway glow, air dead still. Two adults square up, fully in frame, feet on the concrete: a compact Japanese woman in a red tracksuit with a high ponytail, and a tall Dutch man with a blonde buzz in a white tee. Each grabs one ankle behind them and hops in, slamming shoulders and chests, driving the other back three or four metres in ragged circles until one lands hard on both feet, laughing. One continuous shot tracks sideways at a steady walking pace. Bright energetic sports-ad color, hard white light, no one else on the apron.

Grey overcast hangs low over a Kyoto bay, where a plank boardwalk runs past stone lanterns and a moored pontoon; the water lies dead calm. Four adults work in pairs on the weathered decking. A thickset Japanese man in his forties swings a rice sack chest-high to a tall Kenyan woman in her thirties, who absorbs the weight and fires it back. Opposite them a compact Peruvian woman in her fifties and a lean Dutch man in his twenties trade a heavier sack. All four begin fully in frame, boots on the planks; walkers watch from behind the railing. The last catcher then staggers toward the camera and ends partly out of frame. One continuous shot, a slow pan from left to right.

Blue hour drains the color from a grain silo loading yard near the Kyoto coast, dusty concrete slab underfoot, steel chutes and idle conveyors overhead, surf breaking heavily against the rip-rap beyond the fence. Four adults hold a loose square on the slab, all fully in frame, feet planted: a tall Iranian man in a black dobok top, a compact Japanese woman with a tight braid, a muscular Black man in white, a rangy Vietnamese woman in navy. Each takes a turn firing spinning hook kicks and back kicks at pads held for them, whipping around on one spot, dust flaring off the concrete. One continuous shot, handheld, circles slowly at chest height. Moody neo-noir blues, nobody else in the yard.

Fog sits motionless over a merchant's walled courtyard in Kyoto, its floor patterned Mediterranean ceramic — cobalt and ochre stars ringing a dry stone basin, a bent persimmon at one corner. Six adults work that tile within a few meters. Three East Asian men in dark tracksuits hurl a ball low and flat; three women — a stocky Māori keeper in green, a lean Ethiopian in charcoal, a freckled redhead in navy — fling themselves sideways, smother rebounds, and scramble back to a set stance. Neighbors watch from a wooden gallery behind lattice railings, never on the tile. All six start planted, fully framed, and stay in frame; one continuous shot, the camera easing slowly inward.

Rain falls in fine threads over a painted crossing plaza beside a fjord ferry quay, its asphalt slabbed with turquoise and ochre blocks, a rusted signal mast leaning at the edge, black water and cliffs beyond. Exactly two adults hold one square of it: a tall broad-shouldered Somali-Norwegian man in his thirties wearing a mustard windbreaker, and a wiry white woman near fifty in grey thermals and red gloves. Both start fully in frame, boots on the glossy painted asphalt, and stay there, stickhandling a puck in tight figure-eights through four cones without leaving their patch, toe-drags snapping spray. Distant traffic streaks red and white light trails across the reflections. One continuous shot, the camera tracking sideways at a steady walking pace.

Golden hour lies thick on a terraced olive shelf cut into a fjord slope, silver leaves motionless, a dry-stone retaining wall crumbling at one end and a low hand-built cairn marking the drop to the water. Six adults occupy the dusty pale earth: a stocky Filipino man in teal shorts, a freckled redhead woman in a cream tank, a bald East African man in navy, a curvy Latina in lilac, a lean Korean woman in orange, a grey-bearded Sámi man in denim. All six stand fully framed, bare feet planted, then fold one leg up and collide shoulder-first in hopping duels, laughing, staggering, never leaving their small circles of dust. Air is utterly still. One continuous shot, slowly orbiting them.

Flat overcast light sits over a birch clearing above a fjord mouth, where sawn stumps bleed sap, orange survey tape sags between trunks, and swell booms against unseen rocks below, filling every pause. Three adults work the packed earth and leaf litter: a heavyset Māori man in a faded green shell, a small sinewy Vietnamese woman in black leggings, a pale ginger-bearded man in a torn grey hoodie. All three begin fully in frame and on their feet, then pair off — one drops to hands while another lifts his ankles and drives him three metres across the litter, they swap, they crash and reset. Documentary grain, mud on palms. One continuous shot, a slow dolly-out revealing more of the surroundings.

Between long dunes at a fjord head lies a wide flat of firm red sand, staked with survey pylons wrapped in magenta and cyan neon tubing that stain the grains violet; an orange marker flag stands seventy metres out under a cold starless sky. One woman has the place to herself, a lean Brazilian in her late twenties, short bleached curls, lime crop top and black shorts. She stands fully in frame first, bare feet on the sand, then drops prone at a scratched line, explodes up and sprints the entire flat, arms pumping, finishing in a full horizontal dive that rips red spray as she snatches the flag. Nothing else moves. One continuous shot, handheld, slowly circling at chest height.

Deep in an old fjordside gymnastics hall only two practice lamps burn, carving three adults out of near-blackness above the blue spring carpet; chalk bins glow faintly, a climbing rope hangs coiled, worn tape lines cross the floor. There are three: a broad Nigerian man in his forties in a black singlet, a compact Japanese woman with a long braid in maroon, and a rangy Slovak man in grey. All stay fully in frame with feet on the carpet, anchored on one taped line, hauling a thick rope in ratcheting heaves, heels skidding, then one side buckles and the trio collapses laughing into the mats before resetting. Air is dead still. One continuous shot, tracking sideways at a steady walking pace.

Blue hour settles over a whitewashed cement rooftop above a fjord village, where scarlet chilies dry on mesh racks and pale drying nets are pegged in rows; below, breakers thump against black rock, a steady pulse under the quiet. Two adults own a clear square of the terrace: a slim Indian man in his mid-twenties in a coral tee, and a tall grey-haired white woman in her fifties in a teal jumpsuit. Both remain fully in frame, sneakers on the cement, spinning colour-guard flags in bright arcs, then launching synchronised double-rotation tosses that catch the last violet light before slapping back into their palms. Cheerful, snappy, sparkling. The camera tracks sideways at a steady walking pace through one continuous shot.

A smooth red sandstone bench juts over a fjord where fog banks pour uphill in slow grey rolls, swallowing rusted drill cores and a stack of split firewood; a bald tractor tire lies flat on the rock. Six adults ring it at blue hour: a burly Turkish man in a soaked grey tee, a tattooed white woman with a shaved head, a lanky Ethiopian man in orange, a stocky Chilean woman in black, a bearded Icelander in flannel, a broad Pacific Islander woman in navy. All six stay fully in frame, boots planted on the sandstone, alternating overhead sledgehammer strikes onto the rubber, grunting, breath steaming. Plain, unglamorous, sweat-lit. One continuous shot from a static tripod at eye level.

At blue hour a fjordside sawmill yard glows cobalt: spruce logs stacked in ziggurats, torn tarpaulins and pennants snapping violently in a hard downvalley wind, a gantry crane silhouetted against the last pale water. One man works it alone, a solid Punjabi-Norwegian in his thirties, thick beard, a bright yellow kurta over track pants, boots on the sawdust-covered dirt. He begins fully in frame, then bursts into bhangra: high scissor hops, arms punched overhead, dropping into squat kicks that fling sawdust, working two metres forward until, in the final seconds, he closes on the lens and his upper body passes partly out of frame. Punchy, athletic, joyous. One continuous shot, tracking sideways at a steady walking pace.

An emptied exhibition hall in a fjord-side congress centre stretches into shadow: grey commercial carpet seamed with gaffer tape, half-struck booth frames like ribcages, coiled cable runs, warm tungsten work lamps on stands throwing long amber pools. Only one person is inside: a lean Dominican man in his early forties, close-cropped hair, charcoal henley, dark jeans, shoes flat on the carpet, fully in frame. He winds up, drives off an imaginary rubber and fires a ball down the long aisle into a stacked pallet, then jogs the length of the hall to fetch it and repeats, covering many metres. Noir shadows, airless stillness, nothing else moving. One continuous shot from a static tripod at eye level.

A small fjord-town curling rink has been rigged with magenta and cyan stage lamps that pool across the pebbled ice; leftover paper scraps and confetti tumble slowly through the beams, catching on the hacks and the painted house rings. Four adults skid there in sneakers: a compact Thai woman in a yellow jersey, a tall Ghanaian man in white, a stocky Polish man in red, a broad-shouldered Mexican woman in blue. All four start fully in frame, feet on the ice, then scramble after a soft ball with broomsticks, sliding, pivoting, colliding and recovering within a few metres of the button. Fast, bright, advert-clean energy. One continuous shot, a slow dolly-in toward them.

On a clifftop hard court above a fjord, acrylic-coated concrete has faded to seafoam and rust; a netless post leans, and golden-hour light rakes across it while flickering neon from a harbour sign and slow searchlights sweep the water below. Six adults share it: a tall Kenyan woman in white, a chubby Danish man in green, a sinewy Peruvian man in purple, a tattooed Japanese woman in black, a silver-haired Portuguese woman in coral, a broad Samoan man in grey. The six open fully framed, shoes on the court, then hurl a disc between them, sprinting a few metres and laying out flat in full-extension dives. Late on, one skids toward the lens, shoulders leaving frame. One continuous shot with a slow left-to-right pan.

Heavy snow drifts down onto a rippled tidal sand flat at a fjord mouth, melting the instant it lands in the ankle-deep sheet water; a stranded wooden dinghy tilts nearby and long kelp lines mark the last tide. Five adults stand in one shallow pool: a broad Inuit man in a red anorak, a slim Egyptian woman in a blue rain shell, a curly-haired Italian man in olive, a tall Nigerian-Norwegian woman in pink, a stout grey-bearded man in yellow. All five stay fully in frame, bare feet in the water, stomping enormous splashes at each other, scooping and flinging sheets of spray, never stepping out of their small ring. Bright and gleeful. One continuous shot, panning slowly left to right.

Golden hour lights a quarry bench cut high into a fjord wall in Norway: pink granite blocks resting on timber cribbing, a listing gantry, black water far below. Nothing stirs. Three adults toe a scratched mark in the compacted aggregate, then drop to all fours. A powerful Norwegian woman in her forties, ginger hair, black thermal, drives a lateral bear crawl to the first marker; a rangy Ivorian man in his twenties, yellow tee, tears past her forward; a stocky Filipino man in his fifties reverses into a backward crawl for the return leg. They cover twenty-five meters and back, all three fully in frame with hands and feet on the bench. One continuous shot, a slow dolly-out revealing the whole terrace.

Daylight cuts in shafts from high windows of a fjord-side athletics hall, haze drifting over the blue polyurethane while moving spotlights sweep the lanes. Six adults travel the straight with ribbons: a tall Norwegian woman in her thirties leads with overhead spirals into a split leap, followed by a wiry Kenyan man in his twenties trailing a snake along the track, a broad Korean woman in her forties turning through a boomerang toss, and three more in deep-blue and copper unitards chaining chassés and pivots. They cover thirty meters, all six beginning fully in frame with feet on the track; the leader then sweeps toward the lens, ending partly out of frame. Spectators watch from tiered seats. One continuous shot, a slow orbit around them.

Inside a fjord-shore aircraft hangar the great door stands half open on black water; low practice lamps pool on the painted grey concrete while haze-machine fog and slow spotlights carve visible beams over chalked court lines and hanging cargo netting, deep shadows swallowing the walls. Three adults train there: a towering Serbian woman with a blonde plait in navy, a compact Filipino man in white, a broad-chested Congolese man in maroon. All three stay fully in frame, shoes on the concrete, working a spike drill — three-step approach, arms swinging back, a hard leap and cracking swing at a ball tossed by a teammate, landing and shuffling two metres to reset. Enormous, operatic scale. One continuous shot, orbiting slowly around them.

Fine rain lacquers a decommissioned airstrip on a fjord terrace, grooved asphalt mirroring a low pewter sky; faded runway numerals bleed at the edges, a rusted windsock mast stands bare, and a chain-link fence sags toward the treeline. Six adults occupy a stretch of it: a wiry Bangladeshi man in orange, a tall Finnish woman in grey, a heavy Angolan man in white, a freckled woman with cropped hair in green, a middle-aged Chinese man in black, a broad Sámi woman in red. All six remain fully framed, boots splashing the wet asphalt, spinning weighted flags and launching tosses while shifting a few metres between formations. Plain, rough, unpolished. One continuous shot, dollying slowly out.

Two adults circle on the pale limestone forecourt of a fjord-side museum, its rust-red steel canopy and granite fountain misting behind them under soft overcast daylight. One continuous shot: the camera tracks sideways at a steady walking pace. A tall Nigerian man in his thirties, shaved head, olive trousers, white tank, sways low; a stocky Finnish woman in her fifties, ash-blonde braid, teal crop top and grey sweatpants, answers with a sweeping meia-lua de compasso, then drops into negativa and escapes with an au batido. Both start fully framed, feet planted on stone. Birch leaves swirl low across the ground. Visitors watch from the balcony railing above. Near the end the woman lunges toward the lens and her shoulder passes out of frame.

Storm light presses low over a cracked black-asphalt court between a fjord seawall and a red boathouse, faded paint lines underfoot and a bent chain net overhead. Five adults battle in the key. A wiry Korean man in his twenties, grey sleeveless hoodie, attacks the baseline and finishes a reverse layup; a broad Samoan woman in her thirties, cornrows, euro-steps through traffic off two feet; two lanky Dutch players in their forties, mustard shorts, rotate to help while a silver-haired Brazilian man in his fifties contests the finish. Dead leaves skid across the asphalt. Locals watch from a bench behind the fence. All five stay fully in frame, sneakers on the paint. One continuous shot, a handheld camera slowly circling at chest height.

Rain glazes the raked red dirt of a ballfield infield built on a fjord flat; the backstop netting sags, faded chalk baselines dissolve, and far across the water fireworks bloom silently over a dark ridge, throwing brief pink onto the puddles. Two adults face off on the dirt: a compact Japanese-Norwegian woman in her thirties in a navy training top, and a tall silver-haired Ghanaian man in white. Both start fully in frame, feet on the wet clay, then drive through lunging bamboo-sword strikes, shouting on each cut, sliding a few metres up and down an invisible line. In the last seconds he lunges hard at the camera and his shoulder passes out of frame. One continuous shot, tracking sideways at a steady walking pace.

Night turns a red-painted cycle expressway on a fjord causeway into a ribbon of colour: guardrail lamps burn pink and cold blue, wet tarmac doubles them, and petals skim low along the surface in long drifting lines. Four adults use the empty lane: a willowy Ethiopian woman in lavender, a muscular Argentine man in white, a tall Norwegian man with long fair hair in slate, a curvy Korean woman in gold. All four begin fully in frame, feet on the tarmac, then launch into grand allegro — split leaps and bounding jetés carrying them diagonally the length of the lane, arms unfurling, hair lifting. Soft, hypnotic, saturated. One continuous shot, a slow dolly-out revealing the causeway and dark water.

On a crusted white salt pan below fjord cliffs, five adults kick through ankle-deep brine inside a low timber weir, orange marker flags snapping on bamboo poles, a rusted sluice gate half-submerged nearby. The camera holds still on a tripod at eye level for one continuous shot. Light rain lacquers the crust to polished silver. A freckled Irish woman scoops a sheet of water with her shin; a burly Ghanaian man answers with a two-footed stomp; three others, a slender Peruvian woman, a bearded Greek man, a tattooed Vietnamese woman, wheel and slap spray in wide arcs. All five begin fully framed, barefoot on salt. Torn tarpaulin whips behind them. One sprints at the lens and exits frame at the waist.

Golden hour floods a hillside apple orchard above a fjord, trees heavy with russet fruit, a leaning ladder and crates at the row's end. One continuous shot: the camera cranes down from high above the canopy to eye level. Six adults stand on clover and mown grass, all fully in frame from the first moment and staying there. Two turners, a grey-bearded Turkish man and a compact Filipino woman, whip a pair of sash ropes; four jumpers take turns entering the beat — a lanky Romanian man doing criss-cross steps, a red-haired Uruguayan woman dropping into a push-up bounce, a burly Zambian man pivoting on one leg, a silver-haired Nepali woman counting them in. The air is dead still; only bodies and rope move.

Rain hammers a synthetic pitch wedged under a fjord cliff, green fibres flattened and puddled, splashes bursting at every step; rust-streaked floodlight pylons stand unlit and a torn advertising hoarding flaps blank along the touchline. Overcast light drains all colour to slate and moss. Four adults train there: a heavy-shouldered Ghanaian man in black, a tall Estonian woman with a wet blonde bun, a compact Mexican man in grey, a broad Punjabi woman in navy. All four start fully in frame, boots on the turf, then hoist partners into fireman's carries and sprint the length of the pitch, water exploding underfoot, before dumping and swapping to run back. Cold noir tones. One continuous shot, a slow dolly-out revealing more of the pitch.

Mist smokes off a lavender field terraced above a fjord, the rows still grey-purple at sunrise, a drystone hut at the far end, and beyond the ridge a road where headlights draw long streaking trails through the haze. Three adults work the chalky gravel path: a broad Mongolian man in a white training jacket, a lean Nigerian woman with braids in blue, a stocky Sicilian man in black. All three begin fully in frame, bare feet on gravel, drilling hip throws in rotation — grip, turn in, load the hip, sweep the partner over and down onto the path, then swap roles fast. In the final seconds one rises straight toward the lens, cropping at the waist. One continuous shot, tracking sideways at walking pace.

Light rain darkens a strip of cracked soil along the edge of a sunflower field planted on a fjord terrace; the heavy heads hang still and glossy, an irrigation pipe rusts in the furrow, and a squat wooden crate sits on the wet earth. Exactly one adult is present, a tall Kenyan woman in her late twenties, shaved head, a soft grey longsleeve and black shorts, trainers on the soil, fully in frame from the first moment. She runs three steps and kong-vaults the crate, hands punching down, legs threading through, landing and rebounding back over it again and again within a few metres. On the last repetition she vaults straight at the camera, her legs leaving frame. One continuous shot, dollying slowly in.

A storm builds over a brickyard set on a fjord flat: fired clay tiles laid flat as a working floor, a squat kiln stack, pallets of green bricks under sagging plastic, and a sky like wet slate that makes every red surface glow. Nothing stirs but the people. Five adults hold one small patch: a wiry Cuban man in a yellow shirt, a curvy Polish woman in a red dress, a tall Ethiopian woman in mint, a stocky Hawaiian man in white, a silver-haired Frenchwoman in blue. All five stay fully in frame, shoes on the tiles, whipping through lindy hop aerials — over-the-back flips and hip-slide throws, landings smacking the clay — never leaving their spot. One continuous shot, a slow left-to-right pan.

A fjord road tunnel, closed to traffic: unpainted rock walls sweat behind orange barrier drums, sodium fittings replaced by bright even overhead lamps flattening every shadow. Six adults line up on the asphalt, all fully framed at the start, feet on the tarmac: a shaven-headed Egyptian man rips an icky-shuffle down a taped grid, a red-haired Danish woman follows with in-in-out-out hops, and behind them a bearded Moroccan man, a wiry Haitian woman, a heavyset Finnish man and a silver-haired Malian woman chain lateral scissor steps and a hard reverse step. Air hangs dead still. In one continuous shot the camera cranes down from the ventilation gantry to eye level; finally the Danish woman accelerates at the lens until her torso crops the frame.

Floodlights blaze over a freight depot platform on a fjord quay, weathered concrete scarred by pallet corners, stacked containers throwing hard-edged shadows, a parked forklift and a coil of mooring rope at the far end. The night is windless. Two adults have the platform: a compact Japanese man in his twenties in a white tee and red shorts, and a tall muscular Colombian woman with a high ponytail in black. Both begin fully in frame, feet on the concrete, then kick into handstands and race the length of the platform on their hands, hopping and correcting, covering twenty metres before turning back. Bright, punchy, advert-crisp. She finishes hand-walking toward the lens until her arms fill and exit frame. One continuous shot, a slow dolly-out.

Rails curve away into a tunnel mouth beside an outdoor station platform on a fjord line; the tactile-edged concrete glows amber in golden hour, an iron bench and a steel luggage trolley sit unused, and the air is dead calm. Two adults train on the platform — a hulking Icelandic man in his forties, chalk dust on his grey vest, and a powerfully built Trinidadian woman with cropped hair in a black singlet. Both stay fully in frame, boots planted on the concrete, taking turns to wrap a heavy round stone, lap it and drive it onto the trolley bed before rolling it down and resetting, never leaving one metre of platform. Explosive, bright, sports-commercial punch. One continuous shot with a slow dolly-out.

Blue hour turns a wind-packed snowfield on a fjord plateau to cobalt and lilac, sastrugi ridges casting faint blue shadows, a leaning trail cairn dusted white, black peaks folding into deeper valleys behind. The air has gone completely still. Two adults face off: a broad Kazakh man in his thirties in a red rashguard, and a tall Nigerian-Danish woman with braided hair in a grey singlet. Both stand fully in frame, boots on the crusted snow, then shoot doubles, sprawl, clinch and throw each other with hip-and-shoulder trips, scrambling back up in bursts of powder and driving each other across a few metres. Breath steams; snow sticks to their arms. Bright, kinetic, high-contrast. One continuous shot, dollying slowly in.

Fog pours through the arcade of a stone monastery cloister perched over a fjord, softening the columns and a dry central well; dusty afternoon wind hazes the light and grit skitters across worn flagstone. A handful of visitors watch from behind the arcade railing, none on the courtyard floor. Four adults use the open stone: a stocky Peruvian man in ochre, a tall Swedish woman with a short bob in cream, a bearded Lebanese man in olive, a wiry Ghanaian woman in indigo. All four start fully framed, shoes on flagstone, then crouch in a line and leapfrog over one another in a rolling chain, palms slapping backs, advancing a few metres and reversing. Dreamlike, soft-focus warmth. One continuous shot with a slow left-to-right pan.

Wooden rakes lean against a low wall on a broad concrete drying patio cut into a fjord slope, burlap sacks folded in a stack, dawn mist thinning over the water and, far below, a coast road where headlights smear long trails through the vapour. Three adults own a bare circle of slab: a lean Ecuadorian man in his twenties in a white tank, a powerful Nigerian woman with a wrapped headscarf in black, a compact Korean man in a red hoodie. All three stay fully in frame, feet on the concrete, cycling power moves in one spot — windmills spiralling on the shoulders, flares swinging, a long headspin — then popping upright to hit freezes. Epic, sweeping scale. One continuous shot, a slow dolly-out.

On the black painted plywood of a small fjord-town proscenium stage, colored lamps throw magenta and green pools; hemp lines and a half-flown backdrop hang above, the seats beyond are empty and dark, and the air is perfectly still. Five adults stand on the boards: a wiry Ivorian man in a green tracksuit, a tall Bosnian woman with a blonde ponytail, a stocky Chilean man in a striped shirt, a broad Pakistani woman in black, a grey-stubbled Portuguese man in white. All five stay fully in frame, shoes on the plywood, keeping a football alive with insteps, thighs, shoulders and heads, flicking it between them without leaving their marks. Unvarnished, handheld-real, misses and all. One continuous shot, slowly orbiting the group.

Fog rolls across a raised park terrace above a fjord at blue hour, curling past a cast-iron railing and a bench with peeling paint; the crushed decomposed granite underfoot is damp and dark, and the town lights below are reduced to smudges. Three adults hold one small square of it: a burly Estonian man in a grey beanie and black shell, a compact Filipina woman in a red fleece, a tall Somali man in olive. All three remain fully in frame, boots on the granite, stickhandling a ball through a tight line of cones — toe-drags, quick between-the-legs pulls, rapid hand switches — heels barely shifting from their footprints. Plain, cold, documentary honesty. One continuous shot, a slow left-to-right pan.

Snow falls hard on a coal stockyard beside a fjord jetty, whitening the crests of black heaps while the ground stays a bruised smear of coal dust and slush; a conveyor gantry cuts overhead and a lone lamp on a pole makes every flake glow. Three adults occupy one flat patch: a lean Vietnamese man in his thirties in a black gi top, a tall Nigerian woman with a shaved head in dark grey, a broad-shouldered Russian man in navy. All three stay fully in frame, bare feet on the dust, unleashing spinning hook and tornado kicks that fling arcs of wet black grit into the lamplight, resetting on the same spot. One continuous shot, craning down from high above to eye level.

A colonnaded arcade inside a fjord-town cultural centre: pink-flecked terrazzo underfoot, whitewashed pillars marching away, tall windows throwing hard bright shafts across the floor. One continuous shot, handheld, circling slowly at chest height. Four adults hold their patch of terrazzo, feet planted, fully in frame the whole way. A tall Kenyan woman in a lilac tracksuit pounds two balls in alternating rhythm; a stocky Chilean man snaps a snatch-back hesitation, then wraps the ball behind his back; beside them a freckled Scottish man and a short-haired Japanese woman trade low pocket dribbles and a quick spider drill. Paper scraps tumble past their ankles. Onlookers lean over the mezzanine railing above, clapping the tempo.

Inside a fjord hydro plant's turbine hall, checker plate steel rings underfoot between rows of green painted casings; rigged neon and colored stage lamps splash ruby and cyan across the metal while big ventilation fans stir loose paper and dust into slow spirals. Exactly two adults command a clear span of the deck: a fiery Andalusian woman in her forties in a black fringed skirt and red shawl, and a slim Angolan man in a high-waisted grey suit. Both remain fully in frame, heels on the plate, drumming zapateado bursts that ring off the steel, arms curling into sharp braceo, spinning tight on their own footprints. Bright, snappy, joyfully theatrical. One continuous shot, handheld, circling at chest height.

Harsh midday sun bleaches a film backlot street built on a fjord flat: plywood shopfronts with blank unlettered signboards, scaffolding braced behind them, a scissor lift parked askew, and a snow machine on a tower sending flakes drifting glittering through the light beams. Exactly one adult stands on the painted asphalt, a broad-shouldered Ghanaian-Norwegian man in his thirties, close beard, faded maroon tee, grey sweatpants, shoes flat on the ground, fully in frame from the start. He works a ball hard along a few metres of the street — low crossovers, between-the-legs pulls, behind-the-back snaps, hesitations and hard stops — sweat darkening his shirt. Grainy, unstaged, documentary flatness. One continuous shot, slowly orbiting him.

Rain streaks a broad grey asphalt parade ground beside an old fjord garrison, white formation lines dissolving into spreading puddles, bare flagpoles in a row, a squat brick guardhouse at the perimeter. A scattering of watchers sits under the roof of the raised viewing stand, none on the tarmac. Four adults stand in the open: a slender Ethiopian woman in a soaked lilac top, a stocky Danish man in white, a tall Vietnamese man in charcoal, a broad Nigerian woman in seafoam. All four stay fully in frame, shoes on asphalt, ripping speed-rope work in one spot — crossovers, double-unders, side swings — cords slinging fine spray with every rotation. Soft, hazy, hypnotic. One continuous shot, dollying slowly in.

Inland of a fjord, a cracked white salt crust runs to a low ridge under flat overcast light, its polygons brittle as old porcelain; leaning survey stakes and a stripped timber log are the only features, and the air hangs entirely motionless. Four adults are out on it: a heavy-set Māori man in a black tee, a tall Latvian woman with a wet-look bun in grey, a muscular Sudanese man in olive, a compact Bolivian woman in navy. All four begin fully in frame, boots on the crust, then shoulder the log together and jog it a long way across the flat, breathing in cadence, before dropping it in one synchronised heave. Cold, desaturated, severe. One continuous shot, tracking sideways at a steady walking pace.

Deep beneath a Venetian bus terminal, one athlete crouches on the epoxy-coated concrete of a vast island parking garage, arrows painted between empty bays, a flickering neon strip light buzzing while a maintenance searchlight sweeps the pillars. She is a tall Black woman in her late twenties, braided hair tied back, wearing a lime crop top and violet shorts. Bright even overhead lighting floods everything. In one continuous shot she is fully framed, feet planted, then explodes from a mock block start, driving low through the first six strides and covering many meters down the aisle. A slow dolly-in closes on her as she surges, energy crackling.

Two adults square off on interlocking concrete pavers in the inner courtyard of a pastel Venetian apartment block, laundry lines strung overhead, an old stone wellhead capped with iron in the corner. One is a stocky Filipino man in his thirties in a red sleeveless top; the other a lean white woman near forty with a blonde ponytail and teal joggers. Hazy afternoon wind lifts dust in low ribbons across the ground. One continuous shot: both start fully in frame, feet down, then trade spinning hook kicks and back kicks across a few meters, laughing. The slow dolly-in pushes closer until the man steps toward the lens and his shoulders leave the frame.

Six adults work the travertine tile of a Venetian hotel rooftop pool deck, folded loungers pushed aside, a copper bell tower and the open lagoon beyond the parapet where waves keep breaking against the breakwater. Three pairs: a broad Samoan man in grey, a wiry Korean woman in orange, a freckled Irish man in navy, a silver-haired Italian woman in white, a young Nigerian woman in yellow, a bearded Turkish man in black. Hazy windblown afternoon light dulls the colors. In one continuous shot, all six stay fully in frame with feet on the tile, drilling bump-set-hit pepper within a couple of meters, handheld camera circling slowly at chest height.

Golden hour lies flat along a long pedestrianized shopping street in Venice, granite setts polished by centuries, shuttered arcades on both sides, wrought-iron lamp posts casting long stripes. The air is completely still. Two adults train here: a tall Ethiopian woman in her mid-thirties in a coral singlet, and a broad-shouldered Argentine man near fifty with grey stubble and a white tank. One continuous shot begins with both fully framed, feet on the stone, then each runs a long approach, snapping into crossover steps and releasing a training javelin down the empty street. The slow dolly-in follows; the woman charges toward the lens and finishes cropped at the waist.

Night on a packed-dirt farmyard on the Venetian mainland: a leaning hay barn, a rusted tractor under a tarp, one floodlight on a crooked pole washing everything in soft dreamlike white. The air hangs perfectly still, dust hovering unmoved. Two adults stand there — a slim South Asian man in his twenties in a mustard tee, and a muscular Afro-Brazilian woman near thirty with a shaved head and a plum tracksuit. Both remain fully in frame, feet on the dirt, and never leave their small patch. In one continuous shot they trade a football back and forth without letting it touch the dirt — instep taps, thigh cushions, looping headers, quick heel flicks — while the camera drifts in a slow orbit around them.

Mist hangs low over a red rubber tartan oval on the Venetian mainland at sunrise, plane trees dripping beyond the fence, a single low concrete stand where a scatter of spectators sits behind a railing, well off the track. The air is dead calm. One adult occupies the lane: a lean white man in his early forties, close-cropped grey hair, black long sleeves and dark trousers, a snare drum harnessed at his hip. Muted noir tones, everything charcoal and rust. Filmed as one continuous shot from a static tripod at eye level, he marches the whole straight, feet on the track, hammering rolls and snapping crisp pivot turns as he crosses the frame.

Inside a disused cold-store warehouse near the Venetian port, frosted concrete stretches between rows of empty hanging rails and shuttered chill doors; two industrial fans stir loose packing paper and glittering dust through the beams of warm tungsten work lamps. Three adults stand there in the amber gloom: a tall Somali woman with locs in a black bodysuit, a compact Vietnamese man in his thirties in grey, and a heavyset white woman near fifty in a rust jacket. Each grips a long streamer. One continuous shot: all three begin fully framed, feet on the frost, then sprint the length of the aisle trailing ribbons while the handheld camera circles slowly at chest height.

A blinding gypsum flat stretches behind the old saltworks of the Venetian lagoon, powdery white sand ridged into low dunes, rusted vent pipes exhaling slow ropes of steam, a collapsed evaporation shed on the horizon. Hazy windblown afternoon light flattens the scene. Six adults toe a ragged start line: a bald Ghanaian man in blue, a tanned Greek woman in her forties in white, a redheaded Scottish man, a petite Japanese woman in green, a broad Mexican man in orange, a lanky Dutch woman in grey. In one continuous shot all six begin fully framed, standing with feet on the sand, then drop into prone starts, explode forward, sprint twenty meters and dive for buried flags. Handheld camera circles at chest height.

An old badminton hall on the Venetian mainland: green vinyl matting, sagging nets pushed to one side, big pedestal fans pushing loose scoresheets and dust across the floor. Low practice lights leave deep shadows; a handful of spectators watch from wooden bleachers along the wall, none stepping onto the court. Three adults train on one small square of vinyl: a broad Uzbek man in his forties in a white gi, a compact Black woman in her twenties in blue, and a wiry Portuguese man in grey. One continuous shot, everyone fully in frame with feet planted, as they rotate through repeated o-goshi hip-throw entries, lifting and lowering. The camera tracks sideways at a walking pace.

Light rain glazes the concrete crest roadway of a reservoir dam in the hills above Venice, white lane lines running into fog, warning masts and a cable-drum hut at the far end, the still water black below. Six adults pair off on the wet slab: a tall Kenyan woman in pink, a burly Croatian man in yellow, a Thai woman in her thirties in white, a lanky Colombian man in green, a silver-haired French woman in teal, a young Egyptian man in orange. Three hold Thai pads. One continuous shot keeps all six fully framed, feet on the concrete, firing snapping roundhouse kicks within a couple of meters as the camera orbits slowly around them.

Late afternoon on a Venetian working quay: grey cobble setts scoured smooth, moored barges lying still against timber posts, laundry lines slack between ochre walls. Hazy dust-laden wind hangs in the air; nothing else moves but the four dancers. One continuous shot with a slow orbit around them. A shaved-headed Somali man drives a heavy stomp, then rips a jab sequence across his chest; a broad Polish woman answers with a whipping arm swing that snaps her whole ribcage; a lean Mexican man buck-hops backward into a hard stomp-kill; a silver-braided Indian woman shoulders in with staccato hits. Nobody else is on the quay. From the first frame all four stay fully framed on the setts, working within a few metres.

Shafts of daylight fall through high clerestory windows onto the tiled concrete of a sealed tram-line platform beneath Venice, the boarded-over track trench running away into darkness, enamel wayfinding plates stripped bare, dust motes hanging in the beams. The air is still. One adult stands in the light: a muscular Indonesian man in his late twenties, hair tied in a short knot, wearing a bright cyan shirt and white trousers, all crisp and energetic. In one continuous shot he begins fully framed with both feet on the tiles, then drops into a deep crouch and chains explosive pouncing leaps down the entire platform. The camera pans slowly from left to right, holding him.

Bruise-purple storm clouds pile above a closed street on the Venetian causeway, asphalt still dry, a wide white crosswalk under foot, shuttered kiosks and a lifted barrier at the corner; far off, headlights of moving traffic drag long light trails across the overpass. One adult stands on the crosswalk: a statuesque Māori woman in her thirties, dark hair braided tight, in a gold tunic and black leggings, gripping a colour-guard flag. Epic and cinematic. One continuous shot holds her fully in frame, feet rooted to the same patch of asphalt, as she rips the flag through fast spins and launches high tosses, catching cleanly. The camera orbits slowly around her.

A palazzo ballroom on the Grand Canal: warped parquet, chandeliers unlit, tall arched windows throwing shafts of daylight, and a rented lighting rig outside painting flickering neon and sweeping searchlight beams across the frescoed ceiling. Spectators lean over the gilded balcony, none on the floor. Four adults play below — a tall Senegalese man in white, a compact Italian woman near forty in red, a blonde Norwegian man in his twenties, and a curvy Peruvian woman in gold. Dreamy, saturated, slow-glowing. One continuous shot from a static tripod at eye level: all four stay fully framed, feet on the wood, driving power shots and full volleys the length of the hall.

Sunrise mist softens a railway station forecourt in Venice, dark basalt setts sloping toward the canal steps, a shuttered ticket kiosk, coloured paper scraps from last night's festival tumbling through the air. Onlookers cluster behind steel barriers at the edges, off the paving where the action happens. Two adults fence there: a lean Iranian man in his thirties and a tall Danish woman near fifty, both in white jackets, sport foils in hand, masks on. Crisp, bright, advertising energy. In one continuous shot both stay fully in frame with feet on the setts, exchanging long lunges and parry-riposte counters up and down the forecourt as the camera dollies slowly out.

Floodlights on scaffold poles wash a stretch of cropped dry grass outside Venice, round hay bales at the edge, a line of blank banner flags and loose tarpaulin whipping hard in the wind, black countryside beyond. Five adults spread across the turf: a broad Ukrainian man in his forties in blue, a small Tamil woman in fuchsia, an athletic Black man in his twenties in white, a freckled Australian woman in green, and a bearded Lebanese man in grey. Bright, punchy, sporty. One continuous shot keeps all five fully framed with feet on the grass, vaulting one after another over crouched partners, each landing and dropping into a crouch so the chain creeps a few meters. Camera tracks sideways at a steady walking pace.

An open-air festival stage stands on the Venetian breakwater, aluminium deck bolted over the rocks, black truss towers bare of banners, a storm sky bearing down and heavy surf exploding against the seawall behind. Four adults line up: a rangy Sudanese man in charcoal, a muscular Bulgarian woman in her thirties in deep red, a stocky Japanese man in slate, and a tall Cuban woman with cropped hair in navy. Moody, high-contrast, noir. One continuous shot from a static tripod at eye level: all four start fully framed, feet on the deck, then race head-to-head to a taped finish line, the leader ending close and cropped at the edge of frame.

A long gravel service road runs between white storage tanks at a refinery on the Venetian mainland, pipe racks arching overhead, a striped safety gate standing open, hazy windblown afternoon light bleaching the sky. The air is otherwise still. Three adults train on the loose grey stone: a tall Moroccan woman in her thirties in electric blue, a broad-chested Serbian man near forty in white, and a young Haitian man in bright orange. Bright, punchy, commercial energy. In one continuous shot all three remain fully in frame with feet on the gravel, striking driven shots off the bounce and first-time half-volleys that ricochet from a tank wall and send them chasing far down the road, while the camera orbits slowly around them.

Neon tubes along a boardwalk bar throw pink and cyan over a beach volleyball court on the Venetian Lido, the fine sand freshly raked, net posts wrapped in foam, breakers folding white in the darkness behind. Spectators crowd the raised bar deck above, none on the sand. Two adults face each other, each holding a padded practice stick: a broad Fijian man in his thirties in a black rash guard, and a lean Estonian woman near forty with a bleached crop and grey shorts. Gritty, documentary-plain. One continuous shot keeps both fully framed with feet in the sand as they spar within a few meters, striking and slipping away. The camera dollies slowly in.

Fine white coral sand runs to the water on a beach beside a Venetian lagoon resort, a neon-strung bar throwing magenta over the shore, upturned rowing skiffs at the treeline, and fireworks blooming silently far out over the sea. Four adults stand in a line facing away from a row of planted flags: a tall Jamaican woman in her twenties in yellow, a stocky Finnish man in white, a wiry Malaysian man in red, and a strong-shouldered Chilean woman near forty in cobalt. Bright, kinetic, sporty. One continuous shot: all four hold still, fully in frame with feet on the sand, then drop prone, explode up, sprint the long stretch and dive for the flags. Handheld camera circles slowly at chest height.

Sunrise mist hangs over a lagoon-side metal recycler outside Venice: walls of baled aluminium cubes, a snarled heap of bicycle frames, a chipped weighbridge hut with a striped boom. Two adults claim a clean square of oil-stained concrete while the camera dollies slowly out in one continuous shot, revealing the stacks. A round-shouldered Puerto Rican woman in an orange fleece tucks the iron ball under her jaw, glides back across her heel and punches it skyward with a laughing shout; a lanky Norwegian man in a grey beanie mirrors the sequence, then bounces on his toes. From the first beat both stand feet-planted on that patch, fully in frame throughout. Fat snowflakes drift through the low golden beams.

Inside a Venetian cathedral nave stripped for restoration, worn stone flagstones stretch between marble columns, a scaffold tower rises into the dark vault, and a rigger's console throws flickering neon and slow sweeping searchlight beams across the apse. Low moody lamps leave the aisles in deep shadow. Two adults stand in the central strip: a tall Sri Lankan woman in her thirties in a scarlet bodysuit, and a lean Belgian man near fifty in black, each holding a long silk streamer. Epic and cinematic. One continuous shot: both begin fully framed, feet on the stone, then sprint and gallop the whole nave trailing ribbons; the camera dollies out as the man passes close and leaves frame partly cropped.

Thunderheads stack over a cathedral forecourt square in Venice, sandstone paving swept clean, a boarded market stall against a brick campanile, and far across the water the causeway traffic smears into long light trails. One adult occupies the empty square: a powerfully built Kazakh man in his thirties, hair shaved at the sides, wearing a slate tank top and dark shorts. The mood is vast and cinematic, the light bruised and heavy. One continuous shot opens with him fully in frame, feet flat on the stone, before he drops onto hands and toes and bear-crawls hard across several meters and back. The camera orbits slowly around him throughout, keeping him whole in frame.

A shallow lake behind the Venetian lagoon has frozen over, snow dusting the ice into pale streaks; a boathouse strung with neon tubing spills red and blue across the surface, and warm steam drifts from a pumping-station vent at the bank. One adult skates there: a lean Canadian-Chinese woman in her late twenties, hair in a high bun, wearing a white jacket and turquoise leggings, blades flashing. Bright, energetic, advertisement-clean. In one continuous shot she stays fully in frame with skates on the ice, working backward crossovers within a few meters and snapping quick pivot transitions from backward to forward and back again. The camera dollies slowly toward her as she carves.

A flat, wave-worn rock shelf edges the Venetian shoreline, tide pools catching the magenta glow of a neon-lit seafront frontage, a squat lighthouse dark against the sky, hung lanterns unmoving in the still night air. Five adults link hands: a tall Icelandic woman in her thirties in silver, a compact Bangladeshi man in ochre, a broad Greek man near fifty in black, a young Kenyan woman in white, and a lanky Czech woman in blue. Dreamy, saturated, music-video soft. One continuous shot: all five start fully framed, feet on the rock, then whip a crack-the-whip chain that flings the tail runner toward the lens until she is partly cropped. The camera tracks sideways at a steady walking pace.

Soft overcast daylight lies over a beachfront promenade near Venice, its black-and-white mosaic paving swirling in long waves, shuttered gelato kiosks and bent tamarisk trees behind, the sea flat and silver. Onlookers watch from a raised café terrace above the promenade wall, none on the mosaic. One adult performs below: a wiry Brazilian man in his late twenties, curly hair, black vest and loose grey trousers. Grand, cinematic, weighty. Shot as one continuous take from a static tripod at eye level, he never leaves his single patch of mosaic, launching a cork, then a 540 kick, then a butterfly twist, landing each cleanly with both feet back on the stone.

Floodlight masts blaze over a hospital rooftop helipad in Venice, the painted concrete circle and its faded touchdown ring glossy with damp, aerials and a windsock at the parapet, while fog banks roll through and swallow the skyline in slow surges. One adult stands in the middle: a compact Puerto Rican woman in her thirties, dark curls tied up, in a bright coral tee and white shorts. Playful, upbeat, breezy. The camera cranes down from high above to eye level in one continuous shot; she starts fully in frame with feet on the pad, then kicks up and walks on her hands a few meters, adding springy handstand hops before dropping back down.

An idled car assembly hall on the Venetian mainland: half-built body shells hang from an overhead conveyor, yellow safety lines run across the epoxy-coated concrete, tool trolleys parked in the gloom. Low practice lamps carve deep shadows; one lone adult stands in a small pool of light. She is a middle-aged Trinidadian woman with a greying afro, in a black tank, rolled work trousers and battered tap shoes. Feet on the floor and fully in frame from the first beat, she drills a fast riff-walk, snaps into three pullbacks, then rattles a wing and closes with heel-drop syncopation. The camera never moves, locked on its tripod at eye level for one continuous shot. Nothing else stirs.

Under a glass canopy, a transit plaza on the Venetian mainland glows with bright even overhead lighting: grey porcelain tile, brushed-steel ticket columns, potted olive trees, and confetti-like paper scraps tumbling in the draught from the doors. Nobody else is here. Four adults train in two pairs — a heavyset Georgian man in his forties, a tall Ivorian woman in white, a compact Filipina near thirty, and a rangy Swedish man in blue, all in judo jackets. Noir shadows pool under the columns. One continuous shot keeps all four fully framed with feet on the tile, staying on one small footprint as they drill uchi-mata entries and hip throws. The camera dollies slowly in.

Amidships on a laid-up container feeder moored in the Venetian lagoon: painted grey steel deck streaked with rust, lashing rods stacked against a hatch coaming, a coil of mooring line by the rail. Overcast daylight sits soft and shadowless, the air completely still. One weathered adult, a sinewy Argentinian man in his forties, black compression shirt, faded green cargo shorts, bare feet, starts fully framed and planted on the plating. He takes three quick steps, floats a side aerial with no hands touching, lands, and immediately chains a running front tuck into a low roll along the deck. He remains fully in frame. The camera dollies slowly backward, opening out to the cranes and grey water, one continuous shot.

Inside a caged octagon rigged in a converted Venetian boat shed, chain-link fencing throws lattice shadows over the black vinyl mat; haze drifts and two spotlights sweep across it while a hard floodlight rakes in from stage left. Exactly two adults occupy the canvas, each on a single spot, fully framed and grounded from first frame to last. A shaven-headed Iranian man in red shorts whips into a sprint-step rhythm, then punches out a triple-under that blurs the cable. Opposite him, a tall Ethiopian woman with tight braids and a grey rash guard scissors her feet, folds her arms into a crossing, and finishes on one leg. Sweat sprays in the beams. One continuous shot, the camera locked on a tripod at eye level.

A municipal ice rink on the Venetian mainland sits half-lit: white ice with faded painted lines, dasher boards scarred by pucks, haze-machine fog drifting while moving spotlights sweep in slow blades of light. Spectators sit in the dim stands beyond the boards, none on the ice. Five adults skate: a tall Russian-Armenian woman in black, a slender Vietnamese man in white, a broad Norwegian man in navy, a Black woman near forty in deep green, and a small Italian woman in burgundy. Cinematic and grand. The camera tracks sideways at a steady walking pace through one continuous take; all five stay fully in frame, blades on the ice, springing into jumps within a few meters and landing on clean gliding edges.

Storm light presses down on a small university library plaza in Venice, herringbone brick laid tight, a bronze reading-figure statue on a plinth, bicycle racks along a low balustrade where students crowd to watch from the raised terrace, off the brick. The air is dead still before the rain. One adult stands alone in the open: a compact Mexican-American woman in her late twenties, hair in a tight bun, in a bright white tee and red shorts. Bright and sporty despite the sky. The camera cranes down from high above to eye level in one continuous shot as she holds her single spot, feet on the brick, snapping standing back tucks and standing flips.

An old roller skating rink on the Venetian mainland: glossy maple hardwood, a dusty mirror ball hanging motionless above, faded pennant bunting, and low moody practice lights leaving the corners deep in shadow. Nothing in the air stirs. Spectators sit on carpeted benches behind the barrier, none on the wood. Six adults hold a tight circle — a tall Trinidadian man in gold, a Vietnamese woman in lilac, a Black woman with a bleached crop in orange, a slim Spanish man in green, a curvy Somali woman in white, a bearded German man in pink. Playful and bright. The camera dollies slowly out through one continuous take while all six stay fully in frame, feet on the maple, vogue-spinning into sharp death-drop dips.

An indoor pool on the Venetian mainland: non-slip ceramic tile around still turquoise water, lane reels parked at the shallow end, harsh floodlights blasting in from one side wall so shadows stretch long across the deck. Nothing else moves. Five adults line up on the tile: a tall Nepali man in his thirties in blue trunks and a rash guard, a muscular Black woman in red, a freckled Irish woman near fifty in white, a lean Brazilian man in yellow, and a stocky Korean woman in grey. Dreamy and glowing. One continuous shot: all five start fully framed with feet down, sprinting a few metres in bursts and freezing mid-stride; the camera orbits slowly as one runner passes close and exits frame partly.

Rain streaks the striped tarmac of a race circuit pit lane outside Venice, puddles splashing under the drips from the garage awnings, roller shutters half down, tyre trolleys parked and abandoned. Fans line the far side behind the pit wall, off the tarmac entirely. One adult runs here: a tall Ivorian-French woman in her thirties, hair braided into a crown, in a silver jacket and black leggings, gripping a long streamer that unfurls behind her. Soft, dreamy, saturated. The camera cranes down from high above to eye level in one continuous shot; she begins fully framed, feet on the wet ground, then sprints the length of the lane and finishes close, cropped at the shoulders.

A film sound stage on the Venetian mainland: matte black floor, a white cyclorama curving at one end, thick cable runs taped down, a red hose reel mounted on a rolling frame. Harsh floodlights blast from one side, carving hard-edged shadows; the air is completely still and nobody else is present. Two adults work the floor: a broad Ghanaian-Italian man in his thirties in a yellow tee, and a short, strong Slovak woman near forty with a blonde bob in navy overalls. Playful and upbeat. In one continuous shot both start fully in frame, feet on the floor, then sprint the hose out across the whole stage and drop the nozzle. The camera dollies slowly in.

The great hall of a Venetian courthouse stands empty at night, checkerboard marble stretching between fluted columns, tarped scaffolding against one wall, warm tungsten work lamps clamped to the balustrade throwing amber pools. The air is utterly still. One adult occupies the floor: a tall Iranian-German woman in her forties, silver hair cropped short, wearing a long black tunic and loose trousers, a plain wooden staff in her hands. Grand, cinematic, hushed. Filmed as one continuous take, she stays fully in frame with feet on the marble, moving only a couple of meters as she spins the staff through body rolls, behind-the-back passes and clean vertical tosses. The camera dollies slowly out.

Golden hour turns a fine grey gravel outwash plain inland of Venice to warm ash, braided stream beds glinting between the bars, wind-bent poplars along a levee, low dust blowing steadily across the stones. Five adults train there: a tall Estonian man in his thirties in white, a powerful Nigerian woman in orange, a wiry Indian man in blue, a broad Argentine woman near fifty in grey, and a young Albanian man in black. Raw and documentary. In a single continuous shot the camera dollies slowly outward across the plain; all five stay fully in frame, boots on the gravel, pounding long approaches, breaking into crossover steps and hurling javelins far downfield.

Overcast light flattens a skatepark on the Venetian mainland, its smooth cast-concrete flat bottom ringed by a graffiti-splashed bowl and a rusted quarter pipe, while stray snowflakes drift through the pale beams over the fence. Watchers perch on the coping ledge above, off the flat. Four adults grapple on the bare concrete: a compact Turkish woman in her thirties in red, a broad Samoan man in grey, a lanky Ukrainian man in white, and a strong Black woman near forty in purple. Playful and bright. Filmed as one continuous shot that pans slowly from left to right, all four remain fully in frame with feet on the concrete, shooting double-leg takedowns, driving through and resetting.

One continuous shot tracks sideways at a steady walking pace across a cramped boxing loft above a Havana bakery, its canvas patched with grey tape, a rusted fan turning overhead, low practice lamps leaving the corners in deep shadow. Two adults hold the middle of the mat: a lean Afro-Cuban woman in a coral tank with taped wrists, and a broad man in his forties with silver stubble and navy trunks. Both stand fully framed, feet on the canvas, then trade fast jabs, slip and roll under hooks, pivoting within a couple of metres. Street neon flickers through the shutters and searchlight beams sweep the brick; spectators pack benches beyond the ropes.

A crane move drops from high above the rafters down to eye level in one continuous shot, revealing a disused Havana weaving hall where rows of silent looms flank a chalk-marked plank aisle and thread spools sit furred with lint. Exactly one adult occupies the floor: a compact South Asian woman in her thirties, black braid pinned up, lime shorts and a white cropped tee. She begins standing fully in frame, both bare feet on the boards, drops onto hands and toes, then bear-crawls hard down the aisle, hips low, palms slapping wood. Daylight spears through high windows while steam drifts lazily from floor vents. Nobody else is present.

Fog hangs motionless between the leaning green culms of a bamboo grove behind a crumbling Havana aqueduct, dry leaves carpeting the packed earth, a moss-furred stone channel half-buried at the edge. One adult stands there: a tall Black man in his late twenties, close-cropped hair, charcoal compression top, faded orange shorts, both feet clearly on the soil at the start. The camera orbits him slowly in one continuous shot as he explodes between four low cones, touching the ground at each turn, cutting back and forth across five metres of leaf litter, heels throwing up dust. Epic, muted, monumental; no other person appears.

Bright even lamps flood a school gymnasium in central Havana, its maple court glossy over a faded painted crest, boarded windows lining the upper wall. Three adults hold one spot near the centre circle: a heavyset Latina woman in a mustard tracksuit, a wiry East Asian man in black with a white headband, and a tall mixed-race woman with bleached curls in a grey vest. All three are fully in frame with shoes planted from the first moment. A single continuous shot dollies slowly toward them as they erupt into krump — jarring stomps, chest pops, whipping arm swings — feet never leaving their small patch. The air is still, the hall empty.

Bruised storm clouds press down on a wide civic plaza in Havana paved with polished granite, a dry fountain basin at one side and a weathered obelisk casting no shadow. Four adults stand spread across the stone, all fully in frame with feet down: a stocky white-Cuban man in a red singlet, a slender Ethiopian woman in teal, a broad-shouldered Filipino man in grey, and a silver-haired woman in her fifties wearing white. One continuous shot dollies steadily toward them as they burst into full sprints across twenty metres, then snap into absolute frozen poses mid-stride, then explode again. The air is dead calm before rain; nobody else is anywhere.

Warm tungsten work lamps on tripods carve orange pools out of a cavernous rolling mill on Havana's industrial edge, cold rollers looming in the half-dark, oil stains blooming on the steel plate floor. Five adults stand anchored on that plate, each fully visible from the first beat: a bald Black man in a black tank, a freckled redheaded woman in olive, a lean Vietnamese man in navy, a heavy-armed Latino man in maroon, and a tattooed woman with a shaved head in charcoal. In one continuous shot the camera dollies slowly out, widening the shadowed hall while they hammer battle ropes into whipping waves and thunderous slams, feet rooted. Air still, noir-dark, nobody else.

Low practice lamps leave most of a small Havana gallery hall in deep shadow — pale oak planks, three unlit canvases leaning against a brass rail, a dusty empty pedestal. Three adults claim one bright patch of floor and never leave it: a curly-haired Cuban woman in a scarlet skirt, a spare older man with grey temples in a black shirt, and a young mixed-race dancer in emerald. All are fully in frame, heels on the oak, from the opening moment. One continuous shot dollies gently in as they drive percussive zapateado bursts, heels drumming the boards, arms curling overhead in sharp braceo. Playful, bright-hearted energy; the room is otherwise empty and perfectly calm.

Harsh midday sun bleaches the stamped-concrete concourse ring of a Havana ballpark, shuttered kiosks along one wall, a painted stripe curling around a pillar. Two adults occupy the flat slab: a rangy Afro-Caribbean man in a white sleeveless top, and a muscular Korean woman in her thirties wearing purple. Both start fully in frame with shoes on the concrete. A single continuous shot cranes down from high above to eye level while they fire rubber dodgeballs hard at each other, twisting away, ducking, and diving flat onto the warm stone before scrambling up within a few metres. Air utterly still, shadows short and severe; no one else is present.

A passing shower has left a crushed-brick tennis court behind a Havana sports club glossy and dark, the air now dead calm, a sagging net and a rusted umpire chair off to one side. Four adults work the wet clay, all fully framed with feet down from the start: a broad Cuban man in indigo, a petite Japanese woman in white, a lanky ginger-bearded man in grey, and a tall Black woman in yellow. In one continuous shot the camera dollies slowly outward, opening up the motionless palms beyond the fence, as they pair off with bamboo shinai — crisp overhead strikes, sliding lunges, quick retreats across a couple of metres, sandals skidding on the slick clay. Cheerful, bright, no one else around.

Blue hour over a private tennis lawn behind a crumbling Havana mansion: close-mown turf, sagging net posts, bougainvillea spilling over a coral-stone wall. Five adults line up beside a padded low box dragged onto the grass. One continuous shot, the camera orbiting slowly around them. A compact Cuban woman with copper curls sprints and punches a dive-kong across the box; a broad Sudanese man follows with a speed vault; three more, a wiry Thai man, a tanned Australian woman, a bearded Portuguese man, queue and answer in turn, landing soft on the turf. All five start fully framed, feet down. Neighbours watch from a balcony above. Traffic light trails streak beyond the wall. The final vaulter charges the lens and leaves frame chest-high.

Golden light rakes a broad concrete esplanade along Havana's harbour, rusted mooring bollards spaced down the slabs, a listing crane far across the water, a low seawall catching spray. Three adults begin fully in frame with feet on the concrete: a long-legged Somali woman in lilac, a compact Latino man in cream, and a silver-braided woman in her forties wearing sky blue. Petals and dry leaves swirl low across the slabs. One continuous shot dollies gently inward as they run flat out, slapping a baton from hand to hand at full speed down the esplanade; the final runner accelerates straight at the camera and ends partly outside the frame. Dreamy, warm, unpeopled otherwise.

Fog banks roll steadily through the mown lawn quad of a Havana office campus, softening the glass wings and squat concrete planters into grey shapes. Two adults stand on the grass, both fully in frame, shoes sinking slightly: a heavily built Māori man in a black tank, and a strong-shouldered white woman in her thirties with a blonde bun and a green tee. A handheld camera circles them slowly at chest height in one continuous shot while they take turns flipping a battered tractor tyre end over end down a short lane, dropping into deep squats, driving it up, chasing it forward. Colleagues watch from a raised walkway behind railings. Punchy and bright.

A squash court in a Havana sports club has been rewired for a night shoot: magenta and cyan stage lamps wash the pale hardwood, flicker across the glass back wall, and searchlight beams sweep the white plaster. One dancer works the floor, a broad-shouldered Punjabi man in his thirties, mustard kurta knotted at the waist, loose white trousers, bells at his ankles. Fully framed and grounded at the start, he bounces a driving chaal across two metres, snaps into jumping knee-lifts, throws both arms overhead and spins out of a squat. Spectators press against the glass wall behind. The camera tracks sideways at a walking pace, one continuous shot; near the end he closes in and his head crops out.

Mist lies in the hollows of a golden grassland east of Havana at sunrise, a lone thorn tree, leaning fence posts, a ridge of blue hills behind. Six adults stand on the short grass, all fully in frame with feet down: a huge Samoan man in grey, a wiry Black woman in red, a bearded Turkish man in white, a freckled woman in teal, a stocky Japanese man in black, and a tall Latina in ochre. The camera orbits slowly in one continuous shot as they form three pairs, each carrier hoisting a partner across the shoulders and sprinting thirty metres through the wet grass, boots tearing green streaks. Air dead still, monumental, no one else.

A black storm ceiling hangs over a packed gravel crossroads beyond Havana, a leaning signpost stripped bare, cane fields on three sides, a tin-roofed shed rattling. Leaves and husks swirl low across the stones. Six adults hold the crossing, every one fully in frame with boots on gravel: a broad Cuban man in olive, a lean Sudanese woman in white, a red-haired man in grey, a compact Thai woman in maroon, a bald older man in black, and a tall woman in denim. In one continuous shot the camera cranes down from high overhead to eye level while they spar in pairs with padded practice sticks — cracking strikes, ducks, quick side-steps across a few metres.

Haze drifts between towering bare racking in an empty Havana distribution warehouse, tungsten work lamps glowing amber while moving spotlights slide across polished concrete. A chalked wooden platform stands mid-aisle beside a heavy grey stone ball. Exactly one adult is present: a thickset Pacific Islander man in his thirties, forearms taped, black shorts and a faded burgundy shirt, fully in frame with both feet on the floor. One continuous shot cranes down from the rack tops to eye level as he squats, laps the stone onto his thighs and drives it up onto the platform again and again, staying on one spot. Dreamy, floating, entirely alone.

Haze curls under moving spotlights in a night-time ballet studio in Havana — black marley underfoot, chipped wooden barres, a tall bare brick wall where the mirrors were stripped out. Six adults work the floor, all fully in frame with feet on the vinyl at the start: a sinewy Black man in grey sweats, a small Chinese woman in purple, a bearded man in his forties in white, a tall Latina in orange, a blonde woman in olive, and a young man in red. The camera tracks sideways at walking pace in one continuous shot while they spin weighted poi in fast weaves, butterflies and body turns, shifting a couple of metres. Raw, observational, unlit corners swallowing them.

Haze machine fog pools around squat pillars in a damp concrete bunker hall beneath Havana, moving spotlights raking dripping vaults and a rusted blast door at the far end. Two adults stand on the bare slab, both fully in frame with feet down: a rangy Black man in a grey compression top, and a powerful Mexican woman in her thirties with a low ponytail and dark blue kit. One continuous shot cranes down from the vault ceiling to eye level as they run sharp routes down the hall, cutting off pillars, twisting to snag over-the-shoulder catches on the run. Moody and low-key; near the end he sprints past the lens and finishes half out of frame.

Bright ceiling panels light a small Havana dojo laid with green tatami, a faded cloth banner on the wall, sliding shutters half open, a worn shoe rack by the door. Haze drifts and two soft spotlights swing slowly across the mats. Three adults stand in a triangle, all fully in frame with bare feet on the tatami: a chunky Cuban man in white, a slight Vietnamese woman in a red rash guard, and a tall ginger-bearded man in grey. A tripod camera holds steady at eye level for one continuous shot while they pass juggling clubs in a fast rotating feed, doubles crossing between them, bodies pivoting and shifting a couple of metres. Cheerful and crisp.

The ice is gone from a Havana rink for the season, leaving a painted concrete slab ringed by scuffed boards and hanging tungsten work lamps that glow honey-colored. Two big floor fans push loose paper and dust skittering across the paint. Two adults hold one small square of slab, both fully in frame with heels down from the first beat: a stately Afro-Cuban woman in a fuchsia ruffled skirt, and a lean older man with a silver ponytail in black. In one continuous shot the camera cranes down from the roof trusses to eye level while they hammer alternating zapateado bursts, arms sweeping into high braceo. Upbeat and warm; no one else.

Deep shadows swallow a Havana bus depot hall where yellow bay stripes run across cracked asphalt, service pits gape empty and cables hang from the girders. Only a few low practice lamps burn, leaving the far doors nearly black. One adult stands there, fully in frame with both feet on the asphalt: a compact Chinese-Cuban man in his thirties, hair tied back, sleeveless black top, loose red trousers. One continuous shot dollies slowly toward him as he sinks into a deep crouch and explodes forward in successive pouncing leaps, low then high, crossing bay after bay down the hall. The air is completely still. Epic, cavernous, entirely unpeopled.

Blue hour drains the color from a faded surface parking lot near Havana's seawall, ghostly stall lines still visible, one lamp post snapped at the base, dry leaves swirling low over the asphalt. Three adults stand fully in frame with feet on the tarmac: a long-limbed Black woman in silver-grey, a slender Japanese man in soft white, and a broad-shouldered Latina in dusty rose. One continuous shot dollies slowly inward while they launch grand allegro leaps along a long diagonal — split jumps, sweeping arms, quiet landings that scatter the leaves — travelling the full length of the lot. Dreamy, saturated dusk tones; the lot holds nobody else.

Misty sunrise light diffuses over a flat of fine grey volcanic ash near the Havana coast, scattered black boulders and bleached driftwood breaking the plain, surf crashing white beyond a low berm. Exactly one adult stands on the ash, fully in frame with both feet planted: a powerfully built Greek-Cuban woman in her forties, hair scraped back, a plain slate singlet and grey shorts, ash dusting her calves. A tripod camera watches from eye level in one unbroken shot as she settles, winds back, spins through a tight discus rotation on one spot and releases with a grunt, ash puffing under her pivot foot. Plain, documentary, unglamorous. Nobody else is anywhere near.

Dusk turns a striped natural-grass pitch in a Havana stadium to steel blue, the terraces empty, floodlight pylons dark, a single gate hanging open. Three adults stand on the turf, all fully in frame with boots down: a thickset Nigerian man in black, a lean Argentine man in charcoal, and a tall Slavic woman in deep green. A tripod camera holds a fixed eye-level angle for one continuous shot while they drive resisted sprints across the pitch, thick tow bands stretched taut behind them, torsos angled forward, cleats tearing grass as they cover thirty metres. The evening air is dead calm. Noir shadows, muted color, absolutely no one else in the bowl.

Tungsten lamps hang low over a converted garage gym in Havana, black rubber tiles underfoot, a chalk bin in the corner, gymnastic rings still swaying, the roller door pushed halfway up. Exactly one adult is inside: a wiry Filipino man in his late twenties, tattooed forearms, a plain grey vest and blue shorts, fully in frame with both feet on the tiles. One continuous shot cranes down from above the rings to eye level as he spins a long wooden staff in fast figure-eights, rolls it across his shoulders and flicks it into a spinning toss, catching it while shifting a metre or two. Playful and upbeat; the air is still.
