Golden hour floods a drained dry dock in the Havana shipyard, its wet concrete floor dulled to a matte sheen, keel blocks lined like teeth, a towering caisson gate at the far end. Fine dust blows low across the slab. Two adults stand fully in frame with shoes on the concrete: a lithe Black man in his twenties in white and gold, and a compact Ukrainian woman in her thirties in dark red. A tripod camera holds one continuous eye-level shot while each builds a pounding run-up down the dock, hits a chalked mark, drives up into a long jump and lands hard, skidding to a stop. Amber light, deep shadow, nobody else.

Fog banks roll in across a wide beach west of Havana under soft overcast light, the packed damp sand marked by a curving tide line of broken shells and a half-buried wooden groyne. Exactly one adult stands there, fully in frame with bare feet on the sand: a strong-legged Afro-Latina woman in her thirties, hair wrapped in cloth, faded grey leotard and cut-off track pants. A tripod camera records one continuous eye-level shot while she runs and launches grand allegro leaps along a diagonal, legs splitting wide, sand bursting from each takeoff as she covers twenty metres and drifts in and out of the mist. Plain, unpolished, documentary. No one else on the beach.

Sunset gilds a vineyard outside Havana where wire trellises run in long parallel rows and a tractor lane of compacted soil cuts between them; far beyond the vines a highway drags streaks of headlight past the horizon. Three adults stand on the soil, all fully in frame with boots down: a barrel-chested Cuban man in a canvas shirt, a lean Ethiopian woman in grey coveralls, and a bearded man in his fifties in faded blue. The camera pans slowly left to right in one continuous shot while they haul a coiled fire hose out at a dead sprint down the lane, unreeling it in a snaking line before dropping it flat. Epic, dust-lit, otherwise deserted.

Rain glazes the black granite of a sunken plaza in Havana's bank district, glass office walls rising on three sides, dry concrete planters holding leggy palms. Two adults hold one spot on the wet stone, both fully in frame with feet planted from the opening moment: a broad-shouldered Kenyan man in a bright yellow rash top, and a petite Spanish woman in her thirties with a russet crop and turquoise leggings. A fixed tripod camera at eye level captures one continuous shot as they spin poi in blistering weaves, butterflies and sharp body turns, water flicking off the cords. The air is otherwise still. Onlookers cluster at the railing above, never on the granite.

Daylight spears in through the open portal and two ventilation shafts of a half-bored road tunnel under Havana, striping the raw shotcrete floor while steam drifts from grated vents and rebar arches curve overhead. Six adults hold their own patches of floor, every one fully in frame with feet down: a huge Cuban man in grey, a sinewy Korean woman in black, a tattooed man in olive, a broad Nigerian woman in white, a bearded Slav in navy, and a slight Peruvian man in red. In one continuous shot the camera tracks sideways at walking pace as they hammer burpees — chests to shotcrete, snapping up into explosive jumps, hands clapping overhead.

Bright banks of lamps flatten every shadow in a shipyard fabrication shed in Havana: a rust-stained steel deck, a silent gantry crane overhead, stacks of cut plate leaning in the bays. Four adults stand fully in frame with boots on the plate: a heavyset Black man in orange coveralls, a tall Cuban woman in grey, a stocky Japanese man in blue, and a red-haired woman in her forties in green. A tripod camera holds one continuous eye-level shot while they link hands in a chain and whip into a crack-the-whip spin, the anchor pivoting hard, the tail runner flung wide across a few metres before skidding to a halt. Still air, epic scale, no onlookers.

Floodlights blaze from one side of a Havana fencing hall, throwing long shadows across the metallic piste laid over grey rubber, scoring reels idle at each end, a wooden gallery running above. Six adults stand on the strip, all fully in frame with feet down: a tall Black woman in white, a stocky Cuban man in maroon, a slim Indian man in grey, a blonde woman in navy, a bearded man in black, and a young Latina in gold. The camera pans slowly left to right in one continuous shot as they march snare drums a few paces up the piste, sticks flashing, snapping crisp pivot turns. Spectators watch from the gallery. The lead drummer advances until he is half out of frame.

Low lamps leave the corners of an old Havana tobacco barn in near darkness, light pooling on the wide plank floor beneath empty drying racks that hang like ribs. Four adults each hold a fixed spot with a ball tee before them, all fully in frame with boots on the boards: a burly Dominican man in a grey sleeveless shirt, a lean white-Cuban woman in denim, a tall Black man in navy, and a wiry older man with a white moustache in tan. The camera pans slowly left to right in one continuous shot while they load, rotate and crack bat through ball, one after another, hips whipping, feet never travelling. Still air, epic and shadowed, nobody else.

Steam creeps from floor vents across a derelict brick factory hall in Havana, tungsten work lamps throwing amber cones over broken brick tile and the black mouths of dead kilns. Three adults each own a small patch of floor, all fully in frame with feet planted: a heavy-shouldered Cuban man in a black tank, a lean Somali woman in dark green, and a grey-templed man in his fifties wearing a rust-colored tee. One continuous shot dollies slowly backward, opening up the ruined hall around them while they hoist medicine balls overhead and hammer them down into the tile again and again, dust bursting up, brick fragments skittering. Hard shadows, noir mood, entirely unpeopled.

Portable floodlights blast a circular stone threshing floor on a farm outside Havana, its flagstones ringed by a knee-high wall, woven baskets stacked at the edge, dark cane fields swallowing everything beyond. Two adults stand fully in frame with feet on the stone: a broad Black man in a worn grey shirt, and a tough, freckled woman in her thirties with a dark bob and a maroon vest. The camera orbits them slowly in one continuous shot as she grips his ankles and he powers forward on his hands, wheelbarrow-style, scrambling several metres across the flagstones before they swap and go back. The night is dead still. Harsh light, deep shadow, nobody else.

Late golden sun rakes a flat mesa top above the Havana coast, hardpan cracked and studded with scrub tufts, the cliff edge dropping away where surf pounds white far below. Five adults stand on the hardpan, all fully in frame with spikes on the ground: a tall Caribbean man in white, a broad Polish woman in red, a lean Egyptian man in grey, a muscular Black woman in teal, and a bearded man in his forties in navy. In one continuous shot the camera dollies slowly out, revealing the whole plateau while they run in crossover steps and launch javelins in bright arcs. The last thrower charges toward the lens and finishes partly out of frame.

Light rain slicks the concrete pavers of a Havana rooftop terrace, two dented water tanks on stilts behind and a skyline of peeling pastel facades stretching to the harbour. Exactly one adult is on the pavers: a sturdy Afro-Cuban woman in her thirties, short bleached hair, a black long-sleeve top and grey shorts, fully in frame with both feet down before she begins. A tripod camera holds one continuous eye-level shot as she drops prone, then explodes up into a three-metre burst, resets seated, snaps up again, then falls sideways and scrambles into another start. The air is still, water beading everywhere. Neighbours watch from a balcony behind railings across the gap.

Where the Cuban coast road ends, a plain of tight-packed dark pebbles runs to a cliff edge; surf explodes white below and hazy afternoon wind hauls dust sideways through the light. One adult works alone: a stocky Filipino man in his fifties, sun-bleached vest, leather gloves, canvas trousers powdered pale. He stands on a single patch of stone, fully in frame from the first instant and never leaving it. Gripping the twine of a square straw bale, he swings it between his knees and launches it onto a rusted flatbed trailer, catches his breath, hauls the next one higher, then a third that thumps and slides. Chaff hangs in the haze. The camera stays fixed at eye level, one continuous shot.

Golden light lies flat over a dry lakebed outside Havana, pale clay split into salt-rimmed plates, a single rusted post leaning where a jetty once stood, low hills smudged at the horizon. Exactly one adult stands on the clay, fully in frame with boots down: a rangy Colombian man in his thirties, dark curls, a white long-sleeve shirt and black shorts. One continuous shot dollies slowly toward him as he strikes a ball with thumping power shots, chases it far across the playa, and hammers a full volley out of the air, dust puffing at each plant. The air is perfectly still; near the end he runs at the camera and ends partly cropped.

Dusty afternoon haze softens a closed highway overpass arcing above Havana, faded lane markings running its length, cracked concrete barriers and dead lamp posts leaning over the drop. Three adults stand on the asphalt, all fully in frame with shoes down: a tall Black woman in white with long streamers on a wand, a slight Vietnamese man in pale green, and a broad-shouldered Latina in rose. In one continuous shot the camera cranes down from high above the barriers to eye level as they sprint and gallop the length of the deck, ribbons unspooling in long bright trails behind them. The air is still and warm. Dreamlike, sunlit, no one else.

Rain drums on the tar-and-gravel membrane of a converted Hanoi textile loft rooftop, where rusted water tanks and sagging laundry lines frame a small clear deck. Five adults spar with foam-padded practice sticks: a tall Vietnamese man in yellow shorts, a stocky Black woman in teal, a lean South Asian man in red, a middle-aged white woman in grey, a wiry Vietnamese woman in orange. They trade quick overhead swings, duck under sweeps, pivot two steps and splash puddles, staying within a few meters. Soft overcast daylight, playful energy, nobody else present. One continuous shot with a slow pan from left to right; all five stay fully framed, feet on the wet roof.

Harsh midday sun bleaches an abandoned drive-in lot outside Hanoi: leaning speaker posts, a torn projection screen, a delivery of builder's sand dumped on cracked asphalt and gravel. One man, forties, broad-shouldered, Vietnamese, in a sweat-soaked grey tank top and canvas trousers, digs a shovel deep and flings arc after arc of sand, stamping the blade down, twisting his hips, shifting two paces along the pile. Behind the perimeter fence spectators lean on a railing, none on the lot itself. Festival fireworks pop faintly in the far washed-out sky. Gritty documentary texture, unfiltered grain. One continuous shot, a slow dolly-in toward him, his boots always on the asphalt and his whole body in frame.

Neon arches throw magenta and lime across the painted steel plate of a riverside festival pier in Hanoi, moored barges rocking beyond, strings of pennants snapping hard in the wind. Four adults own one bright square of deck: a muscular Vietnamese man in a white vest, a tall Afro-Brazilian woman in cobalt, a slim Korean man in silver, a fortyish Latina woman in orange. Each coils, swings their arms and rips a standing back tuck, landing on the same spot, then a tuck-jump and another flip in rhythm. Festival crowds watch from a raised viewing balcony behind railings, off the deck. Bright energetic ad tone. One continuous shot, camera slowly orbiting; all four stay fully in frame, feet on steel.

Golden hour lies long over a terraced tea plantation north of Hanoi, the walkway a strip of trodden red earth between clipped green bushes, bamboo drying racks stacked at the edge. The air is perfectly still. Three adults in worn training jackets drill hip throws: a broad Vietnamese man in blue, a compact Japanese woman in white, a tall Kenyan man in faded navy. Two grip sleeve and lapel, one loads uke across his hip in a smooth o-goshi, sets him down, then they rotate partners and repeat, shuffling only a couple of meters of dirt. Playful, warm, upbeat. One continuous shot, handheld camera circling slowly at chest height, all three fully visible with feet planted.

Inside a faded grand hotel lobby in Hanoi, dust turns in shafts of daylight falling from tall arched windows onto polished marble; brass columns and a dry tiled fountain surround one open patch of floor. A neon sign outside flickers and a sweeping searchlight rakes the ceiling, painting rose and cyan bands over everything. Two dancers hold that single spot: a lean Vietnamese woman in a smoke-grey leotard, hair in a low knot, and a broad-shouldered Nigerian man in loose black trousers. She whips a chain of fouetté turns, he answers with double pirouettes, arms opening, both spotting hard. Dreamy, saturated, hypnotic. One continuous shot with a slow pan from left to right; both stay fully framed, feet on marble.

Cold neon from a crusher shed and a string of blue lamps washes the packed sand floor of a gravel pit outside Hanoi; conveyor towers stand dark above the flat. The night air is dead calm. Three adults stand at the line, fully in frame with feet on the sand, then drop prone, chins on hands, heels to camera: a tall Vietnamese woman in scarlet, a stocky white man in yellow, a sinewy Ethiopian man in green. On a whistle they scramble up and sprint fifteen meters, throwing themselves full-length into a dive for a single upright cloth flag, sand exploding. Dreamy, cool, glowing. One continuous shot as the camera cranes down from high above to eye level; all three stay fully in frame.

Mist hangs low over a harvested field beside a Hanoi ring road, straw stubble stiff with dew, tilted power poles vanishing into white, headlight trails streaking behind a distant embankment. One athlete works alone: a muscular Vietnamese woman in her thirties, hair braided tight, wearing a lilac crop top and black tights. She squats, swings both arms and rips a standing broad jump, lands absorbing, immediately bounds again, three explosive jumps forward and a hopping walk-back, covering only a few meters of stubble. Sunrise light is pale and clean; her breath shows. Bright, energetic sports-ad polish. One continuous shot, the camera orbiting slowly around her while she stays fully in frame with feet on the ground.

A wide sandbar of pale river sand sits in a half-dry channel outside Hanoi, bleached driftwood snags at the edge, a low bamboo footbridge crossing behind, hazy afternoon light thickening over dusty bluffs. Nothing else moves. Three performers hold one spot each: a tall Vietnamese man in a white sash, a curvy Filipina woman in emerald, a silver-haired white woman in crimson. They spin tall silk flags in tight figure-eights, snap them flat, then launch synchronized high tosses that spiral above frame and drop back into their hands, knees bending, feet barely shifting on the sand. Bright, punchy, athletic. One continuous shot with a slow pan from left to right; all three remain fully framed and grounded.

A converted warehouse skate park in Hanoi: smooth plywood transitions, spray-mottled walls, clerestory windows dropping hard shafts of daylight through haze-machine fog while spotlights swing lazily overhead. Three adults play on the flat plywood floor: a lanky Vietnamese man in lime, a powerful Samoan woman in purple, a freckled ginger man in white. They hurl foam dodgeballs hard, sidestep, and throw themselves into shoulder rolls, popping straight back up, all within a few meters. Playful, bright, comic timing. One continuous shot, camera tracking sideways at a steady walking pace; the three start fully in frame with feet on the plywood, then the lanky man charges the lens and ends cropped at the waist.

Light rain glazes the reinforced concrete of a container quay on the Red River port in Hanoi; gantry legs, mooring bollards and stacked reefer boxes reflect in the wet slab, harbor lamps doubling in the sheen. The air itself is still. Five adults run the open apron trailing long silk streamers: a broad Vietnamese man in red, a tall Sudanese woman in white, a wiry Japanese man in yellow, a stocky Polish woman in blue, a lean Vietnamese woman in pink. They sprint the full width, cut, gallop back, ribbons snaking behind. Playful, bright, cheerfully commercial. One continuous shot with a handheld camera circling slowly at chest height; all five stay fully in frame, feet slapping wet concrete.

Compacted fine gravel runs down the tree-lined median of a Hanoi boulevard, plane trees arching overhead, golden light slanting between trunks; beyond the far end, surf rumbles and flashes white. Five throwers work one circle of gravel, all fully in frame with feet down: a heavy-set Vietnamese man in a grey singlet, a broad Māori woman in navy, a bearded Turkish man in black, a lanky Vietnamese woman in orange, a silver-templed Black man in maroon. Each crouches low, glides back across the ring and drives the iron ball out with a grunt, feet resettling on the same spot. Onlookers watch from behind the roadside railing, off the gravel. Gritty documentary realism, one continuous shot, static tripod camera at eye level.

Blue hour settles over a small grass airstrip outside Hanoi, a corrugated tin hangar and a faded windsock at one end, low hills fading to indigo; snowflakes drift improbably through the hangar floodlight beams, glittering. Three players take the mown turf: a rangy Vietnamese man in a black kit, a powerful Brazilian woman in white, a broad Algerian man in deep green. They drive the ball the length of the strip, chase it down, then strike full volleys out of the air, sprinting thirty meters between attempts, boots tearing turf. Epic, wide, cinematic. One continuous shot as the camera cranes down from high above to eye level; all three stay fully in frame with feet on grass.

Floodlights buzz over a disused toll plaza on the edge of Hanoi: shuttered booths, a sagging canopy, faded lane arrows painted on concrete, fog banks rolling through the empty lanes and swallowing the far booths. One player occupies a single lane — a lean Vietnamese man in his late twenties, shaved head, black long-sleeve and taped shins, holding a wooden stick. He dances a ball through a line of orange cones, toe-drags, pulls it wide, then reverses back down the row, shifting only a few meters. Moody neo-noir contrast, halos in the mist. One continuous shot, the camera craning down from high above to eye level; he stays fully in frame, shoes on concrete throughout.

On the raw poured concrete slab of an unfinished Hanoi high-rise, rebar stubs bristle at the edge, torn plastic sheeting hangs limp, and the city skyline glows deep blue behind. No wind, nothing else moving. Three dancers hold one small patch: a stocky Punjabi man in a saffron kurta, a tall Vietnamese woman in fuchsia, a slender mixed-race man in cream. Arms hoisted overhead, index fingers up, they bounce through high bhangra hops, snap into deep squat kicks, shoulders shrugging in time, feet returning to the same square meter. Dreamy, saturated, floating. One continuous shot, camera tracking sideways at a steady walking pace past them; all three stay fully in frame with feet on concrete.

An open-air amphitheatre carved into a park hillside outside Hanoi: a flat concrete stage rimmed by chipped blue benches, a banyan leaning over the top row, still dust-hazed afternoon light. Four adults own the stage and nobody else is around. A grinning Korean woman with a pink-streaked bob whips a one-armed cartwheel into an aerial; a stocky Nigerian man answers with two side aerials in a row; a freckled Czech man and a tall Indonesian woman chase them down the stage with alternating hands-free turns, laughing between attempts. All four begin fully framed, shoes flat on the concrete. The tripod stays still at eye level, one continuous shot, until the Indonesian woman bounds close and her legs pass out of frame.

A flat alpine meadow bench high above the Hanoi highlands catches the last blue-hour light: short flowering turf, a lichened stone cairn, ridgelines stacking away into gloom. The air is dead still, grass unmoving. Five adults cross the bench in tumbling lines: a rangy Vietnamese man in olive, a strong Nepali woman in rust, a tall Black man in charcoal, a stocky white woman in mustard, a slim Vietnamese woman in slate. Each links cartwheel into cartwheel into a snapping round-off, travelling twenty meters from one side of frame to the other, boots thudding turf. Grainy, documentary-plain, unglamorous. One continuous shot as the camera cranes down from high above to eye level; all five stay fully in frame throughout.

Heavy snow falls on a humpbacked stone arch bridge outside Hanoi, its cobbles slick and white-dusted, carved balustrades capped in powder, a frozen canal beneath. Five athletes work the roadway in pairs and one solo: a burly Vietnamese man in navy, a tall Somali woman in white, a compact Chilean man in orange, a broad Russian woman in black, a wiry Vietnamese woman in red. Waist belts and stretch bands snap tight as each leans hard forward and drives short choppy strides the length of the bridge, partners anchoring, then swapping and driving back. Playful and bright despite the cold. One continuous shot with a slow pan from left to right; all five stay fully in frame, feet on cobblestone.

A small Hanoi yoga studio at night: light bamboo flooring, mats folded into a corner, unlit paper lanterns overhead, and one harsh floodlight raking in from a side doorway so shadows stretch long across the boards. The room is completely still. Two performers face each other three meters apart — a lean Vietnamese man in a black tee, and a tall Ukrainian woman in a burgundy top, hair loose. They pass wooden clubs in crossing arcs, doubling the tempo, spinning under a self-throw, stepping to catch. Epic, dramatic, high-contrast. One continuous shot from a static tripod at eye level; both start fully framed with feet on bamboo, then the man steps in close and ends cropped mid-chest.

A low-ceilinged wrestling room in a Hanoi sports institute, red foam matting seamed with black tape, faded weight-class charts, practice lamps dimmed so the figures read as silhouettes with rimmed shoulders. Six adults each claim a square of mat, planted and fully in frame from the first instant to the end. A barrel-chested Bulgarian man drives a boxer-skip; a lean Ecuadorian woman rises into rapid criss-crosses; a shaven-headed Korean man swings the rope sideways then drops back into a double bounce; a tattooed Swiss woman, a rangy Tanzanian man and a silver-haired Uzbek woman hammer heel-taps until the cables hiss. Air in the room is dead still, dust hanging. The camera sits locked on a tripod at eye level for one continuous shot.

An old rail viaduct in Hanoi has been rebuilt into an elevated linear park: tapered concrete planks underfoot, wild grasses in trough planters, steam curling up from street vents below and drifting between the balustrades under flat overcast light. Four adults use one clear stretch: a broad Vietnamese man in a faded grey tee, a tall Kenyan woman in olive, a compact Vietnamese woman in yellow, a bearded white man in navy. They chain cartwheels into round-offs, rebounding upright, walking back two paces and going again within a few meters. Plain, gritty, documentary-flat colour. One continuous shot, the camera orbiting slowly; all four start fully framed on the planks, then the bearded man rounds off toward the lens and ends half out of frame.

Under a Hanoi ring road, a pedestrian underpass runs tiled and empty: cream wall tiles, a dead ticket kiosk, orange tungsten work lamps clamped to the ceiling throwing long warm streaks down the concrete. One adult stands centre-tunnel, a rangy Colombian man in his late twenties, black vest, taped wrists, wide grey trousers. Feet on the tiles and fully framed from the opening instant, he hammers a repeating jab-and-swing combination, drops onto one knee for a low hit, then explodes upright and stamps the floor hard enough to shake dust. Loose paper scraps tumble past him on a draught. The handheld camera circles slowly at chest height, one continuous shot, and he never leaves the frame.

Inside a commercial glasshouse outside Hanoi, benches of orchids stretch away under bright even ceiling lamps; misting pipes hang dry and a wide concrete aisle runs arrow-straight between them. Four adults dance there, nobody else in the building. A tall Senegalese man in a white shirt leads a slender Vietnamese woman in a red wrap dress through a double-turn cross-body pass into a cuddle wrap; beside them a silver-haired Spanish woman and a stocky Brazilian man trade fast right turns and a low dip. All four begin fully framed with feet on the concrete. The air is still. One continuous shot: the camera cranes down from above the glazing bars to eye level, and one dancer spins close, shoulder leaving frame.

Light rain has left the painted concrete of a parking garage roof deck in Hanoi glossy and gleaming with lamp glow, fog banks rolling across the low parapet and blurring the tower blocks beyond. Four adults race the deck upside down: a lean Vietnamese man in yellow, a powerful Colombian woman in white, a tall Indian man in navy, a compact Vietnamese woman in pink. All four stand upright on the wet concrete, then kick to handstands and walk on their palms the length of the bay, bouncing forward in handstand hops before dropping and running the return leg on their hands. Playful, bright, joyful. One continuous shot with a handheld camera circling slowly at chest height; all four stay fully in frame.

Misty sunrise softens a cobbled old-quarter square in Hanoi, shuttered arcades on three sides, an iron water pump in the middle, and stray snowflakes drifting through the low sun beams. Two dancers work one spot of rounded cobblestones: a broad-shouldered Vietnamese man in braces and rolled sleeves, and a wiry Australian woman in a swinging blue skirt and flat shoes. He swings her out, she springs, and she flies over his hip in a lindy hop aerial, landing clean on the beat before they whip straight into another. Early risers watch from a raised arcade step behind railings, off the cobbles. Bright, punchy, energetic. One continuous shot, camera orbiting slowly; both stay fully framed with feet down between throws.

A refrigerated dock bay behind a Hanoi market: hanging plastic curtain strips sway at the doorway, stacked blue fish crates drip, a dock leveller tilts toward the empty bay. Cold vapour rolls from ceiling vents and one bank of floodlights rakes across the sealed concrete from the left, leaving the rest dark. Four adults train here alone. A muscular Croatian woman drives a jab-cross-hook combination into mitts held by a grey-templed Kenyan man; two metres away a Malaysian man in his twenties snaps doubled jabs while a tattooed Dutch woman feeds him. All four start fully framed, feet on concrete. One continuous shot tracking sideways at walking pace; the Croatian woman advances until her arm passes out of frame.

Rain has left the mown grass of a balloon launch field outside Hanoi soaked and glass-bright, folded envelopes lying in slack heaps, wicker baskets tipped on their sides, floodlight glare pooling in the wet. Nothing else stirs. Three dancers take a small patch: a stocky Vietnamese man in a dark maroon shirt, a tall Punjabi woman in an emerald kurta, a lean older Black man in cream. Arms lifted overhead, they hammer high hops, drop into squat kicks that fling spray, and shrug their shoulders in tight rhythm, ranging only a couple of meters. Moody neo-noir: low key, deep greens, hard highlights. One continuous shot with a slow dolly-in toward them; all three stay fully in frame, feet on grass.

Heavy snow falls across a high chalk downland north of Hanoi's hill country, short springy turf whitening between exposed chalk scars, a lone weathered stone marker and a fence of leaning posts running to the ridge. One adult trains there, a broad Maori man in his thirties, black thermal top, taped fingers, wet canvas shoes. Fully framed with both feet on the turf from the first moment, he sprints four strides at a low chalk block, plants both palms, tucks his knees through in a single explosive punch, lands clean and rolls out. Snow and stray paper scraps tumble together in the wind. The camera dollies slowly in toward him; he stays entirely within frame. One continuous shot.

Blue hour settles on a granite dome above a Hanoi valley, the rock split by rain-worn channels, a toppled survey cairn at the lip, a bent basketball hoop bolted to a steel post. Four adults own the slab: a rangy Ivorian man in a black tank, a compact Vietnamese woman with a shaved undercut, a heavyset Serbian man in grey, a tall Chilean woman in orange. Balls slam on stone as they trade an in-and-out fake into a behind-the-back change of hand, a stutter step killed by a hard pull-back, a low double pound. From the opening frame all four stay fully in frame, feet on granite. Distant headlight trails streak the valley road. One continuous shot tracking sideways at a walking pace.

Midday sun hammers a drained paddy outside Hanoi, karst hills stacked hazily behind it. The floor is cracked dry mud studded with stubble; a bamboo drying frame leans at the far bund and a lime-dusted line has been scratched across the flat. One adult crouches into blocks improvised from two planks: a lean Jamaican woman in her thirties, cropped bleached hair, navy singlet, chalk on her palms. She holds fully in frame, both feet down, shadow pooled tight beneath her. On an unseen signal she erupts, driving low through six punching strides, arms shearing the heavy air as she crosses the paddy, staying fully in frame. Nothing else moves. One continuous shot, the camera panning slowly left to right.

Warm tungsten work lamps light the grey concrete infield of a Hanoi velodrome, the steep timber track banking up on all sides, spare wheels leaning against a rail. The air is entirely still. Three performers cross the infield: a slender Vietnamese woman in violet, a tall Bulgarian man in white, a strong Nigerian woman in gold. Long ribbons on wands carve spirals and snaking waves as each runs the length of the concrete, launching split leaps and chaîné turns, ribbons trailing metres behind. A handful of spectators sit in the stands above the banking, none on the infield. Bright, punchy, sports-ad clarity. One continuous shot with a slow pan from left to right; all three stay fully framed, feet on concrete.

Neon work lamps flood the sawn white floor of a marble quarry outside Hanoi, cut blocks stacked in pale walls, wire-saw grooves ruling the stone, a shallow bed of grit at one end. The night is windless. One athlete runs it alone: a tall Vietnamese woman in her twenties, powerfully built, hair coiled, in a silver crop top and black briefs. She accelerates twenty meters along the marble, hits the board with a slamming stride, hangs with knees driving forward, and lands deep in the grit, forearms flung back. Moody neo-noir: cold cyan light, hard shadows, breath visible. One continuous shot with the camera orbiting slowly around her; she starts fully framed with feet on marble and stays fully in frame.

Blue dusk fills a small brick-paved village square near Hanoi: red pavers laid in herringbone, an old banyan spreading over one corner, shuttered market stalls, and far off, headlight trails smearing along a raised road. Six adults cluster in one spot: two turners, a stocky Vietnamese man in grey and a tall Ivorian woman in white, swing two long ropes in opposing arcs while a lean Vietnamese woman in red, a bearded Iranian man in olive, a broad Mexican woman in yellow and a slight Korean man in blue take turns bouncing in, knees snapping high, criss-crossing feet, ducking out. Grainy, plain documentary look. One continuous shot, handheld camera circling slowly at chest height; all six stay fully in frame.

Thick fog drifts across a cricket ground on Hanoi's outskirts, swallowing the sightscreen and the low pavilion; the rolled dry clay strip stays crisp underfoot while everything beyond ten meters goes soft grey. Five adults play on the clay: a tall Vietnamese man in orange, a strong Dutch woman in white, a compact Vietnamese woman in navy, a lanky Nigerian man in green, a stocky Chilean woman in red. They rip a pepper drill in pairs and a rotating third — forearm bump, high set, controlled spike — shuffling a couple of meters and diving low for digs. Spectators line the boundary rail beyond, off the pitch. Light, grinning, commercial warmth. One continuous shot from a static tripod at eye level, everyone fully framed.

Snow sifts over a solar farm outside Hanoi, dusting rows of tilted panels that stretch to the horizon; between them runs a service strip of compacted red dirt where dry leaves skate and swirl low across the ground. One athlete uses it: a wiry Vietnamese man in his thirties, close-cropped hair, in a mud-flecked grey tracksuit and battered spikes. He builds a long run-up down the strip, stamps a takeoff, cycles his legs through the air and thumps down into loose dirt, sliding forward before he stands and trudges back. Rough, unpolished documentary texture, flat cold light. One continuous shot, camera tracking sideways at a steady walking pace; he stays fully in frame with feet on the dirt.

Vast shafts of daylight drop from clerestory glass into a disused foundry casting hall in Hanoi, striping a floor of packed black sand; ladle hooks hang from the roof trusses and cold moulds sit in rows. The air is dead calm, dust hanging in the beams. Two adults are lashed ankle to ankle by a strip of cloth: a tall Vietnamese woman in a mustard jumpsuit and a broad-shouldered Greek man in a grey tee. They lurch into a three-legged sprint, find a rhythm, gallop twenty meters across the hall, stumble, catch each other and charge on, laughing. Dreamy, golden, floating dust. One continuous shot with a handheld camera circling slowly at chest height; both stay fully framed.

A flat sheet of dark basalt pavement stretches under a hazy, dusty afternoon wind outside Hanoi, cooling cracks running like veins, a single tractor tire dumped in the middle and, far off, headlight trails smearing along a ridge road. Two adults work that tire: a heavily muscled Vietnamese man, shirtless with taped wrists, and a broad Brazilian woman in a black sports top and grey shorts. They alternate sledgehammer strikes with wooden handles, hips snapping, the rubber booming and shuddering, both rooted on the same square meter of rock, sweat cutting through dust. Deep-shadow noir grade, bronze skin against slate stone. One continuous shot with a handheld camera circling slowly at chest height; both stay fully in frame.

Rain slicks the concrete paver blocks of a lane between container stacks in a Hanoi yard, sodium lamps smearing orange on the wet, fog rolling down the corridor and softening the boxes at the far end. One pitcher owns the lane: a tall Vietnamese woman in her thirties, athletic, dark ponytail, in a charcoal warm-up jacket and white pants. She winds up, lifts her knee high, strides long and fires a ball down the lane into a hanging net, then walks several meters back and repeats, working her way along the corridor. Noir palette: cold shadows, hard amber highlights. One continuous shot, a slow dolly-in toward her; she remains fully in frame with feet on the pavers.

Blue hour lies over a black volcanic sand beach on the coast east of Hanoi, a ragged driftwood line marking high tide, sharp basalt stacks standing offshore, the flat sand firm and windless. One player works it alone: a broad-shouldered Vietnamese man in his late twenties, in a white long-sleeve, navy shorts and cleats. He takes a five-step drop back across the sand, resets his feet, and rifles a long spiral downfield, then sprints to fetch another ball and drops back again, covering twenty meters of beach. Crisp, high-contrast sports-ad colour. One continuous shot from a static tripod at eye level; he starts fully framed with feet on sand, then jogs toward the lens and ends cropped at the thighs.

Heavy snow slants across an airport apron near Hanoi, settling on painted guidance lines, on parked baggage tugs and on the huge hangar doors behind; beyond the perimeter, surf pounds a nearby shore, white lines flashing in the gloom. Six dancers hold one lit patch of concrete: a stocky Vietnamese man in scarlet, a tall Punjabi woman in gold, a lean Ethiopian man in white, a broad Vietnamese woman in turquoise, a bearded white man in orange, a petite Thai woman in magenta. Arms overhead, they pound high hops, snap into squat kicks and shoulder shrugs, feet never leaving their small squares. Saturated, poster-clean sports colour. One continuous shot, a slow dolly-in toward them; all six stay fully framed.

Hard noon sun bleaches a seaside wooden promenade at a faded resort town south of Hanoi: weathered grey decking, a shuttered shelter, a rusted rail, and flat glassy water with no wind at all. Two throwers stand on one section of planking, a chalk-scuffed circle marked out. A heavy-set Vietnamese man in his forties, in a navy singlet, crouches low, glides backward and drives the iron ball out with a roar; a tall Latvian woman with cropped white-blonde hair, in a black training top, answers with the same glide, chest exploding upward, feet resettling in the same spot. Monumental scale, heroic stillness. One continuous shot with a slow pan from left to right; both stay fully framed on the decking.

Dust hangs gold over the loading yard of a Balinese rice-silo complex, where a rusted conveyor arm leans above stacked jute sacks and corrugated towers. Four adults hold one patch of dusty concrete slab: a broad-shouldered Javanese man in a teal tank top and a slim silver-haired white woman swing two long ropes, while a compact Black woman in orange shorts and a lanky South Asian man in white trade double-dutch entries, knees snapping, feet drumming inside a metre of ground. A flickering neon sign and a sweeping security searchlight cut the haze. One continuous shot, the camera tracking sideways at a steady walking pace, everyone fully framed.

Motionless fog sits chest-deep in a walled courtyard behind a shuttered Balinese seaside hotel, its arches chipped, its fountain dry, its floor a wide field of blue-and-ochre patterned ceramic tile that stays plainly visible underfoot. Six adults spar in three pairs across a few metres: a heavy Balinese man in red wraps slipping under jabs, a freckled redhead woman rolling her shoulders, a grey-bearded Black man countering, a tall Korean woman pivoting, a sinewy Sri Lankan woman in navy and a stocky Dutch man in cream. Cold shafts pick out breath. One continuous shot, a slow dolly-in; all six begin fully framed with feet on the tile, and near the end the redhead drives forward and her torso passes partly out of frame.

Storm light presses low over a Balinese crossroads plaza whose painted asphalt carries an enormous mural of waves, half-worn by traffic; sandbags line the kerb and palm crowns thrash beyond. One adult stands there — a wiry Filipino man in his thirties, shaved head, faded purple jersey, taped ankles — pounding a basketball through crossovers, between-the-legs pull-backs and a hard stutter that shifts him two metres and back. Bystanders watch from behind the plaza railings only. A failing neon shopfront stutters pink while a searchlight rakes the underside of the clouds. One continuous shot, handheld, slowly circling at chest height; he stays fully in frame throughout, feet always on the paint.

Blue hour settles on a terraced olive trial grove planted high above Balinese rice valleys, gnarled trunks in rows, a crumbling stone wall at the edge, lanterns unlit. Frangipani petals swirl low across the dusty pale earth, where four adults hold a single small square of ground. A stocky Māori man in braces whips a lithe Chinese woman in a yellow swing dress over his hip; she flips clean and lands. Beside them a tall Ethiopian woman in green and a grey-templed white man in a striped shirt trade their own aerial, catching, landing, resetting on the spot. All four stay fully in frame, feet returning to the earth between throws, in one continuous shot with a slow dolly-out revealing more of the terraces.

Work floodlights on tripods bleach a clearing cut into Balinese teak forest, where a felled trunk, a battered blue water drum and coils of hose sit at the margins; the packed earth and leaf litter underfoot reads clearly in the glare. Six adults form a swaying line only a few metres long — a burly Sundanese man scooping, a silver-cropped white woman pivoting, a young Nigerian man lunging, a Vietnamese woman in a soaked vest, a broad Fijian woman and a rangy Egyptian man in mud-streaked shirts — hurling full pails hand to hand, water arcing and slapping down. The air is otherwise dead still. One continuous shot, a slow dolly-in; all six stay fully framed with boots on the leaf litter.

Behind the coastal dunes of eastern Bali stretches a wide interdune flat of firm red sand, ringed by scrub-crested ridges and a line of leaning bamboo marker poles. Six adults are strung across it in three exchange zones — a long-legged Kenyan woman, a broad Balinese man in blue, a pale Australian woman with a blonde plait, a Brazilian man in yellow, a Japanese man in white, a tall Somali woman — sprinting flat out and slapping batons into upturned palms, spikes ripping shallow trenches as they cross the frame. Hazy afternoon light softens the distance; the air itself is calm. One continuous shot, a slow dolly-out; all six begin fully framed with spikes on the sand and stay in frame as they run.

Inside a Balinese gymnastics hall the practice lights sit low and moody, deep shadows pooling between chalk bins and stacked folded mats; the sprung carpet floor glows dull blue. Four adults share a few metres of it: a rangy Dutch man in grey shorts snaps a flying disc sidearm, a muscular Indonesian woman in maroon lays out horizontal to catch it, a bearded Iranian man dives to defend, and a short Black woman with locs skims the surface for the trailing throw. Spectators stay up on the bleachers behind the rail. A faulty neon strip flickers, a searchlight sweeps the high windows. All four start upright on the carpet and stay fully framed in one continuous shot from a static tripod at eye level.

Night floodlights blaze across a whitewashed cement rooftop terrace in a Balinese market town, trays of split red chilies drying to the parapet, black water tanks and bent aerials behind. Papery chili husks lift and drift through the beams like snowflakes. Four adults work a single square of the cement: a powerful Samoan man in a white singlet launches a petite Indian woman in a red skirt into a swing-out aerial, catching her clean, while a freckled Irish man and a broad-hipped Colombian woman mirror the flip beside them, resetting instantly. Nobody else is up here. One continuous shot from a static tripod at eye level, all four framed throughout.

Golden hour rakes a broad shelf of smooth red sandstone above a Balinese river gorge, its surface pocked with wind-scoured rain pans, a lone pandan clinging at the lip. Air and dust hang perfectly still. One adult crosses it — a lean, sun-weathered Aboriginal Australian man in his late thirties, cropped grey-flecked hair, dust-grey shorts, bare chest sheened with sweat — bursting from a crouch into a long sprint, breaking into galloping bounds, two five-metre ribbons of ochre cloth knotted at his wrists snapping out behind him as he covers thirty metres of rock. One continuous shot, a slow dolly-in that keeps him whole in frame.

Soft overcast light flattens a Balinese sawmill yard: stacked teak logs, a rust-streaked tin roof, torn blue tarps and pennants whipping hard in a strong onshore wind. Sawdust-covered dirt runs level between two piles. Two adults race there across a few metres — a thickset Balinese man in his fifties, sleeves cut off, forearms pale with dust, and a tall Ukrainian woman with a blonde bun and taped gloves — driving flat shovels in and flinging long arcs of sawdust sideways into their bins, stepping, scooping, heaving again as the loose fabric cracks overhead. Nobody else is present. One continuous shot, a slow pan from left to right; both stay fully in frame, boots planted on the sawdust.

An emptied exhibition hall on the Balinese convention circuit stretches long and bright under even overhead lighting, grey commercial carpet marked with taped booth outlines, bare truss and coiled cable drums at the far wall, air conditioning holding everything still. Three adults line up shoulder to shoulder on the carpet: a heavily built Tongan man in a black compression top, a short sinewy Mexican woman in lime, and a long-striding Danish man with sandy hair. They explode forward together and race forty metres to a strip of tape, arms pumping, chests thrown. No one else occupies the hall. One continuous shot, handheld, slowly circling at chest height; all three start fully framed, feet on the carpet, and stay in frame.

Harsh floodlights strike from one side of a curling sheet in a Balinese leisure-rink annexe, throwing hard shadows over pebbled ice, faded house rings and scuffed white boards. Five adults hold their own small patches of ice, each in bulky pads: a barrel-chested Croatian man, a compact Thai woman, a tall Black man with a shaved head, a freckled Canadian woman, and a wiry Balinese man. On a shouted count they drop into butterfly slides, flare their pads at low shots, snap gloves shut and rise, over and over on the spot. Onlookers stay in the tiered gallery beyond the boards. One continuous shot, a slow pan left to right; all five stay fully in frame, feet on the ice.

Rain streaks slant across a Balinese school tennis court, splashing shallow puddles on the acrylic-coated concrete beside a sagging net and a mossy chain-link fence; hazy afternoon light glows behind the squall. Three adults in soaked kit — a tall Balinese man in white with a snare slung high, a broad Black woman in gold braid, and a bespectacled Chinese man with drumsticks flashing — hammer a rolling cadence, marching four steps forward, snapping a crisp pivot turn, backing up, spinning again inside the service boxes. Water leaps at every heel plant. Nobody else is on the court. One continuous shot, a slow dolly-in; all three stay fully in frame, boots on the wet acrylic.

Midday sun burns white on a Balinese tidal flat drained to the reef line, rippled wet sand running out for hundreds of metres past a stranded outrigger hull and a row of bamboo fish stakes. Fog banks roll in off the water and shred around them. Six adults — a stocky Balinese fisherman in cut-offs, a tattooed white woman, a young Kenyan man, a broad Peruvian woman, a grey-haired Japanese man, a lanky Turkish woman — take short run-ups and hurl themselves headfirst into flat belly-slides, skidding metres through the film of water, scrambling up soaked and grinning. One continuous shot, a slow dolly-out; all six stay framed.

Thick fog fills a working bench of a limestone quarry in the Balinese hills, softening the sawn walls, the idle crusher and the pale drill holes into ghosts. Compacted rock aggregate spreads flat and grey below. Two adults ferry water along it, twenty metres and back, in a two-person brigade: a tall Balinese woman in her forties, headscarf soaked, arms corded, swings brimming pails to a stocky ginger-bearded man in a torn olive shirt, who runs them down the bench, dumps them into a drum, and sprints the empties back. Nothing else stirs in the still air. One continuous shot, a slow pan from left to right; both stay fully in frame, boots on the aggregate.

Shafts of daylight fall through high clerestory windows of a Balinese indoor athletics shed, striping a blue polyurethane track; steam drifts steadily from floor vents and glows where the light cuts it. One adult occupies a few metres of lane: a broad-chested Brazilian man in his late twenties, dark curls tied back, black shirt, orange boots, rolling a football through fast step-overs, chopping it behind his standing leg, exploding two metres left, then cutting hard back right. Spectators remain up in the shadowed stands beyond the barrier. Epic, cool-toned quiet. One continuous shot from a static tripod at eye level, the man fully in frame.

Colored stage lights and cold neon tubes wash a disused Balinese airfield hangar, catching a half-draped fuselage, rolling tool chests and painted grey concrete that runs unbroken across the floor. The air is dead still. All four stand on the concrete, then race the length of it: a huge Fijian man in a magenta singlet with a slim Korean woman shouldered across his back, and a broad-backed Polish woman in blue hauling a compact Sudanese man, both carriers driving thirty metres, dropping their partners cleanly, swapping roles and powering back. Nobody else is inside. One continuous shot with the camera tracking sideways at a steady walking pace, keeping all four fully framed.

Blue hour leaves an abandoned coastal runway in Bali glowing faintly, grooved asphalt cracked and threaded with grass, tilted approach lights leaning toward a flat grey sea. Everything is windless. Four adults launch down the centreline: a rangy Somali woman in silver, a tanned Italian man with a greying ponytail, a strong Balinese woman in violet, and a young Black man in white, each trailing five-metre gauze streamers from their wrists as they sprint, break into galloping leaps, and sweep across the whole width of the frame. No one else is out here. One continuous shot, a slow pan from left to right; all four begin fully framed with feet on the asphalt and stay in frame.

Hazy afternoon light hangs still and warm over the pale limestone forecourt of a Balinese art museum, a sculpted fountain standing dry, a carved stone gate behind, dust motes suspended rather than blowing. Two adults work a few metres of the flat apron: a tall Ghanaian woman in a saffron tunic and a lean Japanese man in charcoal, each whipping a silk guard flag through fast spins, drop-turns and shoulder rolls before launching high double tosses that hang against the sky and drop back into their hands. Visitors watch only from behind the rope line at the gate. One continuous shot, handheld, slowly circling at chest height; both stay fully in frame, feet on the limestone.

Golden hour floods a cliff-top asphalt basketball court in south Bali, its painted black surface faded to charcoal, one hoop bent, torn plain banners and loose netting snapping on the fence in a hard sea wind. Two adults attack the same key: a heavyset Balinese man in a sleeveless grey shirt driving baseline for a reverse layup, and a tall Black woman with a braided crown in navy answering with a stutter, a long euro-step and a soft finish, both resetting inside a few metres. Watchers cluster outside the fence on the grass verge. One continuous shot, handheld, slowly circling at chest height; both stay fully in frame, feet on the asphalt.

Neon spill from a strip of signage beyond the outfield tints a Balinese ballpark magenta and green, the raked red dirt of the infield freshly combed, chalk lines crisp, a rust-flecked chain-link backstop rising behind. The night is windless. One adult holds the dirt beside second base: a compact Filipina woman in her early thirties, hair scraped into a knot, black training top, bare feet — snapping spinning hook kicks past an imaginary head, landing balanced, then whipping back kicks with a sharp exhale, never leaving her metre of ground. Spectators sit up in the bleachers behind the fence. One continuous shot, a slow dolly-out.

Light rain glosses a red painted tarmac cycle expressway outside a Balinese new town, concrete barriers on both sides, an overpass dripping overhead, palm silhouettes beyond; the wet lane mirrors the sodium glow. One adult owns it: a broad-shouldered Cuban man in his forties, close-cropped grey hair, black sleeves pushed up, glove on his left hand. He sets, lifts his knee, drives through a full pitching windup and fires down the lane, then crow-hops fifteen metres after each throw, working steadily toward the lens. One continuous shot, a slow orbit; by the end he has closed on the camera and his shoulders pass out of frame.

Bruised storm cloud stacks over coastal salt pans in north Bali, bunded squares of crusted white salt flat stretching to a thatched drying hut and a row of weathered wooden rakes. Dry leaves and torn blossom skitter low across the crust ahead of the rain. One adult drives through the frame: a heavily muscled Māori woman in her thirties, hair whipped loose, black harness biting across her shoulders, towing a weighted sled twenty-five metres in a deep forward lean, short savage steps, then turning and hauling it back. The scene is otherwise empty. One continuous shot, a slow pan from left to right, dreamlike and desaturated.

Blue hour drains color from a highland apple orchard above a Balinese crater lake, clipped rows of trees, leaning ladders, mist pooling between trunks; the clover and grass floor lies flat and dark, the air unmoving. Five adults work a tight few metres in noir shadow: a huge Balinese man in a black vest hoists a fifty-kilo grain sack and heaves it chest-high to a broad Russian woman, who pivots and passes it on to a wiry Nigerian man, a stocky Vietnamese woman and a grey-stubbled Greek man, each catching, absorbing, throwing again. No one else is among the trees. One continuous shot, a static tripod at eye level.

Dusk holds a Balinese artificial turf pitch in deep blue, green synthetic fibres almost black, a sagging goal net at one end, unlit floodlight masts and bamboo scaffolding rising against the last light. Nothing moves in the air. One adult attacks a short shuttle on the turf: a powerfully built Egyptian man in his late twenties, shaved head, grey compression top, hands and toes only, ripping a fast bear crawl five metres to a cone, slapping it, reversing without standing, hips low, breath tearing. Spectators stay behind the perimeter rail. Epic, cold, cinematic. One continuous shot, a slow dolly-in, the man entirely in frame.

Rain sweeps a chalky gravel path cutting through highland lavender trial rows in Bali, splashing puddles between drying racks and snapping plastic sheeting, hazy afternoon light glowing behind the shower. Three adults hold their own circles on the gravel: a hulking Serbian man in a soaked red singlet, a broad Balinese woman with taped fingers, and a lean Black man in blue. Each winds back, sweeps into a full spinning turn on the ball of one foot and rips a discus away low and flat, arms following through, feet resettling on the same spot. Nobody else is here. One continuous shot, the camera craning down from high above to eye level.

Fog rolls in slabs across a Balinese upland smallholding, swallowing the sunflower rows so only the nearest heads show, their stalks black. A bare strip of cracked soil runs along the field edge, a coil of irrigation hose and a leaning wooden stake marking its start. Two adults stand there at the beginning, fully framed, feet in the dust: a sinewy Ethiopian man in faded grey sweats and a broad-shouldered Danish woman in a black long-sleeve. They take turns pounding out long alternate-leg bounds down the strip, each landing punched into a driving single-leg hop and a final stretched stride. The camera dollies back through the murk, one continuous shot; the woman finally surges close and half exits frame.

A low slate storm ceiling presses down on a Balinese brickworks yard floored with fired clay tiles, stacks of green bricks under sacking, a squat kiln chimney trailing thin smoke. The air is utterly still, waiting. One adult moves through a few square metres: a lean Balinese man in his thirties, hair loose to his shoulders, black trousers, no shirt, spinning weighted sock poi in fast three-beat weaves, threading them behind his back, dropping into a turn as the cords hiss past his ribs. Shadowless grey light, deep noir contrast, nobody else in the yard. One continuous shot, a slow pan from left to right.

Harsh floodlights blast in from one side of a Balinese road tunnel closed for works, throwing the three figures' shadows fifty metres along asphalt still tinged orange by sodium lamps; cable trays and stacked cones line the walls. The air is dead calm. Three adults shoulder a heavy teak log — a barrel-chested Samoan man at the front, a tall Norwegian woman in the middle, a wiry Balinese man at the rear — jogging it steadily down the tunnel, calling a rhythm, then dropping it in unison with a crack, reshouldering and pressing on. Nobody else is inside. One continuous shot, a slow dolly-in.

Depot floodlights turn a Balinese rail freight platform into a hard-edged stage: weathered concrete, stacked containers, half-open roller doors and a cargo scale hanging dead motionless on its chain. The night air is still. Five adults hit a tight formation across a few metres — a slender Korean man in white leather, a curvy Balinese woman in chrome, a tall Black woman with a high ponytail, a compact Chilean man in black, and a broad Indian woman in cobalt — snapping into synchronized point-and-freeze choreography, arms slicing on the beat, chests popping, dropping to knees and rebounding as one. Nobody else appears. One continuous shot from a static tripod at eye level.

Blue hour on a sleepy Balinese branch-line platform: yellow tactile studs edging the concrete, a corrugated awning on iron posts, a hand-cranked signal lever rusted upright, rails vanishing into palms. Two adults volley a ball back and forth. A grinning Chilean woman with a high ponytail and a coral tank digs low with locked forearms, floats a clean set to herself, and drives a controlled down-ball across four metres; a broad Ghanaian man in a yellow vest platforms it back, pops it high, and swings again. Sand skims across the platform in the offshore breeze, catching the last light. Both stay on the concrete and fully in frame the whole time, as the camera orbits them slowly in one continuous shot.

Portable floodlights glare on a freak snow crust capping the upper slope of a Balinese volcano, wind-packed and grey-white between black ash cones and bamboo guide poles; rain slants through the beams and pocks the crust into shallow splashing puddles. Three adults each claim a metre of it: a heavyset Balinese man in a soaked bomber jacket, a tanned German woman with cropped bleached hair, and a lean Black man in a hooded top. They toprock loose and cocky, then drop hands to the snow and rip six-step circles, sleet flying off their heels. Gritty, documentary, unlit by anything else. One continuous shot, a slow pan left to right.

Light rain lacquers the worn flagstone of a hillside monastery cloister in Bali until the carved columns and a dripping stone cistern double themselves in the wet. Six adults line up as three wheelbarrow pairs on the flat court: a broad Balinese man gripping the ankles of a sinewy Portuguese woman, a tall Nigerian woman holding a compact Japanese man's legs, and a red-haired Scottish man steering a strong Bolivian woman. On a shout they scramble a few metres across the stone, palms slapping, spray flying, then swap roles and scramble back. Robed onlookers stay under the arcade behind the columns. One continuous shot, a slow pan from left to right.

A soft overcast afternoon flattens the light on a coffee drying patio in the Balinese highlands, where raked beds of red cherries edge a swept smooth concrete slab and bamboo rakes lean on a shed; far off across the valley, festival fireworks burst silently above the ridge. Four adults claim their own small squares of concrete: a grinning Balinese man in a bright orange tee, a curvy Filipina woman in denim, a lanky Black man with a bucket hat, and a short white woman with a pink buzz cut. Each struts a bouncy toprock then drops into whirling six-step footwork. One continuous shot from a static tripod at eye level.

Daylight cuts in through open loading doors and a high clerestory of a Balinese proscenium theatre, laying hard shafts over a black painted plywood deck strewn with half-struck flats and coiled rope. Loose confetti from a past show tumbles through the beams. Five adults in keeper gloves work a few metres of deck: a tall Serbian man, a compact Balinese woman, a broad Black man with a shaved head, a lithe Chinese woman and a grey-bearded Argentine, each launching sideways to palm a low ball away, hitting the boards, rolling and snapping upright. The audience remains seated beyond the stage lip. One continuous shot, the camera tracking sideways at a walking pace.

A raised granite-gravel terrace in a Balinese hilltop park, hemmed by carved stone urns and a low balustrade, blue dusk still glowing behind the volcano ridge; work lights on tripods throw beams that catch drifting flakes of artificial snow. Five adults hold small, separate patches of crushed granite, each fully in frame and grounded from the first instant to the last. A wiry Filipino man swings a raiz that lands facing back; a shaved-headed Russian woman fires a touchdown hook kick; a broad Kenyan man scoots into a hyper turn; two more, a lean Peruvian woman and a tattooed Japanese man, punch a gainer and a jumping crescent. Gravel sprays underfoot. The camera dollies slowly out, one continuous shot.

Misty sunrise seeps grey-gold across the coal stockyard of a Balinese power station, black coal dust ground packed hard between a conveyor bridge, a parked dozer and a mountain of coal; torn paper scraps tumble and lift on eddies of air. Four adults move through a few metres of the dust in noir half-light: a tall Balinese woman with a wooden staff whipping figure-eights, a heavyset Black man rolling his staff across his shoulders, a wiry Iranian man in his fifties tossing his spinning into the mist, and a broad Polish woman catching hers behind her back. Nobody else appears. One continuous shot, a slow dolly-in.

Low practice bulbs leave a colonnaded arcade inside an old Balinese trade hall in deep shadow, the terrazzo floor glinting faintly between square columns and shuttered stalls; scraps of paper drift and turn in the dark air like slow confetti. One adult anchors a single spot on the terrazzo: a broad-backed Filipino man in his forties, hair sweat-flattened, black shorts, no shirt, driving heavy battle ropes into fast alternating waves that snake away down the arcade, then hauling both ends overhead and slamming them into the floor. Nobody else is inside. Moody noir contrast. One continuous shot, the camera tracking sideways at a steady walking pace.

Harsh floodlights rake in from one side of a decommissioned turbine hall in Bali, glancing off checker plate steel decking, swollen green turbine casings and a stalled gantry crane; loose paper scraps tumble slowly through the beams like drifting confetti. Two adults work a few metres of the deck: a heavily built Balinese woman in a sleeveless denim shirt hooks a straw bale and swings it up to a lean, grey-streaked Lebanese man in a dusty vest, who catches, pivots and heaves it onto a stack that grows past his head. Dreamlike, dust-glittered, nobody else present. One continuous shot, a slow pan from left to right.

Soft overcast light sits on a film studio backlot street in Bali, false shopfronts propped from behind, paper lanterns strung overhead, a prop handcart parked at the kerb; the painted asphalt pavement runs flat and clean. The air is completely still. One adult tears down it: a stocky Balinese man in his thirties, grinning, red suspenders over a white tee, hauling a fire hose off its reel at a full sprint, canvas snapping out behind him for thirty metres before he drops the nozzle and skids to a stop. One continuous shot, the camera tracking sideways at a walking pace; he finishes close, cropped at the knees.

Floodlight towers wash a disused drill square deep in red-dirt country, its faded white parade markings ghosting across flat grey asphalt, rusted flagpoles leaning above a wire fence. Two adults are alone here: a broad-shouldered Maori man in his forties wearing a mustard singlet, and a slim Korean woman in her late twenties in teal shorts, hair in a high knot. In one continuous shot the camera orbits them slowly while shredded paper scraps tumble weightlessly through the beams. Both start fully in frame, feet planted, then tear thirty metres in explosive bursts and snap into absolute stillness on command. On the final burst the man charges the lens and ends partly out of frame.

Golden light rakes a vast cracked salt pan, its white crust splitting into curling polygons that stretch toward a low ochre escarpment; a single rusted survey marker throws a long shadow. One adult stands there alone, a tall Somali-Australian woman in her thirties, lean and corded, wearing a rust-orange crop top and grey compression shorts, braids bound tight. The air is dead still, nothing moving but her. She sets her feet, coils low, whips through a full turning wind-up and launches a discus, then resets and repeats. One continuous shot, the camera orbiting slowly around her while the flat salt stays visible beneath her spiking feet, and she remains fully framed throughout.

Beneath a mining company's administration block, a cavernous parking undercroft runs off into darkness, painted bay stripes glossing across epoxy-coated concrete, squat pillars streaked with tyre rubber. Haze machine fog hangs thick, sliced by moving spotlights and by pale shafts of daylight dropping from clerestory slots high in the wall. Nobody else is down here. One adult, a stocky Brazilian man in his early thirties with a shaved head, a lime jersey and navy shorts, snaps a ball through fast step-overs, drags it back, then cuts hard three metres left and right. One continuous shot; the camera dollies slowly outward, revealing more of the bright floor, and he stays fully in frame.

Wind carries fine red dust through the inner courtyard of a three-storey mining-town apartment block, where interlocking concrete pavers form a tight grid around a corrugated water tank and a dying bottlebrush. A busted neon sign above the stairwell flickers pink while a sweeping searchlight from somewhere beyond the roofline crosses the walls. Two adults work the middle: a wiry Filipino man near forty in black shorts, and a tall red-haired woman in her twenties wearing a grey vest. They trade sharp jabs and hooks, slipping and rolling under each other's punches, drifting only a couple of metres. Residents watch from the upper balconies, never on the pavers. One continuous shot, camera slowly dollying out.

Mist hangs over the rooftop pool deck of a desert-highway hotel, first sun bleeding pale gold across light travertine tile still cool from the night; steam drifts lazily from roof vents and pools around ankles. Five adults occupy the deck and no one else does: a silver-haired Greek woman, a stocky Nigerian man in ochre, a slender Vietnamese dancer in lilac, a freckled man in olive, a broad Chilean woman in deep blue. Each holds one spot, spotting hard through clean pirouettes that spill into whipping fouetté sequences, arms slicing the vapour. One continuous shot with the camera orbiting slowly; all five stay fully framed, feet returning to the visible tile.

Light rain glazes the granite setts of an outback town's pedestrian mall, turning the stone into a dark mirror of shuttered awnings, a dead fountain and a corrugated verandah dripping steadily. The street is completely deserted. One adult, a compact Egyptian-Australian man in his late twenties with a beanie, cranberry windbreaker and black track pants, drops onto the wet stone. He grinds through continuous windmills, kicks up into airy flares, then balances a slow headspin before freezing on one elbow, never leaving his single small patch. Everything around him is calm and quiet. One continuous shot, the camera dollying slowly out to reveal the empty mall, keeping him fully in frame.

Night settles on the packed-dirt yard of a cattle station, where a hand-built shed carries a buzzing neon sign in cyan and magenta that stains the ground; a galvanised trough and a stack of drums sit at the edge, and steam curls from a vent pipe on the shed wall. One adult is present, a heavyset Samoan woman in her mid-thirties, hair scraped back, wearing a white tank and black leggings. She drops chest to dirt, snaps her feet in, and rockets into a full jump, clapping overhead, repeating fast without shifting off her single spot. One continuous shot, camera orbiting slowly, the flat dirt clearly visible beneath her.

Improbable snow falls thick over a red rubber tartan oval on the edge of an outback town, dusting lane numbers, a rusting tin grandstand and the dark gums beyond the fence, while torn paper scraps tumble on the wind with the flakes. Three adults own the track: a lanky Indian man in his twenties in a purple hoodie, a broad Polish woman near forty in yellow, and a silver-bearded man in charcoal grey. They chase one another the full length of the frame, cutting hard, skidding on the wet rubber, lunging for tags. Spectators huddle in the grandstand, never on the track. One continuous shot, camera locked on a static tripod at eye level.

Behind an outback abattoir, a cold-store warehouse breathes white air; frosted concrete stretches between iced pallet stacks and empty hanging racks, and low practice lamps carve deep shadows across the ribbed walls. The air is utterly still. Three adults stand alone in a pool of dim light: a compact Japanese woman in her thirties wearing burgundy, a tall Ethiopian man in his twenties in grey, and a pale, muscular man near forty in navy. Each swings, sits, and rips a standing back tuck, landing on the same frosted square, then repeats with tighter tucks. One continuous shot, the camera dollying slowly in while all three remain fully in frame.

Soft overcast light flattens a sea of powdery white gypsum, wind-carved ridges running to a half-buried fence line and one skeletal dead tree. Nothing stirs but two adults: a stocky Mexican man in his thirties in a faded red tee, and a tall blonde woman near fifty in a green singlet, both barefoot and chalky to the knees. They take three bounding steps, launch headfirst, and belly-flop into the soft flat, exploding powder, then scramble up laughing and dive again a few metres along. One continuous shot with the camera panning slowly left to right; near the end the man dives toward the lens and ends partly out of frame.

A corrugated-tin sports hall in an outback township holds a single green vinyl badminton court, its white lines fresh, ceiling fans idle under flat, bright, even overhead lighting; the air inside is completely still. One adult occupies the court, a lean Sri Lankan woman in her late twenties, hair braided, wearing a plum crop top and white shorts. She skips at blistering speed, snapping the rope into crossovers, then stacking double-unders and a burst of high-knee sprints without straying from one square metre of mat. Locals watch from bleacher rows behind the sideline, never stepping onto the court. One continuous shot, the camera orbiting her slowly, feet always visible on the vinyl.

Thick fog drifts along the crest roadway of an outback hydroelectric dam, swallowing the spillway gate housings and the guard rail so only white lane lines lead into grey; fine sand skims low across the concrete. Four adults are alone up here: a tall Sudanese man in cobalt, a compact Italian woman in white, a broad Korean man in orange, a lithe woman near forty in mint. They cross the frame on a long diagonal in soaring grand jetés, chaînés between leaps, chasing one another the length of the crest. One continuous shot, a handheld camera circling slowly at chest height; all four stay fully in frame with feet on the concrete.

Harsh midday sun hammers a straight canal quay in an outback irrigation town, cobble setts bleached, a rusted lock gate and a row of dead poplars throwing knife-edge shadows across the walkway. Improbable snowflakes drift through the hard beams, glinting before they vanish. Two adults are the only figures: a rangy Trinidadian man in his thirties in a black shirt, and a broad-jawed Turkish woman near forty in a slate coat, sleeves shoved up. She hunts him along the quay, both covering long ground, cutting off the stone, doubling back, lunging for the tag. One continuous shot, the camera panning slowly left to right, both fully in frame throughout.

Under a ghost mining town, a sealed subway platform survives intact: cracked tiled concrete, blank enamel signage boards, a dead escalator throat gaping in shadow. Low practice lamps leave most of it black, and loose paper scraps tumble down the tunnel on a draught. One adult works alone, a thickset Croatian man in his fifties, forearms roped, wearing a sweat-dark grey shirt and canvas trousers. He hooks small hay bales, swings them from his hips and hurls them up onto a stack that grows past his shoulder, stepping only a couple of metres between throws. One continuous shot from a static tripod at eye level, the tiled floor clearly visible beneath him.

Snow lies over a closed main street of a highway town, softening verandah shopfronts, a dead traffic signal and the painted crosswalk bars still legible on the asphalt. The air is calm, the fall settled, no one else anywhere on the strip. Three adults command it: a broad Argentine man near forty in a black jacket, a tall Kenyan woman in her twenties in scarlet, and a stocky Tongan man in navy. They drive a ball the length of the street, ripping step-overs, chopping sharp cuts past each other, spraying slush from the tarmac. One continuous shot, the camera dollying slowly in while all three stay fully framed.

A faded grand ballroom in a century-old outback hotel: honeyed parquet, a dust-furred chandelier, tall shuttered windows, and rigged stage lights throwing neon magenta and lime bars across the wood. Two adults hold the centre, a heavyset Mongolian man in his forties in a white gi jacket and a compact Afro-Brazilian woman in her thirties in blue. Gripping sleeve and lapel, she turns in tight, loads him across her hips and drills o-goshi again and again, both bodies slapping down and springing back up on the same small patch of parquet. Onlookers watch from the mezzanine balcony, never on the floor. One continuous shot with the camera orbiting slowly around them.

Blue hour settles over the forecourt of a remote railway station, dark basalt setts still holding the day's heat, an iron platform canopy and a stilted water tower cut flat against the deepening sky while distant headlights streak long light trails along the highway behind. Two adults face off on the stone: a lean Iranian man in his thirties in a white dobok, and a powerful Ghanaian woman near forty in black with a red belt. They pivot and unleash spinning hook kicks and back kicks at pads, holding one tight patch, exhaling sharply. Travellers watch from behind the platform railing. One continuous shot, the camera craning down from high above to eye level.

Heavy snow falls over cropped dry grass rolling to a sagging wire fence and a leaning windmill pump, the flakes settling in the tussocks; otherwise the plain is perfectly calm and utterly empty of anyone else. Three adults spread across it: a rangy Puerto Rican man in his twenties in a teal long-sleeve, a strong Danish woman near forty in cream, and a stocky Cree man in his thirties in brown. They break long routes across the frame, planting and cutting, hauling in over-the-shoulder catches at full stride. One continuous shot from a static tripod at eye level; on the last route the woman sprints straight at the camera and ends partly out of frame.

Night in the outback and a festival main stage stands empty of music: an aluminium deck rigged on scaffold, neon tubes glowing pink and cyan along the truss, red dust plain and dark scrub stretching beyond the barriers. Two adults anchor heavy ropes to the deck cleats. A powerful Maori woman in a black crop top and shorts drives lateral snakes that hiss across the metal, then hauls both arms into rainbow arcs; opposite her, a stocky Icelandic man with a blond beard throws grappler swings hip to hip and finishes by driving the ropes down in a whole-body slam. Both stay fully framed, boots planted on the deck throughout. The air is dead calm. One continuous shot, camera dollying slowly out.

Fog rolls thick along a gravel service road inside an outback refinery, blurring pipe racks, a flare stack's dull orange tip and rows of storage tanks into grey slabs; the air itself is otherwise motionless. Four adults march the road with no one else in sight: a wiry Vietnamese man in his twenties, a tall freckled woman near forty, a broad Māori man in his fifties, and a compact Colombian woman, all in plain navy work shirts with snare drums slung at the hip. They hammer tight rudiments, cover twenty metres of gravel, snap crisp pivot turns and drive back. One continuous shot, the camera dollying slowly in, all four fully framed.

Dusty afternoon wind combs a raked sand court beside an outback swimming lagoon, tugging faded shade sails and the slack net while steam curls from a pump-house vent at the court's edge. Four adults hold their own squares of sand: a stocky Fijian man in his thirties, a lean Portuguese woman in her twenties, a tall Ethiopian woman near forty, and a broad-chested man with a grey buzzcut. Each pivots and rips spinning hook and roundhouse kicks, heels blasting fans of sand into the sunlit haze, feet returning to the same footprints. Onlookers line the low fence beyond the sideline. One continuous shot, camera dollying slowly out.

Night on a remote coral-sand beach: a cluster of fishing shacks glows with tubes of neon green and violet, spilling colour across white sand, tinnies moored dark at the water's edge and a low dune line behind. The air hangs still. Four adults play alone on the flat sand — a wiry Malay man in his twenties, a tall Ukrainian woman near forty, a heavyset Islander man, a lean woman in her thirties with cropped bleached hair — running two or three steps before launching headfirst into full-length belly-flop dives, sand fanning up in the neon. One continuous shot, the camera craning down from high above to eye level; all four stay fully in frame.

Sunrise mist hangs pink over an outback scrap yard where crushed car bodies stack into rusting towers, a magnet crane sits idle and rain streaks down, splashing wide puddles across the oil-stained concrete lane. Five adults run it alone: a huge Tongan man in his thirties, a lean Scottish woman in her twenties, a broad Punjabi man near fifty, a tall Ivorian woman, and a stocky man with a red beard, all in mismatched training kit. Strung in a diagonal line, they sprint the length of the yard flicking a ball backwards hand to hand, boots hammering water. One continuous shot, camera panning slowly left to right, everyone fully framed.
