Inside a sandstone cathedral in a former gold town, worn flagstones run between empty pews toward a plain stone altar; steam drifts from a floor grate and thick shafts of daylight fall from the high windows, slicing the gloom into cold blue-grey blades. Two adults are the only souls: a tall Lebanese-Australian man in his forties in a dark shirt, and a stocky Norwegian woman in her thirties in charcoal, their inside ankles bound with a strip of cloth. They lurch into a three-legged sprint, find rhythm, stagger, catch each other, and hammer back the way they came across a few metres of stone. One continuous shot, the camera panning slowly left to right.

Dust-laden afternoon wind sweeps a sandstone-paved cathedral forecourt in an old outback town, hazing a dry fountain basin, three iron lamp posts and a shuttered almshouse wall; far off above the rooftops, fireworks bloom in silent bursts of gold and green. One adult holds the square alone: a solid Punjabi man in his forties, beard bound, in a deep indigo kurta and loose white trousers. Arms thrown overhead, he drives into springing bhangra hops, drops into squat kicks and pumps his shoulders, ranging only a couple of metres over the visible paving. One continuous shot, the camera orbiting slowly around him while he stays fully in frame.

A rink on a frozen salt lake in the outback interior: snow-dusted ice ringed by orange cones, a plywood goal frame, a ute parked on the shore. Fine rain glazes the surface until it shines. Four adults skate hard: a broad Inuk woman in a red jersey, a lean Portuguese man in navy, a tall Nigerian woman in grey, a grizzled Canadian man in black. They stride backward across the whole width of the frame, snapping mohawk turns and heel-to-heel pivots, chasing each other in looping passes. Wet confetti tumbles across the ice. All four begin fully framed with blades on the ice; late on, one sweeps past the lens and half leaves frame. One continuous shot, the camera dollying out.

Hazy, dusty wind blows across a wave-worn rock shelf beneath ochre cliffs, ankle-deep pools spread flat over the smooth stone around a rusted mooring ring and a spine of barnacled ledge. From a shack on the headland a broken neon sign flickers, and a searchlight sweeps out over the water and back across the shelf. Two adults splash there alone: a lean Japanese man in his twenties in board shorts, and a strong Māori woman in her thirties in a black rash vest. They stomp huge sheets of water at each other, kick low arcs, dodge and counter, ranging a few metres. One continuous shot, camera orbiting slowly.

Golden hour floods a beachfront promenade paved in black-and-white wave-pattern mosaic, running past a row of ragged palms and a shuttered kiosk while heavy surf breaks and hisses along the sand below, spray catching the light. One adult is out there alone: a lean Chilean woman in her thirties, hair in a tight bun, wearing a bronze leotard and grey shorts. She sprints the length of the promenade, snaps a round-off into a back handspring and rips a high back tuck, sticks it, then powers another pass the other way. One continuous shot, the camera dollying slowly out to reveal the whole promenade; she stays fully in frame.

Golden light lies flat across the painted concrete circle of a helipad crowning a small outback hospital, its faded white ring chalky, a limp windsock and two aerial masts standing against a gum-lined ridge. The evening is entirely still and no one else is up here. Three adults play: a broad Sri Lankan man in his forties in a grey tee, a compact Ukrainian woman in her twenties in coral, and a tall man with sun-bleached curls. Two hoist the third's ankles and drive her forward on hands across the pad, swapping roles and racing back. One continuous shot, handheld camera circling slowly at chest height; at the end one crawls past the lens, partly out of frame.

An idle vehicle assembly hall sits silent behind a mining town: epoxy-coated concrete marked with yellow walkway lines, a dead overhead conveyor, half-built chassis frames on trestles. Harsh floodlights blast in from one side, throwing long hard shadows; the air is motionless. Three adults, and only three, grip hands in a chain — a squat Greek man in his fifties in overalls, a tall Somali woman in her twenties in a grey tee, and a muscular man with a blond ponytail. They wind up and whip the chain around, the tail runner flung wide, boots skidding across the shining floor before they reset. One continuous shot, camera dollying slowly out.

Under a long glass canopy, an outback transit plaza glows: grey porcelain tile polished by foot traffic, concrete planters holding dusty palms, and low ticket boxes forming a spine down the middle. Floodlights blaze in hard from one side, laying stark shadows over the tiles; nothing else moves in the still air. Two adults train alone on the floor: a wiry Bangladeshi man in his twenties in a black hoodie, and a strong Croatian woman near forty in olive. Each sprints three steps, plants both palms and kongs cleanly over a low box, landing running, then circles back for another. Commuters watch from behind a railing. One continuous shot, camera panning slowly left to right.

At an inland shipbreaking yard, a beached freighter's weather deck runs long and flat, painted steel scabbed with rust around raised cargo hatches and a slab-sided deckhouse, while harsh midday sun bleaches everything and fog banks roll through, briefly swallowing the bow. One adult works the deck alone: a rangy Jamaican-Australian man in his thirties, shirtless in faded blue shorts, chalk on his hands. He pounds out a long run-up along the steel, hits his mark, drives up and lands hard, then paces back for another. One continuous shot, the camera craning down from high above to eye level; on his last approach he sprints past the lens and ends partly out of frame.

A tin-roofed roadhouse gym holds an octagon cage, its vinyl-covered mat scuffed pale, chain-link fence taut, ceiling vents leaking slow curls of steam under bright, flat, even overhead lighting. Two adults face each other on the mat: a tall Korean-Australian woman in her thirties in a navy keikogi, and a heavyset Belgian man near fifty with a grey topknot. Gripping wooden practice swords, they lunge, snap strikes to the head and wrist, slide back, and press forward again across a few metres. Spectators press against the railing outside the cage. One continuous shot, the camera dollying slowly in until the man steps toward the lens and ends partly out of frame.

An improbable ice rink fills a vast machinery shed on the edge of red country: white ice scored with painted lines, roller doors part-open so dusty shafts of daylight fall in hard columns, and drifts of paper confetti tumbling slowly through the beams from a rig above. Three adults hold the ice alone: a lean Estonian man in his twenties in black, a compact Indian-Australian woman near forty in maroon, and a broad woman with cropped white hair. Each anchors on one spot, winding into upright spins that pull tight into fast scratch spins, blades hissing. Locals watch from behind the boards. One continuous shot, camera orbiting slowly.

Late afternoon in the plaza outside an outback university library: herringbone brick, a steel sun sculpture, dusty haze softening the sandstone facade. The air is motionless. Five adults form a loose ring. A tall Sri Lankan woman in a lime windbreaker attacks with punch-and-drag steps; a heavyset Norwegian man snaps a shoulder rock into a jumping foot-stomp; a lanky Mexican man rips a hard chest hit; two more, a short-haired Korean woman and a bearded Egyptian man, clap the count and answer with shoulder-driven hits. All five begin fully framed on the brick. The camera cranes down to eye level in one continuous shot, and the Korean woman closes in until her arms crop out of frame.

A roller rink laid into a wheat-belt town's old picture theatre: glossy maple boards where the seating once bolted down, a dead mirror ball, sagging bunting, low practice lamps leaving the corners in deep shadow, and steam creeping from a vent along the skirting. One adult trains alone, a powerful Iranian-Australian woman in her thirties, hair tied back, in a black long-sleeve and grey shorts. She swings her arms, explodes into a standing broad jump, sticks the landing on the wood, immediately rebounds into another, chaining four bounds down a few metres of floor before turning and going again. One continuous shot, the camera panning slowly left to right, keeping her fully in frame.

Inside a small outback aquatic centre, non-slip ceramic tile surrounds a still pool, a lane-rope reel and stacked kickboards at the far end; haze machine fog thickens the air and moving spotlights swing through it while low practice lamps keep the rest in deep shadow. Three adults have the deck to themselves: a striking Spanish-Australian woman in her forties in a scarlet skirt, a lean Kurdish man in his twenties in black, and a broad woman with cropped grey hair in ivory. Each holds one spot, drumming rapid zapateado heel bursts on the tile while arms curl and snap overhead. One continuous shot, camera dollying slowly out.

Low golden sun rakes the pit lane of a desert race circuit, striped tarmac glowing between empty garage bays, a scaffold timing tower and a torn banner slapping in the warmth; steam bleeds from a vent beside the fuel bay, catching the light. Three adults work the lane alone on the tarmac: a rawboned Irish man in his forties, a solid Samoan woman in her thirties, and a tall man with close-cropped grey hair, all in dark drill uniforms. They sprint the lane hauling a fire hose off its reel, flaking it out long behind them, then drop the line and turn back. Spectators watch from behind the pit wall. One continuous shot, camera panning slowly left to right.

A cavernous sound stage in a desert studio complex: matte black floor stretching away, painted flats leaning against a cyclorama wall, and warm tungsten work lamps hanging low, pooling amber. The air is dead still and nobody else is inside. Five adults spread across the floor — a bright-eyed Filipina woman in her twenties, a heavyset Ghanaian man, a lithe man with a ginger beard, a tall Peruvian woman in her forties, a compact Korean man. They loft hoops high, spin them back along the floor, sprint after them and dive cleanly through as they roll, crossing the whole stage. One continuous shot, camera dollying slowly in; all five stay fully in frame.

Neon from a broken sign across the street flickers through the tall windows of an old outback courthouse, a searchlight sweeping past to shiver colour over squat sandstone columns and a brass rail, while daylight drops in thick shafts onto checkerboard marble. Alone in the great hall, a compact Argentine woman near forty — thick calves, faded grey tee, black shorts — sinks into a deep load. Bang: a standing broad jump lands her two squares up the marble, and she rebounds straight into two more bounds, walks the few metres back, and fires the chain again. One continuous shot, camera panning slowly left to right; she never leaves the frame.

Dawn mist hangs over a broad grey outwash fan south of Mexico City, where meltwater once spread fine gravel flat between two black lava ridges and thin steam creeps from fissure vents. Six adults stand spaced across that gravel, each anchored to a thick rope: a tall Mestizo man in a red singlet, a stocky Black woman in teal, a wiry older Asian man, a broad blonde woman, a lean Afro-Latino man, a muscular brown-skinned woman in grey. They hold their footprints, ripping alternating waves then double slams that spray grit. One continuous shot, the camera craning down from high above to eye level. All six stay fully framed.

Golden light rakes a neighbourhood skatepark in Mexico City, rain falling in bright threads while puddles blink across the smooth cast-concrete flat bottom; a paint-scarred quarterpipe and a bent handrail sit at the edges. Three adults claim the dry centre. A compact Mexican woman with box braids skips forward and throws a webster, one foot punching her over with no hands down; a bearded Lebanese man answers with a hands-free front walkover; a tall Swedish woman links a light run-up into a floating no-hand cartwheel that splashes on landing. All three begin fully framed, shoes on wet concrete, and none of them ever leaves frame. The camera glides slowly in toward them, one continuous shot.

Inside a cramped Tepito gym, a single ring fills the room: sagging taped ropes, a rust-spotted bucket in one corner, hand-painted training slogans faded past reading on the tarp walls. Warm tungsten work lamps clamp to the beams and burn amber on the worn canvas mat. Two adults work there and no one else: a heavyset Mexican man in navy shorts with a shaved head, and a rangy Black woman in a maroon rashguard, hair in tight cornrows. Gripping body locks, they drill throw after throw on one spot, dumping each other to canvas and scrambling straight back up. One continuous shot, static tripod at eye level, both fully framed, air still.

Rows of dead looms line a disused weaving hall in a Mexico City textile mill, their cast frames furred with lint, wooden plank flooring silvered by decades of thread dust. Tungsten work lamps swing low while industrial fans stir loose paper slips and glittering dust through the beams, giving everything a soft, dreaming haze. Six adults dance in three pairs: a tall Nigerian woman in copper satin, a slight Mexican man in braces, a silver-haired white woman in emerald, a broad Filipino man, a redheaded woman in plum, a bearded Mestizo man. They swing out and flip partners over their hips, travelling only a few meters. One continuous shot, handheld camera circling slowly at chest height.

Behind a Xochimilco nursery, a bamboo grove opens into a clearing of packed earth strewn with dry leaves, tarped seedbeds stacked along one wall of canes. The daylight is soft and overcast, and far beyond the bamboo tops, fiesta fireworks keep bursting in pale, smoky flowers. One adult works alone here: a broad-shouldered Mexican woman in her forties, grey tank top, forearms dusted, hair knotted with a bandana. She attacks a mound with a long shovel, driving the blade in and flinging fast arcs of soil sideways, shifting a step or two along the pile between digs. One continuous shot, a slow orbit around her, her boots always on the leafy ground.

An old parish school gym in Colonia Roma holds a maple court polished by generations of sneakers, faded painted keys, and radiators breathing steam that curls through the beams of warm tungsten work lamps hung from the rafters. On the wooden bleachers along the far wall, a dozen spectators sit watching, none of them stepping onto the boards. Two adults duel on the hardwood: a tall Mexican woman in white kit with a dark ponytail, and a stocky Korean man, sleeves rolled. Blades flick — she lunges long, he parries and ripostes, both advancing and retreating a few meters. One continuous shot, slow dolly-in, both fencers fully in frame throughout, feet on the maple.

Golden hour rakes low across a granite civic plaza outside a mid-century ministry building, its dry fountain basin littered with fallen jacaranda, a service grate exhaling slow steam that drifts gold through the pillars. Nobody else occupies the square. One adult stands on the polished pavers: a slender Afro-Mexican man in his thirties, black hair cropped, wearing a lilac shirt and loose grey trousers that catch the light. He locks into robotic pops, chest hits snapping on an unheard beat, arm waves rolling shoulder to fingertips, dime stops and neck isolations, his sneakers never leaving their single square meter of stone. One continuous shot from a static tripod at eye level; he stays fully framed.

A shuttered steel mill's rolling floor stretches into darkness — idle roller tables, a crane hook hanging still, steel plate underfoot streaked with old scale. Somebody has rigged neon tubes and colored stage lights along the gantry, so magenta and cyan pool across the metal while the air stays perfectly motionless. One adult performs alone: a lean white man in his late twenties, dark curls, black vest, silver-taped trousers. He whips a large hoop into a high toss, rolls it down his back, then dives clean through it as it spins, chasing it two or three meters and resetting. One continuous shot, camera panning slowly left to right, keeping him wholly in frame.

In an emptied San Rafael gallery hall, unhung frames lean against lime-washed walls, picture wire coils on a trestle, and pale oak planks run the length of the room. Shafts of daylight fall through tall windows, catching scraps of packing paper and confetti that tumble slowly through the air. Two adults labor there, nobody else: a broad Mexican man in his fifties, grey stubble and a rust-colored work shirt, and a tall Ethiopian woman in a blue tank top, sleeves of muscle. They heave a heavy sand-filled sack chest to chest, catching, absorbing, and firing it back, shuffling a couple of meters. One continuous shot, camera tracking sideways at a steady walking pace, both fully framed.

Thick fog fills the outer concourse plaza of a Mexico City stadium: shuttered ticket windows, a spiral vehicle ramp fading into white, banners hanging limp above stamped concrete. Distant fireworks thud and bloom, smearing orange through the murk. Six adults claim the empty plaza — a tall Mestizo man in black, a compact Japanese woman in yellow, a bald Black man in grey, a curvy white woman in crimson, a bearded Mexican man in olive, a tattooed Latina in white. Three crouch low while the others sprint and leapfrog over their backs, then swap roles, covering only a few meters. One continuous shot as the camera dollies slowly out, revealing more concrete; all six stay fully in frame.

Overcast light flattens a crushed red-brick clay court inside a walled Polanco club: ivy swallowing the chain fence, a peeling umpire chair, the net rolled and leaning. Behind that fence, a handful of members watch from a shaded terrace, never setting foot on the clay. Five adults play on it — a rangy Black man in a white tee, a short Mexican woman with cropped bleached hair, a middle-aged Indian man in navy, a pale woman with a red bandana, a heavyset Mestizo man. A disc skims flat; two of them lay out full-stretch, thumping into clay and rising in red dust. One continuous shot, camera craning from high down to eye level.

A close-mown grass tennis lawn sits behind clipped hedges at a lakeside Chapultepec club, its net rolled up beside a wooden roller, chalk lines faint on turf. Overcast daylight keeps colors clean while a low wind swirls leaves and petals across the grass. Nobody else is around. Six adults form a rope station: a stocky Mexican woman in bright orange, a tall Kenyan man in blue, a freckled white woman in mint, a lean Vietnamese man in yellow, a broad Black woman in fuchsia, a grey-haired man in white. Two pairs turn ropes; the other two jump fast double dutch, knees snapping, staying on one spot. One continuous shot, a slow dolly-in; everyone stays fully framed.

Harsh midday sun bleaches a broad concrete esplanade running beside a canal in the city's south, iron mooring rings set in the slabs, dusty palms lining the far bank, a viaduct crossing behind. Wind spins leaves and bougainvillea petals low across the concrete. Spectators lean on the railing above the water, all of them off the slab. Two adults do the work: a burly Samoan man in a cut-off orange shirt and a tall Mexican woman in black with a chalked shoulder. Shouldering a heavy timber together, they jog it clean across the frame, then drop it in one synchronized crash. One continuous shot, the camera craning down from high overhead to eye level.

Neon signage from surrounding Santa Fe glass towers washes pink and blue over a mown lawn quad at night, sprinkler heads glinting, a low concrete planter box serving as a loading platform. The air is dead calm and the campus is deserted. Five adults ring the stone: a huge Mexican man with a chalk-dusted beard, a tall Black woman in a grey singlet, a thick-set Turkish man, a blonde woman with taped forearms, and a wiry Afro-Latino man. One after another they lap a heavy atlas stone, drive the hips, and roll it onto the ledge, never shifting off their spot. One continuous shot, a slow orbit around the group, everyone fully in frame.

A cramped squash court in an aging Condesa club: white walls scuffed with years of ball marks, a red service line half worn away, pale hardwood dulled underfoot, tungsten work lamps behind wire cages throwing warm pools. The air is completely still and the glass back wall shows an empty corridor. One adult occupies the box — a compact Mexican woman in her thirties, tattooed forearms, black tank top, hair scraped into a bun. She spins weighted poi at speed: three-beat weaves, butterflies, turns under the arms, cords humming past her ears, her bare feet planted on a single square meter. One continuous shot, camera panning slowly left to right, keeping her whole body in frame.

Late afternoon wind drags dust across a stretch of short golden grass at the edge of a highland ranch, barbed-wire fence posts flying strips of faded ribbon and a torn tarp that snaps and flutters. No one else is out there. One adult occupies the field: a lean Mexican man in his twenties, sun-faded blue cap, white sleeves, dirt on his knees. He toes an improvised rubber, rocks into a full windup, and hurls hard down the grass, then jogs after each ball to repeat the throw further along. Filmed in one continuous shot with a handheld camera circling slowly at chest height; near the end he strides toward the lens until his shoulders pass out of frame.

Light rain glazes a packed gravel crossroads outside a highland village north of the capital — a leaning signpost stripped of its plate, a whitewashed cinder-block shrine, wet stones throwing back grey sky. The air is otherwise still, no wind, no traffic, nobody watching. Two adults rehearse on the gravel: a slim Mexican man in a black cropped jacket, bleached fringe stuck to his forehead, and a taller Chinese woman in a wine-red tracksuit. They snap through unison choreography — sharp points, body rolls, hard freezes, a synced spin — trading places within a couple of meters, water flicking off their sleeves. One continuous shot, handheld camera circling slowly at chest height, both fully framed.

Stripped steel racking runs down both sides of an empty distribution warehouse aisle in Vallejo, polished concrete shining under bright even overhead lighting, faded lane decals arrowing off toward loading doors. Torn packing slips and shreds of paper tumble through the aisle. Nobody staffs the building. Two adults face off there: a thickset Mexican man in a grey hoodie with a taped wrist, and a short Colombian woman in a black tee, hair in a tight bun. They fire rubber balls hard at each other, twisting away, ducking, diving flat onto the concrete and scrambling up, ranging a few meters. One continuous shot, a slow orbit around the pair; both stay fully in frame.

A ballet rehearsal studio above a Centro arcade has its cracked mirror hidden under grey cloth, barres pushed to the wall, black marley vinyl scuffed with rosin. A single bank of harsh floodlights burns from one side, and steam creeps in from a radiator vent, catching the beams. Six adults work in three tied pairs: a tall Mexican woman in maroon, a wiry Black man in grey, a stocky Korean woman in blue, a bearded white man in a torn tee, an Afro-Latina in yellow, a broad-shouldered older man in green. Ankles bound, they stagger and sprint the room's width, stumbling, laughing, correcting. One continuous shot, slow dolly-in, all six fully framed.

A disused civil-defence hall beneath Mexico City: bare damp concrete underfoot, blast doors hanging open, water beading on riveted columns. High slit windows throw hard pale shafts through the dark, dust hanging motionless in them. Two adults train alone. A heavyset Mexican man in a sleeveless grey sweatshirt grips the low handles of a plate-loaded sled and drives it four metres across the slab, calves shaking, breath fogging; a tall Ukrainian woman with a blonde braid and black leggings hauls it back hand-over-hand on a thick rope, then takes her own turn on the handles. Both stay planted on the concrete and fully in frame from first moment to last. One continuous shot, the camera orbiting slowly around them.

Above a Doctores market sits a small dojo floored in green tatami, brush-inked scrolls on the wall, a shoe rack by the sliding door, tungsten work lamps hanging on cords. A narrow raised gallery behind a wooden railing holds a few watchers, none of them on the mats, and the air hangs still. Two adults train below: a heavy Mexican man in a worn white gi and a lithe Brazilian woman with a dark braid in blue. Gripping sleeve and lapel, they drill hip throws in turns — load, lift, dump — then scramble on the tatami before resetting a meter or two away. One continuous shot, camera craning from high above down to eye level.

The ice is gone for the season, leaving a painted concrete slab inside scarred dasher boards, faded circles still showing under low practice lights that leave the empty seating in deep shadow. The air is dead still, the building otherwise deserted. Three adults own the slab: a bright-eyed Mexican woman in a pink bomber and white boots, a slim Thai man in a mint tracksuit, and a tall Black woman with box braids in electric blue. They hit unison choreography with sharp finger points, hip pops, head snaps and quick freezes, holding their spots on the concrete. One continuous shot from a static tripod at eye level, all three fully in frame the whole time.

Inside a municipal bus depot's parking hall, numbered bays stripe the asphalt, a fuel island stands unmanned, and tungsten work lamps on long cords throw warm cones down the empty rows. Nothing stirs; the buses are out on route. One adult plays there: a rangy Afro-Mexican man in his late twenties, sleeveless orange jersey, shorts, worn high-tops. He hammers the ball through crossovers, snaps it between the legs, drops a hesitation, spins back, and repeats down a couple of bays. Filmed in one continuous shot, the camera tracking sideways at a steady walking pace; in the final beats he drives straight at the lens and his upper body leaves the frame.

Fog sits thick on a vast surface parking lot behind a shuttered Iztapalapa appliance warehouse — faded asphalt, bent light poles, a stripped neon sign still flickering over the loading doors while a security searchlight sweeps slow arcs through the haze. Nobody else is out. Two adults fence across the tarmac: a tall Mexican woman in a white jacket, dark hair braided tight, and a broad-chested white man in his forties, grey at the temples, mask under one arm at the start. They advance, lunge deep, parry and riposte, driving each other the length of the lot and back. One continuous shot from a static tripod at eye level; both stay fully in frame, feet on asphalt.

Golden hour turns a fine grey ash plain below a smoking cone into a sea of warm dunes, dead pines standing skeletal at the rim, thin steam leaking from cracks in the ground and drifting sideways. No one else crosses this emptiness. Three adults play: a broad Mestizo man in a black tank top, ash to the knees; a wiry white woman in a mustard tee, hair loose; and a tall Sudanese man in grey. A disc floats out and they sprint, then lay out horizontally, catching and crashing into ash that erupts around them, ranging a few meters. One continuous shot, camera dollying slowly out to reveal more plain; all three stay fully framed.

Light rain sheens the striped natural grass of a big empty stadium at night, the stands black and vacant, flickering neon hoardings pulsing along the touchline while two searchlights sweep slow beams across the wet turf. One adult occupies the pitch: a tall Mexican woman in her thirties, wet dark hair slicked back, a charcoal leotard, calves shining. She carves huge spirals with a long ribbon, running it in figure-eights, throwing leap after leap, spinning through turns as she travels from one penalty area toward halfway. One continuous shot, camera panning slowly from left to right to follow her; she remains fully in frame, bare feet on grass.

A converted Guerrero garage now serves as a crossfit box: pull-up rigs bolted to brickwork, bumper plates stacked in colors, a half-open roller shutter, black rubber tiles across the floor. Neon strips and colored stage lights pulse magenta and lime while a searchlight beam flickers in through the shutter gap. Two adults train, nobody else present: a powerfully built Afro-Mexican woman in a lime crop top, and a lean Japanese man in black with taped fingers. They set into starting blocks, explode out on a shout, drive four hard strides across the tiles, then walk back and reset. One continuous shot from a static tripod at eye level, both fully in frame.

A drained dry dock floor lies wet under night: rows of keel blocks, steel ladders climbing the mossy walls, coiled hoses, neon dock signage staining the puddles green and red. Something like snow — flecks of ash and foam — drifts through the lamp beams. One adult is down there alone: a stocky Mexican man in his thirties, hooded sweatshirt cut at the sleeves, wet boots, a bucket of balls at his feet. He rocks into a full windup and fires hard along the dock floor, walking to fresh balls between throws. One continuous shot, the camera dollying slowly out; at the end he strides toward the lens and passes partly out of frame.

Rain falls over a wide grey-sand beach south of the capital, the packed damp sand glossy underfoot; a stranded fishing panga and a leaning net pole mark the spot. Air is still. Five adults form a ring and keep one ball alive: a wiry Mexican man in a soaked white tee digs it off his forearms; a tall Somali woman sets it high; a freckled Irish man swings a controlled roll shot across the circle; a stocky Korean woman digs again; a grey-haired Argentinian woman feathers an overhand pass back. All five start fully framed, barefoot on sand. The camera orbits them slowly, one continuous shot, and at the end one lunges toward the lens and leaves frame from the waist.

Fog drowns a vineyard on volcanic soil, hiding everything but two rows of gnarled vines strung on rusting wire and the compacted tractor lane between them, where rain streaks down and puddles jump. Nobody watches. Four adults perform in the mud: a striking Mexican trans woman in a soaked white slip, a tall Black man in a black mesh top, a compact Filipina in silver, and a lean bearded man in red. Arms cut hard lines, hands frame faces, then each whips into a spin and collapses backward into a death-drop dip, rising again on the same patch of earth. One continuous shot, camera dollying slowly out to reveal the rows; all four stay fully framed.

Between two bank towers, a sunken plaza of black granite holds a dry reflecting channel and a green-bronze relief wall, its steps far outside the frame and the flat stone floor bare. Overcast light softens everything while a low wind chases fallen leaves and petals across the granite. Four adults occupy it: a broad Mexican man in a gold sash-belted tunic, a small athletic Vietnamese woman in red, a tall Afro-Brazilian man in black, and a silver-haired Mestiza in white. Borrowing lion-dance mechanics without costume, they sink into deep crouches, then pounce forward in explosive paired leaps, landing low, prowling a few meters. One continuous shot from a static tripod at eye level.

Deep in a half-bored metro tunnel under Mexico City, sprayed shotcrete curves overhead, rebar mesh waiting on one wall, ventilation ducts running the length. Big fans push loose paper and grey dust drifting through a bank of floodlights raking from the left. Four adults mark a chalk board on the floor. A slim Colombian woman with a shaved head takes a five-stride run-in, drives one hop, stretches a long step and lands soft in a squat; a broad Tongan man repeats it with more power; two others, a bearded Iranian man and a tall Belgian woman, follow and scuff their marks. All four stay fully framed, shoes on shotcrete, throughout. One continuous shot, the camera easing slowly in toward them.

One continuous shot inside a cavernous barge-fabrication shed east of Mexico City, where a half-welded pontoon hull rests on timber blocks and a lime-green crane cab hangs idle overhead. Five adults stand together on the rust-stained steel plate floor, feet planted: a tall Black man in a tangerine tank top, a stocky Filipina woman in teal shorts, a lean white man in white joggers, a silver-haired Mexican woman in a magenta crop top, a broad South Asian man in cobalt blue. They launch a relay of round-offs into linked cartwheels, hands slapping steel, covering ten meters. Warm tungsten work lamps burn through haze-machine fog while spotlights sweep. The camera tracks sideways at a steady walking pace. All five stay fully framed throughout.

Long metallic pistes stripe the rubber floor of a fencing hall in an old sports institute, score reels dangling from stanchions, faded club banners hanging in the still, warm tungsten glow. Tonight the strips carry rows of small orange cones instead of blades, and nobody else is in the building. Six adults stand one per station: a broad Mexican man in a black jersey, a tall Nordic woman with a blonde plait, a wiry Afro-Cuban man, a stocky Japanese woman, a bearded older Mestizo, a tattooed white woman. Each stickhandles a ball fast through the cones, toe-drags and dekes, feet fixed on one spot. One continuous shot, camera tracking sideways at a steady walking pace.

An emptied barn on the city's rural edge has had its bales shoved to the walls, leaving wide plank flooring worn pale by boots. Bright even lamps hang from the tie beams, while through gaps in the siding a flickering roadside neon and a passing searchlight throw restless colored bars across the wood. Two adults face each other, alone: a rangy Mexican man in a black shirt with taped knuckles, and a broad-shouldered Ukrainian woman in a grey tee, hair braided. They rifle rubber balls hard, jackknife aside, and dive along the planks to escape, working within a few meters. One continuous shot, a slow dolly-in; both remain fully in frame.

Inside an abandoned brick factory hall, a collapsed kiln arch yawns at the far end, pallets of unfired blocks slump against a pillar, and the floor is a patchwork of broken brick tile. Tungsten work lamps on tripods pool amber into the dark; the air is utterly still. Three adults train, no one else: a heavily built Mexican man with a shaved head in black, a lean Somali woman in a grey long-sleeve, and a silver-bearded white man in a faded singlet. They load and fire standing broad jumps, sticking landings, then chain repeat bounds down the hall for a few meters. One continuous shot, camera panning slowly left to right, all three fully in frame.

Floodlights on a pole light an old flagstone threshing floor above a highland village, its low stone wall crowned with drying maize husks, dark hills beyond where fiesta fireworks burst in green and gold. No spectators; four adults stand upright and fully framed on the stones: a stocky Mexican man in a red tee, a tall Black woman in grey, a wiry Peruvian woman with a long braid, and a bearded white man in blue. Dropping onto hands and feet, they bear-crawl hard across the flagstones, hips low, palms slapping, racing shoulder to shoulder. One continuous shot, camera tracking sideways at walking pace; near the end one crawler angles at the lens and passes partly out of frame.

A flat mesa top of hardpan and sparse scrub runs to a sheer edge, distant ranges stacked beneath a bruised anvil of storm cloud that has not yet broken; the air is heavy and completely still. Five adults gather on the hardpan with two long ropes: a broad Mexican woman in a purple tank top, a lanky Ghanaian man in yellow, a short white woman with cropped grey hair, a muscular Mestizo man in black, and a slim Korean woman in orange. Two pairs turn, one jumps, feet drumming a single patch of dirt, then they swap turners. One continuous shot, handheld camera circling slowly at chest height, all five fully in frame.

A Condesa rooftop terrace of concrete pavers is edged with potted palms and squat black water tanks, the skyline of low apartment blocks and antenna forests fading into soft overcast light. On a neighboring roof, a few onlookers lean over their parapet, well off the terrace, and the air is entirely calm. Two adults rehearse here: a slender Mexican woman in a pale blue two-piece with a high ponytail, and an androgynous Black dancer in a cream oversized shirt and wide trousers. They land unison points, wrist flicks, and hard body freezes, mirroring each other and swapping sides within a couple of meters. One continuous shot, slow dolly-in; both stay fully in frame.

Light rain leaves a plain of tight-packed dark pebbles glossy and reflective, a rusted fence line running off toward a low volcanic cone, an empty stretch of desert with no wind at all. Three adults are out here alone with training sleds: a grinning Mexican man in a bright yellow tee, a powerful Black woman in navy with a taped shoulder, and a lean white man in a red cap. Heads down, they drive the loaded sleds in sprints clear across the flat, pebbles crunching, laughing between efforts. One continuous shot, the camera craning down from high overhead to eye level; at the end the yellow-shirted man pushes past the lens, partly out of frame.

Rain drums onto a vast cracked pale clay flat south of Dubai, where rusted survey stakes lean beside a sagging wire fence and a stranded cargo pallet darkens with water. One man in his thirties, wiry, South Asian, black curls plastered flat, wears a mustard kurta over grey track pants. He drives into bhangra high hops, knees snapping up, then drops to squat kicks with both arms punched overhead, shifting only a couple of metres as puddles explode around his heels. Soft overcast daylight flattens the colour; rain streaks slant through the frame. No one else is present. One continuous shot, the camera slowly orbiting him, his feet always on the clay and his whole body in frame.

Blue hour settles over a sealed overpass on the edge of Dubai, its lane markings freshly painted, orange cones stacked against the barrier, distant tower silhouettes stacked like teeth. Two women stand fully in frame at the near end: one tall and Black with braids coiled tight, in a teal singlet; the other stocky and Filipina, cropped bleached hair, red shorts. They set into three-point stances, explode together, and drive the full length of the asphalt toward a strip of tape stretched across the far lanes, arms hammering, finishing side by side. Air is dead calm, sky deepening indigo, nobody watching anywhere. One continuous shot from a static tripod at eye level, both runners in frame throughout.

Rain has just glazed the tar-and-gravel membrane of a converted warehouse roof in Dubai's old industrial belt; dented satellite dishes and a lopsided water tank crowd the parapet, and fine sand skitters low across the wet surface. One man, mid-twenties, Emirati, athletic and long-limbed, wears a lime training top and white shorts. He drops a ball, smashes a laced power shot into the parapet, meets the rebound on the half-volley, then leaps into a full scissor volley, landing hard and resetting within a few strides. Light rain leaves the roof mirror-bright with reflections. The rooftop is otherwise deserted. One continuous shot, the camera dollying slowly outward to reveal the surrounding rooftops, keeping him entirely in frame.

Golden light rakes a forgotten drive-in outside Dubai: rows of rusted speaker poles, a torn screen sagging on scaffolding, steam curling from a service vent behind the projection hut. Two adults face off on the cracked asphalt and gravel — a lean Japanese man in his forties, silver-streaked ponytail, white jacket, and a broad Brazilian woman in her twenties, copper braid, blue jacket. With sport foils they trade explosive lunges, parry-ripostes and fleches, chasing each other twenty metres down the lane, sneakers grinding grit. Spectators perch on a low bleacher behind the far railing, well off the lot. One continuous shot, the camera craning from high above down to eye level, both fencers fully framed.

Hazy afternoon wind pushes dust along a painted steel festival deck on a Dubai creekside pier, strung bulbs swinging above and dark dhow hulls moored beyond the edge. Neon panels flicker and a searchlight sweeps across the plates. Three adults work the deck: a tall Nigerian woman in an orange crop top, a stocky Korean man in navy, a freckled Australian man in white. One launches a deep pass; the other two burst downfield, cut hard on the steel, and pull in over-the-shoulder catches thirty metres away before flipping the ball back. No bystanders anywhere. One continuous shot, the camera tracking sideways at a steady walking pace, all three fully in frame with feet on the plate.

Soft overcast light lies over a terraced plantation walkway in the hills behind Dubai, trodden red earth between clipped green hedgerows, stacked wicker crates and a leaning irrigation pipe. Fine dust skims low across the path. One woman — mid-forties, Iranian, compact and muscular, black hair knotted, grey vest and maroon leggings — begins face-down on the earth, then snaps up on a clap, driving three hard strides before sinking back to a seated start and firing out again the other way, staying within a few metres. Nobody else appears on the terraces. One continuous shot, the camera craning down from high above to eye level, keeping her whole body in frame throughout.

Daylight falls in hard shafts through the tall windows of a Dubai hotel atrium, striking polished marble beneath a hanging glass sculpture and two brass palm trees. Haze machine fog pools at ankle height and a house spotlight drifts across it. Two adults hold the centre: a slim Thai man in his late twenties, bleached undercut, silver jacket; a tall Ethiopian woman in her thirties, high ponytail, lilac suit. They lock into razor-sharp unison choreography — synchronized point-and-freeze arms, chest isolations, quarter-turn pivots and a low drop — never leaving their single square metre of stone. The lobby is otherwise empty. One continuous shot, the camera tracking sideways at a steady walking pace, both dancers fully framed.

Late golden sun floods the packed sand floor of a quarry pit outside Dubai, where a silent conveyor rig, tall gravel cones and an idle loader ring the working level. The air is completely still. Three adults stand on their own marks: a heavyset Samoan man in a grey sleeveless top, a broad-shouldered Ukrainian woman with a blonde bun and black tights, a lean Sudanese man in faded red. Each in turn crouches, glides back across a single spot, whips the hips open and punches a steel shot out over the sand, then holds the reverse without stepping away. No spectators break the emptiness. One continuous shot from a static tripod at eye level, all three fully in frame.

Thick fog swallows a harvested field of straw stubble on Dubai's inland farm belt; a rusted baler and a skeletal wind pump loom half-visible, and dry leaves skitter low across the stalks. Two adults lean into a thick rope: a burly Turkish man in his fifties, grey beard, brown workshirt; a tall Jamaican woman in her thirties, shaved head, olive tank. They heave in alternating surges, heels furrowing the stubble, one dragged two metres before rooting and hauling back until both crash down and scramble upright, still gripping. Nobody else stands in the fog. One continuous shot, the camera dollying slowly outward to reveal the field's grey vastness, both figures fully in frame.

A storm sky presses low over a dry riverbed sand bar outside Dubai, bleached driftwood snagged against squat concrete bridge piers while dust ribbons run across the pale sand. Six adults train in three pairs: a stocky Mexican woman in yellow wraps, a rangy Somali man in black, a freckled Irish woman, a broad Chinese man, a silver-haired Greek man, a compact Vietnamese woman. Mitts crack as they fire jab-cross-hook combinations, pivoting and shuffling a few metres. All six stand fully framed with feet in the sand at the start; then the nearest pair advances and passes partly out of frame at the edge. One continuous shot, the camera dollying slowly inward.

Low practice lights carve deep shadows across the smooth plywood flat of an indoor Dubai skate park, quarter-pipes rising behind and a taped-off foam pit at the edge. Big fans stir loose flyers and dust into slow spirals. Two adults square off: a lanky Dutch man in his twenties, blond mop, purple hoodie; a muscular Colombian woman in her thirties, curls tied back, grey tee. Dodgeballs whip between them at full force; each twists away, ducks under a screamer, then dives flat and rolls back upright, ranging a few metres across the boards. The park is empty besides them. One continuous shot, the camera orbiting slowly around the pair, both fully in frame.

Light rain lacquers the reinforced concrete apron of a container quay in Dubai, gantry crane legs straddling the far end, coiled hawsers pooled by a bollard, and distant fireworks blooming silently over the water. Two adults work the wet slab: a tall Kenyan man in his thirties, close-shaved, orange long-sleeve; a broad-hipped Polish woman in her forties, ginger braid, navy top. She fires a long spiral; he sprints forty metres along the quay, plants a cut on the slick concrete, looks back over his shoulder and reels the ball in, then jogs it home. The quay is deserted. One continuous shot, the camera tracking sideways at a walking pace, both fully in frame.

Heavy snowfall blankets the compacted gravel median of a broad Dubai boulevard, settling on bare ornamental trees, cast-iron benches and a dry ornamental basin. The air itself is calm, flakes falling straight down. Four adults occupy the strip: a burly Argentinian man in a green thermal, a lean Indian woman in purple, a tall Norwegian man in white, a stocky Haitian woman in black. They alternate five-step drop-backs, sliding in the pocket and launching long spirals to receivers breaking twenty metres down the median, boots crunching gravel. Onlookers watch from behind railings on the far pavement. One continuous shot from a static tripod; after the opening the nearest thrower jogs toward the lens and leaves frame partly.

Light rain has left the mown turf of a small private airstrip outside Dubai glossy and dark, a limp windsock over a corrugated tin hangar and faded threshold markings bleeding into the grass. The air hangs motionless. Five adults drill in the wet: a squat Georgian man with cauliflower ears, a tall Brazilian woman with a black braid, a wiry Egyptian man in grey, a broad Canadian woman in maroon, a shaven-headed Nepali man. They shoot repeated double-leg takedowns, penetration step, drive, lift and controlled finish, resetting a couple of metres each time. Nobody else is out here. One continuous shot, handheld and circling slowly at chest height; late on, one wrestler drives toward the lens and edges out of frame.

Floodlights blaze over an abandoned toll plaza on a Dubai ring road, six empty booths dark behind glass, barrier arms frozen upright, white lane paint slicing the concrete. Nothing stirs but the dancers. Six adults fill two lanes: a rangy Trinidadian man in a black vest, a heavy-built Turkish woman in denim, a slim Malay man in white, a tall Russian woman with a platinum crop, a bearded Lebanese man, a compact Ghanaian woman. They hammer krump — stomps that shudder the concrete, jagged chest pops, whipping arm swings and buck-ups — surging a few metres and snapping back. No one watches. One continuous shot, the camera dollying slowly out to reveal the whole plaza, all six framed.

Neon spill from surrounding towers washes a raw poured concrete slab high on an unfinished Dubai high-rise, rebar bundles stacked at the core and safety netting billowing at the open edge. Scraps of paper confetti tumble through the coloured light. Five adults stand at their own plyo boxes: a thickset Peruvian man in a grey hoodie, a tall Somali woman in teal, a stocky Croatian man, a lean Japanese woman with a short bob, a bearded Pakistani man in red. They dip and launch onto the boxes, land soft, step down and reload, each staying on one square of slab. The deck is otherwise deserted. One continuous shot from a static tripod at eye level.

Blue hour deepens over an open-air amphitheatre stage in Dubai, its flat concrete apron flanked by cable spools and two skeletal sound towers, house strings unlit. The air is entirely still. Three adults spread across the slab: a tall Sudanese woman in a white tank, a stocky Portuguese man with a beard and blue shorts, a wiry Korean woman in yellow. A disc snaps low between them and they attack it — a full horizontal layout dive, a skid across the concrete, a quick pop pass and a second stretching dive a few metres on. Audience members watch from tiered seating behind a low rail, off the stage. One continuous shot from a static tripod at eye level.

Harsh midday sun bleaches a broad shelf of short flowering turf above the mountain road east of Dubai, a boulder cairn at one end and a rusted cattle gate at the other, petals and dry leaves whirling low over the grass. Three adults march the bench: a tall Icelandic man with a red beard in navy, a compact Bolivian woman with a black bun, a lean Nigerian man in white. Snares strapped high, they hammer rolls and accents while crossing thirty metres in step, then snap crisp pivot turns and counter-march back. Nobody else stands on the meadow. One continuous shot, the camera panning slowly left to right, all three fully in frame throughout.

Soft overcast light greys a cobbled stone arch bridge spanning a dry wadi outside Dubai, mossy parapets and squat iron lamps lining the roadway while dry leaves swirl across the rounded stones. Five adults work a lane: a barrel-chested Serbian man in a yellow tee, a tall Rwandan woman in pink, a stocky Chilean man, a broad Finnish woman with a blonde plait, a grinning Indonesian man in orange. Taking turns, they squat, grip and flip a heavy tractor tire end over end down a few metres of cobble, whooping and slapping hands between reps. The bridge is closed and empty. One continuous shot from a static tripod at eye level, all five fully framed.

A small yoga studio on a Dubai mezzanine, cleared of props: light bamboo boards, rolled mats stacked in a corner, a wall of frosted glass. One work light blasts in from the side so bodies read half-lit; two industrial fans push loose paper and dust skidding along the boards. Three adults perform on their own squares of floor, feet down and fully in frame from the opening instant to the last. A lean Sudanese man in a mesh top runs a fast hands-and-arms sequence; a curvy Filipina woman in emerald snaps a pirouette and drops backward flat to the boards; a grey-haired Brazilian woman duckwalks a tight circle and freezes. The camera cranes down to eye level, one continuous shot.

Hard floodlights from one wall throw long shadows over a red foam mat in a Dubai training room, taped circles worn pale and climbing ropes hanging in the corner; leftover paper confetti still tumbles down from the vents. Six adults pair off: a springy Uzbek man in blue, a tall Danish woman with a sandy braid, a broad Egyptian man, a compact Thai woman in green, a bearded Italian man, a strong-shouldered Kenyan woman. One partner fakes high, the other drops levels, snatches both legs and drives to a soft lifted finish, then they bounce apart a couple of metres and swap, grinning. No spectators. One continuous shot, the camera craning down from high above to eye level, all six fully in frame.

Neon signage floods an elevated linear park walkway threading between Dubai blocks, tapered concrete planks underfoot, wild planter beds and cable railings glowing pink and cyan while a searchlight sweeps overhead. Two adults train in the colour: a bouncy Cuban man in his twenties, tight curls, white singlet; a tall Vietnamese woman in her thirties, straight black hair tied back, mint hoodie. They shadow box facing one another, snapping doubles, slipping imagined counters, rolling under and skipping laterally three or four metres along the planks, grinning through the drill. Nobody else walks the deck. One continuous shot, the camera dollying slowly outward to reveal the glowing corridor, both boxers fully in frame with feet on the concrete.

Coloured tube lights wash a tiled pedestrian underpass beneath a Dubai interchange, condensation beading on a conduit and a haze of fog hanging as a spotlight swings along the tunnel. Three adults play the length of it: a lean Ethiopian man in bright blue, a stocky Mexican woman in a pink windbreaker, a tall Swedish man with a red topknot. On a shouted call they burst into flat sprints down the tiles, then freeze absolutely still mid-stride — arms flung, one heel raised — before exploding again a few metres the other way. The underpass holds nobody else. One continuous shot, handheld, circling slowly at chest height with all three fully in frame.

Shafts of daylight cut through the high glass of an enormous commercial greenhouse outside Dubai, striking a wide concrete service walkway between towering tomato vines and rows of dormant misting pipes. The air is dead still, dust hanging in the beams. One man — early forties, Māori, thickly built, dark hair buzzed short, black compression top and grey shorts — sets his hands on a weighted sled and drives it sprinting the length of the aisle, shoulders low, feet clawing concrete, breath ragged. No one else works the house. One continuous shot, the camera dollying slowly toward him; after starting fully framed with both feet planted, he pushes right up to the lens and passes partly out of frame.

The open top deck of a Dubai multi-storey car park, painted concrete striped with faded bay markings, a squat lift housing and glass towers hazing away in the drizzle. Rain streaks down and bursts in shallow puddles under soft overcast light. One adult trains up here alone: a powerfully built Ukrainian woman in her forties, tacky-smeared forearms, black singlet, cropped copper hair. Feet planted, fully in frame throughout, she wraps a heavy concrete sphere, laps it onto her thigh, roars, and extends it up onto a chest-high stack of pallets, then rolls it down and repeats twice, water flying off the stone. The camera cranes down from high above to eye level in one continuous shot.

Golden hour gilds a cobbled square in Dubai's heritage quarter, coral-stone arcades and a dry tiled fountain enclosing the rounded stones, with fine white flakes drifting through the low beams. Five adults, boots planted and all fully framed, labour along one lane: a hulking Bulgarian man in a grey vest, a broad Tanzanian woman in yellow, a stocky Korean man, a tall Lebanese woman with a dark ponytail, a bearded Chilean man. They squat, grip and flip a scarred tractor tire end over end across five metres of cobble, shouting counts. Onlookers crowd behind wooden railings under the arcades, off the stones. One continuous shot, handheld and circling at chest height; finally one lifter steps toward the lens, half leaving frame.

Daylight knifes through clerestory windows into an enclosed loading dock bay in Dubai, catching roller shutters, stacked pallets and steel dock-leveller plates on the sealed concrete; haze fog rolls low and a work spotlight swings across it. Three adults, fully framed with feet down, move in a line: a compact Chinese man in a red sash and black trousers, a lithe Malaysian woman in gold, a broad Cambodian man in white. Borrowing lion-dance mechanics without costume, they sink into deep crouches, spring forward in synchronized pounces, land wide and stamp, ranging a few metres down the bay. Nobody else is inside. One continuous shot from a static tripod at eye level; at the end the lead dancer pounces close and exits frame partly.

Blue dusk on a launch field at the desert's edge outside Dubai, mown short grass ringed by a low fence of steel pins, an orange windsock hanging slack on its mast, inflation fans strapped to a flatbed, dune ridges dark on the horizon. Six adults play a chasing game across the whole width of the field: an Emirati woman in a coral tracksuit jinks left, checks back, and lunges to slap a shoulder; a rangy Ghanaian man swerves away; a stocky Bolivian woman, a bald Polish man, a tall Indian woman and a bearded Australian man scatter and reverse. All six begin fully framed with shoes on grass and stay in frame. The camera pans slowly left to right, one continuous shot.

A bruised storm sky hangs over a chalk plateau on the escarpment above Dubai, short springy turf pocked with flint scatter, a wind-bent thorn bush and a leaning stone marker. The air has gone eerily still before the rain. Three adults, fully framed and feet down, contest a disc: a tall Ghanaian man in a yellow jersey, a compact Slovak woman with a blonde plait, a lean Emirati man in white. The disc skims flat and they attack it — a full-stretch layout across the turf, a scrambling reset, a second one-handed diving grab a few metres away. No one else is up here. One continuous shot, the camera dollying slowly in; at the end the nearest player rises into the lens, partly leaving frame.

Light rain glazes a bare grey granite plateau in the ranges outside Dubai, water sheeting off the slabs, a small stone cairn and a rusted survey bolt the only marks. The air is otherwise calm. Two adults square off on a single dry patch: a grinning Portuguese man in his forties, close-cropped grey hair, teal shorts; a wiry Ugandan woman in her twenties, dyed orange twists, white crop top. Feet nailed to that patch, they trade shadow-boxing rounds — flicking lead hooks, ducking beneath phantom overhands, weaving shoulder to shoulder with tight pivots inside a metre — laughing between flurries. Nobody else is on the rock. One continuous shot from a static tripod at eye level, both fully in frame throughout.

Misty sunrise seeps across a drained, cracked-mud paddy on Dubai's farmland fringe, bamboo drying racks leaning at the bund and steam curling off a warm irrigation outfall. Four adults hold their own patches of dry mud: a heavyset Puerto Rican man in a grey henley, a tall Japanese woman with a low ponytail, a lean Nigerian man in black, a stocky Czech woman with a blonde crop. Each loads onto a back leg and rips a bat through a ball perched on a tee, hips clearing, follow-through winding them around without a step off the spot, then sets another ball. No one else in the fields. One continuous shot, the camera panning slowly left to right, all four fully framed throughout.

Warm tungsten work lamps glow over the flat grey concrete infield of a Dubai velodrome, the steep timber banking curving overhead, coiled cables and a scaffolding tower parked at the apron while steam drifts from a floor vent. Five adults command the centre: a slim Korean man with a mint-dyed fringe, a tall Nigerian woman in silver, a compact Turkish woman in black, a sharp-jawed Filipino man in white, a broad Brazilian man in red. They snap through unison choreography — point-and-hold arms, hard body waves, synchronized drops and quarter turns — shifting only a few metres. An audience fills the far seating above the banking. One continuous shot, the camera orbiting slowly around them, all five fully in frame with shoes on the concrete.

Fog rolls in thick over a marble quarry's cutting floor outside Dubai, white sawn stone glowing beneath it, a silent wire saw rig and stacked blocks looming at the edges while stone dust streams low across the slabs. Two adults march the open floor: a tall Ukrainian man in his forties, greying buzz cut, black uniform jacket; a compact Jamaican woman in her twenties, twisted locs pinned up, gold-trimmed jacket. Snare drums slung high, they hammer a bright cadence while covering twenty-five metres of marble in lockstep, then throw crisp pivot turns and counter-march, sticks flashing. The quarry is deserted. One continuous shot, the camera dollying slowly out to reveal the pale expanse, both fully in frame.

Dusty afternoon wind hazes a brick-paved square in a village on Dubai's outskirts, dust hanging gold between clipped plane trees, an old iron well head and a stuttering neon shopfront whose glow flickers over the pavers as a searchlight rakes past above. Three adults stand close in a tight triangle: a bearded Armenian man in a black shirt, a small Filipina woman with a pixie cut and mustard jacket, a tall Danish man in grey. Clubs whirl between them in fast crossing passes, doubles and behind-the-back throws, feet planted on their own bricks. Nobody else crosses the square. One continuous shot, the camera dollying slowly inward, all three fully framed with feet on the pavers.

Dusty wind hazes a cricket ground outside Dubai, the rolled dry clay strip pale between worn outfield grass, a leaning sightscreen, a heavy roller parked by the boundary rope and steam wisping from a groundsman's vent. One man — late twenties, Jamaican, springy and long-legged, short locs, bright red singlet and white shorts — starts fully in frame, both feet on the clay at the far end, then accelerates thirty metres down the clay, hits his mark, drives a knee skyward and sails into a long jump, landing hard and skidding forward. The ground is empty of anyone else. One continuous shot, handheld and circling slowly at chest height; late in the take he runs at the lens and passes partly out of frame.

Soft overcast light dulls a compacted red dirt service strip running between tilted panel rows on a Dubai solar farm, grey inverter cabinets humming at intervals while a maintenance beacon flickers and a survey searchlight sweeps the array. Five adults work the dirt: a tall Ethiopian woman in emerald, a slim Argentinian man in white, a broad Malaysian woman in gold, a bearded Estonian man in navy, a compact Colombian woman in violet. Silk flags whip through fast spins, tosses arcing high before they step under and catch clean, drifting only a few metres between exchanges. No one else is on site. One continuous shot, the camera orbiting slowly around them, all five fully in frame.

A decommissioned foundry casting hall in Dubai's industrial belt: floor of packed black moulding sand, a hulking ladle crane parked overhead, sand moulds stacked like coffins along one wall. Magenta and green stage lamps have been rigged in the roof trusses, and confetti scraps tumble through the beams. One adult performs, a compact Tunisian woman in her twenties, silver leggings, black crop top, hair in twin buns. Fully framed with bare feet in the sand at the start, she rips a fast three-beat weave, folds the poi into butterflies at her hips, then turns a full circle beneath them. The camera pans slowly left to right, one continuous shot, as she strides toward the lens and her head crops out of frame.

Golden hour lights a flat basalt pavement in the black rock country beyond Dubai, fissures venting thin steam between stacked cairns and a rusted trail marker. Three adults grip hands in a chain: a rangy Somali man in a grey tee, a strong Polish woman with a blonde ponytail and orange top, a stocky Filipino man in blue. They wind up, running a wide circle across the dark rock, the chain accelerating until the anchor plants and the tail runner is slung outward, sprinting twenty metres across the pavement before wheeling back to rejoin. Nobody else is on the lava. One continuous shot, the camera panning slowly left to right, all three fully in frame.

Misty sunrise softens a narrow corridor between towering container stacks in a Dubai yard, concrete paver blocks underfoot, scattered twist-locks and a lopsided ladder against corrugated steel. The air is still, everything hushed and pearl-grey. Four adults work a lane: a barrel-chested Nigerian man in a yellow tee, a tall Kazakh woman with a black braid, a stocky Irish man freckled and grinning, a broad Indonesian woman in teal. Taking turns, they wedge fingers under the tread and heave a scarred tractor tire up onto its face, chasing it six metres down the pavers, palms slapping between reps. No one else is in the yard. One continuous shot, handheld and circling slowly at chest height, all four fully framed.

Golden hour turns a black volcanic sand beach beyond Dubai into a sheet of dark glitter, basalt boulders humped at the tideline and a bleached driftwood spar half-buried above the calm, barely breathing surf. Two adults lock up on one patch of sand: a wiry Thai man in his thirties, shaved head, red shorts and hand wraps; a tall Trinidadian woman in her twenties, box braids tied high, black crop top. Hands clasped behind each other's neck, they battle for the plum, twisting and pulling as knees drive up into the body in hard alternating strikes, heels never leaving their metre of sand. The beach is empty, both fighters fully framed throughout. One continuous shot, the camera tracking sideways at a steady walking pace.

One woman owns a wide slab of painted concrete on the apron outside a Shanghai maintenance hangar, yellow taxi guidelines curving under her boots, a folded jet bridge and an idle tow tractor parked far behind. She is Black, mid-thirties, tall and long-limbed, in a scarlet ruffled skirt and cropped white top. From the first beat she stands fully in frame, both feet planted, then rips into a zapateado burst — hammering heel-toe triplets, a sharp golpe, arms spiralling upward in slow braceo before another louder volley. Soft overcast daylight, still air, nobody else. Filmed as one continuous shot with a slow dolly-in, bright and buoyant.

Blue hour drapes a weathered wooden promenade on the Shanghai coast, its driftwood railing bleached pale, a rusted tide gauge bolted at one end, scattered breakwater blocks catching the last light while surf keeps thudding against them. Three adults hold the deck: a stocky Georgian man in his forties with a shaved head and grey vest, a slim Korean woman around thirty in teal harem pants, a red-bearded Irish man in a black tank. All three begin fully visible, feet on the planks, then drive poi into fast three-beat weaves, butterfly patterns and turning spirals, cords whistling. Grand and cinematic, no onlookers, captured in one continuous shot as the camera dollies slowly outward.

Rain glazes the dusty concrete slab of a grain-handling yard outside Shanghai, four squat steel silos rising behind a tipped hopper chute, spilled kernels pasted into the wet sheen. Four adults start together, whole bodies in frame, shoes flat on the slab: a broad Samoan man in an orange work shirt, a wiry Vietnamese woman in grey joggers, a freckled Dutch woman with a blonde braid, a lean Ethiopian man in navy. They explode into sprint bursts across ten meters, then snap into rigid freezes, one wobbling, before bursting again; near the end the Samoan man surges straight toward the lens and leaves frame at the waist. One continuous shot, camera panning slowly left to right, epic and severe. No one else is present.

Ochre and cobalt ceramic tiles pave a small Mediterranean-style courtyard tucked behind a Shanghai lane house, a dry stone cistern at its center, potted lemon trees along a low arcade. Two adults work the tile: a compact Puerto Rican man near thirty in a lime tracksuit, and a tall Chinese woman in her late twenties with a bleached buzzcut and denim shorts. Both stay fully in frame, feet down, before he drops into continuous windmills and she chains flares into a brief headspin, spraying rain from splashing puddles under harsh midday sun breaking through the shower. Neighbors watch only from the arcade balcony behind the railing. Cheerful and punchy, filmed as one continuous shot with the camera tracking sideways at a walking pace.

A repainted intersection plaza in Shanghai glows under drizzle, giant orange chevrons stretched across the asphalt, stubby bollards ringing the edge, a shuttered noodle stall dark on the corner while fog banks roll low through the crossing. One man commands it — Nigerian, early forties, heavy shoulders, in a yellow jersey and black shorts. He begins fully in frame with both feet on the wet paint, then attacks a volleyball spike approach: three-step run, arm swing back, a hard jump and cracking hit that skids the ball over the puddles. He repeats it closer until his torso fills and overflows the frame. Spectators cluster behind the barrier railings only. Bright sports-ad energy, one continuous shot, slow pan from left to right.

Golden hour on a terraced olive grove in the hills west of Shanghai, dusty pale earth swept flat between gnarled trunks, a coil of drip line and a stack of harvest nets at the terrace wall. Four adults pair off and race on their hands. A sinewy Kenyan man walks fast on his palms while a broad Latvian woman grips his ankles and drives him forward; alongside, a tattooed Vietnamese woman crawls with a heavyset Italian man holding her shins, both grunting as they cover four metres. Dust puffs under every hand. The air is still, low sun stretching their shadows. All four begin standing on the earth, fully framed, and stay in frame. One continuous shot craning down to eye level.

Night in a bamboo-fringed forest clearing outside Shanghai, a single floodlight on a tripod throwing a hard cone across packed earth and wet leaf litter; snowflakes drift through the beam and vanish. A stacked timber pallet box sits at the centre. Three adults work it in rotation, feet on the ground, fully framed from the first instant to the last, none leaving frame. A rangy Nigerian man in black thermals sinks and explodes up, landing silent on the box; a compact Japanese woman with short-cropped hair steps down and rebounds instantly; a broad Georgian man with a heavy beard doubles up two jumps in a row, breath smoking. The camera stays locked at eye level on its tripod, one continuous shot.

Mist softens sunrise over a firm red-sand interdune flat near the Shanghai coast, dune crests rippling behind, half-buried fence posts leaning in a broken line, a skin of fine sand hissing sideways across the ground. Three adults hold their spots: a tall Brazilian woman around thirty in a white gi top and cropped leggings, a stocky Japanese man in his forties with a headband, and a grey-locked Caribbean man in loose black trousers. Framed fully, bare feet gripping the sand, they fire spinning kicks in rotation — tornado kick, spinning hook, a low sweep that throws a red plume into the drifting dust. Nobody else for kilometers. Epic and vast, rendered as one continuous shot with a slow pan from left to right.

Inside a Shanghai training gym, a blue spring carpet floor stretches under harsh floodlights raking in from one side, a chalk bucket and folded landing mats stacked against the wall, white tape marking the corners. One athlete works alone: a Korean-American man in his late twenties, lean and heavily muscled, in a black singlet and orange shoes. He sets fully in frame, feet on the carpet, then loads into a crouched block start and detonates — hips rising, first three drive strides low and violent across two meters — before walking back and repeating with more snap. The air is completely still, the gym empty of anyone else. One continuous shot, handheld camera circling slowly at chest height, cinematic and severe.

Misty sunrise settles on a Shanghai rooftop terrace where wide trays of red chilies dry across whitewashed cement, a squat water tank in one corner and empty clotheslines sagging overhead. One woman uses the clear strip: Colombian, early thirties, athletic with a high ponytail and a mint jersey over black shorts. She stands fully in frame, both feet on the cement, then hammers soccer power shots against the parapet — plant, drive, laces through the ball — before flicking one up and catching it on a full volley that cracks off the wall, chasing rebounds a couple of meters either way. Nothing else stirs; the terrace is hers alone. Playful and bright, one continuous shot from a static tripod at eye level.

Light rain leaves a smooth red sandstone bench above a Shanghai reservoir rain-slicked, shallow potholes brimming, a rusted survey pin driven near the lip, the valley falling away behind. Six adults line up: a tall Ghanaian man in a silver jacket, a petite Thai woman in pleated white, a broad Kazakh man in black leather, a freckled Australian woman with copper hair, a slim Chinese man in an oversized grey coat, a curvy Brazilian woman in cobalt. Everyone is fully in frame with feet on the stone throughout, hitting sharp unison choreography — synchronized point-and-lock arms, body rolls, a hard drop to half-squat, quick head snaps. Nobody watches. Monumental in scale, held in one continuous shot while the camera pushes slowly inward.

Sawdust-blanketed dirt spreads through a timber sawmill yard on Shanghai's outskirts, log piles stacked shoulder-high, a silent conveyor angling toward a shed whose kiln vents leak slow ribbons of steam into the misty sunrise. One dancer takes the swept patch: a Dominican man in his mid-twenties, wiry, in a mustard windbreaker, baggy grey pants and white sneakers. Fully in frame with both feet down from the first moment, he toprocks with bouncing Indian-step and crossovers, then drops onto one hand into fast six-step footwork, circling his own axis before popping back upright. No one else is working. Upbeat and playful, told in one continuous shot as the camera dollies slowly outward to reveal the whole yard.

An emptied exhibition hall in a Shanghai convention centre after the stands come down: grey commercial carpet running to the horizon of the room, taped floor grids, a lone forklift parked by a shuttered service door. Even ceiling panels wash everything flat white while steam creeps from floor vents in slow sheets. Two adults shoulder a scaffold-length timber pole. A broad Kazakh woman with a cropped fringe leads, a wiry Egyptian man behind her; together they jog the pole diagonally across the whole hall, boots thudding the carpet, then count aloud and drop it in perfect unison with a boom. Both stand fully framed on the carpet at the start and never leave frame. One continuous shot from a fixed eye-level tripod.

A curling rink in a Shanghai sports club, borrowed for hockey drills: pebbled ice with painted house rings showing, a scoreboard frame dark, shafts of daylight dropping from clerestory windows onto the surface. One adult tends a net dragged onto the sheet, a thickset Chinese-Canadian woman in her thirties, white pads, mismatched blue jersey, cage mask, catching glove flashing. Skates on the ice, fully framed from the first instant to the last, she drops into the butterfly, seals both pads, kicks a loose puck out to the corner, pushes back up, shuffles across her crease and smothers another. Air hangs still. Spectators watch from a raised viewing gallery behind glass. One continuous shot, the camera tracking sideways at walking pace.

A faded green acrylic hard court sits inside a plane-tree-lined Shanghai tennis club, windscreen fabric rippling along the fence, a net-post crank rusted orange, blossom petals swirling low over the surface. Three adults take the baseline area: a stocky Lebanese man near forty in a coral polo, a tall Swedish woman with a blonde bob in navy, and a slim Japanese woman in her twenties wearing yellow. All three remain fully in frame, shoes on the acrylic, running a fast pepper triangle — forearm bump, quick set, controlled downward hit, everyone shuffling a couple of meters to dig low balls and reset. Club members lean on the railing outside the fence. Sunny, playful and commercial, one continuous shot orbiting slowly around them.

Drizzle beads on a rippled tidal sand flat below Shanghai, stranded bamboo fishing poles leaning in the shallows, a distant outfall pipe venting slow steam across the horizon, the wet sand throwing back the pale sky. Three adults line up: a broad Tongan man in a red rash vest, a lean Ukrainian woman with a bleached crop, and a bearded Egyptian man in grey shorts. All are fully in frame with bare feet planted, then bend to steel drums and shove them into a rolling race, sprinting bent double for twenty meters, sand spraying, barrels slewing and getting wrestled straight. Not a soul besides them. Bright and athletic, one continuous shot as the camera cranes down from high above to eye level.

On a quarry bench cut into a hillside outside Shanghai, compacted rock aggregate makes a flat pad below terraced grey walls, torn tarps and marker flags whipping hard in strong wind under harsh midday sun. Six adults gather: a heavy-shouldered Fijian woman in orange, a wiry Sudanese man in white, a short Chinese woman with pigtails in pink, a tanned Italian man in a vest, a tall Norwegian woman in denim, and a stocky Peruvian man in green. Everyone stays fully in frame, boots on the gravel — four turning two long ropes while pairs jump in for fast double dutch, high knees, quick switch-outs, and back to turning. No spectators anywhere. Sun-bleached and boisterous, one unbroken continuous shot tracks sideways at a walking pace.

Low practice lights leave a Shanghai indoor sprint track in deep shadow, blue polyurethane gleaming faintly, a banked corner curving into darkness, torn paper scraps tumbling through the air from an open loading door. Three adults use the infield straight: a tall Somali woman in a black long-sleeve, a stocky German man with a red beard in grey, and a compact Vietnamese man in a white tee. All three begin fully in frame with shoes on the track, then trade flying-disc work — a flat throw drawing a full-extension layout dive that skids a few meters, the catcher popping up to launch the next while a third bids low. Teammates watch from the balcony rail above. Noir-cool, one continuous shot tracking sideways at walking pace.

Haze fills a Shanghai aircraft hangar, painted grey concrete stretching between a parked tug rig and towering doors, moving spotlights sweeping cones through the fog under low, deep-shadowed practice lights. Five adults occupy the floor: a burly Croatian man in black, a lithe Jamaican woman with box braids in silver, a short Chinese man in a grey vest, a red-haired Scottish woman in navy, and a broad Iranian man in olive. All five are fully in frame with feet on the concrete, then fall into wheelbarrow relays — hands slapping fast across three meters while partners grip ankles, then rotating roles and firing back, breath loud in the empty space. Nobody else present. Moody neo-noir, one continuous shot from a static tripod at eye level.

A disused runway outside Shanghai bakes under harsh midday sun, grooved asphalt scored with faded threshold bars, tilted approach lights rusting off to the side, fine dust streaming low across the surface. One man works the centerline: Afro-Cuban, early thirties, densely muscled, in cut-off grey shorts and no shirt, wrists taped. He stands fully in frame, feet on the asphalt, then kicks into a handstand and walks fifteen meters down the markings, breaking into a chain of springy handstand hops, correcting a wobble with a shoulder shrug.
