As he nears the lens his legs rise out of frame. Playfully upbeat, entirely deserted, filmed as one continuous shot with a slow dolly-in.

Heavy snowfall settles over a museum forecourt in Shanghai, pale limestone paving swept in patches, a fountain basin rimmed with ice, a bronze abstract sculpture catching flakes on its shoulders. Two adults claim a cleared square: a Persian woman in her late twenties, slight and quick, in a plum long-sleeve and black tights, and a stocky Danish man near fifty with white stubble, in a grey thermal. Both stay fully in frame with shoes on the stone, whipping speed ropes through fast singles, then crossover after crossover, then a burst of double-unders that flicks snow off the paving. Nobody else out in the cold. Dreamy and hushed, told in one continuous shot as a handheld camera circles slowly at chest height.

Storm light presses down on a cramped outdoor basketball court between Shanghai lane houses, painted black asphalt bleeding faded key lines, a bent rim over a plywood board, chain-link fence rattling as rain streaks in and puddles jump. Two adults grip up: a heavyset Mongolian man around forty in a white judogi, and a lean Puerto Rican woman in her thirties with a tight bun, wearing a blue gi. Both stand fully in frame, bare feet on the wet paint, drilling repeated o-goshi — grip, turn-in, hip loading, partner rolled over and slapping out, then swapping tori and uchikomi again on the spot. Residents watch from behind the fence. Gritty documentary texture, one continuous shot with a slow dolly-in.

Harsh midday sun bleaches a ballpark infield in suburban Shanghai, freshly raked red dirt combed in arcs, chalk baselines crisp, a chain backstop throwing lattice shadows near an empty dugout. One athlete owns the mound area: a Ghanaian-British woman in her late twenties, broad-shouldered, hair in cornrows, wearing a black sports top and grey shorts with hands wrapped. Fully in frame with cleats in the dirt, she shadow boxes — double jab, cross, a rolling slip under an imagined hook, pivot right, then a fast three-punch combination that kicks dust off her back foot as she covers two meters and circles back. Air completely still, stands empty. The whole drill holds in one continuous shot, static tripod at eye level, light and quick.

Golden hour rakes along an elevated bicycle expressway in Shanghai, its red painted tarmac glowing between curved perforated noise walls, the darkening skyline stacked beyond, everything perfectly still. One runner uses the closed lane: a Turkish-German man in his mid-thirties, tall and rangy, in a black long-sleeve and dark shorts, hair slicked back. He starts fully in frame with spikes on the tarmac, then drives into a hurdle row set down the lane, attacking each barrier with a snapped lead leg and flat trail knee, three strides between, covering thirty meters and easing down at the far end. No other person on the deck. Cool noir palette, one continuous shot from a static tripod at eye level.

Heavy snow drifts across coastal salt evaporation pans south of Shanghai, a crusted white flat divided by low earthen dikes, a wooden rake abandoned in the brine, ankle-deep water lying in slabs of grey glass. Three adults wade the shallow pan: a weathered Uyghur man in his fifties in rolled canvas trousers, a strong Nepali woman around thirty in a red fleece, and a young Polish man with wet blond hair in a soaked hoodie. All three stay fully in frame, feet in the water, launching stomp-splashes at each other, scooping sheets of brine with cupped hands, dodging and countering across three meters. No onlookers. Raw documentary feel, one continuous shot as the camera orbits slowly around them.

Six adults hold a wedge in a Pudong heritage orchard, dwarf apple trees pruned into low bowls, a stone irrigation channel frozen at the row's edge. Flat dim light of heavy snowfall drains all color; the air stays motionless. Three women — one tall and dark-skinned in crimson, one stocky East Asian woman in teal, one wiry redhead in slate — and three broad-shouldered men in grey-trimmed white spin weighted silk flags, snap them flat, then stride a few metres apart and back, releasing synchronized quad tosses and catching behind the back. Clover and grass show clearly beneath their boots. All six stay fully framed, feet on the grass, in one continuous shot as the camera cranes from high above down to eye level.

Neon spills from signage above a caged synthetic turf pitch in Shanghai, green fibers glowing sour lime, searchlights sweeping the sky and flickering tubes strobing across the chain fence and bare goal frame. Three adults work the full length: a heavily built Fijian man in a black compression top, a tall Belarusian woman with a blonde ponytail in red, and a lean Malaysian man in white. All three begin fully in frame with cleats on the turf, then shoulder a padded log and jog it the length of the pitch in tight step, calling cadence, before dropping it flat together with a thud and pounding back the other way. Nobody else inside the cage. Bright sports-ad punch, one continuous shot with a slow dolly-out.

A storm sky hangs bruised and low over a lavender field on Shanghai's western fringe, a chalky gravel service path cutting between purple rows, distillation sheds at the end venting slow steam into the heavy air. One athlete uses the path: a Māori-Chinese woman in her early thirties, powerfully built, hair in a topknot, wearing a white singlet and burgundy shorts. She stands fully in frame with spikes on the gravel, then runs a long approach — building speed, breaking into crossover steps, hips turning, blocking hard on the front leg and hurling a javelin that arcs away over the rows. Not another person in sight. Playful, punchy energy, one continuous shot with a handheld camera circling slowly at chest height.

Thunderheads stack over a sunflower field outside Shanghai, a strip of cracked dry soil running along its edge, heavy heads drooping toward the earth, a rusted irrigation valve standing at the corner. The air hangs dead still. Five adults square off: a tall Senegalese man in white fencing whites, a compact Korean woman with a bob, a broad Hungarian man in his fifties, a freckled Irish woman with red hair, and a slender Indonesian man. All five stay fully in frame with feet on the soil, working sport foils in shifting pairs — advance, deep lunge, blade-clearing parry and immediate riposte, retreat a meter, reset and go again. Nobody watching. Epic and severe, one continuous shot with a slow pan from left to right.

A lone woman in her late thirties, Ethiopian, close-cropped hair, wearing an ochre tank and black shorts, works a wet courtyard of fired clay tiles behind a shuttered Shanghai kiln workshop, where stacked green bricks and a rusted chimney lean over the wall. Light rain glosses the tiles to a dark shine; torn red paper scraps tumble past her knees. She loads deep, springs forward off both feet, sticks the landing, rebounds instantly into a single-leg skater bound left, then right, and finishes with a tuck-jump stop. One continuous shot, camera panning slowly left to right; she stays fully in frame, feet on the tile.

A road tunnel under Shanghai sits closed to traffic, asphalt still oil-dark beneath dead sodium fixtures while a single work floodlight rakes hard from one side, glazing the tiled walls and throwing enormous shadows down the bore. Six adults train in three pairs: a heavy Uzbek man in red shorts, a lithe Brazilian woman in black, a tattooed Australian man, a compact Thai woman in yellow, a rangy Sudanese man, and a stocky Chinese woman in blue. All stay fully in frame with bare feet on the asphalt, locking plum clinches and driving alternating knees into pads, breaking, swiveling, re-clinching within a meter or two. Nobody else. Air dead still. Neo-noir mood, one continuous shot with a slow dolly-out.

Four adults toe an improvised chalk line on the long weathered concrete platform of a disused Shanghai freight depot, container gantries frozen behind them, a faded semaphore post at the far end. Overcast daylight sits flat and shadowless; nothing moves but the runners. On a shouted count they explode into a four-abreast sprint, driving forty meters down the platform toward a rope stretched between two bollards — a broad Han man in a black singlet, a lean Nigerian woman in yellow, a freckled European woman in grey, a silver-haired Filipino man in red. The handheld camera circles slowly at chest height in one continuous shot; all four remain fully framed, feet striking concrete.

Rain slicks the tactile-edged concrete of a suburban Shanghai commuter platform, closed for the night, its yellow tiles glossy and its awning dripping between two dead vending kiosks. Far beyond the tracks, fireworks bloom and fade in low orange bursts. Four adults — a heavyset Kenyan man, a compact Japanese woman with a braid, a tall pale man in a soaked hoodie, a middle-aged Indian woman in navy — shoulder a lacquered timber beam and jog it eighty meters along the platform, calling cadence, then drop it flat in unison and reset. Shot in one continuous take, the camera cranes from high overhead down to eye level; all four stay fully in frame.

Hazy amber afternoon light, thick with blown dust and ice crystals, washes a frozen reservoir field outside Shanghai, where wind has carved the packed snow into long ridges beside a leaning fence of bamboo poles. Distant fireworks pop silently above the treeline. Three adults in bright puffers — a grinning Brazilian man in lime, a tall Korean woman in magenta, a bearded Scandinavian man in orange — burst forward twenty meters in a scramble, then freeze mid-stride like statues, wobble, and go again, laughing. All three start fully in frame with boots on the crusted snow; in one continuous shot from a static tripod at eye level, the lime-clad man charges the lens and ends partly out of frame.

Night floodlights on scaffolding blast a temple cloister in western Shanghai, worn flagstones running between red lacquer columns and a bronze incense urn brimming with rainwater. Rain streaks through the beams and kicks up splashing puddles. Two men hold one spot at the courtyard's center: a heavyset Māori dancer in a dripping black vest, and a slim silver-haired Vietnamese man in white. They trade dime-stops on the beat, lock into square tutting frames at the chest, then pass a wave from shoulder to fingertip across the gap between them before hitting a slow glide-freeze. Monks and onlookers watch from the raised arcade behind the railing. One continuous shot, camera dollying slowly outward; both stay fully framed.

Light rain leaves a coffee bean drying patio glossy on a bluff south of Shanghai, its smooth concrete slab swept clear except for a pair of wooden rakes, a low seawall in front and surf hammering the rocks below. One dancer works a single spot: a Peruvian woman in her mid-thirties, muscular calves, black hair scraped into a bun, wearing a faded grey leotard and torn warmers. She stands fully in frame, feet on the wet concrete, then whips into pirouettes — a clean double, a triple with a fought landing — and links straight into a chain of fouettés, spotting hard, water flicking from her shoes. Nobody else. Unvarnished documentary feel, one continuous shot with a slow dolly-in.

Black painted plywood covers a proscenium stage in a small Shanghai theater, hemp ropes descending at the wings, a half-struck painted backdrop hanging crooked, smoke drifting from a floor vent into harsh floodlights raking from one side. One dancer takes the deck: a Haitian man in his early thirties, heavy build, hair in short twists, in a baggy orange tee and grey sweats. He begins fully in frame with sneakers on the plywood, then krumps hard — stomping down, chest pops snapping, arm swings whipping past his head, jab-steps carrying him three meters downstage until his shoulders push past the frame edge. The house is empty. Bright and playful, one continuous shot craning down from high above to eye level.

Snow falls steadily on a raised park terrace in Shanghai, crushed decomposed granite crunching underfoot, snow-dusted ginkgos leaning over a curved concrete bench, dark lanterns unlit while brown leaves skitter low across the ground. One dancer works the flat center: a Vietnamese-French woman in her late twenties, athletic, black hair in twin buns, wearing a padded olive vest, wide grey pants and white sneakers. Fully in frame with both feet on the granite, she toprocks with a bouncing kick-step and cross, then plants a hand and drops into circling six-step footwork, knees skimming the grit, rising into a freeze two meters from where she started. Nobody else in the park. Cool noir tone, one continuous shot craning down from overhead to eye level.

Misty sunrise turns a coal stockyard beside a Shanghai river plant into pale gold vapor: black dust ground raked into long ridges, a stopped bucket conveyor overhead, a cooling tower fading into haze. The air is dead calm. One woman works there alone — mid-forties, Ghanaian, muscular shoulders, hair wrapped in a grey cloth, wearing a sleeveless indigo top and loose canvas trousers. She runs a waxed hardwood staff through figure-eight spins at the hips, rolls it across her shoulders and down one arm, steps a few meters sideways, snaps it into a high vertical toss, and catches it blind behind her back. In one continuous shot the camera cranes from far overhead down to eye level; she stays fully framed, boots on the dust.

Harsh floodlight rakes down a colonnaded arcade walkway inside an old Shanghai exchange building, speckled terrazzo polished dull, marble columns marching in pairs, industrial floor fans blasting dust and loose paper along the floor. Three adults use the straight: a broad Māori woman in navy, a slight Chinese man in a red singlet, and a bearded Portuguese man in grey. All three stay fully in frame with shoes on the terrazzo, chaining standing broad jumps between column bases, then linking alternating bounds for four metres, thudding down, walking back and firing again. Office workers watch from behind the mezzanine railing above. Rough, unpolished documentary flavor, told in one continuous shot as the camera dollies slowly outward down the colonnade.

Dust-thick shafts of daylight drop through the clerestory windows of a decommissioned Tokyo turbine hall, striping a checker plate steel floor between two capped generator casings and a hanging chain hoist. Loose paper scraps tumble slowly through the beams. Four adults stand in a tight square, each holding their patch of floor: a wiry Senegalese man in a charcoal waistcoat, a curvy Japanese woman in dark green, a tall red-haired woman in black, a stocky Chilean man in grey. They rip shuffle-ball-changes in unison, break into alternating pullbacks, then answer one another with a rattling five-tap wing before locking into a paddle-and-roll. One continuous shot; the camera dollies slowly back, revealing the cavernous hall, all four fully framed, boots on the steel.

Night floodlights blaze over a deserted studio backlot in western Tokyo, where false timber shopfronts and a plywood noodle stall line a street of painted asphalt. One woman works there alone — mid-thirties, Southeast Asian, muscular shoulders, mustard tee, cuffed denim, red work gloves. She starts fully in frame, boots planted on the asphalt, then hauls a hay bale off a prop cart, jogs it the whole length of the shopfronts and hurls it hip-high onto a growing stack at the far end, sprinting back across the street for the next. Pink petals and dry leaves swirl low across the pavement around her boots. Playful upbeat energy, no one else anywhere, one continuous shot with a slow pan from left to right.

Storm light presses low over the vast flat grey asphalt of an old garrison parade ground in eastern Tokyo, bare flagpoles clanging, a concrete reviewing stand along one side. A single man occupies the emptiness: fifty-ish, Japanese, silver-templed, lean and sinewy in a black singlet and slate shorts. He attacks a scuffed plyo box with repeated jumps, landing soft, stepping down, exploding again, hands slicing the heavy air, feet never leaving one small patch of asphalt. Far behind him, spectators lean on the railing of the raised stand, well off the tarmac. Distant fireworks burst beneath the bruised clouds. Neo-noir contrast, one continuous shot, camera tracking sideways at a steady walking pace.

Floodlight masts throw hard white pools across a drained salt-evaporation pan on Tokyo Bay reclaimed land, its cracked white crust flaking underfoot, container gantries black on the horizon. Five adults train there and nobody else: a burly Polynesian man in a lime tank, a tall Indian woman with a long braid and teal shorts, a stocky Korean man in white, a freckled redhead in orange, a silver-haired Black woman in cobalt. Each stands over a battered tractor tire, driving sledgehammer strikes down in alternating grips, hips snapping, chalk dust puffing on impact. The air is dead calm and the crust stays sharply visible. Bright energetic sports-ad color, one continuous shot, a slow orbit around the people.

On the lowest parking level of a Tokyo office tower, warm tungsten work lamps clamped to pipes light a stretch of epoxy-coated concrete between yellow bay numbers and a row of hissing vent grilles. One goalkeeper occupies the empty deck: a broad Nigerian woman in her twenties, hair in twists, padded green jersey, grey shorts, scuffed gloves. She shuffles, then throws herself sideways to smother a rolling ball, scrambles up, sets, dives the other way, covering only a few metres of floor. Steam drifts from the vents and hangs in the lamp beams; her breath shows in it. Gritty documentary texture, grain and sweat, one continuous shot filmed by a static tripod camera at eye level.

Hazy dust-warmed afternoon light slants into the inner courtyard of an aging Tokyo housing block, where interlocking concrete pavers ring a dead fountain, laundry racks and dented mail lockers. The air itself is motionless. One woman trains on the pavers: forty-odd, Brazilian, thick-thighed, hair scraped back, black long-sleeve and faded burgundy leggings. She drops to her chest, snaps her feet in, launches into a full jump with a clap overhead, and repeats, sinking lower each round, palms grinding grit. Residents watch from the balcony walkways above, none of them down on the paving. Moody neo-noir shadow, one continuous shot as the camera cranes down from high above to eye level.

Rain falls lightly on the travertine tile of a boutique hotel pool deck high over Tokyo, teak loungers stacked to one side, a glass parapet holding back a haze of rooftops. Two dancers own the wet stone and no one else is up here. A slim Filipino man in a soft grey unitard and a tall blonde woman in a coral wrap-top mark each other, then spiral into pirouettes, doubles into triples, before she chains fouetté turns while he holds a slow attitude spin beside her. Rain streaks flash through the light and puddles splash under their turning feet. Bright, buoyant, feel-good mood; one continuous shot, the camera in a slow orbit around the people.

Heavy snow pours down a shuttered pedestrian shopping street in Tokyo, unlit paper lanterns overhead, granite setts swept into a long clear lane between stalls. Two runners work that lane alone — a rangy Kenyan man in a slashed yellow singlet and a stocky Japanese woman in violet thermals, both breathing steam. They explode from a start line, sprint twenty metres, slap a cone, cut back hard, and shuttle past each other again and again, boots skidding and gripping the wet stone, covering the whole street. Torn festival paper and confetti tumble through the snow between the shopfronts. Bright, punchy sports-ad energy, no bystanders at all, one continuous shot from a handheld camera slowly circling at chest height.

Mist burns pink over a small farmyard on Tokyo's western outskirts: packed dirt swept smooth between a tin barn, stacked plastic crates and a leaning persimmon tree. Rain streaks slant through the sunrise and puddles splash and ripple across the yard. Two dancers use a few metres of that dirt and nobody else appears. A lean Vietnamese man in a soaked white tee and green cargos toprocks, shoulders loose, then drops to six-step footwork, hands printing the mud; opposite him a tanned woman with cropped bleached hair and a rust tracksuit answers, sliding into her own circle before both freeze. Dreamy music-video softness, hair sticking wet. One continuous shot, handheld camera slowly circling at chest height.

Golden hour lies long across a suburban Tokyo athletics oval, red rubber tartan glowing, chain fence and an unlit scoreboard behind the empty back straight. The air is completely still. Five adults play a stop-start sprint game and there is nobody else on the track: a tall Ethiopian woman in black, a heavy-shouldered white man in navy, a small Thai woman in silver, a bearded Turkish man in grey, a stringy Chinese man in maroon. They burst from a curve, cross the whole frame in a flat run, then lock into sudden statue freezes on a call, one wobbling, before tearing away again. Neo-noir shadows stripe the lanes. One continuous shot, camera tracking sideways at a steady walking pace.

Frost furs the racking of a Tokyo cold-store hall, plastic strip curtains hanging dead still, and someone has clamped neon and colored stage lights to the beams so magenta and cold green wash the frosted concrete floor. One man works there, alone in the freezing quiet: mid-forties, Māori, heavyset, shaved head, thermal vest under an open hoodie, tape on both wrists. Boots planted, he drives a sledgehammer down onto a truck tire, switching lead hands every few blows, ice dust jumping off the rubber, breath billowing pink in the light. Gritty documentary framing, coarse grain, sweat steaming off his forearms. One continuous shot with a slow pan from left to right.

Blue hour settles over a broad gypsum flat behind Tokyo's dune ridge, a leaning survey post and a rope fence the only marks on the powdery white sand. One fighter stands in the middle of it and no one else is there: a mid-thirties Iranian woman, whipcord lean, black hair knotted tight, dark rash guard, cropped white trousers, bare feet. She pivots and fires spinning hook kicks, then jumping back kicks, each rotation blasting a fan of pale sand into the dim air, her footprint never leaving one small crater. Petals blown from somewhere inland skate low across the ground around her. Epic cinematic scale, one continuous shot, camera craning down from high above to eye level.

A community badminton hall in Tokyo has its nets folded away, leaving a green vinyl mat court under clamped tungsten work lamps and a rig of moving spotlights cutting haze-machine fog. Four adults share it, nobody else inside. A stocky Japanese man in a white gi top and a tall Ghanaian woman in red hold hand paddles chest-high; facing them, a lanky Argentinian man in blue and a broad-shouldered Korean woman with a shaved side sprint two steps, spring, and snap flying front kicks and jumping roundhouses into the pads, landing, resetting, swapping roles within a few metres. Cracks echo. Sunny, upbeat commercial gloss. One continuous shot, camera tracking sideways at a steady walking pace.

Light rain glosses the concrete crest roadway of a dam in Tokyo's western mountains, white lane lines running between a low parapet and two squat valve towers, reservoir black on one side. Two people are up here and no one else. A broad Samoan woman in a soaked orange shirt grips the ankles of her partner, a slight Japanese man in grey with taped fingers, and he powers forward on his hands along the lane line, elbows locking, water splashing off his palms; after four metres they swap and come back. Wet leaves and petals skitter low across the concrete around them. Bright energetic sports-ad snap. One continuous shot with a slow dolly-in toward the people.

Blue hour drains the color from a Tokyo canal quay, grey cobble setts running between iron mooring bollards and brick warehouse arches, the water flat and violet. Six adults in navy drill trousers and suspenders work the quay, nobody else near: two Japanese women, a huge Fijian man, a freckled European man, a slim Peruvian woman, a grey-bearded Black man. They haul a flaked hose off a reel and sprint it out along the whole length of the quay, the line snaking behind them, then drop and dress it, chests heaving. On the far bank, traffic light trails streak past in long ribbons. Dreamy music-video haze, one continuous shot with a slow pan from left to right.

A sealed subway platform under Tokyo still has its tiled concrete floor, empty signage frames and a dark trackbed; someone has rigged neon and colored stage lights along the tunnel mouth and set big fans blowing, so loose paper and dust stir constantly through the beams. Four adults race the length of the platform inside burlap sacks — a broad Mexican man in a red shirt, a tall Somali woman in green, a stocky Japanese woman in white, a rangy Dutch man in black. They bound in huge hops, one crashes and rolls, scrambles upright, and all four surge for a chalk finish line. Epic, cavernous scale, nobody else present, one continuous shot with a slow pan from left to right.

Snow falls thick and windless onto a closed Tokyo crossing, softening the painted crosswalk stripes on the asphalt beneath a dark shuttered department store. Six adults play across a few metres of that road: a towering Sudanese man in yellow, a stocky Japanese man in black, a red-haired woman in teal, a compact Indonesian woman in white, a bearded white man in grey, a lean Korean woman in purple. A disc floats and they hurl themselves flat out, laying out horizontally to fingertip-catch it, sliding through slush, popping up to reset. Onlookers stay packed behind steel barriers along the sidewalk, off the road. Moody neo-noir palette, one continuous shot with a slow dolly-out revealing more of the surroundings.

Harsh floodlights stand on one side of a faded Tokyo hotel ballroom, raking the parquet wood and throwing chandelier shadows across sheeted tables; steam drifts from floor vents and hangs blue in the beams. Three boxers work a small square of the floor: a heavy-browed Russian man in red gloves, a wiry Jamaican woman with cornrows and blue gloves, and a compact Japanese man refereeing footwork in black. The two spar light and quick, slipping, rolling under hooks, pivoting off the ropes of an imaginary ring, drifting a couple of metres and back. Guests watch from the mezzanine gallery above, none on the floor. Soft, drifting music-video mood. One continuous shot, handheld camera slowly circling at chest height.

Snow falls heavily across a train station forecourt in Tokyo, dark basalt setts swept bare in one patch between bicycle racks and a bare ginkgo, the lit glass concourse wall glowing behind. One man trains there: late twenties, Japanese-Peruvian, thick forearms, hair plastered wet, black sleeveless top, grey joggers. Feet rooted in a low stance, he whips two heavy battle ropes into alternating waves, then rises and slams them down together, snow bursting off the coils with every strike. Dead leaves swirl low around his shoes. Commuters watch from behind the barrier at the concourse doors, none stepping onto the stone. Gritty documentary grain, one continuous shot with a slow dolly-in toward the people.

Dusty haze blows across a cropped dry grass terrace on a Tokyo river floodplain, a gravel levee and steel pylons behind, the distant expressway drawing traffic light trails through the murk. One woman occupies the empty grass: mid-thirties, Icelandic, enormously strong, sandy hair braided back, chalked forearms, black singlet and tan knee sleeves. She squats over a smooth concrete atlas stone, laps it onto her thigh, drives her hips and rolls it onto a waist-high platform, drops it, resets, and does it again, feet never leaving one flattened patch of grass. Grit stings; she snorts and grips harder. Loud, sunlit commercial punch. One continuous shot, handheld camera slowly circling at chest height.

Midday sun hammers an open-air festival main stage on Tokyo's waterfront, aluminium deck plates ticking with heat, truss towers and blank banner walls framing three facing pairs. Six adults hold the deck: a tall Senegalese woman in gold, a wiry Japanese man in white, a broad Croatian man in blue, a small Indian woman in green, a tattooed Australian woman in black, a grey-ponytailed Chilean man in red. Each pair passes juggling clubs across a metre of deck, six-count showers escalating into fast doubles, clubs spinning bright against the sky. Confetti scraps tumble through the air over them. The audience stays packed below at the front barrier, off the stage. Epic cinematic feel, one continuous shot, camera tracking sideways at a steady walking pace.

Soft overcast daylight flattens a gravel service road running beside a Tokyo bayside refinery, pipe racks and a cold flare stack rising behind a chain fence, an elevated highway smearing traffic light trails across the far background. Two adults race there with nobody else around: a heavy-set Turkish man in a grey coverall with the sleeves knotted, and a lean Japanese woman in a blue tee and canvas gloves. Each shoves an empty steel barrel on its side, jogging bent over, palms slapping the drum to keep it rolling straight over loose stones, sprinting a few metres to a chalk line, spinning the barrel and driving back. Crisp, high-octane commercial energy, one continuous shot, camera tracking sideways at a steady walking pace.

Golden hour turns the raked fine sand of a bayside volleyball court in Tokyo amber, the net sagging, a concrete seawall and pine row behind. The evening air is completely still. One goalkeeper begins fully in frame, both bare feet planted in the sand: a mid-twenties Japanese-Brazilian man, curly hair, loose lilac jersey, black shorts, taped fingers. He dives left to palm a ball away, rolls up, resets, dives right, spraying sand a few metres either way. Walkers watch from the seawall promenade, never on the court. Then he sprints straight at the lens to smother a loose ball and ends partly out of frame. Dreamy music-video glow. One continuous shot, camera craning down from high above to eye level.

On a Tokyo island cove, fine white coral sand runs between black volcanic rocks where a hot-spring vent breathes steam that drifts low across the beach in the golden hour light. One man plays alone there: forty-ish, Korean, thick-chested, sun-bleached hair, faded green shorts, sand caked to his shins. He hurls a wooden hoop out with backspin so it rolls back to him, sprints alongside it down the beach, then dives head-first through the returning hoop, tucks, rolls up out of the sand and chases it again, covering thirty metres of shoreline. Raw reportage texture, hard grain, real sweat. One continuous shot, camera tracking sideways at a steady walking pace.

Blue dusk sinks over a scrap metal yard on Tokyo's industrial fringe, oil-stained concrete cleared between walls of crushed car cubes and an idle magnet crane; tarpaulins and torn flags snap hard in a strong wind. Five adults train on the concrete, alone in the yard: a towering Dutch woman in white, a stocky Japanese man in navy, a Sri Lankan woman with a bun in yellow, a bald Puerto Rican man in grey, a freckled young man in green. They pepper in shifting pairs — forearm bump, tight set, controlled downward hit — shuffling two or three metres, the odd player rotating in. Saturated, high-contrast commercial punch. One continuous shot with a slow dolly-out revealing more of the surroundings.

A deconsecrated cathedral nave in Tokyo has been stripped of pews, leaving a long diagonal of worn stone flagstones between scaffolded arches; low moody practice lights leave deep shadow, haze-machine fog rolls, and moving spotlights sweep the columns. Three dancers cross the whole length and no one else is inside. A tall Ukrainian man in black tights, a slender Japanese woman in a smoke-grey leotard and a muscular Brazilian woman in deep green launch grand jetés one after another down the diagonal, each landing softly, chasséing, and firing again, arms carving the fog, travelling from the far wall almost to the camera's side. Moody neo-noir color. One continuous shot, camera tracking sideways at a steady walking pace.

Floodlights wash the sandstone paving of a cathedral forecourt in Tokyo at night, a dry fountain and shut iron gates at one end, plane trees motionless in dead-calm air. Four adults haul a heavy timber log across the square: a huge Tongan man, a short sinewy Japanese woman, a bearded Israeli man, a tall Kenyan woman with a shaved head, all in dark shirts darkened further with sweat. Shoulder to shoulder, they jog the log the full width of the forecourt, calling the count, then drop it on a shout and it thuds against the stone. Onlookers stand behind the gate railings only. Hard neo-noir chiaroscuro, one continuous shot, handheld camera slowly circling at chest height.

Blue hour turns a frozen lake in Tokyo's western highlands to slate and lavender, a half-buried wooden jetty and a wall of black conifers at the shore, the air utterly still. Two adults are out on the snow-dusted ice with nobody else in sight: a heavyset Russian-Japanese man in a battered orange parka and a small wiry Filipina woman in a patched blue shell. They take long running starts, then throw themselves down — he belly-first with arms out, she feet-first on her back — and skid ten metres across the ice, laughing, scrambling up on their knees and running back for another go. Gritty documentary handheld feel. One continuous shot with a slow dolly-in toward the people.

A black storm ceiling presses low over a wave-worn rock shelf on the Bōsō coast east of Tokyo, tide pools glinting in its dimples, a bent fishing marker and torn orange banner snapping in the gale beside it. One woman owns the shelf: late twenties, Afro-Japanese, powerful legs, box braids flying, neon-yellow crop top and black track pants. She sinks into a low buck stance, slams a heel into the rock, snaps her torso open, whips both arms across her chest, then punches through a jab-step combo and kills it off with a hard freeze, shifting two meters between hits. One continuous shot from a static tripod at eye level; she stays fully framed throughout.

Thick fog swallows a beachfront promenade in Tokyo, its black-and-white mosaic paving curling away in waves, palms reduced to grey ghosts, steam rising from drain vents along the seawall. Four throwers work a marked circle on the mosaic: a colossal Samoan man in a stretched grey singlet, a broad Ukrainian woman with chalked hands, a shaven-headed Japanese man in navy, and a tall Nigerian woman in red. Each in turn crouches, glides back across the circle, whips the hips open and punches the shot away into the fog, grunting, then resets on the same spot. Onlookers line the seawall steps well behind them. Epic cinematic mood. One continuous shot from a static tripod camera at eye level.

Noon sun glares off a rooftop helipad above central Tokyo, its painted concrete circle bleached almost white, antenna masts and a gritty parapet behind, fine dust blowing low across the deck in ribbons. Two adults stand inside the circle and the roof is otherwise deserted: a tall Sudanese-Japanese woman in a lilac crop top and black shorts, and a compact Greek man with a grey-streaked beard in a washed-out blue tee. Their ropes blur, whipping into crossovers, then bursts of double-unders, feet ticking on the same square metre of concrete, shadows hard beneath them, sweat flicking into the dust. Dreamy music-video shimmer in the heat haze. One continuous shot with a slow pan from left to right.

Inside a shuttered Ōta-ward scooter plant, magenta and cyan stage lamps rigged to the overhead conveyor hooks pour color across epoxy-coated concrete marked with faded yellow walkway grids; stacked empty parts trolleys line one wall. The air is dead still. Three adults work a triangle a few meters wide: a broad Samoan man in a black tank, a lean Egyptian woman with a shaved head in violet, and a grey-bearded Dutch man in navy. They keep a ball alive — forearm pass low, high set, controlled downward spike, dig, repeat — sprawling and recovering on the slick floor. One continuous shot, a handheld camera circling slowly at chest height; all three remain fully in frame.

Under the glass canopy of a Tokyo transit plaza, low moody practice lights leave deep shadow across grey porcelain tile, dark ticket gates and dormant escalators barely catching the glow. The air inside is completely still. Three adults claim a small patch of tile and nobody else is around: a compact Japanese man in black, a tall Ethiopian woman in a maroon leotard and joggers, and a stocky Chilean man in slate. One after another they set, swing their arms and throw standing back tucks, knees snapping in, landing on the same tile square; the last adds a standing full twist and staggers half a step. Moody neo-noir contrast. One continuous shot, camera craning down from high above to eye level.

Thick fog rolls over the painted steel weather deck of a container ship berthed in Tokyo Bay, hatch covers beaded with damp, a yellow crane pedestal vanishing aft. Cherry petals blown from shore swirl low across the deck plates. Four adults in bright warm-ups pound two basketballs on the steel: a tall Sudanese woman in orange, a compact Japanese man in white, a broad Mexican man in teal, a blonde Australian woman in pink. They snap low crossovers, thread between-the-legs into behind-the-back wraps, and trade quick hesitation combos within a few meters. Everyone begins fully framed, feet on deck; as the camera pans slowly from left to right, the orange-clad woman drives at the lens and ends partly out of frame. One continuous shot.

In a basement fight gym in Tokyo, a small octagon cage sits under neon and colored stage lights, its vinyl-covered mat glowing violet, blank banners taped to the chain-link, haze-machine fog rolling as spotlights swing across it. One dancer is inside and no one else is anywhere in the room: a mid-thirties Japanese-Colombian man, lean and tattooed, black tank, loose grey sweats, high-tops. He toprocks along the cage wall, shoulders rocking, then drops into fast six-step footwork, palms flat on the mat, sweeping his legs in a circle before rising into a freeze and shuffling a couple of metres to start again. Moody neo-noir color. One continuous shot with a slow dolly-in toward the dancer.

Warm tungsten work lamps hang low over a Tokyo ice rink after hours, throwing amber pools across white ice with faded painted lines; haze-machine fog drifts and a pair of moving spotlights sweep the empty benches. Two adults are out on the ice in boots, alone in the building: a curvy Japanese woman in a red puffer and a rangy Ghanaian man in a green windbreaker. They take long running starts and hurl themselves into slides, she belly-first with arms spread, he feet-first spinning, skating the length of the rink and racing back to do it again. Then he slides right toward the lens and ends partly out of frame. Dreamy music-video glow. One continuous shot, handheld camera slowly circling at chest height.

Fog sits thick on a university library plaza in Tokyo, herringbone brick underfoot, a bronze sundial and packed bike racks softening into grey, lit reading-room windows glowing above; beyond the hedge, traffic light trails streak past in long smears. Five adults skip rope on the brick, the plaza otherwise deserted: a tall Somali man in a lemon hoodie, a round-cheeked Japanese woman in pink, a wiry Italian man in white, a tattooed Korean woman in mint, a grey-haired Canadian woman in orange. Ropes hiss into high-knee speed steps, then side-swing openers rolling into rattling triple-unders, each pair of shoes ticking on one small square of brick. Playful upbeat commercial brightness. One continuous shot; the camera cranes down from overhead to eye level.

Harsh floodlights rake in from one side of a 1980s Tokyo roller rink, throwing long hard shadows over glossy maple boards; a disco ball hangs dark above a painted planet mural. Torn confetti drifts down through the beams. Three adults each claim a single spot near center: a muscular Jamaican woman in red, a short wiry Japanese man in electric blue, a tall grey-templed Turkish man in white. They hammer two-ball pound dribbles at knee height, drop into scissor drills passing the ball front-to-back between their feet, then spin it around their ankles in fast spider taps. Spectators watch from the lounge behind the rink barrier. One continuous shot, slow pan from left to right; all three stay fully framed, sneakers on the maple.

Harsh floodlights blaze in from one side of an indoor Tokyo pool hall, skimming the non-slip ceramic tile of the deck and turning the flat turquoise water into a silent slab; lane reels and starting blocks sit unused and the air is completely still. Two dancers stand on the tile, alone in the hall: a striking Spanish-Japanese woman, forties, black hair oiled back, a red skirt and hard-soled shoes, and a slim Filipino man in a black shirt and boots. They erupt into zapateado, heels drilling the tile in accelerating bursts, arms sweeping overhead in slow braceo, chins high, feet never leaving their spots. Bright energetic sports-ad crispness. The handheld camera circles them slowly at chest height through one continuous shot.

Blue-hour dusk settles over the pit lane of a mountain circuit north of Tokyo: striped tarmac boxes, roller doors half down on empty garages, a tyre stack under a dead timing board. The air is completely still. Four adults kick to handstands on the painted lines — a rangy Kenyan man, a stocky Japanese woman in a cropped hoodie, a tattooed Brazilian woman, a pale Finnish man in shorts — and race twelve meters on their hands, breaking into shuffling hops. Spectators watch from the terrace balcony above the garages. All four begin fully framed with feet down; in one continuous shot the camera cranes from overhead to eye level as the Kenyan man walks past it, ending partly out of frame.

Inside a cavernous Rio sound stage, pale shafts of daylight fall through high clerestory windows onto a matte black floor scuffed by old dolly track and coiled cables. One continuous shot from a static tripod at eye level holds two adults, both fully in frame with feet planted from the first beat. A tall Afro-Brazilian woman in a scarlet fringed dress leads a wiry silver-haired Japanese-Brazilian man in a charcoal shirt through a burst of triple spins, then a sweeping cross-body lead that carries them two meters sideways and back. The air is perfectly still; only their heels, hems and hands cut the light. Epic, hushed, monumental.

Sunlight drops in hard columns through the high arched windows of an old Rio courthouse hall, where torn dockets and paper scraps tumble slowly above a checkerboard marble floor between brass rails and empty oak benches. The camera pans slowly left to right in one continuous shot. Four adults stand fully visible, feet on the marble: a broad Black woman in cobalt warmups, a lean white man with a ginger beard, a stocky Korean-Brazilian man in yellow, a tall brown-skinned woman with braids. They rock into full pitching windups, driving leg lifts and snapping hard throws to each other across a few meters. Near the end the ginger-bearded man strides at the lens and his shoulder leaves frame.

Snow falls thickly over a wide grey gravel outwash flat under Rio's ridgelines, where a rusted culvert pipe and two bent marker posts are the only landmarks; the air itself is windless, flakes dropping straight down. One continuous handheld shot circles slowly at chest height. A single man — mid-thirties, brown-skinned, shaved head, mud-flecked green kit and battered boots — begins fully in frame with both feet on the gravel, then drives a ball forty meters across the plain, chasing it, striking a low power shot, jogging on and hammering a full running volley that kicks grit and slush. Grainy, cold, documentary-plain; he stays entirely within frame.

Harsh midday sun bleaches the smooth cast concrete flat bottom of a hillside Rio skatepark, its bowl lip chipped, its faded paint sun-ghosted, a sagging chain fence beyond. Nothing stirs but the athletes. In one continuous shot a slow dolly-out gradually reveals more of the empty park. Six adults — three men, three women, Black, white and mixed, in bright mismatched singlets of tangerine, lime and violet — start fully in frame with bare feet on the concrete, then pair off for double-leg takedown drills: level change, penetration step, lift and controlled set-down, alternating attacker and defender. Playful, sunny, upbeat. Late in the take one woman drives forward until she is cropped at the waist.

A cramped Rio gym: a single boxing ring with a scuffed canvas mat, sagging ropes, warm tungsten work lamps clamped to the rafters, steam curling from a wall vent and glowing amber in the beams. Spectators crowd bleachers well outside the ropes, never on the canvas. One continuous shot from a static tripod at eye level. Alone inside the ring, one muscular Black woman in her forties with cornrows, purple tank and grey shorts stands fully in frame, feet wide on the canvas, and hoists a heavy medicine ball overhead before smashing it down between her boots — again and again, hips snapping, breath visible in the steam. Epic, cathedral-dark, monumental.

Rows of dead looms rust in a derelict Rio weaving hall, warm tungsten work lamps throwing long shadows across a wooden plank floor while big fans stir loose paper and lint through the beams. One continuous shot, static tripod, eye level; all six adults remain fully in frame with feet on the boards throughout. They pair off — a lanky white man with a topknot, a squat Afro-Brazilian woman in olive, a grey-templed Lebanese-Brazilian man, a tattooed blonde, a broad Indigenous woman, a lean man in oxblood — and spar with padded practice sticks: overhead strikes, parries, slipping steps and quick counters within a couple of meters. Neo-noir, smoky, low-key and hard-edged.

Soft overcast light filters into a bamboo grove clearing outside Rio, stalks creaking, a sagging rope swing hanging still while dry leaves swirl low across packed earth. One continuous shot pushes slowly toward two adults, both fully in frame with feet on the ground at the start and never leaving frame. A stocky Afro-Brazilian man in a black vest grips the ankles of a tall pale woman with cropped bleached hair in a rust tracksuit; she powers forward on her hands in a hard wheelbarrow crawl across three meters, they wheel around, swap roles and charge back. Muted greens, deep shadow, neo-noir stillness broken by scrabbling hands.

Low moody practice lamps hang over a small Rio club basketball court, polished maple hardwood glossed with reflections, haze thick in the air while two spotlights sweep slowly across faded key lines and a dented scorer's table. Camera pans slowly left to right, one continuous shot. Four adults begin fully in frame, feet on the hardwood: a rangy Black man in red gloves, a compact white woman with a braid, a broad Japanese-Brazilian man, a freckled woman in grey. They spar in pairs — jabs, slipping, rolling under hooks, short pivots inside a few meters — breath and shoulders working. Documentary-raw. One boxer drifts toward the lens and ends half cropped.

Golden hour breaks under the rain over a granite civic plaza in downtown Rio, a dry tiered fountain behind, polished pavers sheeting with water while rain streaks flare gold and puddles burst underfoot. Onlookers press behind a low railing at the plaza edge, none on the stone. One continuous shot, a slow dolly-out that widens to the whole square. Four adults hold the center, fully in frame with feet on the granite the entire take: a heavyset Black man in soaked denim, a wiry Indigenous woman in orange, a tall bald white man, a curvy woman with copper twists. They krump — hard stomps, chest pops, whipping arm swings — spray flying off every hit. Epic, burnished, thunderous.

Harsh floodlights rake one side of a Rio steel mill rolling floor, gantries overhead, idle rollers cold, haze hanging so the beams turn solid and two spotlights sweep across the scarred steel plate underfoot. One continuous shot, the camera slowly dollying out to reveal the vast shed. Five adults hold the light, all fully in frame with feet on the plate throughout: three women and two men — Black, white, Nikkei-Brazilian — in matched charcoal and oxblood tailoring. They snap through sharp unison choreography: knife-edge arm points, quarter-turn hits, a low drop into a slide step, chest isolations, shifting two meters as a block. Neo-noir, lacquered, ice-cold.

Neon tube artworks flicker along the white walls of a Rio gallery hall while colored stage lights sweep the pale oak plank floor, a searchlight beam crawling past an empty plinth. One continuous shot tracks sideways at a steady walking pace. One man — mid-forties, mixed-race, heavy through the shoulders, sleeveless grey shirt, tape on his wrists — stands fully in frame with boots planted on the oak beside a battered tractor tire, and never leaves frame or his spot. He hauls a sledgehammer overhead and drives it down onto the rubber, rebound absorbed, hips reloading, strike after strike, magenta and cyan light strobing over his back. Epic, cathedral-cool, monumental.

Night on a stadium concourse plaza in Rio: stamped concrete stretching between concrete pylons, neon signage flickering pink and green above shuttered kiosks, searchlights sweeping the sky. Fans jam the ramp balconies and press behind mesh barriers, all off the concrete. One continuous shot, slow dolly-out opening the plaza wide. Five adults crouch into starting blocks, fully in frame with feet down: a towering Black man in electric blue, a compact white woman in citrus yellow, a broad Filipino-Brazilian man, a lean woman with a shaved head, a stocky man in white. They explode out together, driving low through first strides and sprinting hard across the plaza, the widening frame holding all five whole throughout. Bright, punchy, kinetic.

Blue hour settles over a red clay tennis court in the Rio hills, crushed brick dust glowing violet, torn sponsor banners on the fence, confetti and paper scraps tumbling through the cooling air. Spectators sit in low stands beyond the fence, none on the clay. Handheld, the camera orbits slowly at chest height in one continuous shot. Six adults line the baseline, feet rooted in the clay, each holding one spot the whole take: a shaven-headed Black man, a silver-haired white woman, a stocky Korean-Brazilian man, a braided Indigenous woman and two wiry brown-skinned men in slate, teal and bone kit. They raise medicine balls overhead and hammer them into the clay in rolling waves, dust bursting around their ankles. Epic, dusk-lit, enormous.

Light rain glazes a close-mown grass tennis lawn on a Rio estate, the sagging net dark, a single pole lamp catching improbable snowflakes drifting through its beam above the reflective turf. In one continuous shot the frame slides in a slow pan from left to right. Three adults grapple within a single small patch, all fully in frame with feet on the grass throughout: a heavy-shouldered Afro-Brazilian man in a black rash guard, a wiry ash-blonde woman in navy, a broad Mongolian-Brazilian man in maroon. They cycle takedown entries, a hip throw, a sprawl, a scramble to knees and back up, bodies steaming and slick. Neo-noir: silver, wet, and hushed.

Blue hour on a riverside concrete esplanade in Rio, broad slabs running past bollards and two moored barges, dry leaves and petals swirling low along the ground in the offshore breeze. A few onlookers sit on the seawall above, off the walkway. One continuous shot from a static tripod at eye level; both athletes stay fully in frame with feet on the concrete throughout. A tall Black woman in a mustard crop top and a heavyset white man with a grey buzzcut in navy sprint shuttle runs between chalk cones, touching down, cutting hard and driving back across ten meters, shoes squealing on damp slab. Grainy, unglamorous, breath-loud.

Dusty hazy wind blows across a corporate campus quad in Rio, glass towers on three sides, distant traffic light trails streaking along the overpass beyond a hedge, a stalled fountain in the corner. A static tripod at eye level records it all as one continuous shot. Two adults begin fully in frame with feet on the mown lawn: a springy young Vietnamese-Brazilian woman in a lilac tracksuit and a lanky freckled man in a mint tee. They tear across the grass in linked cartwheels and round-offs, chaining five or six in a row from one side of the quad to the other, laughing. Bright, buoyant, commercial. At the end she round-offs toward the lens and finishes cropped at the knees.

Bright even overhead lighting floods a small squash court in a Rio sports club: pale hardwood, scuffed white walls streaked with ball marks, a glass back wall reflecting the empty corridor. The air is dead still. A handheld camera circles slowly at chest height, one continuous shot. A single athlete — a broad-shouldered Afro-Brazilian woman in her thirties, hair in a high puff, wearing a slate crop top and white shorts — starts fully in frame with both feet on the wood and stays entirely in frame. She loads deep and fires a standing broad jump, sticks the landing, rebounds into two more bounds, turns at the wall and chains them back across four meters, wood booming under each touchdown. Epic, stark, monumental.

Light rain silvers a stretch of short golden grass on the savanna edge beyond Rio, a half-built hay stack leaning beside a rack of tarps and pennants whipping hard in the wind, wet blades mirroring the pale sky. One continuous shot drifts slowly inward toward two adults, both fully in frame with feet on the grass for the entire take, working from one spot. A sturdy Black man in a soaked ochre shirt and a tall Ukrainian-Brazilian woman with a wet braid swing hay bales up hand-to-hand, heaving each one onto the growing stack, straw scattering into the rain. Dreamy, washed pastel, slow and hypnotic.

Golden hour at a rural gravel crossroads on the bluff above a Rio cove, a leaning signpost stripped of its plates, a dumped pile of pale sand at the verge, waves crashing white on the rocks below. The camera tracks sideways at a steady walking pace in one continuous shot. One man — early thirties, brown-skinned, compact and grinning, in a sun-faded turquoise shirt and rolled canvas trousers — stands fully in frame with boots on the packed gravel and shifts only a couple of meters along the pile. He digs and flings shovel after shovel of sand in bright arcs that catch the low sun, racing himself, dust glowing. Cheerful, warm, upbeat and sun-drenched.

An emptied distribution warehouse in Rio's port zone: a long polished concrete aisle between bare steel racking, magenta and cyan stage lights rigged high, floor fans dragging loose paper and dust through the beams. A static tripod at eye level records one continuous shot, keeping both wrestlers whole in frame on the concrete from first second to last. A powerfully built Black man in a teal singlet and a compact white woman with a red ponytail in grey drill double-legs straight on the bare floor: collar tie, fake high, dive to the far knee, run the pipe and finish flat, then reset and switch roles, sneakers barking on concrete. Bright, saturated, high-energy sports-ad polish.

Shafts of daylight cut through the tall windows of a Rio ballet rehearsal studio, falling across black marley vinyl, wooden barres and a wall of peeling grey paint. Nothing moves in the air. One continuous shot slowly dollies out to reveal the full room. Two adults hold the floor, fully in frame with feet planted the whole time: a broad Afro-Brazilian man in a sleeveless charcoal top and a tall silver-haired white woman in navy leggings. They heave a heavy sandbag between them — swing, launch, absorb the catch in a deep squat, pivot and send it back — a few meters of ground covered, chalk dust hanging in the light. Epic, austere, monumental.

Beneath Rio, a long underground bunker hall of bare damp concrete, a shallow drainage channel running its length, harsh floodlights blazing from one side so the far end vanishes into black. The air is dead calm. A static tripod at eye level watches without cutting, one continuous shot. A single athlete stands fully in frame with both feet on the concrete and never shifts off her spot: a tall, athletic Colombian-Brazilian woman in her late twenties, hair in a tight bun, wearing a lime tank and black shorts. She wrenches a medicine ball across her body in rotational side slams, left hip then right, ripping it into the floor and snatching the rebound up, rep after rep. Punchy, bright-contrast, sports-ad energy.

A small Rio judo dojo, green tatami mats laid tight, faded cloth banners on the wall, low practice lamps leaving the corners in deep shadow. Students kneel in a line against the wall, off the mat, watching. The air is completely still. Filmed as one continuous shot, the camera retreats steadily and the whole dojo opens up behind it. One man — late thirties, brown-skinned, stocky and heavily muscled, in a white gi with the jacket knotted at his waist — stays fully in frame with bare feet on the tatami, holding a single spot. He fires repeated box jumps onto a low plyo box, landing soft, stepping down, exploding up again. Grainy, unvarnished, hard-breathing.

An off-season Rio ice rink stripped to its painted concrete slab, scarred dasher boards and a dead scoreclock ringing the empty pad, bright even overhead lighting flattening every shadow. Spectators watch from the tiered seats behind the boards, none on the slab. In one continuous shot the camera eases steadily inward. Four adults start fully in frame with feet on the concrete: a broad Black man in scarlet, a compact Japanese-Brazilian woman in white, a rangy freckled man, a muscular woman with buzzed hair. Right on the painted slab they drill double-leg takedowns — snap-down setups, penetration steps, drives and quick resets. Crisp, bright, upbeat. One wrestler charges the camera and ends cropped at the chest.

A cavernous Rio bus depot hall stands empty, asphalt marked with faded bay stripes, concrete fuel pillars and a hanging tire rack, floodlights blasting from one side while big extractor fans send loose paper and dust skating across the ground. One continuous shot, the camera gliding sideways at a steady walking pace. Four adults stay fully in frame with feet on the asphalt throughout: a lanky Black man in canary yellow, a curvy white woman in pink, a broad Bolivian-Brazilian man, a wiry woman with box braids. They dribble the length of several bays, firing step-overs, sharp scissor cuts and stop-turns, weaving past each other. Playful, poppy, bouncing with color.

Floodlights on tall poles wash a huge empty surface parking lot in Rio, faded asphalt seamed with tar, a single toppled cart against the chain fence, improbable snowflakes drifting slowly through the beams. Throughout, one continuous shot travels sideways at a steady walking pace, keeping him fully in frame. One man — early forties, mixed-race, thickset with a greying beard, in a plain grey sweatshirt and black track pants — starts with both cleats on the asphalt, then works the lot end to end: five-step drop-backs, resetting, rolling out twenty meters and launching long tight spirals into the dark. Grainy, cold, documentary-honest.

Rain glazes a wide volcanic ash plain outside Rio, fine grey ash packed dark and reflective, a scraped-flat runway strip and a shallow landing pit gouged out of it, dry leaves swirling low across the ground. A handheld camera circles slowly at chest height for one continuous shot, keeping her fully in frame from first step to last. A single athlete — a tall Ethiopian-Brazilian woman in her twenties with a high fade, in a fuchsia crop top and white shorts — begins with both spikes on the ash, then rips through a long run-up across the plain, hits the board, hangs, and lands in a spray of wet ash. Bright, joyful, splashy.

Blue hour over an empty natural grass football stadium in Rio, mowing stripes running toward a bare goalmouth, the stands unlit and silent, floodlight towers black against a deepening sky. Not a breath of wind. The camera creeps slowly closer across one continuous shot. One woman — early thirties, pale-skinned with dark hair loose to her shoulders, in an oversized ivory shirt and shorts — begins fully in frame with boots on the turf and stays in frame throughout, carrying the ball twenty-five meters across the pitch with elastico flicks, hard outside-foot cuts and stop-turns spun back the other way. Dreamy and weightless: dew mist, indigo shadow, soft-edged blue light.

A Rio crossfit box after hours: black rubber tiles, a welded pull-up rig, chalk buckets and stacked plates, low practice lamps carving deep shadows between them. The air hangs still. The handheld camera prowls a slow chest-height circle in one continuous shot, all three fully in frame with feet on the rubber the whole take. A grinning stocky Black man in a coral tee, a tall Syrian-Brazilian woman with a thick ponytail, and a wiry grey-haired white man pass a heavy sandbag in a triangle — rotational toss over the shoulder, catch absorbed chest-deep, pivot and rip it on — laughing, shuffling a couple of meters between throws. Bright color, playful bounce, commercial warmth.

Dusty hazy wind blows through a Rio shipyard dry dock, the wet concrete floor streaked with runoff between huge timber keel blocks and the rust-scaled bow of a half-stripped hull. One continuous shot slowly orbits the runners. Four adults, all fully in frame with feet on the concrete throughout: a towering Black man in slate, a lean white woman with a bleached crop, a broad Indigenous man in brick red, a rangy woman with long dark braids. They run relay exchanges the length of the dock, sprinting flat out, calling, slapping the baton up into waiting palms and driving on, spray flicking off their spikes. Epic, sun-hazed, cathedral-scaled.

Soft overcast daylight flattens a wide beach north of Rio, packed damp sand stretching to a driftwood tangle, dry leaves and petals skating low over the surface in the sea breeze. One continuous shot sweeps a slow pan from left to right; all six start fully in frame with feet on the sand. Six adults — a broad Black man with locs, a wiry white woman, a stocky Nikkei-Brazilian man, a tall Indigenous woman and two lean brown-skinned men in grey, plum and sand tones — sprint three or four steps and launch into headfirst belly-flop dives, skidding along the wet sand, scrambling up and going again in staggered waves. Neo-noir mood: silver light, heavy shadow, spray hanging.

Dusty hazy afternoon wind sweeps a vineyard tractor row in the hills behind Rio, compacted soil packed hard between gnarled vine rows on trellis wire, a rusted water tank at the end of the lane. In one continuous shot the handheld frame swings in a slow chest-height arc, all six fully in frame with feet on the soil the entire time. Six adults hold their spots in a loose line — a heavyset Black man, a wiry Japanese-Brazilian woman, a bald white man, a tall woman with copper locs, a broad Indigenous man, a lean woman in ochre — and krump hard: heel stomps punching dust up, chest pops, elbows firing out into buck jumps and sudden freezes. Epic, golden, monumental.

Rain slicks the black granite of a sunken plaza in Rio's bank district, glass office walls rising on all sides, paper scraps and shredded receipts tumbling down into the well of the square. One continuous shot dollies slowly toward the pair; both stay fully in frame with feet on the granite throughout. A cheerful round-faced Filipina-Brazilian woman in a canary raincoat and a lanky brown-skinned man with a beard in a red hoodie face off two meters apart, passing juggling clubs in fast crossing volleys, adding spins and doubles, ducking a fumble and recovering with a grin, shoes splashing. Bright, saturated, bouncy commercial cheer.

Deep in a Rio tunnel under construction, raw shotcrete floor runs between rebar ribs and a parked spoil skip, thick haze swallowing the work lights while daylight from the distant portal falls in hard shafts through gaps in the shuttering, spotlights swinging across the fog. One continuous shot slowly orbits the players. Three adults begin fully in frame with feet on the shotcrete: a tall Black man in graphite, a compact white woman with a wet braid, a stocky Korean-Brazilian man. They carry the ball twenty meters down the bore, firing step-overs, scissors and sharp cutbacks. Neo-noir, cold and smoky. One dribbles at the lens and ends half out of frame.

A disused hull-fabrication shed on Rio's Ilha do Governador dock: rust-stained steel plate underfoot, a curved barge bow section propped on timber blocks, green welding screens folded against a wall of ventilation louvers. Daylight stabs through high dirty windows, thickened by haze-machine fog as two rigged spotlights sweep slowly. One man moves in a clearing a few meters wide — Afro-Brazilian, thirties, lean and sinewy, shirtless under an open denim vest, red drawstring pants, bare feet. He winds a cheat-step, snaps a hooking 540 kick past a hanging chain, lands, immediately swings through a low cork, and finishes with a butterfly twist. Filmed as one continuous shot, the camera orbits slowly around him; he stays fully in frame.

A Rio fencing hall lit only by low practice lamps and the flicker of neon signs beyond its windows, searchlights sweeping in through the glass across the metallic piste strip laid over dark rubber flooring, reel cables coiled at the edges. The camera pans slowly left to right in one continuous shot; all six remain fully in frame with feet on the floor. Six adults dance there: a shaven-headed Black woman in gauzy lilac, a lanky white man in aqua, a Nikkei-Brazilian woman with waist-length braids, and three more in ash-grey — spinning long ribbon wands into rolling spirals and figure-eights, chaining leaps and chaîné turns while drifting two or three meters along the strip. Dreamy, iridescent, floating.

Inside a timber barn outside Rio, colored stage lights are clamped to the beams, washing the wide plank floor in magenta and teal, hay bales stacked in the corner beside a hanging block and tackle. The air is quiet and still. In one continuous shot the camera cranes down from high in the rafters to eye level. Three adults hold fixed spots, fully in frame with feet on the boards throughout: a beaming heavyset Black woman in yellow, a lanky white man with a topknot, a compact Peruvian-Brazilian man in blue. They rip through burpees — drop, chest to plank, snap the feet in, explode into a clapping jump — landing hard, boards booming. Bright and gleefully upbeat.

An abandoned brick factory hall on Rio's outskirts, broken brick tile underfoot, dead beehive kilns along one wall, low practice lamps throwing deep shadow while confetti and torn paper tumble down through the broken roof lights. One continuous shot orbits slowly around the pair, both fully in frame with feet on the tile the whole time. A springy Afro-Brazilian man in white cotton trousers and a grinning tattooed woman with a bleached crop trade capoeira: rocking ginga, an au cartwheel, a sweeping meia-lua, ducking esquiva dodges, circling three meters of floor. Playful, warm-lit, buoyant.

A round flagstone threshing floor sits on a clifftop above a Rio fishing village, neon bar signs glowing pink and green from the lane below, a stone roller shoved to one side, waves crashing hard on the rocks beyond. The camera pans slowly left to right in one continuous shot. Three adults stay fully in frame with feet on the flagstones: a tall Black man in a white mesh top, a compact Chinese-Brazilian woman in cobalt, a broad-shouldered woman with a bleached buzzcut. They snap through sharp unison choreography — knife-point arms, quarter-turn hits, a synchronized drop and slide step — shifting two meters as one. Bright, punchy, high-gloss.

Blue hour on a mesa top plateau high above the Rio hinterland, hardpan cracked and dotted with sparse scrub, a leaning survey cairn at the rim, fog banks rolling in low and swallowing the drop-off. One continuous shot orbits slowly around the group; all six stay fully in frame with feet on the hardpan the entire time, holding their spots. Six adults in matched black coats over grey — three women and three men, Black, white, Indigenous and Nikkei-Brazilian — cut every count as one: blade-straight arm points, staccato head turns, a chest-pop freeze, then a knee dip and rise timed to the same beat. Neo-noir: cold indigo, silhouettes cutting the mist.

region: Utah salt flats and red-rock desert, USA
caption: Five adults hold the sun-bleached concrete pavers of a hotel roof terrace above a red-rock town, a hazy salt-flat skyline and a rusted water tank standing behind them, a dead-still afternoon thick with dust light. All five begin fully in frame, feet planted on the pavers, and none leaves it. A tall Black woman in a charcoal crop top, a stocky Latino man in slate shorts, a lean white man in a maroon tank and a broad Korean woman in black leggings knit a basket; the fifth, a wiry Indian woman in silver, loads, rockets upward, snaps a toe-touch and drops into their cradle catch. One continuous shot, a slow pan from left to right, moody amber-and-shadow neo-noir.

region: Utah salt flats and red-rock desert, USA
caption: Blue hour settles over a desert pavement flat of tight-packed dark pebbles, a low red mesa fading violet behind leaning survey stakes and a bleached tire rut. One man is here and nobody else: mid-thirties, Filipino, compact and muscular, in a bright citrus tank, white track pants and clean sneakers. He starts fully in frame, both feet down, then attacks — Indian-step toprock, kick-out shuffle, then he drops to hands and rips six-step around a tight circle before popping back up, covering only a couple of meters. Loose paper scraps and confetti tumble past his shoulders on the cooling air. One continuous shot, a slow dolly-out revealing the wide plain, punchy and energetic.

region: Utah salt flats and red-rock desert, USA
caption: Golden hour lays amber light across a dry lakebed west of the Great Salt Lake, pale clay cracked into wide polygons, a lone survey stake at the edge. Nothing stirs in the air. Two adults trade a wooden hoop across a few meters of clay: a broad-shouldered Korean-American man in a mustard tee, and a freckled woman in her forties with a copper braid and denim shorts. She rolls the hoop with backspin so it returns to her; he dives head-first through it as it passes, rolls out of the landing, then flicks it back spinning. Both start fully framed on the clay; in one continuous shot the camera pans slowly left to right as he charges it and ends partly out of frame.

region: Utah salt flats and red-rock desert, USA
caption: Floodlights blaze on a closed overpass above a red-rock canyon, lane paint crisp on the asphalt, barrier flags and loose tarps whipping hard in a night wind. Four adults, alone for miles, start fully in frame, boots on the asphalt, staying in frame: a tall Somali woman in a rust hoodie, a barrel-chested Samoan man in a black tee, a sinewy white woman with a bleached crop, and a lanky Vietnamese man in navy coveralls. They lock into a brigade a few meters long, heaving sloshing steel pails hand to hand, water leaping and slapping the asphalt, the last man dumping and firing the empty back down the line. One continuous shot cranes down from high above to eye level, bright and athletic.

region: Utah salt flats and red-rock desert, USA
caption: Hazy afternoon light softens a tar-and-gravel roof membrane atop an old brick loft in a desert rail town, a hand-painted water tank and dead vines on the parapet. Two adults share the roof, nobody else: a Thai man in his late twenties, slim, in a cropped ivory shirt and wide black trousers, and a Nigerian woman in her thirties with a high ponytail, in a lilac blazer over cycling shorts. Both stay fully in frame, feet rooted to one patch of gravel, locked into a mirrored routine — wrist isolations, a snapping point to the horizon, a hard chest pop held as a freeze. Dry leaves and petals swirl low around their ankles. One continuous shot, a slow orbit around them, dreamy pastel color.

region: Utah salt flats and red-rock desert, USA
caption: Rain has just passed over an abandoned drive-in lot beneath desert cliffs; the cracked gravel-strewn asphalt lies wet and reflective, tilted speaker poles and a torn screen looming, the air now dead still. Five adults, no one else, start fully in frame with boots on the asphalt: a broad Māori man in a soaked grey shirt, a Ukrainian woman with a blonde bun, a wiry Ethiopian man, a heavyset white woman in black, and a Chilean man in a green windbreaker. Shouldering a long timber together, they jog the length of the lot, water spraying from their boots, then bark a count and drop the log flat in unison. One continuous shot, a slow dolly-out revealing the lot, cold noir blues and sodium orange.

region: Utah salt flats and red-rock desert, USA
caption: Bruised purple storm clouds stack over a festival pier on the Great Salt Lake's south marina: painted steel plate decking, strings of dead bulbs swaying between posts, steam curling from a vent grate near the shuttered ticket booth. Two adults run routes down thirty meters of deck — a rangy Somali-American man in a yellow jersey, and a powerfully built woman with a blonde ponytail in navy. He fires a spiral, she plants hard, breaks on a deep post, tracks the ball over her outside shoulder and hauls it in at full stride, then jogs back to reset. Festivalgoers watch from a raised viewing platform behind the railing. One continuous shot; the camera cranes down from high above to eye level, both fully framed.

region: Utah salt flats and red-rock desert, USA
caption: Harsh midday sun hammers a trodden red-earth walkway between terraced tea rows in a canyon pocket, bamboo drying racks and a leaking irrigation pipe to one side while low fog banks roll through the bushes. Five adults, nobody else, all fully in frame with feet on the earth: a stocky Turkish man and a tall Kenyan woman hold thai pads; a Danish woman with a shaved head and a broad Mexican man hammer alternating right roundhouse kicks into them, driving the holders back a few meters and resetting. The fifth, a lean Indonesian man in a faded singlet, counts the round and slaps the pads. Grain, sweat, handheld reality — one continuous shot from a handheld camera slowly circling at chest height.

region: Utah salt flats and red-rock desert, USA
caption: Bright ceiling panels wash a hotel lobby in a red-rock resort town, its honed marble floor matte between sandstone columns and a dry fountain, haze breathing through the space while a moving spotlight sweeps slow bars of light. Four adults and no one else stand fully in frame, feet on the marble: a rangy Egyptian man in black shorts, a compact Peruvian woman in a purple sports top, a freckled Australian man, and a tall Cambodian woman with taped wrists. In two pairs they lock plum clinches, ripping knees into braced pads, pummeling for inside control, breaking and re-clamping across a couple of meters. One continuous shot from a static tripod camera at eye level, hard noir shadow and cold contrast.

region: Utah salt flats and red-rock desert, USA
caption: Neon strip lamps bolted to idle crusher rigs throw pink and cyan across a gravel pit floor of packed sand, stacked screening drums and a conveyor arm frozen overhead; the night air hangs completely still. Six adults work the pit alone, all fully in frame, feet on the sand: a burly Fijian man, a small Vietnamese woman in a yellow vest, a red-bearded Scot, a Colombian woman with sleeve tattoos, a bald Black man in a cutoff, and a wiry Iranian man. They stretch a brigade clear across the frame, hurling sloshing pails hand to hand while runners sprint the empties back, water flashing in the neon and pocking the sand. One continuous shot, a slow dolly-out revealing the lit pit, upbeat and joyful.

region: Utah salt flats and red-rock desert, USA
caption: Thin mist drifts low over a harvested wheat field on a Utah bench, straw stubble combed in long harvester lines, a leaning irrigation wheel and pink sunrise glow behind it. Torn paper scraps drift and tumble through the mist. Three adults in soft pastel training kit — a tall Ethiopian-American woman, a slim Argentinian man with a topknot, a broad silver-haired woman in lilac — take turns pacing off a run-up, sprinting twenty meters, hopping off one leg, stretching a long step, and landing the final jump in a tilled soft patch. All begin fully framed on the stubble; as the camera pans slowly from left to right, the topknot man sprints toward the lens and ends partly out of frame. One continuous shot.

region: Utah salt flats and red-rock desert, USA
caption: Dusty haze gilds a wide pale sand bar in a dry riverbed, towering varnished canyon walls rising on both sides and a bleached cottonwood snag half-buried at the bend; the air is utterly still. A single dancer occupies the emptiness: a Brazilian man in his thirties, long-muscled, barefoot, in loose black trousers and a rust-colored open shirt. Standing fully in frame with both feet in the sand, he opens with a slow port de bras, then attacks a long diagonal — chassé into soaring grand jeté, saut de chat, tour jeté, sand puffing at each landing as he covers the bar end to end. One continuous shot, the camera craning down from high above to eye level, vast and cinematic.

region: Utah salt flats and red-rock desert, USA
caption: Colored stage lights and moving spotlights slice haze-machine fog inside a converted hangar skate park, smooth plywood flats spread between a scuffed quarter pipe and a paint-scarred plywood wall. Four adults hold one patch of floor, all fully in frame with feet on the plywood: a lean Dominican man in a satin tracksuit, a muscular Norwegian woman in white, a heavyset Pakistani man in a green tee, and a short Chinese woman with pink-tipped hair. Trading turns on the same spot, they burn windmills, swing into flares, and spike into a spinning headspin, the others hyping and marking time in place. Onlookers watch from the raised deck behind the railing, off the floor. One continuous shot, a slow dolly-out, saturated dreamlike glow.

region: Utah salt flats and red-rock desert, USA
caption: Sunrise mist softens a reinforced concrete quay beside a salt-flat shipping canal, weathered containers stacked in blocks and a dormant gantry crane standing over cold bollards; nothing moves but the people. Six adults are alone here, all fully in frame with feet on the concrete: a shaven-headed Greek man in a black windbreaker, a tall Ghanaian woman in a maroon tracksuit, a stocky Uzbek man, a freckled Canadian woman with a ginger bun, a slim Brazilian man in yellow, and a broad Filipina in grey. Tight in one ring, they keep a ball alive — laces, thigh, chest, header — flicking it across the circle with rainbow scoops and around-the-world touches, feet barely leaving their spots.
