Blue-hour dusk over a small skatepark carved into a Peruvian hillside, its flat bottom a smooth grey concrete floor between a chipped quarter pipe and a rusted rail. Four adults in helmets and light pads — a muscular Colombian woman with a shaved side, a lean Vietnamese man in red, a tall Nordic woman with a blonde bun, a stocky Black man in navy — start fully framed, shoes on the concrete. They pair off and spar with foam-wrapped practice sticks: quick overhead cuts, sliding parries, a shoulder-dip counter, feet shuffling within a couple of metres. Fog banks slide over the rim of the bowl. Onlookers perch on the fence above. One continuous shot, a handheld camera circling slowly at chest height.

A tiny boxing ring fills a whitewashed gym in a Puno side street: worn canvas mat, sagging ropes wrapped in electrical tape, a hand-painted scoreboard nailed to the corner post. Torn paper scraps tumble through the air, kicked up and drifting, while harsh floodlights hit hard from one side and leave the far corner nearly black. Two adults hold the center, feet on the canvas: a slender Vietnamese woman in her late twenties in a silver slip dress, and a bearded Latino man in his forties, heavy-chested, in an open cream shirt. They stay in one spot, ripping continuous double spins and pulling each other through tight cross-body leads, canvas squeaking. Both stay fully in frame. One continuous shot, a slow dolly-in. Dreamy, music-video color.

A vast highland weaving hall, rows of idle looms receding into gloom, lint and torn paper pattern scraps tumbling through shafts of daylight from clerestory windows. Two adults hold the plank floor: a broad-shouldered Peruvian man in his forties, bare-armed in a grey vest, and a tall Nigerian woman with cropped hair in ochre trousers. Rooted to their spots, they spin long wooden staffs in blurring figure-eights, roll them across shoulders and behind the back, snap into low guards, then flick vertical tosses and catch them without a step. Dust hangs gold in the light; nobody else is in the hall. One continuous shot from a static tripod camera at eye level, both figures fully framed.

Mist hangs in a bamboo grove on a cloud-forest terrace above the Urubamba, culms creaking, packed earth strewn with dry curled leaves, a leaning stone shrine wrapped in faded ribbon. Beyond the stalks a roadside neon sign flickers and a highway searchlight sweeps, splashing color through the mist. One adult works the clearing: a lean Brazilian man in his late twenties, buzzed hair, barefoot, in charcoal shorts and a sleeveless white top, forearms dusty. Starting upright with both feet on the earth, he snaps no-hand cartwheels across a few meters and lands them into a front aerial, leaves bursting up at each touchdown. He stays fully in frame. One continuous shot from a static tripod at eye level. Bright, energetic, athletic tone.

A school gymnasium in Cajamarca holds a medium court of polished maple hardwood, its faded key lines overlapping older markings, folded bleachers strapped to the wall, a bent hoop with a knotted net. Air is completely still; only the people move. Bright even overhead lighting flattens everything into hard shadowless glare that the color grade pushes cold and noir. Four adults occupy a few meters of the boards: a broad-shouldered Māori man in black, a slim Ukrainian woman with a blonde plait in grey, a middle-aged Chinese man in maroon, and a tall Afro-Latina in olive. Paired off, they drive padded-stick sparring — fast diagonal strikes, blocks, slipping steps that squeak on the wood. All four stay fully in frame. One continuous shot, slow dolly-in.

Harsh noon sun hammers the polished granite pavers of a deserted civic plaza in a Peruvian mountain town, a dry bronze fountain at one edge, torn festival paper still tumbling across the stone. Five adults work the space: a heavy-set Andean man hoists a wiry white woman across his shoulders; a tall Somali woman lifts a compact Chinese man the same way; a grey-bearded Brazilian runs ahead calling the pace. All five are fully in frame at the start, feet on the granite, then the carriers sprint the length of the plaza, swap loads and haul back. Snow peaks stand beyond the rooftops; no one else is around. One continuous shot, a slow dolly-out revealing more of the plaza.

Warm tungsten work lamps pool on the steel plate floor of a dormant rolling mill high in the Andes, idle roller tables and a hanging chain hoist fading into shadow. Two adults own the aisle: a lean Peruvian sprinter in his thirties, black singlet, taped fingers, and a taller Russian woman with a platinum crop in a rust-red kit. Both stand fully framed on the plating, then attack a line of training hurdles set down the bay, lead leg snapping flat, trail knee driving through, five clearances each before they slow at the far end and jog back. Steam drifts from a wall vent through the lamplight. One continuous shot, the camera in a slow orbit around them.

A quiet contemporary gallery in Cusco: pale oak planks, white walls hung with large unframed canvases of blank colour fields, a single black bench. One woman stands alone in the middle, mid-twenties, Peruvian-Japanese, athletic, with a high ponytail, an orange mesh jersey and black shorts. Feet planted on the boards, fully in frame, she starts working an orange ball — pounding it low, whipping it behind her back, snapping it between her legs into a hesitation, then a sharp retreat dribble and a spin that keeps her inside a two-metre patch. The air is perfectly still under bright even ceiling lights. Nobody else is present. One continuous shot, a handheld camera circling slowly at chest height.

Golden hour on the outer concourse of a highland Peruvian stadium: stamped concrete plaza, shuttered turnstiles, a curling exit ramp. Six adults line up abreast — a rangy Bolivian man, a broad Kenyan woman with a shaved head, a red-haired Scot, a compact Thai woman, a bearded Argentine, a tall Black woman in white. Each stands fully framed with a battered steel drum, feet on the concrete. On a shout they tip the drums onto the rim and run them the full width of the plaza, hands slapping metal, barrels rumbling and wobbling, the leaders pulling ahead. The evening air is dead calm and the plaza empty. One continuous shot, the camera craning down from high above to eye level.

Midday sun burns down on a crushed red-brick tennis court behind a stone hacienda in the Andes, the net sagging, chalk lines faded, eucalyptus beyond. Four adults train in pairs on the clay, fully in frame from the first moment: a shaven-headed Samoan man holding thai pads for a lean Peruvian woman with taped shins, and a grey-haired Dutch woman holding for a young Black man in blue shorts. The strikers fire switch-step low kicks into the pad, follow with a driving mid-body round kick and a snapped push-kick, then reset, dust puffing red at every pivot. The air is motionless. One continuous shot, a slow dolly-in toward the four.

Soft grey daylight over a close-mown grass tennis lawn beside a highland Peruvian country club, the net posts bare, a hedge of red geraniums shedding petals that swirl low across the turf. Three adults crouch into starting blocks laid on the grass: a powerful Jamaican woman in yellow, a slim Korean man in white, a freckled Australian woman with a brown braid. All three are fully in frame, spikes set on the lawn. They rock into set position, then explode out low, driving four hard strides with shins nearly flat, decelerate after a few metres, walk back and reload twice more. One continuous shot, a slow dolly-out revealing the lawn, hedges and pale mountains behind.

Storm light presses down on a riverside esplanade of broad concrete slabs in a Peruvian valley town, a muddy river running fast below the parapet and steam curling from a drain vent at the wall. Four adults in bright kit stand fully framed on the slabs: a tall Ecuadorian woman with braids, a stocky Polish man, a lean Somali man in green, a sturdy white woman in pink. In two pairs they hammer a pepper drill — forearm bump, crisp set, controlled downward hit, dig and repeat — bodies dropping low, shoes scraping grit. Thunderheads pile over the ridge. One continuous shot, a slow dolly-in until the nearest player backpedals toward the lens and her legs slip out of frame.

Mist and thin rain at sunrise over the lawn quad of a highland Peruvian tech campus, glass blocks half-dissolved in cloud, a shallow sand landing pit cut into the grass. Two adults stand fully framed on the wet turf: a powerfully built Haitian man in a black compression top, and a tall Peruvian woman with a soaked black ponytail in grey. Each takes a long run-up down the grass, feet splashing through puddles, hits the board, drives one knee sky-high and sails into the sand, then trudges back for another attempt. Colleagues watch from a balcony rail behind the glass. One continuous shot, a slow dolly-out widening on the quad as the man jogs close and his head crops out of frame.

A single squash court in a small Andean sports club, pale hardwood scuffed with black shoe marks, a red service line, a glass back wall. Warm work lamps clamped above the walls light three adults standing fully framed on the boards: a curvy Peruvian woman with copper-dyed curls, a wiry Indian man in a striped tee, a tall blonde Danish woman in dungarees. Each swings soft weighted poi on cords, cutting fast butterfly weaves in front of the chest, flipping to trailing planes behind the shoulders and turning under the cords, each shifting a couple of metres across the boards. Friends crowd the glass wall behind, grinning. The air is still. One continuous shot, the camera craning down from high above to eye level.

Low golden sun across an open stretch of puna grassland, short tawny grass combed flat, dust streaming low over the ground, a line of dark hills far behind. Two adults set themselves side-on to the camera at the left edge of the frame, fully visible: a broad-chested Ethiopian man in a white singlet, and a strong-legged Peruvian woman with a black bun in a red crop and shorts. They settle into three-point crouches on the grass, freeze, then rip forward, hips low, arms tearing, and accelerate the whole width of the frame in long driving strides before easing off at the right edge. Nobody else is out here. One continuous shot, a static tripod camera at eye level.

Light rain slicks a packed gravel crossroads high in the sierra, water pooling in wheel ruts and mirroring the sky, a tilted wooden signpost with its lettering worn away, a low adobe wall, poplars behind. Six adults gather on the wet gravel: a burly Mongolian man in indigo, a small silver-haired Peruvian woman in white, a tall Dutch woman in her thirties in green, a wiry Cuban man in grey, a broad Turkish woman in black, and a young bearded Norwegian in red. Facing off in pairs, they cut with kendo shinai — sharp overhead strikes with long lunging steps, gravel crunching, water flicking up. All six stay fully in frame. One continuous shot, craning down from high above to eye level. Playful, upbeat.

An empty distribution warehouse aisle in the Andes: polished concrete running between towering bare pallet racks, a forgotten pallet of shrink-wrap at the end, torn packing paper and confetti-like label scraps tumbling slowly through the air under even white ceiling lights. Three adults hold one spot on the concrete, fully in frame: a slender Peruvian man with shoulder-length hair, a curvy Cameroonian woman in a lilac tracksuit, a middle-aged Korean woman with a silver crop. Two turn long ropes in opposite arcs while the third skips inside them, knees snapping high, adding quick criss-crosses and half-turns without leaving her footprint; then they swap. One continuous shot, a slow pan drifting left to right.

A ballet rehearsal studio converted from a chapel in a Peruvian mountain town: black marley vinyl underfoot, a barre along a cracked plaster wall, tall mirrors turned to face away. A single hard floodlight rakes in from the left, and steam seeps from a floor vent across the vinyl. Three adults work a low padded box: a compact Peruvian woman with a tight bun, a tall Angolan man in black, a broad Russian woman with a bleached crop. Standing fully framed, they take short run-ups, punch both hands onto the box and shoot their legs through in fast kong vaults, landing clean and circling back within a few metres. One continuous shot, static tripod camera at eye level.

Deep under an Andean hillside, a damp concrete bunker hall lit by strings of warm work lamps, seeping walls, a rusted blast door propped open. Six adults in white fencing jackets and mesh masks — a heavyset Peruvian man, a slight Vietnamese woman, a tall ginger-bearded man, a Black woman with a shaved head, a wiry Chilean man, a silver-haired white woman — begin fully framed, shoes on the wet floor. Three bouts run at once, blades clattering: quick advances, deep lunges, circular parries and snapping ripostes that chase opponents ten metres down the hall. The air is dead still. One continuous shot, a slow orbit around them as one fencer presses forward past the lens, her mask cropping out of frame.

A cramped village dojo in the Peruvian highlands, green tatami squares taped at the seams, worn judo belts hung on nails, a plain clock on the wall under flat even ceiling lights. Two adults trade a battle in the middle of the mats: a burly Peruvian man in his fifties, sleeveless, greying hair, and a lean Kenyan woman in her twenties with box braids and a black tank. Both stay fully in frame, bare feet gripping the tatami. He answers her with a heavy stomp series and crossing arm swings; she replies with jab-outs, a shuddering torso hit and a lurching buck-hop, both ranging a couple of metres. The air is completely still. One continuous shot, handheld camera circling slowly at chest height.

An off-season ice rink stripped of ice: a painted concrete slab ringed by scuffed dasher boards under bright even ceiling lights, big drying fans roaring and dragging dust and loose paper across the floor. Five adults in mismatched training gear stand fully framed on the slab — a stocky Peruvian man, a tall Nigerian woman with braids, a bearded Ukrainian in a hoodie, a small Filipina in a headband, a lanky Black man in grey. Each drills a ball in a tight square: hard low pounds, a snap between the legs, a behind-the-back wrap, a hesitation and a hard first step. Locals watch from the seating tiers. One continuous shot, handheld camera circling at chest height as one player drives past the lens, half-cropped.

A cavernous bus depot hall in the Andes, empty numbered bays striped in yellow across cracked asphalt, one coach up on jacks in the far corner, strings of warm tungsten work lamps overhead. A single man dances on one bay stripe: mid-thirties, Punjabi, stocky and strong, in a bright turquoise kurta over track pants, a printed scarf knotted at his waist. Fully in frame from the first moment, feet on the asphalt, he bounces his shoulders, springs into high double hops with both hands flicking above his head, drops into a squat and kicks one leg out, then rises again, never leaving his spot. The hall is silent and still. One continuous shot, camera tracking sideways at a steady walking pace.

A vast empty parking lot on the outskirts of a highland Peruvian market town, faded asphalt with ghost lines, a bent light mast, torn plastic banners snapping on a wire fence in the dusty afternoon wind. Five adults in dark hakama and armour hold the middle of the lot, fully framed, bare feet flat on the tarmac: a barrel-chested Japanese man, a lean Peruvian woman, a tall Nigerian man, a compact white woman with grey hair, a young Korean man. They pair off and rotate, driving forward with sliding stamping steps, wooden shinai cracking down onto head and wrist targets, shouting on each strike. Grit hazes the air. One continuous shot, the camera craning down from high above to eye level.

Golden hour lays long copper light across a volcanic ash plain beneath a scarred cinder cone, fine grey ash unmarked but for one line of footprints, bleached stumps standing where a forest burned. The air is utterly still. A single adult occupies the plain: a powerfully built Mexican woman in her late twenties, thick thighs, hair braided tight, wearing an electric blue crop top and black shorts, ash caked to her calves. Leaning hard against a resistance band anchored to a buried stake, she grinds out driving resisted sprints a few meters forward, ash exploding from each stride, then walks back and attacks again. She stays fully in frame with feet on the ash. One continuous shot, a slow dolly-in. Bright, punchy sports-ad energy.

Misty sunrise inside a highland football stadium, mown stripes silvered with dew, floodlight pylons fading into cloud, grit drifting low over the turf near the touchline. One woman occupies the centre circle: early forties, Chinese-Peruvian, powerfully built, hair tied back, wearing a crimson sash over a black training top and loose gold trousers. Fully in frame from the first moment, boots on the grass, she sinks into a deep wide crouch, holds, then explodes upward into a pouncing leap, lands soft, pivots low and springs again, clawed hands stabbing forward, covering only a few metres. Scattered early spectators watch from the lower stand. One continuous shot, the camera craning down from high above to eye level.

A converted warehouse gym in Arequipa: black rubber tiles, steel racks loaded with bumper plates, a chalk bucket, climbing ropes hanging slack. Shafts of daylight drop from high industrial windows and print bright rectangles on the floor, dust hanging in them. The room is otherwise still. One adult stands in a bright rectangle: a tall Ukrainian woman in her twenties, long neck, ash-blonde hair in a low bun, wearing a smoke-grey leotard and rolled-down black tights over bare feet. Holding a single spot, she spins clean double pirouettes, then whips into a fouetté sequence, working leg snapping out and in, spotting hard, arms opening and closing. She stays fully in frame. One continuous shot, handheld, slowly circling at chest height. Dreamy, soft-glow music-video color.

A drained dry dock at a lake shipyard on the altiplano, its floor slick wet concrete between blocked keel supports and a rust-streaked caisson gate. Harsh floodlights on masts turn the puddles white; fireworks bloom silently over the lake in the distance. Four adults in worn work clothes run a relay along the dock floor: a squat Aymara man, a tall freckled woman with a ginger plait, a lanky Sudanese man, a broad Chinese woman in a headscarf. All start fully framed, boots on the concrete, then sprint their legs and slap a steel bar into waiting hands, spray flying. Nobody else is here. One continuous shot, camera tracking sideways at a steady walking pace.

Soft overcast daylight flattens a wide firm sand flat along a highland lake, packed damp sand ribbed by receded water, reed beds hissing at the margin, a beached wooden skiff half sunk in silt. Petals torn from lakeside shrubs swirl low across the ground. A single adult stands fully in frame on the sand: a wiry Peruvian man in his forties, weathered face, close grey hair, in navy swim shorts. He settles prone, then at a shout snaps up, sprints hard across many meters of the flat and launches into a full extended dive to snatch an upright rubber flag, skidding through wet sand. He stays fully in frame. One continuous shot, panning slowly from left to right. Dreamy, muted, cinematic.

Between two long trellised rows of a highland Peruvian vineyard, the tractor lane is compacted dust-grey soil, vines heavy with dark fruit, an irrigation pump shed venting white steam at the row's end. Six adults pair up in the hazy afternoon wind: a sinewy Chilean man, a tall Ghanaian woman, a red-cheeked Belgian woman, a stocky Quechua man, a young Black man in a vest, a broad Korean woman. All six stand fully framed, shoes on the soil, then three drop to their hands while their partners grab their ankles and drive them down the lane in a scrambling wheelbarrow race, arms slapping dust, turning back after a few metres. One continuous shot, a slow pan from left to right.

Thick fog fills a sunken plaza in the banking quarter of a highland Peruvian city, black granite paving darkened with damp, a dry fountain basin and glass towers dissolving above. Dead eucalyptus leaves skate low across the stone. Four adults are anchored on their own squares, fully in frame: a heavily muscled Brazilian woman in black, a wiry Peruvian man in a grey tee, a bald Nigerian man, a tall Slavic woman with a blonde braid. Each grips a thick rope looped to a bollard and hammers alternating waves, then double-arm slams that whip the ropes into blurred coils, knees bent, feet never shifting. One continuous shot, a slow pan travelling from left to right.

Inside an unfinished road tunnel bored through an Andean ridge, the floor is raw grey shotcrete, ribbed steel arches overhead, a coiled ventilation duct running along one wall and venting warm steam. Strings of tungsten work lamps throw amber light down the bore. Five adults in training kit stand fully framed on the shotcrete: a broad Peruvian woman with a topknot, a lean Somali man, a bearded Portuguese man, a small Japanese woman in yellow, a tall Black woman in a blue vest. On a whistle they explode into shuttle sprints between orange cones, slapping the ground at each turn, chests heaving, five metres out and five back. One continuous shot, camera tracking sideways at a steady walking pace.

A shipyard fabrication shed above a mountain lake, floor of rust-stained steel plate, half-welded hull sections looming, a gantry rail and stacked plate offcuts. One floodlight blasts in from the left, cutting a hard white wedge and leaving the rest in blue-black shadow. A single man works the lit patch: late twenties, Peruvian, tall and rangy, in a black singlet and pale shorts, hair damp. Fully framed with both feet on the plate, he steps left-right-close, swings both arms back, hurls himself upward and slings his hitting hand through the air in a full spike swing, lands, resets, repeats harder. Nothing else moves in the shed. One continuous shot, handheld camera circling slowly at chest height.

A converted fencing hall in an Andean university: a metallic piste strip laid over dark rubber flooring, tall industrial fans at the far end pushing dust and loose sheets of paper past the walls, bright even lights overhead. Two adults in white judo jackets stand fully framed on the strip: a broad, thick-necked Peruvian woman in her thirties with a black bun, and a slim, older Japanese-Brazilian man with grey at his temples. They drill an entry over and over — she grips his lapel and sleeve, turns in, loads him across her hip and lifts, and he rolls out and rises, then they swap roles, breathing hard, staying on the strip. One continuous shot, handheld camera circling slowly at chest height.

Inside an empty stone-walled barn high in the Peruvian sierra, six adults begin flat-footed on wide plank wood, one square meter each. Tungsten work lamps on tripods pour amber across the boards; shredded festival paper tumbles from the rafters. A broad Quechua man in a maroon tank whips a cheat-set swing kick into a full airborne twist. A lean Black woman with locs answers with a gainer flash. A silver-haired white man in grey sweats pops a back tuck with a half turn; a stocky Filipina in denim drills hook-kick-to-hyperspin; two mestizo brothers in orange and teal trade low aerial twists, landing on their own planks. One continuous shot, handheld camera circling slowly at chest height, gritty documentary grain, all six fully in frame.

An abandoned brick factory hall in the sierra: floor of broken brick tile, cracked and shifting underfoot, two beehive kilns with collapsed mouths, a conveyor frame stripped of belts. Shafts of daylight fall through shattered clerestory windows, and a big derelict fan still turning in the draft stirs paper and brick dust through the beams. One adult runs the hall: a broad-shouldered Peruvian man in his forties, shaved head, in heavy navy trousers, a soot-marked shirt and boots. Starting upright and fully framed, he sprints the length of the floor unreeling a canvas hose behind him, dust exploding at each step, then slams it down and charges the camera, ending partly out of frame. One continuous shot, handheld, slowly circling at chest height. Dreamy, hazy.

Floodlights bleach an old stone threshing floor tucked behind a Seoul hillside village, stacked clay jars along one wall, black tiled eaves cutting the night above. Three adults begin fully in frame, feet planted on worn flagstone: a tall Korean woman in a charcoal wrap dress, a stocky Black man in an emerald sleeveless top, a lean older white woman with silver braids in deep plum. In one continuous shot the camera pans slowly left to right while they carve overlapping ribbon spirals, snapping into chaîné turns and low split leaps within a few meters. The braided woman then advances toward the lens, her shoulder and trailing ribbon passing partly out of frame. Air is dead still, shadows hard and inky.

Blue hour glows over a broad hardpan plateau east of Seoul, sparse scrub tufts, a rusted radio mast pinned to the far rim, valley haze below. Three adults stand fully visible on the flat, dusty ground: a compact Korean man in a lemon tracksuit, a broad-shouldered Latina woman in orange shorts and white tee, a wiry South Asian man in sky-blue. One continuous shot, the camera tracking sideways at an easy walking pace as they explode into sprints across many meters, then slam into comic frozen poses — arms flung, one balanced on a single foot — before bursting off again, laughing. Dry leaves and petals skitter low across the hardpan around their shoes. All three stay fully framed.

Bruised storm clouds stack over a Seoul rooftop terrace of grey concrete pavers, a bent antenna cluster in one corner, glass towers crowding the horizon before the rain lands. A single adult man — mid-thirties, Korean, sinewy, in a faded maroon hoodie and black shorts — stays fully in frame, sneakers on the pavers, working a basketball through hard crossovers, between-the-legs strings and sharp pull-back retreats inside a couple of meters. Stray snowflakes drift oddly through the last blades of light between buildings. Spectators watch from a railed walkway one roof over, never on his terrace. One continuous shot from a static tripod at eye level, unpolished and documentary-plain.

Stadium-style floodlights blaze across a wide flat of tight-packed dark pebbles beside a Seoul ring road, stacked shipping crates and a chain fence marking the edge. Two adults hold one spot, both fully in frame with feet firmly down: a burly Korean man in a canary singlet, and a tall Nigerian woman in white with turquoise sleeves. One continuous shot, the camera tracking sideways at a steady walking pace as they take turns dropping into a low glide across the throwing circle, whipping hip and chest open and punching the shot skyward with a bright shout, then bouncing on their toes to reset. Behind them distant traffic streaks into long red-and-white light trails. Bright, cheerful, energetic.

Sunrise mist hangs low over a cracked pale clay playa west of Seoul, salt-white fissures running to the horizon, one leaning power pylon and a rusted irrigation pump breaking the emptiness. Three adults start fully framed, bare feet and soft shoes flat on the clay: a Korean woman with a high bun in coral, a middle-aged Black man in cream, a freckled redhead in mint. The camera cranes down from high above to eye level in one continuous shot as they launch a chain of grand jetés along a long diagonal, covering many meters with soaring split leaps and running assemblés. None of them leaves the frame. Dust and dry petals swirl low, kicked into pale ribbons by their landings. Sunny, buoyant, commercial.

Golden hour paints a closed overpass north of Seoul, lane paint bleached to ghost stripes, dented crash barriers along both edges, cranes glowing beyond the guardrail. Three adults appear fully in frame on the asphalt: a muscular Korean man in a black compression top, a tall Ethiopian woman in violet, a stocky white man in grey. In one continuous shot a handheld camera circles slowly at chest height while two of them lean hard into resistance bands anchored by the third, chopping short powerful strides that drag them a few meters before the anchor releases and they burst free. The air is windless and warm. The violet-clad woman then charges the lens, torso filling and leaving the frame's edge.

Rain hammers a tar-and-gravel loft rooftop in Seoul while golden light slips through torn clouds, streaking the puddles around a squat brick water tank and a row of rusted vents. Three adults stay fully in frame, boots planted on the gritty membrane: a broad Korean woman in a soaked lime jacket, a lean Middle Eastern man in orange, a grey-bearded Black man in navy. One continuous shot, the camera tracking sideways at a steady walking pace as they race with wide shovels, biting into a gravel heap and flinging glittering wet arcs into a bin two meters away, feet skidding and resetting, water bursting under every stomp. Bright, punchy, sports-ad energy, breath and spray flying.

Blue hour drains color from an abandoned drive-in lot on Seoul's fringe: cracked asphalt speckled with gravel, a peeling white screen, rows of dead speaker posts. Strong wind whips torn banner lines and loose plastic sheeting into snapping arcs. Three adults hold a single small patch of ground, fully in frame, feet down: a Korean woman in a slit red dress, a tall Brazilian man in a black shirt, a silver-haired white woman in graphite. One continuous shot orbits slowly around them as they fire off triple spins, cross-body leads and hammerlock turns, heels scraping the asphalt. A scattering of onlookers watches from a raised concession terrace beyond the lot, never on the asphalt. Moody, shadow-cut, neo-noir.

Sunrise mist rolls off the Han across a festival pier decked in painted steel plate, fat mooring bollards and a string of unlit paper lanterns swaying above the water. Three adults are fully in frame from the first moment, cleats ringing on the metal: a compact Korean man in a bright yellow kit, a tall Kenyan woman in white and red, a stocky Portuguese man in teal. The camera cranes down from high above to eye level in one continuous shot as they whip crosses in and smash full volleys and half-volley drives at a portable net, sprinting a few meters between strikes. Cherry petals swirl low across the plate around their feet. Cheerful, sunlit, commercial gloss.

Overcast light flattens a trodden red-earth walkway running between clipped tea terraces on hills south of Seoul, a tin roasting shed nearby breathing steam from its vents, drying racks tilted along the slope. A single adult — a Korean woman in her forties, lean and wiry, black leggings, faded rust windbreaker, hair knotted tight — begins fully in frame with both shoes on the packed earth. One continuous shot orbits slowly around her as she attacks a flat agility ladder: high-knee ins-and-outs, lateral shuffles, icky-shuffle patterns, feet drumming the dirt within a couple of meters. Steam drifts across the frame. Near the end she strides toward the camera and her torso crops out of frame. Raw, handheld documentary texture.

A deserted hotel lobby in Seoul: polished marble floor, brass planters holding stiff palms, a long lacquered reception counter swallowed by shadow. Low practice lamps carve deep pools of darkness, gold rims on every edge, air perfectly still. Two adults stand fully in frame, feet flat on the stone: a tall Korean man in a wide-shouldered ivory suit, and a curvy Afro-Caribbean woman in a black bodysuit with long gloves. One continuous shot, the camera craning down from high overhead to eye level as they hold a single spot, snapping duckwalks into hand performance, whipping fast spins and dropping into sharp death drops before floating back up. Dreamy, slow-blooming, music-video haze.

Soft overcast light fills a worked-out sand and gravel pit outside Seoul: terraced grey walls, an idle rusted conveyor, tire ruts pressed into packed sand. Far beyond the rim, fireworks bloom silently in the pale sky. Two adults are fully in frame, barefoot on the sand: a slim Korean man in a washed-blue tank, and a strong-shouldered white woman with cropped bleached hair in a mustard tee. One continuous shot, the camera dollying slowly toward them as they alternate leapfrog vaults, each crouching low while the other plants both hands on their back and swings clear, landing in a spray of grit, then crouching in turn — the pair travelling only a few meters. Dreamy, drifting, softly lit.

Golden hour sets a cut wheat field near Seoul alight, straw stubble bristling underfoot, round bales throwing long shadows, a leaning scarecrow post against a blue ridgeline. Odd snowflakes drift through the low beams. Three adults occupy one tight patch, fully in frame, boots in the stubble: a heavy-set Korean man in a black singlet, a tall Somali woman in deep green, a grey-templed white man in charcoal. One continuous shot; the camera descends on a crane from high above down to eye level while each in turn coils into a full discus wind-up, sweeping a slow preliminary swing, spiralling through the turn and firing the disc away with a grunt, then bracing hard. Cold shadows, moody contrast, neo-noir stillness.

Light rain glazes a pale sand bar in a dry riverbed under a Seoul bypass, concrete pilings marching overhead, a steaming drain pipe venting white vapor along the bank, driftwood snagged in the shallows. One adult — a Korean man in his late twenties, rangy, shaved head, in a soaked grey vest and black briefs-cut shorts — starts fully in frame, spikes set in wet sand. One continuous shot as the camera dollies slowly out, revealing more of the riverbed while he drives through a row of hurdles staggered down the bar, lead leg snapping over each rail, three strides between, covering a long stretch of ground. Steam curls across him. Grainy, unglamorous, documentary honesty.

Daylight falls in hard shafts through high clerestory windows of a converted warehouse skate park in Seoul, plywood quarter pipes curving in the gloom, a taped-off flat pad of smooth plywood at the center. Flickering neon tubes and a sweeping searchlight rig throw restless color across the ramps. One adult — a broad-built Filipino man in his thirties, tattooed forearms, white tank and loose red joggers — stands fully in frame, feet fixed on one spot on the plywood. One continuous shot, the camera holding a slow orbit around him as he spins weighted poi into fast weaves, butterflies and behind-the-back turns, whipping his torso through crisp half-turns while the cords blur into bright discs. Bright, kinetic, sports-ad snap.

Dust-hazed afternoon wind sweeps a container quay on Seoul's river port: stacked steel boxes in faded colors, gantry crane legs straddling the reinforced concrete, mooring lines groaning. Sweeping searchlights and a flickering neon strip on the terminal stutter through the haze. Two adults stand fully in frame, cleats on the concrete: a powerful Korean man in a black long-sleeve, and a tall Jamaican woman in silver-grey. One continuous shot, the camera dollying slowly out to reveal the quay's depth as she rips a long route down the pier, planting hard, snatching the ball over her shoulder at full stride while he sprints in coverage. She then keeps driving toward the lens and finishes partly out of frame. Cold, cinematic, neo-noir.

Rain lacquers a compacted gravel median walk down a wide Seoul boulevard, plane trees dripping overhead, iron benches empty, lamplight smeared across the wet stones. The air is otherwise motionless. A single adult — a broad-shouldered Korean woman around forty, in a rain-dark teal keeper jersey, padded gloves, black shorts — stays fully in frame, boots pressed into the gravel. One continuous shot, the camera tracking sideways at a steady walking pace as she throws herself low to smother a rolling ball, pops up spitting water, dives high the other way with both gloves, and scrambles back to a set stance, all inside a few meters. Muted noir palette, slick reflections, shadowed and severe.

Harsh noon sun bleaches a small grass airstrip outside Seoul, its mown turf striped by mower passes, a faded windsock hanging dead on its pole, a corrugated tin hangar shimmering at the far end. Nothing stirs but the performer. One adult — a lithe Korean man in his twenties, gold silk sash over loose white trousers, bare chest, hair tied back — stands fully in frame, feet on the turf. One continuous shot, the camera panning slowly from left to right as he sinks into deep lion-dance crouches, then explodes into long pouncing leaps that carry him far across the strip, landing in wide stances, twisting, springing again. Dreamlike, sun-drunk, gauzy music-video air.

Dead booths stand in a row across a disused toll plaza on Seoul's outer ring, blue-hour light draining the concrete lanes and their faded white arrows, weeds pushing through the expansion joints beneath a dead overhead gantry. The air hangs still. Five adults stay fully in frame, shoes on the painted concrete: a wiry Korean man in a rolled-sleeve shirt, a curvy Colombian woman in fuchsia, a tall Korean woman in slate, a grizzled white man in denim, a broad Black man in cream. One continuous shot with the camera dollying slowly toward them while they trade partners across a few meters — copa turns, inside-turn cross-body leads, quick hand changes and shoulder shimmies. Plain, unstyled, documentary observation.

Midday sun hammers the raw poured concrete slab of an unfinished Seoul tower, rebar stubs bristling at the edges, orange safety netting bellying against the skyline, stacked formwork panels casting knife shadows. The air is entirely still. Three adults are fully in frame, boots on the slab: a lean Korean woman in white, a heavyset Māori man in navy, a tall blond man in faded red. One continuous shot, the camera panning slowly left to right as they surge across the long deck, chipping the ball up, meeting it with full-swing volleys that crack against a plywood target, chasing rebounds many meters downfield. Bleached highlights, glassy haze, a floating dreamlike music-video calm.

Noon glare floods the flat concrete stage of a hillside amphitheater above Seoul, empty tiered stone seating rising behind, cable spools and a dented speaker stack shoved into the wings. Far below, expressway traffic drags long light trails through the valley haze. Three adults are fully in frame, palms and shoes on the concrete: a compact Korean man in a grey tee, a tall Vietnamese woman in olive, a broad-chested white woman in faded orange. One continuous shot, the camera sweeping a slow pan from left to right while two pair up for hard wheelbarrow crawling — hands slapping fast across a few meters, legs gripped high — then swap so the third takes a turn. Sweaty, plain, documentary looseness.

Midday sun burns over a flat alpine meadow bench high above a Seoul valley, short flowering turf clipped by wind, a boulder cairn at the edge, blue ridges stacked to the horizon. Nothing moves in the air. Four adults hold one small patch, all fully in frame with boots on the turf: a thick-necked Korean man in black, a tall Sudanese woman in white, a stocky Argentinian woman in maroon, a bearded ginger man in grey. One continuous shot, the camera tracking sideways at a steady walking pace while each in turn crouches, glides low across the mark and punches the shot out with a bark of effort, then resets on the same spot. Flat, unfiltered documentary look.

Hard noon light strikes a cobblestone roadway across an old stone arch bridge on Seoul's outskirts, mossy parapets, iron lantern posts, glare bouncing off the river beneath. The day is windless and silent. Four adults occupy one tight spot, fully in frame, bare feet on the rounded cobbles: a compact Korean man in a white judogi, a tall Russian woman in blue, a broad Korean woman in white, a lean Turkish man in blue. One continuous shot, a handheld camera circling slowly at chest height as they drill hip throws in pairs — grip, turn in, load the hip, sweep the partner over and steer them down — then swap roles and repeat. Deep shadows, bleached stone, austere neo-noir mood.

A small Seoul yoga studio glows under low practice lamps, deep shadows collecting between rolled mats and a rack of wooden blocks; loose paper scraps and confetti tumble through the beams from an open transom. Two adults are fully in frame, bare feet on light bamboo flooring: a stocky Korean woman in a bright coral crop top and black shorts, and a tall lanky Indian man in a white tank and blue shorts. One continuous shot, a slow orbit circling the pair as they fold one leg up, arms crossed, and hop into each other with sharp shoulder bumps, hopping and jostling across two meters, laughing, both fighting to stay upright. High-energy, punchy, sports-ad brightness.

Low practice lights cut deep shadow across a Seoul wrestling room: a wide red foam mat, padded walls, a tattered rope hanging in one corner, big floor fans dragging dust and loose paper across the surface. Three adults stand fully in frame, bare feet on the foam: a thick-set Korean man in a navy singlet, a tall Ukrainian woman in maroon, a compact Black man in charcoal. Held in one continuous take, the camera glides sideways at a steady walking pace as they clamp one ankle behind them and hop into collisions — shoulders driving, chests thudding, bodies staggering a few meters before one crashes down and springs up grinning. Heroic contrast, dust in the beams, epic and cinematic weight.

A decommissioned rail viaduct in Seoul now carries an elevated linear park, tapered concrete planks underfoot, planted grasses in steel troughs, the last blue light after sunset thinning overhead while expressway traffic below smears into long trails. Three adults are fully in frame, shoes on the planks: a slight Korean woman in a black bomber, a tall Iranian man in olive, a heavyset white woman with a shaved head in denim. One continuous shot, the camera holding a slow orbit while they whip glowing poi through windmills, buzzsaw spins and thread-the-needle passes, pivoting hard and stepping a couple of meters along the walkway. Plain, handheld, documentary flatness; only sweat and rope-blur.

Harsh floodlights blast in from one end of a tiled pedestrian underpass in Seoul, ribbed concrete ceiling, chipped wall tiles, a dead vending alcove halfway along. Industrial fans stir litter and grey dust into the beams. Two adults stand fully in frame, shoes squeaking on the tiled concrete: a barrel-chested Korean man in a soaked black tee, and a tall Polish woman with a braid in a rust singlet. One continuous shot, a slow pan travelling left to right while they lean back on a thick hemp rope, hauling in ragged surges, heels skidding a meter each way, until one rips a huge heave and both stagger and crash down hard. Towering shadows, epic cinematic scale.

Bright overhead lamps flood a long aisle of a commercial glass greenhouse outside Seoul: benched seedling trays receding in rows, misting pipes hissing above, condensation crawling down the panes while neon glow and a sweeping searchlight flicker through the glass from the road. Six adults are fully in frame, boots on the wide concrete walkway: two Korean men and a Korean woman in dark work shirts, a tall Ghanaian woman in grey, a stocky Mexican man in green, a lean white man in navy. Across one continuous take the camera moves sideways at a steady walking pace while they shoulder a heavy timber and jog it far down the aisle, counting cadence, then slam it down in unison. Hard shadows, cold noir tone.

Dusty afternoon wind scours the open top level of a Seoul parking garage: painted concrete bays with peeling yellow lines, a squat stair tower, low dust snaking across the deck in pale ribbons. One adult — a broad-shouldered Korean woman in her thirties, muscular forearms, red technical tee, black cargo pants, hair in a tight knot — starts fully in frame, boots on the concrete. One continuous shot; the camera paces sideways beside her at a steady walking pace as she rips a flat hose off a reel and sprints its full length across the deck, the canvas snapping out behind her, then plants her feet, slams the nozzle down and drops into a crouch. Bright, punchy, sports-ad drive.

Noon sun blazes off rounded cobblestones in an old-town square in Seoul, a capped stone well at its center, shuttered hanok shopfronts with dark timber beams closed on every side, air utterly still. Three adults stand fully in frame, bare feet spread on the stones: a thick-limbed Korean man in a grey rash guard, a tall Bulgarian woman in black, a compact Black man in maroon. The camera slides sideways at a steady walking pace through one continuous shot as they drill double-leg takedowns in rotating pairs — a hard level change, a driving penetration step, a lift and controlled drive a couple of meters before the finish, then an instant reset. Monumental shadows, epic cinematic grandeur.

Neon tubes and colored stage lamps wash a truck loading dock bay in a Seoul warehouse, magenta and cyan sliding over stacked pallets, a half-raised roller door, a rubber dock bumper streaked black. The air is dead calm. One adult — a lean Korean man in his late twenties, close-cropped hair, black kit with silver trim — stands fully in frame, boots planted on sealed concrete, never leaving his spot. One continuous take keeps the camera drifting sideways at a steady walking pace while he juggles a football in a fast unbroken string: laces, thigh, thigh, shoulder, header, a flick behind the standing leg and a catch on the instep. Deep saturated shadows, monumental, cinematic scale.

Floodlights on portable masts carve a cold white oval out of a hot-air balloon launch field near Seoul: mown short grass, folded envelopes bundled beside wicker baskets, a black tree line beyond the reach of the beams. Nothing else moves in the night air. Two adults are fully in frame, running shoes on the grass: a tall Korean woman with a long ponytail in a charcoal bodysuit, and a broad Greek man in a dark grey tee. A slow orbit swings around them in one continuous shot while they tear across the field in long sprints and galloping side-steps, meters of silver streamer snapping and coiling behind each of them. Hard-edged shadows, cool blue-black neo-noir.

Thick fog drowns a chalk-turf plateau on the ridges outside Seoul, springy grass over pale stone, scattered flint, a half-seen barbed fence dissolving into the white. Rain streaks through the murk and splashes in shallow puddles across the turf. One adult — a Korean woman in her early thirties, athletic, in a bright tangerine jersey and white shorts, soaked hair stuck to her cheek — begins fully in frame with both shoes on the ground. One continuous shot, a slow dolly-out steadily widening onto more of the plateau while she drills spike approaches within a few meters: three-step run, hard double-leg plant, huge arm swing and a cracking contact. Finally she runs at the lens and passes half out of frame. Cheerful, bouncy energy.

Hazy wind-blown afternoon light spreads across a bare grey granite plateau above a rocky coast east of Seoul, wind-scoured slabs seamed with quartz, a leaning stone cairn, waves smashing white on the rocks far below. One adult — a stocky Korean man in his forties, in a sun-faded yellow jersey, grey pants and a worn glove — stands fully in frame, cleats on the granite. Throughout one continuous shot the camera travels sideways at a steady walking pace as he winds up, lifts his knee high, strides long and fires a hard throw down the slab, then jogs after the ball dozens of paces to a new mark and repeats the delivery. Sunlit, upbeat, breezy commercial polish.

Neon from a roadside strip beyond a low dike stains a drained rice paddy near Seoul in magenta and green, the cracked dry mud tiled into curling plates, stubble rows still visible, dust hissing low across the surface in the night wind. One adult — a wiry Korean man in his twenties, bare-chested with a black waistband and taped wrists — starts fully in frame, feet on the mud. One continuous shot in which the camera descends on a crane from high above to eye level as he runs a long tumbling pass far across the paddy: hurdle, round-off, whipping back handspring, then a high back tuck that lands hard, dust jumping around his heels. Cold shadows, saturated noir color.

Warm tungsten work lamps hang over the infield of a Seoul velodrome, the steep timber banking curving away on all sides, a flat grey concrete floor at the center, steam drifting from a vent grate near the tunnel mouth. One adult — a compact Korean man in his late twenties, in a white tee, olive cargos and a knit cap — stays fully in frame, sneakers on the concrete, holding one spot. Onlookers lean over the safety railing high on the banking, never on the infield floor. One continuous shot rides sideways at a steady walking pace while he drops into windmills, snaps into airy flares and screws into a spinning headspin. Bright, vivid, sports-ad punch.

Light rain glosses the sawn white marble floor of a quarry cut into hills north of Seoul, blade-scored benches stepping up the pale walls, a wire-saw rig parked in the shadow, snowflakes wandering through the work lights' beams. Four adults hold a tight patch, all fully in frame, shoes on the wet stone: a lean Korean woman in black, a towering Sudanese man in white, a stocky Spanish man in grey, a silver-haired white woman in navy. One continuous shot: handheld, the lens prowls a slow circle at chest height while each hammers a basketball through low crossovers, between-the-legs strings and behind-the-back snaps, staying on one spot. Cold reflections, ink-black shadows, neo-noir gloom.

Floodlights on a fishing village square near the Seoul coast throw a hard white pool over red brick pavers, a stone water trough at one side, drying nets hung on poles, surf booming against the seawall just beyond. Four adults are fully in frame, shoes on the brick: a compact Korean man in a black tee, a tall Nigerian woman in gold, a stocky white woman in red, a lanky Korean man in grey. One continuous shot, a slow dolly-in creeping toward them as they blast rubber balls at each other, twisting away, ducking and rolling across a few meters. Late in the take the gold-clad woman lunges at the lens and finishes cropped at the frame edge. Grand, dramatic, cinematic.

Harsh noon sun bleaches the rolled clay centre strip of a cricket ground squeezed between apartment towers on the Han riverside in Seoul, sightscreens grey, stumps leaning. Torn festival paper tumbles across the clay in the heat haze. One man is alone out there: late thirties, Korean, shaven-headed and heavily built through the shoulders, in a black tee and dark shorts, chalk on his palms. He stands fully framed, bare feet on the strip, then kicks into a handstand and walks the length of the pitch on his hands, ribs locked, adding a run of sharp double-hand hops before dropping down at the far end. One continuous shot, handheld camera circling slowly at chest height, contrast hard, shadows inky.

Soft overcast light lies flat over a compacted red dirt access strip running between rows of tilted solar panels outside Seoul, grey inverter cabinets humming at intervals, a service road beyond where headlights drag long trails through the hazy grey distance. Two adults are fully in frame, hands and toes pressed into the dirt: a lean Korean man in a pale grey tee, and a strong-built Danish woman in a faded lilac tank. One continuous shot as the camera dollies slowly out, opening up the endless array while they race bear-crawling far down the strip, hips low, palms slapping the earth, kicking up fine red dust and pulling ahead of one another. Soft, floating, dreamy music-video haze.

A foundry casting hall on the Tibetan plateau, floor of packed black moulding sand raked smooth, daylight dropping in dusty shafts from high dirty windows. Two adults train in a bright patch of that light: a rangy Tibetan man in his twenties with a shaved head and loose orange shorts, and a stocky German woman in her forties with a blonde crop and a white rash guard. Both start fully framed, bare feet printing the sand. She holds paddles high; he skips a switch step, snaps a jumping front kick into the pad, lands, then whips a spinning back kick, and they trade roles. The air is perfectly still. One continuous shot, camera craning down from high above to eye level.

Three adults, alone on a flat dark basalt pavement veined with cracked hexagonal slabs high on the plateau, stay planted in a tight triangle barely a metre wide. A wiry Brazilian man in his twenties wears a yellow windbreaker; a broad-shouldered Nigerian woman in her thirties wears a magenta tracksuit; a lean Japanese man in his forties wears white overalls. One continuous shot: they bounce through bright toprock, then drop hands to stone and spin crisp six-step footwork, kick out, pop back up laughing, feet never leaving their spot. Thick fog hangs motionless around them, softening a distant glacier ridge. A handheld camera circles slowly at chest height, all three fully framed.

Rain glosses concrete paver blocks in a freight yard on the Tibetan plateau, corrugated container stacks rising into a corridor with snow peaks looming beyond. Exactly three adults occupy it and nobody else: a silver-haired Finnish woman in a navy jersey, a broad Mongolian man in his thirties in oxblood pads, a slim Ethiopian man in his twenties in a steel-grey hoodie. In one continuous shot they weave a puck through orange cones with quick stick dekes, shoulders dropping, blades scraping wet stone, then flick sharp passes between them. Reflections shiver under their boots; the air is otherwise still. A slow dolly-out reveals more of the yard while all three remain fully in frame.

Misty sunrise over a black volcanic sand cove on a vast highland lake beneath plateau cliffs, a bleached driftwood line and a ruined stone jetty marking the far edge. Six adults and no one else start shoulder to shoulder, feet in the sand, fully in frame: two women with copper and black braids in teal and coral shirts, four men in mustard, white, olive and purple, ages twenty to fifty, mixed Andean, Somali, Danish and Filipino. In one continuous shot they crouch, shove wooden barrels forward and sprint bent-double, barrels drumming, sand spraying, crossing the beach in a ragged laughing line. Wind-driven waves crash and foam behind them. A slow dolly-in glides toward the racers, everyone staying visible.

A slow dolly-in drifts toward four adults on the painted concrete of an apron beside a lonely plateau hangar, faded yellow taxi markings curving underfoot, a parked fuel bowser silhouetted in pale sunrise mist. Nobody else is present. They begin motionless and complete in frame, spikes on the concrete: a wiry Kenyan woman in a lilac singlet, a broad Czech man with a blond ponytail, a lanky Tamil man in dove-grey, a strong Maori woman in her forties in seafoam. One continuous shot follows them jogging out along the markings, breaking into crossover strides and launching javelins in long dreamy arcs, chests open, back legs whipping through, covering the apron's length. The air is glassy still; sunrise gilds their breath.

Night rain lacquers weathered wood decking on a promenade above a plateau lake, cast-iron lamps burning amber, a moored ferry hulk creaking beyond the railing where a scatter of onlookers watches from behind the ironwork, none stepping onto the boards. Three adults hold the deck: a tattooed Puerto Rican man in black, a rangy Dutch woman in her thirties in a wet grey shell, a compact Chinese man in oxblood. One continuous shot, all three planted and fully framed at first, then they run and kong vault a low crate, hands slapping wet timber. The last traceur charges the lens and finishes half out of frame. A handheld camera circles slowly at chest height.

Between towering corrugated silos and a skeletal conveyor gantry on the Tibetan plateau, a dusty concrete slab lies dark with rain and glinting. Three adults own it, no one else: a powerful Samoan woman in a slate jersey, a lanky Sudanese man in white sleeves, a bearded Russian man in his forties in charcoal. All three stand fully in frame, cleats on wet concrete, before exploding into work. In one continuous shot they run long routes across the slab, cutting hard at the gantry legs, twisting to haul in over-the-shoulder catches at full stride. Snowflakes drift through the low beams of light, bright against the gloom. A slow dolly-out unveils the yard's iron scale.

Heavy snowfall softens a patterned ceramic courtyard inside an old plateau caravanserai, a carved arcade running the perimeter and a dry fountain crusted white. Six adults hold one spot at its centre, all fully in frame with boots on tile: three women, three men, aged twenty to forty-five, Uyghur, Irish, Colombian and Ghanaian, in cobalt and gold uniforms. Spectators watch from the raised arcade behind the columns, never entering the tiled floor. One continuous shot: four bases lock grips, dip and hurl a flyer skyward through the falling snow while the sixth teammate spots beneath with arms raised, she hits a straddle, then folds into their cradle. The camera cranes down from high above to eye level.

A storm sky bruises purple above a painted asphalt crossroads in a plateau town, prayer-flag lines hanging motionless overhead and shuttered tea shops ringing the square. Six adults, three couples, plant themselves on the bright road paint and stay entirely in frame: a red-haired Scottish woman, a Haitian man in suspenders, an Uzbek woman in polka dots, a Vietnamese man in mint, a silver-bearded Argentinian man, a Zulu woman in canary yellow. Onlookers cheer from a low wall and balconies, off the road. One continuous shot: swing-outs snap into aerials, partners flipping over hips and landing in place, shoes squeaking. The camera pans slowly from left to right.

On a walled terrace of stunted olive trees in a dry plateau valley, the flat is bare pale earth, silvery leaves shivering in a hazy afternoon wind, prayer flags on a post at the edge. Far below, headlights streak along a highway in long trails. One woman holds the centre of the terrace: early thirties, Tibetan, wiry and strong, in a fitted electric-blue top, white leggings and a red sash. Fully in frame with both boots planted, she cranks a long silk flag through fast drop-spins, snaps the pole flat, then punches a high toss into the wind, spots it and catches the shaft clean, never moving her feet. One continuous shot, a slow orbit around her.

Snow falls thickly into a clearing among gnarled plateau junipers, a fallen trunk on one side and a half-buried cairn on the other. Two adults stand on packed earth and leaf litter, fully in frame from the first breath: a heavy-set Maori man in his forties in a black thermal, and a tall Belarusian woman in her twenties, blond crop, deep-red fleece. One continuous shot: she crouches, he plants both hands on her back and vaults over, drops into a crouch himself, and she leaps him in turn, the pair travelling only a few metres and back through the drifts. Snow bursts from their boots; nothing else stirs. Handheld, the camera drifts in a slow circle at chest height.

Fog rolls thick over a firm red sand flat between plateau dunes, a leaning survey post the only landmark, rain streaking down and puddles bursting underfoot. Two adults march the flat alone, framed head to toe from the start: a broad Trinidadian woman in her thirties in a white-and-cyan uniform, and a wiry Korean man in his twenties with bleached hair in the same colors, both carrying snare drums. One continuous shot: they hammer a driving cadence, stride the length of the flat, execute crisp pivot turns and reverse, sticks flashing, water leaping around their boots. The camera cranes down from high above to eye level as they pass.

Low practice lamps carve deep shadows across a spring carpet floor in a plateau training hall, chalk bins and a rolled tumbling strip along the wall, big industrial fans stirring loose paper and dust through the beams. Two adults hold a single spot in the middle, wholly in frame: a compact Algerian man in his twenties, red headband and black joggers, and a tall Swedish woman in her thirties in a violet leotard and grey shorts. Teammates watch from bleachers beyond the low barrier. One continuous shot: he throws a cork, she answers with a snapping 540 kick, then both spin butterfly twists, landing on the same square metre. Handheld, the camera circles them slowly at chest height.

Sunrise mist wraps a whitewashed cement rooftop where trays of red chilies dry beside stacked clay pots, ridgelines fading blue behind. Four adults and nobody else stand rooted on the cement, all fully in frame: a broad-armed Nepali man in a faded green shirt, a Turkish woman in her forties with grey-streaked hair, a young Brazilian man in a torn white vest, and a slight Filipina woman in navy. The air is dead calm. One continuous shot, plain and unglamorous: three lock wrists into a basket, dip twice, and punch the flyer straight up over the chilies, her arms tight, before she drops back into their cradle. A static tripod camera watches at eye level.

Sunrise mist pools in a gorge below a broad sweep of smooth red sandstone, wind-carved pockets in the rock and a single stunted pine clinging at the rim. Three adults, alone up here, begin side by side with feet on stone and every limb in frame: a freckled Australian woman in her thirties, teal shirt; a stocky Peruvian man in orange; a tall Congolese man in his forties in white. In one continuous shot they take off across the slickrock, flipping a rugby ball backwards down the line, chasing, cutting, whooping, covering thirty metres of rock in bright easy joy. Air perfectly still. A slow dolly-out opens up the sandstone expanse around them.

Fog hangs between log stacks in a plateau sawmill yard, an idle bandsaw shed dripping, distant road traffic smearing into thin light trails beyond the fence. Three adults are the only people here: a lean Kenyan man in his twenties in faded blue, a heavyset Bulgarian woman in her thirties in grey, a sinewy Cambodian man in a black tee. They crouch into starting positions on sawdust-covered dirt, whole bodies in frame. One continuous shot: they explode out, drive hard through the first strides, sawdust kicking up, and pound down the yard, the nearest runner storming past the lens and leaving frame half-cropped. The camera pans slowly from left to right.

A vast plateau exhibition hall stands half-struck: skeleton booth frames, taped cable runs, endless grey commercial carpet. Warm tungsten work lamps burn on stands while leftover rig neon flickers and a sweeping searchlight rakes the far wall. One adult occupies the floor, no one else: a huge Icelandic man in his thirties, red beard, black singlet and chalked hands, entirely in frame with boots on the carpet. In one continuous shot he squats over a steel keg, rips it up and hurls it backward over his shoulder, watching it thump down behind him, then strides two paces and sets up again, roaring. A slow dolly-out reveals the hall's emptiness around him.

A curling rink in a plateau border town, its pebbled ice glinting under a bank of hard floodlights set on one side, the rest of the hall drowned in haze and slow-moving spotlights. One man defends a battered practice net at the near house: mid-forties, Mongolian, thickset, in scuffed white pads and a plain dark jersey, breath steaming. He begins fully in frame, skates flat on the ice, then drops repeatedly into a butterfly, thighs sealing the surface, flaring one pad to kick an imaginary rebound away, snapping his glove hand across his chest, and driving back up, all inside the same small ring of scraped ice. Spectators watch from tiered benches behind glass. One continuous shot, a slow orbit around him.

A bruised storm sky presses down on a cracked acrylic hard court beside a plateau schoolhouse, sagging net, rusted chain fence rattling, scraps of paper tumbling across the baseline. Six adults work the court, all fully in frame with feet on the faded paint, and no one else stands on it: three pairs in worn singlets, a stocky Kazakh man, a tall Nigerian woman, a grey-templed Italian man, a young Mexican woman, a broad Indian man, a lean Ukrainian woman. Locals lean on the fence outside, watching from there. One continuous shot, unpolished: they circle, shoot double-leg takedowns, drive a few steps, land, reset and go again. The camera cranes down from high above to eye level.

Snow blows across a rippled wet sand flat beneath dark plateau cliffs, stranded net floats and a wrecked skiff half-sunk in the tide line, surf breaking grey behind. One adult is out there, nobody else: a wiry Ivorian man in his late twenties, cropped hair, mud-flecked red shirt, black shorts, both feet on the sand and fully in frame at the start. One continuous shot, raw and observational: he rolls the ball, snaps step-overs, cuts hard left, drives thirty metres along the flat spraying water, then pushes the ball straight at the lens and passes so close he ends half out of frame. The camera tracks sideways at a steady walking pace.

Blue hour settles over a quarry bench cut into a plateau flank, terraced rock walls stepping up behind an abandoned crusher, dust blowing low across compacted aggregate. Five adults and no one else stand in a rough line, whole bodies in frame, boots crunching stone: a weathered Chilean woman in her forties, a young Somali man in a torn hoodie, a broad Polish man in coveralls, a slim Thai woman in grey, a bearded Iraqi man in khaki. One continuous shot: they burst into sprints across the bench, then freeze mid-stride, wobbling, and go again. The closest runner ends cropped at the frame edge as a slow dolly-out widens the quarry.

Warm tungsten work lamps pool along a blue polyurethane sprint track inside a plateau fieldhouse, a banked turn curving away and a dark timing gantry overhead. Four adults, two couples, hold a single spot on the lanes, fully in frame throughout: a Cuban man in his thirties in a loose ivory shirt, a Sri Lankan woman in a plum dress, a silver-haired French man, a Nigerian woman in shimmering gold. Athletes rest on bleachers beyond the barrier, off the track. One continuous shot, dreamy and slow-glowing: hands lift, the women spool through triple spins, the men sweep cross-body leads, hips rolling, feet whispering on rubber. A handheld camera circles the couples slowly at chest height.

Colored stage lights wash a painted grey concrete hangar floor on the plateau, the vast door cracked open onto blue snow peaks, gantry rigging bleeding magenta and teal. Five adults occupy the floor and nobody else appears: a tall Ukrainian woman in silver, a compact Japanese man in violet, a muscular Cameroonian man in white, a red-haired Canadian woman, a lean Turkish man in black. All stay on one spot, entirely in frame. Confetti scraps tumble slowly through the beams. One continuous shot: four bases lock a basket, dip, and float the flyer up into the drifting paper, arms sweeping, before catching her softly. The camera pans slowly from left to right.

On the grooved asphalt of a decommissioned high-altitude airstrip, six adults form a tight ring: a broad-shouldered Tibetan man in a rust tank top, a lean Brazilian woman with braids and yellow shorts, a wiry Korean man in grey sweats, a stocky Nigerian woman in white, a silver-haired Dutch man, a tattooed Chilean woman in green. Pairs trade low sweeping compass kicks, drop into shoulder-down dodges, then spring up into one-handed cartwheel kicks while the rest rock a side-to-side base step and swap in. Dusty afternoon haze blurs faded threshold paint and a rusted windsock mast, the haze hanging motionless, runway deserted. One continuous shot, the camera craning down from high above to eye level, all six fully framed with feet on asphalt.

Dust hangs golden in the afternoon wind over a pale limestone forecourt of a plateau museum, a shallow fountain lying flat and unmoving and heavy bronze doors shut behind. Four adults stand on the stone, complete in frame: a Colombian woman in her thirties in lavender, a slender Vietnamese man in white, a broad Croatian man in his forties, a Zambian woman with braids in coral. Visitors linger on the steps and behind the fountain rail, never on the paving where the four work. One continuous shot, softly dreamlike: they burst between cone lines a few metres apart, touching down, spinning, sprinting back, hair swinging. A slow dolly-in drifts toward them.

Blue hour deepens over a black-painted asphalt court in a plateau schoolyard, a bent hoop with a chain net, a faded mural wall and jagged mountains behind. One adult plays: a lean Dominican woman in her twenties, high bun, bright orange tank, white shorts, both sneakers on the paint and all of her in frame from the first beat. Onlookers sit on a raised concrete ledge beyond the sideline, off the court. One continuous shot with punchy energy: she attacks from the wing, crosses over, drives three strides and finishes a euro-step layup, rebounds and repeats the other way. A handheld camera circles her slowly at chest height.

Floodlights blaze over a raked red dirt infield on the plateau, chain backstop glittering, black peaks massed beyond the outfield fence, confetti scraps whirling through the light columns. Two adults face the diamond alone, fully in frame with cleats in the dirt: a towering Serbian man in his thirties, dark stubble, sleeveless slate top, and a powerful Jamaican woman in her twenties, braided crown, crimson shirt. One continuous shot with grand sweeping weight: they crouch behind wooden barrels, drive them forward and sprint the length of the baseline, dirt exploding, barrels booming across the diamond, chests heaving at the far bag. The camera orbits slowly around them.

Night floodlights pour along a red-painted cycle highway threading the plateau, slim guard posts ticking past and wind turbines standing dark against the sky. Five adults are the only souls on the tarmac: a bright-eyed Indonesian woman in her twenties, a lanky Ghanaian man, a freckled Australian man in his thirties, a compact Peruvian woman, a grey-haired Portuguese man, all in candy-colored kit, all fully in frame at the start. One continuous shot, breezy and cheerful: they sprint the lane in a strung-out chain, slapping baton handoffs at full speed, whooping as each new runner tears away. A static tripod camera at eye level holds the whole line.

Blue hour turns crusted white salt pans lilac on a plateau flat, low mud dikes dividing the squares and a rusted sluice gate standing crooked. Rain streaks down and puddles jump. Two adults, nobody else, stand ankle-deep and fully in frame: a grinning Kenyan man in his twenties in a soaked yellow tee, and a stocky Danish woman in her thirties, blond bob, aqua shorts. One continuous shot, bright and kinetic: they stomp huge sheets of brine at each other, skid, scoop with both arms, chase in tight circles across two or three metres of shallow water, howling. A slow dolly-out widens across the shining pans.

Dusk blues an apple orchard on the plateau, gnarled rows heavy with small fruit, a leaning ladder abandoned mid-row and steam curling from a ground vent between the trunks. Two adults face off on clover and grass, both wholly in frame: a broad Georgian man in his forties, beard, mustard flannel, and a tall Ethiopian woman in her twenties in a dusty rose top. One continuous shot, hazy and lyrical: they lean back on a thick rope, heels ploughing green, hauling in surging jerks, sliding a metre one way then the other until the rope slips and both crash laughing into the clover. A camera tracks sideways at a steady walking pace.

Dusty afternoon wind sweeps a green synthetic turf pitch high on the plateau, pop-up goals shivering and low stone bleachers ringing the field where onlookers sit well clear of the turf. Four adults hold two spots on the pitch, all fully in frame: a lean Thai woman in her twenties in electric blue, a broad Nigerian man holding pads, a copper-haired Irish woman in white, a compact Japanese man in grey pads. One continuous shot, punchy and bright: the strikers whip roundhouse kicks into the pads, shins cracking, hips turning over, then switch stance and unload the other leg without shifting from their marks. The camera cranes down from high above to eye level.

Fog banks roll between ridges above a chalky gravel path cutting through lavender rows on the plateau, a roofless stone hut anchoring the far end, dusty wind combing the purple. Five adults, no one else, begin planted and fully in frame: a poised Korean woman in her thirties, a rangy Hungarian man, a silver-haired Spanish woman, a broad Nigerian man, a slight Chilean man, all in white sport fencing jackets with masks and light foils. One continuous shot, soft and dreamlike: they advance and retreat in rotating pairs, one fencer waiting en garde, lunging deep along the gravel, blades ticking, parry-riposte exchanges carrying them the length of the path. The camera cranes down from high above to eye level.

Hazy wind rattles a sunflower field on the plateau while fog slides between the rows and spills onto a strip of dry cracked soil edged by a leaking irrigation pipe. Four adults, and absolutely nobody else, plant their hands on weighted sleds, feet in the dirt, whole bodies in frame: a beaming Filipina woman in her thirties in lime, a hefty Ukrainian man in orange, a tall Kenyan man in sky blue, a freckled Canadian woman in fuchsia. One continuous shot, bouncy and fun: they drive the sleds twenty metres down the strip, legs pistoning, dust puffing, then collapse grinning against the pipe. The camera pans slowly from left to right.

Mist pools over a plateau brick-maker's yard, raw adobe blocks curing under reed mats, a kiln chimney breathing pale smoke. Four adults stand on the fired clay tiles: a tall Tibetan woman in a faded teal jersey, a stocky Mexican man in orange shorts, a slender Vietnamese man with a headband, a freckled Irish woman with a red ponytail. Split into two duos, they keep a ball alive with low forearm digs, high looping sets and soft roll shots angled at a partner's chest, scooping dying balls off the tiles. Sunrise light stays soft, the air motionless, the yard empty of others. One continuous shot, a handheld camera circling slowly at chest height, all four fully in frame, feet on the tiles.

A road tunnel through the plateau sits closed to traffic, sodium lamps spilling amber on asphalt, a taped-off lane and dripping ventilation ducts overhead, deep shadows swallowing the far bore. Two adults are alone inside, both fully in frame with shoes on the asphalt: a chirpy Nepali woman in her twenties in a marigold shirt, and a burly Dutch man in his forties, buzzcut, teal overalls. One continuous shot, playful and quick: they run a two-person bucket brigade, swinging sloshing pails hand to hand and hustling them thirty metres down the lane, water arcing and slapping, both laughing at the slippery mess. The camera pans slowly from left to right.

A storm sky hangs low over a freight depot platform on the plateau, rusted boxcars parked alongside, a sagging steel canopy and pooled shadow between its posts. Two adults occupy the weathered concrete, whole bodies in frame at the start: a severe Estonian woman in her thirties, black bob, charcoal coat, and a wiry Korean man in his forties in a slate shirt. One continuous shot, noir and cold-toned: they spin wooden hoops down the platform, chase them, roll under one, then dive headlong through another and pop up sprinting, covering the platform's whole length. The air is heavy and still. A camera tracks sideways at a steady walking pace.

Sunrise mist floods an open railway platform on the plateau, snowflakes drifting through shafts of light beside a riveted iron shelter and a single glowing signal down the line. One adult stands alone on tactile-edged concrete, entirely in frame: a powerfully built Ethiopian man in his thirties, close-cropped hair, black long-sleeve and slate trousers. One continuous shot with sweeping cinematic weight: he winds up, throws a cork with a knee tucked tight, lands, immediately snaps a 540 kick, then floats a butterfly twist along two metres of platform, breath and snow blowing off his shoulders. The camera orbits slowly around him.

A dark storm sky presses on a windswept snowfield below plateau ridges, buried fence posts marking a lost boundary and a ruined stone hut at the edge. Six adults, no one else in sight, stand on crusted wind-packed snow, all fully in frame: a red-cheeked Mongolian woman, a lanky Norwegian man, a stocky Peruvian man, a Ghanaian woman in a bright parka, a bearded Turkish man, a young Korean woman. One continuous shot, rough and observational: they scoop and hurl snowballs, sprinting between the posts, ducking, diving flat and rolling up caked white. The camera cranes down from high above to eye level.

Butter lamps glow in an alcove of a plateau monastery cloister, snow settling on worn flagstone between carved pillars and frosted copper prayer wheels. Rooted on one square of stone, six adults keep every limb in frame: a slender Tibetan woman in her twenties, a broad Samoan man, a Portuguese woman with grey curls, a young Kenyan man, an Indian man in his forties, a Finnish woman in white. Monks and lay visitors look on from the shaded arcade, none stepping onto the flags. One continuous shot, hushed and dreamlike: wrists lock into a basket, the group dips, and the flyer floats up through falling snow before settling into their cradle. The camera dollies slowly in.

Harsh midday sun glares off a smooth concrete drying patio on a plateau slope, wooden bean rakes leaning against a tin-roof shed while a sudden shower streaks down and puddles pop across the slab. Six adults work in three pairs, nobody else present, all fully in frame with bare feet on wet concrete: a stocky Uzbek man, a tall Brazilian woman, a grizzled Japanese man in his fifties, a young Nigerian woman, a lean Mexican man, a broad Ukrainian woman, in worn white and blue jackets. One continuous shot, unvarnished: they turn in for o-goshi hip throws, load partners across the hip, drop them, then swap roles. A static tripod camera at eye level.

Magenta and cyan stage lights carve two adults out of the dark on a black painted plywood deck of a downtown Los Angeles proscenium house, gilded box seats and a dusty velvet valance framing them. One continuous shot cranes down from high above the fly rails to eye level. A tall Black woman with cornrows in a rust tank top and a stocky Latino man in a grey singlet grip a thick hemp rope, heaving in alternating surges, boots skidding, dropping to one knee and hauling again within a couple of metres. Both stay fully in frame, feet planted on the visible boards. Silent onlookers watch only from the seats beyond the pit rail.
