On a raised park terrace above a Los Angeles reservoir, crushed decomposed granite crunches under two adults, a rusted chain-link goal frame bolted at one end and a wall of eucalyptus behind. Soft overcast daylight flattens the colours while, far off, fireworks burst silently over the hills. One continuous shot tracks sideways at a steady walking pace. A wiry Korean-American man in a faded green keeper jersey and a broad-shouldered white woman in black shorts alternate diving saves, punching a ball clear, rolling up through the grit and resetting. Both begin fully in frame with feet on the ground; later she surges toward the lens and ends partly out of frame. No one else is anywhere near.

Grey overcast light drains all colour from a coal stockyard beside a shuttered Los Angeles power station, where black coal dust lies in long ridged windrows and a rusted stacker conveyor arcs overhead toward a boarded transfer tower. The air is dead still; nothing moves except one man. He is lean and middle-aged, South Asian, shaved head, in a black sleeveless top and loose charcoal trousers, and he drops into a deep crouch before exploding forward in low pounce leaps, hands slapping the dust, then sinking and springing again, covering the width of the frame. One continuous shot from a static tripod at eye level keeps him whole and the flat black ground plainly visible. Nobody else exists here.

Warm tungsten work lamps clamped to cracked columns pool light across the terrazzo floor of a long colonnaded arcade inside an abandoned Los Angeles civic building, taped-up glass doors at the far end. Beyond the openings, restless neon and a swinging searchlight bar the speckled stone with colour. One continuous shot from a static tripod at eye level. Six adults, all fully in frame, feet on the stone, spar in three pairs with padded sticks: a burly Samoan man in a red rash guard, a slim Ethiopian woman in blue, a grey-bearded white man, a young Filipina in yellow, a tattooed Mexican-American woman, a lanky Black man in white. They trade overhead strikes, slip aside, counter, all within a few paces. Nobody watches.

Shafts of daylight fall from a clerestory high in a derelict turbine hall in Los Angeles, striping the checker plate steel deck between two capped turbine casings and a hanging gantry hook. Neon tubes stutter along one wall and a searchlight rakes the girders, colouring the haze. One continuous shot dollies slowly in toward four adults, all fully framed with boots on the plate. A broad Nigerian-American man in a black tee and a red-haired white woman in a grey hoodie trade padded-stick strikes; beside them a compact Japanese-American woman and a silver-templed Chicano man weave, parry and counter, shuffling only a few feet either way. The vast hall stays otherwise empty and cold.

Harsh midday sun bleaches a deserted backlot street at a Los Angeles studio: false brownstone facades with hollow windows, a prop fire hydrant, painted asphalt seamed with tape marks. The air hangs completely still. One continuous shot from a static tripod at eye level holds two adults fully in frame a metre apart, feet planted, never leaving their spots. A tall Black man with locs tied back, in a sand-coloured tank and black shorts, hoists a heavy medicine ball overhead and drives it into the pavement, catching the bounce; opposite him a muscular white woman in a maroon crop top and grey leggings mirrors him, then twists to slam side to side. Their shadows are hard and short. Nobody else is on the street.

Bruised storm clouds press down on a cracked asphalt parade ground at a decommissioned coastal base in Los Angeles, flagless poles clanging in a row, a low sea wall beyond where waves break white and heavy. Rain has not yet fallen. One continuous shot cranes down from high overhead to eye level, holding two adults locked together on one spot, both wholly in frame. A shaven-headed Vietnamese-American man in black shorts and a tall Afro-Latina woman with taped wrists in a grey sports bra fight for the clinch, hands sliding to the neck, driving alternating knees into each other's guard, twisting and resetting without their feet leaving a small patch of visible tarmac. The empty ground stretches away, no bystanders at all.

Two work floodlights on a tilted mast throw hard white cones across a salt pan north of Los Angeles, the cracked crust glowing pale between weathered survey stakes; low dust streams across the ground and vanishes into the dark. One continuous shot dollies slowly inward. A rangy Native American man in a dust-grey henley and a solid blonde woman in a black long-sleeve heave a heavy sand sack between them, swinging it low, launching it in an arc, absorbing the catch with bent knees and pivoting to throw again. Both start fully in frame, boots crunching the salt; near the end he steps toward the lens and passes partly out of frame. The flats are otherwise deserted.

Down in an underground Los Angeles parking level dressed for a party, pink and green tubes are zip-tied to the pipework and colour the epoxy-coated concrete; two big floor fans push loose flyers and dust skating across the slab between numbered stalls. One woman occupies the space: athletic, Puerto Rican, box braids gathered high, in a bright orange crop tee, teal shorts and white boxing boots. One continuous shot pans slowly left to right with her as she shadow boxes, snapping doubled jabs, slipping an imaginary counter, rolling under and firing a hook, bouncing a few metres along the empty bay with the floor clearly visible under her feet. She stays fully in frame throughout. Nobody else is down here.

Dusty hazy afternoon light hangs over the inner courtyard of a stucco Los Angeles apartment block, interlocking concrete pavers underfoot, a dry tiled fountain in the corner and bougainvillea spilling off a second-floor rail. The air itself is calm. One continuous shot dollies slowly out to reveal more of the courtyard. Three adults form a short brigade: a compact Vietnamese woman in a lime tee, a bearded white man in a blue work shirt, and a tall Somali-American woman in a coral tank. They sling full water pails hand to hand, water leaping over the rims and darkening the pavers, then sprint the empty buckets back a few metres, laughing and reloading. All stay fully framed. No neighbours appear.

A storm sky presses violet over the downtown towers beyond the glass parapet of a hotel rooftop pool deck in Los Angeles; light travertine tile rings the pool and dry petals from a planter swirl low across it. One dancer holds the deck: a slender Black man in a canary-yellow mesh top, white trousers and heeled boots. One continuous shot dollies slowly toward him as he whips through hand performance, snaps a triple spin on the spot and drops into a clean death-drop dip, rebounds and repeats, staying fully in frame on a single square metre of tile with his feet always on the visible floor. Guests watch from behind the glass of the bar above, none of them on the deck.

Thick fog swallows the ends of a pedestrianized shopping street in Los Angeles, granite setts wet and shining, iron planters and rolled shutters fading into white; rain streaks past and puddles spit under each touch. One continuous shot pans slowly from left to right across four adults, all four framed from the opening beat, each rooted to their own spot. A cheerful Brazilian-American man in a bright teal jacket juggles with alternating insteps; a tall Black woman in a pink windbreaker pops the ball thigh to thigh; a stocky Korean man in orange heads it repeatedly; a freckled white woman in yellow flicks it up behind her and catches it on her neck. Shoppers watch from under an arcade behind a low railing.

Golden hour rakes across a packed dirt farmyard east of Los Angeles, a leaning red barn with a broken vane, a galvanised trough and feed sacks strung from a beam; warm rain streaks through the light and pocks the dust into little craters. One continuous shot orbits slowly around three adults, all fully in frame. A wiry Mexican-American woman in a lemon tee, a tall Black man in a blue tank and a stocky white man in a red shirt explode into short sprints across a few metres of mud, then freeze mid-stride on a shout, arms flung out, wobbling, before bursting off again in the other direction. The yard holds no one else.

Storm light bruises the sky over a red rubber tartan oval at an old Los Angeles college, hurdles stacked at the rail and lane numbers ghosted by wear; club neon stutters beyond the fence and a searchlight sweeps the empty dark bleachers. One continuous shot tracks sideways at a walking pace past five adults, all five fully in frame throughout, each holding their own patch of track. A silver-haired Cuban man, a tall Black woman in a wine dress, a muscular white man in black, a compact Filipina in emerald and a lean Indian-American woman spin through doubles and triples, snap into cross-body leads with invisible partners, shoulders sharp, heels grinding the rubber. Nobody watches from the stands.

Inside a cold storage warehouse in Los Angeles, ice furs the steel racking and a plastic strip curtain hangs stiff at the far door; harsh floodlights from one side rake the frosted concrete, while a failing tube stutters and a beam swings across the aisle. Breath fogs. One continuous shot dollies slowly in on three adults, all fully framed with boots on the frost. A heavy Turkish-American man in a worn white gi drills o-goshi on a lean Black woman in blue, loading her across his hip and setting her down; a grey-haired white woman in judo trousers coaches, then steps in to take the next turn and finishes close, partly out of frame.

Hazy afternoon light hangs heavy over a powdery white gypsum flat outside Los Angeles, leaning fence posts marking an old boundary and a bleached ridgeline dissolving in the dust. The air is oddly still, every footfall printing sharp in the sand. One continuous shot cranes down from high above to eye level as six adults, ankles bound in pairs with cloth strips, lurch into a ragged race across the flat. A tall Black woman and a stocky white man find a rhythm; a Vietnamese-American man and a redheaded woman stumble and haul each other up; an Indian-American woman and a bearded Latino man overtake them, spraying gypsum. All six stay fully in frame throughout. The flat is otherwise deserted.

Bright even overhead lighting floods a municipal badminton hall in Los Angeles, green vinyl mats taped with old court lines, sagging nets pushed to the wall and steam curling out of vents near the ceiling. One continuous shot tracks sideways at a steady walking pace along three adults, all three fully in frame, each anchored beside a batting tee. A powerful Dominican man in a sky-blue jersey drives ball after ball off the tee; beside him a lean Black woman in white takes crisp dry swings, hips whipping through; a stocky Japanese-American man in red loads and uncoils, follow-through humming. Feet never leave their small patches of mat. A handful of onlookers sit up on the bleachers behind the barrier, off the court.

Neon strip lights bolted along the parapet wash green and violet over the concrete crest roadway of a dam outside Los Angeles, white lane lines running between hulking spillway gates, valley lights scattered far below. The night air is perfectly still. One continuous shot tracks sideways at a steady walking pace beside six adults, all whole in frame. A tall Ghanaian-American woman and a compact white man kick up into handstands and hop forward in bursts; a lean Iranian-American man walks eight steps on his hands; a curvy Black woman, a bearded Latino and a tattooed Korean woman follow, wobbling, laughing, dropping their feet back to the concrete and going again over a few metres. No spectators.

Soft overcast daylight sits on a canal-side quay in Los Angeles, grey cobble setts running past iron mooring bollards toward a rusted lift bridge; a broken neon sign on the opposite bank stutters and a boat searchlight sweeps the water and the stone. One continuous shot cranes down from high above the bridge to eye level. A single athlete works the quay: a tall mixed-race woman in her thirties, hair braided tight, in a slate blue singlet and orange spikes. She builds a long accelerating run-up along the setts, hits a chalk mark, drives off one foot into a soaring hitch-kick and lands hard on a sand patch. She stays fully in frame throughout. Onlookers line the far bank behind a railing.

Shafts of daylight drop through grimy high windows onto a decommissioned Los Angeles subway platform, cream tiles crazed, a dead track trench along one edge and a hand-painted destination board stripped bare. Haze machine fog rolls low and two rigged spotlights swing lazily across it. One continuous shot from a static tripod at eye level watches two adults cover ground down the platform. A bouncy Filipino-American man in a lilac tee and a tall white woman with a bleached crop in a mint tracksuit kick to handstands and race, hopping and walking on their hands, tumbling out, resetting and going again. Both begin and remain fully in frame, feet touching the tiled floor between attempts. Nobody else is here.

Under flat overcast light a closed city street in Los Angeles waits, crosswalk stripes running under two adults, a boarded diner with a dead neon arrow on one corner and low dust drifting along the gutter. One continuous shot cranes down from above the traffic signals to eye level. A hulking Samoan man in a black singlet, forearms taped, and a broad white woman with a chalked back in a grey tee take turns lapping a heavy stone sphere, squatting over it, rolling it onto the thigh and driving it up onto a wooden loading platform, then tipping it back down for the next lift. Neither leaves their spot and both stay fully in frame. Onlookers crowd behind barricades far up the block.

Inside a shuttered Art Deco ballroom above a downtown Los Angeles theater, gilded plaster palms flank parquet strewn with dust sheets and stacked banquet chairs. Six adults stand upright on the wood for the first beat: a muscular Black man in maroon, a petite Filipina woman in mint, a tall Ukrainian woman, blonde crop, a bearded Persian man in grey, a broad Samoan man in navy, a silver-haired white woman. Pairing off, each rear partner lifts a teammate's shins while the front partner hand-walks four meters, pivots around a folded chair and charges back before roles swap. Daylight shafts slant from high windows through motionless dust, the room otherwise empty. One continuous shot, a slow pan from left to right, all six fully framed.

Dark basalt setts spread across a train station forecourt in Los Angeles under soft overcast daylight, a stopped clock tower above the arches, ragged palms along an empty taxi rank; a stuttering neon sign on the hotel opposite throws colour and a searchlight drifts across the facade. One continuous shot tracks sideways at a steady walking pace. Three adults chain tumbling across the square, all three fully in frame: a bright-eyed Black woman in a coral tee cartwheels twice into a round-off; a slim Chinese-American man in electric blue follows with a one-armed cartwheel; a freckled white man in white joins, and together they chase each other from one side of the frame to the other. Nobody else is around.

A stormfront stacks black over short-grass prairie north of Los Angeles, cropped dry grass running to a leaning windmill and a sagging barbed fence, the air dead calm before the rain. One man is out there: broad-shouldered, forties, Black, close-cropped hair, in a charcoal sweatshirt and mud-stained trousers, standing in a burlap sack pulled to his waist. One continuous shot cranes down from high above to eye level as he hops hard across the grass toward a fence-post marker, gathers speed, catches a tussock and crashes down, rolls, drags himself upright inside the sack and hops on, covering the whole width of the frame. He stays fully visible. No one else for miles.

Behind the scaffold towers of an open-air festival stage on a Los Angeles field, storm light bleeds purple; the aluminium deck is dulled by rain marks, cables coiled and taped at the edges, fog banks rolling straight through the truss. One continuous shot tracks sideways at a steady walking pace along the deck. Two performers cover the full width: a tall Brazilian woman with a long braid in a silver bodysuit and a lean white man in loose indigo. She flings a hoop out so it rolls, spins and returns; he dives cleanly through another held upright, rolls to his feet, spins his own hoop around his waist and sprints on. Both stay fully in frame, soles on the deck. The field is empty.

Night on a gravel access road behind a Los Angeles tank farm: bulbous white storage spheres, a rusted valve manifold, and the pink-and-violet neon of a car-wash arch glowing beyond the levee. Two adults work the road: a broad-shouldered Ghanaian man in a sleeveless yellow kit, and a lean Argentine woman with a dark braid in black shorts. She lofts a bouncing ball down the gravel; he sprints twenty meters, meets it with a driven laces volley into a chain-link goal, then feeds a low cross back for her side-on scissor strike. Dry leaves skitter low across the stones between their steps. One continuous shot, a static tripod camera at eye level, both fully in frame, feet on gravel throughout; nobody else appears.

Light rain slicks a beach volleyball court in Los Angeles, raked fine sand darkening in patches, a sagging net and a shuttered lifeguard tower behind; a nightclub sign stutters up on the boardwalk and a searchlight swings across the court in slow arcs. One continuous shot dollies slowly in. Five adults grapple in the sand: a heavy Tongan man and a lean Black woman clinch, snap down and scramble; a tattooed white man hits a body-lock throw on a compact Vietnamese-American woman; a tall Latina circles for a single leg. All start fully framed with feet planted. The white man rises and drives toward the lens, ending partly out of frame. No spectators anywhere.

Slate storm cloud stacks over a white coral sand beach near Los Angeles, a driftwood line and a tilted flag pole marking the tide; the air is completely still, the sea glassy and flat. One continuous shot cranes down from high above to eye level. Two adults train the length of the sand: a grinning Black man in a bright yellow tank with a resistance band round his waist and a sturdy white woman in teal anchoring it, digging her heels in. He leans hard forward and drives, knees pumping, hauling her stumbling after him; they reset and go again. Both start fully in frame with feet on the sand, then he charges the camera and finishes partly out of frame. Nobody else.

Floodlights glare across the sorting bay of a rail-side Los Angeles scrap yard, mounds of shredded aluminum banked against a silent conveyor picking line and coils of stripped copper. Two adults circle on the oil-stained concrete: a shaven-headed Brazilian man in a soaked white tank top, and a tall Somali woman in dark leggings, hair wrapped tight. Rocking a low side-to-side base step, she fires a spinning leg sweep at his ankles; he bails into a one-handed cartwheel and answers from a handstand with an inverted heel kick, then both roll out and reset. Rain streaks the floodlight beams and bursts from puddles under their palms. One continuous shot, a slow dolly-in toward them, both fully framed, feet on concrete; the yard is deserted.

Warm tungsten work lamps clamped to scaffolding light the stone flagstones of a deconsecrated cathedral nave in Los Angeles, pews under tarpaulins and a great rose window gone dim above; scraps of paper from a restoration bin tumble through the air. One continuous shot from a static tripod at eye level holds three adults, all three fully in frame, each on their own flagstone. A towering Nigerian-American woman in a bright red singlet laps a heavy stone sphere and drives it onto a timber platform; a barrel-chested Greek-American man with chalked forearms hugs and hoists next; a compact Filipina in blue tips it back down and repeats. Feet never travel more than a step. The vast nave is otherwise empty.

Floodlights washing the west front of a Los Angeles cathedral throw long shadows across the sandstone paving of its forecourt square, a dry fountain basin and a row of iron lamp standards catching the glare. The night is windless. One continuous shot orbits slowly around a single man: mid-thirties, Middle Eastern, dark curls, in a plain grey vest and black joggers. He kicks up into a handstand, walks a dozen paces across the stone, drops, resets and hops on his hands with heels tapping. He begins fully in frame, feet down; later he advances handstand-walking toward the lens and ends partly out of frame. Late visitors watch from the cathedral steps behind the low chain barrier, off the square.

Hazy afternoon light filters through fog banks rolling across a frozen lake, snow-dusted ice stretching past frost-stiff reed clumps and a half-sunk wooden jetty. One continuous shot from a static tripod at eye level. Two adults skate the width of the frame: a broad Black man in a maroon jersey and a lean white woman with a blonde ponytail in navy. They dig into hard crossover sprints, blades biting, then square up and carve violent hockey stops that fling white sprays into the fog, turn and go again the other way. Both begin fully in frame with skates on the ice; at the end she sprints straight at the lens and finishes partly out of frame. Nobody else is out on the lake.

Blue hour after sunset leaves the sky steel over a flat wave-worn rock shelf on the Los Angeles coast, ankle-deep pools spread across the smooth stone, a rusted iron mooring ring and a crumbling seawall behind. The water lies dead calm until they break it. One continuous shot orbits slowly around four adults, all fully framed, bare feet on the rock. A tall Black woman in a red swimsuit stomps a pool into a curtain of spray; a wiry Filipino man in orange shorts kicks water back; a freckled white woman and a stocky Latino man scoop and fling, dodging and skidding across a few metres of shining stone, breath visible. No one else is on the shelf.

Light rain leaves the black-and-white mosaic of a beachfront promenade in Los Angeles glossy and reflective, palms bending, flags and awning fabric snapping hard in the wind past a shuttered kiosk. One continuous shot pans slowly from left to right. Five adults run patterns along the promenade: a broad Black man in a bright orange tee lofts a ball; a lean white woman in yellow breaks on a post route and hauls it in over her shoulder; a compact Korean-American man in green cuts back; a tall Latina in pink and a bearded man in blue sprint deep. All begin fully in frame with feet on the mosaic; one receiver ends her route close, partly out of frame. Onlookers cluster behind the seafront railing.

Midday glare hammers the painted concrete circle of a helipad atop a Los Angeles office tower, an antenna mast and squat plant housings behind, the marker paint chalky with wear; oddly, a stuttering neon sign on the tower opposite and a passing helicopter searchlight throw stray colour across the deck. One continuous shot tracks sideways at a steady walking pace. A single athlete works the circle: a compact Métis man in his late twenties, sleeves cut off, forearms sunburnt, in black shorts and trainers. He stays fully in frame, stickhandling a puck rapidly through a tight ring of cones, toe-dragging, pulling it wide and back, feet shuffling on one spot with the painted ground plain beneath. The rooftop is otherwise deserted.

A decommissioned Los Angeles car plant hums with colored stage light; empty chain-conveyor hooks sway overhead, plastic paint-booth curtains hang open, a parked scissor lift sits in shadow. Three adults hold one spot on the epoxy-coated concrete: two bases — a thick-armed Mexican man in a black compression shirt and a broad Danish woman with a bleached buzz cut — lock wrists while a small, sinewy Japanese woman in violet stands between them, feet flat. They launch her straight up, arms tight, into a half twist, catch her in a cradle, reset, and fire again higher. Haze drifts through swinging spotlights, the floor otherwise deserted. One continuous shot, the camera orbiting slowly; all three stay fully framed.

Under the glass canopy of a Los Angeles transit interchange, grey porcelain tile gleams between steel trusses and a dead escalator bank; commuters watch from a mezzanine railing above, none of them on the tile. Six adults hold their own small squares of floor: a rangy Ethiopian man in a red singlet, a curvy Puerto Rican woman in teal, a pale Polish man with a topknot, a compact Vietnamese woman in grey, an older Black man with a silver beard, a tattooed Australian woman in black. Ropes blur — side-swings into double-unders, criss-cross catches, one of them hammering a triple-under. Air is dead still under flat overhead light. One continuous shot, the camera orbiting slowly, all six fully framed, feet drumming the tile.

Deck floodlights on a docked cargo ship in Los Angeles pour hard light over painted steel plating, lashed containers rising behind and a crane post throwing a black bar of shadow; the harbour night is dead calm. One continuous shot pans slowly from left to right along four adults, each rooted to a small square of deck. A heavy Polynesian man in a grey tee crouches, glides back and punches a shot put out over the rail netting; a tall Black woman with taped fingers coils and releases; a bearded white man chalks up and drives; a stocky Chinese-American woman follows, grunting through the finish. All stay fully in frame, boots on the visible steel. Nobody else is aboard.

Dusty high windows drop pale daylight through the chain-link of a small octagon cage in a converted Los Angeles warehouse gym, the worn vinyl mat scuffed grey in the centre, a taped stool and a hanging heavy bag beyond the fence. The gym is silent and still. One continuous shot dollies slowly in on one woman: mid-forties, Latina, muscular, black hair slicked back, in a purple mesh top, black leggings and bare feet. Duckwalking a tight circle, she catwalks upright, punches out sharp hand performance, then folds a rear leg and slams into a dip, back arched against the mat, floating up on one wrist to hit it again. Her footprint never widens; she stays fully in frame. Nobody else is there.

Harsh floodlights from one side of a Los Angeles ice rink rake the white sheet, painted lines and faceoff circles glowing while the far boards and unlit scoreboard sink into black. The arena air is dead still. One continuous shot orbits slowly around a single skater: a tall Japanese-American man in his thirties, hair tied back, in a dark grey long-sleeve and black trousers, blades bright. He steps into an upright spin, draws his arms in until he blurs, sinks to a low sit spin and rises into a tight scratch spin, all inside a small circle of scratched ice, feet never leaving it. He remains fully in frame. Spectators sit in the shadowed stands above the boards.

Snow pours over the herringbone brick forecourt of a Reykjavik university library, where iron lamp arches throw pale cones and a frost-crusted stone book sculpture sits beside dark glass. One woman in her thirties, Black, with tight coils under a knit band, wears a teal puffer vest over grey thermals. Framed fully from the first second, boots planted on the snow-dusted brick, she fires chest pops and neck hits, then rolls a slow arm wave from wrist to shoulder and back, snapping into a robot freeze. She never leaves her footprint or the frame. Flakes drift through the light beams in one continuous shot as the camera pans slowly from left to right.

Inside a converted harbour-side roller rink, glossy maple boards curve under a low ceiling of dead bulb strings while industrial fans push loose flyers and dust across the floor. One lean man in his late twenties, Korean, hair bleached ash blond, wears a cropped orange tee and black joggers. He begins fully in frame, both feet on the maple, hands raised; then he throws two no-hand cartwheels and a front aerial that carries him a few metres, and on the last landing he strides toward the lens, ending with his torso cropped by the frame edge. Spectators watch from behind the rink barrier only. One continuous shot, camera orbiting slowly, harsh floodlight raking from one side.

Deep shadows pool across the non-slip ceramic tile deck of a municipal swimming hall, where a still lane pool glitters and a chipped blue wave mural climbs the wall; only a few practice lamps burn. Three adults stand fully in frame, feet flat on the tile: a stocky Māori man near forty in yellow board shorts, a tall Nordic woman with a platinum bob in a navy one-piece, a wiry Indian man in red trunks. A disc skims low and they explode sideways, laying out flat, sliding on damp tile, popping up to fling it again. The nearest woman lunges at the camera and leaves frame half-cropped. Swimmers watch from bleachers behind the glass. One continuous shot, slow dolly-out widening the hall.

Blue hour settles over the pit lane of a decommissioned coastal race circuit south of Reykjavik: striped white-and-grey tarmac, shuttered garage doors flaking paint, a rust-streaked timing gantry against a black lava field. One broad-shouldered man in his forties, Brazilian, shaved head, wears a charcoal tracksuit with worn white boots. He holds one small patch of tarmac from the opening beat, feet grounded and his whole body inside the frame, flicking a battered football from laces to thigh to shoulder, catching it on his nape, dropping it back into rapid low taps. Nobody else is anywhere near. Air is dead still. One continuous shot, handheld camera drifting slowly around him at chest height.

A cavernous blacked-out sound stage near the Reykjavik docks: matte black floor, a white cyclorama curve at one end, a heavy truss overhead where spotlights swing through thick haze. Four adults, all fully visible with feet planted before anything begins, hold long ribbons — a freckled Irish woman in lime, a Filipino man in magenta, a silver-haired Danish woman in cyan, a young Nigerian man in tangerine. They burst into a galloping relay, sprinting the length of the floor, cutting figure eights so the streamers snap and coil behind them, then galloping back. Nobody else is present, and all four stay inside the frame. One continuous shot, camera dollying out to reveal the whole stage.

Magenta and cyan stage lamps have been clamped to the columns of a courthouse great hall, washing checkerboard marble and a brass balustrade in candy light; the air is perfectly still. Two adults stand fully in frame with shoes on the stone: a tall Ethiopian woman with braids in a mustard warm-up, and a compact Japanese man near fifty in a purple jersey. They start a fast dribbling duel, crossovers snapping side to side, between-the-legs and behind-the-back combos ringing off marble as they shuffle a few metres and back. Midway the woman attacks straight down the lens and finishes half out of frame. No one else is in the hall. One continuous shot from a static tripod at eye level.

Harsh midday sun bleaches a fine grey gravel outwash plain beneath a distant glacier snout, braided meltwater channels lying still and silver, a line of hand-stacked cairns marking a rough course. Four adults stand fully in frame, feet on gravel, each stepped into a burlap sack: a red-bearded Icelandic man, a Vietnamese woman with a long ponytail, a broad Samoan man, a grey-haired white woman in a windbreaker. They launch into hammering hops, covering many metres, elbows swinging, one crashing sideways and rolling back upright to chase the others. Nobody else exists out here. Nearing the cairns, the leading man hops close to the lens and ends partly cropped. One continuous shot, slow left-to-right pan.

Storm light presses down on a coastal skatepark outside Reykjavik: a smooth cast-concrete flat bottom, tagged coping, a rusted breakwater beyond, the sky bruised purple just before rain. Dead leaves and torn petals swirl low across the concrete. One woman in her early thirties, Mexican, dark hair in a high knot, wears a black long-sleeve and olive cargo pants. From the first beat she is entirely in frame, shoes rooted to one small patch, whipping two tethered poi into fast butterfly weaves, spinning under her own arms, turning tight on the spot as the cords hiss. She stays there throughout, alone. One continuous shot, camera dollying slowly out to reveal the whole bowl.

A small harbour-district gym holds one ring: worn cream canvas scuffed grey at centre, sagging red ropes, a taped corner stool, a single floodlight blasting in hard from the left so half the mat falls into blackness. Everything is silent and still. One man in his fifties, Egyptian, greying stubble and a wiry frame, wears a sleeveless navy top and bare feet on the canvas. Fully framed from the opening second, he keeps to one square metre, whipping poi into fast forward weaves, ducking his shoulder under a wrap, pivoting through a body turn while the cords blur past his ribs. Nobody else is here. One continuous shot from a static tripod at eye level.

Rows of silent looms fill a derelict weaving mill, dust-glazed plank flooring running long between them; a stuttering neon tube buzzes overhead and a searchlight sweeps in through cracked windows while a hard floodlight rakes from one side. Three adults, ankles roped together in a chain, stand fully in frame with feet on the boards: a tall Sudanese woman in a red singlet, a stocky Portuguese man in grey, a freckled Australian woman in blue. They lurch into a stumbling sprint down the aisle, finding a rhythm, hips crashing, then swing back the other way, staying inside the frame throughout. No one else is present. One continuous shot from a static tripod at eye level.

Snow falls thick and windless through a bamboo stand planted at the edge of an Icelandic coastal garden, black lava gravel bordering the path and a rusted greenhouse frame ghosting behind the culms. One adult stands on the packed earth and dry leaves: a lean, dark-skinned man in his thirties, close-cropped hair, wearing a soaked charcoal hoodie and grey joggers. He measures three steps, dives hands-first over a low mossy stone plinth, tucks his knees through, lands into a shoulder roll on the leaf litter, then walks back and clears it again one-handed. Bamboo stalks stay motionless under the snow load. One continuous shot, a slow pan from left to right keeping him fully in frame, feet on the ground; nobody else is here.

Bright even lights fill a school gymnasium: polished maple boards, ox-blood painted keys, a wall of felt banners, folded bleachers half pulled out. Six adults spread across the court, every one fully in frame with bare feet on the wood — a muscular Angolan man in white trousers, a Peruvian woman with a braid, a lanky Swede, a stocky Turkish woman, a Korean man in yellow, a grey-templed Cuban man. Paired off, they swing a low ginga, then fire cartwheels and sweeping kicks that their partners duck under, all within a couple of metres. Adult spectators watch from the bleachers only. Late in the take one man rocks toward the lens, ending half cropped. One continuous shot, the camera orbiting slowly.

A wide civic plaza of polished granite pavers sits under a bruised, thunder-heavy sky, its tilted basalt fountain drained, three flagless poles standing bare against grey government facades. The air is dead calm before the rain. One woman in her mid-forties, Filipina, cropped black hair, wears a faded grey tracksuit and scuffed trainers, a long white streamer knotted at her waist. She starts fully in frame, feet on the stone, then explodes into a hard sprint, breaking into a bounding gallop that carries her right across the plaza and back, the ribbon snaking behind. She stays entirely within frame; the square is otherwise empty. One continuous shot, camera dollying slowly in toward her.

A disused rolling mill: scarred steel plate underfoot, idle roller tables streaked with scale, an overhead crane parked in the rafters, one floodlight blasting from the left so shadows stretch long and hard. Nothing in the building moves but her. A woman in her twenties, Somali, wearing a bright coral tunic over white leggings and taped sneakers, stands fully in frame with feet on the plate. She snaps a silk flag through fast horizontal spins, whips a peggy, then launches a high toss, steps two paces sideways and catches it clean, grinning. Halfway she strides at the lens, finishing partly out of frame. She is alone. One continuous shot, camera orbiting slowly.

An emptied gallery hall: pale oak planks, tall white walls hung with three unlit abstract canvases, bright even ceiling light thinned by drifting haze while two moving spotlights sweep across the boards. One man in his thirties, white with red hair and a fighter's build, wears a scuffed grey hoodie, taped wrists and a beanie. Documentary-plain and fully in frame, feet on the oak from the opening second, he drops into windmills, kicks out a flare with hips swinging above the floor, then screws into a headspin and rides it out before rocking back to his feet — all inside one small patch. No one else is in the room. One continuous shot craning down from above to eye level.

Heavy snow blows across a stadium concourse plaza of stamped concrete, shuttered ticket kiosks along one side, torn sponsor banners and loose tarpaulin cracking in strong wind, the grey sea visible past the ramp. Three adults in navy kendo jackets stand fully in frame, feet on the salted concrete: a broad Icelandic man, a Japanese woman with a low knot, a tall Nigerian-Norwegian man. They drive bamboo shinai through shouted head and wrist strikes, advancing and retreating a few metres, staves cracking together. Fans watch from the railed walkway above, never on the plaza. Near the end one lunges past the lens, ending half cropped. One continuous shot tracking sideways at walking pace.

Dawn mist hangs over a crushed-red-brick clay court behind a shuttered tennis clubhouse; a flickering neon clubhouse sign stains the fence pink and a groundskeeper's searchlight swings slowly across the baseline. One woman near fifty, Jamaican, silver-threaded twists, wears a black training top, teal shorts and clay-stained boots. Fully in frame with studs biting the clay from the first second, she rolls the ball under her sole, snaps double step-overs, then cuts hard left and right within a few metres, spraying dust. Club members watch from behind the perimeter fence, none on the clay. She stays entirely in frame. One continuous shot, handheld camera circling slowly at chest height.

Behind a stone manor near the coast, a close-mown grass court lies under a black wall of cloud minutes before rain, its net sagging, a clipped hedge and a rusted umpire chair edging the lawn. The air hangs completely still. Two adults stand fully in frame, shoes pressed into turf: a lean Vietnamese-French man in a slate shirt, and a strong-shouldered Ghanaian woman in maroon. One crouches, the other vaults over her back with hands slapping shoulders, and they swap instantly, leapfrogging in a chain a few metres along the baseline. No one else is on the property. The man's last vault lands close to the lens, ending him half out of frame. One continuous shot tracking sideways at a steady walking pace.

Midday sun hammers a riverside esplanade of broad concrete slabs, iron mooring rings set into the edge, a green steel footbridge crossing overhead and dark water lying flat and unmoving below. Nothing stirs but the people. Three adults stand fully in frame, feet on the slabs: a tall Kenyan man in charcoal, a plum-haired Polish woman, a slight Thai woman in deep green. They whip long ribbon wands into snaking spirals, then run the length of the esplanade with chained leaps and turns, the silk drawing helices behind them, ending with a sharp three-way pivot. Onlookers watch from the footbridge above, none on the concrete. All three stay in frame. One continuous shot craning down to eye level.

Night sits over a corporate campus quad, mown lawn glowing acid green under neon signage on the glass atrium wall, a dark basalt planter and a half-built stack of small hay bales beside it. The air is still. Three adults stand fully in frame, boots on the grass: a heavyset Argentine man with a black beard, a tall Norwegian woman with a blonde plait, a wiry Bangladeshi man in a work vest. Anchored to one spot, they swing bales up from a pile and hurl them onto the stack, grunting, shoulders wrenching, catching and passing without stepping away. Staff watch from behind the atrium glass. All three remain in frame. One continuous shot tracking sideways at a steady walking pace.

A single squash court, pale hardwood glowing where a floodlight blasts through the glass back wall from one side; the rest sinks into shadow, haze curling and a roving spotlight sliding over the scuffed red service lines and dented tin. Two adults stand fully in frame, feet rooted to one small square of floor: a broad-backed Chilean woman in a black crop top holding focus mitts, and a lean Pakistani man in his forties with taped hands and blue shorts. He fires jab-cross-hook combinations, slips under her sweeping mitt, then doubles up to the body, leather cracking. Neither travels; nobody else is inside. One continuous shot, camera dollying slowly out.

Mist burns off a wide flat of short golden grass beneath dark headlands, low dust streaming across the ground, a leaning fence line of grey posts running out toward the sea. Two adults stand fully in frame, boots in the grass: a huge Tongan man in a mud-streaked white jersey, and a rangy Scottish woman with cropped ginger hair in navy. They break into a long run across the flat, spinning the ball backwards between them in flat lateral passes, cutting angles, accelerating over dozens of metres. No one else is out here. In the final stretch the woman veers into the lens and finishes partly out of frame. One continuous shot, camera orbiting slowly.

Light rain slicks a packed-gravel crossroads far outside town, the ground glossy and throwing back a tilted wooden signpost and a shuttered roadhouse whose neon tube stutters pink; a farm searchlight rakes across the fields. Two adults stand fully in frame, feet on the wet gravel: a tall Puerto Rican man in a soaked white shirt, and a Chinese woman in her forties in a silver jacket. Holding one small patch, they duckwalk, snap into fast vogue spins with hands cutting the air, then collapse backwards into death-drop dips, one leg folded, rising instantly to repeat. Nobody else is out here, and both stay in frame. One continuous shot craning down from high above to eye level.

A vast emptied distribution warehouse: polished concrete running away in a long aisle between towering bare steel racks, warm tungsten work lamps clamped at intervals casting amber pools, the far end lost in dark. Everything is motionless but him. One man in his early thirties, Māori-Chinese, close-cropped hair, wears a rust-orange jersey, black shorts and battered boots. He begins fully in frame, feet on the concrete, then drives the ball down the aisle with rolling step-overs, chopping hard cuts around rack legs and covering thirty metres before wheeling back, sole dragging the ball. He remains entirely in frame; nobody else is present. One continuous shot, camera dollying out to reveal the aisle's scale.

A Reykjavik rehearsal studio glows: mirrors curtained off with black cloth, a barre pushed to the wall, magenta and cyan stage lamps painting the black marley vinyl. Two adults face each other on one spot: a broad Icelandic woman in her forties, freckled, blonde ponytail, holding thick red pads at rib height, and a compact Thai-Canadian man in blue shorts, taped hands, sweat already shining. He fires a low chopping kick to her lead thigh, switches stance, drives a shin into the body pad, then whips a spinning back kick that thumps the leather; she resets in the otherwise empty room. Air still, colors saturated. One continuous shot, a static tripod camera at eye level keeps both fully framed, feet planted on the vinyl.

Below ground, a cold-war bunker hall holds bare damp concrete, a half-open steel blast door, and rusted pipe runs along the vault; someone has strung neon-green and blood-red stage lamps that saturate the walls. The air is utterly still. Three adults stand fully in frame, feet on the concrete: an imposing Ivorian man in black tights, a Russian woman with a severe bun, and a compact Mexican-American woman in violet. Each holds a single spot, spotting hard through doubles and triples, then whipping into fouetté sequences, working leg snapping, chests lifted. Nobody else is down here and all three stay framed. One continuous shot, camera panning slowly from left to right.

A small dojo above a fishing harbour: green tatami mats butted tight, a plain hanging scroll, milky shoji windows, and only two low practice lamps so shadows drown the corners. Nothing else moves. One man in his late twenties, Sri Lankan, wiry with black hair stuck to his forehead, wears white judo trousers and a sweat-soaked grey tee. Fully in frame from the first second, bare feet on the mats, he drops flat to his chest, snaps his knees under him and explodes upward into a full jump with hands overhead, landing and repeating faster, never leaving his single square of tatami. He is alone. One continuous shot tracking sideways at a steady walking pace.

The ice is gone; a Reykjavik arena's painted concrete slab shows faded hockey circles, dented boards, and empty folded seats beyond the glass. Two adults dance mid-slab: a tall Cuban man in a loose cream shirt and dark slacks, and a red-haired Icelandic woman in a swinging emerald dress. Both start fully in frame, feet on the concrete — he leads a spot turn, spirals her through a double inside turn into a hammerlock, unwinds it, then dips her low across the faded circle. Paper scraps tumble slowly through the flat overhead light. Halfway on, he releases her hand and prowls straight at the lens, ending cropped at the chest as she keeps spinning behind. One continuous shot, a slow pan from left to right.

An emptied bus depot parking hall: asphalt marked with wide yellow bay stripes, squat concrete columns, a shut roller door at the far end, and neon tubes rigged in violet and green throwing colored bands over the floor. The air is dead still. Six adults line up fully in frame, spikes on the asphalt — a towering Senegalese man, a Croatian woman with a bleached crop, a stocky Filipino man, a tall Somali woman, a tattooed Italian man, a white woman with a grey braid. They fire off together into a flat-out head-to-head sprint the length of the hall, arms hammering, leaning at a taped finish. All stay in frame; nobody else is present. Held as one continuous shot while the camera orbits slowly.

Blue hour drains color from an empty surface parking lot above the shore: faded asphalt with ghost stall lines, two bent light poles, a low sea wall and black water beyond. Nothing moves in the air. Six adults are fully in frame, shoes on the tarmac — a heavyset Fijian man in white, a Danish woman with a blonde bun, a slight Japanese man in orange, a broad Nigerian woman in green, a bearded Chilean man, a redheaded Canadian woman. A disc skims between them and they hurl themselves into flat layout dives, skidding on hips and forearms across a few metres before scrambling up to throw again. All six remain framed and alone. One continuous shot from a static tripod at eye level.

Dusk holds a volcanic ash plain in cold blue: fine grey ash spread flat to a black crater rim, a few half-buried fence posts leaning, a cold fissure vent far off. The air is completely still. Three adults stand fully in frame, bare feet printing the ash: a tall Korean woman with a shaved undercut in white uniform trousers, a broad Nigerian man with a blue belt, and a lean Iranian man in his forties. They snap spinning hook kicks past each other's heads, pivot into back kicks driving heels through the air, shifting only a couple of metres as ash puffs from their pivots. Nobody else is out here; all stay in frame. One continuous shot tracking sideways at a steady walking pace.

Night swallows a coastal football stadium: striped natural grass, neon advertising hoardings pulsing pink along the touchline, a searchlight sweeping the steep stands, sea wind carrying spray. Six adults stand fully in frame, feet on the turf — a muscular Brazilian man in white, a Vietnamese woman with a tight bun, a lanky Estonian man, a Black British woman in gold, a stocky Mongolian man, a freckled Irish woman. On a shared count they hurdle into running round-offs, snap back handsprings and finish with back tucks, tumbling in lines that carry them right across the pitch. Supporters watch only from the stands. All six stay in frame. One continuous shot dollying slowly in.

A crossfit box after hours: black rubber tiles, a steel rig hung with rings, chalk bins and stacked bumper plates, everything drowned in red and blue stage light while haze curls and a spotlight swings across the floor. Three adults hold the space, fully in frame with bare feet on the rubber: a heavily built Cape Verdean man in white trousers, a small Peruvian woman with a long braid, and a bald Ukrainian man near fifty. Rocking through a swaying ginga, they answer each other with au batido side-flips, low rasteira leg sweeps and snapping esquiva ducks, drifting only a couple of metres apart. No one else is inside; all stay framed. Filmed in one continuous shot, handheld, circling them slowly at chest height.

Rain-black storm cloud presses over a shipyard dry dock: wet concrete floor streaked with rust runoff, rows of timber keel blocks, the shadow of a half-plated hull rising behind, and far out over the harbour fireworks bursting silently. Two adults stand fully in frame, boots on the streaming concrete: a colossal Icelandic man with a red beard in a black singlet, and a thick-set Brazilian woman with taped forearms. Anchored on one spot, they take turns lapping a heavy stone sphere onto their laps and driving it up onto a steel platform, chalk smearing, breath steaming. Nobody else is in the dock; both remain in frame. One continuous shot craning down from high above to eye level.

Night on a wide beach of packed damp sand, a neon fish-shack sign burning cyan and pink at the dune line, bleached driftwood half-buried, black sea lying flat far out. The air hangs still. Three adults stand fully in frame, bare feet in the sand: a tall Nigerian woman with cornrows, a heavyset Norwegian man, and a wiry Japanese-Peruvian man in his forties, all in dark training robes with bamboo shinai. They run kirikaeshi, one holding centre while the others rain alternating diagonal cuts onto his raised shinai, stamping forward and reversing down the sand. Nobody else is out here. On a final driving step the tallest closes on the lens and ends partly out of frame. One continuous shot, the camera dollying slowly out.

Dusty afternoon wind hazes a vineyard tractor row: hard compacted soil rutted by tyres, wire trellises of stunted vines either side, a low stone wall at the end, grit streaming low across the ground. One woman in her late twenties, Ethiopian, hair braided close, wears a scuffed grey singlet, black shorts and dust-caked spikes. Fully in frame with feet on the soil, she settles, then sprints a long run-up down the row, hits her mark, drives her knee up in a hang and lands hard in loose worked earth, dust blooming. She stays wholly in frame and jogs back alone; the vineyard is empty. Plain, unpolished documentary framing. One continuous shot, camera panning slowly left to right.

Below street level in Reykjavik's bank quarter, a sunken granite plaza sits in hazy late-afternoon light, a dry fountain channel and a bronze planter at one edge. Onlookers lean on the railings that ring the rim, high above the playing floor; nobody joins the three adults below. A stocky Kenyan man in a grey tee digs a driven ball upward; a wiry Finnish woman with cropped white hair sets it high; a broad Chilean man cuts it back down with a controlled open-hand shot, and they rotate roles, one sprawling flat to save a low ball. Fireworks bloom silently over the far skyline. One continuous shot, the camera craning from high above down to eye level, all three fully framed, feet on granite.

A road tunnel still under construction runs straight into the rock: raw grey shotcrete floor, ribbed sprayed lining, cable trays bolted along the wall, bright even work lighting flooding everything. The air is dead calm. Six adults stand fully in frame, trainers on the shotcrete — a huge Samoan man, a Slovenian woman with a blonde ponytail, a lean Kenyan man, a tattooed Portuguese woman, a Korean man in red, a grey-haired Brazilian woman. Harnessed to resistance bands and a weighted sled, they drive out in a leaning sprint down the tunnel, chains rasping, then jog back to reset. Nobody else is present and all remain framed. One continuous shot from a static tripod at eye level.

Shafts of daylight drop through high grimy windows into a shipyard fabrication shed, striping a rust-stained steel plate floor beside a parked gantry crane and stacks of cut ribs; paper scraps tumble bright through the beams. Four adults stand fully in frame, shoes on the plate: a tall Haitian woman in white kit, a stocky Hungarian man, an Indonesian woman in her twenties, a silver-bearded Australian man. In two pairs they attack down long lines, lunging deep with sport foils, parrying and riposting, chasing each other the length of the shed and back. Nobody else is inside and all four stay framed. The whole thing is one continuous shot, the camera craning from high overhead down to eye level.

Daylight falls in hard diagonal shafts through the high windows of a fencing hall, catching a metallic piste laid over blue rubber flooring, dormant scoring reels and a rack of masks; loose paper scraps turn slowly in the beams. Five adults are fully in frame, feet and hands on the strip: a broad Nigerian man, a Korean woman with a shaved head, a lanky Norwegian man, a Bolivian woman with a dark plait, a bearded Greek man in his forties. From prone, seated and half-falling starts they explode upright on a clap and burst three metres down the piste, then drop and reset. Nobody else is present; all stay framed. One continuous shot throughout, the handheld camera circling slowly at chest height.

Inside a converted olive-press barn on a Cycladic hillside, wide plank wood glows under bright even overhead bulbs, grain dust silvering the seams between boards. Two adults share the space and nobody else. A stocky Black man in his forties, shaved head, red shorts, braces two thick thai pads; a lean Greek woman in her late twenties, dark braid, teal crop top, faces him. For the first second both stand fully in frame, bare feet planted on the planks. She hammers low kicks into the pads, then rises to body height, pivoting hard, shuffling barely two meters, never leaving frame. Through the open doors a taverna sign flickers and a harbour searchlight sweeps the boards. One continuous shot, slow pan left to right.

Warm tungsten work lamps hang inside the derelict soap factory at Piraeus, throwing amber pools across broken brick tile; rusted flywheels and a collapsed conveyor line the far wall. Five adults, nobody else. A tall Korean man with cropped hair in grey sweats, a red-haired woman in a plum leotard, a broad Nigerian dancer in gold shorts, a silver-haired woman in charcoal, a wiry Greek man in white. All five begin fully in frame, feet on the tile, then launch one after another into soaring grand jetés down a long diagonal, chaining chassé and split leaps the length of the hall, every dancer staying inside the frame. Torn paper scraps tumble through the lamplight. One continuous shot from a static tripod at eye level.

On a circular flagstone threshing floor above a Naxos village, ringed by a knee-high stone wall with a lone fig tree leaning over it, the hazy afternoon wind carries chaff through slanting light. Two women only, both fully in frame from the first second, shoes flat on the stone. A tall Ethiopian woman in her thirties, hair wrapped in orange, and a compact Filipina in her twenties with a blunt bob and lime top, each whip a long ribbon wand into overhead spirals, snapping figure-eights while they jump, turn and land on the same slab, never drifting off their spots. Stray snowflakes drift through the light beams. One continuous shot, a slow dolly-out revealing the terraces, punchy sports-ad energy.

Dawn mist pools in the gorge below a flat-crowned limestone butte in the Greek highlands, a toppled shepherd's cairn and a wind-bent thorn bush the only marks on its hardpan top. One adult stands there alone: a lean woman in her late twenties, olive-skinned with a black braid, barefoot in a rust-red singlet and cropped grey trousers. She marks the line, then throws a hands-free side aerial across the scrub, lands square, links a second immediately, and finishes with a punched front flip that stamps dust from the crust. The air is dead calm, the mist unmoving. One continuous shot, the camera craning from high overhead down to eye level, keeping her fully in frame with feet on the hardpan.

Snow falls straight down over a rooftop terrace in central Athens, the floodlit Acropolis rock hazy beyond a forest of TV aerials and a row of solar water tanks. Two adults work a taped ladder laid on the concrete pavers: a barrel-chested Greek man in a lime windbreaker with grey stubble, and a slim Korean-American woman in a pink beanie and black tights. They rip in-and-out steps down the rungs, snap into lateral shuffles, then hop scissors backwards, breath steaming, laughing when a foot clips the tape. Neighbors cheer from balconies across the light well, none of them on the roof. One continuous shot, the camera orbiting slowly; both stay fully in frame, shoes drumming the snow-dusted pavers.

Floodlights on scaffold masts blast a caldera floor of tight-packed dark pebbles on a volcanic Greek island; pale fumaroles hiss at the rim and a cinder cone looms black behind. Four adults stand out there and nobody else: a heavy-shouldered Brazilian man in his fifties with grey stubble and a white singlet, a tall Somali woman in her thirties in a green rash guard, a freckled Irish man in his twenties, bare-chested, and a stocky Japanese woman in navy. All four are fully in frame, feet on the pebbles, and hold their own square meter throughout, shadow boxing hard: jab-cross-hook chains, deep slips, rolling pivots. Snowflakes drift down through the light beams. One continuous shot from a static tripod at eye level, epic and severe.

Heavy snow and rain sweep a drained lakebed in the Greek interior, its pale clay cracked into plates and pocked with puddles; a line of half-buried fence posts marks the far shore. Five adults pound across it in a ragged line — a heavy-set Maori man in a torn navy jersey, a tall Nigerian woman with beaded braids, a red-bearded Scot in white, a compact Brazilian woman in yellow, a grey-templed Greek man in black. Sprinting, they flick flat passes down the line, loop behind each other and switch direction, boots exploding water. All five start fully framed, feet on clay; near the end the leftmost runner charges the lens and leaves frame at the waist. One continuous shot, handheld, circling slowly at chest height.

A closed elevated bypass above Athens, lane markings still crisp on the asphalt, orange cones toppled along the barrier and neon billboards throbbing pink and cyan against the skyline. A single man is up there, nobody else: mid-twenties, mixed Greek-Caribbean, cornrows, gold-yellow tracksuit, white trainers. He begins fully in frame, both feet on the asphalt, then drops into a deep crouch and springs forward in the low pounce-leaps of a lion dance, landing coiled, twisting, bounding again, covering forty meters of empty roadway. Dry leaves skitter low across the lanes around his landings. One continuous shot, the camera tracking sideways at a steady walking pace, saturated and bright like a sports commercial.

Blue hour settles over the tar-and-gravel roof of a converted garment loft in Athens, where a dead ventilation cowl and a sagging clothesline of dyed cloth stand against violet sky. Two adults hold a single patch of gravel: a broad-shouldered Egyptian man with a shaved head in a black vest, and a freckled Danish woman, hair knotted up, in a faded orange tee. Together they drop chest-to-deck, snap their feet in, and explode into a tuck jump; the next rep finishes with a half-turn jump so they land facing opposite ways, then back again. Nothing else stirs in the still air. One continuous shot, a slow dolly-out revealing rooftops around them, both fully in frame, feet returning to the gravel.

Golden light rakes an abandoned drive-in outside Athens: rows of rusted speaker posts, a peeling white screen tower, weeds bursting through cracked asphalt and gravel. Five adults chase across the lot — a tall Greek woman with a sun-bleached bob in coral, a stocky Samoan man in a green vest, a lanky Indian man in white, a muscular German woman in blue, a silver-haired Jamaican man in yellow. They fan into a shallow diagonal, the ball snapping hand to hand, one man looping behind a teammate to take a blind pop over the shoulder and accelerate away. Dust streams low across the asphalt. One continuous shot, the camera tracking sideways at a steady walking pace; all five stay fully framed, boots pounding the empty asphalt.

Midnight on a festival pier in Piraeus, painted steel deck plates glisten under strings of red and blue neon, the stalls shuttered, a crane barge dark on the water. Four adults take turns at a waist-high stack of pallets: a wiry Greek man with a topknot in black, a tall Ethiopian woman in a cropped white hoodie, a heavy-set Turkish man in grey, a short Filipina woman with a bleached buzz cut. Each runs three steps, plants both hands and shoots legs through the arms, clearing the stack and sticking a crouched landing on the steel before jogging back. Confetti scraps tumble past their shins. One continuous shot, the camera tracking sideways at a steady walking pace; nobody else remains, all four fully framed.

Terraced tea bushes drop toward the sea on a Greek island hillside; a red-earth service path runs between them, a rusted watering drum at one end, cicadas loud in the midday glare. Three adults occupy one spot on the packed earth. A weathered Sri Lankan man and a strong-armed Greek woman with a sun-faded scarf swing two long ropes in opposite arcs; between them a lithe Black woman in a blue tank top skips in, drills fast high-knee runs, spins a full turn without breaking rhythm, then bounces out and back in on the beat. Surf pounds the rocks far below, salt haze rising. One continuous shot, a handheld camera circling slowly at chest height, all three fully framed, feet on the red earth.

The lobby of a shuttered Athens hotel keeps its polished marble floor and brass column collars; colored stage lamps on stands wash the walls magenta and green, a neon strip stutters behind the empty reception desk, and a rented searchlight rakes in through the revolving door. Six adults own the room, no one else. Three men and three women, ages twenty to forty-five, Greek, Ghanaian, Chinese, Colombian, Lebanese, Danish, in tracksuits of teal, cream, red and black. All six start fully in frame, sneakers on the marble, and stay on their own small circles: windmills spinning shoulder to shoulder, flares whipping, a headspin drilling under the flicker. One continuous shot, a slow orbit around them, bright and playful.

Snow drifts down over the packed sand floor of a working sand-and-gravel pit on an Attic ridge; conveyor towers and spoil heaps ring the bowl, a stuttering neon sign on the site office throws red across the sand, and a mast searchlight sweeps in slow arcs. Six adults sprint there and nobody else. Mixed men and women in their twenties to fifties, Greek, Kenyan, Peruvian, Polish, Malay and Egyptian, in bright bibs of orange, lime and blue. All six begin fully in frame, boots on the sand, then scatter into a hard chasing game across the whole pit, cutting, faking, lunging out to slap a shoulder and reversing direction. One continuous shot from a static tripod at eye level, bright sports-ad punch.

Sunrise mist hangs gold over a mown wheat field on the Attic plain, straw stubble bristling underfoot, a stone well-head at one edge and round bales beyond. Two adults run a water relay across it: a burly sunburnt Greek man in a sleeveless denim shirt, and a lithe Kenyan woman in a purple tee and shorts. She hauls two sloshing pails twenty paces, swings one across to him without stopping; he sprints the next stretch and dumps it into a tin trough, then races back with the empty, both grinning as water slaps their legs. Petals and dry leaves whirl low over the stubble. One continuous shot, a slow pan from left to right keeps both fully in frame, feet on the field.

Sunrise mist sits on a wide pale sand bar in a dry island riverbed, oleander thickets crowding both banks and an old stone bridge arching in the distance; far off, faint fireworks pop over the hills. A single woman is down there, nobody else: late thirties, Afro-Greek, powerful shoulders, hair braided tight, navy two-piece kit and bare feet. She lies prone with heels planted, fully in frame, then explodes up at an unheard signal, drives twenty meters up the sand bar and hurls herself into a flat dive, hand snatching a short rubber flag before her chest ploughs the sand. Grit sprays and settles. One continuous shot, camera tracking sideways at a steady walking pace, raw documentary texture.

An indoor skate park in an Athens warehouse is closed: smooth plywood transitions, a low quarter pipe, paper streamers still taped to the roof beams. Three adults stand on the flat run between ramps, feet planted — a heavyset Greek woman with a black braid, a compact Vietnamese man in a yellow jersey, and a tall Nigerian man in white. He hoists the woman across his shoulders in a firm carry and sprints a few meters along the plywood, sets her down, and she immediately loads the smaller man and drives back, all three shouting counts. Confetti scraps drift down through the flat overhead light. One continuous shot, the camera craning from high above to eye level, everyone fully framed.

Light rain lacquers the reinforced concrete of a container quay at Piraeus; stacked boxes wall one side, gantry cranes stalk the other, a neon sign over the gatehouse stutters red into the puddles while a security searchlight swings across the wet slab. Three adults, nobody else. A rangy Greek man in his forties, soaked black shirt; a broad Ukrainian woman in her twenties, bleached crop, grey vest; a stocky Ghanaian man in his thirties, taped wrists. All three set hands and feet on the concrete, fully in frame, then tear off in a bear-crawl race, hips low, palms slapping water, hauling twenty-five meters down the quay. One continuous shot from a static tripod at eye level, cold neo-noir contrast.

Storm light turns an Athens boulevard median violet — a gravel promenade under pollarded plane trees, marble benches, headlight trails streaking on both carriageways behind the railings where commuters pause to watch from the sidewalks. Three adults line up on the gravel, feet down, then race its length: a broad Brazilian woman in a green crop top scoops a slim Lebanese man into a shoulder carry and drives forty meters over the compacted gravel while a rangy blond Australian man paces them, shouting time; at the second bench they swap loads without stopping and pound back. Thunder light flickers; the first drops have not fallen. One continuous shot, the camera tracking sideways at a steady walking pace, all three fully in frame throughout.

Storm cloud stacks tower over a mown turf airstrip on an Aegean island; a windsock hangs limp, a corrugated tin hangar rusts at the threshold, and the air is dead calm before the rain. Six adults occupy the grass, nobody else. Men and women aged twenty to fifty, Greek, Haitian, Swedish, Japanese, Brazilian and Iranian, in knee pads and kit of yellow, white and slate. All six start fully in frame with shoes on the turf and stay inside a few meters of it. In pairs they run the three-step spike approach at a portable net, arms swinging back and up, leaping to hammer the ball down, then jogging back to reset. One continuous shot, a slow orbit around them, crisp and bright.

A deserted toll plaza on the Athens–Corinth road, booths dark, lane paint showing through settled snow on the concrete, a bent barrier arm frozen upright. The air is dead calm, light flat and white off the snow-choked sky. Three adults work one lane, no one else anywhere: a barrel-chested Greek man in a black thermal and a tall Ethiopian woman in red lock wrists to build a cradle, then punch a wiry Ukrainian flyer with a blonde ponytail straight up. She snaps a toe-touch, drops back into their arms, and they reset without stepping off their mark. All three stay fully in frame, boots on the concrete. One continuous shot, the camera orbiting slowly around them.

Site floodlights blaze across a raw poured concrete slab on the fourteenth deck of an unfinished Athens high-rise; rebar stubs bristle at the edges, a tower crane hangs its hook overhead, and the night beyond is black and windless. Two adults are up there and no one else. A tall Ethiopian-Greek man in his twenties, singlet and short shorts, ankles taped; a muscular Danish woman in her thirties, blonde buzz cut, black kit. Both stand fully in frame, spikes on the concrete, then take turns sprinting a long run-up the length of the deck, hitting a chalked board, hanging in the light and landing hard into a spread of trucked-in sand. One continuous shot, a slow pan from left to right, clean sports-ad polish.

Soft overcast daylight flattens the flat concrete stage of a hillside amphitheatre outside Athens; weathered stone tiers curve above it, pines lean over the top row, and pale dust streams low across the boards. Two adults are on the stage itself: a broad Greek-Egyptian man in his forties, shaved head, maroon tee, and a slim Peruvian woman in her twenties, dark ponytail, grey shorts. Spectators sit scattered high in the stone seating, never on the stage. Both athletes stay fully in frame, shoes on the concrete, shuttling between four cones a few meters apart, touching down with one hand and snapping into the opposite direction, again and again. One continuous shot, a slow pan from left to right, soft dreamy music-video color.

Cloud sits below a grassy shelf high on Mount Dirfys, where short flowering turf runs level to a tumbled sheepfold wall and a bent iron gate; the overcast light is flat and colorless, the air motionless. Two adults are on the shelf, nobody else. A wiry Moroccan man in his thirties, black long-sleeve, tapered joggers; a strong-shouldered Estonian woman in her twenties, ash-blonde bun, dark green top. Both stand fully in frame with shoes on the turf and work within a few meters, trading tricks: a 540 kick snapping through the air, a butterfly twist laid out flat, a corkscrew landing heavy on the grass. Breath shows faintly. One continuous shot from a static tripod at eye level, cold neo-noir mood.

Mist rises through a single-arch stone bridge over an island gorge, its cobbles slick at sunrise; wrought-iron lamps stand at each parapet and pale fireworks blossom silently far downstream. Five adults hold the roadway and nobody else. Four in worn white and blue judogi — a heavyset Georgian man, a compact Japanese woman, a tall Nigerian man, a red-haired Scottish woman — and a grey-bearded Greek coach in a tracksuit calling counts. All five are fully in frame, bare feet on the cobbles, staying on one spot. In rotating pairs they drill hip throws: grip, turn in, load the partner across the hip, sweep them over and lower them down, then swap roles. One continuous shot, a slow dolly-in toward them, bright and kinetic.

A small studio in an Athens courtyard building: light bamboo flooring, plaster walls hung with rolled mats, brass work lamps throwing warm tungsten pools, a plant shelf under the shuttered window. The air is completely still and one woman is inside, nobody else — mid-thirties, Sri Lankan, athletic build, hair knotted high, coral sports top and black leggings, bare arms shining. She stands fully in frame with both feet on the bamboo and never leaves that square. The rope blurs into a hum: fast bounce steps, then crossovers whipping past her hips, then a burst of double-unders that snap the floorboards, heels barely rising. One continuous shot, a slow pan from left to right, crisp and upbeat like a sports commercial.

Shafts of daylight cut through high dusty windows into an old wrestling room above an Athens gym; red foam mats cover the floor wall to wall, a rope ladder hangs unused and torn confetti from some earlier celebration still tumbles through the beams. One man trains there, nobody else: early forties, Greek-Armenian, heavy thighs, salt-and-pepper stubble, grey singlet and black shorts. He starts fully in frame, feet on the mat, then attacks a short row of low hurdles set across the room, three sprint strides between each, lead leg snapping over, arms driving, pulling up after a few meters and walking back. One continuous shot, a slow dolly-out revealing the whole room, shadowy neo-noir tone.

Sunrise fog sits on an elevated rail-line park above Athens, its tapered concrete planks wet with dew between rusted track remnants and self-seeded fennel. Two adults claim a clear stretch: a shaven-headed Turkish man in loose black, and a muscular Afro-Brazilian woman in a grey crop top and joggers, chalk on her palms. He takes three cheat steps, swings a hooking 540-degree kick past her raised hand, lands, and she answers with a low inward-twisting flip that whips flat over the planks before she sticks it and slaps his palm. Fog holds motionless around the railings; no one else is up here. One continuous shot, a slow dolly-out that reveals the viaduct stretching away, both fully in frame, feet returning to concrete.

A tiled pedestrian underpass beneath an Athens avenue catches morning sun through slotted vents high in its wall; painted-over graffiti mottles the tiles. Three adults dance on the smooth floor: a silver-haired Cuban man in a burgundy shirt, a curvy Greek woman in a yellow skirt, and a slim Japanese woman in blue. He spins the first partner through a cross-body pass, catches the second on the beat, and sends her under his arm into a double turn while the first shines with a shoulder shimmy and quick heel taps; then all three rotate positions, laughing over echoing claps. The air is dead calm, dust hanging in the light shafts. One continuous shot, a slow pan from left to right, all three fully framed.

A commercial glass greenhouse on the Attic plain stretches away in one long aisle of wide concrete walkway, tomato rows on trellis wires either side, irrigation pipes ticking overhead, bright even lighting hanging in rows; the air inside is warm and motionless. One woman works the aisle, nobody else: late twenties, Colombian, compact and muscular, black hair in a high knot, silver leotard over teal shorts. She stands fully in frame, feet on the concrete, then travels the aisle with a hoop — tossing it spinning ahead, rolling it back to her hand, sprinting after it and diving cleanly through the ring before rising into another throw, covering twenty meters. One continuous shot, handheld camera slowly circling at chest height, gritty documentary look.

The top deck of a seaside parking garage in Piraeus lies empty: painted concrete bays in flaking white, a squat stair kiosk, a bent light pole, and beyond the parapet grey waves keep breaking against the mole with a steady roar. Soft overcast daylight, one man, nobody else — mid-twenties, Greek-Ethiopian, tall and rangy, short twists, blue tee, feet zipped into a burlap sack. He begins standing fully in frame, sack bunched at his waist, both feet on the painted concrete, then bounds forty meters across the deck in fast two-footed hops, arms pumping, throwing himself into a rolling tumble past a chalked finish line. One continuous shot from a static tripod at eye level, hazy and dreamlike.

Soft overcast light fills an empty island old-town square, whitewashed houses with blue shutters, a dry marble wellhead, bougainvillea over an archway; fog banks roll through in slow grey waves. Four adults, nobody else, start fully in frame with shoes on the rounded cobblestones, grinning: a lanky Greek woman in yellow and a stocky Brazilian man in pink hold focus mitts for a short braided-hair woman in mint and a tall grey-haired man in orange. Jab-cross-hook combos crack out, the pairs circling and shuffling a couple of meters over the stones. Mid-round the boxer in mint bounces toward the lens, throws two playful jabs and ends cropped at the shoulders. One continuous shot, static tripod at eye level.

Inside a loading dock bay of a Piraeus warehouse, warm work lamps clamped to the racking throw long shadows over sealed concrete; a rolled dock plate and stacked shrink-wrapped pallets crowd the edges. Four adults each hold a spot with a wooden staff: a lean Greek man in a black tank, a broad Nigerian woman with locs, a stocky Filipino man in olive, a tall Czech woman with a bleached crop. They run figure-eights close to the body, roll a staff across the shoulders and behind the neck, pop it into a low vertical toss, catching blind, then finish with a hard butt-strike stop. Dust hangs unmoving in the lamp beams. One continuous shot, the camera orbiting slowly, all four fully framed, boots planted.

Light rain leaves the mown short grass of a balloon launch meadow outside Athens glazed and reflective; deflated envelopes lie folded in bright ribbons, burner rigs vent slow curls of steam, and low hills fade behind the drizzle. Six adults stand in the field, nobody else. Men and women from their twenties to their fifties — Greek, Rwandan, Chilean, Korean, Turkish, Icelandic — in soaked hoodies and vests of plum, cream and slate. All six stay fully in frame, shoes on the wet turf, each rooted to a single patch, shadow boxing: measured jabs, weaving slips, tight pivots, hooks thrown into the rain. Steam drifts between them. One continuous shot from a static tripod at eye level, soft and dreamlike.

Fog hangs thick and unmoving over a chalk downland top in the Greek uplands, cropped springy turf underfoot, a lichened boundary stone and a wind-stunted hawthorn nearby. Four adults pair off, each pair rooted to one patch of grass: a tall Greek woman in orange and a stocky Korean man in a grey rashguard; a bearded Polish man in blue and a broad Ghanaian woman with braids. Pad holders brace, elbows tight; the kickers snap alternating switch kicks into the leather, left, right, left, then leap into a jumping high kick that folds the pad, laughing as they reset. Nothing else moves in the calm white air. One continuous shot, the camera tracking sideways at a steady walking pace, all four fully framed.
